هائلة وليس وراءها طائل إما أن تكون غير مفهومة عند قائلها بل يصدرها عن
خبط في عقله وتشويش في خياله لقلة إحاطته بمعنى كلام قرع سمعه وهذا هو
الأكثر
وإما أن تكون مفهومة له ولكنه لا يقدر على تفهيمها وإيرادها بعبارة تدل
على ضميره لقلة ممارسته للعلم وعدم تعلمه طريق التعبير عن المعاني بالألفاظ
الرشيقة ولا فائدة لهذا الجنس من الكلام إلا أنه يشوش القلوب ويدهش العقول
ويحير الأذهان أو يحمل على أن يفهم منها معاني ما أريدت بها ويكون فهم كل
واحد على مقتضى هواه وطبعه
وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما حدث أحدكم قوما بحديث لا يفقهونه إلا كان
فتنة عليهم (2) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم كلموا الناس بما يعرفون ودعوا ما
ينكرون أتريدون أن يكذب الله ورسوله (3) وهذا فيما يفهمه صاحبه ولا يبلغه
عقل المستمع فكيف فيما لا يفهمه قائله
فإن كان يفهمه القائل دون المستمع فلا يحل ذكره
وقال عيسى PageV01P036
عليه السلام لا تضعوا الحكمة عند غير أهلها فتظلموها ولا تمنعوها أهلها
فتظلموهم كونوا كالطبيب الرفيق يضع الدواء في موضع الداء
وفي لفظ آخر من وضع الحكمة في غير أهلها فقد جهل ومن منعها أهلها فقد ظلم
إن للحكمة حقا وإن لها أهلا فأعط كل ذي حق حقه
وأما الطامات فيدخلها ما ذكرناه في الشطح وأمر آخر يخصها وهو صرف ألفاظ
الشرع عن ظواهرها المفهومة إلى أمور باطنة لا يسبق منها إلى الأفهام فائدة
كدأب الباطنية في التأويلات فهذا أيضا حرام وضرره عظيم فإن الألفاظ إذا
صرفت عن مقتضى ظواهرها بغير اعتصام فيه بنقل عن صاحب الشرع ومن غير ضرورة
تدعو إليه من دليل العقل اقتضى ذلك بطلان الثقة بالألفاظ وسقط به منفعة
كلام الله  تعالى وكلام رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم فإن ما يسبق منه إلى الفهم
لا يوثق به والباطن لا ضبط له بل تتعارض فيه الخواطر ويمكن تنزيله على وجوه
شتى وهذا أيضا من البدع الشائعة العظيمة الضرر وإنما قصد أصحابها الإغراب
لأن النفوس مائلة إلى الغريب ومستلذة له وبهذا الطريق توصل الباطنية إلى
هدم جميع الشريعة بتأويل ظواهرها وتنزيلها على رأيهم كما حكيناه من مذاهبهم
في كتاب المستظهر المصنف في الرد على الباطنية
ومثال تأويل أهل الطامات قول بعضهم في تأويل قوله تعالى {اذهب إلى فرعون
إنه طغى} أنه إشارة إلى قلبه وقال هو المراد بفرعون وهو الطاغي على كل
إنسان
وفي قوله تعالى {وأن ألق عصاك} أي ما يتوكأ عليه ويعتمده مما سوى الله عز
وجل فينبغي أن يلقيه
وفي قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم تسحروا فإن في السحور بركة (1) أراد به
الاستغفار في الأسحار وأمثال ذلك حتى يحرفون القرآن من أوله إلى آخره عن
ظاهره وعن تفسيره المنقول عن ابن عباس وسائر العلماء وبعض هذه التأويلات
يعلم بطلانها قطعا كتنزيل فرعون على القلب فإن فرعون شخص محسوس تواتر إلينا
النقل بوجوده ودعوة موسى له وكأبي جهل وأبي لهب وغيرهما من الكفار وليس من
جنس الشياطين والملائكة مما لم يدرك بالحس حتى يتطرق التأويل إلى ألفاظه
وكذا حمل السحور على الاستغفار فإنه كان صلى الله عليه وسلم يتناول الطعام
ويقول تسحرو (2) وهلموا إلى الغذاء المبارك (3) فهذه أمور يدرك بالتواتر
والحس بطلانها نقلا وبعضها يعلم بغالب الظن وذلك في أمور لا يتعلق بها
الإحساس فكل ذلك حرام وضلالة وإفساد للدين على الخلق ولم ينقل شيء من ذلك
عن الصحابة ولا عن التابعين ولا عن الحسن البصري مع إكبابه على دعوة الخلق
ووعظهم فلا يظهر لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم من فسر القرآن برأيه فليتبوأ
مقعده من النار (4) معنى إلا هذا النمط وهو أن يكون غرضه ورأيه تقرير أمر
وتحقيقه فيستجر شهادة القرآن إليه ويحمله عليه من غير أن يشهد لتنزيله عليه
دلالة لفظية لغوية أو نقلية ولا ينبغي أن يفهم منه أنه يجب أن لا يفسر
القرآن بالاستنباط والفكر فإن من الآيات ما نقل فيها عن الصحابة والمفسرين
خمسة معان وستة وسبعة
ونعلم أن جميعها غير مسموع من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فإنها قد تكون
متنافية لا تقبل الجمع فيكون ذلك مستنبطا بحسن الفهم وطول الفكر ولهذا قال
صلى الله عليه وسلم لابن عباس رضي الله عنه اللهم فقهه في الدين وعلمه
التأويل (5) PageV01P037
ومن يستجيز من أهل الطامات مثل هذه التأويلات مع علمه بأنها غير مرادة
بالألفاظ ويزعم أنه يقصد بها دعوة الخلق إلى الخالق يضاهي من يستجيز
الاختراع والوضع على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لما هو في نفسه حق ولكن
لم ينطق به الشرع كمن يضع في كل مسألة يراها حقا حديثا عن النبي صلى الله
عليه وسلم فذلك ظلم وضلال ودخول في الوعيد المفهوم من قوله صلى الله عليه
وسلم من كذب علي متعمدا فليتبوأ مقعده من النار (1) بل الشر في تأويل هذه
الألفاظ أطم وأعظم لأنها مبدلة للثقة بالألفاظ وقاطعة طريق الاستفادة
والفهم من القرآن بالكلية فقد عرفت كيف صرف الشيطان دواعي الخلق عن العلوم
المحمودة إلى المذمومة فكل ذلك من تلبيس علماء السوء بتبديل الأسامي فإن
اتبعت هؤلاء اعتمادا على الاسم المشهور من غير التفات إلى ما عرف في العصر
الأول كنت كمن طلب الشرف بالحكمة باتباع من يسمى حكيما فإن اسم الحكيم صار
يطلق على الطبيب والشاعر والمنجم في هذا العصر وذلك بالغفلة عن تبديل
الألفاظ اللفظ الخامس وهو الحكمة فإن اسم الحكيم صار يطلق على الطبيب
والشاعر والمنجم حتى على الذي يدحرج القرعة على أكف السوادية في شوارع
الطرق
والحكمة هي التي أثنى الله عز وجل عليها فقال تعالى {يؤتى الحكمة من يشاء
ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد أوتى خيرا كثيرا} وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم كلمة من
الحكمة يتعلمها الرجل خير له من الدنيا وما فيها (2) فانظر ما الذي كانت
الحكمة عبارة  عنه وإلى ماذا نقل وقس به بقية الألفاظ واحترز عن الاغترار
بتلبيسات علماء السوء فإن شرهم على الدين أعظم من شر الشياطين إذ الشيطان
بواسطتهم يتدرج إلى انتزاع الدين من قلوب الخلق ولهذا لما سئل رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم عن شر الخلق أبى وقال اللهم اغفر حتى كرروا عليه فقال
هم علماء السوء (3) فقد عرفت العلم المحمود والمذموم ومثار الالتباس وإليك
الخيرة في أن تنظر لنفسك فتقتدي بالسلف أو تتدلى بحبل الغرور وتتشبه بالخلف
فكل ما ارتضاه السلف من العلوم قد اندرس وما أكب الناس عليه فأكثره مبتدع
ومحدث وقد صح قول رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بدأ الإسلام غريبا وسيعود
غريبا كما بدأ فطوبى للغرباء فقيل ومن الغرباء قال الذين يصلحون ما أفسده
الناس من سنتي والذين يحيون ما أماتوه من سنتي (4) وفي آخر هم المتمسكون
بما أنتم عليه اليوم (5) وفي حديث آخر الغرباء ناس قليل صالحون بين ناس
كثير ومن يبغضهم في الخلق أكثر ممن يحبهم (6) وقد صارت تلك العلوم غريبة
بحيث يمقت ذاكرها ولذلك قال الثوري رحمه الله إذا رأيت العالم كثير
الأصدقاء فاعلم أنه مخلط لأنه إن نطق بالحق أبغضوه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ق-ه (fa-qāf-hā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deep understanding and comprehension of a matter; the root denotes penetrating insight into the essence of things.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'an, it signifies profound religious understanding that leads to action and fear of God, not mere legal casuistry.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "deep comprehension"; metaphorically extended to jurisprudence, but the original usage was broader.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taṣrīf al-Ism (Semantic Shift via Specification) — The term undergoes takhṣīṣ (specification), narrowing a general term to a restricted technical meaning without complete transfer.
chapters.translation:
Know that the origin of the confusion between the blameworthy sciences and the religious sciences lies in the distortion of praiseworthy names, their alteration, and their transfer—through corrupt motives—to meanings other than those intended by the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) and the first generation. These are five terms: jurisprudence (fiqh), knowledge (ʿilm), divine unity (tawḥīd), remembrance (dhikr), and wisdom (ḥikmah). These are praiseworthy names, and those characterized by them hold positions of religious authority. However, they have now been transferred to blameworthy meanings, so that hearts recoil from condemning those who embody these corrupted meanings, due to the widespread application of these names to them.

**The First Term: Jurisprudence (al-Fiqh)**

They have manipulated this term through specification (takhṣīṣ), not through complete transfer or conversion, by restricting it to knowledge of obscure subsidiary legal rulings in fatwas, grasping the subtleties of their causes, prolixity in discussing them, and memorizing the doctrinal positions related to them. Whoever is more profound in these and more occupied with them is called "the most learned jurist" (al-afqah). Yet in the first era, the name jurisprudence was applied absolutely to knowledge of the path to the Hereafter, awareness of the subtle ailments of the souls, the corrupters of deeds, the power of comprehending the pettiness of this world, intense longing for the bliss of the Hereafter, and the dominance of fear over the heart. Evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: {«ليتفقهوا في الدين ولينذروا قومهم إذا رجعوا إليهم»} [So that they may gain understanding in religion and warn their people when they return to them] (Q 9:122). What produces warning and intimidation is this jurisprudence, not the subdivisions of divorce, manumission, imprecation (liʿān), salam contracts, and leases. For these yield neither warning nor intimidation; rather, exclusive devotion to them perpetually hardens the heart and strips away reverence, as we now observe in those exclusively devoted to them.

He, exalted, said: {«لهم قلوب لا يفقهون بها»} [They have hearts with which they do not understand] (Q 7:179), meaning thereby the realities of faith, not legal fatwas. By my life, jurisprudence and understanding (fahm) are in language two names with one meaning; the discussion concerns customary usage, both ancient and modern.

He, exalted, said: {«لأنتم أشد رهبة في صدورهم من الله»} [You are more fearsome in their breasts than God] (Q 59:13) — attributing their lack of fear of God and their magnification of the creatures' power to their lack of jurisprudence (fiqh). Consider: is that the result of failing to memorize subdivisions of fatwas, or is it the result of lacking the sciences we have mentioned?

The Prophet, peace be upon him, called the delegation that came to him "learned jurists" (ʿulamāʾ fuqahāʾ). Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm al-Zuhrī, may God have mercy on him, was asked: "Who is the most learned jurist among the people of Medina?" He replied: "The most God-fearing of them." As if he were pointing to the fruit of jurisprudence—and piety is the fruit of the inner science, not of fatwas and judicial rulings.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Shall I not inform you of the jurist, the complete jurist?" They said: "Yes." He said: "The one who does not make people despair of God's mercy, does not make them feel secure from God's cunning, does not cut them off from God's spirit, and does not abandon the Qur'an out of desire for something else." When Anas ibn Mālik narrated his saying, peace be upon him: "That I should sit with a people remembering God from dawn until sunrise is dearer to me than freeing four slaves," he said: "I turned to Zayd al-Raqāshī and Ziyād al-Numayrī and said: 'The gatherings of remembrance were not like your gatherings, where one of you preaches to his companions and recites hadiths in rapid succession. Rather, we would sit and remember faith, ponder the Qur'an, gain understanding in religion (natafaqqahu fī al-dīn), and count God's blessings upon us as an act of jurisprudence.'" Thus, pondering the Qur'an and counting blessings were called jurisprudence.

He, peace be upon him, said: "A servant does not attain complete jurisprudence (lā yafqahu al-ʿabd kull al-fiqh) until he detests people for the sake of God, and until he sees the Qur'an as having many facets." It is also narrated as a saying of Abū al-Dardāʾ, may God be pleased with him, with his addition: "Then he turns to his own soul and detests it even more intensely." Farqad al-Sabakhī asked al-Ḥasan about a matter, and he answered him. Farqad said: "But the jurists contradict you." Al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him, said: "May your mother lose you, O Farqad! Have you ever seen a jurist with your own eyes? The jurist is only the one who is ascetic in this world, desirous of the Hereafter, insightful in his religion, constant in worship of his Lord, scrupulous (wariʿ), restraining himself from the honors of the Muslims, chaste regarding their wealth, and sincere toward their community." He did not say in all of that: "the one who memorizes subdivisions of fatwas."

I do not say that the name jurisprudence did not encompass fatwas concerning outward rulings, but it did so by way of generality and inclusiveness, or by way of subsequence (istiṭbāʿ). Their application of it to the science of the Hereafter was more frequent. It has thus become clear that this specification was a deception that impelled people toward exclusive devotion to it and turning away from the science of the Hereafter and the rulings of the hearts. They found in this an ally from natural disposition, for the inner science is obscure, acting upon it is difficult, and attaining through it positions of governance, judgeship, prestige, and wealth is unattainable. Thus Satan found a field to beautify this in hearts, through the specification of the name jurisprudence—a name praiseworthy in the Law.

**The Second Term: Knowledge (al-ʿIlm)**

This was applied to knowledge of God, exalted, His signs, and His acts among His servants and creation. When ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, died, Ibn Masʿūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "Truly nine-tenths of knowledge has died." He defined it with the definite article, then interpreted it as knowledge of God, glorified and exalted. They have also manipulated this through specification, until it became famous mostly for one who engages in disputation with opponents over jurisprudential and other questions. Such a one is called "the scholar" (al-ʿālim) in truth, "the stallion of knowledge" (al-faḥl fī al-ʿilm). Whoever does not practice this or occupy himself with it is counted among the weak and is not numbered among the people of knowledge.

This too is manipulation through specification. But what has come down regarding the virtues of knowledge and scholars is mostly about those who know God, exalted, His rulings, His acts, and His attributes.

It has now become absolutely applied to one who possesses nothing of the religious sciences except dialectical formalities in disputed questions. He is thereby counted among the stallions of the scholars, despite his ignorance of exegesis (tafsīr), hadith reports, the school's doctrine, and other matters. This has become a destructive cause for many creatures among the seekers of knowledge.

**The Third Term: Divine Unity (al-Tawḥīd)**

It has now been made an expression for the craft of dialectical theology (ṣināʿat al-kalām), knowledge of the method of disputation, mastery of the ways of refuting opponents, the ability to expatiate in it by multiplying questions, raising doubts, and composing dilemmas (ilzāmāt). Groups among them have even titled themselves "the people of justice and unity" (ahl al-ʿadl wa al-tawḥīd), and the mutakallimūn have been called "the scholars of tawḥīd." Yet all that is specific to this craft was unknown in the first era; rather, they strongly disapproved of anyone who opened a door to disputation and wrangling. As for what the Qur'an contains of evident proofs that precede the minds to accept them at first hearing, that was known to all. Knowledge of the Qur'an was the whole of knowledge, and tawḥīd among them was an expression for something else that most mutakallimūn do not understand—and if they understood it, they would not be characterized by it. That is: to see all things as from God, may He be exalted, with a vision that severs one's attention from causes and intermediaries, so that one sees all good and evil as from Him alone, may His majesty be exalted. This is an exalted station; one of its fruits is trust in God (tawakkul), as will be explained in the Book of Trust.

Among its fruits also is abandoning complaint against creatures, abandoning anger toward them, and being pleased and submitting to God's decree. One of its fruits was the saying of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, when it was said to him during his illness: "Shall we summon a physician for you?" He said: "The Physician has made me ill." And the saying of another, when he fell ill and was asked: "What did the physician say to you about your illness?" He replied: "He said to me: 'I am the Doer of what I will.'" Evidence for this will come in the Book of Trust and the Book of Tawḥīd.

Tawḥīd has a kernel (lubb) and two husks (qishrān), one farther from the kernel than the other. People have specified the name for the husk and for the craft of guarding the husk, and they have entirely neglected the kernel. The first husk is that you say with your tongue: "There is no god but God" (lā ilāha illā Allāh). This is called tawḥīd in opposition to the trinity (tathlīth) professed by the Christians. But it may issue from a hypocrite whose secret contradicts his public declaration.

The second husk is that there be no contradiction or denial in the heart of the meaning of this statement, but rather the apparent heart encompasses belief in it, as well as affirmation (taṣdīq) of it. This is the tawḥīd of the common people. The mutakallimūn, as mentioned, are the guardians of this husk against the disturbances of the innovators (mubtadiʿah).

The third, which is the kernel, is to see all things as from God, exalted, with a vision that severs one's attention from intermediaries, and to worship Him with a worship that singles Him out, so that one worships none other than Him. Following caprice (hawā) exits from this tawḥīd, for whoever follows his caprice has taken his caprice as his deity. God, exalted, said: {«أفرأيت من اتخذ إلهه هواه»} [Have you seen the one who has taken his caprice as his god?] (Q 25:43). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The most hated deity worshipped on earth in the sight of God is caprice." In truth, whoever reflects knows that the idol-worshipper does not worship the idol but worships his own caprice, for his soul inclines to the religion of his forefathers and he follows that inclination. The soul's inclination to the familiar is one of the meanings expressed by caprice (hawā).

Exiting from this tawḥīd also includes indignation against creatures and attention to them, for how can one who sees all as from God, may He be exalted, be indignant at another? Tawḥīd was an expression for this station—the station of the ṣiddīqūn (the most veracious). See to what it has been diverted, with which husk they have been satisfied, and how they have taken this as a fortress for self-praise and boasting with a name that is praiseworthy, while bankrupt of the meaning that deserves true praise. This is like the bankruptcy of one who rises early, faces the qiblah, and says: "I have turned my face to Him who created the heavens and the earth, as a ḥanīf" — and this is the first lie with which he opens his day to God, if his heart's face is not turned to God, exalted, specifically. For if he means by "face" the outward face, then his face is only turned to the Kaʿbah, and he has only turned it away from other directions. But the Kaʿbah is not a direction for Him who created the heavens and the earth, such that one facing it is facing Him—exalted is He above being bounded by directions and regions.

If he means the heart's face—which is what is intended and required by worship—then how can he be truthful in his saying while his heart is wavering among his worldly concerns and needs, occupied with seeking stratagems to amass wealth and prestige, multiplying means, and entirely turned toward them? When has he turned his face to Him who created the heavens and the earth? This word is an announcement of the reality of tawḥīd. The muwaḥḥid (unifier) is one who sees only the One and turns his face only to Him. This is compliance with His saying, exalted: {«قل الله ثم ذرهم في خوضهم يلعبون»} [Say: God, then leave them in their vain play] (Q 6:91). The intent is not utterance by the tongue, for the tongue is but an interpreter that is truthful at times and lying at others. The locus of God's, exalted, consideration—that which is interpreted—is the heart, which is the mine and source of tawḥīd.

**The Fourth Term: Remembrance and Reminding (al-Dhikr wa al-Tadhkīr)**

God, exalted, said: {«وذكر فإن الذكرى تنفع المؤمنين»} [And remind, for remembrance benefits the believers] (Q 51:55). Many reports have come praising gatherings of remembrance, such as his saying, peace be upon him: "When you pass by the meadows of Paradise, graze therein." It was said: "What are the meadows of Paradise?" He said: "The gatherings of remembrance." In the hadith: "God, exalted, has angels roaming the earth besides the recording angels. When they see gatherings of remembrance, they call one another: 'Come to your quest!' They come, surround them, and listen. Indeed, remember God and remember yourselves." This has been transferred to what you see most preachers in this age persistently practicing: storytelling (qaṣaṣ), poetry, ecstatic utterances (shaṭaḥāt), and absurdities (ṭāmmāt).

As for storytelling, it is an innovation (bidʿah). The predecessors prohibited sitting with storytellers (quṣṣāṣ), saying: "This did not exist in the time of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, nor in the time of Abū Bakr or ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them, until discord (fitnah) appeared and the storytellers appeared." It is narrated that Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, left the mosque saying: "Nothing expelled me but the storyteller; were it not for him, I would not have left."

Ḍamrah said: "I said to Sufyān al-Thawrī: 'We face the storyteller with our faces.' He said: 'Turn your backs to the innovations.'" Ibn ʿAwn said: "I entered upon Ibn Sīrīn, who asked: 'What news today?' I said: 'The governor has forbidden the storytellers from storytelling.' He said: 'He has been guided to what is right.'"

Al-Aʿmash entered the congregational mosque of Basra and saw a storyteller saying: "Al-Aʿmash narrated to us..." He sat in the middle of the circle and began plucking the hair of his armpit. The storyteller said: "O shaykh, will you not be ashamed?" He replied: "I am following the Sunnah while you are in falsehood. I am al-Aʿmash, and I never narrated to you." Aḥmad said: "The most lying of people are the storytellers and the beggars." ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, expelled the storytellers from the congregational mosque of Basra. But when he heard the speech of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, he did not expel him, for he spoke of the science of the Hereafter, reflection on death, alerting to the soul's defects, the corruptions of deeds, the whisperings of Satan, and the way to beware of them. He would remind of God's blessings and graces, the servant's shortcoming in gratitude, the pettiness of this world and its defects, its passing nature, its broken promises, the gravity of the Hereafter and its terrors. This is the praiseworthy reminding (tadhkīr) in the Law, urged in the hadith of Abū Dharr, may God be pleased with him, where he said: "Attending a gathering of remembrance is better than praying a thousand rakʿahs; attending a gathering of knowledge is better than visiting a thousand sick; attending a gathering of knowledge is better than witnessing a thousand funerals." It was said: "O Messenger of God, even better than reading the Qur'an?" He said: "Does the Qur'an benefit except through knowledge?" ʿAṭāʾ, may God have mercy on him, said: "A gathering of remembrance expiates seventy gatherings of frivolity."

The embellishers have taken these hadiths as proof for self-aggrandizement, transferring the name of remembrance to their fabrications, heedless of the path of praiseworthy remembrance. They occupy themselves with stories subject to discrepancies, additions, and omissions, departing from the stories in the Qur'an and adding to them. For among stories, some benefit the listener and some harm, even if true. Whoever opens this door upon himself has truth mixed with falsehood, and benefit with harm. For this reason it was prohibited. Thus Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, may God have mercy on him, said: "How much people need a truthful storyteller!" If the story is from the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, concerning matters of their religion, and the storyteller is truthful with sound transmission, I see no harm in it—let him beware of lying.

As for anecdotes of states that allude to lapses or negligences whose meanings the common people's understanding cannot grasp—or that they were a rare lapse followed by reflections compensated by good deeds that cover them—the common person clings to this in his own negligences and lapses, preparing an excuse for himself, arguing: "Such-and-such was narrated about some shaykh or some great figure. We are all prone to sins, so it is no wonder if I disobey God—one greater than me has disobeyed Him." This gives him audacity toward God, exalted, without his realizing it. After guarding against these two dangers, there is no harm in it. At that point it returns to the praiseworthy stories and what the Qur'an contains and what is sound in authentic books of reports.

Among people there are those who deem it permissible to fabricate stories that encourage obedience, claiming that their intent therein is to call creatures to the truth. This is among Satan's promptings, for truth suffices over falsehood, and what God, exalted, and His Messenger, peace be upon him, have mentioned is ample without invention in preaching. How so, when affected rhymed prose (sajʿ) was disliked and counted as affectation? Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him, said to his son ʿUmar, having heard him use rhymed prose: "This is what makes me dislike you. I will never fulfill your need until you repent." He had come to him for a need. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah regarding rhymed prose of three words: "Beware of rhymed prose, O Ibn Rawāḥah." As if the forbidden affected rhymed prose is what exceeds two words. Thus when the man said regarding the blood-money of a fetus: "How shall we pay blood-money for one who neither drank, nor ate, nor cried, nor wailed—and such a one's claim is void?" the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Rhymed prose like the rhymed prose of the Bedouins."

As for poetry, multiplying it in sermons is blameworthy. God, exalted, said: {«والشعراء يتبعهم الغاوون ألم تر أنهم في كل واد يهيمون»} [And the poets—the misguided follow them. Do you not see that they wander in every valley?] (Q 26:224-225). And He said: {«وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له»} [And We did not teach him poetry, nor does it befit him] (Q 36:69). Most of what preachers habitually use of poetry concerns mutual description in love, the beauty of the beloved, the spirit of union, and the pain of separation. The gathering contains only coarse commoners whose interiors are filled with lusts and whose hearts are not free from attention to beautiful forms. Poetry stirs in their hearts only what is latent therein, so the fires of lust ignite, and they scream and feign ecstasy (tawājud). Most or all of that reverts to a kind of corruption. Only poetry containing admonition or wisdom should be used, by way of citation and familiarity. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, some poetry is wisdom."

If the gathering contained only the elite (khawāṣṣ) whose hearts were known to be immersed in love of God, exalted, and no others were present, then poetry whose outward sense refers to creatures does not harm them, for the listener applies everything he hears to what dominates his heart, as will be established in the Book of Listening (Kitāb al-Samāʿ). For this reason, al-Junayd, may God have mercy on him, would speak before a dozen or so men; if they increased, he would not speak. His gathering never reached twenty. A group gathered at the door of Ibn Sālim's house, and it was said to him: "Speak, for your companions have come." He said: "No, these are not my companions; they are the companions of the gathering. My companions are the elite."

As for ecstatic utterances (shaṭaḥāt), I mean two kinds of speech introduced by some Sufis.

**The first kind** is lengthy, extravagant claims of love for God, exalted, and union (wiṣāl) that dispenses with outward works, until some people reach the point of claiming union (ittiḥād), the lifting of the veil, and vision by sight and direct address by speech. They say: "It was said to us such-and-such, and we said such-and-such." They imitate in this al-Ḥusayn ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥallāj, who was crucified for uttering words of this kind, citing his saying "I am the Truth" (anā al-ḥaqq), and what is narrated of Abū Yazīd al-Bisṭāmī that he said: "Glory be to me, glory be to me!" This is a kind of speech whose harm to the common people is immense, until groups of farmers abandoned their farming and displayed such claims. For this speech is relished by nature, since it contains exemption from works along with self-aggrandizement by attaining stations and states. The stupid are not incapable of claiming this for themselves, nor of catching up garbled, embellished words. Whenever they are denounced for it, they are not incapable of saying: "This denunciation originates from knowledge and disputation—knowledge is a veil, and disputation is an act of the soul. This speech only shines from the interior through the unveiling of the light of truth." This and the like has spread its evil throughout the lands and increased its harm among the common people, until whoever utters anything of it—killing him is better in the religion of God than reviving ten. As for Abū Yazīd al-Bisṭāmī, may God have mercy on him, what is narrated of him is not authentic. Even if he was heard saying it, perhaps he was quoting God, exalted, in speech he repeated to himself—as if one heard him reciting {«إنني أنا الله لا إله إلا أنا فاعبدني»} [Indeed, I am God; there is no god but Me, so worship Me] (Q 20:14). It should not be understood from him except as quotation.

**The second kind of shaṭaḥāt** is incomprehensible words with glittering surfaces and terrifying expressions behind which there is nothing. Either they are incomprehensible to their speaker, issuing from confusion in his mind and disturbance in his imagination, due to his lack of grasp of the meaning of words that struck his ear—and this is the more common. Or they are comprehensible to him, but he is unable to convey them or express them in words that indicate his inner thought, due to his lack of practice in knowledge and his failure to learn the method of expressing meanings in elegant words. There is no benefit in this kind of speech except that it disturbs hearts, bewilders minds, and confounds intellects—or it leads one to understand from them meanings not intended, each person's understanding following his caprice and temperament. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "No one among you narrates to a people a hadith they do not understand, except that it is a trial (fitnah) upon them." And he said: "Speak to people according to what they know; leave what they deny. Do you want God and His Messenger to be denied?" This concerns what the speaker understands but the listener's intellect does not reach—how then with what the speaker himself does not understand? If the speaker understands it but the listener does not, it is not permissible to mention it. Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "Do not place wisdom with those unworthy of it, lest you wrong it; and do not withhold it from those worthy of it, lest you wrong them. Be like the gentle physician who places the medicine at the site of the disease." In another wording: "Whoever places wisdom with those unworthy of it has acted ignorantly, and whoever withholds it from those worthy of it has acted unjustly. Wisdom has a right and has people worthy of it; give every right-holder his right."

As for absurdities (ṭāmmāt), they include what we mentioned regarding shaṭaḥāt, and another matter specific to them: diverting the words of the Law from their understood literal meanings to inner matters from which no benefit precedes to the minds—like the practice of the Bāṭiniyyah in their esoteric interpretations (taʾwīlāt). This too is forbidden, and its harm is immense. For when words are diverted from their literal requirements without clinging to a transmitted authority from the Lawgiver, and without a necessity compelling it from rational proof, this entails the nullification of trust in words, and the benefit of God's speech and His Messenger's speech, peace be upon him, collapses. For what precedes to the understanding is not to be trusted, and the inner has no control—thoughts conflict therein, and it can be applied to many facets. This too is among the widespread innovations of immense harm. Its practitioners intend only to astonish, for souls incline to the strange and relish it. By this path, the Bāṭiniyyah reached the demolition of the entire Law by interpreting its literal meanings and applying them to their own opinions, as we have narrated of their doctrines in the Book of al-Mustaẓhirī, composed in refutation of the Bāṭiniyyah.

An example of the interpretation of the people of absurdities is the saying of some of them regarding His saying, exalted: {«اذهب إلى فرعون إنه طغى»} [Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed] (Q 20:24)—that it is an allusion to one's heart, and that "Pharaoh" means the heart, which is the transgressor over every person. And regarding His saying: {«وأن ألق عصاك»} [And that you cast your staff] (Q 20:19)—meaning whatever one leans upon and relies on besides God, exalted, which one should cast away. And regarding his saying, peace be upon him: "Take the pre-dawn meal, for in the pre-dawn meal there is blessing"—they mean seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours. And similar examples, until they distort the Qur'an from beginning to end from its literal meaning and from its exegesis transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and the other scholars.

Some of these interpretations are known to be false with certainty, such as applying "Pharaoh" to the heart. For Pharaoh was a perceptible person whose existence and Moses' summons to him have reached us through mass transmission (tawātur)—like Abū Jahl, Abū Lahab, and other disbelievers. He is not of the kind of devils and angels that are not perceived by the senses, such that interpretation could extend to his words. Likewise, interpreting the pre-dawn meal as seeking forgiveness—for he, peace be upon him, would consume food and say: "Take the pre-dawn meal" and "Come to the blessed breakfast." These are matters whose falsehood is known through mass transmission and sense perception. Some are known by predominant conjecture, in matters not connected to sensation. All of that is forbidden, error, and corruption of religion for creatures. Nothing of this has been transmitted from the Companions, nor from the Followers, nor from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, despite his intense devotion to calling creatures and preaching to them.

Thus the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever interprets the Qur'an by his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire" appears only for this pattern: that one's purpose and opinion is to establish and confirm a matter, so he drags the Qur'an's testimony to it and imposes it upon it, without any verbal, linguistic, or transmitted evidence testifying to that application. It should not be understood from it that one must not interpret the Qur'an through inference (istinbāṭ) and reflection, for among the verses there are those for which five, six, or seven meanings have been transmitted from the Companions and the exegetes. We know that all of them were not heard from the Prophet, peace be upon him, for they may be mutually contradictory and incapable of combination. Thus they would be inferred through good understanding and lengthy reflection. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said to Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him: "O God, give him understanding in religion and teach him the interpretation (taʾwīl)."

Whoever among the people of absurdities deems permissible such interpretations, knowing that they are not intended by the words, and claims that his purpose is to call creatures to the Creator, resembles one who deems permissible inventing and fabricating upon the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, what is true in itself but which the Law did not utter—like one who fabricates a hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him, for every question he deems true. That is injustice, error, and entry into the threat understood from his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." Rather, the evil in interpreting these words is greater and more immense, for it replaces trust in words and cuts off the path of deriving benefit and understanding from the Qur'an entirely.

You have now known how Satan diverted creatures' motivations from the praiseworthy sciences to the blameworthy ones. All of that is from the deception of the evil scholars (ʿulamāʾ al-sūʾ) by altering names. If you follow these people, relying on the famous name without attending to what was known in the first era, you are like one who seeks honor through wisdom by following whoever is called "wise" (ḥakīm). For the name "wise" has come to be applied to the physician, the poet, and the astrologer in this age—due to heedlessness of the alteration of words.

**The Fifth Term: Wisdom (al-Ḥikmah)**

The name "wise" has come to be applied to the physician, the poet, the astrologer—even to one who rolls dice on the palms of black women in the streets. Yet wisdom is what God, exalted, praised, saying: {«يؤتى الحكمة من يشاء ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد أوتى خيرا كثيرا»} [He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good] (Q 2:269). And he, peace be upon him, said: "A word of wisdom that a man learns is better for him than the world and all that is in it." See what wisdom was an expression for, and to what it has been transferred. Measure the rest of the terms by this, and beware of being deceived by the deceptions of the evil scholars. For their evil upon religion is greater than the evil of the devils, since Satan through them gradually proceeds to wrench religion from the hearts of creatures. For this reason, when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about the worst of creatures, he declined and said: "O God, forgive!" until they repeated it, and he said: "They are the evil scholars."

You have now known the praiseworthy and blameworthy knowledge, and the source of confusion. The choice is yours: whether to look after yourself and follow the predecessors (salaf), or to hang by the rope of delusion and imitate the successors (khalaf). All that the predecessors approved of the sciences has become extinct, and what people have crowded upon—most of it is innovated and newly invented. The saying of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, is sound: "Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger as it began—so blessed are the strangers." It was said: "Who are the strangers?" He said: "Those who repair what people have corrupted of my Sunnah, and who revive what they have killed of my Sunnah." In another version: "They are those who cling to what you are upon today." In another hadith: "The strangers are a few righteous people among many; those who hate them among creatures are more than those who love them." Those sciences have become so strange that mentioning them is detested. Thus al-Thawrī, may God have mercy on him, said: "When you see a scholar with many friends, know that he is a muddler (mukhallit), for if he spoke the truth, they would hate him."

- Root: ق د ر (q-d-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of measure, extent, capacity, or predetermined limit — the boundary beyond which a thing ceases to be what it is.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, denotes the divinely ordained measure of existence (qadar), but here it is applied epistemically — the rightful scope or limit of a science as determined by its purpose.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical measurement; metaphorical usage (majāz) extends to the conceptual boundary of a discipline — its sufficient and necessary range.
- Root: ح م د (ḥ-m-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To praise, commend, or extol — the act of acknowledging excellence or benefit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, praise (ḥamd) is due only to that which is intrinsically good and beneficial; thus "commendable sciences" are those whose pursuit yields genuine spiritual or intellectual benefit.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal praise is verbal; metaphorical praise is the intrinsic worthiness of a thing to be sought — here, the sciences that merit pursuit for the sake of the Hereafter.
- Sībawayh Rule: Idāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "القدر المحمود من العلوم المحمودة" employs a partitive genitive (min) to specify a subset, and the adjectival agreement (المحمود/المحمودة) requires gender and definiteness matching, yielding a precise delimitation of the praiseworthy portion within the broader category.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the exposition of the praiseworthy extent of the commendable sciences — that is, the measure which it is fitting to seek and to master, beyond which pursuit becomes blameworthy or superfluous. Know that the sciences which are commended in the Law and by the intellect are not all to be sought to the same degree; rather, each has a limit (qadr) determined by its end. For the science that is a means to salvation has its measure in what suffices for the attainment of that salvation, and the science that is a means to worldly order has its measure in what suffices for the maintenance of that order. Thus, the praiseworthy extent of each science is that which fulfills its purpose without excess or deficiency, for excess leads to neglect of what is more important, and deficiency leaves the purpose unfulfilled. And this is the balance which the wise have struck, and which the Law has confirmed.

chapters.title_en: The Three Categories of Knowledge: The Blameworthy, the Praiseworthy, and the Sufficient
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن العلم بهذا الاعتبار ثلاثة أقسام قسم هو مذموم قليله وكثيره وقسم
هو محمود قليله وكثيره وكلما كان أكثر كان أحسن وأفضل وقسم يحمد منه مقدار
الكفاية ولا يحمد الفاضل عليه والاستقصاء فيه وهو مثل PageV01P038
أحوال البدن فإن منها ما يحمد قليله وكثيره كالصحة والجمال ومنها ما يذم
قليله وكثيره كالقبح وسوء الخلق ومنها ما يحمد الاقتصاد فيه كبذل المال فإن
التبذير لا يحمد فيه وهو بذل وكالشجاعة فإن التهور لا يحمد فيها وإن كان من
جنس الشجاعة فكذلك العلم
فالقسم المذموم منه قليله وكثيره هو ما لا فائدة فيه في دين ولا دنيا إذ
فيه ضرر يغلب نفعه كعلم السحر والطلسمات والنجوم فبعضه لا فائدة فيه أصلا
وصرف العمر الذي هو أنفس ما يملكه الإنسان  إليه إضاعة وإضاعة النفيس مذمومة
ومنه ما فيه ضرر يزيد على ما يظن أنه يحصل به من قضاء وطر في الدنيا فإن
ذلك لا يعتد به بالإضافة إلى الضرر الحاصل عنه
وأما القسم المحمود إلى أقصى غايات الاستقصاء فهو العلم بالله تعالى
وبصفاته وأفعاله وسنته في خلقه وحكمته في ترتيب الآخرة على الدنيا فإن هذا
علم مطلوب لذاته وللتوصل به إلى سعادة الآخرة وبذل المقدور فيه إلى أقصى
الجهد قصور عن حد الواجب فإنه البحر الذي لا يدرك غوره وإنما يحوم الحائمون
على سواحله وأطرافه بقدر ما يسر لهم وما خاض أطرافه إلا الأنبياء والأولياء
والراسخون في العلم على اختلاف درجاتهم بحسب اختلاف قوتهم وتفاوت تقدير
الله تعالى في حقهم وهذا هو العلم المكنون الذي لا يسطر في الكتب ويعين على
التنبه له التعلم ومشاهدة أحوال علماء الآخرة كما سيأتي علامتهم هذا في أول
الأمر ويعين عليه في الآخرة المجاهدة والرياضة وتصفية القلب وتفريغه عن
علائق الدنيا والتشبه فيها بالأنبياء والأولياء ليتضح منه لكل ساع إلى طلبه
بقدر الرزق لا بقدر الجهد ولكن لا غنى فيه عن الاجتهاد فالمجاهدة مفتاح
الهداية لا مفتاح لها سواها وأما العلوم التي لا يحمد منها إلا مقدار مخصوص
فهي العلوم التي أوردناها في فروض الكفايات فإن في كل علم منها اقتصارا وهو
الأقل واقتصادا وهو الوسط واستقصاء وراء ذلك الاقتصاد لا مرد له إلى آخر
العمر فكن أحد رجلين إما مشغولا بنفسك وإما متفرغا لغيرك بعد الفراغ من
نفسك وإياك أن تشتغل بما يصلح غيرك قبل إصلاح نفسك فإن كنت المشغول بنفسك
فلا تشتغل إلا بالعلم الذي هو فرض عليك بحسب ما يقتضيه حالك وما يتعلق منه
بالأعمال الظاهرة من تعلم الصلاة والطهارة والصوم وإنما الأهم الذي أهمله
الكل علم صفات القلب وما يحمد منها وما يذم إذ لا ينفك بشر عن الصفات
المذمومة مثل الحرص والحسد والرياء والكبر والعجب وأخواتها وجميع ذلك
مهلكات وإهمالها من الواجبات مع أن الاشتغال بالأعمال الظاهرة يضاهي
الاشتغال  بطلاء ظاهر البدن عند التأذي بالجرب والدماميل والتهاون بإخراج
المادة بالفصد والإسهال وحشوية العلماء يشيرون بالأعمال الظاهرة كما يشير
الطرقية من الأطباء بطلاء ظاهر البدن وعلماء الآخرة لا يشيرون إلا بتطهير
الباطن وقطع مواد الشر بإفساد منابتها وقلع مغارسها من القلب وإنما فزع
الأكثرون إلى الأعمال الظاهرة عن تطهير القلوب لسهولة أعمال الجوارح
واستصعاب أعمال القلوب كما يفزع إلى طلاء الظاهر من يستصعب شرب الأدوية
المرة فلا يزال يتعب في الطلاء ويزيد في المواد وتتضاعف به الأمراض فإن كنت
مريدا للآخرة وطالبا للنجاة وهاربا من الهلاك الأبدي فاشتغل بعلم العلل
الباطنة وعلاجها على ما فصلناه في ربع المهلكات ثم ينجر بك ذلك إلى
المقامات المحمودة المذكورة في ربع المنجيات لا محالة فإن القلب إذا فرغ من
المذموم امتلأ بالمحمود والأرض إذا نقيت من الحشيش نبت فيها أصناف الزرع
والرياحين وإن لم تفرغ من ذلك لم تنبت ذاك فلا تشتغل بفروض الكفاية لا سيما
وفي زمرة الخلق من قد قام بها فإن مهلك نفسه فيما به صلاح غيره سفيه فما
أشد حماقة من دخلت الأفاعي والعقارب تحت ثيابه وهمت بقتله وهو يطلب مذبة
يدفع بها الذباب عن غيره ممن لا يغنيه ولا ينجيه مما يلاقيه من تلك الحيات
والعقارب إذا همت به
وإن تفرغت من نفسك وتطهيرها وقدرت على ترك ظاهر الإثم وباطنه وصار ذلك
ديدنا
PageV01P039
لك وعادة متيسرة فيك وما أبعد ذلك منك فاشتغل بفروض الكفايات وراع
التدريج فيها فابتدىء بكتاب الله تعالى ثم بسنة رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم ثم بعلم التفسير وسائر علوم القرآن من علم الناسخ والمنسوخ والمفصول
والموصول والمحكم والمتشابه وكذلك في السنة ثم اشتغل بالفروع وهو علم
المذهب من علم الفقه دون الخلاف ثم بأصول الفقه وهكذا إلى بقية العلوم على
ما يتسع له العمر ويساعد فيه الوقت ولا تستغرق عمرك في فن واحد منها طلبا
للاستقصاء فإن العلم كثير والعمر قصير وهذه العلوم آلات ومقدمات وليست
مطلوبة لعينها بل لغيرها وكل ما يطلب  لغيره فلا ينبغي أن ينسى فيه المطلوب
ويستكثر منه فاقتصر من شائع علم اللغة على ما تفهم منه كلام العرب وتنطق به
ومن غريبه على غريب القرآن وغريب الحديث ودع التعمق فيه واقتصر من النحو
على ما يتعلق بالكتاب والسنة فما من علم إلا وله اقتصار واقتصاد واستقصاء
ونحن نشير إليها في الحديث والتفسير والفقه والكلام لتقيس بها غيرها
فالاقتصار في التفسير ما يبلغ ضعف القرآن في المقدار كما صنفه علي الواحدي
النيسابوري وهو الوجيز والاقتصاد ما يبلغ ثلاثة أضعاف القرآن كما صنفه من
الوسيط فيه وما وراء ذلك استقصاء مستغنى عنه فلا مرد له إلى انتهاء العمر
وأما الحديث فالاقتصار فيه تحصيل ما في الصحيحين بتصحيح نسخة على رجل
خبير بعلم متن الحديث
وأما حفظ أسامي الرجال فقد كفيت فيه بما تحمله عنك من قبلك ولك أن تعول
على كتبهم وليس يلزمك حفظ متون الصحيحين ولكن تحصله تحصيلا تقدر منه على
طلب ما تحتاج إليه عند الحاجة وأما الاقتصاد فيه فأن تضيف إليهما ما خرج
عنهما مما ورد في المسندات الصحيحة
وأما الاستقصاء فما وراء ذلك إلى استيعاب كل ما نقل من الضعيف والقوي
والصحيح والسقيم مع معرفة الطرق الكثيرة في النقل ومعرفة أحوال الرجال
وأسمائهم وأوصافهم
وأما الفقه فالاقتصار فيه على ما يحويه مختصر المزني رحمه الله وهو الذي
رتبناه في خلاصة المختصر والاقتصاد فيه ما يبلغ ثلاثة أمثاله وهو القدر
الذي أوردناه في الوسيط من المذهب والاستقصاء ما أوردناه في البسيط إلى ما
وراء ذلك من المطولات
وأما الكلام فمقصوده حماية المعتقدات التي نقلها أهل السنة من السلف
الصالح لا غير وما وراء ذلك طلب لكشف حقائق الأمور من غير طريقتها ومقصود
حفظ السنة تحصيل رتبة الاقتصار منه بمعتقد مختصر وهو القدر الذي أوردناه في
كتاب قواعد العقائد من جملة هذا الكتاب والاقتصاد فيه ما يبلغ قدر مائة
ورقة وهو الذي أوردناه في كتاب الاقتصاد في الاعتقاد ويحتاج إليه لمناظرة
مبتدع ومعارضة بدعته بما يفسدها وينزعها عن  قلب العامي وذلك لا ينفع إلا مع
العوام قبل اشتداد تعصبهم وأما المبتدع بعد أن يعلم من الجدل ولو شيئا
يسيرا فقلما ينفع معه الكلام فإنك إن أفحمته لم يترك مذهبه وأحال بالقصور
على نفسه وقدر أن عند غيره جوابا ما وهو عاجز عنه وإنما أنت ملبس عليه بقوة
المجادلة
وأما العامي إذا صرف عن الحق بنوع جدل يمكن أن يرد إليه بمثله قبل أن
يشتد التعصب للأهواء فإذا اشتد تعصبهم وقع اليأس منهم إذ التعصب سبب يرسخ
العقائد في النفوس وهو من آفات علماء السوء فإنهم يبالغون في التعصب للحق
وينظرون إلى المخالفين بعين الازدراء والاستحقار فتنبعث منهم الدعوى
بالمكافأة والمقابلة والمعاملة وتتوفر بواعثهم على طلب نصرة الباطل ويقوى
غرضهم في التمسك بما نسبوا إليه ولو جاءوا من جانب اللطف والرحمة والنصح في
الخلوة لا في معرض التعصب والتحقير لا نجحوا فيه ولكن لما كان الجاه لا
يقوم إلا بالاستتباع ولا يستميل الأتباع مثل التعصب واللعن والشتم للخصوم
اتخذوا التعصب عادتهم وآلتهم وسموه ذبا عن الدين ونضالا عن المسلمين وفيه
على التحقيق هلاك الخلق ورسوخ البدعة
PageV01P040
في النفوس
وأما الخلافيات التي أحدثت في هذه الأعصار المتأخرة وأبدع فيها من
التحريرات والتصنيفات والمجادلات ما لم يعهد مثلها في السلف فإياك وأن تحوم
حولها واجتنبها اجتناب السم القاتل فإنها الداء العضال وهو الذي رد الفقهاء
كلهم إلى طلب المنافسة والمباهاة على ما سيأتيك تفصيل غوائلها وآفاتها
وهذا الكلام ربما يسمع من قائله فيقال الناس أعداء ما جهلوا فلا تظن ذلك
فعلى الخبير سقطت
فاقبل هذه النصيحة ممن ضيع العمر فيه زمانا وزاد فيه على الأولين تصنيفا
وتحقيقا وجدلا وبيانا ثم ألهمه الله رشده وأطلعه على عيبه فهجره واشتغل
بنفسه فلا يغرنك قول من يقول الفتوى عماد الشرع ولا يعرف علله إلا بعلم
الخلاف فإن علل المذهب مذكورة في المذهب والزيادة عليها مجادلات لم يعرفها
الأولون ولا الصحابة وكانوا أعلم بعلل الفتاوى من غيرهم بل هي مع أنها غير
مفيدة في علم  المذهب ضارة مفسدة لذوق الفقه فإن الذي يشهد له حدس المفتي
إذا صح ذوقه في الفقه لا يمكن تمشيته على شروط الجدل في أكثر الأمر فمن ألف
طبعه رسوم الجدل أذعن ذهنه لمقتضيات الجدل وجبن عن الإذعان لذوق الفقه
وإنما يشتغل به من يشتغل لطلب الصيت والجاه ويتعلل بأنه يطلب علل المذهب
وقد ينقضي عليه العمر ولا تنصرف همته إلى علم المذهب فكن من شياطين الجن في
أمان واحترز من شياطين الإنس فإنهم أراحوا شياطين الجن من التعب في الإغواء
والإضلال وبالجملة فالمرضي عند العقلاء أن تقدر نفسك في العالم وحدك مع
الله وبين يديك الموت والعرض والحساب والجنة والنار وتأمل فيما يعنيك مما
بين يديك ودع عنك ما سواه والسلام
وقد رأى بعض الشيوخ بعض العلماء في المنام فقال له ما خبر تلك العلوم
التي كنت تجادل فيها وتناظر عليها فبسط يده ونفخ فيها وقال طاحت كلها هباء
منثورا وما انتفعت إلا بركعتين خلصتا لي في جوف الليل
وفي الحديث ما ضل قوم بعد هدى كانوا عليه إلا أوتوا الجدل (1) ثم قرأ ما
ضربوه لك إلا جدلا بل هم قوم خصمون وفي الحديث في معنى قوله تعالى {فأما
الذين في قلوبهم زيغ} الآية هم أهل الجدل الذين عناهم الله بقوله تعالى
فاحذرهم (2) وقال بعض السلف يكون في آخر الزمان قوم يغلق عليهم باب العمل
ويفتح لهم باب الجدل
وفي بعض الأخبار إنكم في زمان ألهمتم فيه العمل وسيأتي قوم يلهمون الجدل
(3) وفي الخبر المشهور أبغض الخلق إلى الله تعالى الألد الخصم (4) وفي
الخبر ما أتى قوم المنطق إلا منعوا العمل (5) والله أعلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge, perception, and comprehension; the faculty by which one discerns the reality of things.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing as it truly is; in the theological sense, it is the means by which the servant knows his Lord and His commands.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used both literally (ḥaqīqah) for certain cognition and metaphorically (majāz) for mere opinion or conjecture when qualified by context.
- Root: ذ-م-م (dh-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Blame, censure, and disapproval; the opposite of praise (ḥamd).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which incurs divine or human reproach due to its harmful or futile nature.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to actions; metaphorical when applied to a person's character as an inherent trait.
- Root: ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Praise, commendation, and approval; the antonym of dhamm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which is worthy of approbation because it leads to felicity in this life and the next.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for acts of gratitude; metaphorical for the state of being praiseworthy in essence.
- Root: ق-ص-د (q-ṣ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Moderation, the middle course, and intentional aim.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The balanced path between excess (ifrāṭ) and negligence (tafrīṭ); in the religious sciences, the measure of sufficiency (kifāyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the middle way; metaphorical for the deliberate pursuit of a goal without extravagance.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Partition (al-Taqsīm bi-al-Sharṭ) — The tripartite division of knowledge is structured through coordinated conditional clauses (fa-minhā... wa-minhā...), each introducing a distinct category with its own governing predicate, requiring the reader to track the syntactic parallelism across the periodic sentence.
chapters.translation:
Know that knowledge, in this consideration, is of three categories: a category whose little and much are both blameworthy; a category whose little and much are both praiseworthy, and the more abundant it is, the better and more excellent it becomes; and a category in which only the measure of sufficiency is praised, while exceeding it and exhausting it is not praised. This is like the states of the body, for among them are those whose little and much are praised, such as health and beauty; among them are those whose little and much are blamed, such as ugliness and bad character; and among them are those in which moderation is praised, such as the expenditure of wealth — for extravagance (tabdhīr) is not praised in it, even though it is a form of spending — and like courage, for recklessness (tahawwur) is not praised in it, even though it is of the genus of courage. Likewise is knowledge.

The blameworthy category, whose little and much are both condemned, is that which has no benefit in religion or this world, for in it there is a harm that outweighs its benefit, such as the science of sorcery (siḥr), talismans (ṭilasmāt), and astrology (nujūm). Some of it has no benefit at all, and devoting one's lifespan — which is the most precious thing a human possesses — to it is sheer waste, and wasting what is precious is blameworthy. And some of it contains a harm that exceeds what one imagines is attained through it of fulfilling some worldly desire, for that is not reckoned against the harm that results from it.

As for the category that is praiseworthy to the utmost limit of exhaustive pursuit, it is knowledge of God Most High, His attributes, His acts, His way (sunnah) in His creation, and His wisdom in ordering the Hereafter upon this world. For this is knowledge sought for its own sake and as a means to attain the felicity of the Hereafter, and expending one's utmost capacity in it to the furthest effort falls short of the limit of what is obligatory. For it is the sea whose depth cannot be reached; rather, those who circle around it hover only along its shores and edges to the extent that is facilitated for them, and none have plunged into its depths except the prophets, the saints (awliyāʾ), and those firmly rooted in knowledge (al-rāsikhūn fī al-ʿilm), according to the disparity of their degrees and the variation of God's decree concerning them. This is the hidden knowledge (al-ʿilm al-maknūn) that is not inscribed in books. What aids in becoming alert to it is learning and witnessing the states of the scholars of the Hereafter, as their sign will come to you at the beginning of this matter. And in the Hereafter, what aids in it is striving (mujāhadah), spiritual discipline (riyāḍah), purifying the heart, emptying it of the attachments of this world, and seeking resemblance in that to the prophets and saints — so that it may become clear to every striver after it according to the measure of provision (rizq), not according to the measure of effort. Yet there is no dispensation from exertion in it, for striving (mujāhadah) is the key to guidance; there is no key to it other than that.

As for the sciences in which only a specific measure is praised, they are the sciences we have mentioned under the communal obligations (furūḍ al-kifāyāt). For in each of these sciences there is a minimal sufficiency (iqtiṣār), which is the least; a moderation (iqtiṣād), which is the middle; and an exhaustive pursuit (istiqṣāʾ) beyond that moderation, to which there is no end until the end of one's life. So be one of two men: either one occupied with yourself, or one free for others after having finished with yourself. And beware of occupying yourself with what sets right others before setting right yourself. For if you are the one occupied with yourself, then occupy yourself only with the knowledge that is obligatory upon you according to what your state requires, and what pertains to it of outward acts — such as learning the prayer, purification, and fasting. But the most important matter, which everyone has neglected, is the knowledge of the attributes of the heart — which of them are praiseworthy and which blameworthy — for no human being is free of blameworthy attributes such as greed (ḥirṣ), envy (ḥasad), ostentation (riyāʾ), pride (kibr), self-admiration (ʿujb), and their sisters. All of these are destructive (muhlikāt), and neglecting them is among the obligatory duties. Indeed, occupying oneself with outward acts resembles occupying oneself with coating the exterior of the body when afflicted with scabies and boils, while being negligent of expelling the morbid matter through bloodletting (faṣd) and purging (ishāl). The vulgar among the scholars (ḥashwiyyat al-ʿulamāʾ) point only to outward acts, just as the quack physicians (ṭarqiyyat al-aṭibbāʾ) point only to coating the exterior of the body. But the scholars of the Hereafter point only to purifying the inward, cutting off the sources of evil by corrupting their roots and uprooting their planting grounds from the heart. The majority have fled to outward acts instead of purifying the hearts because the acts of the limbs are easy while the acts of the hearts are difficult — just as one who finds it hard to drink bitter medicines flees to coating the exterior, so he wearies himself in coating while the morbid matters increase and the diseases multiply thereby.

If you desire the Hereafter, seek deliverance, and flee from eternal destruction, then occupy yourself with the knowledge of the inward maladies and their treatment, as we have detailed in the Quarter of the Destructive Things (Rubʿ al-Muhlikāt). Then that will inevitably lead you to the praiseworthy stations mentioned in the Quarter of the Saving Things (Rubʿ al-Munjiyāt). For when the heart is emptied of the blameworthy, it is filled with the praiseworthy; and when the earth is cleared of weeds, various kinds of crops and fragrant plants grow in it. But if you do not empty it of that, it will not grow this. So do not occupy yourself with the communal obligations (furūḍ al-kifāyāt) — especially while among the masses there is one who has already fulfilled them — for one who destroys himself in what sets right others is a fool. How severe is the folly of one into whose garments vipers and scorpions have entered, intent on killing him, while he seeks a fly-swatter to drive flies away from someone else — someone who neither benefits him nor saves him from what he faces of those serpents and scorpions when they attack him.

And if you have finished with yourself and your purification, and you are able to abandon the outward sin and the inward, and that has become a constant habit (dīdnan) for you and an easy custom — and how far that is from you! — then occupy yourself with the communal obligations and observe gradual progression (tadrīj) in them. Begin with the Book of God Most High, then with the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), then with the science of exegesis (tafsīr) and the rest of the Quranic sciences — the science of the abrogating and abrogated (al-nāsikh wa-al-mansūkh), the separated and connected (al-mafṣūl wa-al-mawṣūl), the unambiguous and the ambiguous (al-muḥkam wa-al-mutashābih) — and likewise in the Sunnah. Then occupy yourself with the branches (furūʿ), which is the science of the school (madhhab) of jurisprudence (fiqh) without the disputations (khilāf); then with the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh); and so on to the remaining sciences, according to what one's lifespan allows and time permits. Do not exhaust your entire life in a single art of them seeking exhaustive pursuit, for knowledge is vast and life is short. These sciences are instruments and preliminaries; they are not sought for their own sake but for something else. And whatever is sought for the sake of another should not cause one to forget the ultimate object sought, nor should one seek an excess of it. So be content from the common run of linguistics with what enables you to understand the speech of the Arabs and to speak it; from its rare forms (gharīb), with the rare forms of the Quran and the rare forms of the ḥadīth; and abandon deep immersion in it. Be content from grammar with what pertains to the Book and the Sunnah. For there is no science except that it has a minimal sufficiency (iqtiṣār), a moderation (iqtiṣād), and an exhaustive pursuit (istiqṣāʾ). We shall point to these in ḥadīth, tafsīr, fiqh, and kalām, so that you may analogize the rest to them.

As for the minimal sufficiency in tafsīr, it is what reaches twice the size of the Quran in volume, as ʿAlī al-Wāḥidī al-Naysābūrī compiled in his work al-Wajīz. The moderation is what reaches three times the size of the Quran, as was compiled in al-Wasīṭ. Whatever is beyond that is an exhaustive pursuit that is dispensable, and there is no end to it until the end of one's life.

As for ḥadīth, the minimal sufficiency is to obtain what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (of al-Bukhārī and Muslim) by verifying a copy against a man expert in the science of the text (matn) of ḥadīth. As for memorizing the names of the transmitters (rijāl), you have been spared that by what those before you have transmitted; you may rely on their books, and you are not obliged to memorize the texts of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, but rather to obtain them in a way that enables you to seek what you need when needed. As for the moderation in it, it is to add to them what is outside them of what is found in the sound musnad collections. As for the exhaustive pursuit, it is what lies beyond that, to encompassing everything transmitted — the weak and the strong, the sound and the defective — along with knowledge of the many chains of transmission and knowledge of the states of the transmitters, their names, and their descriptions.

As for fiqh, the minimal sufficiency is what is contained in the Mukhtaṣar of al-Muzanī (may God have mercy on him), which is what we arranged in Khulāṣat al-Mukhtaṣar. The moderation is what reaches three times its size, which is the measure we presented in al-Wasīṭ of the school. The exhaustive pursuit is what we presented in al-Basīṭ, up to what lies beyond that of the lengthy works.

As for kalām (theology), its purpose is only to protect the creedal beliefs (muʿtaqadāt) transmitted by the People of the Sunnah from the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) — nothing more. Whatever lies beyond that is a seeking to unveil the realities of things from other than their proper path. The purpose of preserving the Sunnah is to attain the rank of minimal sufficiency from it with a concise creed, which is the measure we presented in the book Qawāʿid al-ʿAqāʾid within this very work. The moderation in it is what reaches about a hundred pages, which is what we presented in the book al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād. It is needed for debating an innovator (mubtadiʿ) and opposing his innovation with what corrupts it and uproots it from the heart of the commoner. But that is only useful with the commoners before their partisanship becomes intense. As for the innovator, after he has learned even a little of disputation (jadal), kalām rarely benefits him. For if you refute him, he does not abandon his school; he attributes the failure to himself and supposes that someone else has an answer that he is incapable of — rather, you are merely confounding him through the force of argumentation.

As for the commoner, if he is turned away from the truth by some kind of disputation, he can be returned to it by its like, before partisanship for passions becomes intense. But when their partisanship becomes intense, despair of them sets in, for partisanship is a cause that roots beliefs firmly in souls. And this is among the afflictions of the evil scholars (ʿulamāʾ al-sūʾ), for they exaggerate in partisanship for the truth and look at the opponents with an eye of disdain and contempt. Thus arises from them the claim of retaliation, opposition, and reciprocation; their motives are strengthened to seek the victory of falsehood; and their purpose is reinforced in clinging to what they have been attributed with. Had they come from the angle of gentleness, mercy, and sincere counsel in private — not in the mode of partisanship and belittlement — they would have succeeded. But since prestige (jāh) is only maintained through followers, and nothing attracts followers like partisanship, cursing, and reviling of opponents, they adopted partisanship as their habit and instrument, calling it "defending the religion" and "struggling for the Muslims." Yet in truth, in it lies the destruction of creation and the rooting of innovation (bidʿah) in souls.

As for the disputational matters (khiāfiyyāt) that have been innovated in these later ages, in which have been invented of refinements, compilations, and disputations what was never known among the predecessors — beware of even circling around them, and avoid them as one avoids deadly poison. For they are the chronic disease (al-dāʾ al-ʿuḍāl), and it is what has driven all the jurists to seeking rivalry and vainglory, as the detailed account of their calamities and afflictions will come to you. This speech, perhaps, when heard from its speaker, will elicit the saying: "People are enemies of what they do not know." Do not think that — for the expert has been fallen upon.

Accept this counsel from one who wasted his life in it for a time, and exceeded the earlier ones in it in compilation, verification, disputation, and exposition. Then God inspired him with his right guidance and showed him its defect, so he abandoned it and occupied himself with himself. Do not be deceived by the saying of one who says: "The legal opinion (fatwā) is the pillar of the Law (sharʿ), and its rationales (ʿilal) are known only through the science of disputation." For the rationales of the school are mentioned within the school itself, and what is added to them are disputations unknown to the earlier ones and the Companions — and they were more knowledgeable of the rationales of legal opinions than others. Rather, these disputations, besides being useless for the science of the school, are harmful and corrupting of the taste (dhawq) of fiqh. For what the intuition (ḥads) of the muftī testifies to, when his taste in fiqh is sound, cannot in most cases be made to conform to the conditions of disputation. Whoever has habituated his nature to the formalities of disputation, his mind submits to the requirements of disputation and shrinks from submitting to the taste of fiqh. Only one who seeks fame and prestige occupies himself with it, using as a pretext that he seeks the rationales of the school — and his life may pass away while his concern never turns to the science of the school. So be safe from the devils of the jinn, and beware of the devils of mankind, for they have relieved the devils of the jinn of the toil of seduction and misguidance. In sum, what is approved by the intelligent is that you consider yourself alone in the world with God, with death, the presentation (al-ʿarḍ), the reckoning (al-ḥisāb), Paradise, and the Fire before you. Reflect on what concerns you of what lies before you, and leave aside what is other than that. And peace.

Some of the shaykhs saw one of the scholars in a dream and said to him: "What is the news of those sciences in which you used to dispute and debate?" He spread out his hand and blew into it, saying: "They have all fallen away as scattered dust (habāʾ manthūr), and I have benefited only from two units of prayer (rakʿatayn) that I performed sincerely in the depths of the night."

In the ḥadīth: "No people went astray after having been upon guidance except that they were given disputation (jadal)." {«ما ضل قوم بعد هدى كانوا عليه إلا أوتوا الجدل»} Then he recited: {«ما ضربوه لك إلا جدلا بل هم قوم خصمون»} "They strike it for you only as disputation; rather, they are a contentious people" (Q. 43:58). And in the ḥadīth, regarding the meaning of His saying (Most High): {«فأما الذين في قلوبهم زيغ»} "As for those in whose hearts is deviation" (Q. 3:7) — they are the people of disputation whom God meant by His saying (Most High): {«فاحذرهم»} "So beware of them" (Q. 5:57). And some of the predecessors said: "There will be at the end of time a people for whom the door of action will be closed and the door of disputation opened." And in some reports: "You are in a time in which you have been inspired with action, and there will come a people who will be inspired with disputation." And in the well-known report: "The most hateful of creation to God Most High is the obstinate disputer (al-ald al-khaṣim)." And in the report: "No people were given logic (al-manṭiq) except that they were prevented from action." And God knows best.

### ||| الباب الرابع في سبب إقبال الخلق على علم الخلاف وتفصيل آفات المناظرة والجدل وشروط إباحتها

اعلم أن الخلافة بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم تولاها الخلفاء
الراشدون المهديون وكانوا أئمة علماء بالله تعالى فقهاء في أحكامه وكانوا
مستقلين بالفتاوى في الأقضية فكانوا لا يستعينون بالفقهاء إلا نادرا في
وقائع لا يستغنى فيها عن المشاورة فتفرغ العلماء  لعلم الآخرة وتجردوا لها
وكانوا يتدافعون الفتاوى وما يتعلق بأحكام الخلق من الدنيا وأقبلوا على
الله تعالى بكنه اجتهادهم كما نقل من سيرهم فلما أفضت الخلافة بعدهم إلى
أقوام تولوها PageV01P041
بغير استحقاق ولا استقلال بعلم الفتاوى والأحكام اضطروا إلى الاستعانة
بالفقهاء وإلى استصحابهم في جميع أحوالهم لاستفتائهم في مجاري أحكامهم وكان
قد بقي من علماء التابعين من هو مستمر على الطراز الأول وملازم صفو الدين
ومواظب على سمت علماء السلف فكانوا إذا طلبوا هربوا وأعرضوا فاضطر الخلفاء
إلى الإلحاح في طلبهم لتولية القضاء والحكومات فرأى أهل تلك الأعصار عز
العلماء وإقبال الأئمة والولاة عليهم مع إعراضهم عنهم فاشرأبوا لطلب العلم
توصلا إلى نيل العز ودرك الجاه من قبل الولاة فأكبوا على علم الفتاوى
وعرضوا أنفسهم على الولاة وتعرفوا إليهم وطلبوا الولايات والصلات منهم
فمنهم من حرم ومنهم من أنجح والمنجح لم يخل من ذل الطلب ومهانة الابتذال
فأصبح الفقهاء بعد أن كانوا مطلوبين طالبين وبعد أن كانوا أعزة بالإعراض عن
السلاطين أذلة بالإقبال عليهم إلا من وفقه الله تعالى في كل عصر من علماء
دين الله وقد كان أكثر الإقبال في تلك الأعصار على علم الفتاوى والأقضية
لشدة الحاجة إليها في الولايات والحكومات ثم ظهر بعدهم من الصدور والأمراء
من يسمع مقالات الناس في قواعد العقائد ومالت نفسه إلى سماع الحجج فيها
فعلمت رغبته إلى المناظرة والمجادلة في الكلام فأكب الناس على علم الكلام
وأكثروا فيه التصانيف ورتبوا فيه طرق المجادلات واستخرجوا فنون المناقضات
في المقالات وزعموا أن غرضهم الذب عن دين الله والنضال عن السنة وقمع
المبتدعة كما زعم من قبلهم أن غرضهم بالاشتغال بالفتاوى الدين وتقلد أحكام
المسلمين إشفاقا على خلق الله ونصيحة لهم
ثم ظهر بعد ذلك من الصدور من لم يستصوب الخوض في الكلام وفتح باب
المناظرة فيه لما كان قد تولد من فتح بابه من التعصبات الفاحشة والخصومات
الفاشية المفضية إلى إهراق الدماء وتخريب البلاد ومالت نفسه إلى المناظرة
في الفقه وبيان الأولى من مذهب  الشافعي وأبي حنيفة رضي الله عنهما على
الخصوص فترك الناس الكلام وفنون العلم وانثالوا على المسائل الخلافية بين
الشافعي وأبي حنيفة على الخصوص وتساهلوا في الخلاف مع مالك وسفيان وأحمد
رحمهم الله تعالى وغيرهم وزعموا أن غرضهم استنباط دقائق الشرع وتقرير علل
المذهب وتمهيد أصول الفتاوى وأكثروا فيها التصانيف والاستنباطات ورتبوا
فيها أنواع المجادلات والتصنيفات وهم مستمرون عليه إلى الآن ولسنا ندري ما
الذي يحدث الله فيما بعدنا من الأعصار فهذا هو الباعث على الإكباب على
الخلافيات والمناظرات لا غير ولو مالت نفوس أرباب الدنيا إلى الخلاف مع
إمام آخر من الأئمة أو إلى علم آخر من العلوم لمالوا أيضا معهم ولم يسكنوا
عن التعلل بأن ما اشتغلوا به هو علم الدين وأن لا مطلب لهم سوى التقرب إلى
رب العالمين

### |||| بيان التلبيس في تشبيه هذه المناظرات بمشاورات الصحابة ومفاوضات السلف
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ف (kh-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Succession, replacement, that which comes after; khilāfah denotes the office of succession to prophetic authority.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theologically, it signifies the vicegerency of God's law on earth, entailing both political and religious authority; its legitimacy hinges on qualification (istihqāq).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for temporal succession; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to spiritual inheritance of prophetic knowledge.
- Root: ج-د-ل (j-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To twist, braid tightly; jidāl is the vigorous twisting of discourse in argumentation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quran, jidāl is censured when it seeks victory over truth, but permitted when it defends truth against falsehood (cf. {«وَجَادِلْهُم بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ»}).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical twisting; metaphorical for the rhetorical contortions of disputation that may entangle the soul in pride.
- Root: ف-ت-و (f-t-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A young man (fatā) in his prime; fatwā is the authoritative answer of a mature scholar.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The issuance of legal judgment (iftā') requires both knowledge and moral probity; it is a sacred trust, not a means of worldly gain.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the legal verdict; metaphorical for the scholar's "youthful" vigor in serving the community.
- Root: ع-ز-ز (ʿ-z-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Strength, honor, invincibility; ʿizzah is the state of being unattainable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): True ʿizzah belongs to God alone; human honor is contingent on proximity to Him or distance from worldly power.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical might; metaphorical for the dignity of the scholar who flees from rulers, versus the humiliation of the seeker of favor.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Ḥāl and ʿĀriḍ (Circumstantial Clause and Accidental State) — In the sentence "فأصبح الفقهاء بعد أن كانوا مطلوبين طالبين وبعد أن كانوا أعزة بالإعراض عن السلاطين أذلة بالإقبال عليهم," the predicate (khabar) of kāna is doubled with contrasting circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl), showing the inversion of states through temporal contrast (taḍādd al-ḥālāt).
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that after the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), the rightly-guided and divinely-directed caliphs assumed the succession (khilāfah). They were imams, knowers of God (Exalted is He), jurisprudents in His ordinances, and self-sufficient in issuing legal verdicts (fatāwā) in judicial matters. They did not seek the aid of jurists except rarely, in cases where consultation was indispensable. Thus, the scholars devoted themselves exclusively to the science of the Hereafter and purified themselves for it. They would deflect legal verdicts and all that pertained to the worldly affairs of creation, turning instead to God (Exalted is He) with the full depth of their striving, as is transmitted in their biographies.

Then, when the caliphate passed after them to people who assumed it without merit (istihqāq) and without self-sufficiency in the knowledge of verdicts and ordinances, they were compelled to seek the aid of jurists and to keep them in constant attendance in all their affairs, to consult them in the course of their judgments. There remained, however, from the scholars of the Followers (tābiʿūn), those who persisted upon the first model, clung to the purity of religion, and adhered to the path of the early scholars (salaf). When they were sought, they fled and turned away. The caliphs were thus forced to insistently pursue them to appoint them to judgeships and governance.

When the people of those eras witnessed the honor (ʿizzah) of the scholars and the inclination of the imams and governors toward them — despite the scholars' own aversion to them — they stretched their necks toward the pursuit of knowledge as a means to attain honor and grasp status through the rulers. They threw themselves upon the science of verdicts, presented themselves to the governors, made themselves known to them, and sought appointments and gifts from them. Some were denied, and some succeeded. But the successful one did not escape the humiliation of seeking and the degradation of self-exposure.

Thus, the jurists — after having been sought after — became seekers; and after having been honored through their aversion to the sultans, they became humiliated through their inclination toward them — except for those whom God (Exalted is He) guided in every age from among the scholars of God's religion. In those eras, the greater inclination was toward the science of verdicts and judgments, due to the intense need for them in offices and governance.

Then, after them, there arose from the dignitaries (ṣudūr) and princes those who listened to people's discourses on the foundations of creed (ʿaqāʾid), and their souls inclined toward hearing arguments therein. Their desire for disputation (munāẓarah) and argumentation (jidāl) in theology (kalām) became known. So people threw themselves upon the science of kalām, multiplied their compositions in it, arranged methods of disputation, and extracted arts of contradiction in doctrines. They claimed that their purpose was to defend God's religion, to contend for the Sunnah, and to suppress the innovators — just as those before them had claimed that their purpose in occupying themselves with verdicts and undertaking the judgments of the Muslims was compassion for God's creation and sincere counsel to them.

Then, after that, there arose from the dignitaries those who did not deem it sound to plunge into kalām or to open the door of disputation therein — because of what had been generated from opening that door: monstrous fanaticisms and rampant quarrels leading to the shedding of blood and the ruin of lands. Their souls inclined instead toward disputation in jurisprudence (fiqh) and the clarification of what is preferable between the school of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah (may God be pleased with them both), specifically. So people abandoned kalām and the arts of knowledge, and they rushed en masse upon the points of divergence (khilāf) between al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfah in particular. They became lax regarding divergence with Mālik, Sufyān, Aḥmad (may God have mercy on them), and others. They claimed that their purpose was to extract the subtleties of the Sacred Law, to establish the rationales (ʿilal) of the school, and to lay the foundations of legal verdicts. They multiplied compositions and derivations therein, and arranged types of disputations and classifications — and they continue upon this to the present day. We do not know what God will bring forth in the ages after us.

This, then, is the sole motive for the eager pursuit of disputational matters (khilāfiyyāt) and debates (munāẓarāt) — nothing else. And had the souls of the worldly inclined toward divergence with another imam from among the imams, or toward another science from among the sciences, they would have inclined toward them as well, and would not have ceased to delude themselves with the claim that what they occupy themselves with is the science of religion, and that they seek nothing but nearness to the Lord of the Worlds.
