Thus God — exalted and majestic is He — bestowed favor upon this community by making the pilgrimage their monasticism. He honored the Ancient House (al-bayt al-ʿatīq) by attributing it to Himself — exalted is He — and erected it as a destination for His servants. He made its surroundings a sanctuary (ḥaram) for His House, magnifying its affair. He made ʿArafāt like a gutter (mīzāb) upon the courtyard of His basin, and emphasized the sanctity of the place by prohibiting its game and its trees. He placed it on the model of the courts of kings, which visitors seek from every deep valley and every distant quarter — disheveled and dust-covered, humble before the Lord of the House, submissive to Him, in lowliness before His majesty and meekness before His might, while acknowledging His transcendence above being contained by any house or encompassed by any land — that this might be more complete in their servitude (riqq) and worship (ʿubūdiyyah), and more perfect in their submission and obedience.

For this reason, He imposed upon them therein acts which souls do not find familiar and whose meanings intellects do not attain — such as the casting of pebbles (ramy al-jimār) at the jamarāt, and the repeated traversing between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah. By such acts the perfection of servitude and submission becomes manifest.

For the alms-tax (zakāh) is a kindness whose rationale is understood, and the intellect inclines toward it. Fasting is a breaking of the appetite, which is the instrument of God's enemy, and a vacating of oneself for worship by abstaining from distractions. The bowing and prostration in prayer are humility before God through acts that are the very posture of humility, and souls find familiarity in magnifying God. But as for the repeated traversals of the saʿy, the casting of pebbles, and similar acts — there is no share for the soul in them, no familiarity, and no guidance of the intellect to their meanings. Thus nothing impels one to undertake them except the bare command (al-amr al-mujarrad) and the intention of complying with the command insofar as it is an obligatory command to be followed — nothing more. In this there is a deposing of the intellect from its governance and a turning of the soul and nature away from their familiar ground. For whatever the intellect grasps the meaning of, nature inclines toward it with some inclination; that inclination then assists the command and joins it as an impetus to action, so that the perfection of servitude and submission is scarcely manifested thereby. Therefore he — peace be upon him — said specifically concerning the pilgrimage: "I respond to You (labbaik) with a true pilgrimage, in worship and servitude" — and he did not say this concerning prayer or anything else.

And since the wisdom of God — exalted and majestic is He — requires that the salvation of creatures be tied to their acts being contrary to the inclination of their natures, and that their reins be in the hand of the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ), so that they oscillate in their acts upon the path of submission and the requirement of enslavement — then that whose meanings are not attained is the most powerful kind of devotional act (taʿabbudāt) in purifying souls and turning them from the dictates of nature and temperament toward the dictate of servitude. If you discern this, you will understand that the soul's wonder at these strange acts originates from heedlessness of the secrets of devotional acts. This suffices for understanding the principle of the pilgrimage, God willing.

As for longing (al-shawq): It is only kindled after understanding and the certainty that the House is the House of God — exalted and majestic is He — and that it was placed on the model of the courts of kings. Thus its visitor is a visitor to God and a pilgrim to Him; and whoever intends the House in this world is worthy that his visit not be wasted, but that he be granted the object of the visit at its appointed time — namely, the vision of the noble Face of God in the Abode of Permanence. For the deficient, perishing eye in this world is not prepared to receive the vision of God's Face, cannot bear it, and is not ready to be anointed with it, due to its deficiency. But when it is prolonged with permanence in the Hereafter and purified from the causes of change and annihilation, it becomes prepared for vision and sight. Yet by intending the House and gazing upon it, one becomes deserving of meeting the Lord of the House by virtue of the noble promise.

Thus longing for the meeting of God — exalted and majestic is He — inevitably impels longing for its means. This is in addition to the fact that the lover yearns for everything that has an attribution (iḍāfah) to his Beloved; and the House is attributed to God — exalted and majestic is He — so it is fitting that one yearn for it merely for this attribution, let alone seeking the attainment of the abundant reward promised upon it.

As for resolve (al-ʿazm): Let him know that by his resolve he intends to depart from family and homeland, to emigrate from appetites and pleasures, and to set out toward visiting the House of God — exalted and majestic is He. Let him magnify in his soul the rank of the House and the rank of the Lord of the House. Let him know that he has resolved upon a matter of lofty station and grave import, and that whoever seeks something great risks something great.

Let him make his resolve purely for the Face of God — exalted is He — far from the admixtures of ostentation (riyāʾ) and reputation (sumʿah). Let him be certain that nothing is accepted of his intention and deed except the pure, and that among the most heinous abominations is to intend the House of God and His sanctuary while the intended object is other than Him.

Let him therefore rectify his resolve with himself; its rectification is through sincerity (ikhlāṣ), and its sincerity is through avoiding everything in which there is ostentation and reputation. Let him beware of exchanging that which is lower for that which is better.

As for severing attachments (qaṭʿ al-ʿalāʾiq): Its meaning is the restitution of wrongs (mazālim) and sincere repentance to God — exalted is He — from all sins. For every wrong is an attachment, and every attachment is like a present creditor seizing his collar, calling out against him and saying: "Where are you heading? Do you intend the House of the King of Kings while you are squandering His command in your own home, treating it lightly and neglecting it? Do you not feel shame to approach Him with the approach of a disobedient servant, so that He repels you and does not accept you? If you desire the acceptance of your visit, then execute His commands, restore the wrongs, and repent to Him first from all sins. Sever your heart's attachment from looking back to what is behind you, so that you may be turned toward Him with the face of your heart, just as you are turned toward His House with the face of your outward self."

For if you do not do this, you will have nothing from your journey — first — except toil and misery, and — finally — except expulsion and rejection.

Let him sever attachments to his homeland as one who has been cut off from it and who resolves never to return to it. Let him write his will (waṣiyyah) for his children and family, for the traveler and his wealth are in peril — except for him whom God — exalted is He — protects. Let him remember, when severing attachments for the journey of pilgrimage, the severing of attachments for the journey of the Hereafter, for that is before him imminently. What he advances from this journey is hope for the facilitation of that journey — for it is the final abode, and to it is the return.

He should not be heedless of that journey while preparing for this one.

As for provisions (al-zād): Let him seek them from a lawful source. And when he senses in himself eagerness to amass them in abundance, seeking what will remain through the long journey, unchanged and unspoiled before reaching the destination — let him remember that the journey of the Hereafter is longer than this journey, that its provision is piety (al-taqwā), and that everything else which he supposes to be his provision will lag behind him at death and betray him, leaving nothing with him — like moist food that spoils at the first way-station of the journey, leaving him at the time of need bewildered, needy, with no recourse.

Let him beware that his deeds — which are his provision to the Hereafter — not fail to accompany him after death, but rather be spoiled by the admixtures of ostentation and the turbidity of shortcoming.

As for the mount (al-rāḥilah): When he brings it, let him thank God with his heart for God's — exalted and majestic is He — subjugating beasts to him, to bear from him hardship and lighten his toil.

Let him remember at that point the conveyance he will ride to the Abode of the Hereafter — namely, the bier (janāzah) upon which he will be carried. For the affair of pilgrimage in one respect parallels the affair of the journey to the Hereafter. Let him consider whether his journey upon this mount will be fit to serve as provision for that journey upon that conveyance. How near it is to him! And what does he know — perhaps death is near, and his riding of the bier will precede his riding of the camel. Riding the bier is certain, while the facilitation of the means of travel is doubtful. How then does he take precautions regarding the means of a doubtful journey, and secure himself with provisions and mount, while neglecting the affair of the certain journey?

As for purchasing the two garments of iḥrām: Let him remember at that point the shroud (kafan) and the wrapping therein. For he will don and wrap himself in the two garments of iḥrām near the House of God — exalted and majestic is He — and perhaps his journey to it will not be completed. And he will meet God — exalted and majestic is He — wrapped in the garments of the shroud, inevitably. Just as he does not meet the House of God except in a manner contrary to his customs in dress and appearance, so too he will not meet God after death except in an attire contrary to the attire of this world. And this garment is close to that garment, for there is no stitching in it, just as in the shroud.

As for departing from the city: Let him know at that point that he has left family and homeland, heading toward God — exalted and majestic is He — in a journey that bears no resemblance to the journeys of this world. Let him bring to his heart: what does he intend, where is he heading, and whose visit does he seek? That he is heading toward the King of Kings in the company of His visitors — those who were called and answered, who were made to yearn and so yearned, who were summoned forth and so arose, who severed attachments and parted from creatures, and who turned toward the House of God — exalted and majestic is He — whose affair He magnified, whose station He exalted, and whose rank He raised — consoling themselves with the meeting of the House for the meeting of the Lord of the House, until they are granted the utmost of their hopes and blessed with the vision of their Master.

Let him bring to his heart the hope of arrival and acceptance — not relying on his deeds in departing and leaving family and wealth, but trusting in God's bounty and hoping for the fulfillment of His promise to whoever visits His House. Let him hope that if he does not reach it and death overtakes him on the road, he will meet God — exalted and majestic is He — as one arriving unto Him, since He — glorious is His majesty — said: {«وَمَن يَخْرُجْ مِن بَيْتِهِ مُهَاجِرًا إِلَى اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ يُدْرِكْهُ الْمَوْتُ فَقَدْ وَقَعَ أَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ»} (And whoever departs from his house as an emigrant to God and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him — his reward has indeed fallen due upon God).

As for entering the wilderness toward the mīqāt and witnessing those mountain passes: Let him recall therein what lies between departing this world at death and the mīqāt of the Day of Resurrection — and the terrors and reckonings between them. Let him recall, from the terror of highway robbers, the terror of the questioning of Munkar and Nakīr; from the beasts of the wilderness, the scorpions of the grave and its worms, and the vipers and serpents therein; and from his isolation from family and kin, the desolation (waḥshah) of the grave, its constriction, and its solitude. Let him, amid these fears, be in his deeds and words one who provisions himself for the fears of the grave.

As for iḥrām and the talbiyah from the mīqāt: Let him know that its meaning is the answering of God's — exalted and majestic is He — call. Hope that you may be accepted, and fear that it may be said to you: "No response to you, and no blessedness for you" (lā labayk wa lā saʿdayk). So be oscillating between hope and fear, disavowing your own power and strength, and relying upon God's bounty and generosity. For the time of the talbiyah is the beginning of the affair, and it is the place of peril.

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn — may God be pleased with them both — performed the pilgrimage. When he assumed iḥrām and his mount stood still with him, his complexion turned yellow, he trembled, and shivering overtook him, and he could not utter the talbiyah. It was said to him: "Why do you not say the talbiyah?" He said: "I fear that it may be said to me: 'No response to you, and no blessedness for you.'" When he finally said the talbiyah, he fainted and fell from his mount. He continued to be overtaken by that condition until he completed his pilgrimage.

Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said: I was with Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī — may God be pleased with him — when he intended to assume iḥrām. He did not say the talbiyah until we had traveled a mile; then unconsciousness seized him. He then revived and said: "O Aḥmad, God — exalted is He — revealed to Moses — peace be upon him: 'Command the wrongdoers of the Children of Israel to be sparing in their remembrance of Me, for I remember those of them who remember Me with a curse.' Woe to you, O Aḥmad! It has reached me that whoever performs the pilgrimage from other than its proper place (ḥill) and then says the talbiyah, God — exalted and majestic is He — says: 'No response to you, and no blessedness for you, until you return what is in your hands.' So we are not safe from having that said to us."

Let the one saying the talbiyah recall, when raising his voice with the talbiyah at the mīqāt, his answering of God's — exalted and majestic is He — call, when He said: {«وَأَذِّن فِي النَّاسِ بِالْحَجِّ»} (And proclaim the pilgrimage among the people) — and the calling of creation by the blast of the Trumpet (ṣūr) and their mustering from the graves, and their crowding in the plains of the Resurrection, answering the call of God — exalted is He — and divided into those brought near and those abhorred, those accepted and those rejected — oscillating at the outset between fear and hope, just as the pilgrim oscillates at the mīqāt, not knowing whether the completion of the pilgrimage and its acceptance will be facilitated for him or not.

As for entering Mecca: Let him recall at that point that he has arrived at the sanctuary (ḥaram) of God — exalted is He — in safety. Let him hope that by his entry he will be safe from God's punishment, and let him fear that he may not be worthy of nearness, so that by his entry into the sanctuary he becomes disappointed and deserving of abhorrence. Let his hope prevail in all moments, for the generosity is all-encompassing, the Lord is merciful, the honor of the House is great, the right of the visitor is observed, and the protection of the seeker of refuge who clings is not neglected.

As for the falling of the eye's gaze upon the House: He should bring to mind at that point the greatness of the House in his heart, and imagine as though he were witnessing the Lord of the House, due to the intensity of his magnification of it. Hope that God — exalted is He — will grant you the vision of His noble Face, just as He granted you the vision of His great House. Thank God — exalted is He — for conveying you to this rank and joining you to the company of those arriving unto Him. Recall at that point the pouring of people on the Day of Resurrection toward the direction of Paradise, hoping to enter it all together, and then their division into those permitted entry and those turned away — just as the pilgrims divide into the accepted and the rejected. Do not be heedless of recalling the matters of the Hereafter in anything you see, for all the states of the pilgrim are indications of the states of the Hereafter.

As for the circumambulation (ṭawāf) of the House: Know that it is a prayer (ṣalāh). Bring to your heart therein the magnification, fear, hope, and love that we detailed in the Book of Prayer. Know that by circumambulating you are imitating the angels brought near (al-malāʾikah al-muqarrabūn) who encircle the Throne (al-ʿarsh) and circumambulate around it. Do not suppose that the object is the circumambulation of your body around the House; rather, the object is the circumambulation of your heart with the remembrance of the Lord of the House — so that you begin remembrance only from Him and end only with Him, just as you begin the circumambulation from the House and end with the House.

Know that the noble circumambulation is the circumambulation of the heart in the presence of Lordship (ḥaḍrat al-rubūbiyyah), and that the House is an outward exemplar (mithāl ẓāhir) in the world of dominion (ʿālam al-mulk) for that presence which is not seen by the eye — namely, the world of the unseen dominion (ʿālam al-malakūt) — just as the body is an outward exemplar in the world of witness (ʿālam al-shahādah) for the heart, which is not seen by the eye and which is in the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb).

The world of dominion and witness is a ladder (mirqāh) to the world of the unseen and the malakūt, for him for whom God opens the door. To this correspondence the indication points: that the Much-Frequented House (al-bayt al-maʿmūr) in the heavens is opposite the Kaʿbah — for the angels' circumambulation of it is like the circumambulation of humans around this House. And since the rank of most creatures fell short of such circumambulation, they were commanded to imitate them to the extent possible, and were promised that whoever imitates a people is of them. And the one capable of such circumambulation is the one of whom it is said that the Kaʿbah visits him and circumambulates around him — as some of those granted unveiling (mukāshifūn) saw concerning certain saints of God — exalted and majestic is He.

As for the touching of the Black Stone (al-istilām): Hold the conviction at that point that you are pledging allegiance (mubāyaʿah) to God — exalted and majestic is He — upon His obedience. So firm your resolve to fulfill your pledge, for whoever betrays in the pledge deserves abhorrence. Ibn ʿAbbās — may God be pleased with him — narrated from the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — that he said: "The Black Stone is the right hand of God — exalted and majestic is He — in the earth, by which He clasps hands with His creatures, just as a man clasps hands with his brother."

As for clinging to the curtains (astār) of the Kaʿbah and pressing against the multazam: Let your intention in pressing be the seeking of nearness, out of love and longing for the House and the Lord of the House, seeking blessing through contact, and hoping for protection from the Fire for every part of your body — not for the House. Let your intention in clinging to the curtain be importunity in seeking forgiveness and asking for security — like the sinner clinging to the garments of the one he has wronged, imploring him for pardon, showing him that he has no refuge from him except in him, no recourse except his generosity and pardon, and that he will not release his hem except upon pardon and the granting of security for the future.

As for the saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah in the courtyard of the House: It resembles the servant's oscillation in the courtyard of the king's palace, coming and going, time after time — manifesting sincerity in service and hoping to be observed with the eye of mercy — like one who entered upon the king and came out not knowing what the king will decree concerning him — acceptance or rejection — so he keeps oscillating in the palace courtyard, time after time, hoping to be shown mercy the second time if not the first. Let him recall, while oscillating between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, his oscillation between the two pans of the Balance (mīzān) in the plains of the Resurrection. Let him represent al-Ṣafā as the pan of good deeds and al-Marwah as the pan of evil deeds. Let him recall his oscillation between the two pans, gazing at the preponderance and deficiency, oscillating between punishment and forgiveness.

As for the standing at ʿArafāt (al-wuqūf): Recall, by what you see of the crowding of creation, the raising of voices, the diversity of languages, and the following of each group its leader in the oscillations at the sacred sites (mashāʿir) — following them and proceeding by their proceeding — the plains of the Resurrection, the gathering of nations with the prophets and leaders, each nation following its prophet, hoping for their intercession (shafāʿah), and their bewilderment upon that single plain between rejection and acceptance. When you recall that, bind your heart to supplication (ḍarāʿah) and entreaty (ibtihāl) to God — exalted and majestic is He — and you will be mustered in the company of the successful and the shown-mercy. Affirm your hope of response, for the standing-place is noble, and mercy only reaches all creation from the presence of Majesty through the mediation of the precious hearts — the pegs (awtād) of the earth.

The standing-place is never devoid of a stratum of the substitutes (abdāl) and pegs, and a stratum of the righteous and masters of hearts. When their aspirations unite, their hearts are emptied for supplication and entreaty, their hands are raised to God — exalted is He — their necks are stretched forth, and their eyes gaze toward heaven, united in a single aspiration upon the seeking of mercy — do not suppose that their hope will be disappointed, their effort wasted, or that a mercy that would overwhelm them will be withheld. Therefore it was said: Among the greatest sins is to attend ʿArafāt and suppose that God — exalted is He — has not forgiven him. As if the uniting of aspirations and the seeking of support through proximity to the abdāl and awtād, gathered from the far quarters of the lands, is the secret of the pilgrimage and the utmost of its object. There is no path to drawing down the mercy of God — exalted is He — like the uniting of aspirations and the mutual aid of hearts at a single moment.

As for the casting of the pebbles (ramy al-jimār): Intend thereby submission to the command, manifesting servitude and worship, and rising to mere compliance — with no share for the intellect or the soul therein. Then intend thereby the imitation of Abraham — peace be upon him — when Satan — may God curse him — appeared to him at that place to cast doubt into his pilgrimage or tempt him to disobedience. God — exalted and majestic is He — commanded him to cast stones at him, driving him away and cutting off his hope.

If it occurs to you that Satan appeared to him and he saw him, and therefore cast at him — "but as for me, Satan does not appear to me" — know that this thought is from Satan himself, and that he is the one who cast it into your heart to weaken your resolve in the casting, and to make you imagine that it is a deed with no benefit, resembling play, so that you do not occupy yourself with it. Drive him away from yourself by earnestness and vigor in the casting, in spite of Satan's nose.

Know that outwardly you cast pebbles at the jamrah (ʿAqabah), but in reality you cast at the face of Satan and break his back thereby. For the rubbing of his nose is only achieved by your compliance with the command of God — exalted and majestic is He — magnifying Him by the bare command, with no share for the soul or the intellect therein.

As for the slaughtering of the sacrificial animal (hady): Know that it is a drawing near (taqarrub) to God — exalted is He — by virtue of compliance. Make the offering complete, and hope that God will emancipate from the Fire, for every part of it, a part of you. Thus the promise has come. So the larger the offering and the more numerous its parts, the more comprehensive is your ransom from the Fire.

As for visiting Medina: When your eye falls upon its walls, recall that it is the city that God — exalted and majestic is He — chose for His Prophet — peace be upon him — and made the destination of his emigration (hijrah). It is his abode in which he instituted the obligations of his Lord — mighty and majestic is He — and his sunnah, in which he struggled against his enemy and manifested his religion, until God — exalted is He — took him unto Himself. Then He made his burial place therein, and the burial place of his two ministers (wazīrayn) who upheld the truth after him — may God be pleased with them both.

Then represent in your soul the places where the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — set his feet in his comings and goings therein. There is no place your foot treads but that it is a place of his noble feet. So do not place your foot upon it except with tranquility (sakīnah) and awe (wajal).

Recall his walking and his strides through its streets. Imagine his humility and tranquility in walking, and what God — exalted is He — deposited in his heart of the greatness of His knowledge and the elevation of His mention — joined with His own mention, so that He coupled his mention with His own, and nullified the deed of whoever violated his sanctity, even by raising his voice above his voice.

Then recall what God — exalted is He — bestowed upon those who attained his companionship and were blessed with witnessing him and hearing his speech. Intensify your regret over what has eluded you of his companionship and the companionship of his companions — may God be pleased with them.

Then recall that you have missed his vision in this world, and that you are in peril regarding his vision in the Hereafter. Perhaps you will not see him except with regret, and between you and his acceptance of you there may be interposed your evil deeds — as he — peace be upon him — said: "People will be raised up to me, and they will say: 'O Muḥammad!' I will say: 'O Lord, my companions!' He will say: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' I will say: 'Away with them, and far removed!'" So if you violate the sanctity of his law — even in a single moment — do not feel safe from the interposition between you and him, due to your deviation from his clear path.

Yet let your hope be great that God — exalted is He — will not interpose between you and him, after He has granted you faith and brought you forth from your homeland for the sake of visiting him — not for trade, nor any share in this world, but purely for your love of him and your longing to look upon his traces and the wall of his grave — since your soul consented to travel for that alone, having missed his vision. How worthy you are that God — exalted is He — should look upon you with the eye of mercy!

When you reach the Mosque: Recall that it is the courtyard that God — exalted is He — chose for His Prophet — peace be upon him — and for the first Muslims and their most excellent company. The obligations of God — exalted is He — were first established in that courtyard, and it gathered the best of God's creation, living and dead. Let your hope in God — exalted is He — be great, that He will show you mercy by your entering it. Enter it humbly, magnifying it.

How worthy is this place to evoke humility from the heart of every believer — as was related of Abū Sulaymān, who said: Uways al-Qaranī — may God be pleased with him — performed the pilgrimage and entered Medina. When he stood at the door of the Mosque, it was said to him: "This is the grave of the Prophet — peace be upon him." He fainted. When he revived, he said: "Take me out, for no land is pleasurable to me in which Muḥammad — peace be upon him — is buried."

As for visiting the Messenger of God — peace be upon him: You should stand before him as we have described, and visit him dead as you would visit him alive. Do not approach his grave except as you would approach his noble person were he alive. Just as you would observe the sanctity of not touching his person or kissing it, but rather stand at a distance, standing before him — so do likewise. For touching and kissing of shrines is the custom of the Christians and Jews.

Know that he is aware of your presence, your standing, and your visit, and that your greeting (salām) and prayer (ṣalāh) reach him. So represent his noble image in your imagination, placed in the grave before you, and bring to your heart the greatness of his rank. For it has been related from him — peace be upon him — that God — exalted is He — has appointed an angel over his grave who conveys to him the greeting of whoever greets him from his community. This is for one who has not attended his grave in person — how then for one who has left his homeland and crossed the wilderness out of longing to meet him, contenting himself with the sight of his noble shrine, having missed the sight of his noble countenance? And he — peace be upon him — said: "Whoever prays upon me once, God prays upon him ten times." This is his recompense for praying upon him with his tongue — how then for attending his grave in person with his body?

Then approach the pulpit (minbar) of the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and imagine the Prophet — peace be upon him — ascending the pulpit. Represent in your heart his radiant countenance as though upon the pulpit, with the Emigrants (muhājirūn) and Helpers (anṣār) — may God be pleased with them — surrounding him, and he — peace be upon him — urging them to the obedience of God — exalted and majestic is He — with his sermon. Ask God — exalted and majestic is He — not to separate between you and him on the Day of Resurrection.

This is the function of the heart in the rites of the pilgrimage.

When he has completed all of it, he should bind his heart to sorrow (ḥuzn), concern (hamm), and fear (khawf) — that he does not know whether his pilgrimage has been accepted and he has been established in the company of the beloved, or whether his pilgrimage has been rejected and he has been joined to the expelled. Let him ascertain this from his heart and his deeds. For if he finds his heart has increased in aversion to the Abode of Delusion (dār al-ghurūr) and in turning toward the Abode of Intimacy with God — exalted is He — and finds his deeds balanced upon the scale of the Sacred Law — let him trust in acceptance. For God — exalted is He — accepts only from one He loves; and whom He loves, He takes charge of, and manifests upon him the traces of His love, and wards off from him the assault of His enemy Iblīs — may God curse him.

If that appears upon him, it indicates acceptance. But if the matter is otherwise —

chapters.arabic_text:
### || كتاب آداب تلاوة القرآن

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي امتن على عباده بنبيه المرسل صلى الله عليه وسلم وكتابه
المنزل الذي لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه تنزيل من حكيم حميد
حتى اتسع على أهل الأفكار طريق الاعتبار بما فيه من القصص والأخبار واتضح
به سلوك المنهج القويم والصراط المستقيم بما فصل فيه من الأحكام وفرق بين
الحلال والحرام فهو الضياء والنور وبه النجاة من الغرور وفيه شفاء لما في
الصدور ومن خالفه من الجبابرة قصمه الله ومن ابتغى العلم في غيره أضله الله
هو حبل الله المتين ونوره المبين والعروة الوثقى والمعتصم الأوفى وهو
المحيط بالقليل والكثير والصغير والكبير لا تنقضي عجائبه ولا تتناهى غرائبه
لا يحيط بفوائده عند أهل العلم تحديد ولا يخلقه عند أهل التلاوة كثرة
الترديد هو الذي أرشد الأولين والآخرين ولما سمعه الجن لم يلبثوا أن ولوا
إلى قومهم منذرين {فقالوا إنا سمعنا قرآنا عجبا يهدي إلى الرشد فآمنا به
ولن نشرك بربنا أحدا} فكل من آمن به فقد وفق ومن قال به فقد صدق ومن تمسك
به فقد هدي ومن عمل به فقد فاز وقال تعالى {إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له
لحافظون} ومن أسباب حفظه في القلوب والمصاحف استدامة تلاوته والمواظبة على
دراسته مع القيام بآدابه وشروطه والمحافظة على ما فيه من الأعمال الباطنة
والآداب الظاهرة وذلك لا  بد من بيانه وتفصيله وتنكشف مقاصده في أربعة أبواب
الباب الأول في فضل القرآن وأهله
الباب الثاني في آداب التلاوة في الظاهر
الباب الثالث في الأعمال الباطنة عند التلاوة
الباب الرابع في فهم القرآن وتفسيره بالرأي وغيره

### ||| الباب الأول في فضل القرآن وأهله وذم المقصرين في تلاوته
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-ن-ن (m-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Bestowal of a favor (minnah) with weight and gravity; a benefaction that obliges gratitude.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine grace (imtinān) as an act of munificence untainted by prior claim or recompense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal conferral of a concrete boon; here metaphorical for the sending of the Prophet and Book as the greatest favor.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — "بنبيه المرسل وكتابه المنزل" links two explicative objects of "امتن" without repetition of the preposition, marking them as a single composite grace.
chapters.translation:
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.

Praise be to Allah, Who conferred His favor upon His servants through His sent Prophet (peace be upon him) and His revealed Book — falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy — until the path of reflection (iʿtibār) widened for people of insight through what it contains of narratives and reports, and by it the course of the upright way and the straight path became clear, through what He detailed therein of rulings and the distinction between the lawful and the unlawful. For it is the radiance and the light; through it is deliverance from delusion; in it is healing for what lies in breasts. Whoever opposes it among the tyrants, Allah crushes him; whoever seeks knowledge elsewhere, Allah leads him astray. It is the firm rope of Allah, His manifest light, the trustworthy handhold, and the most faithful refuge. It encompasses the little and the much, the small and the great. Its wonders never cease, nor do its marvels come to an end. No delimitation encompasses its benefits among the people of knowledge, nor does frequency of repetition wear it out among the people of recitation. It is that which guided the first and the last. When the jinn heard it, they did not delay but turned to their people as warners, {«فقالوا إنا سمعنا قرآنا عجبا يهدي إلى الرشد فآمنا به ولن نشرك بربنا أحدا»} ("So they said: 'Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord'"). Thus, whoever believes in it has been granted success; whoever speaks by it has spoken truthfully; whoever clings to it has been guided; whoever acts by it has attained felicity. And He, exalted, said: {«إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له لحافظون»} ("Indeed, We — it is We Who sent down the Remembrance, and indeed, We are its Preservers"). Among the causes of its preservation in hearts and codices is the constancy of reciting it and persisting in studying it, along with the fulfillment of its etiquettes and conditions, and the safeguarding of what it contains of inward acts and outward manners. This necessarily requires its clarification and detailing, and its aims unfold in four chapters:

Chapter One: On the virtue of the Qur'an and its people.
Chapter Two: On the outward etiquettes of recitation.
Chapter Three: On the inward acts during recitation.
Chapter Four: On understanding the Qur'an and its interpretation by personal opinion (tafsīr bi'l-ra'y) and otherwise.

### ||| Chapter One: On the virtue of the Qur'an and its people, and the censure of those who fall short in its recitation.

chapters.title_en: The Excellence of the Qur'an
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||| فضيلة القرآن

قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من قرأ القرآن ثم رأى أن أحدا أوتي أفضل مما أوتي
فقد استصغر ما عظمه الله
PageV01P272
تعالى (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما من شفيع أفضل منزلة عند الله تعالى من القرآن
لا نبي ولا ملك ولا غيره (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو كان القرآن في إهاب ما مسته النار (3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أفضل عبادة أمتي تلاوة القرآن (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أيضا إن الله عز وجل قرأ طه ويس قبل أن يخلق
الخلق بألف عام فلما سمعت الملائكة القرآن قالت طوبى لأمة ينزل عليهم هذا
وطوبى لأجواف تحمل هذا وطوبى لألسنة تنطق بهذا (5)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم خيركم من تعلم القرآن وعلمه (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول الله تبارك وتعالى من شغله قراءة القرآن عن
دعائي ومسألتي أعطيته أفضل ثواب الشاكرين (7)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاثة يوم القيامة على كثيب من مسك أسود لا
يهولهم فزع ولا ينالهم حساب حتى يفرغ ما بين الناس رجل قرأ القرآن ابتغاء
وجه الله عز وجل والخ أم به قوما وهم به راضون (8)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أهل القرآن أهل الله وخاصته (9)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن القلوب تصدأ كما يصدأ الحديد فقيل يا رسول
الله وما جلاؤها فقال تلاوة القرآن وذكر الموت (10)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لله أشد أذنا إلى قارىء القرآن من صاحب القينة
إلى قينته (11)
الآثار قال أبو أمامة الباهلي اقرءوا القرآن ولا تغرنكم هذه المصاحف
المعلقة فإن الله لا يعذب قلبا هو وعاء للقرآن
وقال ابن مسعود إذا أردتم العلم فانثروا القرآن فإن فيه علم  الأولين
والآخرين
وقال أيضا اقرءوا القرآن فإنكم تؤجرون عليه بكل حرف منه عشر حسنات أما
إني لا أقول الحرف ألم ولكن الألف حرف واللام حرف والميم حرف
وقال أيضا لا يسأل أحدكم عن نفسه إلا القرآن فإن كان يحب القرآن ويعجبه
فهو يحب الله سبحانه ورسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم وإن كان يبغض القرآن فهو
يبغض الله سبحانه ورسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم
وقال عمرو بن العاص كل آية في القرآن درجة في الحنة ومصباح في بيوتكم
وقال أيضا من قرأ القرآن فقد أدرجت النبوة بين جنبيه إلا أنه لا يوحى إليه
وقال أبو هريرة PageV01P273
إن البيت الذي يتلى فيه القرآن اتسع بأهله وكثر خيره وحضرته الملائكة
وخرجت منه الشياطين وإن البيت الذي لايتلى فيه كتاب الله عز وجل ضاق بأهله
وقل خيره وخرجت منه الملائكة وحضرته الشياطين
وقال أحمد بن حنبل رأيت الله عز وجل في المنام فقلت يا رب ما أفضل ما
تقرب به المتقربون إليك قال بكلامي يا أحمد قال قلت يا رب بفهم أو بغير فهم
قال بفهم وبغير فهم
وقال محمد بن كعب القرظي إذا سمع الناس القرآن من الله عز وجل يوم
القيامة فكأنهم لم يسمعوه قط
وقال الفضيل بن عياض ينبغي لحامل القرآن أن لا يكون له إلى أحد حاجة ولا
إلى الخلفاء فمن دونهم فينبغي أن تكون حوائج الخلق إليه
وقال أيضا حامل القرآن حامل راية الإسلام فلا ينبغي أن يلهو مع من يلهو
ولا يسهو مع من يسهو ولا يلغو مع من يلغو تعظيما لحق القرآن
وقال سفيان الثوري إذا قرأ الرجل القرآن قبل الملك بين عينيه
وقال عمرو بن ميمون من نشر مصحفا حين يصلي الصبح فقرأ منه مائة آية رفع
الله عز وجل له مثل عمل جميع أهل الدنيا
ويروى أن خالد بن عقبة جاء إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وقال اقرأ
علي القرآن فقرأ عليه إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى الآية
فقال له  فأعاد فقال والله إن له لحلاوة وإن عليه لطلاوة وإن أسفله لمورق
وإن أعلاه لمثمر وما يقول هذا بشر (1)
وقال الحسن والله ما دون القرآن من غنى ولا بعده من فاقة
وقال الفضيل من قرأ خاتمة سورة الحشر حين يصبح ثم مات من يومه ختم له
بطابع الشهداء ومن قرأها حين يمسي ثم مات من ليلته ختم له بطابع الشهداء
وقال القاسم بن عبد الرحمن قلت لبعض النساك ما ههنا أحد نستأنس به فمد
يده إلى المصحف ووضعه على حجره وقال هذا
وقال علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه ثلاث يزدن في الحفظ ويذهبن البلغم
السواك والصيام وقراءة القرآن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ض-ل (faḍl)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Superabundance, surplus, and preeminence in rank or merit
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Excellence as a divinely conferred distinction, not acquired merit
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to God's grace; metaphorical when applied to creatures
- Root: ق-ر-أ (qara'a)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To gather, collect, and recite; the act of assembling letters into speech
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Recitation as the verbal embodiment of divine revelation
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for oral recitation; extended to encompass study and teaching
- Root: ش-ف-ع (shafāʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pair, join, and intercede; making an odd number even
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Intercession as the act of adding one's plea to another's deficiency
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for intercession; metaphorical when attributed to the Qur'an as a speaking entity
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Inna (إن الشرطية) — The protasis introduced by 'man' (whoever) governs the apodosis, establishing a universal legal principle through nominalization.
chapters.translation:
I say — may God Most High grant us and you success — let us now expound the excellence of the Qur'an, that the soul may be stirred to embrace its recitation and to revere its sanctity.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an and then sees that someone has been given something better than what he has been given, has indeed deemed small what God Most High has magnified."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no intercessor of greater station with God Most High than the Qur'an — neither prophet, nor angel, nor any other."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Were the Qur'an to be within a hide, the Fire would not touch it."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "The most excellent act of worship of my community is the recitation of the Qur'an."

And he, peace be upon him, also said: "Verily God, Mighty and Majestic, recited Ṭāhā and Yāsīn a thousand years before He created creation. When the angels heard the Qur'an, they said: 'Blessed is the community upon whom this is revealed! Blessed are the bellies that carry this! Blessed are the tongues that utter this!'"

And he, peace be upon him, said: "The best of you is he who learns the Qur'an and teaches it."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "God, Blessed and Exalted, says: 'Whoever is occupied by the recitation of the Qur'an from supplicating Me and asking of Me, I shall give him the most excellent reward of the thankful.'"

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Three persons on the Day of Resurrection shall be upon a mound of black musk, neither terror shall frighten them, nor reckoning shall reach them, until judgment is finished among mankind: a man who recited the Qur'an seeking the Face of God, Mighty and Majestic, and a man who led a people with it while they were pleased with him."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "The people of the Qur'an are the people of God and His elect."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Verily hearts rust just as iron rusts." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is their polish?" He said: "Recitation of the Qur'an and remembrance of death."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "God is more attentive to the reciter of the Qur'an than the master of a songstress is to his songstress."

The Reports of the Companions and Successors:

Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī said: "Recite the Qur'an, and let not these suspended codices deceive you, for God does not torment a heart that is a vessel for the Qur'an."

Ibn Masʿūd said: "If you desire knowledge, then scatter the Qur'an, for in it is the knowledge of the ancients and the later ones."

He also said: "Recite the Qur'an, for you are rewarded for it — for every letter of it, ten good deeds. I do not say that 'alif-lām-mīm' is one letter, but rather alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter."

He also said: "Let none of you ask about himself except through the Qur'an. If he loves the Qur'an and it delights him, then he loves God, Glorified and Exalted, and His Messenger, peace be upon him. And if he detests the Qur'an, then he detests God, Glorified and Exalted, and His Messenger, peace be upon him."

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said: "Every verse in the Qur'an is a degree in Paradise and a lamp in your houses."

He also said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an has had prophethood folded between his sides, except that revelation is not sent down to him."

Abū Hurayrah said: "Verily the house in which the Qur'an is recited expands with its inhabitants, its good increases, the angels attend it, and the devils depart from it. And verily the house in which the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, is not recited narrows upon its inhabitants, its good diminishes, the angels depart from it, and the devils attend it."

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: "I saw God, Mighty and Majestic, in a dream and said: 'O Lord, what is the most excellent thing by which those who draw near draw near to You?' He said: 'By My Speech, O Aḥmad.' I said: 'O Lord, with understanding or without understanding?' He said: 'With understanding and without understanding.'"

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: "When the people hear the Qur'an from God, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, it will be as though they had never heard it before."

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: "It behooves the bearer of the Qur'an that he have no need of anyone — not of the caliphs nor of those beneath them. Rather, the needs of creation should be directed to him."

He also said: "The bearer of the Qur'an is the bearer of the banner of Islam. It behooves him not to play with those who play, nor to be heedless with those who are heedless, nor to engage in frivolity with those who engage in frivolity — in reverence for the right of the Qur'an."

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: "When a man recites the Qur'an, the King is placed between his eyes."

ʿAmr ibn Maymūn said: "Whoever spreads open a codex while praying the morning prayer and recites from it one hundred verses, God, Mighty and Majestic, raises for him the equivalent of the deeds of all the people of the world."

It is related that Khālid ibn ʿUqbah came to the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and said: "Recite the Qur'an to me." So he recited to him: {«Verily God commands justice, excellence, and giving to near kin»} — the verse. He said to him: "Recite again." So he repeated it. Then he said: "By God, verily it has sweetness, and verily upon it is beauty, and verily its lower part is lush with leaves, and verily its upper part is fruitful. And no human could utter this."

Al-Ḥasan said: "By God, there is no richness apart from the Qur'an, nor any poverty after it."

Al-Fuḍayl said: "Whoever recites the concluding portion of Sūrat al-Ḥashr upon rising in the morning and then dies that day, is sealed with the seal of the martyrs. And whoever recites it upon the evening and then dies that night, is sealed with the seal of the martyrs."

Al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: "I said to one of the ascetics: 'There is no one here with whom we may find companionship.' So he stretched his hand to the codex, placed it upon his lap, and said: 'This.'"

And ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, said: "Three things increase retention and remove phlegm: the toothstick, fasting, and the recitation of the Qur'an."

chapters.title_en: On the Blame of the Recitation of the Negligent — Book II, Chapter on the Outward Etiquettes of Recitation (Ten in Number)
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||| في ذم تلاوة الغافلين

قال أنس بن مالك رب تال للقرآن والقرآن يلعنه وقال ميسرة الغريب هو
القرآن في جوف الفاجر وقال أبو سليمان الداراني الزبانية أسرع إلى حملة
القرآن الذين يعصون الله عز وجل منهم إلى عبدة الأوثان حين عصوا الله
سبحانه بعد القرآن
وقال بعض العلماء إذا قرأ ابن آدم القرآن ثم خلط ثم عاد فقرأ قيل له مالك
ولكلامي وقال ابن الرماح ندمت على استظهاري القرآن لأنه بلغني أن أصحاب
القرآن يسألون عما يسأل عنه الأنبياء يوم القيامة
وقال ابن مسعود ينبغي لحامل القرآن أن يعرف بليله إذا الناس ينامون
وبنهاره إذا الناس يفرطون وبحزنه إذا الناس يفرحون وببكائه إذا الناس
يضحكون وبصمته إذا الناس يخوضون وبخشوعه إذا الناس يختالون وينبغي لحامل
القرآن أن يكون مستكينا لينا ولاينبغي له أن يكون جافيا ولا مماريا ولا
صياحا ولا صخابا ولا حديدا
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أكثر منافقي هذه الأمة قراؤها (2) وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم اقرأ القرآن ما نهاك فإن لم ينهك فلست تقرؤه (3) وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم ما آمن بالقرآن من استحل محارمه (4) وقال بعض السلف PageV01P274
إن العبد ليفتتح سورة فتصلي عليه الملائكة حتى يفرغ منها وإن العبد
ليفتتح سورة فتلعنه حتى يفرغ منها فقيل له وكيف ذلك فقال إذا أحل حلالها
وحرم حرامها صلت  عليه وإلا لعنته
وقال بعض العلماء إن العبد ليتلو القرآن فيلعن نفسه وهو لا يعلم يقول
{ألا لعنة الله على الظالمين} وهو ظالم نفسه ألا لعنة الله على الكاذبين
وهو منهم
وقال الحسن إنكم اتخذتم قراءة القرآن مراحل وجعلتم الليل جملا فأنتم
تركبونه فتقطعون به مراحله وإن من كان قبلكم رأوه رسائل من ربهم فكانوا
يتدبرونها بالليل وينفذونها بالنهار
وقال ابن مسعود أنزل القرآن عليهم ليعملوا به فاتخذوا دراسته عملا إن
أحدكم ليقرأ القرآن من فاتحته إلى خاتمته ما يسقط منه حرفا وقد أسقط العمل
به
وفي حديث ابن عمر وحديث جندب رضي الله عنهما لقد عشنا دهرا طويلا وأحدنا
يؤتى الإيمان قبل القرآن فتنزل السورة على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم فيتعلم
حلالها وحرامها وآمرها وزاجرها وما ينبغي أن يقف عنده منها
ثم لقد رأيت رجالا يؤتى أحدهم القرآن قبل الإيمان فيقرأ ما بين فاتحة
الكتاب إلى خاتمته لا يدري ما آمره ولا زاجره ولا ما ينبغي أن يقف عنده منه
ينثره نثر الدقل (1) وقد ورد في التوراة يا عبدي أما تستحي مني يأتيك كتاب
من بعض إخوانك وأنت في الطريق تمشي فتعدل عن الطريق وتقعد لأجله وتقرؤه
وتتدبره حرفا حرفا حتى لا يفوتك شيء منه وهذا كتابي أنزلته إليك انظر كم
فصلت لك فيه من القول وكم كررت عليك فيه لتتأمل طوله وعرضه ثم أنت معرض عنه
أفكنت أهون عليك من بعض إخوانك يا عبدي يقعد إليك بعض إخوانك فتقبل عليه
بكل وجهك وتصغي إلى حديثه بكل قلبك فإن تكلم متكلم أو شغلك شاغل عن حديثه
أومأت إليه أن كف وها أنا ذا مقبل عليك ومحدث لك وأنت معرض بقلبك عني
أفجعلتني أهون عندك من بعض إخوانك

### ||| الباب الثاني في ظاهر آداب التلاوة وهي عشرة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ذ م م (dh-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Blame, censure, dispraise — the opposite of praise (ḥamd); denotes the act of condemning a quality or deed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theological censure tied to moral accountability (taklīf); blame is merited when an act violates divine command despite knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in reference to speech; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to states — e.g., the Qur'an "cursing" a reciter is a figurative attribution of the consequence to the cause.
- Root: ت ل و (t-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, to recite sequentially; recitation (tilāwah) implies tracing letters in order, and by extension, following the injunctions.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Recitation is of two kinds: mere utterance (tilāwah al-lafẓ) and obedient enactment (tilāwah al-ḥukm); the latter is the true purpose.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for vocal recitation; metaphorical for compliance — "he recited the Qur'an" meaning he enacted it.
- Root: غ ف ل (gh-f-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Neglect, heedlessness, absence of heart from awareness; the opposite of vigilance (yaqaẓah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A blameworthy state of the soul wherein the intellect fails to govern the faculties; distinct from ignorance (jahl) as it implies capacity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the heart's absence; metaphorical for the reciter who utters without understanding — a "negligent reciter" is a majāz of the whole for the part.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In phrases like "the reciter of the Qur'an, the Qur'an curses him," the pronoun (hu) refers back to the subject (tālī), establishing a causal nexus through grammatical resumption (rabṭ bi-al-ḍamīr), which is essential for parsing the conditional-like constructions in the reported sayings.
chapters.translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the path of vigilance and save us from the way of the negligent:

Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Many a reciter of the Qur'an recites while the Qur'an curses him."

Maysarah said: "The stranger (al-gharīb) is the Qur'an within the belly of the wicked."

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "The Zabāniyah (the angels of punishment) are swifter to seize the bearers of the Qur'an who disobey Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than they are to seize the idol-worshippers — because they disobey Allah, Glorified be He, after having received the Qur'an."

One of the scholars said: "When the son of Adam recites the Qur'an, then mixes (corrupts his practice), then returns to reciting, it is said to him: 'What is the matter with you and My speech?'"

Ibn al-Rimmāḥ said: "I regretted having memorized the Qur'an, for it reached me that the companions of the Qur'an will be asked on the Day of Resurrection about what the prophets are asked about."

Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It behooves the bearer of the Qur'an to be known by his night when people sleep, by his day when people are negligent, by his grief when people rejoice, by his weeping when people laugh, by his silence when people engage in idle talk, and by his humility when people strut proudly. And it behooves the bearer of the Qur'an to be meek and gentle; it does not behoove him to be harsh, nor quarrelsome, nor loud-voiced, nor clamorous, nor sharp-tempered."

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The majority of the hypocrites of this community are its reciters (qurrāʾ)."

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Recite the Qur'an as long as it forbids you; if it does not forbid you, then you are not truly reciting it."

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "He has not believed in the Qur'an who deems lawful its prohibitions."

One of the Salaf said: "Indeed, a servant opens a sūrah, and the angels pray for him until he finishes it; and indeed, a servant opens a sūrah, and it curses him until he finishes it." It was said to him: "How is that?" He said: "If he deems lawful its lawful and deems unlawful its unlawful, they pray for him; otherwise, it curses him."

One of the scholars said: "Indeed, a servant recites the Qur'an and curses himself without knowing. He says: {«Aye, the curse of Allah be upon the wrongdoers»} (Hūd 11:18) — and he is a wrongdoer to his own soul. And he says: {«Aye, the curse of Allah be upon the liars»} (Āl ʿImrān 3:61) — and he is among them."

Al-Ḥasan (al-Baṣrī) said: "You have taken the recitation of the Qur'an as stages (marāḥil) and made the night a camel; you ride it and traverse its stages with it. But those before you saw it as letters (rasāʾil) from their Lord; they would ponder them by night and execute them by day."

Ibn Masʿūd said: "The Qur'an was sent down to them to act upon it, so they took its study as the deed. Indeed, one of you recites the Qur'an from its opening to its closing, not dropping a single letter, while he has dropped acting upon it."

In the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar and the ḥadīth of Jundub (may Allah be pleased with them both): "We lived for a long time, and one of us would be given faith before the Qur'an. Then a sūrah would be sent down upon Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), and he would learn its lawful, its unlawful, its commands, its prohibitions, and what he should pause at within it. Then I have seen men who are given the Qur'an before faith; one of them recites from the opening of the Book to its closing, not knowing its command, nor its prohibition, nor what he should pause at within it — he scatters it as one scatters unripe dates (daqal)."

And it has been related in the Torah: "O My servant, are you not ashamed before Me? A letter comes to you from one of your brothers while you are walking on the road, so you turn aside from the road and sit down for its sake, and you read it and ponder it letter by letter, so that nothing of it escapes you. Yet this is My Book, which I have sent down to you — look at how much speech I have detailed in it for you, and how many times I have repeated to you therein, so that you might contemplate its length and its breadth — and then you turn away from it. Am I then more insignificant to you than one of your brothers? O My servant, one of your brothers sits with you, and you turn your whole face toward him and incline your whole heart to his speech. If a speaker speaks or an occupier occupies you from his speech, you gesture to him to be silent — and here I am, turning toward you and speaking to you, while you turn your heart away from Me. Have you then made Me more insignificant to you than one of your brothers?"

### ||| Book II: On the Outward Etiquettes of Recitation — and they are ten.
