وكل ما ذكره صحيح وإنما النظر في الكلة وتزيين الحيطان بالديباج فإن ذلك
لا ينتهي إلى التحريم إذ الحرير يحرم على الرجال قال رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم هذان حرام على ذكور أمتي حل لإناثها (5)
وما على PageV02P015
الحائط ليس منسوبا إلى الذكور ولو حرم هذا لحرم تزيين الكعبة بل الأولى
إباحته لموجب قوله {قل من حرم زينة الله} لا سيما في وقت الزينة إذا لم
يتخذ عادة للتفاخر
وإن تخيل أن الرجال ينتفعون بالنظر إليه ولا يحرم على الرجال الانتفاع
بالنظر إلى الديباج مهما لبسه الجواري والنساء
والحيطان في معنى النساء إذ لسن موصوفات بالذكورة
وأما إحضار الطعام فله آداب خمسة
الأول تعجيل الطعام فذلك من  إكرام الضيف وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من
كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليكرم ضيفه (1)
ومهما حضر الأكثرون وغاب واحد أو اثنان وتأخروا عن الوقت الموعود فحق
الحاضر في التعجيل أولى من حق أولئك في التأخير إلا أن يكون المتأخر فقيرا
أو ينكسر قلبه بذلك فلا بأس في التأخير وأحد المعنيين في قوله تعالى {هل
أتاك حديث ضيف إبراهيم المكرمين} أنهم أكرموا بتعجيل الطعام إليهم دل عليه
قوله تعالى {فما لبث أن جاء بعجل حنيذ} وقوله {فراغ إلى أهله فجاء بعجل
سمين} والروغان الذهاب بسرعة وقيل في خفية وقيل جاء بفخذ من لحم وإنما سمي
عجلا لأنه عجله ولم يلبث
قال حاتم الأصم العجلة من الشيطان إلا في خمسة فإنها من سنة رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم إطعام الضيف وتجهيز الميت وتزويج البكر وقضاء الدين
والتوبة من الذنب (2)
ويستحب التعجيل في الوليمة قيل الوليمة في أول يوم سنة وفي الثاني معروف
وفي الثالث رياء
الثاني ترتيب الأطعمة بتقديم الفاكهة أولا إن كانت فذلك أوفق في الطب
فإنها أسرع استحالة فينبغي أن تقع في أسفل المعدة
وفي القرآن تنبيه على تقديم الفاكهة في قوله تعالى وفاكهة مما يتخيرون
{ثم قال} ولحم طير مما يشتهون ثم أفضل ما يقدم بعد الفاكهة اللحم والثريد
فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم فضل عائشة على النساء كفضل الثريد على سائر
الطعام فإن جمع إليه حلاوة بعده فقد جمع الطيبات
ودل على حصول الإكرام باللحم قوله تعالى في ضيف إبراهيم إذ أحضر العجل
الحنيذ أي المحنوذ وهو الذي أجيد نضجه وهو أحد معنى الإكرام أعني تقديم
اللحم
وقال تعالى في وصف الطيبات وأنزلنا عليكم المن والسلوى المن العسل
والسلوى اللحم سمي سلوى لأنه يتسلى به عن جميع الإدام ولا يقوم غيره مقامه
ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم سيد الإدام اللحم ثم قال بعد ذكر المن
والسلوى كلوا من طيبات ما رزقناكم فاللحم والحلاوة من الطيبات
قال أبو سليمان الداراني رضي الله عنه أكل  الطيبات يورث الرضا عن الله
وتتم هذه الطيبات بشرب الماء البارد وصب الماء الفاتر على اليد عند الغسل
قال المأمون شرب الماء بثلج يخلص الشكر
وقال بعض الأدباء إذا دعوت إخوانك فأطعمتهم حصرمية وبورانية وسقيتهم ماء
باردا فقد أكملت الضيافة
وأنفق بعضهم دراهم في ضيافة فقال بعض الحكماء لم نكن نحتاج إلى هذا إذا
كان خبزك جيدا وماؤك باردا وخلك حامضا فهو كفاية
وقال بعضهم الحلاوة بعد الطعام خير من كثرة الألوان والتمكن على المائدة
خير من زيادة لونين PageV02P016
ويقال أن الملائكة تحضر المائدة إذا كان عليها بقل فذلك أيضا مستحب ولما
فيه من التزين بالخضرة
وفي الخبر إن المائدة التي أنزلت على بني إسرائيل كان عليها من كل البقول
إلا الكراث
وكان عليها سمكة عند رأسها خل وعند ذنبها ملح وسبعة أرغفة على كل رغيف
زيتون وحب رمان فهذا إذا اجتمع حسن للموافقة
الثالث أن يقدم من الألوان ألطفها حتى يستوفي منها من يريد ولا يكثر
الأكل بعده وعادة المترفين تقديم الغليظ ليستأنف حركة الشهوة بمصادفة
اللطيف بعده وهو خلاف السنة فإنه حيلة في استكثار الأكل
وكان من سنة المتقدمين أن يقوموا جملة الألوان دفعة واحدة ويصففون القصاع
من الطعام على المائدة ليأكل كل واحد مما يشتهي
وإن لم يكن عنده إلا لون واحد ذكره ليستوفوا منه ولا ينتظروا أطيب منه
ويحكى عن بعض أصحاب المروءات أنه كان يكتب نسخة بما يستحضر من الألوان
ويعرض على الضيفان
وقال بعض الشيوخ قدم إلى بعض المشايخ لونا بالشام فقلت عندنا بالعراق
إنما يقدم هذا آخرا فقال وكذا عندنا بالشام ولم يكن له لون غيره فخجلت منه
وقال آخر كنا جماعة في ضيافة فقدم إلينا ألوان من الرءوس المشوية طبيخا
وقديدا فكنا لا نأكل ننتظر بعدها لونا أو حملا فجاءنا بالطست ولم يقدم
غيرها فنظر بعضنا إلى بعض فقال بعض الشيوخ وكان مزاحا إن الله تعالى يقدر
أن يخلق رءوسا بلا أبدان قال وبتنا تلك الليلة جياعا نطلب فتيتا إلى السحور
فلهذا  يستحب أن يقدم الجميع أو يخبر بما عنده
الرابع أن لا يبادر إلى رفع الألوان قبل تمكنهم من الاستيفاء حتى يرفعوا
الأيدي عنها فلعل منهم من يكون بقية ذلك اللون أشهى عنده مما استحضروه أو
بقيت فيه حاجة إلى الأكل فيتنغض عليه بالمبادرة وهي من التمكن على المائدة
التي يقال إنها خير من لونين فيحتمل أن يكون المراد به قطع الاستعجال
ويحتمل أن يكون أراد به سعة المكان
حكى عن الستوري وكان صوفيا مزاحا فحضر عند واحد من أبناء الدنيا على
مائدة فقدم إليهم حمل وكان صاحب المائدة بخل فلما رأى القوم مزقوا الحمل كل
ممزق ضاق صدره وقال يا غلام ارفع إلى الصبيان فرفع الحمل إلى داخل الدار
فقام الستوري يعدو خلف الحمل فقيل له إلى أين فقال آكل مع الصبيان فاستحيا
الرجل وأمر برد الحمل
ومن هذا الفن أن لا يرفع صاحب المائدة يده قبل القوم فإنهم يستحيون بل
ينبغي أن يكون آخرهم أكلا
كان بعض الكرام يخبر القوم بجميع الألوان ويتركهم يستوفون فإذا قاربوا
الفراغ جثا على ركبتيه ومد يده إلى الطعام وأكل وقال
بسم الله ساعدوني بارك الله فيكم وعليكم وكان السلف يستحسنون ذلك منه
الخامس أن يقدم من الطعام قدر الكفاية فإن التقليل عن الكفاية نقص في
المروءة والزيادة عليه تصنع ومراءاة لا سيما إذا كانت نفسه لا تسمح بأن
يأكلوا الكل إلا أن يقدم الكثير وهو طيب النفس لو أخذوا الجميع ونوى أن
يتبرك بفضلة طعامهم إذ في الحديث لا يحاسب عليه
أحضر إبراهيم بن أدهم رحمه الله طعاما كثيرا على مائدته فقال له سفيان يا
أبا إسحاق أما تخاف أن يكون هذا سرفا فقال إبراهيم ليس في الطعام سرف
فإن لم تكن هذه النية فالتكثير تكلف
قال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه نهينا أن نجيب دعوة من يباهي بطعامه وكره
جماعة من الصحابة أكل طعام المباهاة
ومن ذلك كان لا يرفع من بين يدي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فضلة طعام
قط  لأنهم كانوا لا يقدمون إلا قدر الحاجة ولا يأكلون تمام الشبع
وينبغي أن يعزل أولا نصيب أهل البيت حتى لا تكون أعينهم طامحة إلى رجوع
شيء منه فلعله لا يرجع فتضيق صدورهم وتنطلق في الضيفان ألسنتهم ويكون قد
أطعم الضيفان ما يتبعه كراهية قوم وذلك خيانة في حقهم
وما بقي من الأطعمة فليس للضيفان أخذه وهو الذي تسميه الصوفية الزلة إلا
إذا صرح
PageV02P017
صاحب الطعام بالإذن فيه عن قلب راض أو علم ذلك بقرينة حاله وأنه يفرح به
فإن كان يظن كراهيته
فلا ينبغي أن يؤخذ وإذا علم رضاه فينبغي مراعاة العدل والنصفة مع الرفقاء
فلا ينبغي أن يأخذ الواحد إلا ما يخصه أو ما يرضى به رفيقه عن طوع لا عن
حياء
فأما الانصراف فله ثلاثة آداب
الأول أن يخرج مع الضيف إلى باب الدار وهو سنة وذلك من إكرام الضيف وقد
أمر بإكرامه قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليكرم
ضيفه وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن من سنة الضيف أن يشيع إلى باب الدار قال
أبو قتادة قدم وفد النجاشي على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقام يخدمهم
بنفسه فقال له أصحابه نحن نكفيك يا رسول الله فقال كلا إنهم كانوا لأصحابي
مكرمين وأنا أحب أن أكافئهم وتمام الإكرام طلاقة الوجه وطيب الحديث عند
الدخول والخروج وعلى المائدة
قيل للأوزاعي رضي الله عنه ما كرامة الضيف قال طلاقة الوجه وطيب الحديث
وقال يزيد بن أبي زياد ما دخلت على عبد الرحمن بن أبي ليلى إلا حدثنا
حديثا حسنا وأطعمنا طعاما حسنا
الثاني أن ينصرف الضيف طيب النفس وإن جرى في حقه تقصير فذلك من حسن الخلق
والتواضع قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الرجل ليدرك بحسن خلقه درجة الصائم
القائم ودعي بعض السلف برسول فلم يصادفه الرسول فلما سمع حضر وكانوا قد
تفرقوا وفرغوا وخرجوا فخرج إليه صاحب المنزل وقال قد خرج القوم فقال هل بقي
بقية قال لا قال فكسرة  إن بقيت قال لم تبق قال فالقدر أمسحها قال قد غسلتها
فانصرف يحمد الله تعالى فقيل له في ذلك فقال قد أحسن الرجل دعانا بنية
وردنا بنية فهذا هو معنى التواضع وحسن الخلق
وحكى أن أستاذ أبى القاسم الجنيد دعاه صبي إلى دعوة أبيه أربع مرات فرده
الأب في المرات الأربع وهو يرجع في كل مرة تطييبا لقلب الصبي بالحضور ولقلب
الأب بالانصراف فهذه نفوس قد ذللت بالتواضع لله تعالى واطمأنت بالتوحيد
وصارت تشاهد في كل رد وقبول عبرة فيما بينها وبين ربها فلا تنكسر بما يجري
من العباد من الإذلال كما لا تستبشر بما يجري منهم من الإكرام بل يرون الكل
من الواحد القهار
ولذلك قال بعضهم أنا لا أجيب الدعوة إلا لأني أتذكر بها طعام الجنة أي هو
طعام طيب يحمل عنا كده ومؤنته وحسابه
الثالث أن لا يخرج إلا برضا صاحب المنزل وإذنه ويراعي قلبه في قدر
الإقامة وإذا نزل ضيفا فلا يزيد على ثلاثة أيام فربما يتبرم به ويحتاج إلى
إخراجه قال صلى الله عليه وسلم الضيافة ثلاثة أيام فما زاد فصدفة (1)
نعم لو ألح رب البيت عليه عن خلوص قلب فله المقام إذ ذاك ويستحب أن يكون
عنده فراش للضيف النازل قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فراش للرجل وفراش
للمرأة وفراش للضيف والرابع للشيطان (2)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-ي-ف (ḍ-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes "to incline, to lean toward, to lodge as a guest"; the guest (ḍayf) is so named because he inclines toward the host's hospitality, and the host (muḍīf) inclines toward honoring him.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Hospitality (ḍiyāfah) is a comprehensive act of worship uniting generosity (karam), brotherhood in faith, and emulation of prophetic practice; its reward is tied to sincere intention (niyyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is lodging and feeding; metaphorically extended to all forms of honoring the guest, including cheerfulness of face and kind speech.
- Root: د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To call, summon, invite; also to supplicate. The invitation (daʿwah) is the initiating act that brings the guest into the host's sphere of honor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, daʿwah is the call to God; in social ethics, it is the summons to a meal, which the Prophet made a right (ḥaqq) upon the believer.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal calling; metaphorically, the invitation carries a moral obligation of response (ijābah), as declining without cause is disobedience.
- Root: أ-ك-ل (ʾ-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To eat, consume; the act of ingestion. In the context of hospitality, eating is the culminating act of the guest's acceptance of the host's honor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Eating is a mundane act elevated to worship through intention—whether to strengthen oneself for obedience, to honor a brother, or to follow prophetic sunnah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal consumption of food; metaphorically, "eating" the food of the pious is aiding obedience, while eating with the wicked strengthens transgression.
- Root: ع-ز-م (ʿ-z-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To resolve, intend firmly; also to invite with insistence. The host's resolve (ʿazm) in inviting reflects sincerity versus ostentation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Firm intention (ʿazīmah) distinguishes acts of worship from habits; in hospitality, it determines whether feeding is an act of piety or pride.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal determination; metaphorically, the host's insistence on the guest eating is a sign of genuine welcome versus mere formality.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., "if he knows his brother's heart is pleased...") and exceptions ("except if the host insists from pure heart") to delineate precise legal and ethical boundaries, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis for accurate rendering.
chapters.translation:
I say: The loci of etiquettes in this matter are six: first, the invitation; then the response; then the presence; then the serving of food; then the eating; then the departure. Let us proceed to their explanation, God willing.

**On the Virtue of Hospitality**

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Do not burden the guest so that you make him detest you, for whoever detests the guest has detested God, and whoever detests God, God detests him."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no good in one who does not host guests."

The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, passed by a man who had many camels and cattle, yet he did not host him. He then passed by a woman who had a few sheep, and she slaughtered one for him. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Look at these two—these characters are in the hand of God; whomever He wills to grant a good character, He does."

Abū Rāfiʿ, the freed slave of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: A guest descended upon him, and he said: "Tell so-and-so the Jew: a guest has descended upon me, so lend me some flour until Rajab." The Jew said: "By God, I will not lend it except with a pledge." So he informed the Prophet, who said: "By God, I am trustworthy in heaven and trustworthy on earth. Had he lent me, I would have repaid him. Go with my coat of mail and pledge it with him."

Abraham the Friend, peace and blessings of God be upon him, whenever he wished to eat, would go out a mile or two seeking someone to share his midday meal with him. He was nicknamed "Abū al-Ḍayfān" (Father of Guests). Due to the sincerity of his intention, his hospitality has endured at his shrine to this very day—no night passes without a group eating at his place, from three to ten to a hundred. The custodian of the place said: "To this day, no night has ever been without a guest."

The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked: "What is faith?" He said: "Feeding food and spreading peace."

And he, peace be upon him, said regarding expiations and degrees: "Feeding food, praying at night while people sleep."

And he was asked about the accepted pilgrimage (ḥajj al-mabrūr), and he said: "Feeding food and kind speech."

Anas, may God be pleased with him, said: "Any house that no guest enters—the angels do not enter it."

The reports concerning the virtue of hospitality and feeding are beyond enumeration. Let us then mention its etiquettes.

**Regarding the Invitation**

The inviter should direct his invitation to the pious rather than the wicked. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said in his supplication for one whom he had invited: "May the righteous eat your food."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Do not eat except the food of a pious man, and let none eat your food except a pious man."

He should specifically intend the poor rather than the rich. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The worst food is the food of the wedding feast to which the rich are invited and the poor are not."

He should not neglect his relatives in his hospitality, for neglecting them is a cause of estrangement and severing of kinship ties. Likewise, he should observe order among his friends and acquaintances, for singling out some causes estrangement in the hearts of the rest.

He should not intend by his invitation ostentation and boasting, but rather the drawing of brothers' hearts, the emulation of the Messenger of God's, peace be upon him, sunnah in feeding food, and bringing joy to the hearts of the believers.

He should not invite one whom he knows would find it burdensome to respond, and who, if he attended, would be harmed by the attendees for some reason.

He should not invite anyone except one whose response he desires. Sufyān said: "Whoever invites someone to food while disliking his response bears a sin; and if the invitee responds, then he bears two sins—because he compelled him to eat against his will, and had he known that, he would not have eaten."

Feeding the pious is assistance in obedience, while feeding the wicked is strengthening in transgression. A tailor said to Ibn al-Mubārak: "I sew clothes for the sultans—do you fear that I am among the helpers of the oppressors?" He said: "No. The helpers of the oppressors are those who sell you the thread and needle. As for you, you are among the oppressors themselves."

**Regarding the Response**

The response is an emphatic sunnah, and some have held it obligatory in certain cases. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Were I invited to a sheep's trotter, I would respond; and were a foreleg gifted to me, I would accept."

The response has five etiquettes:

**First:** That he not distinguish the rich by responding while refusing the poor—for that is the arrogance that is prohibited. For this reason, some refrained from responding altogether, saying: "Waiting for the broth is humiliation." Another said: "When I place my hand in another's bowl, my neck has bowed to him." Among the arrogant are those who respond to the rich but not the poor—and this contradicts the sunnah. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, would respond to the invitation of a slave and to the invitation of a poor man.

Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with them both, passed by a group of poor people who were begging on the road, having spread out pieces of bread on the sand and eating, while he was on his mule. He greeted them, and they said: "Come to the midday meal, O son of the daughter of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him." He said: "Yes, indeed—God does not love the arrogant." So he descended, sat with them on the ground, ate, then greeted them, mounted, and said: "I have responded to you, so respond to me." They said: "Yes." So he appointed a known time for them; they attended, and he served them the finest food and sat eating with them.

As for the saying of one who said: "Whose bowl I place my hand in, my neck has bowed to him"—some have said this contradicts the sunnah. But it is not so. For it is humiliation only when the inviter does not rejoice in the response, does not regard it as a favor conferred, and sees it as a debt owed to him by the invitee. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, would attend because he knew that the inviter regarded it as a favor and saw it as an honor and a treasure for himself in this world and the next. Thus this varies according to circumstance. Whoever is suspected of finding the feeding burdensome, doing it only for ostentation or with affectation—responding to him is not from the sunnah; rather, the better course is to offer an excuse. For this reason, some of the Sufis said: "Do not respond except to the invitation of one who sees that you have eaten your own provision, that he has returned to you a trust that was yours with him, and who sees that you have a favor upon him in accepting that trust from him."

Sarī al-Saqaṭī, may God have mercy on him, said: "Alas for a morsel for which there is no liability upon God and no obligation upon any creature."

When the invitee knows there is no favor in it, he should not refuse.

Abū Turāb al-Nakhshī, may God's mercy be upon him, said: "Food was offered to me and I refused, so I was afflicted with hunger for fourteen days—and I knew it was its punishment."

It was said to Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, may God be pleased with him: "Everyone who invites you, go to him." He said: "I am a guest—I lodge wherever they lodge me."

**Second:** That he should not refrain from responding due to the distance of the journey, just as he should not refrain due to the poverty of the inviter or his lack of status. Rather, any distance that can ordinarily be borne should not be a cause of refusal. It is said in the Torah or some books: "Walk a mile to visit the sick; walk two miles to accompany a funeral; walk three miles to respond to an invitation; walk four miles to visit a brother in God." The response to the invitation and the visit were given precedence because in them is the fulfillment of the right of the living, which takes priority over the dead. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Were I invited to a sheep's trotter at al-Ghamīm, I would respond." That is a place several miles from Medina, where the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, broke his fast in Ramadan when the news reached him, and shortened the prayer during his journey.

**Third:** That he should not refrain because he is fasting, but rather attend. If he knows that his brother would be pleased by his breaking the fast, let him break it and reckon in his breaking the fast—by the intention of bringing joy to his brother's heart—what he would reckon in the fast itself, and more. This applies to the voluntary fast. If he does not ascertain his brother's joy, let him affirm it outwardly and break the fast. But if he ascertains that the host is merely affecting courtesy, let him offer an excuse. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to one who excused himself by fasting: "Your brother has gone to trouble for you, and you say, 'I am fasting.'"

Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Among the best of good deeds is honoring one's companions by breaking the fast." Thus breaking the fast is an act of worship with this intention and a good character trait, and its reward surpasses the reward of the fast itself. And whenever he does not break his fast, then his hospitality is kind words, incense, and pleasant conversation. It has been said: "Kohl and oil are one of the two readings."

**Fourth:** That he refrain from responding if the food is of doubtful legality (shubhah), or the place or the spread carpet is from unlawful means, or if a reprehensible thing is established in the place—such as spreading silk brocade, using silver or gold vessels, depicting animals on the ceiling or wall, hearing flutes and instruments of amusement, occupying oneself with any kind of play, sport, jest, and game, or listening to backbiting, tale-bearing, falsehood, slander, and lying—and similar matters that prevent the response and its desirability, rendering it forbidden or disliked. Likewise, if the inviter is an oppressor, an innovator, a wicked person, an evil person, or one who affects courtesy seeking ostentation and pride.

**Fifth:** That he not intend by his response the gratification of the belly's desire, thus becoming a laborer in the affairs of this world. Rather, let him beautify his intention so that by responding he becomes a laborer for the hereafter. This is by intending emulation of the sunnah of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, in his saying: "Were I invited to a sheep's trotter, I would respond." And he intends caution from disobedience to God Almighty, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever does not respond to the inviter has disobeyed God and His Messenger." And he intends honoring his believing brother, following his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever honors his believing brother, it is as if he has honored God." And he intends bringing joy to his heart, in compliance with his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever brings joy to a believer has brought joy to God." And he intends with that the visitation of him, to be among those who love each other for God's sake, since the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, made mutual visiting and mutual giving for God's sake a condition of that. The giving has been realized from one side, so the visiting is realized from his side as well. And he intends safeguarding himself from being ill-thought-of in his refusal, and from tongues being loosened against him by attributing to him arrogance, bad character, contempt for a Muslim brother, or the like.

These are six intentions that attach his response to the acts of nearness individually—how much more so collectively! Some of the predecessors used to say: "I love to have an intention in every act, even in food and drink." And concerning this, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Actions are but by intentions, and every man shall have what he intended. So whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was to a worldly gain he seeks or a woman he marries, his emigration is to that which he emigrated to."

The intention only takes effect in permissible acts and acts of obedience. As for prohibited acts, it does not. For if one intended to bring joy to his brothers by helping them drink wine or another unlawful thing, the intention would not benefit, and it cannot be said: "Actions are but by intentions." Rather, if one intended by raiding—which is an act of obedience—ostentation and seeking wealth, he would turn away from the direction of obedience. Likewise, a permissible act wavering between aspects of good and otherwise becomes attached to the aspects of good by intention. Thus the intention takes effect in these two categories, not in the third.

**Regarding the Presence**

Its etiquette is that he enter the house and not take the seat of honor, seizing the finest place, but rather humble himself. He should not prolong their waiting, nor hasten so as to surprise them before full preparation. He should not constrict the space upon the attendees by crowding. Rather, if the master of the house gestures to him a place, he should not oppose him at all—for he may have arranged in his mind a place for each person, and opposing him would disturb him. And if some of the guests gesture to him to move up as an honor, let him humble himself. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Verily, from humility before God is being content with the lower place in the gathering."

He should not sit facing the door of the women's chamber and their concealment. He should not gaze excessively at the place from which the food emerges, for that is a sign of greed. He should single out with greeting and inquiry those nearest to him when he sits.

If a guest enters for overnight stay, the master of the house should acquaint him upon entry with the direction of the qiblah, the latrine, and the place of ablution. Thus did Mālik do with al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with them both.

Mālik washed his hands before the food, before the people, and said: "Washing before food is for the master of the house first, because he invites people to his generosity, so it is fitting that he precede them in washing; and at the end of the meal, he delays his washing, waiting for someone to enter and eat, so that he may eat with him."

If he enters and sees a reprehensible thing, let him change it if he is able; otherwise, let him denounce it with his tongue and depart. The reprehensible includes spreading silk brocade, using silver and gold vessels, depictions on walls, hearing instruments and flutes, the presence of unveiled women, and other forbidden things. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: "If he sees a kohl container whose top is silver-plated, he should leave." He did not permit sitting except with a silver clasp. And he said: "If he sees a canopy (kullah), he should leave, for that is affectation with no benefit—it neither repels heat nor cold, nor conceals anything." Likewise, he said one should leave if he sees the walls of the house covered with silk brocade as the Kaʿbah is covered.

He said: "If one rents a house containing a depiction, or enters the bathhouse and sees a depiction, he should scratch it out; if he cannot, he should leave."

All that he mentioned is sound. However, the consideration regarding the canopy and adorning walls with silk brocade—for that does not reach the level of prohibition, since silk is forbidden to men. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "These two are forbidden to the males of my nation, permissible for its females." What is on the wall is not attributed to males. And were this forbidden, then adorning the Kaʿbah would be forbidden. Rather, the better course is its permissibility, due to the import of His saying: {«Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God»}—especially at times of adornment, when it is not adopted as a habit of pride. And if one imagines that men benefit by looking at it—it is not forbidden for men to benefit by looking at silk brocade whenever slave-girls and women wear it. And walls are in the category of women, for they are not described by masculinity.

**Regarding the Serving of Food**

It has five etiquettes:

**First:** Hastening the food, for that is part of honoring the guest. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest." Whenever the majority have arrived and one or two are absent, delayed beyond the appointed time, the right of the present in hastening takes precedence over the right of the absent in delaying—unless the delayed one is poor or his heart would be broken by that, in which case there is no harm in delaying. One of the two meanings in His saying, exalted: {«Has the story of the honored guests of Abraham reached you?»} is that they were honored by hastening the food to them. This is indicated by His saying: {«And he did not tarry until he brought a roasted calf»} and His saying: {«Then he turned quickly to his family and brought a fat calf»}—and "turning quickly" (rawaghān) means going swiftly; it was also said: in secret; and it was said: he brought a thigh of meat. It was only called a calf (ʿijl) because he hastened it (ʿajjalahu) and did not delay.

Ḥātim al-Aṣamm said: "Haste is from Satan, except in five things, for they are from the sunnah of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him: feeding the guest, preparing the dead, marrying the virgin, repaying debt, and repenting from sin."

Hastening the wedding feast is recommended. It was said: "The feast on the first day is a sunnah, on the second it is generosity, and on the third it is ostentation."

**Second:** Ordering the foods by presenting fruit first, if available—for that is more fitting in medicine, as it is quicker to transform and should settle at the bottom of the stomach. In the Qur'an there is an indication of presenting fruit first in His saying: "And fruit from what they choose {«then said»} and flesh of fowl from what they desire." Then the best of what is presented after fruit is meat and tharīd (bread soaked in broth). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The superiority of ʿĀʾishah over women is like the superiority of tharīd over all other foods." If one adds sweetness after it, he has gathered all the good things.

The attainment of honor through meat is indicated by His saying regarding Abraham's guests, when he presented the roasted calf (ḥanīdh)—that is, well-cooked—and this is one of the meanings of honor, namely presenting meat. And He said, exalted, in describing the good things: "And We sent down upon you manna and quails"—manna is honey, and quails (salwā) is meat, so called because one is consoled (yatasallā) by it from all other condiments, and nothing else takes its place. For this reason, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The master of condiments is meat." Then He said after mentioning manna and quails: "Eat of the good things We have provided you"—so meat and sweetness are among the good things.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Eating good things begets contentment with God." These good things are completed by drinking cold water and pouring lukewarm water on the hands when washing. Al-Maʾmūn said: "Drinking water with ice purifies gratitude." Some men of letters said: "When you invite your brothers and feed them ḥusrumiyyah and būrāniyyah and give them cold water to drink, you have perfected hospitality." Some spent dirhams on hospitality, and a sage said: "We had no need of this—if your bread is good, your water cold, and your vinegar sharp, that suffices." Some said: "Sweetness after food is better than a multitude of dishes, and being at ease at the table is better than two extra dishes."

It is said that the angels attend the table when there is greens upon it—that too is recommended, for the adornment of greenness. In the report: "The table that was sent down upon the Children of Israel had upon it all kinds of greens except leeks." Upon it was a fish with vinegar at its head and salt at its tail, and seven loaves, upon each loaf an olive and a pomegranate seed. This, when combined, is good for harmony.

**Third:** That he present the most delicate of the dishes first, so that those who desire it may take their fill of it, and not eat much afterward. The habit of the luxurious is to present the coarse first, so that the appetite is rekindled by encountering the delicate afterward—and this contradicts the sunnah, for it is a stratagem for eating much. It was from the sunnah of the early generations to bring out all the dishes at once and arrange the bowls of food upon the table, so that each person eats what he desires. If one has only a single dish, let him mention it so they may take their fill of it and not wait for something better.

It is related of one of the men of magnanimity that he would write out a list of the dishes he had prepared and present it to the guests. Some of the elders said: "A single dish was presented to one of the elders in Syria, and I said: 'With us in Iraq, this is only presented last.' He said: 'And so with us in Syria.' And he had no other dish, so I was embarrassed before him." Another said: "We were a group at a hospitality, and roasted heads were presented to us—cooked and dried—and we did not eat, waiting for another dish or a roast lamb after it. Then he brought the basin and presented nothing else. We looked at one another, and one of the elders, who was humorous, said: 'God Almighty is able to create heads without bodies.' He said: 'And we spent that night hungry, seeking crumbs until dawn.'" For this reason, it is recommended to present everything at once, or to inform them of what one has.

**Fourth:** That he not hasten to remove the dishes before they have been able to take their fill, until they lift their hands from them. For perhaps among them is one for whom the remainder of that dish is more desirable than what has been brought, or he still has need to eat, and it would be spoiled for him by the hastening. This is part of being at ease at the table, which is said to be better than two dishes—it may mean cutting off haste, or it may mean spaciousness of place.

It is related of al-Sattūrī, who was a humorous Sufi: he attended the table of one of the worldly people, and a roast lamb was presented. The master of the table was miserly. When he saw the people tearing the lamb apart, each tearing a piece, his chest tightened and he said: "O boy, raise it to the children." So the lamb was raised into the house. Al-Sattūrī stood up running after the lamb. It was said to him: "Where are you going?" He said: "I will eat with the children." The man was ashamed and ordered the lamb returned.

From this art is that the master of the table should not lift his hand before the people, for they would be shy. Rather, he should be the last of them to eat. One of the generous men would inform the people of all the dishes and leave them to take their fill. When they neared completion, he would kneel on his knees, extend his hand to the food, eat, and say: "In the name of God—help me, may God bless you and upon you." The predecessors used to approve of this from him.

**Fifth:** That he present food in sufficient quantity. For less than sufficiency is a deficiency in magnanimity, and more than it is affectation and ostentation—especially if his soul does not permit them to eat it all. Unless he presents much while being pleased in soul if they took it all, intending to seek blessing in the leftover of their food, since in the hadith: "It is not accounted against him." Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, may God have mercy on him, presented much food upon his table, and Sufyān said to him: "O Abū Isḥāq, do you not fear this is extravagance?" Ibrāhīm said: "There is no extravagance in food." If this intention is not present, then abundance is affectation.

Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, said: "We were forbidden to respond to the invitation of one who boasts with his food." And a group of the Companions disliked eating the food of ostentation. From this was that no leftover food was ever raised from before the Messenger of God, peace be upon him—because they would only present what sufficed, and they would not eat to full satiety.

He should first set aside the portion of the household, so that their eyes do not long for the return of something from it—for perhaps it will not return, and their chests would tighten and their tongues would loosen against the guests. Then he would have fed the guests what is followed by the dislike of a people—and that is treachery against them.

As for what remains of the foods, it is not for the guests to take—this is what the Sufis call "the slip" (zallah)—unless the master of the food explicitly permits it from a content heart, or one knows it by the indication of his state and that he would rejoice in it. If one suspects his dislike, it should not be taken. And when one knows his contentment, one should observe justice and fairness with one's companions—no one should take except what is his share, or what his companion agrees to willingly, not out of shyness.

**Regarding the Departure**

It has three etiquettes:

**First:** That he go out with the guest to the door of the house—and this is a sunnah, and it is part of honoring the guest, which has been commanded. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Verily, from the sunnah of the guest is that he be escorted to the door of the house." Abū Qatādah said: "The delegation of the Negus arrived upon the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he stood up to serve them himself. His companions said: 'We will suffice you, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'No—they honored my companions, and I love to repay them.'" The completion of honor is cheerfulness of face and kind speech upon entry, upon exit, and at the table. It was said to al-Awzāʿī, may God be pleased with him: "What is the honor of the guest?" He said: "Cheerfulness of face and kind speech." Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād said: "I never entered upon ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā except that he told us a good hadith and fed us good food."

**Second:** That the guest depart with a contented soul, even if some shortcoming occurred in his regard—for that is from good character and humility. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Verily, a man attains by his good character the rank of the one who fasts and prays." One of the predecessors was invited by a messenger, but the messenger did not find him. When he heard, he attended—but they had dispersed, finished, and left. The master of the house came out to him and said: "The people have left." He said: "Is there any remainder?" He said: "No." He said: "A crumb, if any remains?" He said: "None remains." He said: "The pot—let me wipe it." He said: "It has been washed." So he departed praising God Almighty. He was questioned about that and said: "The man did well—he invited us with intention and refused us with intention." This is the meaning of humility and good character.

It is related that the teacher of Abū al-Qāsim al-Junayd was invited by a boy to his father's invitation four times, and the father refused him all four times—yet he returned each time to comfort the boy's heart by attending and the father's heart by departing. These are souls that have been tamed by humility before God Almighty and have found tranquility in monotheism, and they have come to witness in every refusal and acceptance a lesson between themselves and their Lord. They are not broken by what occurs from servants of humiliation, just as they are not delighted by what occurs from them of honor. Rather, they see all as from the One, the Subduer. For this reason, some said: "I do not respond to the invitation except because I am reminded by it of the food of Paradise"—that is, it is good food that bears away from us its toil, its burden, and its reckoning.

**Third:** That he not depart except with the contentment and permission of the master of the house, and he should observe his heart regarding the length of stay. When he descends as a guest, he should not exceed three days—for perhaps the host would become weary of him and need to expel him. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Hospitality is three days; whatever exceeds that is charity." Yes—if the master of the house insists upon him from a pure heart, then he may stay at that point. And it is recommended that one have a bed for the guest who descends. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "A bed for the man, a bed for the woman, a bed for the guest—and the fourth is for Satan."

chapters.title_en: A Chapter Gathering Scattered Virtuous and Lawful Etiquettes and Prohibitions
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| فصل يجمع آدابا ومناهي طيبة وشرعية متفرقة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of refined conduct, discipline of the self, and cultivated manners (adab) — both inward disposition and outward practice.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Adab as the trained habit of the soul toward virtuous action, aligning with prophetic guidance and divine command.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense (ḥaqīqah) of prescribed behavioral norms, not metaphorical embellishment.
- Root: ن-ه-ي (n-h-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Prohibition, forbidding, restraint from action — the counterpart to command (amr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sharʿī prohibitions (manāhī) as divine boundaries delineating lawful from unlawful in religious practice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of interdiction; no metaphorical extension here.
- Root: ش-ر-ع (sh-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Path to water; then legislated law (sharīʿah) as the clear way of divine guidance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sharʿī denotes what is revealed and codified by God through the Prophet — binding legal-moral norms.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage: "lawful" (sharʿī) as opposed to customary or rational alone.
- Root: ف-ص-ل (f-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, division, chapter — a distinct section demarcating a topic.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A structural unit in composition, here marking a new thematic segment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of partitioning; no figurative nuance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal sentence with fronted topic (mubtadaʾ) — "فصل يجمع..." (A chapter that gathers...) — where the predicate is an incomplete verbal clause (ṣilah) attached to the relative pronoun, establishing a definitive, self-contained heading.
chapters.translation: I say: This is a chapter that gathers together scattered virtuous etiquettes and lawful prohibitions, drawn from the prophetic way and the divine law, which the seeker of the Hereafter ought to observe in his daily conduct.

chapters.title_en: On the Etiquette of Eating: Diverse Reports and Their Harmonization
chapters.arabic_text:
الأول حكي عن إبراهيم النخعي أنه قال الأكل في السوق دناءة (3)
وأسنده إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وإسناده قريب
وقد نقل ضده عن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما أنه قال كنا نأكل عهد رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم PageV02P018
ونحن نمشي ونشرب ونحن قيام (1)
ورؤي بعض المشايخ من المتصوفة المعروفين يأكل في السوق فقيل له في ذلك
فقال ويحك أجوع في السوق وآكل في البيت فقيل تدخل المسجد قال أستحي أن أدخل
بيته للأكل فيه
ووجه الجمع أن الأكل في السوق تواضع وترك تكلف من بعض الناس فهو حسن وخرق
مروءة من بعضهم فهو مكروه وهو مختلف بعادات البلاد وأحوال الأشخاص فمن لا
يليق ذلك بسائر أعماله حمل ذلك على قلة المروءة وفرط الشره ويقدح ذلك في
الشهادة ومن يليق ذلك بجميع أحواله وأعمالهفي ترك التكلف كان ذلك منه
تواضعا
الثاني قال علي رضي الله عنه من ابتدأ غذاءه بالملح أذهب الله عنه سبعين
نوعا من البلاء ومن أكل في يوم سبع تمرات عجوة قتلت كل دابة في بطنه ومن
أكل كل يوم إحدى وعشرين زبيبة حمرا لم ير في جسده شيئا يكرهه واللحم ينبت
اللحم والثريد طعام العرب والبسقارجات تعظم البطن وترخي الأليتين ولحم
البقر داء ولبنها شفاء وسمنها دواء والشحم يخرج مثله من الداء ولن تستشفي
النفساء بشيء أفضل من الرطب والسمك يذيب الجسد وقراءة القرآن والسواك
يذهبان البلغم ومن أراد البقاء ولا بقاء فليباكر بالغداء وليكرر العشاء
وليلبس الحذاء ولن يتداوى الناس بشيء مثل السمن وليقل غشيان النساء وليخف
الرداء وهو الدين
الثالث قال الحجاج لبعض الأطباء صف لي صفة آخذ بها ولا أعدوها قال
لا تنكح من النساء إلا فتاة ولا تأكل من اللحم إلا فتيا ولا تأكل المطبوخ
حتى يتم نضجه ولا تشربن دواء إلا من علة ولا تأكل من الفاكهة إلا نضيجها
ولا تأكلن طعاما إلا أجدت مضغه وكل ما أحببت من الطعام ولا تشربن عليه فإذا
شربت فلا تأكلن عليه شيئا ولا تحبس الغائط والبول وإذا أكلت بالنهار فنم
وإذا أكلت بالليل فامش قبل أن تنام ولو مائة خطوة
وفي معناه قول العرب تغد تمد تعش تمش يعني تمدد كما قال الله تعال ثم ذهب
إلى أهله يتمطى أي يتمطط
ويقال إن حبس البول يفسد الجسد كما يفسد النهر ما حوله إذا سد مجراه
الرابع في الخبر قطع العروق مسقمة وترك العشاء مهرمة (2)
والعرب تقول ترك الغداء يذهب بشحم الكاذة يعني الآلية وقال بعض الحكماء
لابنه يا بني لا تخرج من منزلك حتى تأخذ حلمك أي تتغذى إذ به يبقى الحلم
ويزول الطيش  وهو أيضا أقل لشهوته لما يرى في السوق
وقال حكيم لسمين أرى عليك قطيفة من نسج أضراسك فمم هي قال من أكل لباب
البر وصغار المعز وأدهن بجام بنفسج وألبس الكتان
الخامس الحمية تضر بالصحيح كما يضر تركها بالمريض هكذا قيل
وقال بعضهم من احتمى فهو على يقين من المكروه وعلى شك من العوافي وهذا
حسن في حال الصحة ورأى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم صهيبا يأكل تمرا وإحدى
عينيه رمداء فقال
أتأكل التمر وأنت رمد فقال يا رسول الله إنما آكل بالشق الآخر (3)
يعني جانب السليمة فضحك رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
السادس أنه يستحب أن يحمل طعام إلى أهل الميت ولما جاء نعي جعفر بن أبي
طالب قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن آل جعفر شغلوا بميتهم عن صنع طعامهم
فاحملوا إليهم ما يأكلون (4)
فذلك سنة
وإذا قدم ذلك إلى الجمع حل الأكل منه ما يهيأ للنوائح والمعينات عليه
بالبكاء والجزع PageV02P019
فلا ينبغي أن يؤكل معهم
السابع لا ينبغي أن يحضر طعام ظالم فإن أكره فليقلل الأكل ولا يقصد
الطعام الأطيب رد بعض المزكين شهادة من حضر طعام سلطان فقال كنت مكرها فقال
رأيتك تقصد الأطيب وتكبر اللقمة وما كنت مكرها عليه وأجبر السلطان هذا
المزكي على الأكل فقال إما أن آكل وأخلي التزكية أو أزكي ولا آكل فلم يجدوا
بدا من تزكيته فتركوه
وحكي أن ذا النون المصري حبس ولم يأكل أياما في السجن فكانت له أخت في
الله فبعثت إليه طعاما من مغزلها على يد السجان فامتنع فلم يأكل فعاتبته
المرأة بعد ذلك فقال كان حلالا ولكن جاءني على طبق ظالم وأشار به إلى يد
السجان وهذا غاية الورع
الثامن حكي عن فتح الموصلي رحمه الله أنه دخل على بشر الحافي زائرا فأخرج
بشر درهما فدفعه لأحمد الجلاء خادمه وقال اشتر به طعاما جيدا وأدما طيبا
قال فاشتريت خبزا نظيفا وقلت لم يقل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لشيء
اللهم بارك لنا فيه  وزدنا منه (1)
سوى اللبن فاشتريت اللبن واشتريت تمرا جيدا فقدمت إليه فأكل وأخذ الباقي
فقال بشر أتدرون لم قلت اشتر طعاما طيبا لأن الطعام الطيب يستخرج خالص
الشكر أتدرون لم لم يقل لي كل لأنه ليس للضيف أن يقول لصاحب الدار كل
أتدرون لم حمل ما بقي لأنه إذا صح التوكل لم يضر الحمل
وحكى أبو علي الروذباري رحمه الله تعالى أنه اتخذ ضيافة فأوقد فيها ألف
سراج فقال له رجل قد أسرفت فقال له ادخل فكل ما أوقدته لغير الله فأطفئه
فدخل الرجل فلم يقدر على إطفاء واحد منها فانقطع
واشترى أبو علي الروذباري أحمالا من السكر وأمر الحلاويين حتى بنوا جدارا
من السكر عليه شرف ومحاريب على أعمدة منقوشة كلها من سكر ثم دعا الصوفية
حتى هدموها وانتهبوها
التاسع قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه الأكل على أربعة أنحاء: الأكل بإصبع من
المقت وبإصبعين من الكبر وبثلاث أصابع من السنة (2)
وبأربع وخمس من الشره وأربعة أشياء تقوي البدن: أكل اللحم وشم الطيب
وكثرة الغسل من غير جماع ولبس الكتان
وأربعة توهن البدن: كثرة الجماع وكثرة الهم وكثرة شرب الماء على الريق
وكثرة أكل الحموضة
وأربعة تقوي البصر: الجلوس تجاه القبلة والكحل عند النوم والنظر إلى
الخضرة وتنظيف الملبس
وأربعة توهن البصر: النظر إلى القذر والنظر إلى المصلوب والنظر إلى فرج
المرأة والقعود في استدبار القبلة
وأربعة تزيد في الجماع: أكل العصافير وأكل الإطريفل الأكبر وأكل الفستق
وأكل الجرجير
والنوم على أربعة أنحاء
فنوم على القفا وهو نوم الأنبياء عليهم السلام يتفكرون في خلق السموات
والأرض ونوم على اليمين وهو نوم العلماء والعباد ونوم على الشمال وهو نوم
الملوك ليهضمهم طعامهم ونوم على الوجه وهو نوم الشياطين
وأربعة تزيد في العقل: ترك الفضول من الكلام والسواك ومجالسة الصالحين
والعلماء
وأربعة هن من العبادة: لا يخطو خطوة إلا على وضوء وكثرة السجود ولزوم
المساجد وكثرة قراءة القرآن وقال أيضا عجبت لمن يدخل الحمام على الريق ثم
يؤخر الأكل بعد أن يخرج  كيف لا يموت وعجبت لمن احتجم ثم يبادر الأكل كيف لا
يموت وقال: لم أر شيئاانفع في الوباء من البنفسج يدهن به ويشرب
والله اعلم بالصواب PageV02P020

- Root: د-ن-ء (danāʾa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lowness, baseness, despicableness; a deficiency in moral worth or social dignity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A trait opposed to noble character (murūʾa); an act diminishing one's standing before God and men.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to physical lowness; metaphorical here for moral degradation in social custom.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ḥukm bi al-ʿādah (Anchoring a legal-moral judgment to customary practice, rendering it relative to time and place).
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [matter] — it is narrated of Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī that he said: "Eating in the marketplace is baseness." He attributed this to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and its chain of transmission is sound. Yet the opposite is transmitted of Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both), who said: "We used to eat during the era of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) while walking, and we would drink while standing." And a certain renowned shaykh of the Sufis was seen eating in the marketplace, and it was said to him regarding that. He replied: "Woe to you! I am hungry in the marketplace, and I eat at home?" It was said: "Do you then enter the mosque?" He said: "I am ashamed to enter His house for the purpose of eating therein."

The reconciliation of these [reports] is that eating in the marketplace is an act of humility and abandonment of affectation for some people, hence it is good; while for others it is a breach of manly virtue (murūʾa), hence it is disliked. It varies according to the customs of lands and the conditions of persons. For one to whom such behavior is incongruous with his other deeds, it is attributed to deficiency in virtue and excess of greed, and it impugns his legal testimony. But for one to whom it is congruous with all his states and deeds, in his abandonment of affectation, it is an act of humility from him.

The second [matter]: ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) said: "Whoever begins his meal with salt, God removes from him seventy kinds of affliction. Whoever eats seven ʿajwa dates in a day, it kills every creature in his belly. Whoever eats twenty-one red raisins each day, he will not see in his body anything he dislikes. Meat grows flesh, and tharīd is the food of the Arabs. Pastries enlarge the belly and slacken the buttocks. Beef is a disease, its milk a cure, and its butter a medicine. Fat expels disease of its like. A woman in postpartum will never be healed by anything better than fresh dates. Fish dissolves the body. Reciting the Qurʾān and using the toothstick remove phlegm. Whoever desires longevity — though there is no longevity — let him eat breakfast early, repeat the evening meal, wear sandals, and let people treat themselves with nothing like clarified butter. Let him reduce intercourse with women, and let him lighten his cloak — that is, his religion."

The third [matter]: Al-Ḥajjāj said to one of the physicians: "Describe for me a regimen which I may adopt and not exceed." He said: "Do not marry any woman except a virgin; do not eat any meat except that of a young animal; do not eat cooked food until its cooking is complete; do not drink any medicine except for an ailment; do not eat any fruit except its ripe one; do not eat any food unless you chew it thoroughly. Eat whatever food you desire, but do not drink over it. And if you drink, do not eat anything over it. Do not withhold stool or urine. If you eat by day, sleep; if you eat by night, walk before you sleep, even a hundred steps." In its meaning is the saying of the Arabs: "Eat breakfast, then stretch; eat supper, then walk" — meaning stretch out, as God Most High said: {«ثُمَّ ذَهَبَ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ يَتَمَطَّىٰ»} (Then he went to his family, strutting) — i.e., stretching himself. And it is said that withholding urine corrupts the body just as a river corrupts what surrounds it when its channel is dammed.

The fourth [matter]: In the report: "Cutting the veins is debilitating, and abandoning the evening meal is aging." The Arabs say: "Abandoning breakfast removes the fat of the kādha" — meaning the tail. And one of the sages said to his son: "O my son, do not leave your house until you have taken your ḥilm" — i.e., eaten breakfast, for by it reason (ḥilm) is preserved and rashness departs. It also lessens his appetite for what he sees in the marketplace. And a sage said to a fat man: "I see upon you a velvet cloak woven from your molars — from what is it?" He said: "From eating the core of wheat, young goats, anointing with violet oil, and wearing linen."

The fifth [matter]: "Strict dieting harms the healthy just as abandoning it harms the sick" — thus it is said. And one of them said: "Whoever diets is certain of discomfort and doubtful of well-being." This is good in a state of health. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) saw Ṣuhayb eating dates while one of his eyes was inflamed, and he said: "Do you eat dates while you are suffering from ophthalmia?" He replied: "O Messenger of God, I only eat with the other side" — meaning the healthy side. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) laughed.

The sixth [matter]: It is recommended to carry food to the family of the deceased. When the news of Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib's death arrived, he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The family of Jaʿfar have been occupied with their dead from preparing their own food, so carry to them what they may eat." That is thus a sunna. And if such food is presented to a gathering, it is permissible to eat from it. But what is prepared for the wailing women and those who assist them in weeping and lamentation — it should not be eaten with them.

The seventh [matter]: One should not attend the food of a tyrant. If compelled, let him eat little and not seek the choicest food. A certain examiner of witnesses (muzakkī) rejected the testimony of one who attended a sultan's meal. The man said: "I was compelled." He replied: "I saw you seeking the choicest morsels and enlarging your bites — you were not compelled in that." And the sultan forced this examiner to eat, whereupon he said: "Either I eat and abandon the examination, or I examine and do not eat." They found no alternative but to accept his examination, so they left him. And it is narrated that Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī was imprisoned and did not eat for days in the prison. He had a sister in God, who sent him food from her spinning work by the hand of the jailer. He refused and did not eat. The woman reproached him afterward, and he said: "It was lawful, but it came to me on the tray of a tyrant" — pointing to the jailer's hand. This is the utmost scrupulousness (waraʿ).

The eighth [matter]: It is narrated of Fatḥ al-Mawṣilī (may God have mercy on him) that he entered upon Bishr al-Ḥāfī as a visitor. Bishr brought out a dirham, gave it to his servant Aḥmad al-Jallāʾ, and said: "Buy with it good food and fine relish." He said: "So I bought clean bread, and I said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said of nothing, 'O God, bless us in it and increase us from it,' except milk. So I bought milk, and I bought good dates, and I presented it to him. He ate, and took the remainder." Then Bishr said: "Do you know why I said, 'Buy good food'? Because good food extracts pure gratitude. Do you know why he did not say to me, 'Eat'? Because it is not for the guest to say to the host, 'Eat.' Do you know why he carried what remained? Because when trust in God (tawakkul) is sound, carrying does no harm."

And Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī (may God Most High have mercy on him) narrated that he prepared a banquet and lit therein a thousand lamps. A man said to him: "You have been extravagant." He said to him: "Enter and extinguish whatever lamp you have lit for other than God." The man entered and was unable to extinguish a single one of them, so he was silenced. And Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī bought loads of sugar and ordered the confectioners until they built a wall of sugar with battlements and prayer niches upon carved columns, all of sugar. Then he invited the Sufis until they demolished it and plundered it.

The ninth [matter]: Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: "Eating is of four kinds: eating with one finger is from miserliness, with two fingers from pride, with three fingers from the sunna, and with four or five from greed. Four things strengthen the body: eating meat, smelling perfume, frequent washing without intercourse, and wearing linen. Four things weaken the body: frequent intercourse, excessive worry, drinking much water on an empty stomach, and eating much sour food. Four things strengthen the eyesight: sitting facing the qibla, applying kohl at sleep, looking at greenery, and cleaning one's garments. Four things weaken the eyesight: looking at filth, looking at a crucified person, looking at a woman's private parts, and sitting with one's back to the qibla. Four things increase sexual desire: eating sparrows, eating the greater itrifal, eating pistachios, and eating watercress. Sleep is of four kinds: sleeping on the back — the sleep of the prophets (peace be upon them), reflecting on the creation of the heavens and the earth; sleeping on the right side — the sleep of scholars and worshippers; sleeping on the left side — the sleep of kings, to digest their food; and sleeping on the face — the sleep of devils. Four things increase intellect: abandoning superfluous speech, using the toothstick, and sitting with the righteous and the scholars. Four things are acts of worship: not taking a step except in a state of ablution, frequent prostration, adhering to the mosques, and frequent recitation of the Qurʾān." He also said: "I marvel at one who enters the bathhouse on an empty stomach and then delays eating after exiting — how does he not die? And I marvel at one who is cupped and then hastens to eat — how does he not die?" And he said: "I have seen nothing more beneficial during an epidemic than violet — anointed with it and drunk."

And God knows best what is correct.

chapters.arabic_text:
### || كتاب آداب النكاح وهو الكتاب الثاني من ربع العادات من كتاب إحياء علوم الدين

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي لا تصادف سهام الأوهام في عجائب صنعه مجرى ولا ترجع
العقول عن أوائل بدائعها إلا والهة حيرى ولا تزال لطائف نعمه على العالمين
تترى فهي تتوالى عليهم اختيارا وقهرا
ومن بدائع ألطافه أن خلق من الماء بشرا فجعله نسبا وصهرا وسلط على الخلق
شهوة اضطرهم بها الحراثة جبرا واستبقى بهم نسلهم إقهارا وقسرا
ثم عظم أمر الأنساب وجعل لها قدرا فحرم بسببها السفاح وبالغ في تقبيحه
ردعا وزجرا وجعل اقتحامه جريمة فاحشة وأمر إمرا وندب إلى النكاح وحث عليه
استحبابا وأمرا فسبحان من كتب الموت على عباده فأذلهم به هدما وكسرا ثم بث
بذور النطف في أراضي الأرحام وأنشأ منها خلقا وجعله لكسر الموت جبرا تنبيها
على أن بحار المقادير فياضة على العالمين نفعا وضرا وخيرا وشرا وعسرا ويسرا
وطيا ونشرا والصلاة والسلام على محمد المبعوث بالإنذار والبشرى وعلى آله
وأصحابه صلاة لا يستطيع لها الحساب عدا ولا حصرا وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد فإن النكاح معين على الدين ومهين للشياطين وحصن دون عدو الله
حصين وسبب للتكثير الذي به مباهاة سيد المرسلين لسائر النبيين فما أحراه
بأن تتحرى أسبابه وتحفظ سننه وآدابه وتشرح مقاصده وآرابه وتفصل فصوله
وأبوابه
والقدر المهم من أحكامه ينكشف في ثلاثة أبواب
الباب الأول في الترغيب فيه وعنه
الباب الثاني في الآداب المرعية في العقد والعاقدين
الباب الثالث في آداب المعاشرة بعد العقد إلى الفراق

### ||| الباب الأول في الترغيب في النكاح والترغيب عنه

اعلم أن العلماء قد اختلفوا في فضل النكاح فبالغ بعضهم فيه حتى زعم أنه
أفضل من التخلي لعبادة الله واعترف آخرون بفضله ولكن قدموا عليه التخلي
لعبادة الله مهما لم تتق النفس إلى النكاح توقانا  يشوش الحال ويدعو إلى
الوقاع
وقال آخرون الأفضل تركه في زماننا هذا وقد كان له فضيلة من قبل إذ لم تكن
الأكساب محظورة وأخلاق النساء مذمومة
ولا ينكشف الحق فيه إلا بان نقدم أولا ما ورد من الأخبار والآثار في
الترغيب فيه والترغيب عنه ثم نشرح فوائد النكاح وغوائله حتى يتضح منها
فضيلة النكاح وتركه في حق كل من سلم من غوائله أو لم يسلم منه

### |||| ا الترغيب في النكاح
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ك-ح (n-k-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning: sexual union (al-waṭʾ) and the contractual bond of marriage; also used for the act of wedlock itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, nikāḥ signifies the lawful covenant (ʿaqd) that legitimizes intimacy, tied to divine command and prophetic sunnah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the marriage contract; metaphorical (majāz) for the act of coition when context implies it.
- Root: ش-ه-و-ة (sh-h-w-t) [Note: root ش repeated per text; anchor for شهوة]
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Appetite, desire, craving — specifically the innate drive toward sensual gratification.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, shahwah is the divinely implanted inclination that tests human discipline; its lawful channeling is marriage.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical appetite; metaphorical for any overpowering inclination of the soul.
- Root: ح-ر-ث (ḥ-r-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Plowing, tilling the earth; extended to the act of procreation (ḥarth) as sowing seed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Quranic metaphor for sexual intercourse leading to offspring (cf. {«نِسَاؤُكُمْ حَرْثٌ لَكُمْ»} — "Your women are a tilth for you").
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for agriculture; metaphorical for the generative act in marriage.
- Root: ن-س-ب (n-s-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lineage, kinship, relation by blood or marriage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Genealogical connection that God honored, making its preservation a legal and moral imperative.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for blood relation; metaphorical for social honor tied to ancestry.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Inshāʾ vs. Khabar (Declarative vs. Performative) — The opening doxology (ḥamdalah) is inshāʾ (performative praise), while the subsequent sentences shift to khabar (declarative statements) about God's acts, requiring careful tracking of nominal (jumlah ismiyyah) vs. verbal (jumlah fiʿliyyah) clauses for temporal and aspectual nuance.
chapters.translation:
In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, against whose wondrous handiwork the arrows of fancies find no course to run, nor do intellects turn back from the first of His marvels save as bewildered and perplexed. And the subtleties of His blessings upon the worlds cease not to follow in succession — they pour upon them by choice and by compulsion.

Among the marvels of His subtle kindness is that He created from water a human being, then made him kin by lineage and by marriage. And He imposed upon creation a lust (shahwah) by which He compelled them to the tilling (ḥarth) — by force — and preserved through them their progeny — by domination and constraint. Then He magnified the matter of lineages (ansāb) and assigned to them a station, forbidding thereby fornication (sifāḥ), and He went to extremes in rendering it vile — as a deterrent and a rebuke. He made its commission a heinous crime and a grave affair, and He summoned to marriage (nikāḥ), urging it upon them — as a recommendation and a command.

Glory be to Him who wrote death upon His servants, and thereby humbled them — as demolition and breaking. Then He scattered the seeds of sperm into the furrows of wombs, and from them He originated a creation, making it a mending for the break of death — as a notification that the seas of decrees overflow upon the worlds — with benefit and harm, good and evil, hardship and ease, folding and unfolding.

And prayers and peace be upon Muhammad, sent forth with warning and glad tidings, and upon his family and his companions — a prayer that reckoning cannot count nor enumerate — and abundant peace.

To proceed: Verily, marriage is an aid to religion, a humiliator of devils, a fortress against the enemy of God — a stronghold — and a cause for the multiplication by which the Master of the Messengers boasts over the rest of the prophets. How fitting it is that its causes be sought, its sunan and etiquettes be preserved, its aims and purposes be expounded, and its chapters and gates be detailed.

The essential portion of its rulings unfolds in three chapters:

- Chapter One: On encouragement toward it and discouragement from it.
- Chapter Two: On the etiquettes observed in the contract and regarding the two contracting parties.
- Chapter Three: On the etiquettes of cohabitation after the contract until separation.

### Chapter One: On Encouragement Toward Marriage and Discouragement From It

Know that the scholars have differed concerning the merit of marriage. Some went to extremes in it, even claiming that it is superior to devoting oneself exclusively to the worship of God. Others acknowledged its merit, but gave precedence to devoting oneself to God's worship over it — whenever the soul does not yearn toward marriage with a yearning that would disturb one's state and summon one to intercourse.

And others said: The better course is to abandon it in our own time, though it possessed merit in former times — when earnings were not forbidden and the morals of women were not blameworthy.

The truth in this matter is not disclosed except by first presenting what has come down of reports and traditions (āthār) concerning encouragement toward it and discouragement from it. Then we shall explain the benefits (fawāʾid) of marriage and its perils (ghawāʾil), so that therefrom the merit of marriage — and of abandoning it — becomes clear for each person who is safe from its perils or not safe from them.

### Sub-section: The Encouragement Toward Marriage
