When the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, returned from a journey, he said before entering Medina: "Do not come upon your women at night." Two men violated this and hurried ahead, and each saw in his home what he disliked. (1)

In the famous report: "The woman is like a rib — if you straighten it, you break it. So leave her, and enjoy her with her crookedness." (2) — This concerns refining her character.

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There is a jealousy that God, Mighty and Majestic, hates — the jealousy of a man over his family without cause for suspicion." (3) For that is from the ill suspicion we have been forbidden; indeed, {«some suspicion is sin»}.

ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Do not be excessively jealous over your family, lest you be accused of evil because of it."

As for jealousy in its proper place, it is indispensable and praiseworthy. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "God is jealous, and the believer is jealous. God's jealousy is that a believing man should commit what God has forbidden him." (4)

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Do you wonder at the jealousy of Saʿd? By God, I am more jealous than him, and God is more jealous than me." (5) For the sake of God's jealousy, He forbade indecencies, both open and hidden. And none loves an excuse more than God — for this He sent warners and bearers of good tidings. And none loves praise more than God — for this He promised Paradise.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "On the night of my night journey, I saw in Paradise a palace with a maiden in its courtyard. I asked: 'Whose palace is this?' It was said: 'ʿUmar's.' I wanted to look at her, but I remembered your jealousy, O ʿUmar." ʿUmar wept and said: "Shall I be jealous of you, O Messenger of God?" (6)

Al-Ḥasan used to say: "Do you leave your women to jostle with the coarse foreigners in the markets? May God curse the one who is not jealous."

He, upon him be peace and blessings, said: "There is a jealousy God loves, and a jealousy God hates; and there is a pride God loves, and a pride God hates. The jealousy God loves is jealousy in the case of suspicion; the jealousy God hates is jealousy without suspicion. The pride God loves is a man's pride in himself at the time of battle and at the moment of impact; the pride God hates is pride in falsehood." (7)

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I am indeed jealous, and no man who is not jealous is but inverted of heart." (8)

The way that suffices instead of jealousy is that men should not enter upon her, and she should not go out to the markets.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said to his daughter Fāṭimah, peace be upon her: "What is best for a woman?" She said: "That she see no man, and no man see her." He drew her to him and said: {«Offspring, one from another»} (9) — approving her words.

The Companions of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to block up the apertures and holes in walls so that women would not look out at men.

Muʿādh saw his wife looking out through an aperture and struck her. He also saw his wife having given a slave-boy an apple she had bitten from, and struck her.

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Make women unattractive, and they will stay in their chambers." He only said this because they do not desire to go out in shabby appearance.

He said: "Accustom your women to 'no'" — for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, had permitted women to attend the mosque. (1)

The correct view now is to prevent them, except for old women. Indeed, this was deemed correct even in the time of the Companions. ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "If the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had seen what women introduced after him, he would have prevented them from going out." (2)

When Ibn ʿUmar said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Do not prevent the female servants of God from the mosques of God,'" one of his sons said: "Yes, by God, we will prevent them." He struck him and was angry with him, saying: "You hear me saying: 'The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: Do not prevent them,' and you say: 'Yes, we will'?" (3) — He only dared to oppose because he knew the times had changed; and he was only angered because of his openly uttering opposition without showing an excuse.

Likewise, the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, had permitted them to go out on the two festivals specifically. (4) But they should not go out except with the consent of their husbands. Going out now is permissible for a chaste woman with her husband's consent, but staying home is safer. She should not go out except for a necessity — for going out for spectacles and non-essential matters detracts from murūʾah and may lead to corruption. If she does go out, she should lower her gaze from men. We do not say that a man's face is ʿawrah for her, as a woman's face is for him. Rather, it is like the face of a beardless youth for a man — it is forbidden to look only when there is fear of temptation. If there is no temptation, then it is not forbidden — for men have never ceased, throughout the passage of time, to have uncovered faces while women go out veiled. Had men's faces been ʿawrah for women, they would have been commanded to veil, or women would have been prevented from going out except for necessity.

**The Sixth: Moderation in Expenditure**

He should not be stingy toward them in spending, nor should he be extravagant, but rather moderate. God Most High said: {«Eat and drink, and do not be extravagant»} and said: {«Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor stretch it out fully»}. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The best of you is the best of you to his family." (5)

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "A dinar you spend in the path of God, a dinar you spend on a slave, a dinar you give in charity to a poor person, and a dinar you spend on your family — the greatest of them in reward is the one you spend on your family." (6)

It is said that ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, had four wives, and he would buy for each one, every four days, meat for a dirham. Al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him, said: "They were fertile in men, but barren in women and garments."

Ibn Sīrīn said: "It is recommended for a man to prepare for his family every Friday a sweet dish (fālūdhaj)." Sweetness, even if not essential, its total abandonment is stinginess in custom. He should also command her to give in charity the leftover food and what would spoil if left — this is the least degree of goodness. The woman may do this by virtue of the situation without explicit permission from the husband.

He should not reserve a fine food for himself and not feed his family from it — for this embitters hearts and distances one from consorting in kindness. If he is determined to do so, let him eat it secretly so his family does not know. Nor should he describe to them a food he does not intend to feed them. When he eats, he should seat all his dependents at his table. Sufyān, may God be pleased with him, said: "It has reached us that God and His angels send blessings upon a household that eats together."

The most important thing he must observe in expenditure is to feed her from lawful (ḥalāl) means, and not to enter into evil paths for her sake — for that would be an injury against her, not a care for her. We have already cited the reports concerning this when mentioning the harms of marriage.

**The Seventh: That the Married Man Learn the Knowledge of Menstruation and Its Rulings**

He must learn what is necessary to guard against, and teach his wife the rulings of prayer and what is made up from it during menstruation and what is not. For he has been commanded to protect her from the Fire by His saying: {«Guard yourselves and your families from a Fire»}. He must therefore teach her the creed of the People of the Sunnah, remove from her heart every innovation (bidʿah) if she hears one, frighten her with God if she is lax in matters of religion, and teach her what she needs of the rulings of menstruation and istiḥāḍah (prolonged bleeding). The knowledge of istiḥāḍah is lengthy. As for what women must necessarily be guided to concerning menstruation: the clarification of which prayers she must make up. For whenever her blood stops shortly before sunset by the measure of one rakʿah, she must make up the ẓuhr and ʿaṣr prayers; and if it stops before dawn by the measure of one rakʿah, she must make up the maghrib and ʿishāʾ prayers. This is the least of what women must observe.

If the man undertakes her instruction, she has no right to go out to ask the scholars. If the man's knowledge is deficient, but he deputizes for her in asking and informs her of the muftī's answer, she has no right to go out. If neither is the case, then she has the right — indeed the obligation — to go out and ask. The man disobeys God by preventing her. Whenever she has learned what is obligatory upon her, she has no right to go out to a remembrance gathering or to learn supererogatory knowledge except with his consent. Whenever a woman neglects a ruling of menstruation or istiḥāḍah and the man does not teach her, the man incurs sin along with her and shares in her sin.

**The Eighth: If He Has Multiple Wives, He Must Be Just Between Them**

He must not incline to one over another. If he goes on a journey and wishes to take one with him, he should cast lots among them (1) — for this is what the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, did. If he wrongs a woman by taking her night, he must make it up to her, for making it up is obligatory upon him. At that point he needs to know the rulings of division (qasm), and its mention is lengthy.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever has two wives and inclines to one over the other" — in another wording: "and does not treat them justly — will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him leaning." (2)

Justice is only required of him in provision and overnight stay. As for love and intercourse, these are not within his choice. God Most High said: {«You will never be able to be just between women, even if you strive»} — that is, justice in the heart's desire and the soul's inclination; and this is followed by disparity in intercourse.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was just between them in provision and in overnight stays, and would say: "O God, this is my effort in what I possess; I have no power over what You possess and I do not possess" (3) — meaning love.

ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, was the most beloved of his wives to him (4), and his other wives knew this. He was carried around during his illness every day and every night, spending the night with each of them, saying: "Where will I be tomorrow?" One of the women perceived this and said: "He is only asking about ʿĀʾishah's day." They said: "O Messenger of God, we permit you to be in ʿĀʾishah's house, for it is hard on you to be carried every night." He said: "Are you all satisfied with that?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then move me to ʿĀʾishah's house." (5)

Whenever one wife gives up her night to her co-wife and the husband consents, the right is established for her. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to divide between his wives. When Sawdah bint Zamʿah grew old, he intended to divorce her, so she gave her night to ʿĀʾishah and asked him to keep her in marriage so she would be gathered in the company of his wives. He left her, and would not divide for her, giving ʿĀʾishah two nights and his other wives one night each. (1)

But such was his justice and strength that whenever his soul yearned for one of the women outside her turn and he had intercourse with her, he would then circulate that day or night to all his other wives. Among this is what is narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, circulated among his wives in a single night. (2) And from Anas, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, circulated among nine wives in one forenoon. (3)

**The Ninth: Concerning Recalcitrance (Nushūz)**

Whenever a quarrel occurs between them and their affair does not mend — if it is from both sides, or from the man — the wife has no authority over her husband, and he has no power to reform her. Then two arbiters are indispensable: one from his family and one from hers, to look into the matter between them and set it right. {«If they desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony between them»}. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, once sent an arbiter to a quarreling couple, and he returned without having reconciled them. ʿUmar struck him with the whip and said: "God Most High says: {«If they desire reconciliation, God will bring harmony between them»}." The man returned, improved his intention, and dealt gently with them, and reconciled between them.

As for when the recalcitrance is from the woman alone — for men are qawwāmūn over women — he has the right to discipline her and compel her to obedience by force. Likewise, if she abandons prayer, he may compel her to pray by force. But he should proceed gradually in disciplining her: first, he should offer admonition, warning, and intimidation. If that does not succeed, he should turn his back to her in the bed, or separate from her in the bedding, and abandon her while remaining in the house with her — from one night to three nights.

If that does not succeed, he may strike her — a strike that is not severe (ghayr mubarriḥ): one that pains her but does not break a bone, does not draw blood, and does not strike the face, for that is prohibited.

It was said to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: "What is the right of the woman over the man?" He said: "Feed her when you eat, clothe her when you clothe yourself, do not disfigure the face, do not strike except with a non-severe strike, and do not abandon her except in the bed." (4)

He has the right to be angry with her and to abandon her in a matter of religion for ten, twenty, or up to a month. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, did this when he sent a gift to Zaynab and she returned it to him. The wife in whose house he was said: "She has humiliated you — she returned your gift!" (5) — meaning she degraded and belittled you. He said: "You are too insignificant before God to humiliate me." Then he was angry with all of them for a month, until he returned to them.

**The Tenth: The Proprieties of Intercourse**

It is recommended to begin with the name of God Most High, to recite Qul Huwa Allāhu Aḥad first, to say the takbīr and tahlīl, and to say: "In the name of God, the Most High, the Magnificent. O God, make it a goodly offspring, if You have decreed that it should come forth from my loins."

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If any of you, when he approaches his wife, says: 'O God, keep Satan away from me, and keep Satan away from what You have provided us' — then if a child is decreed between them, Satan will not harm him." (1)

When you approach ejaculation, say to yourself without moving your lips: "Praise be to God who created from water a human being, and made him lineage and marriage — and your Lord is All-Powerful."

Some of the people of ḥadīth used to say the takbīr so loudly that the people of the house could hear his voice, then turn away from the qiblah. One should not face the qiblah during intercourse, out of honor for the qiblah. He should cover himself and his wife with a garment. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to cover his head, lower his voice, and say to the woman: "Upon you is tranquility." (2)

In the report: "When one of you has intercourse with his wife, let them not strip completely like two donkeys" (3) — meaning two asses. He should first proceed with gentle speech and kissing. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Let none of you fall upon his wife like a beast falls. Let there be between them a messenger." It was said: "What is the messenger, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The kiss and the speech." (4)

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Three things are from incapacity in a man: that he meet someone he would love to know, and part from him before learning his name and lineage; the second, that someone honor him and he repays the honor poorly; the third, that a man approach his slave-girl or wife and have her before speaking to her, being intimate with her, and lying with her — so that he fulfills his need from her before she fulfills her need from him." (5)

It is disliked (makrūh) for him to have intercourse on three nights of the month: the first, the last, and the middle. It is said that Satan attends intercourse on these nights, and it is said that the devils have intercourse on them. Dislike of this has

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح ق ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of “right” (ḥaqq) as established, obligatory claim, or due; also truth and justice.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ḥaqq denotes what is firmly established by divine command or rational necessity—here, the marital obligations owed by the wife to the husband.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of “due” or “claim”; metaphorical (majāz) extension to “rights” as binding moral-legal duties.
- Root: ن ظ ر (n-ẓ-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To look, examine, consider, or reflect; also to care for or supervise.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In scholarly contexts, naẓar implies systematic deliberation and juridical examination of a subject.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal “gazing”; here used metaphorically as “consideration” or “investigation” of a legal topic.
- Root: ز و ج (z-w-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Pairing, coupling, or marriage; the spouse (zawj/zawjah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Marriage as a divinely ordained pairing, implying mutual rights and duties.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal “mate” or “pair”; in legal discourse, the husband (al-zawj) as the party with specified claims.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase “al-qism al-thānī min hādhā al-bāb” is a definite noun phrase followed by a genitive construction, where “min” introduces a partitive relation; the verb “al-naẓar” is a masdar (verbal noun) functioning as the predicate of an implied nominal sentence, indicating the chapter’s purpose.
chapters.translation: I say: The second division of this chapter is the consideration of the rights of the husband over her (the wife).

chapters.title_en: The Definitive Statement on the Rights of the Husband and the Etiquette of the Wife
chapters.arabic_text:
والقول الشافي فيه أن النكاح نوع رق فهي رقيقة له فعليها طاعة الزوج
مطلقا في كل ما طلب منها في نفسها مما لا معصية فيه وقد ورد في تعظيم حق
الزوج عليها أخبار كثيرة قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أيما امرأة PageV02P056
ماتت وزوجها عنها راض دخلت الجنة (1)
وكان رجل قد خرج إلى سفر وعهد إلى امرأته أن لا تنزل من العلو إلى السفل
وكان أبوها في الأسفل فمرض فأرسلت المرأة إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
تستأذن في النزول إلى أبيها فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أطيعي زوجك فمات
فاستأمرته فقال أطيعي زوجك فدفن أبوها فأرسل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
إليها يخبرها أن الله قد غفر لأبيها بطاعتها لزوجها (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا صلت المرأة خمسها وصامت شهرها وحفظت فرجها
وأطاعت زوجها دخلت جنة ربها (3)
وأضاف طاعة الزوج إلى مباني الإسلام وذكر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
النساء فقال حاملات والدات مرضعات رحيمات بأولادهن لولا ما يأتين إلى
أزواجهن دخل مصلياتهن الجنة (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم اطلعت في النار فإذا أكثر أهلها النساء فقلن لم
يا رسول الله  قال يكثرن اللعن ويكفرن العشير (5)
يعني الزوج المعاشر
وفي خبر آخر اطلعت في الجنة فإذا أقل أهلها النساء فقلت أين النساء قال
شغلهن الأحمران الذهب والزعفران (6)
يعني الحلي ومصبغات الثياب وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها أتت فتاة إلى النبي
صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالت يا رسول الله إني فتاة أخطب فأكره التزويج فما حق
الزوج على المرأة قال لو كان من فرقه إلى قدمه صديد فلحسته ما أدت شكره
قالت أفلا أتزوج قال بلى تزوجي فإنه خير (7)
قال ابن عباس أتت امرأة من خثعم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالت
إني امرأة أيم وأريد أن تزوج فما حق الزوج قال إن من حق الزوج على الزوجة
إذا أرادها فراودها عن نفسها وهي على ظهر بعير لا تمنعه ومن حقه أن لا تعطي
شيئا من بيته إلا بإذنه فإن فعلت ذلك كان الوزر عليها والأجر له ومن حقه أن
لا تصوم تطوعا إلا بإذنه فإن فعلت جاعت وعطشت ولم يتقبل منها وإن خرجت من
بيتها بغير إذنه لعنتها الملائكة حتى ترجع إلى بيته أو تتوب (8)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو أمرت أحدا أن يسجد لأحد لأمرت المرأة أن تسجد
لزوجها من عظم حقه عليها (9)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أقرب ما تكون المرأة من وجه ربها إذا كانت في
قعر بيتها وإن صلاتها في صحن دارها أفضل من صلاتها في المسجد وصلاتها في
بيتها أفضل من صلاتها في صحن دارها وصلاتها PageV02P057
في مخدعها أفضل من صلاتها في بيتها (1)
والمخدع بيت في بيت وذلك للستر ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم والمرأة
عورة فإذا خرجت استشرفها الشيطان (2)
وقال أيضا للمرأة عشر عورات فإذا تزوجت ستر الزوج عورة واحدة فإذا ماتت
ستر القبر العشر عورات (3)
فحقوق الزوج على الزوجة كثيرة وأهمها أمران أحدهما الصيانة والستر
والآخر ترك المطالبة بما وراء الحاجة والتعفف عن كسبه إذا كان حراما
وهكذا كانت عادة النساء في السلف كان الرجل إذا خرج من منزله تقول  له
امرأته أو ابنته إياك وكسب الحرام فإنا نصبر على الجوع والضر ولا نصبر على
النار
وهم رجل من السلف بالسفر فكره جيرانه سفره فقالوا لزوجته لم ترضين بسفره
ولم يدع لك نفقة فقالت زوجي منذ عرفته عرفته أكالا وما عرفته رزاقا ولي رب
رزاق يذهب الأكال ويبقى الرزاق
وخطبت رابعة بنت إسماعيل أحمد بن أبي الحواري فكره ذلك لما كان فيه من
العبادة وقال لها والله مالي همة في النساء لشغلي بحالي فقالت إني لأشغل
بحالي منك ومالي شهوة ولكن ورثت مالا جزيلا من زوجي فأردت أن تنفقه على
إخوانك وأعرف بك الصالحين فيكون لي طريقا إلى الله عز وجل فقال حتى استأذن
أستاذي فرجع إلى أبي سليمان الداراني قال وكان ينهاني عن التزويج ويقول ما
تزوج أحد من أصحابنا إلا تغير فلما سمع كلامها قال تزوج بها فإنها ولية لله
هذا كلام الصديقين قال فتزوجتها فكان في منزلنا كن من جص ففني من غسل أيدي
المستعجلين للخروج بعد الأكل فضلا عمن غسل بالأشنان
قال وتزوجت عليها ثلاث نسوة فكانت تطعمني الطيبات وتطيبني وتقول اذهب
بنشاطك وقوتك إلى أزواجك وكانت رابعة هذه تشبه في أهل الشام برابعة العدوية
بالبصرة
ومن الواجبات عليها أن لا تفرط في ماله بل تحفظه عليه
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يحل لها أن تطعم من بيته إلا بإذنه
إلا الرطب من الطعام الذي يخاف فساده فإن أطعمت عن رضاه كان لها مثل أجره
وإن أطعمت بغير إذنه كان له الأجر وعليها الوزر (4)
ومن حقها على الوالدين تعليمها حسن المعاشرة وآداب العشرة مع الزوج كما
روي أن أسماء بنت خارجة الفزاري قالت لأبنتها عند التزوج إنك خرجت من العش
الذي فيه درجت فصرت إلى فراش لم تعرفيه وقرين لم تألفيه فكوني له أرضا يكن
لك سماء وكوني له مهادا يكن لك عمادا وكوني له أمة يكن لك عبدا لا تلحفي به
فيقلاك ولا تباعدي عنه فينساك إن دنا منك فاقربي منه وإن  نأى فابعدي عنه
واحفظي أنفه وسمعه وعينه فلا يشمن منك إلا طيبا ولا يسمع إلا حسنا ولا ينظر
إلا جميلا
وقال رجل لزوجته
خذي العفو مني تستديمي مودتي ... ولا تنطقي في سورتي حين أغضب
PageV02P058
ولا تنقريني نقرك الدف مرة ... فإنك لا تدرين كيف المغيب
ولا تكثري الشكوى فتذهب بالهوى ... ويأباك قلبي والقلوب تقلب
فإني رأيت الحب في القلب والأذى ... إذا اجتمعا لم يلبث الحب يذهب
فالقول الجامع في آداب المرأة من غير تطويل أن تكون قاعدة في قعر بيتها
لازمة لمغزلها لا يكثر صعودها واطلاعها قليلة الكلام لجيرانها لا تدخل
عليهم إلا في حال يوجب الدخول تحفظ بعلها في غيبته وتطلب مسرته في جميع
أمورها ولا تخونه في نفسها وماله ولا تخرج من بيتها إلا بإذنه فإن خرجت
بإذنه فمختفية في هيئة رئة تطلب المواضع الخالية دون الشوارع والأسواق
محترزة من أن يسمع غريب صوتها أو يعرفها بشخصها لا تتعرف إلى صديق بعلها في
حاجاتها بل تتنكر على من تظن أنه يعرفها أو تعرفه همها صلاح شأنها وتدبير
بيتها مقبلة على صلاتها وصيامها وإذا استأذن صديق لبعلها على الباب وليس
البعل حاضرا لم تستفهم ولم تعاوده في الكلام غيرة على نفسها وبعلها وتكون
قانعة من زوجها بما رزق الله وتقدم حقه على حق نفسها وحق سائر أقاربها
منتظفة في نفسها مستعدة في الأحوال كلها للتمتع بها إن شاء مشفقة على
أولادها حافظة للستر عليهم قصيرة اللسان عن سب الأولاد ومراجعة الزوج
وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم أنا وامرأة سفعاء الخدين كهاتين في الجنة
امرأة آمت من زوجها وحبست نفسها على بناتها حتى ثابوا أو ماتوا (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم حرم الله على كل آدمي الجنة يدخلها قبلي غير أني
أنظر عن يميني فإذا امرأة تبادرني إلى باب الجنة فأقول ما لهذه تبادرني
فيقال لي يا محمد هذه امرأة كانت حسناء جميلة وكان عندها يتامى لها فصبرت
عليهن حتى بلغ أمرهن الذي بلغ فشكر الله لها ذلك (2)
ومن آدابها  أن لا تتفاخر على الزوج بجمالها ولا تزدري زوجها لقبحه فقد
روي أن الأصمعي قال دخلت البادية فإذا أنا بامرأة من أحسن الناس وجها تحت
رجل من أقبح الناس وجها فقلت لها يا هذه أترضين لنفسك أن تكوني تحت مثله
فقالت يا هذا اسكت فقد أسأت في قولك لعله أحسن فيما بينه وبين خالقه فجعلني
ثوابه أو لعلي أسأت فيما بيني وبين خالقي فجعله عقوبتي أفلا أرضى بما رضي
الله لي فأسكتتني
وقال الأصمعي رأيت في البادية امرأة عليها قميص أحمر وهي مختضبة وبيدها
سبحة فقلت ما أبعد هذا من هذا فقالت
ولله مني جانب لا أضيعه ... وللهو مني والبطالة جانب
فعلمت أنها امرأة صالحة لها زوج تتزين له
ومن آداب المرأة ملازمة الصلاح والانقباض في غيبة زوجها والرجوع إلى
اللعب والانبساط وأسباب اللذة في حضور زوجها ولا ينبغي أن تؤذي زوجها بحال
روي عن معاذ ابن جبل قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تؤذي امرأة
زوجها في الدنيا إلا قالت زوجته من الحور العين لا تؤذيه قاتلك الله فإنما
هو عندك دخيل يوشك أن يفارقك إلينا (3)
ومما يجب عليها من حقوق النكاح إذا مات عنها زوجها أن لا تحد عليه أكثر
من أربعة أشهر وعشر وتتجنب الطيب والزينة في هذه المدة قالت زينب بنت أبي
سلمة دخلت على أم حبيبة زوج النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حين توفى أبوها أبو
سفيان بن حرب PageV02P059
فدعت بطيب فيه صفرة خلوق أو غيره فدهنت به جارية ثم مست بعارضيها ثم قالت
والله ما لي بالطيب من حاجة غير إني سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
يقول لا يحل لامرأة تؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر أن تحد على ميت أكثر من ثلاثة
أيام إلا على زوج أربعة أشهر وعشرا (1)
ويلزمها لزوم مسكن النكاح إلى آخر العدة وليس لها الانتقال إلى أهلها ولا
الخروج إلا لضرورة ومن آدابها أن تقوم بكل خدمة في الدار تقدر عليها فقد
روي عن أسماء بنت  أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله عنهما أنها قالت تزوجني الزبير
وما له في الأرض من مال ولا مملوك ولا شيء غير فرسه وناضحه فكنت أعلف فرسه
وأكفيه مؤنته وأسوسه وأدق النوى لناضحه وأعلفه وأستقي الماء وأخرز غربه
وأعجن وكنت أنقل النوى على رأسي من ثلثي فرسخ حتى أرسل إلى أبو بكر بجارية
فكفتني سياسة الفرس فكأنما أعتقني (2)
ولقيني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوما ومعه أصحابه والنوى على رأسي
فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أخ أخ لينيخ ناقته ويحملني خلفه فاستحييت أن أسير
مع الرجال وذكرت الزبير وغيرته وكان أغير الناس فعرف رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم إني قد استحييت فجئت الزبير فحكيت له ما جرى فقال والله لحملك
النوى على رأسك أشد علي من ركوبك معه
تم كتاب آداب النكاح بحمد الله ومنه وصلى الله على كل عبد مصطفى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ق-ق (r-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Servitude, softness, and subjugation; the state of being owned (riqq) as opposed to freedom (ḥurriyyah)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theologically, marriage entails a form of lawful servitude (riqq) of the wife to the husband, mirroring the soul's servitude to God
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense (ḥaqīqah) of legal subordination, not metaphorical exaggeration
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Universal Quantifier (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — "in whatever she is asked" (fī kulli mā ṭalaba) establishes an unrestricted general ruling, qualified only by the exception clause "wherein there is no disobedience" (mimmā lā maʿṣiyata fīhi)
chapters.translation:
I say: The definitive statement on this matter is that marriage is a type of servitude (riqq), for she is his bondswoman. Thus, obedience to the husband is incumbent upon her absolutely, in everything he requests of her concerning her own person, provided it involves no disobedience [to God]. Numerous reports have come down regarding the greatness of the husband's right over her. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: «أيما امرأة ماتت وزوجها عنها راض دخلت الجنة» — "Any woman who dies while her husband is pleased with her shall enter Paradise."

There was a man who had set out on a journey and had enjoined upon his wife not to descend from the upper floor to the lower. Her father was in the lower part, and he fell ill. The woman sent word to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) seeking permission to descend to her father. He said: "Obey your husband." Then her father died, and she again sought his instruction. He said: "Obey your husband." So her father was buried [without her attending]. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) then sent word to her, informing her that Allah had forgiven her father on account of her obedience to her husband.

He (peace be upon him) also said: «إذا صلت المرأة خمسها وصامت شهرها وحفظت فرجها وأطاعت زوجها دخلت جنة ربها» — "When a woman prays her five [daily prayers], fasts her month [of Ramadan], guards her chastity, and obeys her husband, she shall enter the Paradise of her Lord."

He also attached obedience to the husband to the very foundations of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) mentioned women and said: "They are bearers of children, givers of birth, sucklers of infants, and merciful to their offspring. Were it not for what they do to their husbands, the women who pray would enter Paradise."

He (peace be upon him) also said: "I looked into the Fire and found that most of its inhabitants were women." They asked: "Why, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied: "They curse excessively and are ungrateful to their companions (al-ʿashīr)" — meaning the husband with whom one dwells in intimacy.

In another report: "I looked into Paradise and found that the fewest of its inhabitants were women." I asked: "Where are the women?" He said: "The two red things have preoccupied them: gold and saffron" — meaning jewelry and dyed garments.

ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: A young woman came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am a young woman who is sought in marriage, but I dislike marrying. What is the right of the husband over the wife?" He said: "Were there to flow from the crown of his head to his feet pus and matter, and she were to lick it clean, she would still not have rendered his due." She said: "Then shall I not marry?" He said: "Yes, marry, for it is good."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: A woman from Khathʿam came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and said: "I am a woman without a husband, and I wish to marry. What is the right of the husband?" He said: "Among the rights of the husband over the wife is that if he desires her and solicits her person while she is upon the back of a camel, she must not refuse him. And among his rights is that she give nothing from his house except with his permission — for if she does so, the burden of sin falls upon her and the reward is his. And among his rights is that she not observe a supererogatory fast except with his permission — for if she does, she will hunger and thirst, and it will not be accepted from her. And if she leaves her house without his permission, the angels curse her until she returns to his house or repents."

He (peace be upon him) also said: «لو أمرت أحدا أن يسجد لأحد لأمرت المرأة أن تسجد لزوجها من عظم حقه عليها» — "Were I to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would have commanded the woman to prostrate to her husband, due to the greatness of his right over her."

He (peace be upon him) also said: "The closest a woman comes to the Face of her Lord is when she is in the depths of her house. Her prayer in the courtyard of her house is better than her prayer in the mosque; her prayer in her room is better than her prayer in her courtyard; and her prayer in her innermost chamber (makhdaʿ) is better than her prayer in her room." The makhdaʿ is a room within a room — this is for the sake of concealment. For this reason, he (peace be upon him) said: «والمرأة عورة فإذا خرجت استشرفها الشيطان» — "The woman is an ʿawrah (something to be concealed); when she goes out, Satan gazes at her with longing."

He also said: "The woman has ten coverings (ʿawrāt). When she marries, the husband veils one covering; when she dies, the grave veils all ten."

Thus, the rights of the husband over the wife are many, and the most important of them are two: first, her protection and concealment; and second, her refraining from demanding beyond what is needed, and her abstaining from his earnings if they are unlawful. Such was the custom of women among the Salaf (the righteous predecessors). When a man left his home, his wife or daughter would say to him: "Beware of unlawful earning, for we can bear hunger and hardship, but we cannot bear the Fire."

A man among the Salaf intended to travel, and his neighbors disapproved of his journey. They said to his wife: "Why do you consent to his travel when he has left you no provision?" She replied: "Ever since I have known my husband, I have known him as an eater (akkāl); I have never known him as a provider (razzāq). I have a Lord who is the Provider (Razzāq) — the eater passes away, but the Provider remains."

Rābiʿah bint Ismāʿīl sought marriage with Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī, but he disliked this due to his devotion to worship. He said to her: "By Allah, I have no concern for women, for I am occupied with my own state." She said: "I am even more occupied with my own state than you, and I have no desire [for marriage]. But I have inherited abundant wealth from my husband, and I wish to spend it upon your brethren [in faith]. I know you to be among the righteous, so that this may become for me a path to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." He said: "Let me seek permission from my master." He returned to Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī — and he had been forbidding him from marriage, saying: "None of our companions has married except that he changed." But when he heard her words, he said: "Marry her, for she is a friend (waliyyah) of Allah. This is the speech of the ṣiddīqīn (the utterly veracious)." He said: "So I married her, and in our house there was a basin of plaster (kaṣṣ) that was exhausted from the washing of hands of those who hastened to leave after eating — let alone those who washed with ashes (ushnān)."

He said: "I married three other women besides her, and she would feed me delicious foods and perfume me, saying: 'Go with your vigor and strength to your [other] wives.'" This Rābiʿah was likened in Syria to Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah of Basra.

Among the obligatory duties upon her is that she not be negligent with his wealth, but rather preserve it for him. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: «لا يحل لها أن تطعم من بيته إلا بإذنه إلا الرطب من الطعام الذي يخاف فساده فإن أطعمت عن رضاه كان لها مثل أجره وإن أطعمت بغير إذنه كان له الأجر وعليها الوزر» — "It is not lawful for her to feed [others] from his house except with his permission, save fresh food that is feared to spoil. If she feeds with his approval, she receives the like of his reward; if she feeds without his permission, he gets the reward and she bears the sin."

Among her rights upon her parents is that they teach her good companionship and the etiquettes of cohabitation with the husband. It is related that Asmāʾ bint Khārijah al-Fazāriyyah said to her daughter upon her marriage: "You have left the nest in which you grew up and have come to a bed you do not know and a companion you have not befriended. Be for him a earth, and he will be for you a sky; be for him a resting-place (mahād), and he will be for you a pillar (ʿimād); be for him a bondmaid, and he will be for you a slave. Do not cling to him so that he tires of you, nor distance yourself from him so that he forgets you. If he draws near to you, draw near to him; if he withdraws, withdraw from him. Guard his nose, his ear, and his eye — let him smell from you only fragrance, hear from you only goodness, and see from you only beauty."

A man said to his wife:
"Take the forgiving from me, and you will prolong my affection — and do not speak in my fury when I am angered.
Do not peck at me as one pecks a drum once — for you do not know how the unseen will turn out.
Do not multiply complaints, for they drive away love — and my heart will recoil from you, for hearts are fickle.
For I have seen that when love and harm are gathered together in the heart, love does not long remain — it departs."

The comprehensive statement on the etiquette of the woman, without prolongation, is that she remain seated in the depths of her house, devoted to her spindle, not frequently ascending or looking out, speaking little to her neighbors, not entering upon them except in a situation that necessitates entry. She preserves her husband in his absence, seeks his pleasure in all her affairs, and does not betray him in her own person or his wealth. She does not leave her house except with his permission; and if she goes out with his permission, she does so concealed in humble attire, seeking empty places rather than thoroughfares and markets, guarding against any stranger hearing her voice or recognizing her person. She does not make herself known to her husband's friend for her needs; rather, she disguises herself from anyone she suspects might know her or whom she knows. Her concern is the rectification of her own state and the management of her house, devoting herself to her prayers and fasts. If a friend of her husband seeks permission at the door while the husband is absent, she does not inquire [who it is] nor does she engage him in conversation — out of protective jealousy (ghayrah) for herself and her husband. She is content with whatever Allah has provided through her husband, and she gives his right precedence over her own right and the rights of all her relatives. She is clean in her person, ready in all circumstances for his enjoyment should he so wish, compassionate toward her children, guarding their concealment, and restrained in tongue from cursing her children or answering back her husband.

He (peace be upon him) said: «أنا وامرأة سفعاء الخدين كهاتين في الجنة» — "I and a woman with dark cheeks shall be like these two in Paradise" — a woman who was widowed from her husband and confined herself to her daughters until they grew up or died.

He (peace be upon him) also said: "Allah has forbidden every human from entering Paradise before me. But I looked to my right and behold, a woman was hastening before me to the gate of Paradise. I said: 'What is this one, hastening before me?' It was said to me: 'O Muhammad, this is a woman who was beautiful and comely, and she had orphans under her care. She bore them patiently until their affairs reached what they reached, and Allah thanked her for that.'"

Among her etiquettes is that she not boast over her husband of her beauty, nor despise her husband for his ugliness. It is related that al-Aṣmaʿī said: "I entered the desert and behold, there was a woman among the most beautiful of people, married to a man among the ugliest of people. I said to her: 'O woman, do you consent for yourself to be under the likes of him?' She said: 'O man, be silent, for you have spoken ill. Perhaps he has been excellent in what is between him and his Creator, so He made me his reward; or perhaps I have been remiss in what is between me and my Creator, so He made him my punishment. Shall I not then be content with what Allah has chosen for me?' And she silenced me."

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "I saw in the desert a woman wearing a red shirt, with dyed hands, and in her hand a prayer-beads (subḥah). I said: 'How far is this from that!' She said:
'For Allah, from me, is a portion I do not neglect — and for play and idleness, from me, is a portion.'
So I knew she was a righteous woman who had a husband for whom she adorned herself."

Among the etiquettes of the woman is adhering to righteousness and restraint (inqibāḍ) in the absence of her husband, and returning to playfulness, expansiveness, and the means of delight in his presence. She should not harm her husband in any way. It is related from Muʿādh ibn Jabal that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: «لا تؤذي امرأة زوجها في الدنيا إلا قالت زوجته من الحور العين لا تؤذيه قاتلك الله فإنما هو عندك دخيل يوشك أن يفارقك إلينا» — "No woman harms her husband in this world except that his wife from the ḥūr al-ʿīn (the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise) says: 'Do not harm him — may Allah destroy you! For he is only a guest with you; soon he will part from you and come to us.'"

Among the obligations upon her from the rights of marriage, if her husband dies, is that she not observe mourning (ʿiddah) for him more than four months and ten days, and that she avoid perfume and adornment during this period. Zaynab bint Abī Salamah said: "I entered upon Umm Ḥabībah, the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him), when her father Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb had died. She called for perfume containing a yellow dye (khalūq) or something else, and applied it to a slave-girl, then wiped it on her own cheeks. Then she said: 'By Allah, I have no need of perfume, except that I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) say: «لا يحل لامرأة تؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر أن تحد على ميت أكثر من ثلاثة أيام إلا على زوج أربعة أشهر وعشرا» — "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn for a dead person more than three days, except for a husband — four months and ten days."'"

She is obliged to remain in the marital home until the end of the ʿiddah (waiting period), and she may not move to her family nor go out except out of necessity.

Among her etiquettes is that she undertake every service in the house that she is able to perform. It is related from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with them both) that she said: "Al-Zubayr married me, and he had no wealth on earth, no slave, and nothing except his horse and his water-camel (nāḍiḥ). I used to feed his horse, suffice him its upkeep, tend it, pound date-stones for his water-camel, feed it, draw water, stitch its leather bucket (gharb), and knead dough. I used to carry the date-stones on my head from a distance of two-thirds of a parasang (farasakh), until Abū Bakr sent me a slave-girl who sufficed me the tending of the horse — and it was as if she had freed me."

She said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) met me one day while his companions were with him, and the date-stones were upon my head. He said: 'Akh, akh' — commanding his she-camel to kneel so he could mount me behind him. But I felt ashamed to walk with the men, and I remembered al-Zubayr and his jealousy — and he was the most jealous of men. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) perceived that I was ashamed, so he went on. I came to al-Zubayr and told him what had happened. He said: 'By Allah, your carrying the date-stones upon your head is harder upon me than your riding with him.'"

The Book of the Etiquettes of Marriage is completed, by the praise of Allah and His grace. And may Allah send blessings upon every chosen servant.

chapters.arabic_text:
### || كتاب آداب الكسب والمعاش وهو الكتاب الثالث من ربع العادات من كتاب إحياء علوم الدين

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
نحمد الله حمد موحد انمحق في توحيده ما سوى الواحد الحق وتلاشر
ونمجده تمجيد من يصرح بأن كل شيء ما سوى الله باطل ولا يتحاشى
وأن كل من في السموات والأرض لن يخلقوا ذبابا ولو اجتمعوا له ولا فراشا
ونشكره إذ رفع السماء لعباده سقفا مبنيا ومهد الأرض بساطا لهم وفراشا
وكور الليل على النهار فجعل الليل لباسا والنهار معاشا
لينتشروا في إبتغاء فضله وينتعشوا به عن ضراعة الحاجات انتعاشا ونصلي على
رسوله الذي يصدر المؤمنون عن حوضه رواء بعد ورودهم عليه عطاشا
وعلى آله وأصحابه الذين لم يدعوا في نصرة دينه تشمرا وانكماشا
وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد فإن رب الأرباب ومسبب الأسباب
جعل الآخرة دار الثواب والعقاب والدنيا دار التمحل والاضطراب
والتشمر والاكتساب
وليس التشمر في الدنيا مقصورا على المعاد دون المعاش بل المعاش ذريعة إلى
المعاد ومعين عليه فالدنيا مزرعة الآخرة ومدرجة إليها
والناس ثلاثة رجل شغله معاشه عن معاده فهو من الفائزين والأقرب إلى
الاعتدال  هو الثالث الذي شغله معاشه لمعاده فهو من المفتصدين
ولن ينال رتبة PageV02P060
الاقتصاد من لم يلازم في طلب المعيشة منهج السداد ولن ينتهض من طلب
الدنيا وسيلة إلى الآخرة وذريعة ما لم يتأدب في طلبها بآداب الشريعة وها
نحن نورد آداب التجارات والصناعات وضروب الاكتسابات وسننها ونشرحها في خمسة
أبواب
الباب الأول فضل الكسب والحث عليه
الباب الثاني في علم صحيح البيع والشراء والمعاملات
الباب الثالث في بيان العدل في المعاملة
الباب الرابع في بيان الإحسان فيها
الباب الخامس في شفقة التاجر على نفسه ودينه

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-س-ب (kasaba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To acquire, earn, or gain something through effort and seeking; implies deliberate pursuit of provision.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, kasb denotes the human acquisition of acts as a locus of divine power — here, the lawful striving for worldly sustenance as a means to the Hereafter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical earning; metaphorical (majāz) — earning as a spiritual vehicle, i.e., the "trade" of this world for the next.
- Root: م-ع-ا-ش (maʿāsh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That by which one lives; livelihood, subsistence; from ʿaysh (life).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Contrasted with maʿād (the return, the Hereafter); the worldly life as a transient state of living, not an end in itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — daily bread; metaphorical — the entire worldly pursuit as a "field" (mazraʿah) for the afterlife.
- Root: ق-ص-د (qaṣada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To intend, aim, or pursue a middle course; moderation between extremes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iqtisād — the praiseworthy middle path in religion and worldly affairs, balancing maʿāsh and maʿād.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — straight path; metaphorical — the balanced believer who uses the world for the sake of the Hereafter.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — The opening employs parallel verbal clauses (ḥamd, tamjīd, shukr, ṣalāh) with rhythmic cadence (sajʿ), each governed by an implicit verb, requiring the translator to preserve the periodic structure and the authorial first-person voice.
chapters.translation:
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

We praise Allah with the praise of one who affirms His Oneness, annihilating in His unity everything other than the One, the True — and does not shrink [from this declaration]. And we glorify Him with the glorification of one who declares plainly that everything other than Allah is falsehood, and does not hesitate [to say so] — and that all who are in the heavens and the earth could never create a single fly, even if they gathered together for it, nor a single gnat. And we thank Him, for He raised the heaven as a canopy built over His servants, and spread the earth as a carpet for them and a resting place, and folded the night over the day, making the night a garment and the day a means of livelihood (maʿāsh) — so that they may disperse in seeking His bounty, and be revived thereby from the abasement of needs, a true revival. And we send blessings upon His Messenger — from whose Basin the believers drink their fill after arriving upon it thirsty — and upon his Family and Companions, who spared no effort and no zeal in supporting His religion. And abundant peace.

To proceed: The Lord of lords and the Causer of causes has made the Hereafter the abode of reward and punishment, and this world the abode of striving and turmoil, of exertion and acquisition (iktisāb). And exertion in this world is not confined to the Hereafter alone, to the exclusion of livelihood — rather, livelihood is a means (dharīʿah) to the Hereafter and an aid to it. For this world is the tillage of the Hereafter and the path leading to it.

And mankind are three [types]: a man whose livelihood occupies him to the neglect of his Hereafter — he is of the losers. And a man whose Hereafter occupies him to the neglect of his livelihood — he is of the negligent. And the closest to moderation is the third: the one whose livelihood occupies him for the sake of his Hereafter — he is of the moderate (muqtaṣidūn). And none shall attain the rank of moderation (iqtisād) who does not adhere, in seeking his living, to the path of rectitude (sadād). And none shall rise up from seeking this world as a means to the Hereafter and a vehicle to it, unless he is disciplined in that seeking by the etiquettes of the Sacred Law. And now we shall present the etiquettes of trades, crafts, and the various modes of earning, along with their normative practices (sunan), and explain them in five chapters:

Chapter One: On the merit of earning and the exhortation to it.
Chapter Two: On the correct knowledge of buying, selling, and transactions.
Chapter Three: On the exposition of justice in transactions.
Chapter Four: On the exposition of excellence (iḥsān) therein.
Chapter Five: On the merchant's compassion for his own soul and his religion.

### ||| Chapter One: On the Merit of Earning and the Exhortation to It

chapters.title_en: The Virtue of Earning and Seeking Lawful Sustenance (Faḍīlat al-Kasb wa Ṭalab al-Ḥalāl)
chapters.arabic_text:
أما من الكتاب فقوله تعالى وجعلنا النهار معاشا فذكره في معرض الامتنان
وقال تعالى وجعلنا لكم فيها معايش قليلا ما تشكرون فجعلها ربك نعمة وطلب
الشكر عليها
وقال تعالى ليس عليكم جناح أن تبتغوا فضلا من ربكم وقال تعالى وآخرون
يضربون في الأرض يبتغون من فضل الله وقال تعالى فانتشروا في الأرض وابتغوا
من فضل الله وأما الأخبار فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من الذنوب ذنوب لا
يكفرها إلا الهم في طلب المعيشة (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم التاجر الصدوق يحشر يوم القيامة مع الصديقين
والشهداء (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من طلب الدنيا حلالا وتعففا عن المسئلة وسعيا
على عياله وتعطفا على جاره لقي الله ووجهه كالقمر ليلة البدر (3)
وكان صلى الله عليه وسلم جالسا مع أصحابه ذات يوم فنظروا إلى شاب ذي جلد
وقوة وقد بكر يسعى فقالوا ويح هذا لو كان شبابه وجلده في سبيل الله فقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تقولوا هذا فإنه إن كان يسعى على نفسه ليكفها عن
المسئلة ويغنيها عن الناس فهو في سبيل الله وإن كان يسعى على أبوين ضعيفين
أو ذرية ضعاف ليغنيهم ويكفيهم فهو في سبيل الله وإن كان يسعى تفاخرا
وتكاثرا فهو في سبيل الشيطان (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله يحب العبد يتخذ المهنة ليستغني بها عن
الناس ويبغض العبد يتعلم العلم يتخذه  مهنة (5)
وفي الخبر إن الله تعالى يحب المؤمن المحترف (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أحل ما أكل الرجل من كسبه وكل بيع مبرور (7)
PageV02P061
وفي خبر آخر أحل ما أكل العبد كسب يد الصانع إذا نصح (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم عليكم بالتجارة فإن فيها تسعة أعشار الرزق (2)
وروي أن عيسى عليه السلام رأى رجلا فقال ما تصنع قال أتعبد قال من يعولك
قال أخي
قال أخوك أعبد منك
وقال نبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم إني لا أعلم شيئا يقربكم من الجنة ويبعدكم
من النار إلا أمرتكم به وإني لا أعلم شيئا يبعدكم من الجنة ويقربكم من
النار إلا نهيتكم عنه وإن الروح الأمين نفث في روعى إن نفسا لن تموت حتى
تستوفي رزقها وإن أبطأ عنها فاتقوا الله وأجملوا في الطلب أمر بالإجمال في
الطلب ولم يقل اتركوا الطلب ثم قال في آخره ولا يحملنكم استبطاء شيء من
الرزق على أن تطلبوه بمعصية الله تعالى فإن الله لا ينال ما عنده بمعصيته
(3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم الأسواق موائد الله تعالى فمن أتاها أصاب منها
(4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لأن يأخذ أحدكم حبله فيحتطب على ظهره خير من أن
يأتي رجلا أعطاه الله من فضله فيسأله له أعطاه أو منعه (5)
وقال من فتح على نفسه بابا من السؤال فتح الله عليه سبعين بابا من الفقر
(6)
وأما الآثار فقد قال لقمان الحكيم لابنه يا بني استغن بالكسب الحلال عن
الفقر فإنه ما افتقر أحد قط إلا أصابه ثلاث خصال رقة في دينه وضعف في عقله
وذهاب مروءته وأعظم من هذه الثلاث استخفاف الناس به
وقال عمر رضي الله عنه لا يقعد أحدكم عن طلب الرزق يقول اللهم ارزقني فقد
علمتم أن السماء لا تمطر ذهبا ولا فضة
وكان زيد بن مسلمة يغرس في أرضه فقال له عمر رضي الله عنه أصبت استغن عن
الناس يكن أصون لدينك وأكرم لك عليهم كما قال صاحبكم أحيحة
فلن أزال على الزوراء أغمرها ... إن  الكريم على الإخوان ذو المال
وقال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه إني لأكره أن أرى الرجل فارغا لا في أمر
دنياه ولا في أمر آخرته
وسئل إبراهيم عن التاجر الصدوق أهو أحب إليك أم المتفرغ للعبادة قال
التاجر الصدوق أحب إلي لأنه في جهاد يأتيه الشيطان من طريق المكيال
والميزان ومن قبل الأخذ والعطاء فيجاهده وخالفه الحسن البصري في هذا
وقال عمر رضي الله عنه ما من موضع يأتيني الموت فيه أحب إلي من موطن
أتسوق فيه لأهلي أبيع وأشتري
وقال الهيثم ربما يبلغني عن الرجل يقع في فأذكر استغنائي عنه فيهون ذلك
علي
وقال أيوب كسب فيه شيء أحب إلي من سؤال الناس
وجاءت ريح عاصفة في البحر فقال أهل السفينة لإبراهيم بن أدهم رحمه الله
وكان معهم فيها أما ترى هذه الشدة فقال ما هذه الشدة وإنما الشدة الحاجة
إلى الناس
وقال أيوب قال لي أبو قلابة الزم السوق فإن الغنى من العافية يعني الغنى
عن الناس
وقيل لأحمد ما تقول فيمن جلس في بيته PageV02P062
أو مسجده وقال لا أعمل شيئا حتى يأتيني رزقي فقال أحمد هذا رجل جهل العلم
أما سمع قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله جعل رزقي تحت ظل رمحي (1)
وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم حين ذكر الطير فقال تغذو خماصا وتروح بطانا (2)
فذكر أنها تغدو في طلب الرزق وكان أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
يتجرون في البر والبحر ويعملون في نخيلهم والقدوة بهم
وقال أبو قلابة لرجل لأن أراك تطلب معاشك أحب إلي من أن أراك في زاوية
المسجد
وروي أن الأوزاعي لقي إبراهيم بن أدهم رحمهم الله وعلى عنقه حزمة حطب
فقال له يا أبا إسحق إلى متى هذا إخوانك يكفونك فقال دعني عن هذا يا أبا
عمرو فإنه بلغني أنه من وقف موقف مذلة في طلب الحلال وجبت له الجنة
وقال أبو سليمان الداراني ليس العبادة عندنا أن تصف قدميك وغيرك يقوت لك
ولكن ابدأ برغيفيك فأحرزهما ثم  تعبد
وقال معاذ بن جبل رضي الله عنه ينادي مناد يوم القيامة أين بغضاء الله في
أرضه فيقوم سؤال المساجد فهذه مذمة الشرع للسؤال والاتكال على كفاية
الأغيار
ومن ليس له مال موروث فلا ينجيه من ذلك إلا الكسب والتجارة
فإن قلت فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما أوحي إلي أن أجمع المال وكن من
التاجرين ولكن أوحي إلي أن سبح بحمد ربك وكن من الساجدين واعبد ربك حتى
يأتيك اليقين (3)
وقيل لسلمان الفارسي أوصنا فقال من استطاع منكم أن يموت حاجا أو غازيا أو
عامرا لمسجد ربه فليفعل ولا يموتن تاجرا ولا خائنا فالجواب أن وجه الجمع
بين هذه الأخبار تفصيل الأحوال فنقول لسنا نقول التجارة أفضل مطلقا من كل
شيء ولكن التجارة إما أن تطلب بها الكفاية أو الثروة أو الزيادة على
الكفاية فإن طلب منها الزيادة على الكفاية لاستكثار المال وادخاره لا ليصرف
إلى الخيرات والصدقات فهي مذمومة لأنه إقبال على الدنيا التي حبها رأس كل
خطيئة فإن كان مع ذلك ظالما خائنا فهو ظلم وفسق وهذا ما أراده سلمان بقوله
لا تمت تاجرا ولا خائنا وأراد بالتاجر طالب الزيادة فأما إذا طلب بها
الكفاية لنفسه وأولاده وكان يقدر على كفايتهم بالسؤال فالتجارة تعففا عن
السؤال أفضل وإن كان لا يحتاج إلى السؤال وكان يعطى عن غير سؤال فالكسب
أفضل لأنه إنما يعطى لأنه سائل بلسان حاله ومناد بين الناس بفقره فالتعفف
والتستر أوفى من البطالة بل من الاشتغال بالعبادات البدنية وترك الكسب أفضل
لأربعة عابد بالعبادات البدنية أو رجل له سير بالباطن وعمل بالقلب في علوم
الأحوال والمكاشفات أو عالم مشتغل بتربية علم الظاهر مما ينتفع الناس به في
دينهم كالمفتي والمفسر والمحدث وأمثالهم أو رجل مشتغل بمصالح المسلمين وقد
تكفل بأمورهم كالسلطان والقاضي والشاهد فهؤلاء إذا كانوا يكفون من الأموال
المرصدة للمصالح أو الأوقاف المسبلة على الفقراء أو العلماء
فإقبالهم على ما هم فيه أفضل من اشتغالهم بالكسب ولهذا أوحي إلى رسول
الله صلى  الله عليه وسلم إن سبح بحمد ربك وكن من الساجدين ولم يوح إليه أن
كن من التاجرين لأنه كان جامعا لهذه المعاني الأربعة إلى زيادات لا يحيط
بها الوصف ولهذا أشار الصحابة على أبي بكر رضي الله عنهم بترك التجارة لما
ولي الخلافة إذ كان ذلك يشغله عن المصالح وكان يأخذ كفايته من مال المصالح
ورأى ذلك أولى ثم لما توفي أوصى برده إلى بيت المال ولكنه رآه في الابتداء
أولى ولهؤلاء الأربعة حالتان أخريان
أحداهما PageV02P063
أن تكون كفايتهم عند ترك المكسب من أيدي الناس وما يتصدق به عليهم من
زكاة أو صدقة من غير حاجة إلى سؤال فترك الكسب والاشتغال بما هم فيه أولى
إذ فيه إعانة الناس على الخيرات وقبول منهم لما هو حق عليهم وأفضل لهم
الحالة الثانية الحاجة إلى السؤال وهذا في محل النظر والتشديدات التي
رويناها في السؤال وذمه تدل ظاهرا على أن التعفف عن السؤال أولى وإطلاق
القول فيه من غير ملاحظة الأحوال والأشخاص عسير بل هو موكول إلى اجتهاد
العبد ونظره لنفسه بأن يقابل ما يلقي في السؤال من المذلة وهتك المروءة
والحاجة إلى التثقيل والإلحاح بما يحصل من اشتغاله بالعلم والعمل من
الفائدة له ولغيره فرب شخص تكثر فائدة الخلق وفائدته في اشتغاله بالعلم أو
العمل ويهون عليه بأدنى تعريض في السؤال تحصيل الكفاية وربما يكون بالعكس
وربما يتقابل المطلوب والمحذور فينبغي أن يستفتي المريد فيه قلبه وإن أفتاه
المفتون فإن الفتاوى لا تحيط بتفاصيل الصور ودقائق الأحوال ولقد كان في
السلف من له ثلثمائة وستون صديقا ينزل على كل واحد منهم ليلة ومنهم من له
ثلاثون وكانوا يشتغلون بالعبادة لعملهم بأن المتكلفين بهم يتقلدون منة من
قبولهم لمبراتهم فكان قبولهم لمبراتهم خيرا مضافا لهم إلى عباداتهم فينبغي
أن يدقق النظر في هذه الأمور فإن أجر الآخذ كأجر المعطي مهما كان الآخذ
يستعين به على الدين والمعطي يعطيه عن طيب قلب
ومن اطلع على هذه المعاني أمكنه أن يتعرف حال نفسه ويستوضح  من قلبه ما هو
الأفضل له بالإضافة إلى حاله ووقته فهذه فضيلة الكسب وليكن العقد الذي به
الاكتساب جامعا لأربعة أمور الصحة والعدل والإحسان والشفقة على الدين
ونحن نعقد في كل واحد بابا ونبتدئ بذكر أسباب الصحة في الباب الثاني
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-س-ب (K-S-B)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Acquisition, earning, and gathering of provision through one's own effort and labor
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The deliberate pursuit of sustenance (rizq) as an act of worship when coupled with lawful intent and self-sufficiency (taʿaffuf)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "gaining" (kasb) versus metaphorical sense of "earning" as a form of jihād against the soul and Satan
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text employs repeated conditional clauses (in kāna... fa-huwa fī sabīl Allāh) to distinguish between lawful and blameworthy earning based on intention (niyya), requiring precise parsing of the protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the truth of the matter and grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with: The merit of earning and seeking lawful sustenance is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports of the Salaf (may Allah be pleased with them all).

As for the Book, Allah Most High says: {«وَجَعَلْنَا النَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا»} ("And We have made the day a means of livelihood") — and He mentioned it in the context of bestowing favor.

And He Most High says: {«وَجَعَلْنَا لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَعَايِشَ قَلِيلًا مَا تَشْكُرُونَ»} ("And We have made for you therein means of livelihood — little do you give thanks") — so your Lord made it a blessing and demanded gratitude for it.

And He Most High says: {«لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ أَنْ تَبْتَغُوا فَضْلًا مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ»} ("There is no sin upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord").

And He Most High says: {«وَآخَرُونَ يَضْرِبُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَبْتَغُونَ مِنْ فَضْلِ اللَّهِ»} ("And others striking through the land seeking of Allah's bounty").

And He Most High says: {«فَانْتَشِرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَابْتَغُوا مِنْ فَضْلِ اللَّهِ»} ("Then spread through the land and seek of Allah's bounty").

As for the reports (akhbār), he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Among sins are sins that nothing expiates except striving (hamm) in seeking a livelihood." (1)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The truthful merchant will be resurrected on the Day of Judgment with the truthful (ṣiddīqīn) and the martyrs." (2)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever seeks the world lawfully, refraining from asking (taʿaffufan ʿan al-masʾala), striving for his family, and showing compassion to his neighbor, will meet Allah with his face like the full moon on the night of Badr." (3)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) was sitting with his companions one day when they saw a young man of vigor and strength who had gone out early seeking provision. They said: "Woe to this one — if only his youth and vigor were in the path of Allah." The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Do not say this. For if he is striving for himself to keep himself from asking and to make himself independent of people, then he is in the path of Allah. And if he is striving for two weak parents or weak offspring to enrich them and suffice them, then he is in the path of Allah. But if he is striving for pride and boasting (tafākhuran wa takāthuran), then he is in the path of Satan." (4)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Indeed Allah loves the servant who takes up a craft (mihna) to make himself independent of people thereby, and He hates the servant who learns knowledge and takes it as a craft." (5)

And in the report: "Indeed Allah Most High loves the believing skilled worker (al-muʾmin al-muḥtarif)." (6)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The most lawful of what a man eats is from his own earning, and every blessed sale (bayʿ mabrūr)." (7)

In another report: "The most lawful of what a servant eats is the earning of his own hand when he is sincere (naṣaḥa)." (1)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Upon you is trade (tijāra), for in it are nine-tenths of provision." (2)

And it is narrated that Jesus (peace be upon him) saw a man and said: "What are you doing?" He said: "I am worshipping." He said: "Who provides for you?" He said: "My brother." He said: "Your brother is more of a worshipper than you."

And our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I do not know of anything that brings you closer to Paradise and distances you from the Fire except that I have commanded you with it, and I do not know of anything that distances you from Paradise and brings you closer to the Fire except that I have forbidden you from it. And indeed the Trustworthy Spirit (al-Rūḥ al-Amīn) breathed into my heart (nafatha fī rawʿī) that no soul will die until it completes its provision (yastawfī rizqahā), even if it is delayed. So fear Allah and seek provision with excellence (ajmilū fī al-ṭalab)" — he commanded excellence in seeking, and did not say "abandon seeking." Then he said at its end: "And do not let the delay of anything from provision lead you to seek it through disobedience to Allah, for what is with Allah is not attained through His disobedience." (3)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The markets are the tables (mawāʾid) of Allah Most High — whoever comes to them obtains from them." (4)

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "That one of you takes his rope and gathers firewood on his back is better than coming to a man whom Allah has given of His bounty and asking him — whether he gives him or withholds from him." (5)

And he said: "Whoever opens for himself a door of asking (suʾāl), Allah opens for him seventy doors of poverty." (6)

As for the reports of the Salaf (āthār), Luqmān the Wise said to his son: "O my son, enrich yourself through lawful earning against poverty, for no one has ever become poor except that three traits afflicted him: weakness in his religion, weakness in his intellect, and loss of his manliness (murūʾa) — and greater than these three is people's contempt for him."

And ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Let none of you sit back from seeking provision saying, 'O Allah, provide for me' — for you know that the sky does not rain gold or silver."

And Zayd ibn Musallama was planting in his land, and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "You have done well. Be independent of people, for that is more protective of your religion and more honorable for you among them" — as your companion Uḥayḥa said:

"I will not cease to tend al-Zawrāʾ, irrigating it... for the generous one among brothers is he who possesses wealth."

And Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I dislike to see a man idle — neither in the matter of his worldly life nor in the matter of his afterlife."

And Ibrāhīm was asked: "The truthful merchant — is he more beloved to you, or the one devoted to worship (al-mutafarrigh lil-ʿibāda)?" He said: "The truthful merchant is more beloved to me, for he is in a jihād — Satan comes to him from the path of the measure and the scale, and from the path of taking and giving, and he fights him." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī differed with him on this.

And ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "There is no place where death comes to me that is more beloved to me than a place where I am trading in the market for my family — selling and buying."

And al-Haytham said: "Sometimes news reaches me about a man falling into [need], and I remember my independence from him, and that makes it easy for me."

And Ayyūb said: "Earning in which there is something [of hardship] is more beloved to me than asking people."

And a violent wind came at sea, and the people of the ship said to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham (may Allah have mercy on him) — and he was among them: "Do you not see this severity?" He said: "This is not the severity — the severity is the need for people."

And Ayyūb said: "Abū Qilāba said to me: 'Cling to the market, for wealth (al-ghinā) is from well-being (al-ʿāfiya)' — meaning independence from people."

And Aḥmad was asked: "What do you say about a man who sits in his house or his mosque and says, 'I will not do anything until my provision comes to me'?" Aḥmad said: "This is a man who is ignorant of knowledge. Has he not heard the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): 'Indeed Allah made my provision under the shade of my spear'?" (1)

And his saying (peace and blessings be upon him) when he mentioned the bird: "It goes out hungry (khamāṣan) and returns full (biṭānan)" (2) — he mentioned that it goes out seeking provision.

And the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) used to trade on land and sea, and work in their palm groves — and they are the example (al-qudwa).

And Abū Qilāba said to a man: "That I see you seeking your livelihood is more beloved to me than that I see you in the corner of the mosque."

And it is narrated that al-Awzāʿī met Ibrāhīm ibn Adham (may Allah have mercy on them) with a bundle of firewood on his neck, and said to him: "O Abā Isḥāq, until when is this? Your brothers suffice you." He said: "Leave me from this, O Abā ʿAmr — for it has reached me that whoever stands in a position of humility (mawqif madhalla) in seeking the lawful, Paradise becomes obligatory for him."

And Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "Worship with us is not that you stand on your feet while others provide for you. Rather, begin with your two loaves — secure them, then worship."

And Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "A caller will call on the Day of Judgment: 'Where are the enemies of Allah in His earth?' Then the beggars of the mosques (suʾāl al-masājid) will stand up." This is the censure of the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ) for begging and relying on the sufficiency of others.

And whoever has no inherited wealth — nothing saves him from this except earning and trade.

If you say: "But he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'It was not revealed to me to amass wealth and be among the merchants. Rather, it was revealed to me: {«فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُنْ مِنَ السَّاجِدِينَ وَاعْبُدْ رَبَّكَ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَكَ الْيَقِينُ»} ("So glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate, and worship your Lord until certainty comes to you") (3). And it was said to Salmān al-Fārsī: 'Advise us.' He said: 'Whoever among you can die as a pilgrim, or a warrior, or one who populates the mosque of his Lord, let him do so — and let him not die as a merchant or a traitor.'"

The answer is that the way of reconciling these reports is the differentiation of circumstances (tafṣīl al-aḥwāl). We say: We do not claim that trade is absolutely better than everything. Rather, trade is either sought for sufficiency (kifāya), or for wealth (tharwa), or for surplus beyond sufficiency. If surplus beyond sufficiency is sought from it for amassing wealth and hoarding it — not to expend it on good deeds and charities — then it is blameworthy, because it is a turning toward the world whose love is the head of every sin. If, along with that, one is oppressive and treacherous, then it is oppression and transgression. This is what Salmān meant by his saying "do not die as a merchant or a traitor" — he meant by "merchant" the seeker of surplus.

As for when one seeks sufficiency for himself and his children through it, and he is able to suffice them through asking — then trade as a means of refraining from asking (taʿaffufan ʿan al-suʾāl) is better. And if he has no need to ask, and he is given without asking, then earning is better — because he is only given because he is a beggar by the tongue of his state (lisān ḥālih) and a caller among people through his poverty. So refraining (al-taʿaffuf) and concealment (al-tasattur) are more fitting than idleness — nay, more fitting than occupying oneself with bodily acts of worship.

Rather, abandoning earning is better for four [types of] people: a devotee occupied with bodily acts of worship; or a man who has a journey within (sayr bi-al-bāṭin) and work of the heart in the sciences of spiritual states (ʿulūm al-aḥwāl) and unveilings (mukāshafāt); or a scholar occupied with cultivating the outward knowledge (ʿilm al-ẓāhir) by which people benefit in their religion — like the muftī, the exegete (mufassir), the hadith narrator (muḥaddith), and their likes; or a man occupied with the welfare of the Muslims (maṣāliḥ al-muslimīn) who has undertaken their affairs — like the sultan, the judge, and the witness. These, when they are sufficed from the funds designated for public welfare (al-amwāl al-marṣada lil-maṣāliḥ) or the endowments (al-awqāf) made available to the poor or the scholars — then their devotion to what they are engaged in is better than their occupation with earning.

For this reason it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him): {«سَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُنْ مِنَ السَّاجِدِينَ»} ("Glorify the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate") — and it was not revealed to him "be among the merchants," because he combined these four meanings with additional excellences that description cannot encompass.

For this reason the companions advised Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) to abandon trade when he assumed the caliphate, since it would distract him from the public welfare — and he took his sufficiency from the public treasury (māl al-maṣāliḥ) and saw that as more appropriate. Then when he died, he bequeathed its return to the treasury (bayt al-māl) — but he saw it as more appropriate at the beginning.

And for these four [types], there are two further states:

The first: that their sufficiency, upon abandoning earning, comes from the hands of people — from what is given to them as charity (zakāt or ṣadaqa) without any need to ask. Then abandoning earning and devoting oneself to what one is engaged in is more appropriate, for in it is assisting people toward good deeds and accepting from them what is a right upon them and better for them.

The second state: the need to ask. This is a place of deliberation (maḥall al-naẓar). The severities we have narrated concerning asking and its censure indicate outwardly that refraining from asking is more appropriate. But making an absolute pronouncement in this matter without observing the circumstances and the persons is difficult — rather, it is entrusted to the servant's ijtihād and his own consideration, by weighing what is cast upon him in asking — of humiliation (madhalla), the tearing of manliness (hatk al-murūʾa), and the need for burdening others and importunity (ilḥāḥ) — against what accrues from his occupation with knowledge and action of benefit to himself and others. For there may be a person whose benefit to creation and to himself is great in his occupation with knowledge or action, and the attainment of sufficiency becomes easy for him with the slightest hint (adnā taʿrīḍ) in asking. And there may be one for whom it is the opposite. And sometimes the sought and the feared may be balanced — then the seeker (al-murīd) should consult his heart (yastaftī qalbahu), even if the muftīs give him a ruling — for the legal rulings (fatāwā) do not encompass the details of forms and the subtleties of circumstances.

Indeed, among the Salaf there was one who had three hundred and sixty friends, staying with each one of them one night [per year], and among them was one who had thirty — and they occupied themselves with worship because they knew that those who took charge of them were assuming the burden of favor (minna) by accepting their gifts (mabarrāt). So their acceptance of their gifts was a good added to their acts of worship. One should therefore scrutinize these matters deeply — for the reward of the taker is like the reward of the giver, whenever the taker uses it to assist himself in religion and the giver gives it with a willing heart.

Whoever is acquainted with these meanings is able to recognize his own state and seek clarity from his heart as to what is best for him relative to his circumstance and his time.

This, then, is the virtue of earning (faḍīlat al-kasb). And let the contract (al-ʿaqd) by which one earns combine four matters: soundness (al-ṣiḥḥa), justice (al-ʿadl), excellence (al-iḥsān), and compassion for religion (al-shafaqa ʿalā al-dīn). We shall devote a chapter to each one, and we begin with the mention of the causes of soundness in the second chapter.

chapters.title_en: The Second Book on the Science of Acquisition through Sale, Usury, Salam, Hire, Partnership, and Commenda — and the Exposition of the Legal Conditions for the Validity of These Transactions, Which Are the Pivot of Livelihoods in the Sacred Law
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| الباب الثاني في علم الكسب بطريق البيع والربا والسلم والإجارة والقراض والشركة وبيان شروط الشرع في صحة هذه التصرفات التي هي مدار المكاسب في الشرع

اعلم أن تحصيل علم هذا الباب واجب على كل مسلم مكتسب لأن طلب العلم فريضة
على كل مسلم وإنما هو طلب العلم المحتاج إليه والمكتسب يحتاج إلى علم الكسب
ومهما حصل علم هذا الباب وقف على مفسدات المعاملة فيتقيها وما شذ عنه من
الفروع المشكلة فيقع على سبب إشكالها فيتوقف فيها إلى أن يسأل فإنه إذا لم
يعلم أسباب الفساد بعلم جملي فلا يدري متى يجب عليه التوقف والسؤال ولو قال
لا أقدم العلم ولكني أصبر إلى أن تقع لي الواقعة فعندها أتعلم وأستفتي
فيقال له وبم تعلم وقوع الواقعة مهما لم تعلم جمل مفسدات العقود فإنه يستمر
في التصرفات ويظنها صحيحة مباحة فلا بد له من هذا القدر من علم التجارة
ليتميز له المباح عن المحظور وموضع الإشكال عن موضع الوضوح ولذلك روي عن
عمر رضي الله عنه أنه كان يطوف السوق ويضرب بعض التجار بالدرة ويقول لا
يبيع في سوقنا إلا من يفقه وإلا أكل الربا شاء أم أبى وعلم العقود كثير
ولكن هذه العقود الستة لا تنفك المكاسب عنها وهي البيع والربا والسلم
والإجارة والشركة والقراض فلنشرح شروطها

### |||| العقد الأول البيع
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-س-ب (kasaba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To seek, earn, or acquire; the act of drawing benefit through one's own effort and toil.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acquisition (kash) denotes the deliberate pursuit of provision (rizq) through lawful means, aligning the servant's action with divine decree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical garnering; metaphorical (majāz) for the moral earning of merit or sin.
- Root: ف-ق-ه (faqiha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deep comprehension; penetrating understanding beyond surface knowledge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Juridical discernment (fiqh) — the grasp of legal rulings with their evidences, distinguishing lawful from unlawful.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for intellectual insight; extended to religious jurisprudence as the operative sense here.
- Root: ع-ق-د (ʿaqada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tie, bind, or knot; a firm covenant or compact.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual bond (ʿaqd) — the mutual obligation that legally binds two parties in exchange.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical tying; metaphorical for the binding of wills in a transaction.
- Root: ف-س-د (fasada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To spoil, corrupt, or become unsound; the opposite of integrity (ṣalāḥ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Invalidity (fasād) in legal terms — a defect in the contract's conditions that nullifies its religious efficacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical decay; metaphorical for legal corruption of a transaction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Protasis (al-sharṭ al-muqaddar) — In "مهما حصل علم هذا الباب وقف على مفسدات المعاملة" the conditional particle (مهما) governs a compound apodosis, requiring the reader to parse the sequence as cause-and-effect within a single periodic structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the acquisition of the knowledge of this book is obligatory upon every Muslim who earns his livelihood, for the pursuit of knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim — and this refers to the knowledge that is needed. The earner stands in need of the science of acquisition, and whenever he obtains the knowledge of this book, he comes to know the invalidating causes of transactions and thus guards against them. As for the problematic subsidiary cases that escape him, he will fall upon the reason for their difficulty and will pause therein until he asks. For if he does not know the causes of invalidity through a summary science, he will not know when it becomes incumbent upon him to pause and to question. And if he were to say, "I will not advance to knowledge, but I will wait until an incident befalls me — then at that time I will learn and seek a legal opinion," it is said to him: By what means will you know of the occurrence of the incident when you have not learned the summary of the invalidating causes of contracts? For he continues in his transactions, supposing them to be sound and permissible. Thus, this measure of the science of commerce is indispensable for him, so that the permissible may be distinguished for him from the prohibited, and the place of ambiguity from the place of clarity. For this reason, it is narrated from ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — that he used to circulate through the market and strike some of the merchants with a whip, saying: "None shall sell in our market except one who has understanding (fiqh); otherwise he will devour usury (ribā), whether he wills it or not." And the science of contracts is vast, but these six contracts are inseparable from livelihoods: namely, sale (bayʿ), usury (ribā), salam (advance payment), hire (ijārah), partnership (shirkah), and commenda (qirāḍ). So let us expound their conditions.

### The First Contract: Sale (al-Bayʿ)
