- Root: خ-ر-ج (kharaja)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To exit, emerge, be excluded; al-ikhrāj = extraction, removal from a state
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for removing something from its proper domain; here, the removal of unlawful property from one's possession as a legal obligation
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of physical removal; metaphorical (majāz) sense of legal divestment of ownership
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Structure (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The tripartite division (fa-idhā... fa-imma... wa-imma...) establishes exhaustive legal categorization through conditional syntax
chapters.translation:
I say: When unlawful wealth is removed [from one's possession], it has three states:

Either it has a specific owner — then it must be returned to him or to his heir; and if he is absent, one awaits his presence or arranges delivery to him. And if it has yielded increase or benefit, let its profits be gathered until the time of his presence.

Or it belongs to an unspecified owner, and despair has been reached of discovering its source, and one does not know whether he died leaving an heir or not — then return to the owner is impossible, and it is held in abeyance until the matter becomes clear. And perhaps return is impossible due to the multiplicity of owners, like the spoils of war taken unlawfully (ghulūl); for after the warriors have dispersed, how could one gather them? And even if one could, how would one divide a single dinar among a thousand or two thousand? This should be given in charity.

Or it is from the public treasury (fay') and funds reserved for the welfare of all Muslims — then it is spent on bridges, mosques, hospices (ribāṭāt), way-stations on the road to Mecca, and similar things from which every Muslim who passes benefits, so that it becomes common to all Muslims.

The ruling on the first category is beyond doubt. As for giving in charity and building bridges, the judge (qāḍī) should undertake this, and the money should be handed to him if a religious judge is found. But if the judge treats unlawful things as permissible (mustaḥill), then one who hands it to him becomes a guarantor for what he did not guarantee before — so how could this remove an established liability? Rather, let a learned and religious man from the townspeople be appointed as arbiter (taḥkīm), for arbitration is preferable to acting alone. If unable, let him undertake it himself, for the goal is the expenditure [of the wealth].

As for the specific spender, we only seek him for precise channels of expenditure in public welfare; so the act of spending itself should not be abandoned due to inability to find a spender who would be preferable when one is able.

If it is said: What is the proof for the permissibility of giving unlawful wealth in charity? And how does one give in charity what one does not own? Indeed, a group has held this to be impermissible because it is unlawful. It is related of al-Fuḍayl that two dirhams fell into his hand, and when he learned they were not from a lawful source, he threw them among the rocks and said: "I do not give in charity except from what is pure, and I do not approve for others what I do not approve for myself."

We say: Yes, that view has its basis and possibility. But we have chosen the contrary due to the report (khabar), the tradition (athar), and analogy (qiyās).

As for the report: The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, commanded that the poisoned sheep which was presented to him be given in charity, when it spoke to him that it was unlawful — for he said, peace be upon him: "Feed it to the captives." (1)

And when the verse was revealed: {«Alif Lām Mīm. The Romans have been vanquished in the nearest land, and they, after their vanquishing, shall be victors»}, the polytheists denied it and said to the Companions: "Do you not see what your companion says, claiming that the Romans will be victorious?" So Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, made a wager with them by the permission of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. When God fulfilled His promise of truth, and Abu Bakr brought what he had wagered, he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "This is illicit gain (siḥt) — give it in charity." And the believers rejoiced in God's victory, for the prohibition of gambling had been revealed after the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, had permitted him to wager with the disbelievers. (2)

As for the tradition: Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him, purchased a slave-girl but could not find her owner to pay the price. He sought him extensively but did not find him, so he gave the price in charity and said: "O God, this is on his behalf — if he is pleased, then so be it; otherwise, the reward is mine."

Al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him, was asked about the repentance of one who took spoils unlawfully (ghāll), and what should be taken from him after the army had dispersed. He said: "He should give it in charity."

It is related that a man's soul tempted him, and he unlawfully took one hundred dinars from the spoils. Then he came to his commander to return them, but he refused to accept them, saying: "The people have dispersed." He came to Muʿāwiyah, who also refused to accept. He then came to one of the ascetics, who said: "Give a fifth of it to Muʿāwiyah and give the rest in charity." When this reached Muʿāwiyah, he regretted not having thought of that himself. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī, and a group of the scrupulous (warrāʿīn) held this view.

As for analogy: It is said that this wealth is suspended between being lost and being spent on good, since despair has been reached regarding its owner. It is known by necessity that spending it on good is preferable to throwing it into the sea. For if we throw it into the sea, we have deprived ourselves and the owner of it, and no benefit results from it. But if we place it in the hand of a poor man who prays for its owner, the owner obtains the blessing of his prayer, the poor man obtains the fulfillment of his need, and the owner obtains reward without his choice. That reward accrues to the owner without his choice should not be denied — for in the authentic report, the sower and planter have reward in everything that people and birds obtain from their fruits and crops. (3) And that is without their choice.

As for the one who says: "We do not give in charity except from what is pure" — that applies when we seek reward for ourselves. But now we seek deliverance from wrongdoing (maẓlimah), not reward. We have deliberated between wasting and giving in charity, and we have weighed the side of charity over the side of wasting.

And the saying: "We do not approve for others what we do not approve for ourselves" — that is so. But it is unlawful for us due to our independence from it, while for the poor man it is lawful, for the evidence of the Sacred Law has made it lawful. When public welfare necessitates making it lawful, it must be made lawful. And when it is lawful, we have approved for him what is lawful.

I say: He may give in charity to himself and his family if he is poor.

As for his family and household, this is not obscure — for poverty is not negated from them by their being his family and household; rather, they are more deserving of charity than others. As for himself, he may take from it the measure of his need, for he too is poor. If he gave it in charity to a poor man, it would be permissible — and likewise when he himself is the poor one.

Let us also record questions (masā'il) in elucidation of this principle:

**Question 1:** If wealth from the hand of a ruler falls into one's possession — some say it should be returned to the ruler, for he knows best what he has undertaken, so one should delegate to him what he has delegated, and this is better than giving it in charity. Al-Muḥāsibī chose this view, saying: "How can one give it in charity? Perhaps it has a specific owner. And if this were permissible, it would be permissible to steal from the ruler and give it in charity."

Others say: One should give it in charity if one knows that the ruler will not return it to its owner — for returning it is assistance to the wrongdoer and an increase in the means of his wrongdoing; thus returning it to him is wasting the owner's right.

The chosen view: If one knows from the ruler's custom that he will not return it to its owner, then one gives it in charity on behalf of its owner. This is better for the owner — if he has a specific owner — than returning it to the ruler, because perhaps it has no specific owner and is the right of the Muslims, in which case returning it to the ruler is wasting. If it has a specific owner, then returning it to the ruler is wasting, assistance to the unjust ruler, and a loss of the blessing of the poor man's prayer for the owner. This is evident.

If it falls into one's hand from an inheritance, and one did not transgress by taking from the ruler, then it resembles a lost object (luqṭah) concerning which one has despaired of knowing its owner — except that one may not dispose of it by giving in charity on behalf of the owner, but one may take ownership of it. And even if one is wealthy, this is because one acquired it from a permissible source, namely picking it up. Here, the wealth was not obtained from a permissible source, so this affects the prohibition of taking ownership but does not affect the prohibition of giving in charity.

**Question 2:** If wealth with no owner falls into one's hand, and we have permitted him to take the measure of his need due to his poverty — then regarding the measure of his need, there is a consideration which we mentioned in the Book of the Secrets of Almsgiving (Asrār al-Zakāh). Some say: He takes a year's sufficiency for himself and his family. And if he is able to purchase an estate or establish a trade by which he earns for his family, he may do so. This is what al-Muḥāsibī chose. However, he said: The preferable course is to give it all in charity if one finds in oneself the strength of trust in God (tawakkul), and to await God's grace in what is lawful. If unable, he may purchase an estate or establish capital from which he lives honorably. And every day in which he finds lawful sustenance, he refrains from it that day; when it is exhausted, he returns to it. And if he finds specific lawful wealth, he gives in charity the equivalent of what he had spent before, and that becomes a loan (qarḍ) owed by him. Then he eats bread and abstains from meat if he can bear it; otherwise he eats meat without indulgence or extravagance.

What he mentioned admits of no addition. However, his making what he spent a loan owed by him involves consideration. There is no doubt that scrupulousness (waraʿ) requires making it a loan, so that when he finds lawful wealth he gives its equivalent in charity. But whenever this is not obligatory upon the poor man to whom it is given in charity, it is not far that it should not be obligatory upon him either when he takes it for his poverty — especially if it fell into his hand from an inheritance and he did not transgress by usurping or earning it, such that the matter becomes severe upon him.

**Question 3:** If one has in his hand both lawful and unlawful or doubtful (shubhah) wealth, and the total does not exceed his need — then if he has a family, let him single out himself for the lawful, for the proof against him is stronger regarding himself than regarding his servant and family. His minor and adult children — he should guard them from the unlawful unless this leads them to something worse; if it does, he feeds them to the measure of need.

In general, what he fears for others is feared for himself and more so — namely, that he partakes knowingly, while his family perhaps partakes unknowingly, since they did not undertake the matter themselves. So let him begin with the lawful for himself, then for those he supports. And when he deliberates regarding himself between what pertains to his food and clothing versus other expenses — like the fee of the cupper, the dyer, the fuller, the porter, applying lime for hair removal, oil, house maintenance, tending the animal, firing the oven, the price of firewood, and lamp oil — let him single out for the lawful his food and his garment. For what pertains to his body and is indispensable is more deserving of being pure.

When the matter turns between food and clothing, it may be said: Single out food for the lawful, because it mingles with his flesh and blood — and every flesh that grows from the unlawful, the Fire is more deserving of it. As for clothing, its benefit is covering one's nakedness and repelling heat, cold, and eyes from one's skin. This is the more apparent view to me.

Al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī said: Clothing takes precedence, because it remains upon one for a duration, while food does not remain — due to the report that God does not accept the prayer of one who wears a garment purchased for ten dirhams containing one unlawful dirham. (1)

This is possible. But similar reports have come regarding one in whose belly is the unlawful and whose flesh has grown from the unlawful. (2) So attending to the flesh and bone — that they grow from the lawful — is more appropriate. For this reason, al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, vomited what he had drunk in ignorance, so that no flesh would grow from it that would persist and remain.

If it is said: When all of it is directed to one's purposes, what difference is there between oneself and others, or between one direction and another? And what is the basis for perceiving this difference?

We say: This is known from the report that Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, may God have mercy on him, died and left a camel and a slave who was a cupper. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about this, and he forbade the earnings of the cupper. He was asked repeatedly, and he continued to forbid it. It was said: "He has orphans." He said: "Feed the camel with it." (3)

This indicates the difference between what one eats oneself and what one's animal eats. When the path of differentiation is opened, then measure upon it the detailed distinctions we have mentioned.

**Question 4:** Regarding the unlawful wealth in one's hand — if one gives it in charity to the poor, he may be generous with them. If he spends it on himself, let him be restrictive as much as possible. What he spends on his family, let him be moderate — midway between generosity and restriction. Thus the matter has three degrees. If he spends on a guest who arrives while poor, let him be generous with him. If the guest is wealthy, he should not feed him unless in a wilderness or arriving at night having found nothing — for at that time he is poor. If the poor man who has come as a guest is scrupulous (taqiyy), and had he known he would have abstained, then let him present the food and inform him — combining the right of hospitality with the abandonment of deception. For one should not honor his brother with what he dislikes, nor should one rely on the fact that he does not know and thus it will not harm him — for when the unlawful reaches the stomach, it effects hardness of heart even if its possessor does not recognize it. For this reason Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, vomited, having drunk in ignorance. And even though we have ruled it lawful for the poor by the dictate of need — just as we make swine and wine lawful under necessity — it does not thereby join the pure things.

**Question 5:** If the unlawful or doubtful is in the hand of one's parents, let him refrain from eating with them. If they are displeased, he should not comply with them in pure unlawfulness; rather, he should forbid them — for there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to God Almighty. If it is doubtful and his abstention is for scrupulousness, then this is opposed by the fact that scrupulousness requires seeking their pleasure — indeed, it is obligatory. So let him be gentle in abstaining. If unable, let him comply but minimize eating — by making the morsel small and lengthening the chewing — and not be expansive, for that is transgression. The brother and sister are close to this, for their right is also emphasized. Likewise, if his mother clothes him in a garment of doubtful origin and is displeased by his returning it, let him accept it and wear it in her presence, and remove it in her absence. Let him strive not to pray in it except in her presence, praying in it as one compelled. When the causes of scrupulousness conflict, one should attend to these subtleties.

It is related of Bishr, may God have mercy on him, that his mother handed him a fresh date and said: "By my right upon you, eat it." He disliked it but ate it. Then he climbed to an upper room, and his mother climbed behind him and saw him vomiting. He did this only because he wanted to combine her pleasure with protecting his stomach.

It was said to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal: "Bishr was asked whether parents have obedience in doubtful matters, and he said no." Aḥmad said: "This is severe."

It was said to him: "Muḥammad ibn Muqātil al-ʿAbbādānī was asked about it, and he said: 'Be dutiful to your parents' — so what do you say?" He said to the questioner: "I would like you to excuse me, for you have heard what both said." Then he said: "How excellent it is to manage them gently."

**Question 6:** One who has pure unlawful wealth in his hand — the pilgrimage (ḥajj) is not obligatory upon him, nor is a financial expiation (kaffārah) required, for he is bankrupt (muflis). Nor is almsgiving (zakāh) obligatory upon him, for the meaning of zakāh is the obligation of paying out, say, a quarter of a tenth — whereas this one must pay out everything, either as return to the owner if he knows him, or as expenditure to the poor if he does not know the owner.

As for wealth that is doubtful, possibly lawful — if he does not remove it from his hand, the pilgrimage is obligatory upon him, because its being lawful is possible, and the pilgrimage is not waived except by poverty, and his poverty is not established. God Almighty has said: {«And God has imposed upon people the pilgrimage to the House — upon whoever can find a way to it»}. And if giving in charity what exceeds his need is obligatory upon him where the presumption of its unlawfulness prevails, then zakāh is even more deserving of obligation.

If an expiation is incumbent upon him, let him combine fasting and freeing a slave to be delivered with certainty. Some have said: Fasting alone is incumbent upon him, for he has no known means. Al-Muḥāsibī said: Feeding suffices him.

What we choose: For every doubtful matter which we have ruled must be avoided and whose removal from one's hand we have made obligatory — because the probability of the unlawful prevails, as we have mentioned — upon him is the combination of fasting and feeding. As for fasting, because he is bankrupt by legal judgment; as for feeding, because giving all of it in charity has been made obligatory upon him, and it is possible that it is his, in which case the obligation arises from the direction of expiation.

**Question 7:** One who has unlawful wealth in his hand and retains it for need, then wishes to perform voluntary pilgrimage — if he goes on foot, there is no harm, for he will eat this wealth in something other than worship, so eating it in worship is preferable. If he cannot walk and needs additional expense for a mount, it is not permissible to take from it for such a need on the road, just as it is not permissible to purchase a mount in the town. And if he anticipates being able to obtain lawful wealth were he to remain, such that he would be independent of the rest of the unlawful — then remaining in expectation of it is preferable to going on pilgrimage on foot with unlawful wealth.

**Question 8:** One who sets out for obligatory pilgrimage with wealth containing doubt — let him strive that his food be from the pure. If unable, then at least from the time of entering the state of iḥrām until the completion of the pilgrimage rites. If unable, let him strive on the Day of ʿArafah that his standing before God and his supplication not occur at a time when his food is unlawful and his garment is unlawful. Let him strive that there be nothing unlawful in his belly and nothing unlawful on his back. For even though we have permitted this by need, it is a kind of necessity, and we have not joined it to the pure things. If unable, let his heart remain in fear and grief over what he is compelled to consume of what is not pure — perhaps God will look upon him with the eye of mercy and pardon him on account of his sorrow, fear, and aversion.

**Question 9:** Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, may God's mercy be upon him, was asked — a man said to him: "My father died and left wealth, and he used to deal with those whose dealings are disliked." He said: "Leave from his wealth the measure of his profit." He said: "He has debts owed to him and debts upon him." He said: "Pay and collect." He said: "Do you see this?" He said: "Would you leave it withheld by his debt?" What he mentioned is sound, and it indicates that he saw the exercise of discernment (taḥarrī) by extracting the measure of the unlawful — for he said: "Extract the measure of the profit." And he saw that the very substance of his wealth is his property, in exchange for what he had given in the corrupt transactions, by way of set-off and mutual exchange, whenever dealings have multiplied and return has become difficult. And he relied in paying his debt upon what is certain, so it should not be abandoned due to doubt.

### ||| الباب الخامس في إدرارات السلاطين وصلاتهم وما يحل منها وما يحرم

اعلم أن من أخذ مالا من سلطان فلا بد له من النظر في ثلاثة أمور في مدخل
ذلك إلى يد السلطان من أين هو وفي صفته التي بها يستحق الأخذ
وفي المقدار الذي يأخذه هل يستحقه إذا أضيف إلى حاله وحال شركائه في
الاستحقاق

chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-خ-ل (d-kh-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of entering, penetrating, or ingress; also income or revenue entering one's possession.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-legal context, denotes the source or channel (jihah) through which wealth lawfully or unlawfully arrives, tied to the notion of acquisition (kasb) and its moral legitimacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to physical entry; here employed metaphorically (majāz) as the "avenue" or "origin" of fiscal inflow, a standard extension in juristic discourse.
- Root: س-ل-ط (s-l-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Authority, dominance, or overpowering; the one wielding coercive power (sulṭān).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes the possessor of temporal authority whose commands carry binding force in worldly matters; in Ghazali's ethics, a figure whose wealth is morally ambiguous due to acquisitional opacity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "dominion" or "proof"; here it is a metonymy (majāz mursal) for the ruler himself, a common classical usage.
- Root: ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Loosening, dissolving, or becoming permissible; the opposite of prohibition (ḥurmah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, signifies the transition from a state of prohibition to permissibility, contingent upon divine command and ethical conditions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is "untying a knot"; metaphorically applied to the removal of legal restriction, a well-attested figurative extension.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause with Inna (إنّ + الشرطية) — The opening "اعلم أن" (know that) governs a nominal sentence where the complement (khabar) is a conditional structure requiring careful parsing of the three enumerated matters (umūr), each introduced by "في" (in), indicating a genitive dependency that specifies the scope of investigation.
chapters.translation:
Know that whoever takes wealth from a sultan must necessarily examine three matters: the channel through which that wealth entered the sultan's hand — from where it came; the attribute by virtue of which he becomes deserving of taking it; and the amount he takes — whether he deserves it when considered in relation to his own state and the state of his partners in entitlement.

### The First Consideration: The Channels of Income for the Sultan

وكل ما يحل للسلطان سوى الإحياء وما يشترك فيه الرعية قسمان
مأخوذ من الكفار وهو الغنيمة المأخوذة بالقهر والفيء وهو الذي حصل من
مالهم في يده من غير قتال والجزية وأموال المصالحة وهي التي تؤخذ بالشروط
والمعاقدة
والقسم الثاني المأخوذ من المسلمين فلا يحل منه إلا قسمان المواريث وسائر
الأمور الضائعة التي لا يتعين لها مالك والأوقاف التي لا متولي لها أما
الصدقات فليست توجد في هذا الزمان
وما عدا ذلك من الخراج المضروب على المسلمين والمصادرات وأنواع الرشوة
كلها حرام
فإذا كتب لفقيه أو غيره إدرار أو صلة أو خلعة على جهة فلا يخلو من أحوال
ثمانية فإنه إما أن يكتب له ذلك على الجزية أو على المواريث أو على الأوقاف
أو على ملك أحياء السلطان أو على ملك اشتراه أو على عامل خراج المسلمين أو
على بياع من جملة التجار أو على الخزانة
فالأول هو الجزية وأربعة أخماسها للمصالح وخمسها لجهات معينة
فما يكتب على الخمس من تلك الجهات أو على الأخماس الأربعة لما فيه مصلحة
وروعي فيه الاحتياط في القدر فهو حلال بشرط أن لا تكون الجزية إلا مضروبة
على وجه شرعي ليس فيها زيادة على  دينار أو على أربعة دنانير فإنه أيضا في
محل الاجتهاد وللسلطان أن يفعل ما هو في محل الاجتهاد وبشرط أن يكون الذمي
الذي تؤخذ الجزية منه مكتسبا من وجه لا يعلم تحريمه فلا يكون عامل سلطان
ظالما ولا بياع خمر ولا صبيا ولا امرأة إذ لا جزية عليهما
فهذه أمور تراعى في كيفية ضرب الجزية ومقدارها وصفة من تصرف أليه ومقدار
ما يصرف فيجب النظر في جميع ذلك
الثاني المواريث والأموال الضائعة فهي للمصالح والنظر أن الذي خلفه هل
كان ماله كله حراما أو أكثره أو أقله وقد سبق حكمه فإن لم يكن حراما بقي
النظر في صفة من يصرف إليه بأن يكون في الصرف إليه مصلحة ثم في المقدار
المصروف
الثالث الأوقاف وكذا يجري النظر فيها كما يجري في الميراث مع زيادة أمر
وهو شرط المواقف حتى يكون المأخوذ موافقا له في جميع شرائطه
الرابع ما أحياه السلطان وهذا لا يعتبر فيه شرط إذ له أن يعطى من ملكه
لمن شاء أي قدر شاء
وإنما النظر في أن الغالب أنه أحياه بإكراه الأجراء أو بأداء أجرتهم من
حرام
فإن الإحياء يحصل بحفر القناة والأنهار وبناء الجدران وتسوية الأرض ولا
يتولاه السلطان بنفسه
فإن كانوا مكرهين على الفعل لم يملكه السلطان وهو حرام وإن كانوا
مستأجرين ثم قضيت أجورهم من الحرام فهذا يورث شبهة قد نبهنا عليها في تعلق
الكرامة بالأعواض
PageV02P135
الخامس ما اشتراه السلطان في الذمة من أرض أو ثياب خلعة أو فرس أو غيره
فهو ملكه وله أن يتصرف فيه ولكنه سيقضي ثمنه من حرام وذلك يوجب التحريم
تارة والشبهة أخرى وقد سبق تفصيله
السادس أن يكتب على عامل خراج المسلمين أو من يجمع أمواله القسمة
والمصادرة وهو الحرام السحت الذي لا شبهة فيه وهو أكثر الإدرارات في هذا
الزمان إلا ما على أراضي العراق فإنها وقف عند الشافعي رحمه الله على مصالح
المسلمين
السابع ما يكتب على بياع يعامل السلطان فإن كان لا يعامل غيره فماله له
كمال خزانة السلطان
وإن كان يعامل غير السلاطين أكثر فما يعطيه قرض على السلطان وسيأخذ بدله
من الخزانة فالخلل يتطرق إلى العوض
وقد سبق حكم الثمن الحرام
الثامن ما يكتب على الخزانة أو على عامل يجتمع عنده من الحلال والحرام
فإن لم يعرف للسلطان دخل إلا من الحرام فهو سحت محض وإن عرف يقينا أن
الخزانة تشتمل على مال حلال ومال حرام واحتمل ان يكون ما يسلم إليه بعينه
من الحلال احتمالا قريبا له وقع في النفس واحتمل أن يكون من الحرام وهو
الأغلب لأن أغلب أموال السلاطين حرام في هذه الأعصار والحلال في أيديهم
معدوم أو عزيز فقد اختلف الناس في هذا فقال قوم كل ما لا أتيقن أنه حرام
فلي أن آخذه وقال آخرون لا يحل أن يؤخذ مالم يتحقق أنه حلال فلا تحل شبهة
أصلا
وكلاهما إسراف والاعتدال ما قدمنا ذكره وهو الحكم بأن الأغلب إذا كان
حراما حرم وإن كان الأغلب حلالا وفيه يقين حرام فهو موضع توقفنا فيه كما
سبق
لقد احتج من جوز اخذ أموال السلاطين إذا كان فيها حرام وحلال مهما لم
يتحقق أن عين المأخوذ حرام بما روي عن جماعة من الصحابة أنهم أدركوا أيام
الأئمة الظلمة وأخذوا الأموال منهم أبو هريرة وأبو سعيد الخدري وزيد بن
ثابت وأبو أيوب الأنصاري وجرير بن عبد الله وجابر وأنس بن مالك والمسور بن
مخرمة
فأخذ أبو سعيد وأبو هريرة من مروان ويزيد بن عبد الملك
وأخذ ابن عمر وابن عباس من الحجاج
وأخذ كثير من التابعين منهم كالشعبي وإبراهيم والحسن وابن أبي ليلى
وأخذ الشافعي من هرون الرشيد ألف دينار في دفعة
وأخذ مالك من الخلفاء أموالا جمة وقال علي رضي الله عنه خذ ما يعطيك
السلطان فإنما يعطيك من الحلال وما يأخذ من الحلال أكثر
وإنما ترك من ترك العطاء منهم تورعا مخافة على دينه أن يحمل على مالا يحل
ألا ترى قول أبي ذر للأحنف بن قيس خذ العطاء ما كان نحلة  فإذا كان أثمان
دينكم فدعوه وقال أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه إذا أعطينا قبلنا وإذا منعنا لم
نسأل
وعن سعيد بن المسيب أن أبا هريرة رضي الله عنه كان إذا أعطاه معاوية سكت
وإن منعه وقع فيه
وعن الشعبي عن مسروق لا يزال العطاء بأهل العطاء حتى يدخلهم النار أي
يحمله ذلك على الحرام لا انه في نفسه حرام وروى نافع عن ابن عمر رضي الله
عنهما أن المختار كان يبعث إليه المال فيقبله ثم يقول لا أسأل أحدا ولا أرد
ما رزقني الله
وأهدى إليه ناقة فقبلها وكان يقال لها ناقة المختار ولكن هذا يعارضه ما
روي أن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما لم يرد هدية أحد إلا هدية المختار والإسناد
في رده أثبت
وعن نافع أنه قال بعث ابن معمر إلى ابن عمر بستين ألفا فقسمها على الناس
ثم جاءه سائل فاستقرض له من بعض من أعطاه وأعطى السائل
ولما قدم الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما على معاوية رضي الله عنه فقال
لأجيزك بجائزة لم أجزها أحدا قبلك من العرب ولا أجيزها أحدا بعدك من العرب
قال فأعطاه أربعمائة ألف درهم فأخذها
وعن حبيب
PageV02P136
ابن أبي ثابت قال لقد رأيت جائزة المختار لابن عمر وابن عباس فقبلاها
فقيل ما هي قال مال وكسوة
وعن الزبير بن عدي أنه قال قال سلمان إذا كان لك صديق عامل أو تاجر يقارف
الربا فدعاك إلى طعام أو نحوه أو أعطاك شيئا فاقبل فإن المهنأ لك وعليه
الوزر
فإن ثبت هذا في المربي فالظالم في معناه
وعن جعفر عن أبيه أن الحسن والحسين عليهما السلام كانا يقبلان جوائز
معاوية
وقال حكيم بن جبير مررنا على سعيد بن جبير وقد جعل عاملا على أسفل الفرات
فأرسل إلى العشارين أطعمونا مما عندكم فأرسلوا بطعام فأكل وأكلنا معه وقال
العلاء بن زهير الأزدي أتى إبراهيم أبي وهو عامل على حلوان فأجازه فقبل
وقال إبراهيم لا بأس بجائزة العمال إن للعمال مؤنة ورزقا
ويدخل بيت  ماله الخبيث والطيب فما أعطاك فهو من طيب ماله
فقد أخذ هؤلاء كلهم جوائز السلاطين الظلمة وكلهم طعنوا على من أطاعهم في
معصية الله تعالى
وزعمت هذه الفرقة أن ما ينقل من امتناع جماعة من السلف لا يدل على
التحريم بل على الورع كالخلفاء الراشدين وأبي ذر وغيرهم من الزهاد فإنهم
امتنعوا من الحلال المطلق زهدا ومن الحلال الذي يخاف إفضاؤه إلى محذور ورعا
وتقوى
فإقدام هؤلاء يدل على الجواز وامتناع أولئك لا يدل على التحريم
وما نقل عن سعيد بن المسيب أنه ترك عطاءه في بيت المال حتى اجتمع بضعة
وثلاثين ألفا وما نقل عن الحسن من قوله لا أتوضأ من ماء صيرفي ولو ضاق وقت
الصلاة لأني لا أدري أصل ماله كل ذلك ورع لا ينكر واتباعهم عليه أحسن من
اتباعهم على الاتساع ولكن لا يحرم اتباعهم على الاتساع أيضا
فهذه هي شبهة من يجوز أخذ مال السلطان الظالم
والجواب أن ما نقل من أخذ هؤلاء محصور قليل بالإضافة إلى ما نقل من ردهم
وإنكارهم وإن كان يتطرق إلى امتناعهم احتمال الورع فيتطرق إلى أخذ من أخذ
ثلاثة احتمالات متفاوتة في الدرجة بتفاوتهم في الورع فإن للورع في حق
السلاطين أربع درجات
الدرجة الأولى أن لا يأخذ من أموالهم شيئا أصلا كما فعله الورعون منهم
وكما كان يفعله الخلفاء الراشدون حتى أن أبا بكر رضي الله عنه حسب جميع ما
كان أخذه من بيت المال فبلغ ستة آلاف درهم فغرمها لبيت المال وحتى أن عمر
رضي الله عنه كان يقسم مال بيت المال يوما فدخلت ابنة له وأخذت درهما من
المال فنهض عمر في طلبها حتى سقطت الملحفة من أحد منكبيه ودخلت الصبية إلى
بيت أهلها تبكي وجعلت الدرهم في فيها فأدخل عمر إصبعه فأخرجه من فيها وطرحه
على الخراج وقال أيها الناس ليس لعمر ولا لآل عمر إلا ما للمسلمين قريبهم
وبعيدهم
وكسح أبو موسى الأشعري بيت المال فوجد درهما فمر بني لعمر رضي الله عنه
فأعطاه  إياه فرأى عمر ذلك في يد الغلام فسأله عنه فقال أعطانيه أبو موسى
فقال
يا أبا موسى ما كان في أهل المدينة بيت أهون عليك من آل عمر أردت أن لا
يبقى من أمة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم أحد إلا طلبنا بمظلمة ورد الدرهم إلى
بيت المال
هذا مع أن المال كان حلالا ولكن خاف أن لا يستحق هو ذلك القدر فكان
يستبريء لدينه ويقتصر على الأقل امتثالا لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم دع ما
يريبك إلى ما لا يريبك (1)
ولقوله ومن تركها فقد استبرأ لعرضه ودينه (2)
ولما سمعه من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من التشديدات في الأموال
السلطانية حتى قال صلى الله عليه وسلم حين PageV02P137
بعث عبادة بن الصامت إلى الصدقة اتق الله يا أبا الوليد لا تجيء يوم
القيامة ببعير تحمله على رقبتك له رغاء أو بقرة لها خوار أو شاة لها تؤاج
فقال يا رسول الله أهكذا يكون قال نعم والذي نفسي بيده إلا من رحم الله
قال فوالذي بعثك بالحق لا أعمل على شيء أبدا (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إني لا أخاف عليكم أن تشركوا بعدي إنما أخاف
عليكم أن تنافسوا (2)
وإنما خاف التنافس في المآل
ولذلك قال عمر رضي الله عنه في حديث طويل يذكر فيه مال بيت المال إني لم
أجد نفسي فيه إلا كالوالى مال اليتيم إن استغنيت استعففت وإن افتقرت أكلت
بالمعروف
وروي أن ابنا لطاوس افتعل كتابا عن لسانه إلى عمر بن عبد العزيز فأعطاه
ثلثمائة دينار فباع طاوس ضيعة له وبعث من ثمنها إلى عمر بثلثمائة دينار هذا
مع أن السلطان ليس مثل عمر بن عبد العزيز
فهذه الدرجة العليا في الورع
الدرجة الثانية هو أن يأخذ مال السلطان ولكن إنما يأخذ إذا علم أن ما
يأخذه من جهة حلال فاشتمال يد السلطان على حرام آخر لا يضره وعلى هذا ينزل
جميع ما نقل من الآثار أو أكثرها أو ما اختص منها بأكابر الصحابة والورعين
منهم  مثل ابن عمر فإنه كان من المبالغين في الورع فكيف يتوسع في مال
السلطان وقد كان من أشدهم إنكارا عليهم وأشدهم ذما لأموالهم وذلك أنهم
اجتمعوا عند ابن عامر وهو في مرضه وأشفق على نفسه من ولايته وكونه مأخوذا
عند الله تعالى بها فقالوا له إنا لنرجو لك الخير حفرت الآبار وسقيت الحاج
وصنعت وصنعت وابن عمر ساكت فقال ماذا تقول يا ابن عمر فقال أقول ذلك إذا
طاب المكسب وزكت النفقة وسترد فترى
وفي حديث آخر أنه قال إن الخبيث لا يكفر الخبيث وإنك قد وليت البصرة ولا
أحسبك إلا قد أصبت منها شرا
فقال له ابن عامر ألا تدعو لي فقال ابن عمر سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم يقول لا يقبل الله صلاة بغير طهورا ولا صدقة من غلول (3)
وقد وليت البصرة فهذا قوله فيما صرفه إلى الخيرات
وعن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما أنه قال في أيام الحجاج ما شبعت من الطعام
منذ انتهبت الدار إلى يومي هذا وروي عن علي رضي الله عنه أنه كان له سويق
في إناء مختوم يشرب منه فقيل أتفعل هذا بالعراق مع كثرة طعامه فقال أما إني
لا أختمه بخلابه ولكن أكره أن يجعل فيه ما ليس منه وأكره أن يدخل بطني غير
طيب فهذا هو المألوف منهم وكان ابن عمر لا يعجبه شيء إلا خرج عنه فطلب منه
نافع بثلاثين ألفا فقال إني أخاف أن تقتنى دراهم ابن عامر وكان هو الطالب
اذهب فأنت حر
وقال أبو سعيد الخدري ما منا أحد إلا مالت به الدنيا إلا ابن عمر فبهذا
يتضح أنه لا يظن به وبمن كان في منصبه أنه أخذ مالا يدري أنه حلال
الدرجة الثالثة أن يأخذ ما أخذه من السلطان ليتصدق به على الفقراء أو
يفرقه على المستحقين فإن ما لا يتعين مالكه هذا حكم الشرع فيه
فإذا كان السلطان إن لم يأخذ منه لم يفرقه واستعان به على ظلم فقد نقول
أخذه منه وتفرقته  أولى من تركه في يده وهذا قد رآه بعض العلماء وسيأتي وجهه
وعلى هذا ينزل ما أخذه أكثرهم ولذلك قال ابن المبارك إن الذين يأخذون
الجوائز اليوم ويحتجون بابن عمر وعائشة ما يقتدون بهما لأن ابن عمر فرق ما
أخذ حتى استقرض في مجلسه بعد تفرقته ستين ألفا وعائشة فعلت مثل ذلك وجابر
بن زيد جاءه مال فتصدق به وقال رأيت أن آخذه منهم وأتصدق أحب إلي من أن
أدعها في أيديهم وهكذا فعل الشافعي رحمه الله بما قبله PageV02P138
من هرون الرشيد فإنه فرقه على قرب حتى لم يمسك لنفسه حبة واحدة
الدرجة الرابعة أن لا يتحقق انه حلال ولا يفرق بل يستبقي ولكن يأخذ من
سلطان أكثر ماله حلال وهكذا كان الخلفاء في زمان الصحابة رضي الله عنهم
والتابعين بعد الخلفاء الراشدين ولم يكن أكثر مالهم حراما
ويدل عليه تعليل علي رضي الله عنه حيث قال فإن ما يأخذه من الحلال أكثر
فهذا مما قد جوزه جماعة من العلماء تعويلا على الأكثر
ونحن إنما توقفنا فيه في حق آحاد الناس ومال السلطان أشبه بالخروج عن
الحصر فلا يبعد أن يؤدي اجتهاد مجتهد إلى جواز أخذ ما لم يعلم أنه حرام
اعتمادا على الأغلب وإنما منعناه إذا كان الأكثر حراما فإذا فهمت هذه
الدرجات تحققت أن ادرارات الظلمة في زماننا لا تجري مجرى ذلك وأنها تفارقه
من وجهين قاطعين
أحدهما أن أموال السلاطين في عصرنا حرام كلها أو أكثرها وكيف لا والحلال
هو الصدقات والفيء والغنيمة لا وجود لها وليس يدخل منها شيء في يد السلطان
ولم يبق إلا الجزية وأنها تؤخذ بأنواع من الظلم لا يحل أخذها به فإنهم
يجاوزون حدود الشرع في المأخوذ والمأخوذ منه والوفاء له بالشرط ثم إذا نسبت
ذلك إلى ما ينصب إليهم من الخراج المضروب على المسلمين ومن المصادرات
والرشا وصنوف الظلم لم يبلغ عشر معشار عشيره
والوجه الثاني أن الظلمة في العصر الأول لقرب عهدهم بزمان الخلفاء
الراشدين كانوا مستشعرين من ظلمهم ومتشوفين  إلى استمالة قلوب الصحابة
والتابعين وحريصين على قبولهم عطاياهم وجوائزهم وكانوا يبعثون إليهم من غير
سؤال وإذلال بل كانوا يتقلدون المنة بقبولهم ويفرحون به وكانوا يأخذون منهم
ويفرقون ولا يطيعون السلاطين في أغراضهم ولا يغشون مجالسهم ولا يكثرون
جمعهم ولا يحبون بقاءهم بل يدعون عليهم ويطلقون اللسان فيهم وينكرون
المنكرات منهم عليهم فما كان يحذر أن يصيبوا من دينهم بقدر ما أصابوا من
دنياهم ولم يكن يأخذهم بأس فأما الآن فلا تسمح نفوس السلاطين بعطية إلا لمن
طمعوا في استخدامهم والتكثر بهم والاستعانة بهم على أغراضهم والتجمل بغشيان
مجالسهم وتكليفهم المواظبة على الدعاء والثناء والتزكية والإطراء في حضورهم
ومغيبهم
فلو لم يذل الآخذ نفسه بالسؤال أولا وبالتردد في الخدمة ثانيا وبالثناء
والدعاء ثالثا وبالمساعدة له على أغراضه عند الاستعانة رابعا وبتكثير جمعه
في مجلسه وموكبه خامسا وبإظهار الحب والموالاة والمناصرة له على أعدائه
سادسا وبالستر على ظلمه ومقابحه ومساوي أعماله سابعا لم ينعم عليه بدرهم
واحد ولو كان في فضل الشافعي رحمه الله مثلا فإذا لا يجوز أن يؤخذ منهم في
هذا الزمان ما يعلم أنه حلال لإفضائه إلى هذه المعاني فكيف ما يعلم أنه
حرام أو يشك فيه فمن استجرأ على أموالهم وشبه نفسه بالصحابة والتابعين فقد
قاس الملائكة بالحدادين
ففي أخذ الأموال منهم حاجة إلى مخالطتهم ومراعاتهم وخدمة عمالهم واحتمال
الذل منهم والثناء عليهم والتردد إلى أبوابهم وكل ذلك معصية على ما سنبين
في الباب الذي يلي هذا فإذا قد تبين مما تقدم مداخل أموالهم وما يحل منها
وما لا يحل
فلو تصور أن يأخذ الإنسان منها ما يحل بقدر استحقاقه وهو جالس في بيته
يساق إليه ذلك لا يحتاج فيه إلى تفقد عامل وخدمته ولا إلى الثناء عليهم
وتزكيتهم ولا إلى مساعدتهم فلا يحرم الأخذ ولكن يكره لمعان وسننبه عليها في
الباب الذي يلي هذا

- Root: ق-س-م (q-s-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Division, apportionment, distribution into parts; the act of partitioning a whole into its constituent shares.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological-legal categorization of things into lawful (ḥalāl) and unlawful (ḥarām) — a division that determines the moral and eschatological status of an act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of formal classification, not metaphorically; the text is a legal taxonomy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text relies heavily on "if...then" (fa-inna) and "except" (illā) structures to delineate legal categories, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the juridical force.
chapters.translation:
I say: Everything that is lawful for the Sultan, apart from the revivification of dead lands (iḥyāʾ) and what the subjects share in common, is of two divisions.

The first division is what is taken from the unbelievers. This comprises: the spoils of war (ghanīmah) taken by force; the fayʾ, which is what comes into his hand from their wealth without fighting; the poll-tax (jizyah); and the wealth of reconciliation (amwāl al-muṣālaḥah), which is taken by virtue of stipulated conditions and contractual agreements.

The second division is what is taken from the Muslims. From this, nothing is lawful except two categories: inheritances (mawārīth), and all lost or ownerless properties (al-amwāl al-ḍāʾiʿah) for which no owner can be determined, and endowments (awqāf) that have no administrator. As for the alms (ṣadaqāt), they are not to be found in this age [of ours].

Everything other than that — such as the land-tax (kharāj) imposed upon the Muslims, confiscations (muṣādarāt), and the various kinds of bribery (rishwah) — is entirely unlawful (ḥarām).

So when a stipend (idrār), a gift (ṣilah), or a robe of honor (khilʿah) is written [as an assignment] for a jurist (faqīh) or anyone else, by way of a draft [upon a revenue source], it does not fall outside eight possible cases. For it is either written for him: (1) upon the poll-tax (jizyah); (2) upon the inheritances; (3) upon the endowments; (4) upon property that the Sultan has revived; (5) upon property he has purchased; (6) upon the tax-collector of the Muslims' land-tax; (7) upon a merchant from among the traders; or (8) upon the treasury (khizānah).

**The First Case: The Poll-Tax (Jizyah).** Four-fifths of it is for the public interests (maṣāliḥ), and one-fifth is for specific designated purposes. Whatever is written upon that fifth from those designated purposes, or upon the four-fifths for the sake of a public interest, provided that caution (iḥtiyāṭ) is observed in the amount — this is lawful, on the condition that the poll-tax is not imposed except in a legally valid manner (ʿalā wajh sharʿī), without any increase beyond one dīnār or four dīnārs. For even this [amount] is a matter of juristic discretion (ijtihād), and the Sultan may do what falls within the scope of ijtihād. And [it is also conditional] that the dhimmī from whom the poll-tax is taken earns his livelihood from a source not known to be unlawful — so he must not be an agent of a tyrannical Sultan, nor a seller of wine, nor a minor, nor a woman, for there is no poll-tax upon these two [latter]. These, then, are matters to be observed concerning the manner of imposing the poll-tax, its amount, the description of the one to whom it is directed, and the amount that is expended. It is therefore obligatory to consider all of that.

**The Second Case: Inheritances and Lost Properties.** These are for the public interests. The consideration here is whether what the deceased left behind was entirely unlawful, or mostly unlawful, or only slightly unlawful — and its ruling has already preceded. If it was not unlawful, then the consideration remains concerning the description of the one to whom it is directed, namely that there be a public interest in directing it to him; and then concerning the amount expended.

**The Third Case: Endowments (Awqāf).** The same consideration applies here as applies to inheritance, with an additional matter: namely, the condition of the endower (sharṭ al-wāqif), so that what is taken must conform to him in all his stipulated conditions.

**The Fourth Case: What the Sultan Has Revived.** No condition is considered here, for he may give from his own property to whomever he wishes, whatever amount he wishes. The only consideration is that the predominant [likelihood] is that he revived it either by coercing laborers (ikrāh al-ajrāʾ) or by paying their wages from unlawful wealth. For revivification is achieved by digging canals and rivers, building walls, and leveling the earth — and the Sultan does not undertake this himself. If the laborers were coerced into the act, then the Sultan does not own it, and it is unlawful. If they were hired and then their wages were paid from unlawful wealth, this engenders a doubt (shubhah) — and we have already alerted to this in [our discussion of] the attachment of gratuity (karāmah) to compensatory payments (aʿwāḍ).

**The Fifth Case: What the Sultan Has Purchased on Credit (fī al-dhimmah).** Whether it be land, garments for robes of honor, a horse, or anything else — it is his property, and he may dispose of it. However, he will pay its price from unlawful wealth, and that necessitates unlawfulness at times and doubt at other times; and its detailed exposition has already preceded.

**The Sixth Case: A Draft upon the Tax-Collector of the Muslims' Land-Tax (kharāj), or upon One Who Collects the Wealth of Division (qismah) and Confiscation (muṣādarah).** This is the unlawful, the ill-gotten gain (suḥt) concerning which there is no doubt whatsoever. And this is the majority of stipends (idrārāt) in this age of ours — except for what is upon the lands of Iraq, for these are, according to al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him), an endowment (waqf) upon the public interests of the Muslims.

**The Seventh Case: A Draft upon a Merchant Who Deals with the Sultan.** If he deals with no one other than him, then his wealth is like the wealth of the Sultan's treasury. But if he deals with others more than he deals with the Sultans, then what he gives as a loan (qarḍ) to the Sultan — he will take its substitute from the treasury, and thus the defect (khalal) attaches to the compensatory payment (ʿiwaḍ). And the ruling on unlawful price (thaman ḥarām) has already preceded.

**The Eighth Case: A Draft upon the Treasury (khizānah), or upon an Agent in Whose Hands Both Lawful and Unlawful Wealth Accumulate.** If it is not known that the Sultan has any income except from unlawful sources, then it is pure ill-gotten gain (suḥt maḥḍ). But if it is known with certainty that the treasury contains both lawful and unlawful wealth, and it is possible that what is delivered to him specifically is from the lawful — a possibility that is proximate and settles in the soul — and it is also possible that it is from the unlawful, which is the predominant [likelihood] because the majority of the Sultans' wealth in these ages is unlawful, while lawful wealth in their hands is non-existent or scarce — then the people have differed on this. A group said: "Whatever I am not certain is unlawful, I may take it." Others said: "It is not lawful to take anything unless one is certain it is lawful; for no doubtful thing (shubhah) is lawful at all." Both of these are excesses (isrāf). The moderation (iʿtidāl) is what we have already mentioned: namely, the ruling that if the predominant [likelihood] is that it is unlawful, then it is unlawful; and if the predominant is that it is lawful, [then it is lawful]; and if there is certain unlawful [wealth] within it, then it is a place of our suspension (tawaqquf), as has preceded.

Those who permitted taking the wealth of the Sultans when it contains both unlawful and lawful, so long as one is not certain that the specific thing taken is unlawful, have adduced as evidence what is related concerning a group of the Companions (may God be pleased with them) that they lived through the days of the unjust imams and took wealth from them: Abū Hurayrah, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, Zayd ibn Thābit, Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Jābir, Anas ibn Mālik, and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah. Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayrah took from Marwān and Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās took from al-Ḥajjāj. Many of the Followers (tābiʿūn) took from them, such as al-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm, al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Abī Laylā. Al-Shāfiʿī took from Hārūn al-Rashīd one thousand dīnārs in a single payment. Mālik took from the caliphs abundant wealth. And ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) said: "Take what the Sultan gives you, for he only gives you from the lawful, and what he takes from the lawful is more."

As for those who refrained from taking their gifts, they did so only out of scrupulous piety (waraʿ), fearing for their religion lest they be carried to what is not lawful. Do you not see the saying of Abū Dharr to al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays: "Take the stipend as long as it is a free gift (niḥlah); but when it becomes the price of your religion, then leave it." And Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him) said: "When we are given, we accept; and when we are withheld, we do not ask."

It is related from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib that Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him) would remain silent when Muʿāwiyah gave him [something], but if he withheld from him, he would speak against him.

It is related from al-Shaʿbī, from Masrūq: "The stipend will not cease to be with its people until it leads them into the Fire" — meaning that it carries them to the unlawful, not that it is in itself unlawful. And Nāfiʿ related from Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both) that al-Mukhtār used to send him wealth, and he would accept it, then say: "I do not ask anyone for anything, nor do I reject what God has provided me." And a she-camel was gifted to him, and he accepted it — and it was called "the she-camel of al-Mukhtār." But this is counterbalanced by what is related that Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both) did not reject any gift from anyone except the gift of al-Mukhtār — and the chain of transmission for his rejection is more firmly established (athbat).

It is related from Nāfiʿ that he said: Ibn Maʿmar sent to Ibn ʿUmar sixty thousand [dirhams], and he distributed them among the people. Then a beggar came to him, so he borrowed from one of those he had given to, and gave to the beggar.

And when al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī (may God be pleased with them both) came to Muʿāwiyah (may God be pleased with him), he said: "I shall honor you with a gift with which I have honored no Arab before you, and with which I shall honor no Arab after you." He said: So he gave him four hundred thousand dirhams, and he took them.

It is related from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit that he said: "I have indeed seen the gift of al-Mukhtār to Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, and they both accepted it." It was asked: "What was it?" He said: "Wealth and clothing."

It is related from al-Zubayr ibn ʿAdī that he said: Salmān said: "If you have a friend who is an agent (ʿāmil) or a merchant who practices usury (ribā), and he invites you to food or the like, or gives you something, then accept — for the wholesome part (al-mahannaʾ) is for you, and upon him is the sin (wizr)." If this is established concerning the usurer, then the tyrant (ẓālim) is within its meaning.

It is related from Jaʿfar, from his father, that al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn (peace be upon them) used to accept the gifts of Muʿāwiyah.

And Ḥakīm ibn Jubayr said: We passed by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr when he had been appointed as an agent over the Lower Euphrates. He sent to the tithe-collectors (ʿushshār): "Feed us from what you have." They sent him food, and he ate, and we ate with him.

And al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zuhayr al-Azdī said: Ibrāhīm [al-Nakhaʿī] came to my father when he was an agent over Ḥulwān, and he honored him with a gift, and he accepted it. And Ibrāhīm said: "There is no harm in the gift of the agents (juwāʾiz al-ʿummāl), for the agents have their expenses (muʾnah) and their provision (rizq). And into his treasury enters both the foul (khabīth) and the pure (ṭayyib); so what he gives you is from the pure part of his wealth."

All of these took the gifts of the tyrannical Sultans, and all of them censured those who obeyed them in disobedience to God (may He be exalted).

This group claimed that what is transmitted concerning the refusal of a group of the Salaf does not indicate unlawfulness, but rather indicates scrupulous piety (waraʿ) — like the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, Abū Dharr, and other ascetics (zuhhād), for they refrained from the absolutely lawful out of asceticism (zuhd), and from the lawful whose outcome is feared to lead to something prohibited, out of piety and God-consciousness (taqwā). Thus, the boldness of these [who took] indicates permissibility (jawāz), while the refusal of those does not indicate unlawfulness.

And what is transmitted concerning Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib — that he left his stipend in the treasury until it accumulated to thirty-some thousand — and what is transmitted concerning al-Ḥasan — his saying: "I do not perform ablution with the water of a money-changer (ṣayrafī), even if the time of prayer becomes narrow, because I do not know the origin of his wealth" — all of that is piety (waraʿ) that is not to be denied, and following them in it is better than following them in expansion (ittisāʿ). But following them in expansion is not unlawful either.

These, then, are the arguments (shubhah) of those who permit taking the wealth of the tyrannical Sultan.

**The Answer.** What is transmitted concerning the taking of these [Companions] is limited and small in comparison to what is transmitted concerning their rejection and their censure. And even if the possibility of piety (waraʿ) attaches to their refusal, there attach to the taking of those who took three possibilities, differing in degree according to their differing in piety. For piety with respect to the Sultans has four degrees:

**The First Degree:** That one takes nothing at all from their wealth — as the pious among them did, and as the Rightly-Guided Caliphs used to do. So much so that Abū Bakr (may God be pleased with him) calculated all that he had taken from the treasury, which amounted to six thousand dirhams, and he repaid it to the treasury. And so much so that ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) was one day dividing the wealth of the treasury when his daughter entered and took a dirham from the wealth. ʿUmar rose in pursuit of her until the cloak fell from one of his shoulders. The girl entered her family's house weeping, and put the dirham in her mouth. ʿUmar inserted his finger and extracted it from her mouth, and threw it upon the land-tax [pile], and said: "O people, there is nothing for ʿUmar or the family of ʿUmar except what is for the Muslims, their near and their far."

And Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī swept the treasury and found a dirham. He passed by a son of ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) and gave it to him. ʿUmar saw it in the boy's hand and asked him about it. He said: "Abū Mūsā gave it to me." He said: "O Abū Mūsā, was there no household in Medina more contemptible to you than the family of ʿUmar? You intended that there should not remain anyone from the ummah of Muḥammad (peace be upon him) except that we would be sought for an injustice." And he returned the dirham to the treasury.

This was despite the fact that the wealth was lawful — but he feared that he did not deserve that particular amount. So he would clear his religion (yastabriʾ li-dīnihi) and content himself with the least, in compliance with his saying (peace be upon him): {«Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt»} (1), and his saying: {«And whoever abandons it has cleared his honor and his religion»} (2). And because of what he heard from the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) of the severities concerning the wealth of the Sultans — until he (peace be upon him) said, when he sent ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit to collect the alms: "Fear God, O Abū al-Walīd. Do not come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a camel on your neck that grunts, or a cow that lows, or a sheep that bleats." He said: "O Messenger of God, is it so?" He said: "Yes, by Him in Whose hand is my soul — except for him upon whom God has mercy." He said: "Then by Him Who sent you with the truth, I shall never work as an agent for anything ever again." (1)

And he (peace be upon him) said: {«I do not fear for you that you will associate partners with God after me; I only fear for you that you will vie with one another in worldly goods (tanāfus)»} (2). He only feared vying in the final outcome (maʾāl).

And for this reason, ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said in a long hadith in which he mentions the wealth of the treasury: "I have not found myself with respect to it except like the guardian of an orphan's wealth: if I am self-sufficient, I abstain; and if I am in need, I eat from it in a recognized manner (bi-al-maʿrūf)."

And it is related that a son of Ṭāwūs forged a document in his father's name to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and he gave him three hundred dīnārs. So Ṭāwūs sold a property of his and sent to ʿUmar three hundred dīnārs from its price — this despite the fact that the Sultan was not like ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. This, then, is the highest degree of piety.

**The Second Degree:** That one takes the wealth of the Sultan, but only takes it when he knows that what he takes is from a lawful source. The fact that the Sultan's hand contains other unlawful wealth does not harm him. Upon this is to be interpreted all — or most — of what is transmitted of the reports (āthār), or what pertains specifically to the greatest of the Companions and the pious among them — such as Ibn ʿUmar. For he was among the most extreme in piety; how then could he expand [his hand] in the wealth of the Sultan, when he was among the most severe of them in censuring them and the most severe in condemning their wealth? For they gathered before Ibn ʿĀmir while he was in his illness, and he was apprehensive about himself on account of his governorship and his being seized by God (may He be exalted) for it. They said to him: "We indeed hope for good for you: you have dug wells, given water to the pilgrims, and done this and that." Ibn ʿUmar was silent. He said: "What do you say, O Ibn ʿUmar?" He said: "I say that [this is so] when the earning is pure (ṭāba al-maksab) and the expenditure is wholesome (zakat al-nafaqah) — and you shall return [to God] and see." In another hadith, he said: "The foul does not expiate the foul (al-khabīth lā yukaffir al-khabīth), and you have been appointed over Basra, and I do not think you have acquired anything from it but evil." Ibn ʿĀmir said to him: "Will you not pray for me?" Ibn ʿUmar said: "I heard the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) say: {«God does not accept a prayer without purification, nor charity from ill-gotten gain (ghulūl)»} (3) — and you have been appointed over Basra." This is his saying concerning what he [Ibn ʿĀmir] expended upon good works.

And it is related from Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both) that he said in the days of al-Ḥajjāj: "I have not been satiated with food from the day the house was plundered to this day of mine."

And it is related from ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) that he had some barley-gruel (sawīq) in a sealed vessel from which he would drink. It was said to him: "Do you do this in Iraq, with the abundance of its food?" He said: "As for me, I do not seal it because of its vinegar, but I dislike that something be put in it that is not of it, and I dislike that anything other than pure (ṭayyib) enter my belly." This is the familiar [conduct] of them.

And Ibn ʿUmar did not like anything but that it left his possession. Nāfiʿ asked him for thirty thousand, and he said: "I fear that you would acquire the dirhams of Ibn ʿĀmir" — and he was the one who had asked. "Go, you are free." And Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: "There is none of us but that the world inclined him — except Ibn ʿUmar." By this it becomes clear that it cannot be thought of him, and of those who were in his station, that he took wealth he did not know to be lawful.

**The Third Degree:** That one takes what he takes from the Sultan in order to give it in charity to the poor or to distribute it among those who deserve it. For what has no specific owner — this is the ruling of the Sacred Law (sharʿ) concerning it. So if the Sultan, were one not to take from him, would not distribute it and would use it to aid himself in tyranny, then we may say that taking it from him and distributing it is more appropriate than leaving it in his hand. This has been seen by some scholars, and its rationale will come later. Upon this is to be interpreted what most of them took. For this reason, Ibn al-Mubārak said: "Those who take gifts (jawāʾiz) today and adduce Ibn ʿUmar and ʿĀʾishah as evidence — they do not emulate them. For Ibn ʿUmar distributed what he took until he borrowed sixty thousand in his very gathering after its distribution; and ʿĀʾishah did the like; and Jābir ibn Zayd — wealth came to him and he gave it in charity, saying: 'I saw that taking it from them and giving it in charity was more beloved to me than leaving it in their hands.'" And thus did al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) do with what he accepted from Hārūn al-Rashīd: he distributed it among his relatives until he retained not a single grain for himself.

**The Fourth Degree:** That one does not ascertain that it is lawful, nor does he distribute it, but rather retains it — yet he takes from a Sultan whose wealth is predominantly lawful. Such were the caliphs in the time of the Companions (may God be pleased with them) and the Followers after the Rightly-Guided Caliphs; the majority of their wealth was not unlawful. This is indicated by the rationale (taʿlīl) of ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) where he said: "For what he takes from the lawful is more." This is something that a group of scholars has permitted, relying upon the predominant [likelihood]. As for us, we have only suspended [judgment] in this matter with respect to individual persons. And the wealth of the Sultan is more akin to being outside the scope of [definitive] enumeration (al-khurūj ʿan al-ḥaṣr), so it is not far that the ijtihād of a mujtahid might lead to the permissibility of taking what is not known to be unlawful, relying upon the predominant. We have only forbidden it when the majority is unlawful.

So when you understand these degrees, you will realize with certainty that the stipends (idrārāt) of the tyrants in our time do not run in that course, and that they differ from it in two decisive respects (wajhān qāṭiʿān):

**The First Respect:** The wealth of the Sultans in our age is entirely unlawful, or for the most part. And how could it not be? For the lawful [sources] — the alms (ṣadaqāt), the fayʾ, and the spoils (ghanīmah) — have no existence [today], and nothing from them enters the hand of the Sultan. Nothing remains except the poll-tax (jizyah) — and it is taken by various kinds of tyranny by which it is not lawful to take it. For they transgress the limits of the Sacred Law in what is taken, in the one from whom it is taken, and in fulfilling the condition [of protection] for him. Then, when you compare that to what flows to them from the land-tax (kharāj) imposed upon the Muslims, from confiscations (muṣādarāt), from bribes (rishā), and from the kinds of tyranny — it does not amount to a tenth of a tenth of a tenth (ʿushr ʿushār ʿushīrihi).

**The Second Respect:** The tyrants of the first age, by virtue of their proximity to the era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, were conscious of their tyranny and eager to win the hearts of the Companions and Followers, and desirous that they accept their gifts and presents. They would send to them without their asking and without humiliation — rather, they would consider it a favor (minnah) upon themselves that [the gifts] were accepted, and they would rejoice in it. And [the recipients] would take from them and distribute, and would not obey the Sultans in their aims, nor frequent their assemblies, nor multiply their gatherings, nor love their survival. Rather, they would supplicate against them, speak freely against them, and censure their wrongdoings. So there was no fear that they would gain from their religion in proportion to what they gained from their world, and no harm would befall them [for refusing].

But as for now, the souls of the Sultans do not permit a gift except to one in whom they hope to employ [as a tool], to multiply their numbers, to seek aid in their aims, to adorn themselves with his frequenting of their assemblies, and to burden him with the obligation of continuous supplication, praise, commendation, and flattery in their presence and absence. So if the taker did not humble himself — first by asking, second by attending upon service, third by praise and supplication, fourth by assisting them in their aims when sought, fifth by multiplying their numbers in his assembly and procession, sixth by displaying love, allegiance, and support for them against their enemies, and seventh by covering up their tyranny, their repugnant acts, and the evils of their deeds — he would not be graced with a single dirham, even if he were of the virtue of al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him), for example.

Therefore, it is not permissible to take from them in this age what is known to be lawful, because it leads to these [evil] meanings. How then [can one take] what is known to be unlawful, or what is doubtful? Whoever dares upon their wealth and likens himself to the Companions and Followers has compared the angels to the blacksmiths (qāsa al-malāʾikah bi-al-ḥaddādīn).

For in taking wealth from them there is a need for mixing with them, observing their [wishes], serving their agents, enduring humiliation from them, praising them, and frequenting their doors — and all of that is disobedience (maʿṣiyah), as we shall explain in the chapter that follows this one.

So when it has become clear from what has preceded the entry-points (madākhil) of their wealth, and what of it is lawful and what is not — if one could imagine a person taking from it what is lawful, to the extent of his entitlement, while he sits in his house and it is conveyed to him, without needing to attend upon an agent or serve him, nor to praise them or commend them, nor to assist them — then the taking is not unlawful, but it is disliked (makrūh) for reasons upon which we shall alert in the chapter that follows this one.

chapters.title_en: The Second Consideration of This Chapter: On the Measure of What Is Taken and the Description of the Taker
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||||  النظر الثاني من هذا الباب في قدر المأخوذ وصفة الآخذ
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-خ-ذ (ʾ-kh-dh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to take, seize, grasp" — both physically and metaphorically, implying acquisition with intent and agency.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-ʾakhdh denotes the act of receiving or appropriating something, often with moral or legal consequence (e.g., taking what is due or forbidden).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical seizure; metaphorical (majāz) extends to "taking" in the sense of accepting a ruling, measure, or condition.
- Root: ق-د-ر (q-d-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes measure, extent, capacity, or decree — the precise quantity or limit of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, qadr relates to divine decree and also to the moral quantification of actions (e.g., the lawful amount in transactions or alms).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical measurement; metaphorical: the normative limit set by sacred law (ḥadd sharʿī).
- Root: و-ص-ف (w-ṣ-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To describe, attribute, or qualify — the act of delineating characteristics.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theology, ṣifah (attribute) is a technical term for the qualities of an entity, here applied to the moral and legal character of the taker.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: verbal depiction; metaphorical: the ethical or juridical qualification of a person's conduct.
- Sībawayh Rule: **Al-Idāfah (Construct State)** — The phrase "قدر المأخوذ وصفة الآخذ" uses two genitive constructs (muḍāf ilayh), where the first noun (qadr, ṣifah) is grammatically indefinite but semantically specified by the following definite noun, indicating a precise, context-bound determination.
chapters.translation: I say: The second consideration of this chapter concerns the measure of what is taken (qadr al-maʾkhūdh) and the description of the taker (ṣifat al-ākhidh).

chapters.title_en: On the Disposition of Public Treasury Funds and the Rights of Those Entitled Thereto
chapters.arabic_text:
ولنفرض المال من أموال المصالح كأربعة أخماس الفيء والمواريث فإن ما عداه
مما قد تعين مستحقه إن كان من وقف أو صدقة أو خمس فيء أو خمس غنيمة وما كان
من ملك السلطان مما أحياه أو اشتراه فله أن يعطي
PageV02P139
ما شاء لمن شاء
وإنما النظر في الأموال الضائعة ومال المصالح فلا يجوز صرفه إلا إلى من
فيه مصلحة عامة أو هو محتاج إليه عاجز عن الكسب فأما الغني الذي لا مصلحة
فيه فلا يجوز صرف مال من بيت المال إليه هذا هو الصحيح وإن كان العلماء قد
اختلفوا فيه
وفي كلام عمر رضي الله عنه ما يدل على أن لكل مسلم حقا في بيت المال
لكونه مسلما مكثرا جمع الإسلام ولكنه مع هذا ما كان يقسم المال على
المسلمين كافة بل على مخصوصين بصفات
فإذا ثبت هذا فكل من يتولى أمرا يقوم به تتعدى مصلحته إلى المسلمين ولو
اشتغل بالكسب لتعطل عليه ما هو فيه فله في بيت المال حق الكفاية
ويدخل فيه العلماء كلهم أعني العلوم التي تتعلق بمصالح الدين من علم
الفقه والحديث والتفسير والقراءة حتى يدخل فيه المعلمون والمؤذنون
وطلبة هذه العلوم أيضا يدخلون فيه فإنهم إن لم يكفوا لم يتمكنوا من الطلب
ويدخل فيه العمال وهم الذين ترتبط مصالح الدنيا بأعمالهم وهم الأجناد
المرتزقة الذين يحرسون المملكة بالسيوف عن أهل العداوة وأهل البغي وأعداء
الإسلام
ويدخل فيه الكتاب والحساب والوكلاء وكل من يحتاج إليه في ترتيب ديوان
الخراج أعني العمال على الأموال الحلال لا على الحرام فإن هذا المال
للمصالح
والمصلحة إما أن تتعلق بالدين أو بالدنيا فبالعلماء حراسة الدين
وبالأجناد حراسة الدنيا
والدين والملك توأمان فلا يستغني أحدهما عن الآخر
والطبيب وإن كان لا يرتبط بعلمه أمر ديني ولكن يرتبط به صحة الجسد والدين
يتبعه فيجوز أن يكون له ولمن يجري مجراه في العلوم المحتاج إليها في مصلحة
الأبدان أو مصلحة البلاد إدرار من هذه الأموال ليتفرغوا لمعالجة المسلمين
أعني من يعالج منهم بغير أجرة وليس يشترط في هؤلاء الحاجة بل يجوز أن يعطوا
مع من  الغنى
فإن الخلفاء الراشدين كانوا يعطون المهاجرين والأنصار ولم يعرفوا بالحاجة
وليس يتقدر أيضا بمقدار بل هو إلى اجتهاد الإمام وله أن يوسع ويغني وله
أن يقتصر على الكفاية على ما يقتضيه الحال وسعة المال
فقد أخذ الحسن عليه السلام من معاوية في دفعة واحدة أربعمائة ألف درهم
وقد كان عمر رضي الله عنه يعطي لجماعة اثني عشر ألف درهم نقرة في السنة
وأثبتت عائشة رضي الله عنها في هذه الجريدة ولجماعة عشرة آلاف ولجماعة
ستة آلاف وهكذا
فهذا مال هؤلاء فيوزع عليهم حتى لا يبقى منه شيء
فإن خص واحدا منه بمال كثير فلا بأس
وكذلك للسلطان أن يخص من هذا المال ذوي الخصائص بالخلع والجوائز فقد كان
يفعل ذلك في السلف ولكن ينبغي أن يلتفت فيه إلى المصلحة
ومهما خص عالم أو شجاع بصلة كان فيه بعث للناس وتحريض على الاشتغال
والتشبه به فهذه فائدة الخلع والصلات وضروب التخصيصات وكل ذلك منوط باجتهاد
السلطان
وإنما النظر في السلاطين الظلمة في شيئين أحدهما أن السلطان الظالم عليه
أن يكف عن ولايته وهو إما معزول أو واجب العزل فكيف يجوز أن يأخذ من يده
وهو على التحقيق ليس بسلطان والثاني أنه ليس يعمم بماله جميع المستحقين
فكيف يجوز للآحاد أن يأخذوا أفيجوز لهم الأخذ بقدر حصصهم أم لا يجوز أصلا
أم يجوز أن يأخذ كل واحد ما أعطى
أما الأول: فالذي نراه أنه لا يمنع أخذ الحق لأن السلطان الظالم الجاهل
مهما ساعدته الشوكة وعسر خلعه وكان في الاستبدال به فتنة ثائرة لا تطاق وجب
تركه ووجبت الطاعة له كما تجب طاعة الأمراء إذ قد ورد في الأمر بطاعة
الأمراء (1)
والمنع من سل اليد عن مساعدتهم // حديث المنع من سل اليد عن مساعدتهم
أخرجه الشيخان من حديث ابن عباس ليس أحد يفارق الجماعة شبرا فيموت إلا مات
ميتة جاهلية ولمسلم من حديث أبي هريرة من خرج من الطاعة وفارق الجماعة فمات
مات ميتة جاهلية وله من حديث ابن عمر من  خلع يدا من طاعة لقي الله يوم
القيامة ولا حجة له
أوامر وزواجر
فالذي نراه أن الخلافة منعقدة للمتكفل PageV02P140
بها من بني العباس رضي الله عنه
وأن الولاية نافذة للسلاطين في أقطار البلاد والمبايعين للخليفة وقد
ذكرنا في كتاب المستظهري المستنبط من كتاب كشف الأسرار وهتك الأستار تأليف
القاضي أبي الطيب في الرد على أصناف الروافض من الباطنية ما يشير إلى وجه
المصلحة فيه والقول الوجيز أنا نراعي الصفات والشروط في السلاطين تشوفا إلى
مزايا المصالح
ولو قضينا ببطلان الولايات الآن لبطلت المصالح رأسا فكيف يفوت رأس المال
في طلب الربح بل الولاية الآن لا تتبع إلا الشوكة
فمن بايعه صاحب الشوكة فهو الخليفة
ومن استبد بالشوكة وهو مطيع للخليفة في أصل الخطبة والسكة فهو سلطان نافذ
الحكم والقضاء في أقطار الأرض ولاية نافذة الأحكام
وتحقيق هذا قد ذكرناه في أحكام الإمامة من كتاب الاقتصاد في الاعتقاد
فلسنا نطول الآن به
وأما الإشكال الآخر وهو أن السلطان إذا لم يعمم بالعطاء كل مستحق فهل
يجوز للواحد أن يأخذ منه فهذا مما اختلف العلماء فيه على أربع مراتب فغلا
بعضهم
وقال كل ما يأخذه فالمسلمون كلهم فيه شركاء ولا يدري أن حصته منه دانق أو
حبة فليترك الكل وقال قوم له أن يأخذ قدر قوت يومه فقط فإن هذا القدر
يستحقه لحاجته على المسلمين وقال قوم له قوت سنة فإن أخذ الكفاية كل يوم
عسير وهو ذو حق في هذا المال فكيف يتركه وقال قوم
وقال قوم إنه يأخذ ما يعطى والمظلوم هم الباقون
وهذا هو القياس لأن المال ليس مشتركا بين المسلمين كالغنيمة بين الغانمين
ولا كالميراث بين الورثة لأن ذلك صار ملكا لهم
وهذا لو لم يتفق قسمه حتى مات هؤلاء لم يجب التوزيع على ورثتهم بحكم
الميراث
بل هذا الحق غير متعين وإنما يتعين بالقبض
بل هو كالصدقات ومهما أعطي الفقراء حصتهم من الصدقات وقع ذلك ملكا لهم
ولم يمتنع بظلم المالك بقية الأصناف بمنع حقهم هذا إذا  لم يصرف إليه كل
المال بل صرف إليه من المال ما لو صرف إليه بطريق الإيثار والتفضيل مع
تعميم الآخرين لجاز له أن يأخذه والتفضيل جائز في العطاء
سوى أبو بكر رضي الله عنه فراجعه عمر رضي الله عنه فقال إنما فضلهم عند
الله وإنما الدنيا بلاغ
وفضل عمر رضي الله عنه في زمانه فأعطى عائشة اثني عشر ألفا وزينب عشرة
آلاف وجويرية ستة آلاف وكذا صفية
وأقطع عمر لعلي خاصة رضي الله عنهما
وأقطع عثمان أيضا من السواد خمس جنات وآثر عثمان عليا رضي الله عنهما بها
فقبل ذلك منه ولم ينكر
وكل ذلك جائز في محل الاجتهاد وهو من المجتهدات التي أقول فيها إن كل
مجتهد مصيب وهي كل مسألة لا نص على عينها ولا على مسألة تقرب منها فتكون في
معناها بقياس جلي كهذه المسألة ومسألة حد الشرب فإنهم جلدوا أربعين وثمانين
والكل سنة وحق وأن كل واحد من أبي بكر وعمر رضي الله عنهما مصيب باتفاق
الصحابة رضي الله عنهم إذ المفضول ما رد في زمان عمر شيئا إلى الفاضل مما
قد كان أخذه في زمان أبي بكر ولا الفاضل امتنع من قبول الفضل في زمان عمر
واشترك في ذلك كل الصحابة واعتقدوا أن كل واحد من الرأيين حق
فليؤخذ هذا الجنس دستورا للخلافات التي يصوب فيها كل مجتهد
فأما كل مسألة شذ عن مجتهد فيها نص أو قياس جلي بغفلة أو سوء رأي وكان في
القوة بحيث ينقض حكم المجتهد فلا نقول فيها إن كل واحد مصيب بل المصيب من
أصاب النص أو ما في معنى النص
وقد تحصل من مجموع هذا أن من وجد من أهل الخصوص الموصوفين بصفة تتعلق بها
مصالح الدين أو الدنيا وأخذ من السلطان خلعة أو إدرارا على التركات أو
الجزية لم يصر فاسقا بمجرد أخذه وإنما يفسق بخدمته لهم ومعانته إياهم
ودخوله
PageV02P141
عليهم وثنائه وإطرائه لهم إلى غير ذلك من لوازم لا يسلم المال غالبا إلا
بها كما سنبينه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ي-ء (fayʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, restoration; that which returns to the community from enemy property without warfare
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely-designated public revenue category distinct from ghanīmah (spoils of war)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its technical legal sense (ḥaqīqah sharʿiyyah), not metaphorical
- Root: م-ص-ل-ح-ة (maṣlaḥah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That which is sound, upright, beneficial; the opposite of corruption (fasād)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Public welfare as a recognized legal consideration in discretionary governance
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Here denotes the collective interest of the Muslim polity, a technical usage
- Root: ك-ف-ا-ي-ة (kifāyah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sufficiency, that which suffices for one's needs
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The guaranteed subsistence right of those engaged in public service
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of adequacy; not extravagance nor destitution
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the precise scope of permissibility and prohibition in legal reasoning
chapters.translation:
I say: Let us posit the wealth [in question] as being from the funds of public interests (amwāl al-maṣāliḥ), such as four-fifths of the fayʾ (public revenue) and inheritances [with no designated heirs]. For whatever falls outside this — when its rightful recipient has been specifically determined, whether it be from a waqf (endowment), a ṣadaqah (charity), a fifth of the fayʾ, or a fifth of the ghanīmah (spoils) — and whatever belongs to the Sultan's private property, whether he has revived dead land or purchased it, he may give thereof what he wills to whom he wills.

PageV02P139

The consideration here pertains only to the lost funds and the monies of public interests. Such funds may not be disbursed except to one in whom there is a general public benefit, or who is in need of it and incapable of earning. As for the wealthy person in whom there is no public benefit, it is not permissible to disburse treasury funds to him. This is the correct position, even though the scholars have differed concerning it.

In the statement of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) there is an indication that every Muslim has a right in the treasury by virtue of being a Muslim who has multiplied the numbers of Islam. Nevertheless, he did not divide the wealth among all Muslims collectively, but rather among those specifically distinguished by certain qualities.

Now that this is established: whoever undertakes an affair whose benefit extends to the Muslims — such that were he to occupy himself with earning a livelihood, that [public function] would be neglected — he has a right of sufficiency (ḥaqq al-kifāyah) in the treasury.

Included in this category are all the scholars — I mean those [possessing] sciences pertaining to the interests of religion: the science of jurisprudence (fiqh), ḥadīth, exegesis (tafsīr), and Qurʾanic recitation. Even the teachers, the muʾadhdhins (callers to prayer), and the students of these sciences are included therein, for if they are not provided for, they cannot devote themselves to seeking knowledge.

Also included are the workers (al-ʿummāl) — those upon whose labors the worldly interests depend — namely the salaried soldiers (al-ajnād al-murtaziqah) who guard the realm with swords against the people of enmity, the people of transgression, and the enemies of Islam.

Also included are the scribes, the accountants, the agents, and everyone needed for the organization of the revenue bureau (dīwān al-kharāj) — I mean the workers over the lawful funds, not the unlawful, for this wealth is for public interests.

The public interest (al-maṣlaḥah) pertains either to religion or to the world. By the scholars is the guarding of religion, and by the soldiers is the guarding of the world. Religion and sovereignty (al-mulk) are twins; neither is independent of the other.

As for the physician — although no religious matter is connected to his knowledge, yet bodily health is connected to it, and religion follows the body — it is permissible that he, and those like him in the sciences needed for the welfare of bodies or the welfare of lands, receive a stipend (idrār) from these funds, so that they may devote themselves to treating the Muslims — I mean those among them who treat without fee. Need is not a condition for these; rather, they may be given even with wealth.

For the rightly-guided caliphs (al-khulafāʾ al-rāshidūn) used to give to the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār without their being known for neediness. Nor is it limited to a fixed amount; rather, it is left to the ijtihād (independent judgment) of the Imām. He may be generous and enrich, or he may restrict himself to sufficiency, according to what the circumstances and the abundance of the wealth require.

Indeed, al-Ḥasan (peace be upon him) took from Muʿāwiyah in a single payment four hundred thousand dirhams. And ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to give some groups twelve thousand dirhams of pure silver annually. ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) was inscribed in this register, as were some groups with ten thousand and others with six thousand — and so on.

This, then, is the wealth of these [recipients]; it is distributed among them until nothing remains of it. If one person is singled out with a large amount, there is no harm in that.

Likewise, the Sultan may single out from this wealth those with special distinctions with robes of honor (khilaʿ) and gifts (jawāʾiz). This was done among the early generations (al-salaf). However, one should have regard therein for the public interest. Whenever a scholar or a brave man is singled out with a gift, there is in that an encouragement of the people and a stimulation toward engagement [in such pursuits] and emulation of him. This, then, is the benefit of robes of honor, gifts, and various kinds of special allocations — and all of that is entrusted to the ijtihād of the Sultan.

The consideration regarding tyrannical rulers (al-salāṭīn al-ẓalamah) concerns two matters. The first: the tyrannical ruler is obligated to refrain from his governorship — he is either already deposed or obligated to be deposed — so how can it be permissible to take from his hand when, in reality, he is not a ruler? The second: he does not distribute his wealth to all those entitled — so how can it be permissible for individuals to take from him? Is it permissible for them to take the amount of their shares, or is it not permissible at all, or is it permissible for each one to take what he is given?

As for the first: what we hold is that taking one's right is not prohibited. For when the tyrannical ignorant ruler is supported by military might (shawkah), his removal is difficult, and replacing him would ignite an unbearable conflagration of strife (fitnah), then it is obligatory to leave him [in place] and obligatory to obey him, just as obedience to commanders is obligatory.
