ابتداء فتجب مقاطعته انتهاء لأن الحكم إذا ثبت بعلة فالقياس أن يزول
بزوالها وعلة عقد الأخوة التعاون في الدين ولا يستمر ذلك مم مقارفة المعصية
فأقول أما كونه ألطف فلما فيه من الرفق والاستمالة والتعطف المفضي إلى
الرجوع والتوبة لاستمرار الحياء عند دوام الصحبة ومهما قوطع وانقطع طمعه عن
الصحبة أصر واستمر
وأما كونه أفقه فمن حيث إن الأخوة عقد ينزل منزلة القرابة فإذا انعقدت
تأكد الحق ووجب الوفاء بموجب العقد ومن الوفاء به أن لا يهمل أيام حاجته
وفقره وفقر الدين أشد من فقر المال وقد أصابته جائحة وألمت به آفة افتقر
بسببها في دينه فينبغي أن يراقب ويراعي ولا يهمل بل لا يزال يتلطف به ليعان
على الخلاص من تلك الوقعة التي ألمت به
فالأخوة عدة للنائبات وحوادث الزمان وهذا من أشد النوائب والفاجر إذا صحب
تقيا وهو ينظر إلى خوفه ومداومته فسيرجع على قرب ويستحي من الإصرار بل
الكسلان يصحب الحريص في العمل فيحرص حياء منه
قال جعفر بن سليمان مهما فترت في العمل نظرت إلى محمد بن واسع وإقباله
على الطاعة فيرجع إلي نشاطي في العبادة وفارقني الكسل وعملت عليه أسبوعا
وهذا التحقيق وهو أن الصداقة لحمة كلحمة النسب والقريب لا يجوز أن يهجر
بالمعصية ولذلك قال الله تعالى لنبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم في عشيرته {فإن
عصوك فقل إني بريء مما تعملون} ولم يقل إني بريء منكم مراعاة لحق القرابة
ولحمة النسب
وإلى هذا أشار أبو الدرداء لما قيل له ألا تبغض أخاك وقد فعل كذا فقال
إنما أبغض عمله وإلا فهو أخي وأخوة الدين أوكد من أخوة القرابة
ولذلك قيل لحكيم أيما احب إليك أخوك أو صديقك فقال إنما أحب أخي إذا كان
صديقا لي
وكان الحسن  يقول كم من أخ لم تلده أمك ولذلك قيل
PageV02P184
القرابة تحتاج إلى مودة والمودة لا تحتاج إلى قرابة وقال جعفر الصادق رضي
الله عنه مودة يوم صلة ومودة شهر قرابة ومودة سنة رحم مائية من قطعها قطعه
الله
فإذن الوفاء بعقد الأخوة إذا سبق انعقادها واجب
وهذا جوابنا عن ابتداء المؤاخاة مع الفاسق فإنه لم يتقدم له حق فإن تقدمت
له قرابة فلا جرم لا ينبغي أن يقاطع بل يجامل
والدليل عليه أن ترك المؤاخاة والصحبة ابتداء ليس مذموما ولا مكروها بل
قال قائلون الانفراد أولى فأما قطع الأخوة عن دوامها فمنهي عنه ومذموم في
نفسه ونسبته إلى تركها ابتداء كنسبة الطلاق إلى ترك النكاح والطلاق أبغض
إلى الله تعالى من ترك النكاح قال صلى الله عليه وسلم شرار عباد الله
المشاءون بالنميمة المفرقون بين الأحبة (1)
وقال بعض السلف في ستر زلات الإخوان ود الشيطان أن يلقى على أخيكم مثل
هذا حتى تهجروه وتقطعوه فماذا اتقيتم من محبة عدوكم
وهذا لأن التفريق بين الأحباب من محاب الشيطان كما أن مقارفة العصيان من
محابه فإذا حصل للشيطان أحد غرضيه فلا ينبغي أن يضاف إليه الثاني وإلى هذا
أشار عليه السلام في الذي شتم الرجل الذي أتى فاحشة إذ قال مه وزبره وقال
لا تكونوا عونا للشيطان على أخيكم (2)
فبهذا كله يتبين الفرق بين الدوام والابتداء لأن مخالطة الفساق محذورة
ومفارقة الأحباب والإخوان أيضا محذورة وليس من سلم عن معارضة غيره كالذي لم
يسلم وفي الابتداء قد سلم فرأينا أن المهاجرة والتباعد هو الأولى وفي
الدوام تعارضا فكان الوفاء بحق الأخوة أولى هذا كله في زلته في دينه
أما زلته في حقه بما يوجب إيحاشه فلا خلاف في أن الأولى العفو والاحتمال
بل كل ما يحتمل تنزيله على وجه حسن ويتصور تمهيد عذر فيه قريب أو بعيد فهو
واجب بحق الأخوة فقد قيل ينبغي أن تستنبط لزلة أخيك سبعين عذرا فإن لم
يقبله قلبك فرد اللوم على نفسك فتقول لقلبك ما أقساك  يعتذر إليك أخوك سبعين
عذرا فلا تقبله فأنت المعيب لا أخوك فإن ظهر بحيث لم يقبل التحسين فينبغي
أن لا تغضب إن قدرت ولكن ذلك لا يمكن وقد قال الشافعي رحمه الله من استغضب
فلم يغضب فهو حمار ومن استرضى فلم يرضى فهو شيطان
فلا تكن حمارا ولا شيطانا واسترض قلبك بنفسك نيابة عن أخيك واحترز أن
تكون شيطانا إن لم تقبل
قال الأحنف حق الصديق أن تحتمل منه ثلاثا ظلم الغضب وظلم الدالة وظلم
الهفوة
وقال آخر ما شتمت أحدا قط لأنه إن شتمني كريم فأنا أحق من غفرها له أو
لئيم فلا أجعل عرضي له غرضا ثم تمثل وقال
وأغفر عوراء الكريم ادخاره ... وأعرض عن شتم اللئيم تكرما
وقد قيل
خذ من خليلك ما صفا ... ودع الذي فيه الكدر
فالعمر أقصر من معا ... تبة الخليل على الغير
ومهما اعتذر إليك أخوك كاذبا كان أو صادقا فاقبل عذره
قال عليه السلام من اعتذر إليه أخوه فلم يقبل عذره فعليه مثل إثم صاحب
المكس (3)
وقال عليه السلام المؤمن سريع الغضب سريع الرضا (4)
فلم يصفه بأنه PageV02P185
لا يغضب
وكذلك قال الله تعالى والكاظمين الغيظ ولم يقل والفاقدين الغيظ وهذا لأن
العادة لا تنتهي إلى أن يجرح الإنسان فلا يتألم بل تنتهي إلى أن يصبر عليه
ويحتمل وكما أن التألم بالجرح مقتضى طبع البدن فالتألم بأسباب الغضب طبع
القلب ولا يمكن قلعه ولكن ضبطه وكظمه والعمل بخلاف مقتضاه فإنه يقتضي
التشفي والانتقام والمكافأة وترك العمل بمقتضاه ممكن وقد قال الشاعر
ولست بمستبق أخا لا تلمه ... على شعث أي الرجال المهذب
قال أبو سليمان الداراني لأحمد بن أبي الحواري إذا واخيت أحدا في هذا
الزمان فلا تعاتبه على ما تكرهه فإنك لا تأمن من أن ترى في جوابك ما هو شر
من الأول قال فجربته فوجدته كذلك
وقال بعضهم الصبر على مضض الأخ خير من معاتبته والمعاتبة خير من القطيعة
والقطيعة خير من الوقيعة
وينبغي أن لا يبالغ في البغضة عند الوقيعة
قال  الله تعالى {عسى الله أن يجعل بينكم وبين الذين عاديتم منهم مودة}
وقال عليه السلام أحبب حبيبك هونا ما عسى أن يكون بغيضك يوما ما وأبغض
بغيضك هونا ما عسى أن يكون حبيبك يوما ما (1)
وقال عمر رضي الله عنه لا يكن حبك كلفا ولا بغضك تلفا وهو أن تحب تلف
صاحبك مع هلاكك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ه ف و (hafā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A slip, error, or stumble; the act of faltering from rectitude.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral lapse (zallah) that deviates from the straight path (istiqāmah), distinct from deliberate rebellion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical stumble; metaphorical (majāz) for a moral transgression requiring forbearance.
- Root: ق ط ع (qaṭʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cut off, sever, or break a connection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Severance of the bond of brotherhood (ukhuwwah), contrasted with the obligation of wafāʾ (fidelity).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical cutting; metaphorical for social and spiritual rupture.
- Root: و ف ي (wafā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Fulfillment, completion, loyalty to a covenant.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The obligatory fulfillment of contractual bonds, including the covenant of brotherhood.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for paying a debt in full; metaphorical for honoring moral commitments.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Distinguishing the legal ruling for initiating brotherhood (ibtidāʾ) versus maintaining it (dawām), where the conditional clause governs the apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The lapse of a friend is either in his religion, by committing a disobedience, or in your right, by his shortcoming in brotherhood.

As for what is in the religion, from committing a disobedience and persisting upon it, it is upon you to be gentle in advising him, by that which straightens his crookedness, gathers his scattered affairs, and returns his state to righteousness and piety. If you are unable, and he remains persistent, then the paths of the Companions and the Followers have differed regarding the continuation of the right of his love or severing him.

Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) held the view of severance, and said: "When your brother turns away from what he was upon, then hate him from the very place you loved him." He saw this as a requirement of love for Allah's sake and hatred for Allah's sake.

As for Abū al-Dardāʾ and a group of the Companions, they held the contrary view. Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "When your brother changes and turns from what he was upon, do not abandon him for that reason, for your brother bends one time and straightens another."

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said: "Do not sever your brother, nor abandon him for a sin he commits, for he commits it today and leaves it tomorrow." He also said: "Do not relate to the people the slip of the scholar, for the scholar slips a slip, then leaves it." In the report: "Beware of the slip of the scholar, but do not sever him, and await his return."

In the ḥadīth of ʿUmar, he had asked about a brother he had made a brother of, who had gone out to Syria. He asked about him one of those who arrived from there, and said: "What has my brother done?" He said: "That one is the brother of Satan." He said: "Gently!" He said: "He has committed the major sins until he fell into wine." He said: "When you intend to go out, inform me." So when he went out, he wrote to him: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. {«Ḥā Mīm. The revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the Knowing, the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, the Severe in punishment»} — the verse. Then he reproached him beneath it and rebuked him. When he read the letter, he wept and said: "Allah has spoken truly, and ʿUmar has advised me sincerely." So he repented and returned.

It is narrated that two brothers were afflicted, one of them with a passion. His brother showed him his state and said: "I have been stricken with an ailment. If you wish not to bind your companionship with me for Allah's sake, then do so." He said: "I would never dissolve the bond of your brotherhood for the sake of your sin, ever." Then his brother bound himself before Allah not to eat or drink until Allah cured his brother of his passion. He fasted forty days, in all of which he asked him about his passion, and he would say: "The heart remains upon its state." He continued wasting away from grief and hunger until the passion departed from his brother's heart after the forty. He informed him of that, and he ate and drank after he had nearly perished from emaciation and harm.

Likewise, it is narrated of two brothers from the Salaf that one of them turned from uprightness. It was said to his brother: "Will you not sever him and abandon him?" He said: "He is most in need of me at this very time — when he has fallen into his stumble — that I take his hand, be gentle with him in reproach, and pray for his return to what he was upon."

It is related in the Israʾīliyyāt that two worshipping brothers were on a mountain. One of them descended to buy meat from the city for a dirham. He saw a prostitute near the butcher, gazed at her, fell in love with her, drew her to a secluded place, and lay with her. Then he stayed with her for three days, and was too ashamed to return to his brother, out of shame for his offense. He said: His brother missed him and was concerned about his affair. He descended to the city and kept asking about him until he was guided to him. He entered upon him while he was sitting with her, embraced him, and began kissing him and clinging to him. The other denied that he knew him at all, out of extreme shame before him. He said: "Arise, my brother, for I have known your affair and your story, and you have never been more beloved to me nor dearer than at this hour of yours." When he saw that this had not dropped him from his eye, he arose and departed with him.

This is the way of a people, and it is more subtle and more discerning than the way of Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), though his way is more excellent and safer.

If you say: "Why do you say this is more subtle and more discerning? The one who commits this disobedience is not permissible to take as a brother in the first place, so severance is obligatory in the end, because when a ruling is established by a cause, by analogy it is removed by its removal. The cause of the bond of brotherhood is mutual assistance in religion, and that does not continue with the commission of disobedience."

I say: As for its being more subtle, it is due to what it contains of gentleness, attraction, and compassion that leads to return and repentance, through the continuation of shame with the continuation of companionship. Whenever he is severed and his hope for companionship is cut off, he persists and continues.

As for its being more discerning, it is from the perspective that brotherhood is a bond that holds the station of kinship. When it is contracted, the right is affirmed, and fulfillment of what the contract requires becomes obligatory. From fulfillment of it is that one does not neglect his days of need and poverty — and the poverty of religion is more severe than the poverty of wealth. A calamity has befallen him, and an affliction has struck him, by which he has become poor in his religion. He should be watched over and cared for, not neglected. Rather, one should continue to be gentle with him, so that he may be aided toward deliverance from that fall which has struck him.

For brotherhood is a provision for calamities and the vicissitudes of time, and this is among the severest of calamities. The wicked one, when he accompanies a God-fearing man and sees his fear and his perseverance, will soon return and be ashamed of persistence. Nay, the lazy one accompanies the diligent in work, and becomes diligent out of shame before him.

Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān said: "Whenever I slackened in work, I looked at Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ and his devotion to obedience, and my vigor in worship returned to me, laziness departed from me, and I worked upon that for a week."

This is the verification: that friendship is a bond like the bond of lineage, and the relative is not to be abandoned for a disobedience. For this reason, Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet (peace be upon him) regarding his kinsfolk: {«Then if they disobey you, say: I am innocent of what you do»} — and He did not say: "I am innocent of you," observing the right of kinship and the bond of lineage.

To this Abū al-Dardāʾ pointed when it was said to him: "Will you not hate your brother, for he has done such-and-such?" He said: "I only hate his deed. Otherwise, he is my brother, and the brotherhood of religion is more firmly established than the brotherhood of lineage."

For this reason, it was said to a sage: "Which is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He said: "I only love my brother when he is a friend to me."

Al-Ḥasan used to say: "How many a brother has your mother not borne!" For this reason, it was said: "Kinship needs affection, but affection needs no kinship." Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The affection of a day is a connection, the affection of a month is kinship, and the affection of a year is a blood-relative womb — whoever severs it, Allah severs him."

Therefore, fidelity to the bond of brotherhood, when its contraction has preceded, is obligatory.

This is our answer regarding the initiation of brotherhood with the wicked one, for no right has preceded from him. But if kinship has preceded, then by no means should he be severed; rather, he should be treated with courtesy.

The proof of this is that refraining from brotherhood and companionship in the first place is neither blameworthy nor disliked. Nay, some have said that solitude is preferable. As for severing brotherhood after its continuation, it is prohibited and blameworthy in itself. Its relation to refraining from it in the first place is like the relation of divorce to refraining from marriage — and divorce is more hateful to Allah the Exalted than refraining from marriage. He (peace be upon him) said: "The worst of Allah's servants are those who go about with slander, separating between loved ones."

Some of the Salaf said regarding concealing the slips of brothers: "It is the wish of Satan that such a thing be cast upon your brother, so that you abandon him and sever him. So what have you guarded against from the love of your enemy?"

This is because separating between loved ones is among the beloved things of Satan, just as the commission of disobedience is among his beloved things. So when one of his two aims is achieved for Satan, the second should not be added to it. To this the Prophet (peace be upon him) pointed in the case of the man who reviled the man who had committed an indecency, when he said: "Gently!" and rebuked him, saying: "Do not be helpers of Satan against your brother."

By all this, the difference between continuation and initiation becomes clear. For mixing with the wicked is to be guarded against, and parting from loved ones and brothers is also to be guarded against. The one who is safe from the opposition of others is not like the one who is not safe. In initiation, one is safe, so we saw that separation and distance are preferable. In continuation, the two oppose each other, so fidelity to the right of brotherhood is more fitting.

All this concerns his slip in his religion.

As for his slip regarding your right, by that which necessitates estrangement, there is no disagreement that forgiveness and forbearance are preferable. Nay, everything that can be interpreted in a good manner, and for which an excuse, near or far, can be conceived, is obligatory by the right of brotherhood. For it has been said: "You should seek out for your brother's slip seventy excuses. If your heart does not accept it, then return the blame upon yourself, and say to your heart: 'How hard-hearted you are! Your brother excuses himself to you with seventy excuses, and you do not accept it. So you are the blameworthy one, not your brother.'"

If it becomes apparent in such a way that it cannot be interpreted favorably, then one should not become angry if one is able. But that is not possible. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Whoever is provoked to anger and does not become angry is a donkey, and whoever is appeased and does not become satisfied is a devil." So do not be a donkey nor a devil. Appease your heart yourself, on behalf of your brother, and beware of being a devil if you do not accept.

Al-Aḥnaf said: "The right of a friend is that you bear from him three things: the injustice of anger, the injustice of familiarity, and the injustice of a slip."

Another said: "I have never reviled anyone, for if a noble man reviles me, I am more worthy of forgiving him; or if a base man does, I will not make my honor a target for him." Then he recited: "And I forgive the fault of the noble, preserving him, and I turn away from the reviling of the base, out of generosity."

It has been said: "Take from your friend what is pure, and leave that which has turbidity. For life is too short for reproaching a friend over a fault."

Whenever your brother excuses himself to you, whether lying or truthful, accept his excuse. He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever is excused by his brother and does not accept his excuse, upon him is the like of the sin of the tax collector." And he (peace be upon him) said: "The believer is quick to anger and quick to satisfaction." He did not describe him as one who does not become angry.

Likewise, Allah the Exalted said: {«And those who swallow their anger»} — and He did not say: "and those who lack anger." This is because habit does not extend to a man being wounded and not feeling pain; rather, it extends to his being patient upon it and bearing it. Just as feeling pain from a wound is a requirement of the nature of the body, so feeling pain from the causes of anger is the nature of the heart. It cannot be uprooted, but restraining it, swallowing it, and acting contrary to its requirement — for it requires vindictiveness, revenge, and retaliation — is possible. The poet said: "And I am not one to keep a brother whom I do not reproach for his dishevelment — for which man is refined?"

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said to Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī: "When you make a brother in this age, do not reproach him for what you dislike, for you are not safe from seeing in his response something worse than the first." He said: "I tried it, and found it to be so."

Some of them said: "Patience upon the pain of a brother is better than reproaching him, and reproaching is better than severance, and severance is better than slander."

One should not exaggerate in hatred at the time of slander. Allah the Exalted said: {«Perhaps Allah will place between you and those whom you have treated as enemies, affection»}. And he (peace be upon him) said: "Love your beloved moderately, for perhaps he will be your enemy one day. And hate your enemy moderately, for perhaps he will be your beloved one day."

ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Let not your love be infatuation, nor your hatred destruction" — meaning that you love the destruction of your companion along with your own ruin.

chapters.title_en: The Sixth Right: Supplication for One's Brother in Life and After Death
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||||  الحق السادس

الدعاء للأخ في حياته وبعد مماته بكل ما يحبه لنفسه ولأهله وكل متعلق به
فتدعو له كما تدعو لنفسك ولا تفرق بين نفسك وبينه فإن دعاءك له دعاء لنفسك
على التحقيق فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا دعا الرجل لأخيه في ظهر الغيب
قال الملك ولك مثل ذلك (2)
وفي لفظ آخر يقول الله تعالى بك أبدا يا عبدي (3)
وفي الحديث يستجاب للرجل في أخيه ما لا يستجاب له في نفسه (4)
وفي الحديث دعوة الرجل لأخته في ظهر الغيب لا ترد (5)
وكان أبو الدرداء يقول إني لأدعو لسبعين من إخواني في سجودي أسميهم
بأسمائهم
وكان محمد بن يوسف الأصفهاني يقول وأين مثل الأخ الصالح أهلك يقتسمون
ميراثك ويتنعمون بما خلفت وهو منفرد بحزنك مهتم مما قدمت وما صرت إليه يدعو
لك في ظلمة الليل وأنت تحت أطباق الثرى وكان الأخ الصالح يقتدي بالملائكة
إذ جاء في الخبر إذا مات العبد قال الناس ما خلفت وقال الملائكة ما قدم (6)
يفرحون له بما قدم ويسألون عنه ويشفقون عليه ويقال من بلغه موت أخيه
فترحم عليه وأستغفر له كتب له كأنه شهد جنازته وصلى عليه
وروي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال مثل الميت في قبره مثل
الغريق يتعلق بكل شيء ينتظر دعوة من ولد أو والد أو أخ أو قريب (7)
وأنه ليدخل على قبور الأموات من دعاء الأحياء من الأنوار مثل الجبال
وقال بعض السلف الدعاء للأموات بمنزلة الهدايا للأحياء فيدخل الملك على
الميت ومعه طبق من نور عليه منديل من نور فيقول هذه PageV02P186
هدية لك من عند أخيك فلان من عند قريبك  فلان
قال فيفرح بذلك كما يفرح الحي بالهدية

### ||||  الحق السابع الوفاء والإخلاص
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ع-و (da-ʿa-wa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To call, summon, invoke; the core act of requesting or beseeching with the tongue and heart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Supplication (duʿāʾ) as an act of worship and a means of drawing near to Allah, encompassing both request (masʾalah) and praise (thānāʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — verbal calling; metaphorical (majāz) — the heart's turning toward Allah in need, even without utterance.
- Root: غ-ي-ب (ghayb)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That which is absent, hidden, unseen; the opposite of presence (ḥuḍūr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the context of supplication, "in the absence" (ẓahr al-ghayb) signifies the brother's unawareness of the prayer, ensuring sincerity and freedom from ostentation (riyāʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical absence; metaphorical — the heart's absence from the supplicant's awareness, emphasizing pure intention.
- Root: و-ف-ي (w-f-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Completeness, fulfillment, loyalty; to give in full measure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Loyalty (wafāʾ) as a covenant-keeping virtue, here extended to the brother's rights after death.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — fulfilling a debt; metaphorical — the soul's steadfastness in love beyond the grave.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ) — "If a man supplicates for his brother in his absence" (idhā daʿā...), the protasis (sharṭ) and apodosis (jawāb) establish a causal nexus, emphasizing the guaranteed divine response as a grammatical certainty.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sixth right is supplication for one's brother during his life and after his death, for everything he loves for himself, for his family, and for all that pertains to him. So you supplicate for him just as you supplicate for yourself, and you make no distinction between yourself and him — for your supplication for him is, in truth, a supplication for yourself. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«When a man supplicates for his brother in his absence, the angel says: 'And for you the like thereof'»} (2). In another wording, Allah the Exalted says: {«And for you likewise, O My servant, forever»} (3). And in the hadith: {«A man is answered in [his supplication for] his brother what he is not answered in [his supplication for] himself»} (4). And in the hadith: {«The supplication of a man for his brother in his absence is not rejected»} (5).

Abu al-Dardāʾ (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "I supplicate for seventy of my brothers in my prostration, naming them by their names." And Muhammad ibn Yūsuf al-Aṣfahānī used to say: "Where is the like of the righteous brother? Your heirs divide your inheritance and delight in what you have left behind, while he alone is occupied with grief for you, concerned over what you have sent forth and what you have become — supplicating for you in the darkness of the night while you lie beneath the layers of dust." And the righteous brother emulates the angels, for it has come in the report: {«When a servant dies, the people say: 'What has he left behind?' But the angels say: 'What has he sent forth?'»} (6) — they rejoice for him in what he has sent forth, and they ask about him, and they show compassion toward him. And it is said: Whoever is informed of his brother's death, and then shows mercy upon him and seeks forgiveness for him, it is written for him as though he had attended his funeral and prayed over him.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: {«The likeness of the dead in his grave is like the drowning one, clinging to everything, awaiting a supplication from a son, or a father, or a brother, or a relative»} (7). And indeed, there enters upon the graves of the dead, from the supplications of the living, lights like mountains. And one of the Salaf said: "Supplication for the dead is in the position of gifts for the living." The angel enters upon the dead with a tray of light, upon which is a cloth of light, and says: "This is a gift for you from your brother so-and-so, from your relative so-and-so." He said: "And he rejoices at that just as the living rejoices at a gift."

### ||||  The Seventh Right: Loyalty and Sincerity

chapters.title_en: On the Meaning of Fidelity (al-Wafā') and Its Requisites in Brotherhood
chapters.arabic_text:
ومعنى الوفاء الثبات على الحب وإدامته إلى الموت معه وبعد الموت مع
أولاده وأصدقائه فإن الحب إنما يراد للآخرة فإن انقطع قبل الموت حبط العمل
وضاع السعي ولذلك قال عليه السلام في السبعة الذين يظلهم الله في ظله
ورجلان تحابا في الله اجتمعا على ذلك وتفرقا عليه (1)
وقال بعضهم قليل الوفاء بعد الوفاء خير من كثيره في حال الحياة ولذلك روي
أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أكرم عجوزا دخلت عليه فقيل له في ذلك فقال إنها
كانت تأتينا أيام خديجة وإن كرم العهد من الدين (2)
فمن الوفاة للأخ مراعاة جميع أصدقائه وأقاربه والمتعلقين به ومراعاتهم
أوقع في قلب الصديق من مراعاة الأخ في نفسه فإن فرحه بتفقد من يتعلق به
أكثر إذ لا يدل على قوة الشفقة والحب إلا تعديهما من المحبوب إلى كل من
يتعلق به حتى الكلب الذي على باب داره ينبغي أن يميز في القلب عن سائر
الكلاب ومهما انقطع الوفاء بدوام المحبة شمت به الشيطان فإنه لا يحسد
متعاونين على بركما يحسد متواخيين في الله ومتحابين فيه فإنه يجهد نفسه
لإفساد ما بينهما قال الله تعالى وقل لعبادي يقولوا التي هي أحسن إن
الشيطان ينزغ بينهم وقال مخبرا عن يوسف من بعد إن نزغ الشيطان بيني وبين
إخوتي ويقال ما تواخى اثنان في الله فتفرق بينهما إلا بذنب يرتكبه أحدهما
وكان بشر يقول إذا قصر العبد في طاعة الله سلبه الله من يؤنسه
وذلك لأن الإخوان مسلاة للهموم وعون على الدين
ولذلك قال ابن المبارك ألذ الأشياء مجالسة الإخوان والانقلاب إلى كفاية
والمودة الدائمة هي التي تكون في الله وما يكون لغرض يزول بزوال ذلك الغرض
ومن ثمرات المودة في الله أن لا تكون مع حسد في دين ودنيا وكيف يحسده وكل
ما هو لأخيه فإليه ترجع فائدته وبه وصف الله تعالى المحبين في الله تعالى
فقال ولا يجدون في صدورهم حاجة مما أوتوا  ويؤثرون على أنفسهم ووجود الحاجة
هو الحسد
ومن الوفاء أن لا يتغير حاله في التواضع مع أخيه وإن ارتفع شأنه واتسعت
ولايته وعظم جاهه فالترفع على الإخوان بما يتجدد من الأحوال لؤم
قال الشاعر
إن الكرام إذا ما أيسروا ذكروا ... من كان يألفهم في المنزل الخشن
وأوصى بعض السلف ابنه فقال يا بني لا تصحب من الناس إلا من إذا افتقرت
إليه قرب منك وإن استغنيت عنه لم يطمع فيك وإن علت مرتبته لم يرتفع عليك
وقال بعض الحكماء إذا ولي أخوك ولاية فثبت على نصف مودته لك فهو كثير
وحكى الربيع أن الشافعي رحمه الله آخى رجلا ببغداد ثم إن أخاه ولى
السيبين فتغير له عما كان عليه فكتب إليه الشافعي بهذه الأبيات
اذهب فودك من فؤادي طالق ... أبدا وليس طلاق ذات البين
فإن ارعويت فإنها تطليقة ... ويدوم ودك لي على ثنتين
وإن امتنعت شفعتها بمثالها ... فتكون تطليقين في حيضين
وإذا الثلاث أتتك مني بتة ... لم تغن عنك ولاية السيبين PageV02P187
واعلم أنه ليس من الوفاء موافقة الأخ فيما يخالف الحق في أمر يتعلق
بالدين بل الوفاء له المخالفة فقد كان الشافعي رضي الله عنه آخى محمد بن
عبد الحكم وكان يقربه ويقبل عليه ويقول ما يقيمني بمصر غيره فاعتل محمد
فعاده الشافعي رحمه الله تعالى فقال
مرض الحبيب فعدته ... فمرضت من حذري عليه
وأتى الحبيب يعودني ... فبرئت من نظري إليه
وظن الناس لصدق مودتهما أنه يفوض أمر حلقته إليه بعد وفاته فقيل للشافعي
في علته التي مات فيها رضي الله تعالى عنه إلى من نجلس بعدك يا أبا عبد
الله فاستشرف له محمد بن عبد الحكم وهو عند رأسه ليومئ إليه فقال الشافعي
سبحان الله أيشك في هذا أبو يعقوب البويطي فانكسر لها محمد ومال أصحابه إلى
البويطي مع أن محمدا كان قد حمل عنه مذهبه كله لكن كان البويطي أفضل وأقرب
إلى الزهد والورع
فنصح الشافعي لله وللمسلمين وترك المداهنة ولم يؤثر رضا الخلق على رضا
الله تعالى  فلما توفي انقلب محمد بن عبد الحكم عن مذهبه ورجع إلى مذهب أبيه
ودرس كتب مالك رحمه الله وهو من كبار أصحاب مالك رحمه الله
وآثر البويطي الزهد والخمول ولم يعجبه الجمع والجلوس في الحلقة واشتغل
بالعبادة وصنف كتاب الأم الذي ينسب الآن إلى الربيع بن سليمان ويعرف به
وإنما صنفه البويطي ولكن لم يذكر نفسه فيه ولم ينسبه إلى نفسه فزاد الربيع
فيه وتصرف وأظهره
والمقصود أن الوفاء بالمحبة من تمامها النصح لله
قال الأحنف الإخاء جوهرة رقيقة إن لم تحرسها كانت معرضة للآفات فاحرسها
بالكظم حتى تعتذر إلى من ظلمك وبالرضا حتى لا تستكثر من نفسك الفضل ولا من
أخيك التقصير
ومن آثار الصدق والإخلاص وتمام الوفاء أن تكون شديد الجزع من المفارقة
نفور الطبع عن أسبابها كما قيل
وجدت مصيبات الزمان جميعها ... سوى فرقة الأحباب هينة الخطب
وأنشد ابن عيينة هذا البيت وقال لقد عهدت أقواما فارقتهم منذ ثلاثين سنة
ما يخيل إلي أن حسرتهم ذهبت من قلبي
ومن الوفاء أن لا يسمع بلاغات الناس على صديقه لاسيما من يظهر أولا أنه
محب لصديقه كيلا يتهم ثم يلقي الكلام عرضا وينقل عن الصديق ما يوغر القلب
فذلك من دقائق الجيل في التضريب ومن لم يحترز منه لم تدم مودته أصلا
قال واحد لحكيم قد جئت خاطبا لمودتك قال إن جعلت مهرها ثلاثا فعلت قال
وما هي قال لا تسمع علي بلاغة ولا تخالفني في أمر ولا توطئني عشوة
ومن الوفاء أن لا يصادق عدو صديقه
قال الشافعي رحمه الله إذا أطاع صديقك عدوك فقد اشتركا في عدواتك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ف-ي (w-f-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Completeness, fulfillment of a measure or covenant; to be whole and unabated.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Steadfastness in covenant (ʿahd) with God and creation; linked to sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and the completion of love (tamām al-maḥabbah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: fulfilling a debt or vow. Metaphorical: persistence of affection unto death and beyond, as the "measure" of love is its uninterrupted duration.
- Root: ث-ب-ت (th-b-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firmness, stability, standing immovable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Constancy of the heart upon the path of love; the opposite of turning away (iʿrāḍ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical standing. Metaphorical: moral steadfastness in brotherhood despite changing circumstances.
- Root: ن-ز-غ (n-z-gh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To incite, provoke, stir up discord.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Satanic insinuation that ruptures harmony between believers; mentioned in the Quran regarding interpersonal strife.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a goad for beasts. Metaphorical: the devil's subtle prodding of hearts toward enmity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnā') — The phrase "فإن انقطع قبل الموت حبط العمل" employs a conditional (in) with a jussive apodosis, indicating a causal necessity: the cessation of love nullifies prior deeds, a syntactic pattern emphasizing consequence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The meaning of fidelity (al-wafā') is steadfastness upon love and its continuation until death, and after death with one's children and friends. For love is only sought for the Hereafter; if it is severed before death, the deed is rendered void and the effort is wasted. For this reason, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, regarding the seven whom God will shade in His shade: "And two men who loved each other for God's sake, meeting upon that and parting upon that" {«رجلان تحابا في الله اجتمعا على ذلك وتفرقا عليه»}.

And some of them said: "A little fidelity after death is better than much of it during life." For this reason, it is narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) honored an old woman who entered upon him, and when it was said to him about that, he said: "She used to visit us in the days of Khadījah, and indeed, honoring the covenant is part of religion" {«إنها كانت تأتينا أيام خديجة وإن كرم العهد من الدين»}.

Thus, from fidelity to a brother is the observance of all his friends, relatives, and those connected to him. Observing them strikes the friend's heart more deeply than observing the brother himself, for his joy at the care shown to those connected to him is greater—since nothing indicates the strength of compassion and love except their extension from the beloved to all who are connected to him, even to the dog at the door of his house, which should be distinguished in the heart from all other dogs.

Whenever fidelity is severed by the cessation of love, Satan gloats over him. For he does not envy two who cooperate in righteousness as he envies two who are brothers for God's sake and love each other in Him. He strains himself to corrupt what is between them. God the Exalted said: "And say to My servants that they speak that which is best; indeed, Satan sows discord between them" {«وقل لعبادي يقولوا التي هي أحسن إن الشيطان ينزغ بينهم»}. And He said, reporting from Joseph: "After Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers" {«من بعد إن نزغ الشيطان بيني وبين إخوتي»}. And it is said: "No two have become brothers for God's sake and then separated except due to a sin committed by one of them." Bishr used to say: "When a servant falls short in obedience to God, God strips him of the one who brings him comfort." That is because brothers are a solace for worries and an aid upon religion.

For this reason, Ibn al-Mubārak said: "The most delightful of things is the company of brothers and turning to sufficiency." And the enduring affection is that which is for God's sake; whatever is for a purpose vanishes with the vanishing of that purpose.

Among the fruits of affection in God is that it be free of envy in religion and worldly matters. How could he envy him, when all that belongs to his brother returns to him in benefit? With this, God the Exalted described those who love in God, saying: "And they find not in their breasts any need of what they were given, and they prefer others over themselves" {«ولا يجدون في صدورهم حاجة مما أوتوا ويؤثرون على أنفسهم»}. The existence of need (al-ḥājah) is envy.

And from fidelity is that one's state does not change in humility toward his brother even if his rank rises, his authority expands, and his prestige becomes great. For elevating oneself over brothers due to newly acquired circumstances is baseness (lu'm). The poet said:

"Indeed, the noble, when they prosper, remember... those who kept their company in the rough abode."

And one of the predecessors (salaf) advised his son, saying: "O my son, do not accompany anyone unless—when you are in need of him—he draws near to you; when you are independent of him, he does not covet what you have; and when his rank rises, he does not exalt himself over you."

And one of the sages said: "If your brother is appointed to a position of authority and remains upon half of his affection for you, that is much."

Al-Rabīʿ narrated that al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) made a pact of brotherhood with a man in Baghdad. Then his brother was appointed over al-Sībayn and changed toward him from what he had been. So al-Shāfiʿī wrote to him these verses:

"Go—your love from my heart is divorced... forever, and it is not a revocable divorce.
If you relent, then it is one divorce... and your love for me remains upon two.
And if you refuse, I add to it its like... so it becomes two divorces in two menstrual periods.
And when the three come to you from me irrevocably... the governorship of al-Sībayn will not avail you." (Page V02P187)

Know that it is not from fidelity to agree with a brother in what opposes the truth in any matter pertaining to religion. Rather, fidelity to him is opposition. For al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) had made a pact of brotherhood with Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, and he would bring him near, turn toward him, and say: "Nothing keeps me in Egypt but him." Then Muḥammad fell ill, and al-Shāfiʿī visited him, saying:

"The beloved fell ill, so I visited him... and I fell ill from fear for him.
And the beloved came to visit me... and I was cured from my looking at him."

And the people, due to the sincerity of their affection, thought that he would delegate the authority of his study circle (ḥalaqah) to him after his death. So it was said to al-Shāfiʿī during the illness in which he died (may God be pleased with him): "To whom shall we sit after you, O Abū ʿAbd Allāh?" Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam perked up at his head, intending to gesture toward himself. But al-Shāfiʿī said: "Glory be to God! Does Abū Yaʿqūb al-Buwayṭī doubt this?" Muḥammad was broken by this, and his companions inclined toward al-Buwayṭī—even though Muḥammad had transmitted his entire school (madhhab) from him. But al-Buwayṭī was more virtuous and closer to asceticism (zuhd) and scrupulousness (waraʿ).

Thus al-Shāfiʿī gave sincere counsel (naṣīḥah) to God and to the Muslims, and abandoned flattery (mudāhanah), and did not prefer the pleasure of creation over the pleasure of God the Exalted. When he died, Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam turned away from his school and reverted to the school of his father, and studied the books of Mālik (may God have mercy on him)—and he was among the senior companions of Mālik (may God have mercy on him).

And al-Buwayṭī chose asceticism and obscurity; he was not pleased with gathering and sitting in the study circle, and he occupied himself with worship. He composed the book al-Umm, which is now attributed to al-Rabīʿ ibn Sulaymān and known by him. Al-Buwayṭī indeed composed it, but he did not mention himself in it nor attribute it to himself. Then al-Rabīʿ added to it, made changes, and published it.

The point is that fidelity in love is part of its completeness: sincere counsel to God.

Al-Aḥnaf said: "Brotherhood is a delicate jewel; if you do not guard it, it becomes exposed to afflictions. So guard it by restraint (kaẓm) until you excuse yourself to the one you have wronged, and by contentment (riḍā) so that you do not consider much from yourself nor deficiency from your brother."

Among the effects of truthfulness, sincerity, and complete fidelity is that one be intensely distressed at separation, with the nature recoiling from its causes, as was said:

"I have found all the calamities of time... save the parting of beloved ones, to be light in burden."

Ibn ʿUyaynah recited this verse and said: "I have known people whom I parted from thirty years ago, and it does not occur to me that their grief has left my heart."

And from fidelity is that one does not listen to people's reports (balāghāt) against one's friend—especially from one who first appears to be a lover of the friend, so as not to be suspected, then casts the speech casually and transmits from the friend what embitters the heart. For that is among the subtleties of the devil in sowing discord (taḍrīb). Whoever does not guard against it, his affection will never endure at all. One man said to a sage: "I have come seeking your affection in marriage." He said: "If you make its dowry three things, I will do so." He asked: "What are they?" He said: "Do not listen to reports against me, do not oppose me in any matter, and do not lead me into a pitfall (ʿashwah)."

And from fidelity is that one does not befriend the enemy of one's friend. Al-Shāfiʿī (may God have mercy on him) said: "If your friend obeys your enemy, then the two of them have shared in your enmity."

chapters.title_en: The Eighth Right: Easing, Avoiding Affectation, and Lifting Burden
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||||  الحق الثامن التخفيف وترك التكلف والتكليف
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ف-ف (kh-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lightness, diminution of weight; opposite of heaviness (thiqal). In physical and moral senses.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Relief from hardship in religious obligations; God’s mercy in reducing burdens (takhlīf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical lightness; Metaphorical: easing of commands or duties.
- Root: ك-ل-ف (k-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To burden, impose, or charge someone with something; also to adorn or cover (takalluf = affectation, self-imposed difficulty).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taklīf = divine imposition of obligations; takalluf = unnecessary self-imposed hardship or artificiality in speech/action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: loading a beast; Metaphorical: imposing duties beyond necessity, or affecting a manner not natural.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The sequence "التخفيف وترك التكلف والتكليف" uses conjunctive wa (و) to link three distinct yet related concepts, each clarifying the scope of the "right" (ḥaqq) owed to the companion.
chapters.translation: I say: The eighth right [owed to a companion] is easing [in dealings], abandoning affectation (takalluf), and [refraining from] imposing burdens (taklīf) [upon him].

chapters.title_en: On the Etiquette of Brotherhood: The Lifting of Burden and Abandonment of Formality (Fī Ādāb al-Ukhuwwa: Takhfīf al-Muʾna wa Tark al-Takalluf)
chapters.arabic_text:
وذلك بأن لا يكلف أخاه ما يشق عليه بل يروح سره من مهماته وحاجاته ويرفهه
عن أن يحمله شيئا من أعبائه فلا يستمد منه من جاه ومال ولا يكلف التواضع له
والتفقد لأحواله والقيام بحقوقه بل لا يقصد بمحبته إلا الله تعالى تبركا
بدعائه واستئناسا بلقائه واستعانة به على دينه وتقربا إلى الله تعالى
بالقيام بحقوقه وتحمل مؤنته
قال بعضهم من اقتضى من إخوانه ما لا يقضونه فقد ظلمهم ومن اقتضى منهم مثل
ما يقتضونه فقد أتعبهم ومن لم يقتض فهو المتفضل عليهم
وقال بعض الحكماء من جعل نفسه عند الإخوان فوق قدره أثم وأثموا ومن جعل
نفسه في قدره تعب وأتعبهم ومن جعلها دون قدره سلم وسلموا تمام التخفيف بطي
بساط التكليف
PageV02P188
حتى لا يستحي منه فيما لا يستحي من نفسه
وقال الجنيد ما تواخى اثنان في الله فاستوحش أحدهما من صاحبه أو احتشم
إلا لعلة في أحدهما
وقال علي عليه السلام شر الأصدقاء من تكلف لك ومن أحوجك إلى مداراة
وألجأك إلى اعتذار
وقال الفضيل إنما تقاطع الناس بالتكلف يزور أحدهم أخاه فيتكلف له فيقطعه
ذلك عنه
وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها المؤمن أخو المؤمن لا يغتنمه ولا يحتشمه
وقال الجنيد صبحت أربع طبقات من هذه الطائفة كل طبقة ثلاثون رجلا حارثا
المحاسبي وطبقته وحسنا المسوحي وطبقته وسريا السقطي وطبقته وابن الكريبي
وطبقته فما تواخى اثنان في الله واحتشم أحدهما من صاحبه أو استوحش إلا لعلة
في أحدهما
وقيل لبعضهم من نصحب قال من يرفع عنك ثقل التكلف وتسقط بينك وبينه مؤنة
التحفظ
وكان جعفر بن محمد الصادق رضي الله عنهما يقول أثقل إخواني علي من يتكلف
لي وأتحفظ منه وأخفهم على قلبي من أكون معه كما أكون وحدي
وقال بعض الصوفية لا تعاشر من الناس إلا من لا تزيد عنده ببر ولا تنقص
عنده بإثم يكون ذلك لك وعليك وأنت عنده سواء وإنما قال هذا لأن به يتخلص عن
التكلف والتحفظ
وإلا فالطبع يحمله على أن يتحفظ منه إذا علم أن ذلك ينقصه عنده
وقال بعضهم كن مع أبناء الدنيا بالأدب ومع أبناء الآخرة بالعلم ومع
العارفين كيف شئت وقال آخر لا تصحب إلا من يتوب عنك إذا أذنبت يعتذر إليك
إذا أسأت ويحمل مؤنة نفسك ويكفيك مؤنة نفسه
وقائل هذا قد ضيق طريق الأخوة على الناس وليس الأمر كذلك بل  ينبغي أن
يواخى كل متدين عاقل ويعزم على أن يقوم بهذه الشرائط ولا يكلف غيره هذه
الشروط حتى تكثر إخوانه إذ به يكون مواخيا في الله وإلا كانت مواخاته لحظوظ
نفسه فقط
ولذلك قال رجل للجنيد قد عز الإخوان في هذا الزمان أين أخ لي في الله
فأعرض الجنيد حتى أعاده ثلاثا فلما أكثر قال له الجنيد إن أردت أخا يكفيك
مؤنتك ويحتمل أذاك فهذا لعمري قليل وإن أردت أخا في الله تحمل أنت مؤنته
وتصبر على أذاه فعندي جماعة أعرفهم لك
فسكت الرجل
واعلم أن الناس ثلاثة رجل تنتفع بصحبته ورجل تقدر على أن تنفعه ولا تضرر
به ولكن لا تنتفع به
ورجل لا تقدر أيضا على أن تنفعه وتضرر به وهو الأحمق أو السيء الخلق فهذا
الثالث ينبغي أن تتجنبه فأما الثاني فلا تجتنبه لأنك تنتفع في الآخرة
بشفاعته وبدعائه وبثوابك على القيام به وقد أوحى الله تعالى إلى موسى عليه
السلام أن أطعتني فما أكثر إخوانك أي إن واسيتهم واحتملت منهم ولم تحسدهم
وقد قال بعضهم صحبت الناس خمسين سنة فما وقع بيني وبينهم خلاف فإني كنت
معهم على نفسي ومن كانت هذه شيمته كثر إخوانه
ومن التخفيف وترك التكلف أن لا يعترض في نوافل العبادات
كان طائفة من الصوفية يصطحبون على شرط المساواة بين أربع معان إن أكل
أحدهم النهار كله لم يقل له صاحبه صم وإن صام الدهر كله لم يقل له أفطر وإن
نام الليل كله لم يقل له قم وإن صلى الليل كله لم يقل له نم وتستوي حالاته
عنده بلا مزيد ولا نقصان لأن ذلك إن تفاوت حرك الطبع إلى الرياء والتحفظ لا
محالة
وقد قيل من سقطت كلفته دامت ألفته من خفت مؤنته دامت مودته
وقال بعض الصحابة إن الله لعن المتكلفين وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أنا
والأتقياء من أمتي براء من التكلف (1)
وقال بعضهم إذا عمل الرجل في بيت أخيه أربع خصال فقد تم أنسه به (2)
إذا أكل عنده  ودخل الخلاء وصلى ونام
فذكر ذلك لبعض المشايخ فقال بقيت خامسة وهو أن يحضر مع الأهل في بيت أخيه
ويجامعها لأن البيت يتخذ للاستخفاء في الأمور الخمس PageV02P189
وإلا فالمساجد أروح لقلوب المتعبدين فإذا فعل هذه الخمس فقد تم الإخاء
وارتفعت الحشمة وتأكد الانبساط
وقول العرب في تسليمهم يشير إلى ذلك إذ يقول أحدهم لصاحبه مرحبا وأهلا
وسهلا أي لك عندنا مرحب وهو السعة في القلب والمكان ولك عندنا أهل تأنس بهم
بلا وحشة لك منا ولك عندنا سهولة في ذلك كله أي لا يشتد علينا مما تريد
ولا يتم التخفيف وترك التكلف إلا بأن يرى نفسه دون إخوانه ويحسن الظن بهم
ويسيء الظن بنفسه فإذا رآهم خيرا من نفسه فعند ذلك يكون هو خيرا منهم وقال
أبو معاوية الأسود إخواني كلهم خير مني قيل وكيف ذلك قال كلهم يرى لي الفضل
عليه ومن فضلني على نفسه فهو خير مني وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم المرء على
دين خليله ولا خير في صحبة من لا يرى لك مثل ما ترى له (1)
فهذه أقل الدرجات وهو النظر بعين المساواة والكمال في رؤية الفضل للأخ
ولذلك قال سفيان إذا قيل لك ياشر الناس فغضبت فأنت شر الناس أي ينبغي أن
تكون معتقدا ذلك في نفسك أبدا
وسيأتي وجه ذلك في كتاب الكبر والعجب
وقد قيل في معنى التواضع ورؤية الفضل للإخوان أبيات
تذلل لمن إن تذللت له ... يرى ذاك للفضل لا للبله
وجانب صداقة من لا يزا ... ل على الأصدقاء يرى الفضل له
وقال آخر
كم صديق عرفته بصديق ... صار أحظى من الصديق العتيق
ورفيق رأيته في طريق ... صار عندي هو الصديق الحقيقي
ومهما رأى الفضل لنفسه فقد احتقر أخاه وهذا في عموم المسلمين مذموم
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم بحسب المؤمن من الشر أن يحقر أخاه المسلم (2)
ومن تتمة الانبساط وترك التكلف أن يشاور إخوانه في كل ما يقصده ويقبل
إشاراتهم فقد قال تعالى وشاورهم في الأمر وينبغي أن لا يخفي  عنهم شيئا من
أسراره كما روي أن يعقوب ابن أخي معروف قال جاء أسود بن سالم إلى عمي معروف
وكان مواخيا له فقال إن بشر بن الحرث يحب مؤاخاتك وهو يستحي أن يشافهك بذلك
وقد أرسلني إليك يسألك أن تعقد له فيما بينك وبينه أخوة يحتسبها ويعتد بها
إلا أنه يشترط فيها شروطا لا يحب أن يشتهر بذلك ولا يكون بينك وبينه مزاورة
ولا ملاقاة فإنه يكره كثرة الالتقاء فقال معروف أما أنا لو آخيت أحدا لم
أحب مفارقته ليلا ولا نهارا ولزرته في كل وقت وآثرته على نفسي في كل حال ثم
ذكر من فضل الأخوة والحب في الله أحاديث كثيرة ثم قال فيها
وقد آخى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عليا فشاركه في العلم (3)
وقاسمه في البدن (4)
وأنكحه أفضل بناته وأحبهن إليه وخصه بذلك لمؤاخاته (5)
وأنا PageV02P190
أشهدك أني قد عقدت له أخوة بيني وبينه وعقدت إخاءه في الله لرسالتك
ولمسألته على أن لا يزورني إن كره ذلك ولكني أزوره متى أحببت ومره أن
يلقاني في مواضع نلتقي بها ومره أن لا يخفي علي شيئا من شأنه وأن يطلعني
على جميع أحواله فأخبر ابن سالم بشرا بذلك فرضى وسلا به
فهذا جامع حقوق الصحبة وقد أجملناه مرة وفصلناه أخرى ولا يتم ذلك إلا بأن
تكون على نفسك للإخوان ولا تكون لنفسك عليهم وأن تنزل نفسك منزلة الخادم
لهم فتقيد بحقوقهم جميع جوارك
أما البصر فبأن تنظر إليهم نظر مودة يعرفونها منك وتنظر إلى محاسنهم
وتتعامى عن عيوبهم ولا تصرف بصرك عنهم في وقت إقبالهم عليك وكلامهم معك
روي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يعطي كل من جلس إليه نصيبا من وجهه وما
استصغاه أحد إلا ظن أنه أكرم الناس عليه حتى كان مجلسه وسمعه وحديثه ولطيف
مسألته وتوجهه للجالس إليه (1)
وكان مجلسه مجلس حياء وتواضع وأمانة وكان عليه السلام أكثر الناس تبسما
وضحكا في وجوه أصحابه وتعجبا مما يحدثونه به وكان ضحك أصحابه عنده التبسم
اقتداء منهم  بفعله وتوقيرا له عليه السلام
وأما السمع فبأن تسمع كلامه متلذذا بسماعه ومصدقا به ومظهرا للاستبشار به
ولا تقطع حديثهم عليهم بمرادة ولا منازعة ومداخلة واعتراض فإن أرهقك عارض
اعتذرت إليهم وتحرس سمعك عن سماع ما يكرهون
وأما اللسان فقد ذكرنا حقوقه فإن القول فيه يطول ومن ذلك أن لا يرفع صوته
عليهم ولا يخاطبهم إلا بما يفقهون
وأما اليدان فأن لا يقبضهما عن معاونتهم في كل ما يتعاطى باليد
وأما الرجلان فأن يمشي بهما وراءهم مشي الأتباع لا مشي المتبوعين ولا
يتقدمهم إلا بقدر ما يقدمونه ولا يقرب منهم إلا بقدر ما يقربونه ويقوم لهم
إذا أقبلوا ولا يقعد إلا بقعودهم ويقعد متواضعا حيث يقعد
ومهما تم الاتحاد خف حمله من هذه الحقوق مثل القيام والاعتذار والثناء
فإنها من حقوق الصحبة وفي ضمنها نوع من الأجنبية والتكلف فإذا تم الاتحاد
انطوى بساط التكلف بالكلية فلا يسلك به إلا مسلك نفسه لأن هذه الآداب
الظاهرة عنوان آداب الباطن وصفاء القلب
ومهما صفت القلوب استغنى عن تكلف إظهار ما فيها ومن كان نظره إلى صحبة
الخلق فتارة يعوج وتارة يستقيم ومن كان نظره إلى الخالق لزم الاستقامة
ظاهرا وباطنا وزين باطنه بالحب لله ولخلقه وزين ظاهره بالعبادة لله والخدمة
لعباده فإنها أعلى أنواع الخدمة لله إذ لا وصول إليه إلا بحسن الخلق ويدرك
العبد بحسن خلقه درجة القائم الصائم وزيادة PageV02P191
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك ل ف (K-L-F)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To burden, to impose something arduous; takalluf denotes assuming a task with effort and strain, often artificial.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Takalluf is the self-imposition of hardship beyond the natural; in brotherhood, it signifies contrived formality that veils sincere intimacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is the actual bearing of weight; metaphorical (majāz) is the social pretense that weighs upon the heart, severing true affection.
- Root: أ ن س (A-N-S)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sociability, familiarity, the absence of estrangement (waḥshah); istīʾnās is seeking comfort in another's presence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, the soul's repose (sukūn) in the beloved for God's sake, mirroring the heart's intimacy with the Divine.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is physical companionship; metaphorical is the spiritual ease that removes all awkwardness between brethren.
- Root: ح ش م (Ḥ-Sh-M)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Shyness, restraint, or awe that creates distance; iḥtishām is a formality that inhibits free interaction.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral state opposed to true brotherhood; it signals a residual self-consciousness incompatible with pure love in God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is the feeling of shame; metaphorical is the social barrier that, when present, indicates a defect in one of the two brethren.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text frequently employs "لا... إلا" (nothing but) and "من... فـ" (whoever... then) to delineate precise ethical boundaries, requiring careful parsing to preserve the conditional logic of reward and blame.
chapters.translation:
I say: This is achieved by not burdening one's brother with what is difficult for him. Rather, one should give his heart rest from his cares and needs, and spare him from carrying any of his loads—so that he neither seeks from him status nor wealth, nor imposes upon him humility toward himself, nor the checking of his conditions, nor the fulfillment of his rights. Nay, his love should not intend anything save God Most High—seeking blessing through his supplication, finding comfort in his meeting, seeking his aid upon his religion, and drawing near to God Most High by fulfilling his rights and bearing his expenses.

One of them (the early sages) said: "Whoever demands from his brethren what they cannot fulfill has wronged them. Whoever demands from them the like of what they demand from him has wearied them. And whoever demands nothing is the one who bestows favor upon them."

Another of the wise men said: "Whoever places himself among brethren above his rank sins and causes them to sin. Whoever places himself at his rank wearies himself and wearies them. And whoever places himself below his rank is safe and they are safe." The complete alleviation is the folding up of the carpet of obligation (taklīf), until he is not ashamed before him of what he would not be ashamed of before himself.

Al-Junayd said: "Two men never became brethren in God, and then one of them felt estranged from his companion or felt inhibited (iḥtashama) toward him, save due to a defect in one of them."

ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said: "The worst of friends is the one who imposes formality upon you (yatakallafu laka), who makes you need to be cautious with him, and who drives you to apologize."

Al-Fuḍayl said: "People only cut each other off through formality (takalluf). One of them visits his brother and behaves with contrived ceremony toward him, and that severs him from him."

ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The believer is the brother of the believer: he does not exploit him (lā yaghtanimuhu) nor stand on ceremony with him (lā yaḥtashimuhu)."

Al-Junayd said: "I reached four classes of this group (the Sufis), each class comprising thirty men: Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī and his class, Ḥasan al-Musawḥī and his class, Sarī al-Saqaṭī and his class, and Ibn al-Kuraibī and his class. Never did two men become brethren in God, and one of them felt inhibited from his companion or estranged, save due to a defect in one of them."

It was said to one of them: "Whom shall we accompany?" He said: "One who lifts from you the weight of formality, and between whom and you the burden of self-guarding falls away."

Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq (may God be pleased with them both) used to say: "The heaviest of my brethren upon me is the one who behaves with ceremony toward me (yatakallafu lī), and I must guard myself against him. The lightest of them upon my heart is the one with whom I am as I am when alone."

One of the Sufis said: "Do not mix with people save one who does not increase in your estimation through your goodness, nor decrease through your sin—such that it is the same for you and against you, and you are equal in his sight." He only said this because through it one is delivered from formality and self-guarding. Otherwise, nature impels one to guard against him when one knows that this diminishes him in his sight.

Another said: "Be with the sons of this world through good manners (adab), with the sons of the Hereafter through knowledge, and with the knowers (al-ʿārifīn) however you wish."

Another said: "Accompany none save one who repents for you when you sin, apologizes to you when you do ill, bears the burden of your self, and spares you the burden of his own self."

But the one who said this has narrowed the path of brotherhood for people. The matter is not so. Rather, one should take as brother every religious, intelligent person, and resolve to fulfill these conditions oneself, without imposing these conditions upon the other—so that one's brethren may be many. For by this one becomes a brother in God; otherwise, one's brotherhood is only for one's own selfish ends.

For this reason, a man said to al-Junayd: "Brethren have become scarce in this age. Where is a brother for me in God?" Al-Junayd turned away until the man repeated it three times. When he persisted, al-Junayd said to him: "If you seek a brother who spares you your burden and bears your harm—this, by my life, is rare. But if you seek a brother in God, whose burden you bear and whose harm you endure patiently—then I have a group whom I can introduce to you." The man fell silent.

Know that people are of three kinds: a man from whose companionship you benefit; a man whom you are able to benefit without being harmed by him, but from whom you do not benefit; and a man whom you cannot benefit and are harmed by—and he is the fool or the ill-tempered. This third kind you must avoid. As for the second, do not avoid him, for you benefit in the Hereafter through his intercession, his supplication, and your reward for attending to him. God revealed to Moses (peace be upon him): "If you obey Me, how many are your brethren!"—meaning: if you show kindness to them, bear with them, and do not envy them.

One of them said: "I accompanied people for fifty years, and no discord ever occurred between me and them, for I was with them against myself." Whoever has this trait, his brethren become many.

From the alleviation and abandonment of formality is that one does not object to another's supererogatory acts of worship (nawāfil). A group of Sufis used to accompany one another on the condition of equality in four matters: if one of them ate all day, his companion did not say to him "Fast"; if he fasted perpetually, he did not say "Break your fast"; if he slept all night, he did not say "Stand in prayer"; if he prayed all night, he did not say "Sleep." His states were equal in his sight, without increase or decrease—because if they differed, it would inevitably stir nature toward hypocrisy (riyāʾ) and self-guarding.

It has been said: "Whose formality falls away, his intimacy endures; whose burden is light, his love abides."

One of the Companions said: "God has cursed those who impose formality (al-mutakallifīn)." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I and the God-fearing of my community are free of formality (takalluf)."

One of them said: "When a man does four things in his brother's house, his intimacy with him is complete: when he eats with him, enters the privy, prays, and sleeps." This was mentioned to one of the masters, and he said: "A fifth remains: that he be present with the family in his brother's house and have intercourse with her—for the house is made for concealment in these five matters." Otherwise, the mosques are more restful to the hearts of worshippers. When he does these five, brotherhood is complete, inhibition (ḥashmah) is lifted, and ease (inbisāṭ) is confirmed.

The Arabs' saying in their greeting points to this, as one says to his companion: "Marḥaban wa ahlan wa sahlan"—meaning: "You have with us a spacious place (marḥab), which is breadth in heart and place; you have with us family (ahl) with whom you feel at home without estrangement from us; and you have with us ease (suhūlah) in all of that—i.e., nothing you desire is hard upon us."

The alleviation and abandonment of formality is not complete save that one sees oneself as below one's brethren, thinks well of them, and thinks ill of oneself. When he sees them as better than himself, then at that point he is better than them. Abū Muʿāwiyah al-Aswad said: "All my brethren are better than me." It was said: "How is that?" He said: "Each of them sees merit in me over himself, and whoever prefers me over himself is better than me." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "A man is upon the religion of his intimate friend; and there is no good in the companionship of one who does not see for you the like of what you see for him."

This is the least of the degrees—namely, looking with the eye of equality. The perfection is in seeing merit for the brother. For this reason, Sufyān said: "When it is said to you, 'O evil of people,' and you become angry, then you are the evil of people"—meaning: one should always hold this belief about oneself.

The explanation of this will come in the Book of Pride and Self-Conceit (Kitāb al-Kibr wa al-ʿUjb).

Poems have been composed on the meaning of humility and seeing merit for brethren:

"Be humble to one who, when you humble yourself to him, / Sees it as merit, not as folly.
And shun the friendship of one who never ceases / To see merit for himself over friends."

Another said:

"How many a friend I knew through a friend / Became more favored than the old friend!
And a companion I saw on a road / Became, in my sight, the true friend."

Whenever one sees merit for oneself, he has despised his brother—and this is blameworthy among the generality of Muslims. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "It suffices a believer of evil that he despise his Muslim brother."

From the completion of ease and abandonment of formality is that one consults his brethren in everything he intends and accepts their counsel. God Most High said: {«وشاورهم في الأمر»} ("And consult them in the matter") (Āl ʿImrān 3:159). One should also conceal nothing of his secrets from them. It is related that Yaʿqūb, the nephew of Maʿrūf, said: "Aswad ibn Sālim came to my uncle Maʿrūf—and he was his sworn brother—and said: 'Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith desires your brotherhood, but he is ashamed to address you directly. He has sent me to you to ask that you contract between you and him a brotherhood which he may reckon and count upon—except that he stipulates conditions therein which he does not wish to be publicized: that there be no visiting between you and him, nor meeting, for he dislikes frequent encounters.' Maʿrūf said: 'As for me, if I took anyone as brother, I would not love to part from him by night or day. I would visit him at every time and prefer him over myself in every state.' Then he mentioned many hadiths on the merit of brotherhood and love in God, and said therein: 'The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) took ʿAlī as brother, sharing with him in knowledge, dividing with him in body, and marrying him to his best and most beloved daughter, singling him out for that due to their brotherhood. And I call you to witness that I have contracted between me and him a brotherhood, and I have bound his brotherhood in God—for your message and his request—on condition that he not visit me if he dislikes that, but I shall visit him whenever I wish. And tell him to meet me in places where we may encounter each other, and tell him not to conceal from me anything of his affair, and to inform me of all his states.' Ibn Sālim informed Bishr of that, and he was satisfied and found comfort in it."

This encompasses the rights of companionship, which we have summarized once and detailed another time. This is not complete save that you are against yourself for the brethren, and not for yourself against them—and that you place yourself in the station of a servant to them, binding all your limbs to their rights.

As for the eye: that you look at them with a look of affection which they recognize from you; that you look at their virtues and turn a blind eye to their faults; and that you do not avert your gaze from them at the time of their turning toward you and their speaking with you. It is related that the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave each one who sat with him a share of his face, and no one who spoke with him thought that anyone was more honored by him than himself—such that his sitting, his listening, his speech, his gentle questioning, and his turning toward the one seated with him were all of this kind. His gathering was a gathering of modesty, humility, and trustworthiness. He (peace be upon him) was the most smiling and laughing of people in the faces of his companions, and the most wonder-struck at what they related to him. The laughter of his companions in his presence was but a smile, following his example and honoring him (peace be upon him).

As for the ear: that you listen to his speech, delighting in hearing it, affirming it, and showing joy at it; that you do not cut off their speech through contradiction, disputation, interruption, or objection. If a pressing matter overtakes you, you apologize to them. And you guard your ear from hearing what they dislike.

As for the tongue: we have already mentioned its rights, for speech on it would be long. From that is that you do not raise your voice over them, and that you address them only with what they understand.

As for the two hands: that you do not withhold them from aiding them in everything done by hand.

As for the two feet: that you walk with them behind them, the walk of followers, not of the followed; that you do not advance before them save as they advance; that you do not draw near them save as they draw near; that you stand for them when they approach; that you do not sit save when they sit; and that you sit humbly wherever they sit.

Whenever union (ittiḥād) is complete, the burden of these rights becomes light—such as standing, apologizing, and praising—for these are among the rights of companionship and include within them a kind of estrangement and formality. When union is complete, the carpet of formality is folded up entirely, and one proceeds with him only as one proceeds with oneself—for these outward etiquettes are the title of inward etiquettes and the purity of the heart. When hearts are pure, one is spared the formality of displaying what is within them. Whoever's gaze is upon the companionship of creatures is sometimes crooked and sometimes straight; whoever's gaze is upon the Creator, uprightness becomes incumbent upon him outwardly and inwardly. He adorns his inward with love for God and His creatures, and his outward with worship of God and service to His servants—for this is the highest kind of service to God, since there is no reaching Him save through good character (ḥusn al-khuluq). By his good character, the servant attains the rank of the one who perpetually stands in prayer and fasts—and more.

### |||| خاتمة لهذا الباب نذكر فيها جملة آداب العشرة والمجالسة مع أصناف الخلق ملتقطة من كلام بعض الحكماء

إن أردت حسن العشرة فالق صديقك وعدوك بوجه الرضا من غير ذلة لهم ولا هيبة
منهم وتوقير من غير كبر وتواضع مي غير مذلة
وكن في جميع أمورك في أوسطها فكلا طرفي قصد الأمور ذميم
ولا تنظر في عطفيك ولا تكثر الالتفات ولا تقف على الجماعات وإذا جلست فلا
تستوفز وتحفظ من تشبيك أصابعك والعبث بلحيتك وخاتمك وتخليل أسنانك وإدخال
أصبعك في أنفك وكثرة بصاقك وتنخمك وطرد الذباب من وجهك وكثر التمطي
والتثاؤب في  وجوه الناس وفي الصلاة وغيرهما وليكن مجلسك هاديا وحديثك
منظوما مرتبا وأصغ إلى الكلام الحسن ممن حدثك من غير إظهار تعجب مفرط ولا
تسأله إعادته واسكت عن المضاحك والحكايات ولا تحدث عن إعجابك بولدك ولا
جاريتك ولا شعرك ولا تصنيفك وسائر ما يخصك ولا تتصنع تصنع المرأة في التزين
ولا تتبذل تبذل العبد وتوق كثرة الكحل والإسراف في الدهن ولا تلح في
الحاجات ولا تشجع أحدا على الظلم ولا تعلم أهلك وولدك فضلا عن غيرهم مقدار
مالك فإنهم إن رأوه قليلا هنت عندهم وإن كان كثيرا لم تبلغ قط رضاهم وخوفهم
من غير عنف ولن لهم من غير ضعف ولا تهازل أمتك ولا عبدك فيسقط وقارك وإذا
خاصمت فتوقر وتحفظ من جهلك وتجنب عجلتك وتفكر في حجتك ولا تكثر الإشارة
بيديك ولا تكثر الالتفات إلى من وراءك ولا تجث على ركبتيك وإذا هدأ غيظك
فتكلم وإن قربك سلطان فكن منه على مثل حد السنان فإن استرسل عليك فلا تأمن
انقلابه علبك وارفق به رفقك بالصبي وكلمه بما يشتهيه ما لم يكن معصية ولا
يحملنك لطفه بك أن تدخل بينه وبين أهله وولده وحشمه وإن كنت لذلك مستحقا
عنده فإن سقطة الداخل بين الملك وبين أهله سقطة لا تنعش وزلة لا تقال وإياك
وصديق العافية فإنه أعدى الأعداء ولا تجعل مالك أكرم من عرضك وإذا دخلت
مجلسا فالأدب فيه البداية بالتسليم وترك التخطي لمن سبق والجلوس حيث اتسع
وحيث يكون أقرب إلى التواضع وأن تحيي بالسلام من قرب منك عند الجلوس
ولا تجلس على الطريق فإن جلست فأدبه غض البصر ونصرة المظلوم وإغاثة
الملهوف وعون الضعيف وإرشاد الضال ورد السلام وإعطاء السائل والأمر
بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر والارتياد لموضع البصاق ولا تبصق في جهة القبلة
ولا عن يمينك ولكن عن يسارك وتحت قدمك اليسرى
ولا تجالس الملوك فإن فعلت فأدبه ترك الغيبة ومجانبة الكذب وصيانة السر
وقلة الحوائج وتهذيب الألفاظ والإعراب في الخطاب والمذاكرة بأخلاق الملوك
وقلة المداعبة وكثرة الحذر منهم  وإن ظهرت لك المودة وإن لا تتجشأ بحضرتهم
ولا تخلل بعد الأكل عنده وعلى الملك أن يحتمل كل شي إلا إفشاء السر والقدح
في الملك والتعرض للحرم
ولا تجالس العامة فإن فعلت فأدبه ترك الخوض في حديثهم وقلة الإصغاء إلى
أراجيفهم والتغافل عما يجري من سوء ألفاظهم وقلة اللقاء لهم مع الحاجة
إليهم
وإياك أن تمازح لبيبا أو غير لبيب فإن اللبيب يحقد عليك والسفيه يجتريء
عليك لأن المزاح يخرق الهيبة ويسقط ماء الوجه ويعقب الحقد ويذهب بحلاوة
الود ويشين فقه الفقيه ويجريء
PageV02P192
السفيه ويسقط المنزلة عند الحكيم ويمقته المتقون وهو يميت القلب ويباعد
عن الرب تعالى ويكسب الغفلة ويورث الذلة وبه تظلم السرائر وتموت الخواطر
وبه تكثر العيوب وتبين الذنوب
وقد قيل لا يكون المزاح إلا من سخف أو بطر
ومن بلي في مجلس بمزاح أو لغط فليذكر الله عند قيامه قال النبي صلى الله
عليه وسلم من جلس في مجلس فكثر به لغطه فقال قبل أن يقوم من مجلسه ذلك
سبحانك اللهم وبحمدك أشهد أن لا إله إلا أنت أستغفرك وأتوب إليك إلا غفر له
ما كان في مجلسه ذلك (1)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ش ر (ʿ-sh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes association, intimacy, and the tenth part; al-ʿishrah is the company one keeps, and ḥusn al-ʿishrah is the excellence of social conduct.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological ethics, ʿishrah signifies the mutual bond of companionship that mirrors the divine command to treat others with equity and gentleness, as a reflection of God's own attribute of al-Raḥmān.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical cohabitation; metaphorically extended to the moral bearing one adopts in the presence of others, where the "face of contentment" (wajh al-riḍā) is a figurative veil of amiability.
- Root: و ق ر (w-q-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is heaviness, gravity, and dignity; waqār is the settled composure that commands respect without arrogance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tawqīr (reverence) is the due honor paid to rank or virtue, distinct from khawf (fear), as it proceeds from recognition of merit, not intimidation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal weightiness of a load; metaphorical for the moral weight of a person's bearing in society.
- Root: م ز ح (m-z-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Jesting and playful banter; the root carries a sense of lightening or thinning, as in thinning a garment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the ethical framework, muzāḥ is censured when it erodes the gravity (waqār) of the soul and distracts from the remembrance of God; it is permissible only in rare, measured instances.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal jesting; metaphorically, it is described as "tearing the veil of dignity" (kharq al-haybah), indicating its destructive social effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Imperative Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The text employs frequent conditional clauses (e.g., "If you wish... then do X") where the protasis sets a hypothetical ethical scenario and the apodosis delivers the normative command, requiring precise parsing of the verb moods (jazm) to preserve the causal linkage between intention and action.
chapters.translation:
I say: This is a conclusion to this book, in which we mention a compendium of the etiquettes of companionship and assembly with all classes of creation, gleaned from the sayings of certain sages.

If you desire excellence in companionship, then meet your friend and your enemy with a face of contentment, without any abasement toward them, nor awe of them; and with reverence without pride, and humility without humiliation. And be, in all your affairs, in their middlemost course, for both extremes of any matter, when pursued, are blameworthy.

Do not glance sideways at your flanks, nor multiply your turning about, nor stand upon the gatherings of people. And when you sit, do not perch restlessly. Guard yourself against interlacing your fingers, toying with your beard and your ring, picking your teeth, inserting your finger into your nose, excessive spitting and clearing your throat, and driving away flies from your face. Avoid frequent stretching and yawning in the faces of people, whether in prayer or otherwise. Let your sitting place be tranquil, and your speech well-ordered and arranged. Lend ear to good speech from whoever speaks to you, without displaying excessive astonishment, and do not ask him to repeat it. Refrain from jesting tales and anecdotes. Do not speak out of admiration for your son, nor your slave-girl, nor your poetry, nor your compositions, nor anything else that pertains specifically to you. Do not adorn yourself with the adornment of a woman, nor degrade yourself with the degradation of a slave. Beware of excessive kohl and extravagance in oil. Do not be importunate in your requests. Do not embolden anyone toward injustice. Do not teach your family and your children—let alone others—the measure of your wealth; for if they see it as little, you become contemptible in their eyes, and if it is much, you will never attain their satisfaction. Make them fear you without harshness, and be gentle with them without weakness. Do not jest with your slave-woman nor your slave, lest your dignity fall away. And when you dispute, then be grave, guard yourself against your ignorance, avoid your haste, and reflect upon your proof. Do not gesture excessively with your hands, nor turn frequently to those behind you, nor kneel upon your knees. And when your rage has subsided, then speak.

If a ruler brings you near, then be toward him like the edge of a spearhead: if he lets himself be at ease with you, do not feel secure from his turning against you. Deal gently with him as you would deal gently with a child, and speak to him of what he desires, so long as it is not an act of disobedience. Let not his kindness toward you carry you to interpose between him and his family, his children, and his retinue, even if you are deserving of that in his estimation; for the fall of one who interposes between a king and his family is a fall that cannot be lifted, and a slip that cannot be forgiven.

Beware of the friend of prosperity, for he is the most hostile of enemies. Do not make your wealth more honorable than your honor (ʿirḍ). And when you enter an assembly, the etiquette therein is to begin with the greeting of peace (salām), to refrain from stepping over those who preceded you, and to sit where the space widens, and where it is closer to humility. And greet with peace the one who is near you when you sit. Do not sit upon the road; but if you do sit, then its etiquette is the lowering of the gaze, aiding the oppressed, succoring the distressed, assisting the weak, guiding the astray, returning the greeting, giving to the asker, commanding the good and forbidding the evil, and seeking out a place for spitting. Do not spit in the direction of the qiblah, nor to your right, but to your left and beneath your left foot.

Do not sit with kings; but if you do, then its etiquette is the abandonment of backbiting, the avoidance of lying, the safeguarding of secrets, the fewness of requests, the refinement of expressions, grammatical correctness in speech, the mention of the morals of kings, the fewness of jesting, and abundant caution toward them, even if affection appears to you from them. And do not belch in their presence, nor pick your teeth after eating with them. And it is upon the king to tolerate everything except the divulging of secrets, disparagement of the king, and encroachment upon the harem.

Do not sit with the common folk; but if you do, then its etiquette is to refrain from plunging into their discourse, to listen little to their rumors, to feign heedlessness of what passes of their foul expressions, and to be few in meeting them, despite the need of them.

Beware of jesting with an intelligent man or with a foolish one; for the intelligent man bears a grudge against you, and the foolish one grows bold against you. For jesting tears the veil of dignity, causes the water of the face to fall, bequeaths rancor, carries away the sweetness of affection, disgraces the jurisprudence of the jurist, emboldens the fool, lowers one's station with the sage, and makes the God-fearing abhor him. It deadens the heart, distances one from the Lord, Most High, earns heedlessness, and bequeaths abasement. By it, inner secrets are darkened, and inspirations die. By it, faults multiply, and sins become manifest.

And it has been said: Jesting arises only from frivolity or insolent pride.

And whoever is afflicted in an assembly with jesting or clamor, let him remember God at his rising. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever sits in an assembly wherein much clamor occurs, and then says before rising from that assembly: "Glory be to You, O God, and with Your praise; I bear witness that there is no god but You; I seek Your forgiveness and I repent to You" — except that he is forgiven for what occurred in that assembly.»

### ||| الباب الثالث في حق المسلم والرحم والجوار والملك وكيفية المعاشرة مع من يدلي بهذه الأسباب

اعلم أن الإنسان إما أن يكون وحده أو مع غيره وإذا تعذر عيش الإنسان إلا
بمخالطة من هو من جنسه لم يكن له بد من تعلم آداب المخالطة
وكل مخالط ففي مخالطته أدب والأدب على قدر حقه وحقه على قدر رابطته التي
بها وقعت المخالطة
والرابطة إما القرابة وهي أخصها أو أخوة الإسلام وهي أعمها وينطوي في
معنى الأخوة الصداقة والصحبة وإما الجوار وإما صحبة السفر والمكتب والدرس
وإما الصداقة أو الأخوة
ولكل واحد من هذه الروابط درجات
فالقرابة لها حق ولكن حق الرحم المحرم آكد وللمحرم حق ولكن حق الوالدين
آكد
وكذلك حق الجار ولكن يختلف بحسب قربه من الدار وبعده ويظهر التفاوت عند
النسبة حتى إن البلدي في بلاد الغربة يجري  مجرى القريب في الوطن لاختصاصه
بحق الجوار في البلد
وكذلك حق المسلم يتأكد بتأكد المعرفة
وللمعارف درجات فليس حق الذي عرف بالمشاهدة كحق الذي عرف بالسماع بل آكد
منه والمعرفة بعد وقوعها تتأكد بالاختلاط
وكذلك الصحبة تتفاوت درجاتها فحق الصحبة في الدرس والمكتب آكد من حق صحبة
السفر
وكذلك الصداقة تتفاوت فإنها إذا قويت صارت أخوة فإن ازدادت صارت محبة فإن
ازدادت صارت خلة والخليل أقرب من الحبيب فالمحبة ما تتمكن من حبة القلب
والخلة ما تتخلل سر القلب فكل خليل حبيب وليس كل حبيب خليلا وتفاوت درجات
الصداقة لا يخفى بحكم المشاهدة والتجربة فأما كون الخلة فوق الأخوة فمعناه
أن لفظ الخلة عبارة عن حالة هي أتم من الأخوة وتعرفه من قوله صلى الله عليه
وسلم لو كنت متخذا خليلا لاتخذت أبا بكر خليلا ولكن صاحبكم خليل الله (2)
إذا الخليل هو الذي يتخلل الحب جميع أجزاء قلبه ظاهرا وباطنا ويستوعبه
ولم يستوعب قلبه عليه السلام سوى حب الله وقد منعته الخلة عن الاشتراك فيه
مع أنه اتخذ عليا رضي الله عنه أخا فقال علي مني بمنزلة هرون من موسى إلا
النبوة (3)
فعدل بعلي عن النبوة كما عدل بأبي بكر عن الخلة فشارك أبو بكر عليا رضي
الله عنهما في الأخوة وزاد عليه بمقاربة الخلة وأهليته لها لو كان للشركة
في الخلة مجال فإنه نبه عليه بقوله لاتخذت أبا بكر خليلا وكان صلى الله
عليه وسلم حبيب الله وخليله وقد روي أنه صعد المنبر يوما مستبشرا فرحا فقال
إن الله قد اتخذني خليلا كما اتخذ إبراهيم خليلا فأنا حبيب الله وأنا خليل
الله تعالى (4)
فإذن ليس قبل PageV02P193
المعرفة رابطة ولا بعد الخلة درجة وما سواهما من الدرجات بينهما
وقد ذكرنا حق الصحبة والأخوة ويدخل فيهما ما وراءهما من المحبة والخلة
وإنما تتفاوت الرتب في تلك الحقوق كما سبق بحسب تفاوت المحبة والأخوة حتى
ينتهي أقصاها إلى أن يوجب الإيثار بالنفس والمال كما آثر أبو بكر رضي الله
عنه نبينا صلى  الله عليه وسلم وكما آثره طلحة ببدنه إذ جعل نفسه وقاية
لشخصه العزيز صلى الله عليه وسلم فنحر الآن نريد أن نذكر حق أخوة الإسلام
وحق الرحم وحق الوالدين وحق الجوار وحق الملك أعني ملك اليمين فإن ملك
النكاح قد ذكرنا حقوقه في كتاب آداب النكاح

### |||| حقوق المسلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ط (khalata)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intermingling, blending, and mixing of one thing with another; social mixing (mukhālaṭah) as the interpenetration of persons in shared life.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The necessary condition of human sociability (madaniyyah); mixing as the practical means of fulfilling mutual needs, distinct from mere proximity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical blending; metaphorical (majāz) for social intercourse, where the "mixing" is of interests and duties.
- Root: ر-ح-م (raḥima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The womb (raḥim); kinship bond; mercy as its derivative, since mercy flows from the womb-tie.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The specific bond of blood relation (qarābah) that entails obligatory kindness (ṣilah); a graded right (ḥaqq) intensifying with proximity of degree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the womb; metaphorical for the protective compassion due to kin, extending to the "womb" of the community.
- Root: خ-ل-ل (khalla)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A gap or interstice; khullah as the state of intimate friendship that penetrates (yatakhallalu) the heart's core.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The highest degree of love (maḥabbah) in the spiritual hierarchy; exclusive devotion, as in the case of Ibrāhīm and the Prophet ﷺ as "Khalīl Allāh."
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical penetration through gaps; metaphorical for love that permeates every part of the heart, leaving no room for rivals.
