chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ص (khalasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of purity, deliverance, and being freed from entanglement; al-khalāṣ is the act of escaping unharmed from a harmful situation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, khalāṣ denotes salvation from spiritual harm and moral corruption, not merely physical escape.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical escape; metaphorical (majāz) for the soul's liberation from social vices like backbiting and envy.
- Root: ش-ر (sharra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Evil, harm, or wickedness; the opposite of khayr (good), encompassing both active malice and passive corruption.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Shar is any act or trait that distances one from divine proximity; in social context, it is the moral poison emanating from corrupt companionship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for tangible harm; metaphorical for the subtle erosion of faith through association with the wicked.
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, withdrawal, or isolation; ʿuzlah is the deliberate act of distancing oneself from a group.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the spiritual path, ʿuzlah is a protective discipline (riyāḍah) to safeguard the heart from worldly distractions and moral contagion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical separation; metaphorical for inner detachment from the concerns and vices of society.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Causal Clauses (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The text frequently employs conditional constructions (e.g., "if you isolate yourself, you are spared") where the protasis establishes a cause and the apodosis its necessary effect, requiring precise temporal and logical sequencing in translation.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the fourth benefit of seclusion (ʿuzlah) is deliverance (khalāṣ) from the evil of people. For they harm you at one time through backbiting (ghībah), at another through ill suspicion (sūʾ al-ẓann) and false accusation, through fabricated demands and false hopes that are difficult to fulfill, and at yet another time through slander (namīmah) or lying. Perhaps they observe from you certain deeds or words whose inner reality their intellects cannot fathom, and so they store these up as a treasure with them, reserving them for a moment when an opportunity for evil appears. Thus, if you isolate yourself from them, you are spared the need for self-guarding against all of this.

For this reason, one of the sages said to another: "Shall I teach you two verses better than ten thousand dirhams?" He asked, "What are they?" He said:
"Lower your voice if you speak at night, / And look around by day before you speak.
For speech, once uttered, cannot return, / Whether it be ugly or beautiful."

There is no doubt that whoever mingles with people and shares in their affairs is never free from an envier (ḥāsid) or an enemy who thinks ill of him and imagines that he is preparing for hostilities against him, plotting mischief against him, and secretly devising ruin behind his back. For people, whenever their greed for a matter intensifies, {«يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ هُمُ الْعَدُوُّ فَاحْذَرْهُمْ»} ("They think every cry is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them") — and their greed for the world has intensified, so they suspect none but others of greed for it. Al-Mutanabbī said:
"When a man's deeds turn foul, his suspicions turn foul, / And he believes the false imaginings he habitually entertains.
He becomes hostile to his lovers through the words of his slanderers, / And so he wanders in a dark night of doubt."

It has been said: "The companionship of the wicked bequeaths ill suspicion of the righteous."

The kinds of evil that a man encounters from his acquaintances and from those with whom he mingles are many, and we shall not prolong the enumeration of their details; in what we have mentioned there is an indication of their sum total, and in seclusion there is deliverance from all of them. To this pointed the majority of those who chose seclusion.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "Be a brother of the ignorant, and you will be lightened" — and it is narrated as raised (marfūʿ) [to the Prophet].

And the poet said:
"Whoever praises people without testing them, / Then tests them, will blame the one he praised.
He finds comfort in solitude, / While the near and the far bring him loneliness."

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said concerning seclusion: "It is rest from the evil companion."

It was said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr: "Will you not come to Medina?" He replied: "There remains in it none but an envier of blessings or one who rejoices at calamity."

Ibn al-Sammāk said: "A companion of ours wrote to me: 'To proceed — people were once a remedy (dawāʾ) by which one was cured, but they have become a disease (dāʾ) with no cure for it. So flee from them as you would flee from a lion.'"

One of the Bedouins used to keep constant company with a tree and would say: "It is my boon companion, possessing three qualities: if it hears from me, it does not inform against me; if I spit in its face, it bears it from me; and if I carouse against it, it does not grow angry." Al-Rashīd heard this and said: "He has made me abstain from boon companions."

Some of them had attached themselves to notebooks and graves, and it was said to him [about this]. He replied: "I have seen nothing safer than solitude, nor more admonishing than a grave, nor a companion more delightful than a notebook."

Al-Ḥasan, may God be pleased with him, said: "I intended to perform the pilgrimage, and Thābit al-Bunānī — who was also among the friends of God — heard of that and said: 'It has reached me that you intend the pilgrimage, and I would love to accompany you.' Al-Ḥasan said to him: 'Woe to you! Leave us to associate under the veil of God over us. I fear that if we travel together, one of us might see from the other that which we would find loathsome in each other.'"

This is an indication of another benefit in seclusion: the preservation of the veil (satr) over religion, manliness (murūʾah), character, poverty, and all other faults.

God, Glorified be He, has praised those who conceal themselves, saying: {«يَحْسَبُهُمُ الْجَاهِلُ أَغْنِيَاءَ مِنَ التَّعَفُّفِ»} ("The ignorant man thinks them wealthy from their self-restraint"). And the poet said:
"No shame is there if a blessing departs from the free man, / But shame is that comeliness should depart."

A man is never free, in his religion, his worldly affairs, his character, and his deeds, from faults (ʿawrāt) — the first being in religion and the world — whose concealment is [necessary]; safety does not remain with their exposure.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "People were once leaves without thorns; today people are thorns without leaves."

If such is the judgment of his time — and he was at the end of the first century — then one should not doubt that the later [age] is worse.

Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: "Sufyān al-Thawrī said to me, in wakefulness during his life and in a dream after his death: 'Reduce your acquaintance with people, for deliverance from them is severe. I do not reckon that I saw anything I disliked except from one I knew.'"

One of them said: "I came to Mālik ibn Dīnār while he was sitting alone, and a dog had placed its jaw upon his knee. I went to drive it away, and he said: 'Leave it, O man! This one neither harms nor injures, and it is better than an evil companion.'"

It was said to one of them: "What made you isolate yourself from people?" He said: "I feared that my religion might be stripped from me without my perceiving it." This is an indication of the stealthy theft of one's nature from the character of an evil companion.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "Fear God, and beware of people. For they have never mounted the back of a camel but that they have made it lame, nor the back of a steed but that they have hamstrung it, nor the heart of a believer but that they have ruined it."

One of them said: "Reduce your acquaintances, for it is safer for your religion and your heart, and lighter regarding the falling away of obligations from you — because whenever acquaintances multiply, obligations grow great, and fulfilling all of them becomes difficult."

One of them said: "Deny those you know, and do not seek acquaintance with those you do not know."

chapters.title_en: The Fifth and Sixth Benefits of Seclusion, and the Harms of Seclusion
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||| الفائدة الخامسة

أن ينقطع طمع الناس عنك وينقطع طمعك عن الناس
فأما  انقطاع طمع الناس عنك ففيه فوائد فإن رضا الناس غاية لا تدرك
فاشتغال المرء بإصلاح نفسه أولى ومن أهون الحقوق وأيسرها حضور الجنازة
وعيادة المريض وحضور الولائم والإملاكات وفيها تضييع الأوقات وتعرض للآفات
ثم قد تعوق عن بعضها العوائق وتستقبل فيها المعاذير ولا يمكن إظهار كل
الأعذار فيقولون له قمت بحق فلان وقصرت في حقنا ويصير ذلك سبب عداوة فقد
قيل من لم يعد مريضا في وقت العيادة اشتهى موته خيفة من تخجيله إذا صح على
تقصيره
ومن عمم الناس كلهم بالحرمان رضوا عنه كلهم ولو خصص استوحشوا
وتعميمهم بجميع الحقوق لا يقدر عليه المتجرد له طول الليل والنهار فكيف
من له مهم يشغله في دين أو دنيا قال عمرو بن العاص كثرة الأصدقاء كثرة
الغرماء
وقال ابن الرومي
عدوك من صديقك مستفاد ... فلا تستكثرن من الصحاب
فإن الداء أكثر ما تراه ... يكون من الطعام أو الشراب
وقال الشافعي رحمه الله أصل كل عداوة اصطناع المعروف الى اللئام
وأما انقطاع طمعك عنهم فهو أيضا فائدة جزيلة فإن من نظر الى زهرة الدنيا
وزينتها تحرك حرصه وانبعث بقوة الحرص طمعه ولا يرى إلا الخيبة في أكثر
الأحوال فيتأذى بذلك
ومهما اعتزل لم يشاهد وإذا لم يشاهد لم يشته ولم يطمع ولذلك قال الله
تعالى {ولا تمدن عينيك إلى ما متعنا به أزواجا منهم} وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم انظروا الى من هو دونكم ولا تنظروا الى من هو فوقكم فإنه أجدر أن لا
تزدروا نعمة الله عليكم (1)
وقال عون بن عبد الله كنت أجالس الأغنياء فلم أزل مغموما كنت أرى ثوبا
أحسن من ثوبي ودابة أفره من دابتي فجالست الفقراء فاسترحت
وحكى أن المزني رحمه الله خرج من باب جامع الفسطاط وقد أقبل ابن عبد
الحكم في موكبه فبهره ما رأى من حسن حاله وحسن هيئته فتلا قوله تعالى
{وجعلنا بعضكم لبعض فتنة أتصبرون} ثم قال بلى أصبر وأرضى وكان فقيرا مقلا
فالذي هو في بيته لا يبتلى بمثل هذه الفتن
فإن من شاهد زينة الدنيا فأما أن يقوى دينه ويقينه فيصبر الى أن يتجرع
مرارة الصبر وهو أمر من الصبر أو تنبعث رغبته فيحتال في طلب الدنيا فيهلك
هلاكا مؤبدا أما في الدنيا فبالطمع الذي يخيب في أكثر الأوقات فليس كل من
يطلب الدنيا تتيسر له وأما في الآخرة فإيثاره متاع الدنيا على ذكر الله
تعالى والتقرب إليه
ولذلك قال ابن الإعرابي
إذا كان باب الذل من جانب الغنى ... سموت الى العلياء من جانب الفقر
أشار الى أن الطمع يوجب في الحال ذلا

### |||| الفائدة السادسة

الخلاص من مشاهدة الثقلاء والحمقى ومقاساة حمقهم
وأخلاقهم فإن رؤية الثقيل هي العمى الأصغر
قيل للأعمش مم عمشت عيناك قال من النظر الى الثقلاء
ويحكى أنه دخل عليه أبو حنيفة فقال في الخبر {أن من} PageV02P235
سلب الله كريمتيه عوضه الله عنهما ما هو خير منهما (1)
فما الذي عوضك فقال في معرض المطايبة عوضني الله منهما أنه كفاني رؤية
الثقلاء وأنت منهم
وقال ابن سيرين سمعت رجلا يقول نظرت الى ثقيل مرة فغشى علي
وقال جالينوس لكل شيء حمى وحمى الروح النظر الى الثقلاء
وقال الشافعي رحمه الله ما جالست ثقيلا إلا وجدت الجانب الذي يليه من
بدني كأنه أثقل علي من الجانب الآخر
وهذه الفوائد ما سوى الأوليين متعلقة بالمقاصد الدنيوية الحاضرة ولكنها
أيضا تتعلق بالدين
فإن الإنسان مهما تأذى برؤية ثقيل لم يأمن أن يغتابه وأن يستنكر ما هو
صنع الله فإذا تأذى من غيره بغيبة أو سوء ظن أو محاسدة أو نميمة أو غير ذلك
لم يصبر عن مكافأته
وكل ذلك يجر الى فساد الدين وفي العزلة سلامة عن جميع ذلك فليفهم

### ||||  آفات العزلة

اعلم أن من المقاصد الدينية والدنيوية ما يستفاد بالاستعانة بالغير ولا
يحصل ذلك إلا بالمخالطة
فكل ما يستفاد من المخالطة يفوت بالعزلة وفواته من آفات العزلة
فانظر الى فوائد المخالطة والدواعي اليها ما هي وهي التعليم والتعلم
والنفع والانتفاع والتأديب والتأدب والاستيناس والإيناس ونيل الثواب
وإنالته في القيام بالحقوق  واعتياد التواضع واستفادة التجارب من مشاهدة
الأحوال والاعتبار بها
فلنفصل ذلك فإنها من فوائد المخالطة وهي سبع

### |||||  الفائدة الأولى التعليم والتعلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-م-ع (ṭamaʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "craving" or "coveting" — an inward reaching of the soul toward something desired, whether permissible or blameworthy.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭamaʿ denotes the soul's attachment to worldly goods, which fuels avarice (ḥirṣ) and distracts from the Hereafter; its opposite is qunūʿ (contentment) or al-ya's (despair of what others possess).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to the predator's longing for prey; metaphorical (majāz) usage applies to the heart's inclination toward worldly allurements — here, the cutting off of ṭamaʿ is a spiritual discipline, not a physical act.
- Root: ث-ق-ل (thaqula)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes heaviness and weight; a "thaqīl" (burdensome person) is one whose company weighs upon the soul.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ethical discourse, the thaqīl is one whose presence breeds spiritual dullness and whose folly (ḥumq) provokes sin — viewing such a person is termed "the lesser blindness" (al-ʿamā al-aṣghar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal heaviness is physical weight; metaphorical usage transfers this to social and psychological burden, as in the reported sayings of the Salaf.
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is separation and withdrawal from a group or affair.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿUzlah (seclusion) is a middle path — not absolute solitude, but retreat from harmful mixing while preserving necessary communal obligations.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is physical separation; metaphorical is the heart's detachment from worldly concerns even amid people.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs "fa-ammā... fa-" (as for... then) to structure parallel benefits, and "law... la-" (if... then) for counterfactual conditions, requiring careful rendering of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
### The Fifth Benefit

That people's hopes should be cut off from you, and your hope should be cut off from them.

As for the cutting off of people's hopes from you — therein lie benefits. For the satisfaction of people is a goal that is never attained. So a man's occupation with reforming his own soul is more fitting. Among the easiest of obligations and the lightest of them are attending the funeral, visiting the sick, and attending banquets and marriage feasts — and in these there is the wasting of times and exposure to afflictions. Moreover, some of these may be hindered by obstacles, and excuses arise in them, yet one cannot show all of one's excuses. So they say to him: "You fulfilled the right of so-and-so, but you fell short regarding our right" — and that becomes a cause of enmity. For it has been said: "Whoever does not visit the sick at the time of visiting, [the sick man] desires his death, fearing the disgrace of his own shortcoming when he recovers."

And whoever denies all people equally [of his attendance] — they are all pleased with him. But if he singled out some, they would take offense. Yet to include them all in all rights is not within the power of one who devotes himself [to worship] throughout the night and day — so how [could it be] for one who has an important occupation in religion or worldly affairs? ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said: "The abundance of friends is the abundance of creditors."

And Ibn al-Rūmī said:
"Your enemy is acquired from your friend — so do not multiply companions excessively. For the disease, most often seen, comes from food or drink."

And al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: "The root of every enmity is the conferring of favors upon the base."

As for the cutting off of your hope from them — this too is a magnificent benefit. For whoever looks upon the bloom of this world and its adornment, his covetousness is stirred, and by the strength of covetousness his hope is roused — and he sees nothing but disappointment in most circumstances, and is thereby harmed.

And whenever he withdraws, he does not witness; and when he does not witness, he does not desire; and when he does not desire, he does not hope. Therefore God, exalted, said: {«وَلَا تَمُدَّنَّ عَيْنَيْكَ إِلَىٰ مَا مَتَّعْنَا بِهِ أَزْوَاجًا مِّنْهُمْ»} ("And do not extend your eyes to what We have given enjoyment to pairs of them") — and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Look to those who are below you, and do not look to those who are above you, for that is more fitting that you not disparage God's blessing upon you."

And ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: "I used to sit with the rich, and I remained constantly grieved — I would see a garment better than my garment, and a mount more excellent than my mount. Then I sat with the poor, and I found rest."

And it is related that al-Muzanī, may God have mercy on him, came out from the gate of the Jāmiʿ of Fusṭāṭ when Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam approached in his procession — and he was dazzled by what he saw of the excellence of his state and the beauty of his appearance. So he recited the saying of God, exalted: {«وَجَعَلْنَا بَعْضَكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ فِتْنَةً أَتَصْبِرُونَ»} ("And We have made some of you a trial for others — will you be patient?") — then he said: "Yes, I am patient and content." And he was a poor man of little means. So the one who is in his house is not afflicted with such trials.

For whoever witnesses the adornment of this world — either his religion and certainty are strengthened, and he is patient until he swallows the bitterness of patience (and that is a bitterer thing than patience itself), or his desire is stirred, and he schemes in seeking the world, and is destroyed with an everlasting destruction — as for this world, through the hope that is disappointed in most times, for not everyone who seeks the world finds it easy; and as for the Hereafter, through his preferring the goods of this world over the remembrance of God, exalted, and drawing near to Him.

Therefore Ibn al-Aʿrābī said:
"When the door of abasement is on the side of wealth, I ascend to the heights on the side of poverty."
He indicated that hope (ṭamaʿ) necessitates abasement in the present state.

### The Sixth Benefit

Deliverance from witnessing burdensome fools (thuqalāʾ) and from enduring their folly and their manners. For the sight of a burdensome person is the "lesser blindness" (al-ʿamā al-aṣghar).

It was said to al-Aʿmash: "Why have your eyes become dim?" He said: "From looking at burdensome people."

And it is related that Abū Ḥanīfah entered upon him, and he said: "In the report [it is mentioned] that {«مَن سَلَبَهُ اللهُ كَرِيمَتَيْهِ عَوَّضَهُ اللهُ عَنْهُمَا مَا هُوَ خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُمَا»} ('Whoever God deprives of his two precious [eyes], God compensates him with what is better than them') — so what has He compensated you with?" He said, in the vein of jest: "God has compensated me with this: that He has spared me the sight of burdensome people — and you are among them."

And Ibn Sīrīn said: "I heard a man say: 'I looked at a burdensome person once, and I fainted.'"

And Galen said: "Everything has a fever, and the fever of the spirit is looking at burdensome people."

And al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: "I never sat with a burdensome person except that I found the side of my body adjacent to him as though it were heavier upon me than the other side."

These benefits — apart from the first two — pertain to present worldly aims. But they also pertain to religion. For whenever a man is harmed by the sight of a burdensome person, he is not safe from backbiting him, or from disapproving of what God has wrought. And when he is harmed by another through backbiting, or ill-opinion, or envy, or slander, or other than that, he does not restrain himself from requiting him. And all of that leads to the corruption of religion. And in seclusion there is safety from all of that — so let this be understood.

### The Harms of Seclusion

Know that among religious and worldly aims, there are those that are attained through the assistance of others, and that is not obtained except through social mixing (mukhālaṭah). So everything that is attained through mixing is lost through seclusion — and its loss is among the harms of seclusion.

So look at the benefits of mixing and the motives toward it — what are they? They are: teaching and learning; benefiting and being benefited; disciplining and being disciplined; finding companionship and giving companionship; attaining reward and causing [others] to attain it in fulfilling rights; habituating oneself to humility; and acquiring experiences through witnessing circumstances and drawing lessons from them.

Let us detail these, for they are among the benefits of mixing — and they are seven.

### The First Benefit: Teaching and Learning

chapters.title_en: On the Prerequisites of Learning and the Perils of Isolation for the Ignorant
chapters.arabic_text:
وقد ذكرنا فضلهما في كتاب العلم وهما أعظم العبادات في الدنيا
ولا يتصور ذلك إلا بالمخالطة إلا أن العلوم كثيرة وعن بعضها مندوحة
وبعضها ضروري في الدنيا
فالمحتاج إلى التعلم لما هو فرض عليه عاص بالعزلة
وإن تعلم الفرض وكان لا يتأتى منه الخوض في العلوم ورأى الإشتغال
بالعبادة فليعتزل
وإن كان يقدر على التبرز في علوم الشرع والعقل فالعزلة في حقه قبل التعلم
غاية الخسران
ولهذا قال النخعي وغيره تفقه ثم اعتزل فمن اعتزل قبل التعلم فهو في
الأكثر مضيع أوقاته بنوم أو فكر في هوس وغايته أن يستغرق الأوقات بأوراد
يستوعبها ولا ينفك في أعماله بالبدن والقلب عن أنواع من الغرور يخيب سعيه
ويبطل عمله بحيث لا يدري ولا ينفك اعتقاده في الله وصفاته عن أوهام يتوهمها
ويأنس بها وعن خواطر فاسدة تعتريه فيها فيكون في أكثر أحواله ضحكة للشيطان
وهو يرى نفسه من العباد
فالعلم هو أصل الدين فلا خير في عزلة العوام والجهال أعني من لا يحسن
العبادة في الخلوة ولا يعرف جميع ما يلزم فيها
فمثال النفس مثال مريض يحتاج الى طبيب متلطف يعالجه فالمريض الجاهل إذا
خلا بنفسه عن الطبيب قبل أن يتعلم الطب تضاعف لا محالة مرضه
فلا تليق العزلة إلا بالعالم وأما التعليم ففيه ثواب عظيم مهما صحت نية
المعلم والمتعلم
ومهما كان القصد إقامة الجاه والاستكثار بالأصحاب والأتباع فهو هلاك
الدين
وقد ذكرنا وجه ذلك في كتاب العلم
وحكم في العالم في هذا الزمان إن يعتزل إن أراد سلامة دينه
فإنه لا يرى مستفيدا يطلب فائدة لدينه بل لا طالب إلا لكلام مزخرف يستميل
به العوام في معرض الوعظ أو الجدل معقد يتوصل به الى إفحام الأقران ويتقرب
به الى السلطان ويستعمل في معرض المنافسة والمباهاة وأقرب علم مرغوب فيه
المذهب ولا يطلب غالبا إلا للتوصل الى التقدم على الأمثال  وتولي الولايات
واجتلاب الأموال
فهؤلاء كلهم يقتضي الدين والحزم الإعتزال عنهم PageV02P236
فإن صودف طالب لله ومتقرب بالعلم الى الله فأكبر الكبائر الإعتزال عنه
وكتمان العلم منه وهذا لا يصادف في بلدة كبيرة أكثر من واحد أو اثنين إن
صودف
ولا ينبغي أن يغتر الإنسان بقول سفيان تعلمنا العلم لغير الله فأبى العلم
أن يكون إلا لله فإن الفقهاء يتعلمون لغير الله ثم يرجعون الى الله
وانظر الى أواخر أعمار الأكثرين منهم واعتبرهم أنهم ماتوا وهم هلكى على
طلب الدنيا ومتكالبون عليها أو راغبون عنها وزاهدون فيها وليس الخبر
كالمعاينة
واعلم أن العلم الذي أشار اليه سفيان هو علم الحديث وتفسير القرآن ومعرفة
سير الأنبياء والصحابة فإن فيها التخويف والتحذير وهو سبب لإثارة الخوف من
الله فإن لم يؤثر في الحال أثر في المآل
وأما الكلام والفقه المجرد الذي يتعلق بفتاوى المعاملات وفصل الخصومات
المذهب منه والخلاف لا يرد الراغب فيه للدنيا الى الله بل لا يزال متماديا
في حرصه الى آخر عمره
ولعل ما أودعناه هذا الكتاب إن تعلمه المتعلم رغبة في الدنيا فيجوز أن
يرخص فيه إذ يرجى أن ينزجر به في آخر عمره فإنه مشحون بالتخويف بالله
والترغيب في الآخرة والتحذير من الدنيا وذلك مما يصادف في الأحاديث وتفسير
القرآن ولا يصادف في كلام ولا في خلاف ولا في مذهب
فلا ينبغي أن يخادع الإنسان نفسه فإن المقصر العالم بتقصيره أسعد حالا من
الجاهل المغرور أو المتجاهل المغبون وكل عالم اشتد حرصه على التعليم يوشك
أن يكون غرضه القبول والجاه وحظه تلذذ النفس في الحال باستشعار الإدلال على
الجهال والتكبر عليهم فآفة العلم الخيلاء (1)
كما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم
ولذلك حكي عن بشر أنه دفن سبعة عشر قمطرا من كتب الأحاديث التي سمعها
وكان لا يحدث ويقول أني أشتهي أن أحدث فلذلك لا أحدث ولو اشتهيت أن لا أحدث
لحدثت ولذلك قال حدثنا باب من أبواب الدنيا وإذا قال الرجل حدثنا فإنما
يقول أوسعوا لي
وقالت رابعة  العدوية لسفيان الثوري نعم الرجل أنت لولا رغبتك في الدنيا
قال وفيماذا رغبت قالت في الحديث
ولذلك قال أبو سليمان الداراني من تزوج أو طلب الحديث أو اشتغل بالسفر
فقد ركن إلى الدنيا
فهذه آفات قد نبهنا عليها في كتاب العلم والحزم الاحتراز بالعزلة وترك
الاستكثار من الأصحاب ما أمكن بل الذي يطلب الدنيا بتدريسه وتعليمه فالصواب
له إن كان غافلا في مثل هذا الزمان أن يتركه
فلقد صدق أبو سليمان الخطابي حيث قال دع الراغبين في صحبتك والتعلم منك
فليس لك منهم مال ولا جمال إخوان العلانية أعداء السر إذا لقوك تملقوك وإذا
غبت عنهم سلقوك من أتاك منهم كان عليك رقيبا وإذا خرج كان عليك خطيبا أهل
نفاق ونميمة وغل وخديعة فلا تغتر باجتماعهم عليك فما غرضهم العلم بل الجاه
والمال وأن يتخذوك سلما الى أوطارهم وأغراضهم وحمارا في حاجاتهم إن قصرت في
غرض من أغراضهم كانوا أشد أعدائك ثم يعدون ترددهم إليك دالة عليك ويرونه
حقا واجبا لديك ويفرضون عليك أن تبذل عرضك وجاهك ودينك لهم فتعادي عدوهم
وتنصر قريبهم وخادمهم ووليهم وتنتهض لهم سفيها وقد كنت فقيها وتكون لهم
تابعا خسيسا بعد أن كنت متبوعا رئيسا
ولذلك قيل اعتزال العامة مروءة تامة
فهذا معنى كلامه وإن خالف بعض ألفاظه وهو حق وصدق
فإنك ترى المدرسين في رق دائم وتحت حق لازم ومنة ثقيلة ممن يتردد اليهم
فكأنه يهدي تحفة اليهم ويرى حقه واجبا عليهم
وربما لا يختلف اليه ما لم يتكفل برزق له على الإدرار
ثم إن المدرس المسكين قد يعجز عن القيام بذلك من ماله فلا يزال مترددا
الى أبواب السلاطين ويقاسي الذل والشدائد مقاساة الذليل PageV02P237
المهين حتى يكتب له على بعض وجوه السحت مال حرام ثم لا يزال العامل
يسترقه ويستخدمه ويمتهنه ويستذله الى أن يسلم إليه ما يقدره نعمة مستأنفة
من عنده عليه ثم يبقى في مقاساة القسمة على أصحابه إن سوى بينهم مقته
المميزون ونسبوه الى الحمق وقلة التمييز والقصور عن درك  مصارفات الفضل
والقيام بمقادير الحقوق بالعدل وإن فاوت بينهم سلقه السفهاء بألسن حداد
وثاروا عليه ثوران الأساود والآساد فلا يزال في مقاساتهم في الدنيا وفي
مطالبة ما يأخذه ويفرقه عليهم في العقبى
والعجب أنه مع هذا البلاء كله يمني نفسه بالأباطيل ويدليها بحبل الغرور
ويقول لها لا تفتري عن صنيعك فإنما أنت بما تفعلينه مريدة وجه الله تعالى
ومذيعة شرع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وناشرة علم دين الله وقائمة
بكفاية طلاب العلم من عباد الله وأموال السلاطين لا مالك لها وهي مرصدة
للمصالح وأي مصلحة أكبر من تكثير أهل العلم فبهم يظهر الدين ويتقوى أهله
ولو لم يكن ضحكة للشيطان لعلم بأدنى تأمل أن فساد الزمان لا سبب له إلا
كثرة أمثال أولئك الفقهاء الذين يأكلون ما يجدون ولا يميزون بين الحلال
والحرام فتلحظهم أعين الجهال ويستجرئون على المعاصي باستجرائهم اقتداء بهم
واقتفاء لآثارهم
ولذلك قيل ما فسدت الرعية إلا بفساد الملوك وما فسدت الملوك إلا بفساد
العلماء
فنعوذ بالله من الغرور والعمى فإنه الداء الذي ليس له دواء
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Physical separation, withdrawal, setting apart from a group or place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Voluntary seclusion (al-ʿuzlah) as a spiritual discipline, distinct from forced exile; its legitimacy hinges on the state of the learner's soul.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in spatial terms; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the heart's detachment from worldly attachments.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The protasis (law/fa-in) governs the apodosis, requiring precise parsing to distinguish categorical rulings (e.g., 'if he is able... then isolation is loss') from contingent advice.
chapters.translation:
I say: We have already mentioned the excellence of both knowledge and seclusion in the Book of Knowledge, and they are the greatest of acts of worship in this world. Yet this cannot be conceived except through social mixing (mukhālaṭah) — save that the sciences are many, and from some of them there is dispensation (mandūḥah), while some are necessary in this world.

Thus, one who is in need of learning that which is obligatory upon him is disobedient by choosing seclusion. But if he has learned the obligatory duty, and cannot engage in the deeper sciences, and sees that occupying himself with worship is his proper course, then let him seclude himself.

However, if he is capable of excelling in the religious and rational sciences, then seclusion in his case, before learning, is the utmost loss. For this reason, al-Nakhaʿī and others said: "Acquire deep understanding (tafaqqah), then seclude yourself." For whoever secludes himself before learning is, in most cases, wasting his hours in sleep or in reflection upon vain fancies (hawas); and at best, he fills his times with litanies (awrād) that consume them entirely, yet he is not free, in his bodily and heart-driven works, from varieties of self-delusion (ghurūr) that render his striving futile and his deed void — without his even perceiving it. Nor is his belief concerning God and His attributes free from false imaginings (awhām) he conjures and grows fond of, nor from corrupt thoughts (khawāṭir fāsidah) that assail him therein. Thus, in most of his states, he becomes a laughingstock of Satan while imagining himself to be among the devout.

So knowledge is the root of religion; hence there is no good in the seclusion of the common folk and the ignorant — I mean, those who do not know how to worship properly in solitude, nor know all that is incumbent upon them therein.

The parable of the soul is that of a sick man who needs a gentle physician to treat him. If the ignorant patient isolates himself from the physician before learning medicine, his illness will inevitably double. Therefore, seclusion befits none but the learned man.

As for teaching, it carries immense reward whenever the intention of the teacher and the learner is sound. But whenever the aim is to establish prestige (jāh) and to multiply companions and followers, it is the ruin of religion. We have already mentioned this point in the Book of Knowledge.

The ruling for the scholar in this age is to seclude himself if he desires the safety of his religion. For he will not see a seeker who pursues benefit for his faith; rather, there is no seeker except for embellished speech (kalām muzakhraf) by which he sways the common folk under the guise of preaching, or for convoluted disputation (jadal muʿaqqad) by which he attains the refutation of peers, or by which he draws near to the Sultan, or which he employs in the spirit of rivalry and ostentation. The nearest science desired is the legal school (madhhab), which is sought only as a means to surpass one's equals, to assume offices, and to amass wealth. All such persons — religion and prudence demand that one withdraw from them. [Page V02P236]

But if one encounters a seeker for God's sake, drawing near to God through knowledge, then the greatest of grave sins is to withdraw from him and to conceal knowledge from him. Yet such a one is not found in a large town except as one or two, if found at all.

One should not be deluded by the saying of Sufyān: "We learned knowledge for other than God, but knowledge refused to be for anything but God." For jurists learn for other than God, then return to God. Look at the final years of most of them and take heed: they died ruined upon the pursuit of this world, clamoring for it — or turning away from it and renouncing it. But report is not like direct observation (al-khabar laysa ka-l-muʿāyanah).

Know that the knowledge to which Sufyān referred is the science of ḥadīth, the exegesis of the Qurʾān, and the knowledge of the biographies of the Prophets and the Companions. For in these there is intimidation and warning (takhwīf wa-tahdhīr), and they are the cause of arousing fear of God. If this does not take effect immediately, it takes effect in the final outcome.

As for speculative theology (kalām) and bare jurisprudence (fiqh mujarrad) — which pertains to legal verdicts on transactions and the adjudication of disputes, the school (madhhab) and its disagreements — these do not turn the one who desires this world back to God. Rather, he remains persistent in his greed until the end of his life.

Perhaps what we have deposited in this book — if a learner studies it with worldly desire — it may be permissible to grant him license therein, for it is hoped that he will be deterred by it at the end of his life. For it is filled with intimidation by God, persuasion toward the Hereafter, and warning against this world. Such matters are found in the ḥadīth and the exegesis of the Qurʾān, and are not found in kalām, nor in disagreement (khilāf), nor in the madhhab.

So one should not deceive himself. For the negligent one who knows his negligence is more fortunate in state than the deluded ignorant, or the one who feigns ignorance and is duped. Every scholar whose eagerness for teaching intensifies — it is likely that his aim is acceptance and prestige, and his share is the soul's immediate pleasure in feeling superiority over the ignorant and arrogance toward them. For the affliction of knowledge is vainglory (khuyalāʾ), as the Prophet ﷺ said.

For this reason, it is narrated of Bishr that he buried seventeen camel-loads (qanāṭir) of ḥadīth books he had heard, and he would not narrate, saying: "I long to narrate, and therefore I do not narrate. Had I longed not to narrate, I would have narrated." For this reason it was said: "Narrate to us (ḥaddithnā) is a door among the doors of this world; when a man says 'narrate to us,' he is only saying: 'make room for me.'"

And Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah said to Sufyān al-Thawrī: "What an excellent man you are, were it not for your desire for this world." He said: "In what do I desire it?" She said: "In ḥadīth."

For this reason, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "Whoever marries, or seeks ḥadīth, or occupies himself with travel, has leaned toward this world."

These are afflictions (āfāt) we have already warned against in the Book of Knowledge. Prudence demands guarding oneself through seclusion and refraining from multiplying companions as much as possible. Rather, the one who seeks this world through his teaching and instruction — the correct course for him, if he is heedless, in such an age as this, is to abandon it.

How true was Abū Sulaymān al-Khaṭṭābī when he said: "Leave those who desire your company and learning from you, for you have from them neither wealth nor beauty. Brothers in public are enemies in secret. When they meet you, they flatter you; when you are absent, they slander you. Whoever of them comes to you becomes a watcher over you, and when he leaves, he becomes an orator against you. They are people of hypocrisy, backbiting, rancor, and deceit. Do not be deluded by their gathering around you, for their aim is not knowledge but prestige and wealth — that they may take you as a ladder to their desires and a donkey for their needs. If you fall short in any of their aims, they become your fiercest enemies. Then they count their frequent visits to you as a favor upon you, and deem it an obligation due to you, and impose upon you that you expend your honor, your standing, and your religion for them — so you make enemies of their enemies and support their kin, their servants, and their allies. You rise for them foolishly after having been wise, and become for them a base follower after having been a followed leader."

For this reason it was said: "Withdrawing from the common folk is complete manliness (murūʾah tāmmah)."

This is the meaning of his words, even if some of its expressions differ — and it is true and sincere.

For you see the teachers (mudarrisūn) in perpetual servitude, under a binding claim and a heavy obligation, toward those who frequent them. It is as if he is presenting a gift to them, while he deems his right an obligation upon them. Perhaps no one even attends him unless he undertakes to provide a continuous stipend for him. Then the poor teacher may be unable to fulfill that from his own wealth, so he keeps going to the doors of the Sultans, enduring humiliation and hardships with the endurance of the abased and degraded — [Page V02P237] until there is written for him, from some form of illicit gain (suḥt), forbidden wealth. Then the agent (al-ʿāmil) keeps enslaving him, employing him, degrading him, and humiliating him, until he hands over to him what he deems a fresh favor from him upon him. Then he remains in the ordeal of distribution among his companions: if he equalizes between them, the discerning ones resent him and attribute to him foolishness, lack of discernment, and failure to grasp the variations of merit and to fulfill the measures of rights with justice; and if he differentiates between them, the foolish ones lash him with sharp tongues and rise against him with the rising of serpents and lions. So he remains in their ordeals in this world, and in the Hereafter in the reckoning of what he takes and distributes among them.

The wonder is that, with all this affliction, he still deludes himself with falsehoods and dangles them before himself with the rope of self-deception, saying to his soul: "Do not slacken in your work, for you intend, by what you do, the Face of God, and you are disseminating the Law of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and spreading the knowledge of God's religion, and undertaking the sufficiency of the students of knowledge among God's servants. And the wealth of the Sultans has no owner; it is reserved for public interests — and what interest is greater than multiplying the people of knowledge? Through them religion becomes manifest and its people are strengthened."

Had he not been a laughingstock of Satan, he would realize with the slightest reflection that the corruption of the age has no cause except the abundance of such jurists — those who eat whatever they find without distinguishing between the lawful and the unlawful. The eyes of the ignorant fall upon them, and they grow bold in sins by their boldness, following them and tracing their footsteps.

For this reason it was said: "The subjects are corrupted only by the corruption of the kings, and the kings are corrupted only by the corruption of the scholars."

So we seek refuge in God from self-delusion and blindness — for it is the disease for which there is no cure.

chapters.title_en: The Second and Third Benefits: Mutual Benefit and the Discipline of the Self and Others
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||||| الفائدة الثانية النفع والإنتفاع

أما الإنتفاع بالناس فبالكسب والمعاملة
وذلك لا يتأتى إلا بالمخالطة والمحتاج إليه مضطر الى ترك العزلة فيقع في
جهاد من المخالطة أن طلب موافقة الشرع فيه كما ذكرناه في كتاب الكسب فإن
كان معه مال لو اكتفى به قانعا لأقنعه فالعزلة أفضل له إذا انسدت طرق
المكاسب في الأكثر إلى من المعاصي إلا أن يكون غرضه الكسب للصدقة
فإذا اكتسب من وجهه وتصدق به فهو أفضل من العزلة للاشتغال بالنافلة وليس
بأفضل من العزلة للاشتغال بالتحقق في معرفة الله ومعرفة علوم الشرع ولا من
الإقبال بكنه الهمة على الله تعالى والتجرد بها لذكر الله أعني من حصل له
أنس بمناجاة الله عن كشف وبصيرة لا عن أوهام وخيالات فاسدة
وأما النفع فهو أن ينفع الناس إما بماله أو ببدنه فيقوم بحاجاتهم على
سبيل الحسبة
ففي النهوض بقضاء حوائج المسلمين ثواب وذلك لا ينال إلا بالمخالطة
ومن قدر عليها مع القيام بحدود الشرع فهي أفضل له من العزلة إن كان لا
يشتغل في عزلته إلا بنوافل الصلوات والأعمال البدنية وإن كان ممن انفتح له
طريق العمل بالقلب بدوام ذكر أو فكر فذلك لا يعدل به غيره ألبتة

### ||||| الفائدة الثالثة التأديب والتأدب

ونعني به الارتياض بمقاساة الناس والمجاهدة في تحمل أذاهم كسرا للنفس
وقهرا للشهوات
وهي من الفوائد التي تستفاد بالمخالطة وهي أفضل من العزلة في حق من لم
تتهذب أخلاقه ولم تذعن لحدود الشرع شهواته ولهذا انتدب خدام الصوفية في
الرباطات فيخالطون الناس بخدمتهم وأهل السوق للسؤال منهم كبرا لرعونة النفس
واستمدادا من بركة دعاء الصوفية المنصرفين بهممهم الى الله سبحانه
وكان هذا هو المبدأ في الأعصار الخالية والآن قد خالطته الأغراض الفاسدة
ومال ذلك عن القانون كما مالت سائر شعائر الدين فصار يطلب من التواضع
بالخدمة التكثير بالاستتباع والتذرع الى جمع المال والاستظهار بكثرة
الأتباع فإن كانت النية هذه فالعزلة خير من ذلك ولو الى القبر وإن كانت
النية رياضة النفس فهي خير من العزلة في حق المحتاج الى الرياضة وذلك مما
يحتاج إليه في بداية الإرادة فبعد حصول الارتياض ينبغي أن يفهم أن الدابة
لا يطلب من رياضتها عين رياضتها بل المراد منها أن تتخذ
PageV02P238
مركبا يقطع به المراحل ويطوى على ظهره الطريق والبدن مطية للقلب يركبها
ليسلك بها طريق الآخرة وفيها شهوات إن لم يكسرها جمحت به في الطريق فمن
اشتغل طول العمر بالرياضة كان كمن اشتغل طول عمر الدابة برياضتها ولم
يركبها فلا يستفيد منها إلا الخلاص في الحال في عضها ورفسها ورمحها وهي
لعمري فائدة مقصودة ولكن مثلها حاصل في البهيمة الميتة وإنما ترد الدابة
لفائدة تحصل من حياتها فكذلك الخلاص من ألم الشهوات في الحال يحصل بالنوم
والموت ولا ينبغي أن يقنع به كالراهب الذي قيل له يا راهب فقال ما أنا راهب
إنما أنا كلب عقور حبست نفسي حتى لا أعقر الناس وهذا حسن بالإضافة الى من
يعقر الناس  ولكن لا ينبغي أن يقتصر عليه فإن من قتل نفسه أيضا لم يعقر
الناس بل ينبغي أن يتشوف إلى الغاية المقصودة بها
ومن فهم ذلك واهتدى الى الطريق وقدر على السلوك استبان له أن العزلة أعون
له من المخالطة
فأفضل لمثل هذا الشخص المخالطة أولا والعزلة آخرا
وأما التأديب فإنما نعني به أن يروض غيره وهو حال شيخ الصوفية معهم فإنه
لا يقدر على تهذيبهم إلا بمخالطتهم وحاله حال المعلم وحكمه ويتطرق اليه من
دقائق الآفات والرياء ما يتطرق الى نشر العلم إلا أن مخايل طلب الدنيا من
المريدين الطالبين للارتياض أبعد منها من طلبه العلم ولذلك يرى فيهم قلة
وفي طلبة العلم كثرة
فينبغي أن يقيس ما تيسر له من الخلوة بما تيسر له من المخالطة وتهذيب
القوم وليقابل أحدهما بالآخر وليؤثر الأفضل وذلك يدرك بدقيق الاجتهاد
ويختلف بالأحوال والأشخاص فلا يمكن الحكم عليه مطلقا بنفي ولا إثبات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ف-ع (n-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of utility, benefit, and that which yields good outcome in worldly or religious affairs.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Benefit (nafʿ) as that which conduces to the soul's perfection or its preservation; its opposite is harm (ḍarar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for tangible gain; metaphorically for spiritual advantage, as in "benefiting" through intercession or knowledge.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — governing the apodosis of "if he has wealth..." with implicit ellipsis of the subject's state.
chapters.translation:
### ||||| The Second Benefit: Benefit and Mutual Benefit

As for deriving benefit from people, it is through earning and commerce; and this cannot be achieved except through social mixing (mukhālaṭah). One who is in need of this is compelled to abandon seclusion (ʿuzlah) and thus falls into the struggle of social mixing — namely, seeking conformity with the Sacred Law therein, as we have mentioned in the Book of Earning (Kitāb al-Kasb). If he possesses wealth such that, were he content with it, it would suffice him, then seclusion is better for him when the paths of earning are, for the most part, blocked by avenues leading to acts of disobedience — unless his purpose in earning is for charity (ṣadaqah). If he earns from lawful means and gives it in charity, that is better than seclusion devoted to supererogatory acts (nāfilah); yet it is not better than seclusion devoted to attaining verification (taḥqīq) in knowledge of God and knowledge of the religious sciences, nor better than turning with the whole of one's aspiration (himmah) toward God Most High and devoting oneself exclusively thereby to the remembrance of God (dhikr) — I mean, for one who has attained intimacy (uns) with whispered communion with God (munājāt) through unveiling (kashf) and insight (baṣīrah), not through vain fancies and corrupt imaginings.

As for benefit (nafʿ), it is that one benefits people — either with one's wealth or with one's body — by fulfilling their needs in the manner of seeking divine reward (ḥisbah). In rising to accomplish the needs of the Muslims there is great reward, and that is attained only through social mixing. Whoever is capable of this while upholding the limits of the Sacred Law, it is better for him than seclusion — if in his seclusion he would occupy himself only with supererogatory prayers and bodily acts of worship. But if he is one for whom the path of inner heart-work has been opened — through constant remembrance (dhikr) or reflection (fikr) — then nothing else can equal that at all.

### ||||| The Third Benefit: Discipline and Being Disciplined

By this I mean the training (riyāḍah) of oneself through enduring people and striving (mujāhadah) in bearing their harm — as a breaking of the ego (nafs) and a subjugation of the passions (shahawāt). This is among the benefits acquired through social mixing, and it is better than seclusion for one whose character has not yet been refined and whose passions have not yet submitted to the limits of the Sacred Law. For this reason, the servants of the Sufis in the hospices (ribāṭāt) undertook such mixing — mingling with people through their service, and with the people of the marketplace by asking of them — as a means of breaking the ego's arrogance (raʿūnah) and seeking blessing (barakah) from the supplication of the Sufis who turn their aspirations toward God, Glorified be He.

This was the practice in bygone ages. But now, corrupt motives have mingled with it, and it has deviated from its proper norm (qānūn) just as other rites of religion have deviated. Thus, what is sought from humility through service has become the multiplication of followers, a means of amassing wealth, and a show of strength through the abundance of adherents. If such is the intention, then seclusion is better than that — even if it leads to the grave. But if the intention is the training of the ego, then it is better than seclusion for one who stands in need of such training. This is something needed at the beginning of the spiritual path (irādah). Yet after the training is accomplished, one should understand that the beast of burden is not sought for the sake of its training itself; rather, the intent is that it be taken as a mount by which one traverses the stages and upon whose back the road is folded. The body is likewise a mount for the heart, which rides it to traverse thereby the road of the Hereafter. Within it are passions which, if not broken, will bolt with him along the way. Whoever occupies his entire life with training alone is like one who occupies his entire life training his beast and never rides it — gaining from it nothing but immediate relief from its biting, kicking, and goring. That, by my life, is a sought benefit — but the like of it is obtained from a dead animal. Rather, the beast is sought for the benefit derived from its life. Likewise, relief from the pain of passions in the present moment is obtained through sleep and through death — and one should not be content with that, like the monk of whom it was said, "O monk!" and he replied: "I am no monk; I am but a vicious dog who has confined myself so as not to bite people." This is commendable relative to one who does bite people — but one should not stop at it, for one who kills himself also does not bite people. Rather, one should aspire toward the ultimate goal for which this is intended.

Whoever understands this, is guided to the path, and is able to traverse it — it becomes clear to him that seclusion is more helpful to him than social mixing. Thus, for such a person, social mixing is better first, and seclusion last.

As for disciplining others (taʾdīb), I mean thereby that one trains another — this being the state of the Sufi master (shaykh) with his disciples. For he cannot refine them except through mixing with them. His state is that of the teacher, and his ruling is the same. There penetrate into him the same subtle afflictions and ostentation (riyāʾ) that penetrate into the dissemination of knowledge — except that the signs of seeking worldly gain among the disciples who seek training are more remote than among those who seek knowledge. For this reason, one sees few of the former and many of the latter.

One should therefore weigh what is available to him of seclusion against what is available to him of social mixing and the refinement of people, and compare the one with the other, and prefer the better. This is grasped through precise exertion of judgment (ijtihād), and it varies according to circumstances and persons — so that no absolute verdict can be given upon it, neither by negation nor by affirmation.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Benefit: Seeking Companionship and Affection (al-Istī'nās wa al-Īnās)
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||||| الفائدة الرابعة الاستئناس والإيناس

وهو غرض من يحضر الولائم والدعوات ومواضع المعاشرة والأنس وهذا يرجع الى
حظ النفس في الحال
وقد يكون ذلك على وجه حرام بمؤانسة من لا تجوز مؤانسته أو على وجه مباح
وقد يستحب ذلك الأمر الدين وذلك فيمن تستأنس بمشاهدة أحواله وأقواله في
الدين كالأنس بالمشايخ الملازمين لسمت التقوى
وقد يتعلق بحظ النفس ويستحب إذا كان الغرض منه ترويح القلب لتهييج دواعي
النشاط في العبادة فإن القلوب إذا أكرهت عميت ومهما كان في الوحدة وحشة وفي
المجالسة أنس يروح القلب فهي أولى إذ الوفق في العبادة من حزم العبادة
ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله لا يمل حتى تملوا (1)
وهذا أمر لا يستغنى عنه فإن النفس لا تألف الحق على الدوام ما لم تروح
وفي تكليفها الملازمة داعية للفترة وهذا عني بقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن
هذا الدين متين فأوغل فيه برفق والإيغال فيه برفق دأب المستبصرين ولذلك قال
ابن عباس لولا مخافة الوسواس لم أجالس الناس وقال مرة لدخلت بلادا لا أنيس
بها  وهل يفسد الناس إلا الناس فلا يستغني المعتزل إذا عن رفيق يستأنس
بمشاهدته ومحادثته في اليوم والليلة ساعة فليجتهد في طلب من لا يفسد عليه
في ساعته تلك سائر ساعاته فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم المرء على دين خليله
فلينظر أحدكم من يخالل (2)
وليحرص أن يكون حديثه عند اللقاء في أمور الدين وحكاية أحوال القلب
وشكواه وقصوره عن الثبات على الحق والاهتداء الى الرشد ففي ذلك متنفس
ومتروح للنفس فيه مجال رحب لكل مشغول بإصلاح نفسه فإنه لا تنقطع شكواه ولو
عمر أعمارا طويلة والراضي عن نفسه مغرور قطعا
فهذا النوع من الاستئناس في بعض أوقات النهار ربما يكون أفضل من العزلة
في حق بعض الأشخاص PageV02P239
فليتفقد فيه أحوال القلب وأحوال الجليس أولا ثم ليجالس

### ||||| الفائدة الخامسة في نيل الثواب وإنالته

أما النيل فبحضور الجنائز وعيادة المريض وحضور العيدين وأما حضور الجمعة
فلا بد منه
وحضور الجماعة في سائر الصلوات أيضا لا رخصة في تركه إلا لخوف ضرر ظاهر
يقاوم ما يفوت من فضيلة الجماعة ويزيد عليه وذلك لا يتفق إلا نادرا
وكذلك في حضور الإملاكات والدعوات ثواب من حيث إنه إدخال سرور على قلب
مسلم
وأما إنالته فهو أن يفتح الباب لتعوده الناس أو ليعزوه في المصائب أو
يهنوه على النعم فإنهم ينالون بذلك ثوابا وكذلك إذا كان من العلماء وإذن
لهم في الزيارة نالوا ثواب الزيارة وكان هو بالتمكين سببا فيه فينبغي أن
يزن ثواب هذه المخالطات بآفاتها التي ذكرناها وعند ذلك قد ترجح العزلة وقد
ترجح المخالطة
فقد حكي عن جماعة من السلف مثل مالك وغيره ترك إجابة الدعوات وعيادة
المرضى وحضور الجنائز بل كانوا أحلاس بيوتهم لا يخرجون إلا الى الجمعة أو
زيارة القبور وبعضهم فارق الأمصار وانحاز الى قلل الجبال تفرغا للعبادة
وفرارا من الشواغل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ ن س (alif-nūn-sīn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of familiarity, sociability, and dispelling of loneliness; al-īnās denotes the act of comforting or cheering another, while al-istī'nās is the seeking of that comfort for oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-uns is the soul's repose in what is familiar and agreeable, contrasting with al-waḥshah (wilderness/desolation of the heart); it carries a spiritual valence when directed toward the righteous.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes physical proximity and social mixing; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the heart's tranquility through witnessing another's state, as in "uns bi-mushāhadat aḥwālihi."
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The phrase "fa-in kāna... fa-hiya awlā" employs a conditional protasis with a nominal predicate, where the apodosis is a preference judgment, requiring careful parsing of the implied subject (al-mujālasah).
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth benefit is the seeking of companionship and the granting of affection (al-istī'nās wa al-īnās). This is the aim of one who attends banquets, invitations, and places of social mixing and intimacy, and it reverts to the soul's share in the present moment.

This may be unlawful (ḥarām) when it involves keeping company with one whose company is not permissible, or it may be permissible (mubāḥ). And it may be recommended (mustaḥabb) for a religious purpose — namely, in the case of one whose states and words in religion one finds comfort in witnessing, like the intimacy felt with elder shaykhs who adhere steadfastly to the mark of piety (simt al-taqwā).

It may also pertain to the soul's share and be recommended when the intent is to refresh the heart so as to stir the motives of vigor in worship. For hearts, when compelled, grow blind; and whenever there is desolation (waḥshah) in solitude and intimacy (uns) in sitting together that refreshes the heart, then sitting together is more fitting — for moderation in worship is part of prudent worship. For this reason, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«إن الله لا يمل حتى تملوا»} ("Indeed, Allah does not grow weary until you grow weary").

This is a matter that cannot be dispensed with, for the soul does not habituate itself to the truth perpetually unless it is given respite. And imposing upon it constant adherence invites languor. This is what is meant by his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): {«إن هذا الدين متين فأوغل فيه برفق»} ("Indeed, this religion is firm, so enter into it with gentleness") — and entering into it with gentleness is the constant practice of the insightful (al-mustabṣirīn). For this reason, Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Were it not for fear of whisperings (al-waswās), I would not sit with people." And once he said: "I would enter a land with no companion in it." And do people corrupt others except through people? Thus the one who withdraws (al-muʿtazil) is not free from need of a companion whose sight and conversation he finds comfort in for an hour of the day and night. So let him strive in seeking one who will not corrupt for him that hour — and thereby all his other hours. For the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«المرء على دين خليله فلينظر أحدكم من يخالل»} ("A man follows the religion of his intimate friend, so let each of you consider whom he takes as a friend").

And let him be eager that his speech at meeting be concerning matters of religion, the narration of the heart's states, its complaint, and its shortcoming in steadfastness upon the truth and guidance to right conduct (al-rashad). For in that there is a breathing space and a refreshment for the soul, a wide field for everyone occupied with reforming himself — for his complaint never ceases, even if he lived for many long lifetimes. And the one satisfied with himself is deluded, without doubt.

Thus this kind of companionship, in some hours of the day, may be more excellent than seclusion (al-ʿuzlah) in the case of certain persons. So let him first examine therein the states of the heart and the states of the sitter, and then let him sit.

---

The Fifth Benefit: Attaining Reward and Causing Others to Attain It

As for attaining it (al-nayl), that is through attending funerals, visiting the sick, and attending the two festivals (al-ʿīdayn). As for attending the Friday prayer, it is obligatory without exception. And attending the congregational prayer in the rest of the prayers also has no license to abandon it, except out of fear of manifest harm that counterbalances what is lost of the congregation's merit and exceeds it — and that occurs only rarely.

Likewise, in attending marriage contracts and invitations, there is reward insofar as it is bringing joy into the heart of a Muslim.

As for causing others to attain it (īnāluhu), it is that one opens the door for people to visit him when ill, or to offer condolences in afflictions, or to congratulate him upon blessings — for they thereby attain reward. Likewise, if one is among the scholars and permits them to visit, they attain the reward of visitation, and he, through enabling it, is a cause therein. Therefore, one ought to weigh the reward of these social mixings against their afflictions (āfāt) which we have mentioned. And at that point, seclusion may outweigh, or social mixing may outweigh.

For it has been narrated concerning a group of the Salaf — such as Mālik and others — that they abandoned answering invitations, visiting the sick, and attending funerals. Rather, they were the mats of their houses, not going out except to the Friday prayer or to visit graves. And some of them departed the cities and withdrew to the peaks of mountains, devoting themselves entirely to worship and fleeing from distractions.

chapters.title_en: The Sixth Benefit — Humility in Social Intercourse, and the Hidden Perils of Choosing Seclusion
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||||| الفائدة السادسة

من المخالطة التواضع فإنه من أفضل المقامات ولا
يقدر عليه في الوحدة وقد يكون الكبر سببا في اختيار العزلة
فقد روي في الإسرائيليات أن حكيما من الحكماء  صنف ثلثمائة وستين مصحفا في
الحكمة حتى ظن أنه قد نال عند الله منزلة فأوحى الله الى نبيه قل لفلان إنك
قد ملأت الأرض نفاقا وإني لا أقبل من نفاقك شيئا قال فتخلى وانفرد في سرب
تحت الأرض وقال الآن قد بلغت رضا ربي فأوحى الله الى نبيه قل له إنك لن
تبلغ رضاي حتى تخالط الناس وتصبر على أذاهم فخرج فدخل الأسواق وخالط الناس
وجالسهم وواكلهم وأكل الطعام بينهم ومشى في الأسواق معهم فأوحى الله تعالى
إلى نبيه الآن قد بلغ رضاي
فكم من معتزل في بيته وباعثه الكبر ومانعه عن المحافل أن لا يوقر أو لا
يقدم أو يرى الترفع عن مخالطتهم أرفع لمحله وأتقى لطراوة ذكره بين الناس
وقد يعتزل خيفة من أن تظهر مقابحه لو خالط فلا يعتقد فيه الزهد والإشتغال
بالعبادة فيتخذ البيت سترا على مقابحه إبقاء على اعتقاد الناس في زهده
وتعبده من غير استغراق وقت الخلوة بذكر أو فكر وعلامة هؤلاء أنهم يحبون أن
يزاروا ولا يحبون أن يزوروا ويفرحون بتقرب العوام والسلاطين إليهم
واجتماعهم على بابهم وطرقهم وتقبيلهم أيديهم على سبيل التبرك ولو كان
الاشتغال بنفسه هو الذي يبغض إليه المخالطة وزيارة الناس لبغض إليه
زياراتهم له كما حكيناه عن الفضيل حيث قال وهل جئتني إلا لأتزين لك وتتزين
لي
وعن حاتم الأصم أنه قال للأمير الذي زاره حاجتي أن لا أراك ولا تراني
فمن ليس مشغولا مع نفسه بذكر الله فاعتزاله عن الناس سببه شدة اشتغاله
بالناس لأن قلبه متجرد للالتفات إلى نظرهم إليه بعين الوقار والاحترام
والعزلة بهذا السبب جهل من وجوه أحدها أن التواضع والمخالطة لا تنقص من
منصب من هو متكبر بعلمه أو دينه إذ كان علي رضي الله عنه يحمل التمر والملح
في ثوبه ويده ويقول
لا ينقص الكامل من كماله ... ما جر من نفع إلى عياله
وكان أبو هريرة وحذيفة وأبي وابن مسعود رضي الله عنهم يحملون حزم الحطب
وجرب الدقيق على أكتافهم
PageV02P240
وكان أبو هريرة  رضي الله عنه يقول وهو والي المدينة والحطب على رأسه
طرقوا لأميركم
وكان سيد المرسلين صلى الله عليه وسلم يشتري الشيء فيحمله الى بيته بنفسه
فيقول له صاحبه أعطني أحمله فيقول صاحب الشيء أحق بحمله (1)
وكان الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما يمر بالسؤال وبين أيديهم كسر فيقولون
هلم إلى الغداء يا ابن رسول الله فكان ينزل ويجلس على الطريق ويأكل معهم
ويركب ويقول إن الله لا يحب المستكبرين الوجه الثاني أن الذي شغل نفسه بطلب
رضا الناس عنه وتحسين اعتقادهم فيه مغرور لأنه لو عرف الله حق المعرفة علم
أن الخلق لا يغنون عنه من الله شيئا وأن ضرره ونفعه بيد الله ولا نافع ولا
ضار سواه وأن من طلب رضا الناس ومحبتهم بسخط الله سخط الله عليه وأسخط عليه
الناس بل رضا الناس غاية لا تنال فرضا الله أولى بالطلب
ولذلك قال الشافعي ليونس بن عبد الأعلى والله ما أقول لك إلا نصحا إنه
ليس إلى السلامة من الناس من سبيل فانظر ماذا يصلحك فافعله ولذلك قيل
من راقب الناس مات غما ... وفاز باللذة الجسور
ونظر سهل الى رجل من أصحابه فقال له اعمل كذا وكذا لشيء أمره به فقال يا
أستاذ لا أقدر عليه لأجل الناس فالتفت إلى أصحابه وقال لا ينال عبد حقيقة
من هذا الأمر حتى يكون بأحد وصفين عبد تسقط الناس من عينه فلا يرى في
الدنيا إلا خالقه وأن أحدا لا يقدر على أن يضره ولا ينفعه
وعبد سقطت نفسه عن قلبه فلا يبالي بأي حال يرونه
وقال الشافعي رحمه الله ليس من أحد إلا وله محب ومبغض فإذا كان هكذا فكن
مع أهل طاعة الله وقيل للحسن يا أبا سعيد إن قوما يحضرون مجلسك ليس بغيتهم
إلا تتبع سقطات كلامك وتعنيتك بالسؤال فتبسم وقال للقائل هون على نفسك فإني
حدثت نفسي بسكنى الجنان ومجاورة الرحمن فطمعت وما حدثت نفسي بالسلامة من
الناس لأني قد علمت أن خالقهم ورازقهم ومحييهم ومميتهم لم يسلم  منهم
وقال موسى عليه السلام يا رب احبس عني ألسنة الناس فقال يا موسى هذا شيء
لم اصطفه نفسي فكيف أفعله بك وأوحى الله سبحانه وتعالى إلى عزير إن لم تطب
نفسا بأني اجعلك علكا في أفواه الماضغين لم أكتبك عندي من المتواضعين
فإذن من حبس نفسه في البيت ليحسن اعتقادات الناس وأقوالهم فيه فهو في
عناء حاضر في الدنيا {ولعذاب الآخرة أكبر لو كانوا يعلمون} فإذن لا تستحب
العزلة إلا لمستغرق الأوقات بربه ذكرا وفكرا وعبادة وعلما بحيث لو خالطه
الناس لضاعت أوقاته وكثرت آفاته ولتشوشت عليه عباداته
فهذه غوائل خفية في اختيار العزلة ينبغي أن تتقي فإنها مهلكات في صور

chapters.anchors:
- Root: و ض ع (waḍʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To place down low, to lower; al-tawāḍuʿ is the act of lowering oneself, the opposite of elevation and haughtiness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Humility (tawāḍuʿ) is the soul's disposition to abandon the claim of superiority over others; it is the praiseworthy mean between arrogance (kibr) and self-abasement.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical lowering; metaphorical (majāz) — the moral posture of the heart that refuses to seek rank over fellow creatures.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Responsive Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the repeated "fa-" clauses (fa-kharaja, fa-dakhala) mark the apodosis of divine testing, each response being a new divine address.
chapters.translation:
### ||||| The Sixth Benefit

Among the [benefits of] social intercourse is humility, for it is among the most excellent of stations, and one is not capable of it in solitude. And it may be that arrogance is the very cause of choosing seclusion. For it has been related in the Isra'iliyyat that a certain sage among the sages composed three hundred and sixty books of wisdom, until he fancied that he had attained a station with God. So God revealed to His prophet: "Say to so-and-so: You have filled the earth with hypocrisy, and I accept nothing of your hypocrisy." He said: So he withdrew and secluded himself in a subterranean cavern beneath the earth, saying: "Now I have attained the good pleasure of my Lord." Then God revealed to His prophet: "Say to him: You will never attain My good pleasure until you mix with people and bear patiently their harm." So he went out, entered the marketplaces, mixed with the people, sat with them, ate with them, partook of food among them, and walked in the markets alongside them. Then God — exalted be He — revealed to His prophet: "Now he has attained My good pleasure."

How many a one is secluded in his house, his motive being arrogance, and what prevents him from the assemblies is [the fear] that he might not be honored, or not be given precedence, or [the notion] that raising himself above mixing with them is more elevating for his rank and more protective of the freshness of his reputation among the people! And another may seclude himself out of fear that his faults would become manifest were he to mix [with them], so that [people] would not believe in his asceticism and his occupation with worship. He thus takes the house as a veil over his faults, preserving people's belief in his asceticism and devotion — without his solitary hours being absorbed in remembrance or reflection. The mark of these [people] is that they love to be visited but do not love to visit; they rejoice at the drawing near of the common folk and the sultans to them, at their gathering at their door, their knocking, and their kissing of their hands by way of seeking blessing. Had his occupation with himself been truly what made social intercourse and visiting people distasteful to him, then their visits to him would have been equally distasteful — as we have related of al-Fuḍayl, when he said: "Have you come to me except that I might adorn myself for you and you adorn yourself for me?"

And it is related of Ḥātim al-Aṣamm that he said to the amir who visited him: "My need is that I neither see you nor you see me."

So whoever is not occupied with himself in the remembrance of God, his withdrawal from people is caused by his intense occupation with people, for his heart is wholly devoted to attending to their looking upon him with the eye of veneration and respect. And seclusion for this reason is ignorance in several respects:

The first: humility and social intercourse do not diminish the rank of one who is haughty by virtue of his knowledge or his religion. For ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — used to carry dates and salt in his garment and his hand, saying:

"The perfect one loses nothing of his perfection / by what he carries of benefit to his household."

And Abū Hurayrah, Ḥudhayfah, Ubayy, and Ibn Masʿūd — may God be pleased with them all — used to carry bundles of firewood and sacks of flour upon their shoulders. {PageV02P240} And Abū Hurayrah — may God be pleased with him — would say, while he was governor of Medina with the firewood upon his head: "Make way for your amir!"

And the Master of the Messengers — peace be upon him — would buy something and carry it himself to his house. His companion would say to him: "Give it to me, let me carry it," and he would reply: "The owner of the thing has more right to carry it." And al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī — may God be pleased with them both — would pass by beggars with broken pieces of bread before them, and they would say: "Come to the meal, O son of the Messenger of God!" So he would descend, sit on the road, and eat with them, then mount [his ride] and say: {«إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْتَكْبِرِينَ»} "Indeed, God does not love the arrogant" (Q 16:23).

The second respect: the one who busies himself with seeking people's approval of him and improving their belief concerning him is deluded. For had he known God with true knowledge, he would know that the creatures avail him nothing against God, that his harm and his benefit are in God's hand, and that there is no bringer of benefit nor of harm save Him; and that whoever seeks the approval of people and their love at the cost of God's displeasure, God will be displeased with him and will make the people displeased with him. Nay — the approval of people is a goal that is never attained, so the approval of God is more worthy of pursuit.

For this reason al-Shāfiʿī said to Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā: "By God, I say to you nothing but sincere counsel: there is no way to safety from people. So look to what will set you right and do it." And for this reason it was said:

"Whoever watches the people dies of grief, / and the bold one wins the pleasure."

And Sahl looked at a man among his companions and said to him: "Do such-and-such," for a matter he commanded him. He said: "O master, I cannot do it on account of the people." So he turned to his companions and said: "No servant attains the reality of this matter until he is of two descriptions: a servant from whose eye the people have fallen, so that he sees in this world nothing but his Creator, and [knows] that no one is able to harm him or benefit him; and a servant whose own self has fallen from his heart, so that he cares not in what state they see him."

And al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — said: "There is no one but has a lover and a hater. So since it is thus, be with the people of obedience to God." And it was said to al-Ḥasan: "O Abū Saʿīd, there are people who attend your gathering whose only aim is to track the slips of your speech and to vex you with questions." He smiled and said to the speaker: "Put yourself at ease, for I have told myself of dwelling in the Gardens and neighboring the All-Merciful, and so I have hoped; and I have not told myself of safety from the people, for I know that their Creator, their Provider, their Life-giver, and their Death-giver was not safe from them."

And Moses — peace be upon him — said: "O Lord, restrain from me the tongues of the people." He said: "O Moses, this is a thing I have not chosen for Myself — how then shall I do it for you?" And God — glorified and exalted be He — revealed to ʿUzayr: "If your soul is not content that I make you a morsel in the mouths of those who chew, I have not written you with Me among the humble."

So then, whoever confines himself in the house to improve the beliefs and sayings of the people concerning him is in present toil in this world, {«وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ»} "and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew" (Q 16:33). Therefore seclusion is not desirable except for one whose hours are wholly absorbed with his Lord — in remembrance, reflection, worship, and knowledge — such that were people to mix with him, his hours would be lost, his afflictions multiplied, and his devotions disturbed.

These, then, are hidden perils in the choice of seclusion that must be guarded against, for they are destroyers in the guise of saviors.
