### ||| بيان تأديب الله تعالى حبيبه وصفيه محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم بالقرآن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Refinement, disciplined cultivation of character; the root denotes calling, assembling, and training toward excellence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine and prophetic disciplining (taʾdīb) as the inculcation of virtuous dispositions (makārim al-akhlāq) through revealed guidance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense — training and correction; metaphorical extension — the outward comportment (ādāb) as the visible fruit of inward states.
- Root: ظ-ه-ر (ẓ-h-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Outwardness, that which is manifest and perceptible to the senses.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The exterior (ẓāhir) as the locus of bodily acts (aʿmāl al-jawāriḥ), which mirror the interior (bāṭin) dispositions of the heart.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical surface; metaphorical — the visible realm of conduct as a sign (ʿalāmah) of hidden reality.
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Inherent nature, disposition, measure, and proportion; also the act of creation and estimation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Akhlāq as the stable inner constitution (hayʾah rāsikhah) from which actions proceed spontaneously without deliberation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — created form and measure; metaphorical — moral character as the "inner form" of the soul.
- Root: س-ر-ر (s-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The innermost secret, the hidden core of a thing; joy and concealment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sirr (pl. asrār) as the deepest faculty of the heart where divine illumination (anwār ilāhiyyah) is received.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — hidden thing; metaphorical — the heart's secret depth as the source (manbaʿ) of outward acts.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Predication and Apposition (al-ḫabar wa al-ʿaṭf) — The opening sentences employ nominal clauses (jumal ismiyyah) with predicate appositions to establish permanent ontological truths (e.g., "ādāb al-ẓawāhir ʿunwān..."), requiring the translator to preserve the stative, timeless quality of the assertions.
chapters.translation:
In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, who created everything and perfected its creation and ordering, and who disciplined His Prophet Muḥammad — may God bless him and grant him peace — and perfected his discipline, and purified his attributes and moral traits, then took him as His chosen friend and beloved. He granted success in following him to whomever He willed to refine, and deprived of assuming his moral traits whomever He willed to frustrate. May God bless our master Muḥammad, the master of the messengers, and his family, the good and pure, and grant them abundant peace.

To proceed: The etiquettes of the outward (ādāb al-ẓawāhir) are the title-page of the etiquettes of the inward (ādāb al-bawāṭin), and the movements of the bodily members (ḥarakāt al-jawāriḥ) are the fruits of inner thoughts (thamarāt al-khawāṭir). Deeds are the result of moral character (natījat al-akhlāq), and etiquettes are the exudation of knowledges (rashḥ al-maʿārif). The secrets of the hearts (sarāʾir al-qulūb) are the planting-grounds of actions and their springs, and the lights of the inner secrets (anwār al-sarāʾir) are what shine upon the outward, adorning it, making it radiant, and exchanging its unpleasant aspects and defects for beauties.

Whosoever's heart does not humble itself, his bodily members will not humble themselves. And whosoever's breast is not a niche-lamp (mishkāh) for the divine lights, the beauty of prophetic etiquettes will not overflow upon his outward.

I had resolved to conclude the Quarter of Customs (rubʿ al-ʿādāt) of this book with a comprehensive book on the etiquettes of daily living, so that the seeker thereof would not find it burdensome to extract them from all these books. Then I saw that each book of the Quarter of Customs had already covered a portion of the etiquettes, so I deemed their repetition and reiteration burdensome — for seeking repetition is heavy, and souls are naturally disposed to oppose what is repeated. Thus I decided to confine this book to the mention of the etiquettes of the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — and his transmitted moral traits (akhlāqihi al-maʾthūrah) related through chains of transmission (bi-al-isnād). I shall present them gathered together, chapter by chapter, with the chains of transmission omitted, so that therein — along with all the etiquettes — there may be gathered the renewal of faith and its confirmation through the contemplation of his noble moral traits, each single one of which bears witness with certainty that he was the most generous of God's creation, the highest of them in rank, and the greatest of them in worth — how then when they are all combined?

Then I shall add to the mention of his moral traits the mention of his physical constitution (khilqah), then the mention of his miracles (muʿjizāt) which the reports have authenticated — so that all this may express the noble qualities of character and natural disposition, and may extract from the ears of those who deny his prophethood the plug of deafness.

God Almighty is the Guardian of success in following the master of the messengers in moral traits, states, and all the landmarks of religion — for He is the Guide of the perplexed and the Answerer of the call of the distressed.

We shall mention in this book: first, an exposition of God Almighty's disciplining of him through the Qurʾān; then an exposition of the comprehensive sum of his excellent moral traits; then an exposition of a portion of his etiquettes and moral traits; then an exposition of his speech and his laughter; then an exposition of his moral traits and etiquettes regarding food; then an exposition of his moral traits and etiquettes regarding clothing; then an exposition of his forgiveness despite ability [to retaliate]; then an exposition of his overlooking what he disliked; then an exposition of his generosity and munificence; then an exposition of his courage and valor; then an exposition of his humility; then an exposition of his form and physical constitution; then an exposition of the comprehensive sum of his miracles and signs — may God bless him and grant him peace.

### ||| Exposition of God Almighty's Disciplining of His Beloved and Chosen One, Muḥammad — May God Bless Him and Grant Him Peace — Through the Qurʾān

chapters.title_en: The Prophet's (ﷺ) Adornment with Noble Character and the Quranic Discipline of Morals
chapters.arabic_text:
كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كثير الضراعة والابتهال دائم السؤال من
الله تعالى أن يزينه بمحاسن الآداب ومكارم الأخلاق فكان يقول في دعائه
اللهم حسن خلقي وخلقي (1) ويقول اللهم جنبني منكرات الأخلاق (2) فاستجاب
الله تعالى دعاءه وفاء بقوله عز وجل {ادعوني أستجب لكم} فأنزل عليه القرآن
وأدبه به فكان خلقه القرآن
قال سعد بن هشام دخلت على عائشة رضي الله عنها وعن أبيها فسألتها عن
أخلاق رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالت أما تقرأ القرآن قلت بلى قالت
كان خلق رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم القرآن (3)
وإنما أدبه القرآن بمثل قوله تعالى {خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن
الجاهلين}  وقوله {إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى وينهى عن
الفحشاء والمنكر والبغي} وقوله {واصبر على ما أصابك إن ذلك من عزم الأمور}
وقوله {ولمن صبر وغفر إن ذلك لمن عزم الأمور} وقوله {فاعف عنهم واصفح إن
الله يحب المحسنين} وقوله {وليعفوا وليصفحوا ألا تحبون أن يغفر الله لكم}
وقوله {ادفع بالتي هي أحسن فإذا الذي بينك وبينه عداوة كأنه ولي حميم}
وقوله {والكاظمين الغيظ والعافين عن الناس والله يحب المحسنين} وقوله
{اجتنبوا كثيرا من الظن إن بعض الظن إثم ولا تجسسوا ولا يغتب بعضكم بعضا}
ولما كسرت رباعيته وشج يوم أحد فجعل الدم يسيل على وجهه وهو يمسح الدم
ويقول كيف يفلح قوم خضبوا وجه نبيهم بالدم وهو يدعوهم إلى ربهم (4) فأنزل
الله تعالى {ليس لك من الأمر شيء} تأديبا له على ذلك
وأمثال هذه التأديبات في القرآن لا تحصر وهو صلى الله عليه وسلم المقصود
الأول بالتأديب والتهذيب ثم منه يشرق النور على كافة الخلق فإنه أدب
بالقرآن وأدب الخلق به ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم بعثت لأتمم مكارم
الأخلاق (5) ثم رغب الخلق في محاسن الأخلاق بما أوردناه في كتاب رياضة
النفس وتهذيب الأخلاق فلا نعيده ثم لما أكمل الله تعالى خلقه أثنى عليه
فقال تعالى {وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم} فسبحانه ما أعظم شأنه وأتم امتنانه ثم
انظر إلى عميم لطفه وعظيم فضله كيف أعطى ثم أثني فهو الذي زينه بالخلق
الكريم ثم أضاف إليه ذلك فقال {وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم} ثم بين رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم للخلق أن الله يحب مكارم الأخلاق ويبغض سفسافها (6) قال علي
رضي الله عنه يا عجبا لرجل مسلم يجيئه أخوه المسلم في حاجة فلا يرى نفسه
للخير أهلا فلو كان لا يرجو ثوابا ولا يخشى عقابا لقد كان ينبغي له أن
يسارع إلى مكارم الأخلاق فإنها مما تدل على سبيل النجاة
فقال له رجل أسمعته من رسول الله PageV02P358
صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال نعم وما هو خير منه  لما أتى بسبايا طيء وقفت
جارية في السبي فقالت يا محمد إن رأيت أن تخلي عني ولا تشمت بي أحياء العرب
فإني بنت سيد قومي وإن أبي كان يحمي الذمار ويفك العاني ويشبع الجائع ويطعم
الطعام ويفشي السلام ولم يرد طالب حاجة قط أنا ابنة حاتم الطائي
فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يا جارية هذه صفة المؤمنين حقا لو كان أبوك
مسلما لترحمنا عليه خلوا عنها فإن أباها كان يحب مكارم الأخلاق وإن الله
يحب مكارم الأخلاق فقام أبو بردة بن نيار فقال يا رسول الله الله يحب مكارم
الأخلاق فقال والذي نفسي بيده لا يدخل الجنة إلا حسن الأخلاق (1) وعن معاذ
بن جبل عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن الله حف الإسلام بمكارم الأخلاق
ومحاسن الأعمال (2) ومن ذلك حسن المعاشرة وكرم الصنيعة ولين الجانب وبذل
المعروف وإطعام الطعام وإفشاء السلام وعيادة المريض المسلم برا كان أو
فاجرا وتشييع جنازة المسلم وحسن الجوار لمن جاورت مسلما كان أو كافرا
وتوقير ذي الشيبة المسلم وإجابة الطعام والدعاء عليه والعفو والإصلاح بين
الناس والجود والكرم والسماحة والابتداء بالسلام وكظم الغيظ والعفو عن
الناس واجتناب ما حرمه الإسلام من اللهو والباطل والغناء والمعازف كلها وكل
ذي وتر وكل ذي دخل والغلبة والكذب والبخل والشح والجفاء والمكر والخديعة
والنميمة وسوء ذات البين وقطيعة الأرحام وسوء الخلق والتكبر والفخر
والاختيال والاستطالة والبذخ والفحش والتفحش والحقد والحسد والطيرة والبغي
والعدوان والظلم
قال أنس رضي الله عنه
فلم يدع نصيحة جميلة إلا وقد دعانا إليها وأمرنا بها ولم يدع غشا أو قال
عيبا أو قال شينا إلا حذرناه ونهانا عنه (3) ويكفي من ذلك كله هذه الآية
{إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان} الآية وقال معاذ أوصاني رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم فقال يا معاذ أوصيك باتقاء الله وصدق الحديث والوفاء بالعهد
وأداء الأمانة وترك الخيانة وحفظ الجار ورحمة اليتيم ولين الكلام وبذل
السلام وحسن العمل وقصر الأمل ولزوم الإيمان والتفقه في القرآن وحب الآخرة
والجزع  من الحساب وخفض الجناح وأنهاك أن تسب حكيما أو تكذب صادقا أو تطيع
آثما أو تعصي إماما عادلا أو تفسد أرضا وأوصيك باتقاء الله عند كل حجر وشجر
ومدر وأن تحدث لكل ذنب توبة السر بالسر والعلانية بالعلانية (4) فهكذا أدب
عباد الله ودعاهم إلى مكارم الأخلاق ومحاسن الآداب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-ر-ع (ḍ-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Supplication with humility and abasement; stretching forth the hands in earnest entreaty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The state of utter servitude before Allah, combining verbal petition with bodily humility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical lowliness; metaphorical extension to the soul's abasement in prayer.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — "الضراعة والابتهال" functions as coordinated synonyms reinforcing a single semantic field of earnest supplication.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was abundant in humble supplication and earnest entreaty, perpetually asking Allah Most High to adorn him with the beauties of good conduct and the noble traits of character. Thus he would say in his supplication: "O Allah, beautify my outward form and my inward character (khuluqī)," (1) and he would say: "O Allah, protect me from the reprehensible traits of character." (2) Allah Most High answered his supplication, fulfilling His mighty word: {«ادعوني أستجب لكم»} ["Call upon Me, I will answer you"] (Ghāfir 40:60). So He sent down upon him the Quran and disciplined him by it, and his character was the Quran.

Saʿd ibn Hishām said: I entered upon ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her and with her father) and asked her about the character of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). She said: "Do you not read the Quran?" I replied: "Indeed, I do." She said: "The character of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the Quran." (3)

The Quran disciplined him only through such verses as His saying Most High: {«خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين»} ["Take the forgiveness, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant"] (Al-Aʿrāf 7:199), and His saying: {«إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى وينهى عن الفحشاء والمنكر والبغي»} ["Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence, and giving to near relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and transgression"] (Al-Naḥl 16:90), and His saying: {«واصبر على ما أصابك إن ذلك من عزم الأمور»} ["And be patient over what befalls you; indeed, that is of the matters of determination"] (Luqmān 31:17), and His saying: {«ولمن صبر وغفر إن ذلك لمن عزم الأمور»} ["And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters of determination"] (Al-Shūrā 42:43), and His saying: {«فاعف عنهم واصفح إن الله يحب المحسنين»} ["So pardon them and overlook—indeed, Allah loves the doers of good"] (Al-Māʾidah 5:13), and His saying: {«وليعفوا وليصفحوا ألا تحبون أن يغفر الله لكم»} ["And let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?"] (Al-Nūr 24:22), and His saying: {«ادفع بالتي هي أحسن فإذا الذي بينك وبينه عداوة كأنه ولي حميم»} ["Repel with that which is better; then behold, the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend"] (Fuṣṣilat 41:34), and His saying: {«والكاظمين الغيظ والعافين عن الناس والله يحب المحسنين»} ["And those who restrain anger and pardon the people—and Allah loves the doers of good"] (Āl ʿImrān 3:134), and His saying: {«اجتنبوا كثيرا من الظن إن بعض الظن إثم ولا تجسسوا ولا يغتب بعضكم بعضا»} ["Avoid much assumption; indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy, nor backbite one another"] (Al-Ḥujurāt 49:12).

And when his front tooth was broken and his face was wounded on the Day of Uḥud, blood began to flow down his face while he wiped the blood away, saying: "How can a people prosper who have stained the face of their Prophet with blood, while he calls them to their Lord?" (4) Then Allah Most High revealed: {«ليس لك من الأمر شيء»} ["You have no part in the matter"] (Āl ʿImrān 3:128), disciplining him for that.

And examples of such disciplines in the Quran are beyond enumeration. He (ﷺ) was the primary object of discipline and refinement; then from him the light radiated forth to all creation. For he was disciplined by the Quran, and he disciplined creation by it. Therefore he (ﷺ) said: "I was sent only to perfect the noble traits of character." (5) Then he encouraged creation toward the beauties of good conduct by what we have already presented in the Book of the Training of the Soul and the Refinement of Character (Kitāb Riyāḍat al-Nafs wa Tahdhīb al-Akhlāq), so we shall not repeat it.

Then, when Allah Most High had perfected his character, He praised him, saying Most High: {«وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم»} ["And indeed, you are upon an immense character"] (Al-Qalam 68:4). Glory be to Him—how immense is His affair and how complete His beneficence! Then consider His all-encompassing kindness and immense bounty: how He gave, then He praised. For He it is who adorned him with noble character, then attributed that to him, saying: {«وإنك لعلى خلق عظيم»}.

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made clear to creation that Allah loves the noble traits of character and abhors their base and contemptible forms. (6) ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "How astonishing for a Muslim man whose Muslim brother comes to him with a need, yet he does not deem himself worthy of goodness! Even if he hoped for no reward and feared no punishment, he ought still to hasten toward the noble traits of character, for they are among the things that point to the path of salvation."

A man said to him: "Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He replied: "Yes, and what is better than it." When the captives of the tribe of Ṭayy were brought forth, a slave-girl stood among the captives and said: "O Muḥammad, if you see fit to release me, and not let the living Arabs gloat over me—for I am the daughter of the leader of my people, and my father used to protect the honor, free the captive, feed the hungry, serve food, spread peace, and never turn away a seeker of need. I am the daughter of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O slave-girl, these are truly the attributes of the believers. Had your father been a Muslim, we would have shown mercy upon him. Release her, for her father loved the noble traits of character, and Allah loves the noble traits of character."

Then Abū Burdah ibn Niyār stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, does Allah love the noble traits of character?" He said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, none shall enter Paradise except one of good character." (1)

And from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, Allah has fortified Islam with the noble traits of character and the beauties of deeds." (2)

And from that [fortification] are: good companionship, generosity of beneficence, gentleness of demeanor, bestowing kindness, feeding food, spreading peace, visiting the sick Muslim—whether righteous or wicked—following the funeral procession of a Muslim, good neighborliness toward those you neighbor—whether Muslim or disbeliever—honoring the elderly Muslim, accepting the invitation to food and supplicating for the host, pardoning and reconciling between people, generosity, munificence, magnanimity, initiating with the greeting of peace, restraining anger, forgiving people, and avoiding all that Islam has forbidden of frivolity, falsehood, singing, and musical instruments entirely—and every stringed instrument and every wind instrument—and avoiding deceit, lying, miserliness, stinginess, harshness, cunning, treachery, backbiting, corruption between people, severing of family ties, bad character, arrogance, boastfulness, conceit, self-aggrandizement, extravagance, obscenity, lewdness, rancor, envy, superstition, transgression, aggression, and injustice.

Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "He left no beautiful counsel but that he called us to it and commanded us with it, and he left no treachery"—or he said: "no fault"—or he said: "no defect—but that he warned us against it and forbade us from it." (3)

And sufficient from all of that is this verse: {«إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان»} ["Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence"] (Al-Naḥl 16:90).

And Muʿādh said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me counsel, saying: "O Muʿādh, I counsel you to fear Allah, truthfulness in speech, fulfillment of covenants, rendering trusts, abandoning treachery, protecting the neighbor, mercy toward the orphan, gentleness of speech, spreading peace, excellence of deeds, shortness of hope, adherence to faith, deep understanding of the Quran, love of the Hereafter, and dread of the Reckoning, and lowering the wing [in humility]. And I forbid you from cursing a wise man, belittling a truthful man, obeying a sinner, disobeying a just leader, or corrupting the earth. And I counsel you to fear Allah at every stone, tree, and clod of earth, and to repent for every sin—the secret in secret, and the open in open." (4)

Thus did he discipline the servants of Allah and call them to the noble traits of character and the beauties of good conduct.

chapters.title_en: An Exposition of a Compendium of His (ﷺ) Noble Traits, Gathered by Certain Scholars and Culled from the Reports
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان جملة من محاسن أخلاقه التي جمعها بعض العلماء والتقطها من الأخبار

فقال كان صلى الله عليه وسلم أحلم الناس (5)
وأشجع الناس (6)
وأعدل الناس (7)
وأعف الناس لم تمس يده قط PageV02P359
يد امرأة لا يملك رقها أو عصمة نكاحها أو تكون ذات محرم منه (1)
وكان أسخى الناس (2) لا يبيت عنده دينار ولا درهم وإن فضل شيء ولم يجد من
يعطيه وفجأه الليل لم يأو إلى منزله حتى يتبرأ منه إلى من يحتاج إليه (3)
لا يأخذ مما آتاه الله إلا قوت عامه فقط من أيسر ما يجد من التمر والشعير
ويضع سائر ذلك في سبيل الله (4) لا يسأل شيئا إلا أعطاه (5) ثم يعود على
قوت عامه فيؤثر منه حتى أنه ربما احتاج قبل انقضاء العام إن لم يأته شيء
(6) وكان يخصف النعل ويرقع الثوب ويخدم في مهنة أهله (7) ويقطع اللحم معهن
(8) وكان أشد الناس حياء لا يثبت بصره في وجه أحد (9) ويجيب دعوة العبد
والحر (10) ويقبل الهدية ولو أنها جرعة لبن أو فخذ أرنب ويكافيء عليها (11)
PageV02P360
ويأكلها ولا يأكل الصدقة (1) ولا يستكبر عن إجابة الأمة والمسكين (2)
يغضب لربه ولا يغضب لنفسه (3) وينفذ الحق وإن عاد ذلك عليه بالضرر أو على
أصحابه
وعرض عليه الانتصار بالمشركين على المشركين وهو في قلة وحاجة إلى إنسان
واحد يزيده في عدد من معه فأبى وقال أنا لا أنتصر بمشرك (4) وجد من فضلاء
أصحابه وخيارهم قتيلا بين اليهود فلم يحف عليهم ولا زاد على مر الحق بل
وداه بمائة ناقة وإن بأصحابه لحاجة إلى بعير واحد يتقوون به (5) وكان يعصب
الحجر على بطنه مرة من الجوع (6) ومرة يأكل ما حضر ولا يرد ما وجد ولا
يتورع عن مطعم حلال  وإن وجد تمرا دون خبز أكله (7) وإن وجد شواء أكله وإن
وجد خبز بر أو شعير أكله وإن وجد حلوا أو عسلا أكله وإن وجد لبنا دون
خبزاكتفى به وإن وجد بطيخا أو رطبا أكله لا يأكل متكئا (8) ولا على خوان
(9) منديله باطن قدميه (10) لم يشبع من خبز بر ثلاثة أيام متوالية (11) حتى
لقي الله تعالى إيثارا على نفسه لا فقرا ولا بخلا يجيب الوليمة (12)
PageV02P361
ويعود المرضى (1) ويشهد الجنائز ويمشي وحده بين أعدائه بلا حارس (2) أشد
الناس تواضعا وأسكنهم في غير كبر (3) وأبلغهم في غير تطويل (4) وأحسنهم
بشرا (5) لا يهوله شيء من أمور الدنيا (6) ويلبس ما وجد فمرة شملة ومرة برد
حبرة يمانيا ومرة جبة صوف ما وجد من المباح لبس (7) وخاتمه فضة (8) يلبسه
في خنصره الأيمن (9) والأيسر (10) يردف خلفه عبده أو غيره (11) يركب ما
أمكنه مرة فرسا ومرة بعيرا ومرة بغلة شهباء ومرة حمارا ومرة يمشي راجلا
حافيا بلا رداء ولا عمامة ولا قلنسوة يعود المرضى في أقصى المدينة (12) يحب
الطيب ويكره الرائحة PageV02P362
الرديئة (1) ويجالس الفقراء (2) ويؤاكل المساكين (3) ويكرم أهل الفضل في
أخلاقهم ويتألف أهل الشرف بالبر لهم (4) يصل ذوي رحمه من غير أن يؤثرهم على
من هو أفضل منهم (5) لا يجفو على أحد (6) يقبل معذرة المعتذر إليه (7) يمزح
ولا يقول إلا حقا (8) يضحك من غير قهقهة (9) يرى اللعب المباح فلا ينكره
(10) يسابق أهله (11) وترفع الأصوات عليه فيصبر (12) وكان له لقاح وغنم
يتقوت هو وأهله من ألبانها (13) وكان له عبيد وإماء لا يرتفع عليهم في
PageV02P363
مأكل ولا ملبس (1) ولا يمضي له وقت في غير عمل لله تعالى أو فيما لا بد
له منه من صلاح نفسه (2) يخرج إلى بساتين أصحابه (3) لا يحتقر مسكينا لفقره
وزمانته ولا يهاب ملكا لملكه يدعو هذا وهذا إلى الله دعاء مستويا (4) قد
جمع الله تعالى له السيرة الفاضلة والسياسة التامة وهو أمي لا يقرأ ولا
يكتب نشأ في بلاد الجهل والصحارى في فقره وفي رعاية الغنم يتيما لا أب له
ولا أم فعلمه الله  تعالى جميع محاسن الأخلاق والطرق الحميدة وأخبار الأولين
والآخرين وما فيه النجاة والفوز في الآخرة والغبطة والخلاص في الدنيا ولزوم
الواجب وترك الفضول (5) وفقنا الله لطاعته في أمره والتأسي به في فعله آمين
يا رب العالمين
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح ل م (ḥ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Forbearance, clemency, the restraint of the soul upon provocation; the opposite of rash folly (safah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A praiseworthy faculty of the soul that withholds it from the vehemence of anger, rooted in deliberate reason (ʿaql).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in describing a settled character; metaphorical (majāz) if applied to a transient act of self-restraint.
- Root: ش ج ع (sh-j-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Courage, stoutness of heart in battle; the lion is termed shujāʿ.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Firmness of the heart in confronting perils, a virtue of the irascible faculty (al-quwwah al-ghaḍabiyyah) governed by reason.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in martial contexts; extended to moral courage in enduring hardship.
- Root: ع ف ف (ʿ-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abstinence from the unlawful, purity from base desires; the root implies cessation (kuff) from transgression.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's contentment with the licit and its renunciation of the illicit, a perfection of the appetitive faculty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for refraining from what is forbidden; metaphorical for the heart's detachment from worldly allurements.
- Root: س خ و (s-kh-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Generosity, open-handedness; the opposite of bukhl (miserliness).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The readiness to expend wealth in obedience to God, a virtue of the concupiscent faculty (al-quwwah al-shahwāniyyah) disciplined by religion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for giving wealth; metaphorical for magnanimity of spirit in pardoning.
- Root: ح ي ا (ḥ-y-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Shame, modesty, the soul's aversion to blameworthy acts; derived from ḥayāh (life), as it is the life of the heart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A restraining quality that prevents the soul from base deeds, considered a branch of faith (īmān).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for bashfulness before creation; metaphorical for the awe (khashyah) that restrains one before the Creator.
- Root: ت و ض ع (t-w-ḍ-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Humility, lowliness, the opposite of pride (kibr); from wāḍaʿa, to lower oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's recognition of its servitude (ʿubūdiyyah) before God, manifesting in gentle conduct toward creatures.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical lowering; metaphorical for the heart's abasement before the Divine Majesty.
- Root: ع و د (ʿ-w-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To return, to visit repeatedly; ʿiyādah (visiting the sick) implies returning to the patient with care.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A commendable act of neighborliness and brotherhood, fulfilling the right of the Muslim upon the Muslim.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of visiting; metaphorical for the soul's return to God in repentance (tawbah).
- Root: ص ب ر (ṣ-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Patience, endurance, self-restraint in adversity; the camel is termed ṣabūr for its endurance of thirst.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's steadfastness in obedience, abstention from sin, and composure under trial.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for enduring hardship; metaphorical for forbearance toward the ignorant (ḥilm).
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — In enumerating the Prophet's traits, the accusative or nominative predicates are coordinated by wa (and) without repetition of the verb, each clause standing as an independent attribution; the translator must preserve the paratactic flow, rendering each trait as a discrete, verbatim clause rather than subordinating them into modern periodic syntax.
chapters.translation:
I say: The exposition of a compendium of his (peace and blessings be upon him) noble traits, which a certain scholar gathered and culled from the reports.

He said: He (peace and blessings be upon him) was the most forbearing of people (5), and the most courageous of people (6), and the most just of people (7), and the most chaste of people — his hand never touched the hand of a woman whom he did not own by right of slavery, or whose marriage bond was not under his protection, or who was not a close kin within the prohibited degrees (1). And he was the most generous of people (2); no dinar or dirham remained overnight in his possession, and if anything surplus remained and he found no one to give it to, and night overtook him suddenly, he would not return to his dwelling until he had divested himself of it to one in need (3). He took from what God had given him only the provision of his year — the simplest of what he could find of dates and barley — and he placed all the rest in the path of God (4). He did not ask for anything except that he gave it (5); then he would return to his yearly provision and prefer others over himself therein, such that he might perhaps fall into need before the year's end if nothing came to him (6). And he would patch his sandal, and mend his garment, and serve in the chores of his household (7), and cut the meat alongside them (8). And he was the most intensely modest of people — his gaze would not fix itself upon anyone's face (9). And he would accept the invitation of the slave and the free man alike (10). And he would accept the gift, even if it were a sip of milk or a haunch of rabbit, and he would reciprocate for it (11), and he would eat it — but he would not eat charity (ṣadaqah) (1). And he did not deem himself too great to answer the invitation of the slave-girl or the destitute (2). He would become angry for his Lord, but he would not become angry for himself (3); and he would execute the truth even if it redounded to his own harm or to that of his companions.

And victory over the polytheists was offered to him by means of the polytheists, while he was in a state of scarcity and in need of a single man to increase the number of those with him — yet he refused, and said: "I do not seek victory through a polytheist" (4). He found one of the most virtuous and choicest of his companions slain among the Jews, yet he did not act harshly toward them, nor did he exceed the bounds of truth, but rather he paid his blood-wit with a hundred camels — though his companions were in need of a single camel to strengthen themselves with (5). And he would bind a stone upon his belly at times from hunger (6); and at other times he would eat whatever was present, and would not reject what he found, nor would he scruple over a lawful food — if he found dates without bread, he ate them (7); if he found roast meat, he ate it; if he found bread of wheat or barley, he ate it; if he found something sweet or honey, he ate it; if he found milk without bread, he sufficed with it; if he found watermelon or fresh dates, he ate them. He did not eat reclining (8), nor upon a dining-table (9); his napkin was the inner soles of his feet (10). He never filled his belly with wheat bread for three consecutive days until he met God Most High — out of preference for others over himself, not out of poverty nor miserliness (11). He would accept the wedding feast invitation (12), and visit the sick (1), and attend the funerals, and walk alone among his enemies without a guard (2). He was the most humble of people, and the most tranquil of them without pride (3), and the most eloquent of them without prolixity (4), and the most cheerful of them in countenance (5). Nothing of the affairs of this world would terrify him (6). And he would wear whatever he found — at times a wrapped mantle, at times a striped Yemeni cloak, at times a woolen gown — whatever of the permissible he found, he wore (7). And his signet ring was of silver (8); he wore it on his right little finger (9) and on his left (10). He would carry behind him on his mount his slave or another (11). He would ride whatever was possible — at times a horse, at times a camel, at times a gray mule, at times a donkey, and at times he would walk on foot, barefoot, without a cloak, without a turban, and without a cap, visiting the sick in the farthest part of the city (12). He loved perfume and disliked foul odor (1). And he would sit with the poor (2), and eat with the destitute (3), and honor the people of excellence in their moral virtues, and draw near the people of noble lineage through kindness to them (4). He would maintain ties with his kin without preferring them over those who were more virtuous than them (5). He would not treat anyone harshly (6). He would accept the excuse of the one who apologized to him (7). He would jest, but he would say nothing but the truth (8). He would laugh without guffawing (9). He would see permissible play and not disapprove of it (10). He would race with his family (11). And voices would be raised against him, and he would bear it patiently (12). And he had milch camels and sheep, from whose milk he and his household would sustain themselves (13). And he had male and female slaves, and he did not elevate himself above them in food or clothing (1). And no time passed for him except in work for God Most High, or in what was indispensable for him of the rectification of his own soul (2). He would go out to the orchards of his companions (3). He did not despise a poor man for his poverty and chronic affliction, nor did he fear a king for his kingship — he would call both this one and that one to God with an equal call (4). God Most High had gathered for him the virtuous conduct and the perfect governance — and he was unlettered (ummī), not reading nor writing, raised in the land of ignorance and the deserts, in his poverty, in the tending of sheep, an orphan with neither father nor mother. So God Most High taught him all the noble traits and praiseworthy ways, and the reports of the ancients and the later generations, and that wherein lies salvation and triumph in the Hereafter, and felicity and deliverance in this world, and the adherence to duty and the abandonment of excess (5). May God grant us success in obeying him in his command, and in following his example in his deed. Amen, O Lord of the Worlds.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of Further Aspects of His Manners and Moral Traits
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان جملة أخرى من آدابه وأخلاقه

مما رواه أبو البحتري قال ما شتم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أحدا من
المؤمنين بشتيمة إلا جعل لها كفارة ورحمة (6) وما لعن امرأة قط ولا خادما
بلعنة (7) وقيل له وهو في القتال لو لعنتم يا رسول الله فقال إنما بعثت
PageV02P364
رحمة ولم أبعث لعانا (1) وكان إذا سئل أن يدعو على أحد مسلم أو كافر عام
أو خاص عدل عن الدعاء عليه إلى الدعاء له (2) وما ضرب بيده أحدا قد إلا أن
يضرب بها في سبيل الله تعالى وما انتقم من شيء صنع إليه قط إلا أن تنتهك
حرمة الله وما خير بين أمرين قط إلا اختار أيسرهما إلا أن يكون فيه إثم أو
قطيعة رحم فيكون أبعد الناس من ذلك (3) وما كان يأتيه أحد حر أو عبد أو أمة
إلا قام معه في حاجته (4) وقال أنس رضي الله عنه والذي بعثه بالحق ما قال
لي في شيء قط كرهه لم فعلته ولا لامني نساؤه إلا قال دعوه إنما كان هذا
بكتاب وقدر (5) قالوا وما عاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مضجعا إن فرشوا
له اضطجع وإن لم يفرش له اضطجع على الأرض (6) وقد وصفه الله تعالى في
التوراة قبل أن يبعثه في السطر الأول فقال محمد رسول الله عبدي المختار لا
فظ ولا غليظ ولا صخاب في الأسواق ولا يجزى بالسيئة السيئة ولكن يعفو ويصفح
مولده بمكة وهجرته بطابة وملكه بالشام يأتزر على وسطه هو ومن معه دعاة
للقرآن والعلم يتوضأ على أطرافه
وكذلك نعته في الإنجيل
وكان من خلقه أن يبدأ من لقيه بالسلام (7) ومن قاومه لحاجة صابره حتى
يكون هو المنصرف (8) وما أخذ أحد بيده فيرسل يده حتى يرسلها الآخر (9) وكان
إذا لقي  أحدا من أصحابه بدأه بالمصافحة ثم أخذ بيده فشابكه ثم شد قبضته
عليها (10) وكان لا يقوم ولا يجلس إلا على ذكر الله (11) وكان لا يجلس إليه
أحد وهو يصلي إلا خفف صلاته وأقبل عليه فقال ألك حاجة PageV02P365
فإذا فرغ من حاجته عاد إلى صلاته (1) وكان أكثر جلوسه أن ينصب ساقيه
جميعا ويمسك بيديه عليهما شبه الحبوة (2) ولم يكن يعرف مجلسه من مجلس
أصحابه (3) لأنه كان حيث انتهى به المجلس جلس (4) وما رؤي قط ماذا رجليه
بين أصحابه حتى لا يضيق بهما على أحد إلا أن يكون المكان واسعا لا ضيق فيه
وكان أكثر ما يجلس مستقبل القبلة (5) وكان يكرم من يدخل عليه حتى ربما بسط
ثوبه لمن ليست بينه وبينه قرابة ولا رضاع يجلسه عليه (6) وكان يؤثر الداخل
عليه بالوسادة التي تحته فإن أبى أن يقبلها عزم عليه حتى يفعل (7) وما
استصفاه أحد إلا ظن أنه أكرم الناس عليه (8) حتى يعطي كل من جلس إليه نصيبه
من وجهه حتى كأن مجلسه وسمعه وحديثه ولطيف محاسنه وتوجهه للجالس إليه
ومجلسه مع ذلك مجلس حياء وتواضع وأمانة قال الله تعالى فيما رحمة من الله
لنت لهم ولو كنت فظا غليظ القلب لانفضوا من حولك ولقد كان يدعو أصحابه
بكناهم إكراما لهم واستمالة لقلوبهم (9) ويكني من لم تكن له كنية فكان يدعى
بما كناه به (10) ويكني أيضا النساء اللاتي لهن الأولاد واللاتي لم يلدن
يبتدئ لهن الكنى (11) PageV02P366
ويكني الصبيان فيستلين به قلوبهم (1) وكان أبعد الناس غضبا وأسرعهم رضا
(2) وكان أرأف الناس بالناس وخير الناس للناس وأنفع الناس للناس (3) ولم
تكن ترفع في مجلسه الأصوات (4) وكان إذا قام من مجلسه قال سبحانك اللهم
وبحمدك أشهد أن لا إله إلا أنت أستغفرك وأتوب إليك {ثم يقول} علمنيهن جبريل
عليه السلام (5)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ت-م (shatama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To revile, insult, or verbally abuse with harsh words; the act of vilification.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes the moral vice of verbal aggression, contrasted with prophetic forbearance (ḥilm) and pardon (ʿafw).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for verbal abuse; here employed to highlight the Prophet's absolute abstention from it, even when provoked.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The construction "ما... إلا" (negative restriction) governs the apodosis, emphasizing exclusivity of action.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that among the reports transmitted concerning his manners and moral traits is what Abū al-Bukhtarī related, saying: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) never reviled any believer with an insult, except that he made it an expiation and mercy for him. Nor did he ever curse a woman or a servant with a curse. And it was said to him during battle: "O Messenger of Allah, would that you cursed them." He replied: "I was sent only as a mercy, and I was not sent as one who curses." {«إِنَّمَا بُعِثْتُ رَحْمَةً وَلَمْ أُبْعَثْ لَعَّانًا»}

And whenever he was asked to supplicate against someone — Muslim or disbeliever, general or specific — he would turn away from supplicating against him to supplicating for him. He never struck anyone with his hand, except when fighting in the path of Allah the Exalted. And he never took revenge for anything done to him, except when a sanctity of Allah was violated. And he was never given a choice between two matters, except that he chose the easier of them, unless it involved sin or severing of kinship ties — in which case he was the furthest of people from it.

No one came to him — free man, slave, or bondwoman — except that he stood with him in his need. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "By Him who sent him with the truth, he never said to me about anything I did that he disliked: 'Why did you do it?' Nor did his wives rebuke me, except that he would say: 'Leave him; this was only by the Book and decree.'"

They said: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) never found fault with a resting place — if a cushion was spread for him, he lay upon it; and if none was spread, he lay upon the bare ground.

Allah the Exalted described him in the Torah before sending him, in the first line: "Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, My chosen servant — neither harsh nor coarse, nor clamorous in the marketplaces; he does not repay evil with evil, but rather pardons and forgives. His birth is in Mecca, his emigration to Ṭaybah, and his dominion in Syria. He and his companions wear their waist-wrappers at the middle, calling to the Qur'an and knowledge; he performs ablution at his limbs." Likewise was his description in the Gospel.

Among his traits was that he would initiate the greeting of peace (salām) upon whomever he met. And whoever stood with him for a need, he would bear with him patiently until that person himself departed. And no one ever took his hand, such that he would release his hand until the other released it first. And whenever he met any of his companions, he would initiate the handshake, then take his hand and interlace his fingers, then tighten his grip upon it.

He would not stand nor sit except upon the remembrance of Allah. And whenever anyone sat with him while he was praying, he would shorten his prayer and turn to him, saying: "Do you have a need?" Then when that person finished his need, he would return to his prayer.

Most of his sitting was to draw up both his legs together, holding them with his hands, resembling a sitting posture (ḥubwah). And his sitting place could not be distinguished from that of his companions, because he would sit wherever the gathering ended with him. He was never seen stretching his legs among his companions, lest he cause constriction to anyone thereby — except when the place was spacious with no narrowness. And most of his sitting was facing the qiblah.

He would honor whoever entered upon him, to the extent that he might spread his garment for one with whom he had neither kinship nor foster-brotherhood, seating him upon it. And he would prefer the one entering to have the cushion beneath him; if he refused to accept it, he would insist until he did so. And no one ever sought his favor, except that he thought he was the most honored of people to him — such that he gave every sitter his share of his attention, until his sitting, his listening, his speech, his subtle excellences, and his turning toward the one seated with him seemed wholly devoted to him.

Yet with all that, his sitting was a sitting of modesty, humility, and trustworthiness. Allah the Exalted said: {«فَبِمَا رَحْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ لِنْتَ لَهُمْ وَلَوْ كُنْتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ الْقَلْبِ لَانْفَضُّوا مِنْ حَوْلِكَ»} — "By the mercy of Allah you were gentle with them; had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you."

He would call his companions by their kunyahs (honorific surnames), as an honor to them and to win their hearts. And he would give a kunyah to one who had none, so that he would thereafter be called by that kunyah. He would also give kunyahs to women who had children and to those who had not borne children, initiating kunyahs for them. And he would give kunyahs to young boys, thereby softening their hearts toward him.

He was the furthest of people from anger and the quickest of them to contentment. He was the most compassionate of people toward people, the best of people for people, and the most beneficial of people to people. Voices were never raised in his gathering. And when he rose from his gathering, he would say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise; I bear witness that there is no god but You; I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance." Then he said: "Gabriel (peace be upon him) taught them to me."

chapters.title_en: An Exposition of His Speech and Laughter (Peace Be Upon Him)
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان كلامه وضحكه صلى الله عليه وسلم

كان صلى الله عليه وسلم أفصح الناس منطقا وأحلاهم كلاما ويقول (6) أنا
أفصح العرب (7) وإن أهل الجنة يتكلمون فيها بلغة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم
(8) وكان نزر الكلام  سمح المقالة إذا نطق ليس بمهذار وكان كلامه كخرزات
نظمن (9) قالت عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها كان لا يسرد الكلام كسردكم هذا
كان كلامه نزرا وأنتم تنثرون الكلام نثرا (10) قالوا وكان أوجز الناس كلاما
وبذاك جاءه جبريل وكان مع الإيجاز يجمع كل ما أراد (11) وكان يتكلم بجوامع
الكلم لا فضول ولا تقصير كأنه يتبع بعضه بعضا بين كلامه توقف يحفظه سامعه
ويعيه (12) وكان جهير الصوت أحسن الناس نغمة (13) وكان طويل السكوت لا
يتكلم في غير PageV02P367
حاجة (1) ولا يقول المنكر ولا يقول في الرضا والغضب إلا الحق (2) ويعرض
عمن تكلم بغير جميل (3) ويكني عما اضطره الكلام إليه مما يكره (4) وكان إذا
سكت تكلم جلساؤه ولا يتنازع عنده (5) في الحديث ويعظ بالجد والنصيحة (6)
ويقول لا تضربوا القرآن بعضه ببعض فإنه أنزل على وجوه (7) وكان أكثر الناس
تبسما وضحكا في وجوه أصحابه وتعجبا مما تحدثوا به وخلطا لنفسه بهم (8)
ولربما ضحك حتى تبدو نواجذه (9) وكان ضحك أصحابه عنده التبسم اقتداء به
وتوقيرا له (10) قالوا ولقد جاءه أعرابي يوما وهو عليه السلام متغير اللون
ينكره أصحابه فأراد أن يسأله فقالوا لا تفعل يا أعرابي فإنا ننكر لونه فقال
دعوني فوالذي بعثه بالحق نبيا لا أدعه حتى يتبسم فقال يا رسول الله بلغنا
أن المسيح يعني الدجال يأتي الناس بالثريد وقد هلكوا جوعا أفترى لي بأبي
أنت وأمي أن أكف عن ثريده تعففا وتنزها حتى أهلك هرالا أم أضرب في ثريده
حتى إذا تضلعت شبعا آمنت بالله وكفرت به قالوا فضحك رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم حتى بدت نواجذه ثم قال لا بل يغنيك الله بما يغني به المؤمنين
(11) قالوا وكان PageV02P368
من أكثر الناس تبسما وأطيبهم نفسا مالم ينزل عليه قرآن أو يذكر الساعة أو
يخطب بخطبة عظة (1) وكان إذا سر ورضي فهو أحسن الناس رضا فإن وعظ وعظ بجد
وإن غضب وليس يغضب إلا لله لم يقم لغضبه شيء وكذلك كان في أموره كلها (2)
وكان إذا نزل به الأمر فوض الأمر إلى الله  وتبرأ من الحول والقوة واستنزل
الهدى فيقول اللهم أرني الحق حقا فأتبعه وأرني المنكر منكرا وأرزقني
اجتنابه وأعذني من أن يشتبه علي فأتبع هواي بغير هدى منك واجعل هواي تبعا
لطاعتك وخذ رضا نفسك من نفسي في عافية واهدني لما اختلف فيه من الحق بإذنك
إنك تهدي من تشاء إلى صراط مستقيم (3)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ظ-م (naẓama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ordering, stringing together; the arrangement of pearls upon a thread
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Coherent sequential composition reflecting intentional design
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical stringing; metaphorical for eloquent, well-ordered speech
- Root: ض-ح-ك (ḍaḥika)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Laughter; the opening of the mouth in mirth
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A natural human response; in prophetic context, a controlled expression of joy
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for audible laughter; metaphorical for the visible manifestation of inner contentment
- Root: ج-ز-ل (jazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abundance and excellence; cutting decisively
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Speech that is copious in meaning yet precise in expression
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for abundant provision; metaphorical for refined, weighty speech
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ḥāl (Circumstantial Clause) — The descriptive phrases (e.g., "when he spoke," "when he was silent") function as circumstantial qualifiers anchoring the main verbal actions in temporal and modal frames.
chapters.translation:
I say — and success is from God:

**An Exposition of His Speech and Laughter (Peace Be Upon Him)**

He (peace be upon him) was the most eloquent of people in speech and the sweetest of them in utterance. He said: "I am the most eloquent of the Arabs, and the people of Paradise will speak therein in the tongue of Muhammad (peace be upon him)." His speech was measured, his expression generous — when he spoke, he was not a babbler. His words were like pearls strung in order.

ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "He did not pour forth speech rapidly as you pour it forth. His speech was measured, while you scatter words in profusion."

They said: He was the most concise of people in speech, and it was with this that Gabriel came to him. Yet despite this concision, he gathered within it all that he intended. He spoke with comprehensive words (jawāmiʿ al-kalim) — no excess, no deficiency — as though one part followed another in sequence. Between his words there was a pause, such that the listener would retain and comprehend them.

His voice was loud and clear, and he had the most beautiful tone of all people. He was given to long silences, speaking not in what was unnecessary. He never uttered what was reprehensible, and in both pleasure and anger he spoke only the truth. He would turn away from one who spoke with impropriety, and would allude indirectly to that which necessity compelled him to mention but which he disliked to state plainly.

When he fell silent, his companions would speak, and they would not dispute in his presence over any matter of conversation. He would admonish with earnestness and sincere counsel. He said: "Do not strike some parts of the Qurʾān against others, for it was revealed upon multiple aspects."

He was the most smiling of people and the most given to laughter in the faces of his companions, expressing wonder at what they related, and mingling himself with them. Sometimes he would laugh until his molars became visible. The laughter of his companions in his presence was but a smile, following his example and out of reverence for him.

They said: A Bedouin once came to him on a day when his complexion had changed, such that his companions found him unrecognizable. The Bedouin wanted to ask him about it, but they said: "Do not do so, O Bedouin, for we find his complexion changed." He said: "Leave me! By Him who sent him with the truth as a prophet, I shall not leave him until he smiles." He then said: "O Messenger of God, it has reached us that the Messiah — meaning the Dajjāl — comes to people with tharīd (bread soaked in broth) while they have perished from hunger. Do you think — may my father and mother be your ransom — that I should refrain from his tharīd out of abstinence and purity until I perish of hunger, or should I plunge into his tharīd until, when I am satiated, I believe in God and disbelieve in him?"

They said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) laughed until his molars became visible, then said: "No, rather God will suffice you with what He suffices the believers."

They said: He was among the most smiling of people and the most pleasant in spirit — so long as no Qurʾān was being revealed upon him, nor the Hour was mentioned, nor he was delivering an admonitory sermon. When he was pleased and content, he was the most pleasing of people in contentment. When he admonished, he admonished with earnestness. And when he became angry — and he did not become angry except for God — nothing could withstand his anger. Thus was he in all his affairs.

When an affair descended upon him, he would commit the matter to God, disavow all power and strength of his own, and seek the descent of guidance, saying: "O God, show me truth as truth that I may follow it, and show me falsehood as falsehood that I may avoid it. Protect me from its being confused upon me, such that I follow my desire without guidance from You. Make my desire a follower of Your obedience. Take Your satisfaction with Yourself from my self in well-being. Guide me to that wherein there is disagreement of truth, by Your permission. Verily, You guide whom You will to a straight path."

chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان أخلاقه وآدابه في الطعام

كان صلى الله عليه وسلم يأكل ما وجد (4) وكان أحب الطعام إليه ما كان على
ضفف (5) والضفف ما كثرت عليه الأيدي وكان إذا وضعت المائدة قال بسم الله
اللهم اجعلها نعمة مشكورة تصل بها نعمة الجنة (6) وكان كثيرا إذا جلس يأكل
يجمع بين ركبتيه وبين قدميه كما يجلس المصلي إلا أن الركبة تكون فوق الركبة
والقدم فوق القدم ويقول إنما أنا عبد آكل كما يأكل العبد وأجلس كما يجلس
العبد (7) وكان لا يأكل الحار ويقول إنه غير ذي PageV02P369
بركة وإن الله لم يطعمنا نارا فأبردوه (1) وكان يأكل مما يليه (2) ويأكل
بأصابعه الثلاث (3) وربما استعان بالرابعة (4) ولم يأكل بأصبعين ويقول إن
ذلك أكلة الشيطان (5) وجاءه عثمان بن عفان رضي الله عنه بفالوذج فأكل منه
وقال ما هذا يا عبد الله قال بأبي أنت وأمي نجعل السمن والعسل في البرمة
ونضعها على النار ثم نغليه ثم نأخذ مخ الحنطة إذا طحنت فنقليه على السمن
والعسل في البرمة ثم نسوطه حتى ينضج فيأتي كما ترى فقال رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم إن هذا الطعام طيب (6) وكان يأكل خبز الشعير غير منخول (7) وكان
يأكل القثاء بالرطب (8) وبالملح (9) وكان أحب الفواكه الرطبة إليه البطيخ
والعنب (10) وكان يأكل البطيخ بالخبز وبالسكر (11) وربما أكله PageV02P370
بالرطب (1) ويستعين باليدين جميعا وأكل يوما الرطب في يمينه وكان يحفظ
النوى في يساره فمرت شاة فأشار إليها بالنوى فجعلت تأكل من كفه اليسرى وهو
يأكل بيمينه حتى فرغ وانصرفت الشاة (2) وكان ربما أكل العنب خرطا يرى زؤانه
على لحيته كخرز اللؤلؤ (3) وكان أكثر طعامه الماء والتمر (4) وكان اللبن
بالتمر ويسميهما الأطيبين (5) وكان أحب الطعام  إليه اللحم ويقول هو يزيد في
السمع وهو سيد الطعام في الدنيا والآخرة ولو سألت ربي أن يطعمنيه كل يوم
لفعل (6) وكان يأكل الثريد باللحم والقرع (7) وكان يحب القرع ويقول إنها
شجرة أخي يونس عليه السلام (8) قالت عائشة رضي الله عنها وكان يقول عائشة
إذ طبختم قدرا فأكثروا فيها من الدباء فإنه يشد قلب الحزين (9) وكان يأكل
لحم الطير الذي يصاد (10) وكان لا يتبعه والصيد ويحب أن يصاد له ويؤتى به
فيأكله (11) وكان إذا أكل اللحم لم يطأطئ رأسه إليه ويرفعه إلى فيه رفعا ثم
ينتهشه انتهاشا (12) وكان يأكل الخبز والسمن (13) وكان يحب من الشاة الذراع
والكف ومن القدر الدباء ومن الصباغ الخل ومن التمر PageV02P371
العجوة (1) ودعا في العجوة بالبركة وقال هي من الجنة وشفاء من السم
والسحر (2) وكان يحب من البقول الهندباء والباذروج والبقلة الحمقاء التي
يقال لها الرجلة (3) وكان يكره الكليتين لمكانهما من البول (4) وكان لا
يأكل من الشاة سبعا الذكر والأنثيين والمثانة والمرارة والغدد والحيا والدم
ويكره ذلك (5) وكان لا يأكل الثوم ولا البصل ولا الكراث (6) وما ذم طعاما
قط لكن إن أعجبه أكله وإن كرهه تركه وإن عافه لم يبغضه إلى غيره (7) وكان
يعاف الضب والطحال ولا يحرمهما (8) وكان يلعق بأصابعه الصحفة ويقول آخر
الطعام أكثر بركة (9) وكان يلعق أصابعه من الطعام حتى تحمر (10) وكان لا
يمسح يده بالمنديل حتى يلعق أصابعه واحدة واحدة ويقول إنه لا يدري في أي
الطعام البركة (11) PageV02P372
وإذا فرغ قال الحمد لله اللهم لك الحمد أطعمت فأشبعت وسقيت فأرويت لك
الحمد غير مكفور ولا مودع ولا مستغنى عنه (1) وكان إذا أكل الخبز واللحم
خاصة غسل يديه غسلا جيدا ثم يمسح بفضل الماء على وجهه (2) وكان يشرب في
ثلاث دفعات وله فيها ثلاث تسميات وفي أواخرها ثلاث تحميدات (3) وكان يمص
الماء مصا ولا يعب عبا (4) وكان يدفع فضل سؤره إلى من على يمينه (5) فإن
كان من على يساره أجل رتبة قال للذي على يمينه السنة أن تعطي فإن أحببت
آثرتهم (6) وربما كان  يشرب بنفس واحد حتى يفرغ (7) وكان لا يتنفس في الإناء
بل ينحرف عنه (8) وأتى بإناء فيه عسل ولبن فأبى أن يشربه وقال شربتان في
شربة وإدامان في إناء واحد (9) ثم قال صلى الله عليه وسلم لا أحرمه ولكني
أكره الفخر والحساب بفضول الدنيا غدا وأحب التواضع فإن من تواضع لله رفعه
الله وكان في بيته أشد حياء من العاتق لا يسألهم طعاما ولا يتشهاه عليهم إن
أطعموه أكل وما أعطوه قبل وما سقوه شرب (10) وكان ربما قام فأخذ ما يأكل
بنفسه أو يشرب (11) PageV02P373
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-ف-ف (ḍ-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Crowding, pressing together; a thing whose sides are filled with people
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes abundance of participants sharing a meal, implying communal blessing
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical crowding; metaphorically signifies multiplicity of hands reaching food
- Root: ن-ه-ش (n-h-sh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To seize and bite flesh from the bone with the front teeth
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Manner of eating befitting humility, distinct from predatory tearing
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal action of biting; rhetorically marks deliberate, dignified consumption
- Root: ع-ف-و (ʿ-f-w) / ع-ي-ف (ʿ-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To abstain from something due to natural aversion, without prohibition
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Distinguishes personal dislike (karāhah) from legal unlawfulness (taḥrīm)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of turning away; metaphorical for moral restraint in judgment
- Sībawayh Rule: Ḥāl Clause (الْحَال) — Circumstantial accusatives describing the Prophet's posture and actions (e.g., "as one who sits," "biting with his front teeth") provide simultaneous qualifiers to the main verb, requiring careful temporal coordination in translation.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now I shall expound his character and manners in eating.

He, peace and blessings be upon him, ate whatever he found. And the most beloved food to him was that upon which many hands were laid (ḍafaf) — and ḍafaf is that upon which hands multiply. When the table was set, he would say: "In the name of God. O God, make it a thankful blessing by which You join us to the blessing of Paradise." Often, when he sat to eat, he would draw together his knees and his feet as one who sits in prayer — except that one knee would be above the other knee, and one foot above the other foot — and he would say: "I am but a servant; I eat as a servant eats, and I sit as a servant sits." He would not eat hot food, saying: "It is devoid of blessing, and God has not fed us fire — so cool it." He would eat from what was before him, and he would eat with his three fingers, and sometimes he would aid himself with a fourth. He did not eat with two fingers, saying: "That is the eating of Satan." ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may God be pleased with him, brought him fālūdhaj, and he ate from it and said: "What is this, O ʿAbd Allāh?" He replied: "May my father and mother be your ransom — we place clarified butter and honey in a pot, set it upon the fire, then boil it; then we take the marrow of wheat when it is ground, fry it in the butter and honey in the pot, then stir it until it ripens, and it comes as you see." The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, this food is good." He ate barley bread unsifted. He ate cucumber with fresh dates, and with salt. The most beloved of fresh fruits to him were watermelon and grapes. He would eat watermelon with bread and with sugar, and sometimes he ate it with fresh dates, aiding himself with both hands. One day he ate fresh dates with his right hand, and he kept the pits in his left hand. A sheep passed by, so he gestured to it with the pits, and it began eating from his left palm while he ate with his right hand, until he finished and the sheep departed. Sometimes he ate grapes cluster-wise, so that their residue appeared upon his blessed beard like pearls strung. His most frequent food was water and dates. He also ate milk with dates, and he called them "the two most excellent." The most beloved food to him was meat, and he said: "It increases hearing, and it is the master of food in this world and the Hereafter; and had I asked my Lord to feed it to me every day, He would have done so." He ate tharīd with meat and gourd. He loved gourd, saying: "It is the tree of my brother Jonah, peace be upon him." ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "He would say: 'When you cook a pot, multiply therein the gourd (dubbāʾ), for it strengthens the heart of the sorrowful.'" He ate the meat of hunted birds, but he did not pursue the hunt himself; he loved that it be hunted for him and brought to him, and then he would eat it. When he ate meat, he did not lower his head toward it, but raised it to his mouth with a lifting, then bit from it with his front teeth (intihāsh). He ate bread with clarified butter. He loved, of the sheep, the foreleg and the hand; of the pot, the gourd; of condiments, vinegar; and of dates, the ʿajwah. He invoked blessing upon the ʿajwah, saying: "It is from Paradise, and a cure from poison and sorcery." He loved, of vegetables, endive, basil, and the foolish herb called rajlah (purslane). He disliked the two kidneys because of their proximity to urine. He did not eat, of the sheep, seven things: the testicles, the two female organs, the bladder, the gall bladder, the glands, the womb, and the blood — and he disliked that. He did not eat garlic, nor onion, nor leek. He never disparaged any food whatsoever; rather, if it pleased him, he ate it, and if he disliked it, he left it, and if he felt aversion to it, he did not make it hateful to others. He felt aversion to the ḍabb (lizard) and the spleen, yet he did not declare them unlawful. He would lick the dish with his fingers, saying: "The last of the food is the most abundant in blessing." He would lick his fingers of food until they became red. He would not wipe his hand with a napkin until he had licked his fingers one by one, saying: "Indeed, one does not know in which part of the food the blessing lies." When he finished, he would say: "Praise be to God. O God, to You is praise — You fed me and I was satiated, and You gave me drink and I was quenched. To You is praise, unrepudiated, unrelinquished, and not to be dispensed with." When he ate bread and meat specifically, he washed his hands thoroughly, then wiped the excess water over his face. He drank in three draughts, uttering in them three invocations of the Name, and at their ends three praises. He sipped water by suction and did not gulp it down. He would pass the remainder of his drink to the one on his right. If the one on his left was of higher rank, he would say to the one on his right: "The sunnah is that you give; but if you wish, I will prefer them over you." Sometimes he drank in a single breath until he finished. He would not breathe into the vessel, but would turn away from it. A vessel containing honey and milk was brought to him, and he refused to drink it, saying: "Two drinks in one draught, and two relishes in one vessel." Then he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "I do not declare it unlawful, but I dislike pride and the reckoning over the superfluities of this world tomorrow, and I love humility — for whoever humbles himself before God, God raises him." He was, in his own house, more shy than a virgin maiden; he would not ask them for food, nor crave it upon them — if they fed him, he ate; whatever they gave him, he accepted; and whatever they gave him to drink, he drank. Sometimes he would rise and take for himself what he would eat or drink.
