حسن الخلق وقال عطاء ما ارتفع من ارتفع إلا بالخلق الحسن ولم ينل أحد كماله
إلا المصطفى صلى الله عليه وسلم فأقرب الخلق إلى الله عز وجل السالكون
آثاره بحسن الخلق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes measured estimation, proportioning, and the inherent disposition or nature of a thing — both physical form (khalq) and moral temper (khuluq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khuluq is the inward constitution (hayʾah nafsāniyyah) from which actions proceed spontaneously without deliberation; it is the ethical correlate of physical creation (khalq), and its perfection is the very aim of prophetic mission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the divinely-given moral constitution; metaphorically (majāz) extended to acquired habits that become second nature through repeated practice.
- Root: ع-ف-و (ʿ-f-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pardon, to efface, to leave something unpunished; the root also carries the sense of abundance and excess (from which "forgiveness" derives — pardoning what exceeds the limit of requital).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAfw is the deliberate relinquishment of just retribution (qisāṣ) — a virtue ranked above mere justice, and commanded in the Quranic verse cited herein.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "to obliterate" (maḥw); in moral discourse it is a well-established metaphor for wiping away the offense of another as if it had never occurred.
- Root: غ-ض-ب (gh-d-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The boiling and agitation of the blood of the heart seeking vengeance; the most violent of the irascible passions.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ghada b is the combustion of the irascible faculty (al-quwwah al-ghaḍabiyyah) when the animal spirit is stirred; its complete suppression is the defining test of religion, as the Prophet declared in the hadith cited.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the physiological-emotional state; the prophetic command "do not be angry" is a metonymy (kināyah) for restraining its outward expressions and inward indulgence.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In the hadith "he is that you join the one who cuts you off..." the pronominal construction (huwa an taṣila) employs a nominal sentence with an indefinite predicate clause, establishing a definitional equation between good character and its concrete manifestations, a pattern Sībawayh classifies under predicative apposition requiring no copula.
chapters.translation:
I say — God Most High said to His Prophet and Beloved, praising him and manifesting His favor upon him: {«وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ»} ("And indeed, you are upon an immense moral constitution"). And ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, his moral constitution was the Qurʾān."

And a man asked the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, about good character, so he recited the saying of God Most High: {«خُذِ الْعَفْوَ وَأْمُرْ بِالْعُرْفِ وَأَعْرِضْ عَنِ الْجَاهِلِينَ»} ("Take the pardon, command the good, and turn away from the ignorant"). Then he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "It is that you join the one who cuts you off, give to the one who deprives you, and pardon the one who wrongs you."

The hadith: "I was sent to perfect the noble traits of character" — recorded by Aḥmad, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, and it has preceded in the Book of the Etiquettes of Companionship.

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "The heaviest thing placed in the Balance on the Day of Resurrection is God-consciousness (taqwā) and good character." — The hadith "The heaviest thing placed in the Balance is good character" is recorded by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, who declared it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ.

And a man came to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, from before him and said: "O Messenger of God, what is religion?" He said: "Good character." Then he came to him from his right side and said: "O Messenger of God, what is religion?" He said: "Good character." Then he came to him from his left side and said: "What is religion?" He said: "Good character." Then he came to him from behind him and said: "O Messenger of God, what is religion?" So he turned to him and said: "Do you not understand? It is that you do not become angry."

And it was said: "O Messenger of God, what is ill-omen (al-shuʾm)?" He said: "Bad character."

And a man said to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: "Advise me." He said: "Fear God wherever you are." He said: "Add for me." He said: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed that erases it." He said: "Add for me." He said: "Treat people with good character."

The hadith: "God has not beautified a man's physical form and his moral character such that the Fire consumes him" — has preceded in the Book of the Etiquettes of Companionship.

The hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ: "The first thing placed in the Balance is good character" — I have not found an original source for it in this wording. But Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī record from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ: "There is nothing in the Balance heavier than good character," and he (al-Tirmidhī) said: "It is gharīb (unusual)," and in some of its chains he said: "Ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (sound and good)."

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, God has singled out this religion for Himself, and nothing befits your religion except generosity and good character. Indeed, adorn your religion with the two of them."

The hadith: "Good character is the greatest of God's creations" — recorded by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ from the hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir with a weak chain.

And it was said: "O Messenger of God, which of the believers is most perfect in faith?" He said: "The one among them with the best character."

The hadith: "Indeed, you cannot encompass people with your wealth, so encompass them with a cheerful face and good character" — recorded by al-Bazzār, Abū Yaʿlā, and al-Ṭabarānī in Makārim al-Akhlāq from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah; some chains of al-Bazzār have trustworthy narrators.

The hadith: "Bad character corrupts deeds just as vinegar corrupts honey" — recorded by Ibn Ḥibbān in al-Ḍuʿafāʾ from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, and by al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah as well; Ibn Jarīr declared both weak.

The hadith: "Indeed, you are a man whose physical form God has beautified, so beautify your moral character" — recorded by al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq and Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Daghūlī in his Book of Etiquettes; there is weakness in it.

And from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, he said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was the most beautiful of people in face and the best of them in character."

And from Abū Masʿūd al-Badrī, he said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say in his supplication: 'O God, You have beautified my physical form, so beautify my moral character.'"

And from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, he said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to supplicate frequently, saying: 'O God, I ask You for sound health, well-being, and good character.'"

The hadith of Abū Hurayrah: "A man's nobility (karm) is his religion, his manliness (murūʾah) is his intellect, and his good character is his [true] lineage (ḥasab)" — recorded by Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound upon the condition of Muslim, and by al-Bayhaqī. I say: In it is Muslim ibn Khālid al-Zanjī, who has been criticized. Al-Bayhaqī said: "It is also narrated through two other weak chains," then he narrated it as a statement of ʿUmar (mawqūf) and said: "Its chain is sound."

The hadith of Usāmah ibn Sharīk: "I witnessed the Bedouins asking the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: 'What is the best thing given to a servant?' He said: 'Good character.'" — recorded by Ibn Mājah, and it has preceded in the Book of the Etiquettes of Companionship.

The hadith: "Indeed, the most beloved of you to God and the closest of you to me in seating on the Day of Resurrection are those of you with the best character" — recorded by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Ṣaghīr and al-Awsaṭ from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah: "Indeed, the most beloved of you to God are those with the best character." And al-Ṭabarānī records in Makārim al-Akhlāq from the hadith of Jābir: "Indeed, the closest of you to me in seating are those with the best character." Both hadiths have preceded in the Book of the Etiquettes of Companionship.

The hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Three traits — whoever does not possess them, or even one of them, no deed of his is counted" — recorded by al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq with a weak chain, and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Kabīr and in Makārim al-Akhlāq from the hadith of Umm Salamah.

And among his supplications, peace and blessings be upon him, at the opening of prayer was: "O God, guide me to the best of moral traits — none guides to their best except You — and turn away from me their worst — none turns their worst away from me except You."

The hadith of Anas: "Indeed, good character melts away sin just as the sun melts ice" — recorded by al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq with a weak chain; al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ṭayālisī, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās and declared it weak; likewise he narrated it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah and declared it weak as well.

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "From the felicity of a man is good character."

The hadith: "Auspiciousness (al-yumn) is good character" — recorded by al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq from the hadith of ʿAlī with a weak chain.

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him, to Abū Dharr: "O Abū Dharr, there is no intellect like prudent deliberation (al-tadbīr), and no lineage (ḥasab) like good character."

And from Anas, he said: "Umm Ḥabībah said to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: 'What do you think of a woman who has two husbands in this world, then she dies and they both die, and they all enter Paradise — to which of them does she belong?' He said: 'To the one with the better character toward her in this world. O Umm Ḥabībah, good character has carried away the good of this world and the Hereafter.'"

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, the upright Muslim (al-musaddad) attains the rank of the perpetual faster and the perpetual prayer-stander through his good character and the nobility of his station."

The hadith of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: "Indeed, I saw last night a wonder" — recorded by al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq with a weak chain.

The hadith: "Indeed, a servant attains through his good character the greatest of ranks in the Hereafter" — recorded by al-Ṭabarānī, al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq, and Abū al-Shaykh in his Book of Makārim al-Akhlāq and in his Book of the Strata of the Iṣfahānīs, from the hadith of Anas with a good chain.

And it is narrated that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, sought permission to enter upon the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while there were with him women from the women of Quraysh speaking with him and asking much of him, their voices raised above his voice. When ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, sought permission, they hurried to the veil. Then ʿUmar entered while the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was laughing. So ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "What makes you laugh, may my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of God?" He said: "I marvel at these women who were with me — when they heard your voice, they hurried to the veil." So ʿUmar said: "You, O Messenger of God, were more deserving that they should stand in awe of you." Then ʿUmar turned to them and said: "O enemies of your own souls! Do you stand in awe of me and not stand in awe of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him?" They said: "Yes, for you are harsher and more severe than the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him." So he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Enough, O Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb! By Him in Whose hand is my soul, Satan has never met you traversing a path except that he took another path, not your path."

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Bad character is a sin that is not forgiven, and evil suspicion is an offense that reeks."

And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, a servant attains through his bad character the lowest depth of Hell."

THE SAYINGS OF THE PIOUS PREDECESSORS (Āthār):

Luqmān the Wise said to his father: "O my father, which of the traits in a man is best?" He said: "Religion." He said: "And if there are two?" He said: "Religion and wealth." He said: "And if there are three?" He said: "Religion, wealth, and modesty (al-ḥayāʾ)." He said: "And if there are four?" He said: "Religion, wealth, modesty, and good character." He said: "And if there are five?" He said: "Religion, wealth, modesty, good character, and generosity." He said: "And if there are six?" He said: "O my son, if the five traits are gathered in him, then he is pure and God-fearing — God is his protector, and from Satan he is delivered."

And al-Ḥasan said: "Whoever has bad character torments himself."

And Anas ibn Mālik said: "Indeed, a servant attains through his good character the highest rank in Paradise while he is not a worshipper, and attains through his bad character the lowest depth of Hell while he is a worshipper."

And Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "In the breadth of character are the treasures of provision."

And Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "The likeness of the ill-tempered man is like a broken clay pot — it cannot be patched, nor can it be remade into clay."

And al-Fuḍayl said: "That a wicked man of good character should accompany me is more beloved to me than that a worshipper of bad character should accompany me."

And Ibn al-Mubārak accompanied a man of bad character on a journey, and he bore his conduct patiently and treated him gently. When he parted from him, he wept. It was said to him about that, and he said: "I weep for him out of mercy — I parted from him while his character remained with him; it did not part from him."

And al-Junayd said: "Four things raise a servant to the highest ranks even if his deeds and knowledge are little: forbearance (al-ḥilm), humility (al-tawāḍuʿ), generosity, and good character — and it is the perfection of faith."

And al-Kannānī said: "Sufism is character — whoever surpasses you in character has surpassed you in Sufism."

And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Mix with people through [good] character, and separate from them through [your] deeds."

And Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "Bad character is an evil deed with which the abundance of good deeds does not avail; and good character is a good deed with which the abundance of evil deeds does not harm."

And Ibn ʿAbbās was asked: "What is nobility (al-karam)?" He said: "It is what God has clarified in His Mighty Book: {«إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ اللَّهِ أَتْقَاكُمْ»} ('Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most God-conscious of you')." It was said: "Then what is lineage (al-ḥasab)?" He said: "The best of you in character is the most excellent of you in lineage."

And he said: "Every building has a foundation, and the foundation of Islam is good character."

And ʿAṭāʾ said: "None has risen who rose except through good character, and none attained perfection except the Chosen One, peace and blessings be upon him. So the closest of creation to God, Mighty and Majestic, are those who traverse his path through good character."

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Reality of Good Character and Bad Character
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان حقيقة حسن الخلق وسوء الخلق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty, excellence, and perfection in form or act; the opposite of ugliness (qubḥ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥusn in the theological sense denotes moral and intellectual excellence aligned with divine command and rational virtue.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for sensory beauty; metaphorical (majāz) for moral and spiritual excellence.
- Root: س-و-ء (s-w-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Evil, corruption, and moral deficiency; the opposite of ḥusn.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sūʾ signifies that which is blameworthy in action or disposition, opposed to divine approbation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical harm; metaphorical for moral depravity and spiritual vice.
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Innate disposition, nature, or character; also creation and measure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khuluq is the inner form (ṣūrah bāṭinah) of the soul, parallel to khalq as the outer form.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical creation; metaphorical for the stable inner trait of the soul.
- Sībawayh Rule: Idāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "ḥaqīqat ḥusn al-khuluq" employs a chain of annexation, where the first term (ḥaqīqah) governs the second (ḥusn), and the second governs the third (al-khuluq), indicating a precise definitional unpacking of the essence of character.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the exposition of the reality of good character (ḥusn al-khuluq) and bad character (sūʾ al-khuluq).

chapters.title_en: The Reality of Good Character and Its Four Pillars
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الناس قد تكلموا في حقيقة حسن الخلق وأنه ما هو وما تعرضوا
لحقيقته وإنما تعرضوا لثمرته ثم لم يستوعبوا جميع ثمراته بل ذكر كل واحد من
ثمراته ما خطر له وما كان حاضرا في ذهنه ولم يصرفوا العناية إلى ذكر حده
وحقيقته المحيطة بجميع ثمراته على التفصيل والاستيعاب وذلك كقول الحسن حسن
الخلق بسط الوجه PageV03P052
وبذل الندى وكف الأذى وقال الواسطي هو أن لا يخاصم ولا يخاصم من شدة
معرفته بالله تعالى وقال شاه الكرماني هو كف الأذى واحتمال المؤن وقال
بعضهم هو أن يكون من الناس قريبا وفيما بينهم غريبا وقال الواسطي مرة هو
إرضاء الخلق في السراء والضراء وقال أبو عثمان هو الرضا عن الله تعالى وسئل
سهل التستري عن حسن الخلق فقال أدناه الاحتمال وترك المكافأة والرحمة
للظالم والاستغفار له والشفقة عليه وقال مرة أن لا يتهم الحق في الرزق ويثق
به ويسكن إلى الوفاء بما ضمن فيطيعه ولا يعصيه في جميع الأمور فيما بينه
وبينه وفيما بينه وبين الناس وقال علي رضي الله عنه حسن الخلق في ثلاث خصال
اجتناب المحارم وطلب الحلال والتوسعة على العيال وقال الحسين بن منصور هو
أن لا يؤثر فيك جفاء الخلق بعد مطالعتك للحق وقال أبو سعيد الخراز هو أن لا
يكون لك هم غير الله تعالى فهذا وأمثاله كثير وهو تعرض لثمرات حسن الخلق لا
لنفسه ثم ليس هو محيطا بجميع الثمرات  أيضاوكشف الغطاء عن الحقيقة أولى من
نقل الأقاويل المختلفة فنقول الخلق والخلق عبارتان مستعملتان معا يقال فلان
حسن الخلق والخلق أي حسن الباطن والظاهر فيراد بالخلق الصورة الظاهرة ويراد
بالخلق الصورة الباطنة وذلك لأن الإنسان مركب من جسد مدرك بالبصر ومن روح
ونفس مدرك بالبصيرة ولكل واحد منهما هيئة وصورة إما قبيحة وإما جميلة
فالنفس المدركة بالبصيرة أعظم قدرا من الجسد المدرك بالبصر ولذلك عظم الله
أمره بإضافته إليه إذ قال تعالى إني خالق بشرا من طين فإذا سويته ونفخت فيه
من روحي فقعوا له ساجدين فنبه على أن الجسد منسوب إلى الطين والروح إلى رب
العالمين والمراد بالروح والنفس في هذا المقام واحد فالخلق عبارة عن هيئة
في النفس راسخة عنها تصدر الأفعال بسهولة ويسر من غير حاجة إلى فكر وروية
فإن كانت الهيئة بحيث تصدر عنها الأفعال الجميلة المحمودة عقلا وشرعا سميت
تلك الهيئة خلقا حسنا وإن كان الصادر عنها الأفعال القبيحة سميت الهيئة
التي هي المصدر خلقا سيئا وإنما قلنا إنها هيئة راسخة لأن من يصدر منه بذل
المال على الندور لحاجة عارضة لا يقال خلقه السخاء ما لم يثبت ذلك في نفسه
ثبوت رسوخ وإنما اشترطنا أن تصدر منه الأفعال بسهولة من غير روية لأن من
تكلف بذل المال أو السكوت عند الغضب بجهد وروية لا يقال خلقه السخاء والحلم
فههنا أربعة أمور
أحدها فعل الجميل والقبيح
والثاني القدرة عليهما
والثالث المعرفة بهما
والرابع هيئة للنفس بها تميل إلى أحد الجانبين ويتيسر عليها أحد الأمرين
إما الحسن وإما القبيح
وليس الخلق عبارة عن الفعل فرب شخص خلقه السخاء ولا يبذل إما لفقد المال
أو لمانع وربما يكون خلقه البخل وهو يبذل إما لباعث أو لرياء وليس هو عبارة
عن القوة لأن نسبة القوة إلى الإمساك والإعطاء بل إلى الضدين واحد وكل
إنسان خلق بالفطرة قادر على الإعطاء والإمساك وذلك لا يوجب خلق البخل ولا
خلق السخاء وليس هو عبارة عن المعرفة فإن المعرفة تتعلق بالجميل والقبيح
جميعا على وجه واحد بل هو عبارة عن المعنى الرابع وهو الهيئة التي بها
تستعد النفس لأن يصدر منها الإمساك أو البذل فالخلق إذا عبارة عن هيئة
النفس وصورتها الباطنة وكما أن حسن الصورة الظاهرة مطلقا لا يتم بحسن
العينين دون الأنف والفم والخد بل لا بد من حسن الجميع ليتم حسن الظاهر
فكذلك في الباطن أربعة أركان لا بد من الحسن في جميعها حتى يتم حسن الخلق
فإذا استوت الأركان الأربعة واعتدلت وتناسبت حصل حسن الخلق وهو قوة العلم
وقوة الغضب وقوة الشهوة وقوة العدل بين هذه القوى الثلاث
PageV03P053
أما قوة العلم فحسنها وصلاحها في أن تصير بحيث يسهل بها درك الفرق بين
الصدق والكذب في الأقوال وبين الحق والباطل في الاعتقادات وبين الجميل
والقبيح في الأفعال فإذا صلحت هذه القوة حصل منها ثمرة الحكمة والحكمة رأس
الأخلاق الحسنة وهي التي قال الله فيها ومن يؤت الحكمة فقد أوتى خيرا كثيرا
وأما قوة الغضب فحسنها في أن يصير انقباضها وانبساطها على حد ما تقتضيه
الحكمة وكذلك الشهوة حسنها وصلاحها في أن تكون تحت إشارة الحكمة أعني إشارة
العقل والشرع
وأما قوة العدل فهو ضبط الشهوة والغضب تحت إشارة العقل والشرع
فالعقل مثاله مثال الناصح المشير
وقوة العدل هي القدرة ومثالها مثال المنفذ الممضي لإشارة العقل
والغضب هو الذي تنفد فيه الإشارة ومثاله مثال كلب الصيد فإنه يحتاج إلى
أن يؤدب حتى يكون استرساله وتوقفه بحسب الإشارة لا بحسب هيجان شهوة النفس
والشهوة مثالها مثال الفرس الذي يركب في طلب الصيد فإنه تارة يكون مروضا
مؤدبا وتارة يكون جموحا فمن استوت فيه هذه الخصال واعتدلت فهو حسن الخلق
مطلقا ومن اعتدل فيه بعضها دون البعض فهو حسن الخلق بالإضافة إلى ذلك
المعنى خاصة كالذي يحسن بعض أجزاء وجهه دون بعض وحسن القوة الغضبية
واعتدالها يعبر عنه بالشجاعة وحسن قوة الشهوة واعتدالها يعبر عنه بالعفة
فإن مالت قوة الغضب عن الاعتدال إلى طرف الزيادة تسمى تهورا وإن مالت إلى
الضعف والنقضان  تسمى جبنا وخورا
وإن مالت قوة الشهوة إلى طرف الزيادة تسمى شرها وإن مالت إلى النقصان
تسمى جمودا
والمحمود هو الوسط وهو الفضيلة والطرفان رذيلتان مذمومتان والعدل إذا فات
فليس له طرفا زيادة ونقصان بل له ضد واحد ومقابل وهو الجور
وأما الحكمة فيسمى إفراطها عند الاستعمال في الأغراض الفاسدة خبثا وجربزة
ويسمى تفريطها بلها والوسط هو الذي يختص باسم الحكمة
فإذن أمهات الأخلاق وأصولها أربعة الحكمة والشجاعة والعفة والعدل ونعني
بالحكمة حالة للنفس بها يدرك الصواب من الخطأ في جميع الأفعال الاختيارية
ونعني بالعدل حالة للنفس وقوة بها تسوس الغضب والشهوة وتحملهما على مقتضى
الحكمة وتضبطهما في الاسترسال والانقباض على حسب مقتضاها ونعني بالشجاعة
كون قوة الغضب منقادة للعقل في إقدامها وإحجامها ونعني بالعفة تأدب قوة
الشهوة بتأديب العقل والشرع
فمن اعتدال هذه الأصول الأربعة تصدر الأخلاق الجميلة كلها
إذ من اعتدال قوة العقل يحصل حسن التدبير وجودة الذهن وثقابة الرأي
وإصابة الظن والتفطن لدقائق الأعمال وخفايا آفات النفوس ومن إفراطها تصدر
الجربزة والمكر والخداع والدهاء ومن تفريطها يصدر البله والغمارة والحمق
والجنون وأعني بالغمارة قلة التجربة في الأمور مع سلامة التخيل فقد يكون
الإنسان غمرا في شيء دون شيء والفرق بين الحمق الجنون أن الأحمق مقصوده
صحيح ولكن سلوكه الطريق فاسد فلا تكون له روية صحيحة في سلوك الطريق الموصل
إلى الغرض وأما المجنون فإنه يحتار ما لا ينبغي أن يختار فيكون أصل اختياره
وإيثاره فاسدا
وأما خلق الشجاعة فيصدر منه الكرم والنجدة والشهامة وكسر النفس والاحتمال
والحلم والثبات وكظم الغيظ والوقار والتودد وأمثالها وهي أخلاق محمودة
وأما إفراطها وهو التهور فيصدر منه الصلف والبذخ
PageV03P054
والاستشاطة والتكبر والعجب وأما تفريطها فيصدر منه المهانة والذلة والجزع
والخساسة وصغر النفس والانقباض عن تناول الحق الواجب
وأما خلق العفة فيصدر منه السخاء والحياء والصبر والمسامحة والقناعة
والورع واللطافة والمساعدة والظرف وقلة الطمع وأما ميلها إلى الإفراط أو
التفريط فيحصل منه الحرص والشره والوقاحة والخبث والتبذير والتقتير والرياء
والهتكة والمجانة والعبث والملق  والحسد والشماتة والتذلل للأغنياء واستحقار
الفقراء وغير ذلك
فأمهات محاسن الأخلاق هذه الفضائل الأربعة وهي الحكمة والشجاعة والعفة
والعدل والباقي فروعها
ولم يبلغ كمال الاعتدال في هذه الأربع إلا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
والناس بعده متفاوتون في القرب والبعد منه فكل من قرب منه في هذه الأخلاق
فهو قريب من الله تعالى بقدر قربه من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وكل من
جمع كمال هذه الأخلاق استحق أن يكون بين الخلق ملكا مطاعا يرجع الخلق كلهم
إليه ويقتدون به في جميع الأفعال ومن انفك عن هذه الأخلاق كلها واتصف
بأضدادها استحق أن يخرج من بين البلاد والعباد فإنه قد قرب من الشيطان
اللعين المبعد فينبغي أن يبعد كما أن الأول قريب من الملك المقرب فينبغي أن
يقتدى به ويتقرب إليه فإن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لم يبعث إلا ليتمم
مكارم الأخلاق كما قال (1)
وقد أشار القرآن إلى هذه الأخلاق في أوصاف المؤمنين فقال تعالى إنما
المؤمنون الذين آمنوا بالله ورسوله ثم لم يرتابوا وجاهدوا بأموالهم وأنفسهم
في سبيل الله أولئك هم الصادقون فالإيمان بالله وبرسوله من غير ارتياب هو
قوة اليقين وهو ثمرة العقل ومنتهى الحكمة والمجاهدة بالمال هو السخاء الذي
يرجع إلى ضبط قوة الشهوة
والمجاهدة بالنفس هي الشجاعة التي ترجع إلى استعمال قوة الغضب على شرط
العقل وحد الاعتدال فقد وصف الله تعالى الصحابة فقال أشداء على الكفار
رحماء بينهم إشارة إلى أن للشدة موضعا وللرحمة موضعا فليس الكمال في الشدة
بكل حال ولا في الرحمة بكل حال فهذا بيان معنى الخلق وحسنه وقبحه وبيان
أركانه وثمراته وفروعه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Creation, measurement, estimation; the inherent nature or disposition of a thing; the form and constitution of a being.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The inner constitution (al-ṣūrah al-bāṭinah) of the soul, parallel to al-khalq as the outer form; the divinely-given disposition from which actions proceed.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes the physical form (khalq); metaphorical extension (majāz) applies the same root to the inner character (khuluq), establishing a systematic analogy between outward and inward beauty.
- Root: ه-ي-ء (h-y-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Form, state, condition, configuration; the manner in which a thing is composed and arranged.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The stable disposition (hayʾah rāsikhah) of the soul that determines the ease or difficulty of action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense of a settled state, not a transient condition—distinguishing character from occasional acts.
- Root: ع-د-ل (ʿ-d-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Equity, balance, straightness; the mean between two extremes.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The governing virtue that holds the other faculties in due proportion; justice as the regulative principle of the soul.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of weighing and balancing; applied metaphorically to the soul's internal governance of its powers.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Predication with Dual Subjects (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-mubtadaʾ wa al-khabar)—when al-Ghazālī states "الخلق والخلق عبارتان مستعملتان معا" (khalq and khuluq are two expressions used together), the dual predicate requires that both terms share a single semantic field, establishing the parallel between outer and inner form through syntactic coordination.
chapters.translation:
Know that people have spoken concerning the reality of good character (ḥusn al-khuluq)—what it is—yet they have not addressed its true reality but rather addressed its fruits. Then they did not exhaust all its fruits; rather, each one mentioned of its fruits only what occurred to him and what was present in his mind, and they did not direct their attention to stating its definition and its true reality that encompasses all its fruits in detail and comprehensively. This is like the saying of al-Ḥasan: "Good character is a cheerful face, the giving of bounty, and the withholding of harm." Al-Wāsiṭī said: "It is that one neither disputes nor is disputed against, due to the intensity of his knowledge of Allah the Exalted." Shāh al-Kirmānī said: "It is the withholding of harm and the bearing of burdens." Some said: "It is that one be near to people while being a stranger among them." Al-Wāsiṭī said on one occasion: "It is pleasing creation in prosperity and adversity." Abū ʿUthmān said: "It is contentment with Allah the Exalted." Sahl al-Tustarī was asked about good character, and he said: "Its lowest degree is forbearance, abandoning retaliation, mercy toward the wrongdoer, seeking forgiveness for him, and compassion toward him." On another occasion he said: "It is that one does not accuse the Truth concerning provision, but trusts in Him and rests in the fulfillment of what He has guaranteed, thus obeying Him and not disobeying Him in all matters—between him and his Lord, and between him and people." ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Good character consists in three qualities: avoiding forbidden things, seeking what is lawful, and being generous toward one's dependents." Al-Ḥusayn ibn Manṣūr said: "It is that the harshness of creation does not affect you after your contemplation of the Truth." Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz said: "It is that you have no concern other than Allah the Exalted." This and the like of it is abundant, and it is an address to the fruits of good character, not to its essence. Moreover, it is not comprehensive of all the fruits.

Also, the unveiling of the covering from the reality is more appropriate than the transmission of divergent sayings. So we say: al-khalq and al-khuluq are two expressions used together. It is said: "So-and-so is good in khalq and khuluq," meaning good in the inner and the outer. By al-khalq is meant the outward form, and by al-khuluq is meant the inward form. This is because the human being is composed of a body perceived by sight and of a spirit and soul perceived by inner vision (al-baṣīrah). Each of these has a configuration and a form—either ugly or beautiful. The soul perceived by inner vision is greater in rank than the body perceived by sight. For this reason, Allah magnified its affair by ascribing it to Himself, for He the Exalted said: {«إِنِّي خَالِقٌ بَشَرًا مِنْ طِينٍ فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِي فَقَعُوا لَهُ سَاجِدِينَ»} ("Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down before him in prostration.") He thus indicated that the body is attributed to clay, while the spirit is attributed to the Lord of the worlds. By "spirit" and "soul" in this context is meant one and the same thing.

So al-khuluq is an expression for a settled disposition (hayʾah rāsikhah) in the soul from which actions proceed with ease and facility, without need for thought and deliberation. If the disposition is such that beautiful actions, praiseworthy by reason and by Law, proceed from it, that disposition is called good character (khuluq ḥasan). If what proceeds from it is ugly actions, the disposition that is the source is called bad character (khuluq sayyiʾ). We only said that it is a settled disposition because one from whom the giving of wealth proceeds rarely, due to an incidental need, is not said to have the character of generosity (sakhāʾ) unless that is established in his soul with settledness. And we only stipulated that actions proceed from him with ease, without deliberation, because one who forces himself to give wealth or to remain silent during anger, with effort and reflection, is not said to have the character of generosity and forbearance (ḥilm).

Here, then, are four matters:
First: the doing of the beautiful and the ugly (fiʿl al-jamīl wa al-qabīḥ).
Second: the capacity (qudrah) for both.
Third: the knowledge (maʿrifah) of both.
Fourth: a disposition of the soul by which it inclines to one of the two sides, and by which one of the two matters—either the beautiful or the ugly—is rendered easy for it.

Character is not an expression for the act, for there may be a person whose character is generosity yet he does not give, either for lack of wealth or due to an obstacle; and there may be one whose character is miserliness yet he gives, either due to a motive or for ostentation. Nor is it an expression for the capacity, for the relation of capacity to withholding and giving—indeed to both opposites—is one and the same, and every person is created by nature capable of giving and withholding, and that does not necessitate the character of miserliness nor the character of generosity. Nor is it an expression for knowledge, for knowledge pertains to the beautiful and the ugly alike in one and the same manner. Rather, it is an expression for the fourth meaning, namely the disposition by which the soul is prepared for withholding or giving to proceed from it.

So character is an expression for the disposition of the soul and its inward form. And just as the beauty of the outward form absolutely is not completed by the beauty of the eyes alone, without the nose, mouth, and cheek—rather, beauty in all of them is necessary for the outward beauty to be complete—so likewise in the inward there are four pillars (arkān) in all of which beauty is necessary for good character to be complete. When the four pillars are equal, balanced, and proportionate, good character is attained. These are: the power of knowledge (quwwat al-ʿilm), the power of anger (quwwat al-ghaḍab), the power of appetite (quwwat al-shahwah), and the power of justice (quwwat al-ʿadl) that governs these three powers.

As for the power of knowledge, its beauty and soundness consist in its becoming such that by it the discernment of the difference between truth and falsehood in statements, between right and wrong in beliefs, and between the beautiful and the ugly in actions is rendered easy. When this power is sound, the fruit of wisdom (ḥikmah) issues from it—and wisdom is the head of good moral qualities. It is that concerning which Allah said: {«وَمَنْ يُؤْتَ الْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا»} ("And whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good.")

As for the power of anger, its beauty consists in its contraction and expansion being according to the limit that wisdom requires. Likewise, the appetite—its beauty and soundness consist in its being under the direction of wisdom, that is, the direction of reason and the Law.

As for the power of justice, it is the restraining of appetite and anger under the direction of reason and the Law.

So reason—its example is the example of the sincere advisor (al-nāṣiḥ al-mushīr). The power of justice is the capacity, and its example is the example of the executor who carries out the direction of reason. Anger is that in which the direction is executed, and its example is the example of the hunting dog, which needs to be trained so that its release and its restraint are according to direction, not according to the agitation of the soul's appetite. The appetite—its example is the example of the horse ridden in pursuit of game: sometimes it is broken and trained, and sometimes it is headstrong.

So whoever has these qualities equal and balanced in him is good in character absolutely. Whoever has some of them balanced but not others is good in character with respect to that particular meaning only—like one whose some facial features are beautiful but not others. The beauty of the irascible power and its balance is expressed by courage (shajāʿah). The beauty of the appetitive power and its balance is expressed by temperance (ʿiffah). If the irascible power deviates from balance toward the side of excess, it is called recklessness (tahawwur); if it deviates toward weakness and deficiency, it is called cowardice (jubn) and faint-heartedness (khawar). If the appetitive power deviates toward the side of excess, it is called gluttony (sharah); if it deviates toward deficiency, it is called frigidity (jumūd). The praiseworthy is the mean, and it is the virtue; the two extremes are two vices, blameworthy. As for justice, when it is lost, it has no two extremes of excess and deficiency, but rather one opposite and counterpart, which is injustice (jawr).

As for wisdom, its excess—when employed for corrupt purposes—is called cunning (khibth) and craftiness (jarbazah); its deficiency is called foolishness (balah). The mean is that which is exclusively named wisdom.

So the mothers and roots of moral qualities are four: wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice. By wisdom we mean a state of the soul by which it discerns right from wrong in all voluntary actions. By justice we mean a state of the soul and a power by which it governs anger and appetite, driving them according to what wisdom requires and restraining them in their release and contraction according to its requirement. By courage we mean the irascible power being submissive to reason in its advance and its retreat. By temperance we mean the appetitive power being disciplined by the discipline of reason and the Law.

From the balance of these four roots, all beautiful moral qualities proceed. For from the balance of the power of reason arises good management, sharpness of mind, penetrating judgment, correctness of opinion, and discernment of the subtleties of actions and the hidden defects of souls. From its excess arise craftiness, deceit, trickery, and cunning. From its deficiency arise foolishness, inexperience (ghamārah), stupidity (ḥumq), and madness (junūn). By inexperience I mean lack of experience in affairs along with soundness of imagination—for a man may be inexperienced in one thing but not another. The difference between stupidity and madness is that the stupid person's aim is sound, but his way of proceeding is corrupt, so he has no sound deliberation in traversing the path that leads to the goal. As for the madman, he chooses what he ought not to choose, so the very root of his choosing and preferring is corrupt.

As for the character of courage, from it proceed generosity (karam), valor (najdah), manliness (shahāmah), self-mastery (kasr al-nafs), forbearance (iḥtimāl), clemency (ḥilm), steadfastness (thabāt), suppression of rage (kaẓm al-ghayẓ), dignity (waqār), affability (tawaddud), and the like—and these are praiseworthy moral qualities. As for its excess, namely recklessness, from it proceed arrogance (ṣalaf), ostentation (badhakh), fury (ishtishāṭah), pride (takabbur), and self-conceit (ʿujb). As for its deficiency, from it proceed abasement (mahānah), humiliation (dhillah), anguish (jazaʿ), baseness (khisāsah), smallness of soul (ṣighar al-nafs), and shrinking from claiming the obligatory right.

As for the character of temperance, from it proceed generosity (sakhāʾ), modesty (ḥayāʾ), patience (ṣabr), forbearance (musāmaḥah), contentment (qanāʿah), scrupulousness (waraʿ), gentleness (lutf), helpfulness (musāʿadah), elegance (ẓarf), and lack of avarice (qillat ṭamaʿ). As for its inclination toward excess or deficiency, from it arise greed (ḥirṣ), gluttony (sharah), shamelessness (waqāḥah), wickedness (khibth), extravagance (tabdhīr), miserliness (taqtīr), ostentation (riyāʾ), shamelessness (hatk), frivolity (majānah), jesting (ʿabath), flattery (malaq), envy (ḥasad), gloating (shamātah), self-abasement before the rich, contempt for the poor, and other such things.

So the mothers of the excellences of moral character are these four virtues—wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice—and the rest are their branches.

None attained the perfection of balance in these four except the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. People after him are varied in their proximity to and distance from him. So whoever is near to him in these moral qualities is near to Allah the Exalted to the measure of his proximity to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. Whoever combines the perfection of these moral qualities deserves to be among creation a king obeyed, to whom all creation returns and whom they follow in all actions. Whoever is stripped of all these moral qualities and is characterized by their opposites deserves to be expelled from among lands and servants, for he has drawn near to the accursed, banished Satan—so he ought to be banished, just as the former is near to the angel brought near—so he ought to be followed and drawn near to. For the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent only to perfect the noble traits of character, as he said.

The Quran has pointed to these moral qualities in the descriptions of the believers, for He the Exalted said: {«إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا وَجَاهَدُوا بِأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَنْفُسِهِمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الصَّادِقُونَ»} ("The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah—those are the truthful.") So belief in Allah and His Messenger without doubt is the strength of certainty (quwwat al-yaqīn), and it is the fruit of reason and the culmination of wisdom. Striving with wealth is the generosity that returns to the restraining of the appetitive power. Striving with the self is the courage that returns to the employment of the irascible power under the condition of reason and the limit of balance. And Allah the Exalted described the Companions, saying: {«أَشِدَّاءُ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ»} ("Harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves")—an indication that harshness has its place and mercy has its place. So perfection is not in harshness in every case, nor in mercy in every case.

This, then, is the elucidation of the meaning of character, its goodness and its badness, and the elucidation of its pillars, its fruits, and its branches.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Malleability of Moral Traits through Disciplined Training
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان قبول الأخلاق للتغيير بطريق الرياضة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ل (q-b-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "acceptance, reception, or capacity to receive" — here, the inherent receptivity of a thing to alteration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, denotes the ontological possibility of change (imkān al-taghayyur) as opposed to necessary immutability — aligning with the Ashʿarī doctrine of accident (ʿaraḍ) and acquired character (khulq) as contingent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of "accepting" an external influence; metaphorical (majāz) extension to moral traits as passive recipients of formative action.
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q) — *Note: This root is excluded per your instruction (خ already used). I will instead anchor on the second key root:*
- Root: ر-ي-ض (r-y-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "taming, breaking in (an animal), disciplining, or exercising" — from the practice of training a mount to obedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In spiritual ethics, riyāḍah denotes the systematic subjugation of the lower self (nafs) through repetitive acts, rendering virtue second nature (malakah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for physical training; metaphorical extension to moral character as a field to be cultivated and habituated.
- Sībawayh Rule: **Naʿt Sababī (Attributive Qualification)** — The genitive construction "قبول الأخلاق للتغيير" (acceptance of moral traits for change) functions as a nominal sentence with an implicit predicate, where the masdar (verbal noun) governs its object via the preposition "لِ" (for/to), indicating purpose or directedness — a standard pattern for expressing capacity and potentiality.
chapters.translation: I say: Know — may God guide you — that the exposition of the acceptance of moral traits (akhlāq) for change through the path of disciplined training (riyāḍah) is a matter whose truth is attested by both rational necessity and witnessed experience. For the moral trait is not an unalterable essence (jawhar thābit) fixed in the soul from its origin, but rather a disposition (hayʾah) that arises from the repetition of acts, and whatsoever arises through repetition may be transformed through the repetition of its opposite. Just as the wild beast is tamed by persistent exercise, and the stubborn horse is rendered obedient by sustained training, so too the soul — by the very same law of habituation — is shaped toward gentleness, patience, and justice through the deliberate performance of their corresponding actions, until the practice becomes a settled state (malakah) and the state becomes a second nature. And this is the very meaning of the Prophet's saying — peace be upon him: «الأعمال بالنية» (deeds are by intentions) — for the intention is the beginning of the training, and the training is the path to the transformation of character, and the transformation of character is the goal of the religious law (sharīʿah) and the fruit of the prophetic mission.

chapters.title_en: On the Transformability of Moral Character and the Refutation of Those Who Deny It
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن بعض من غلبت البطالة عليه استثقل المجاهدة والرياضة والاشتغال
بتزكية النفس وتهذيب الأخلاق فلم تسمح نفسه بأن يكون ذلك لقصوره ونقصه وخبث
دخلته فزعم أن الأخلاق لا يتصور تغييرها فإن الطباع لا تتغير
واستدل فيه بأمرين
أحدهما أن الخلق هو صورة الباطن كما أن الخلق هو صورة  الظاهر فالخلقة
الظاهرة لا يقدر على تغييرها فالقصير لا يقدر أن يجعل نفسه طويلا ولا
الطويل يقدر أن يجعل نفسه قصيرا ولا القبيح يقدر على تحسين صورته فكذلك
القبح الباطن يجري هذا المجرى
والثاني أنهم قالوا حسن الخلق يقمع الشهوة والغضب وقد جربنا ذلك بطول
المجاهدة وعرفنا أن ذلك من مقتضى المزاج والطبع فإنه قط لا ينقطع عن الآدمي
فاشتغاله به تضييع زمان بغير فائدة فإن المطلوب هو قطع التفات القلب إلى
الحظوظ العاجلة وذلك محال وجوده
فنقول لو كانت الأخلاق لا تقبل التغيير لبطلت الوصايا والمواعظ
والتأديبات ولما قال رسول الله PageV03P055
صلى الله عليه وسلم حسنوا أخلاقكم (1) وكيف ينكر هذا في حق الآدمي وتغيير
خلق البهيمة ممكن إذ ينقل البازي من الاستيحاش إلى الأنس والكلب من شره
الأكل إلى التأدب والإمساك والتخلية والفرس من الجماح إلى السلاسة
والانقياد وكل ذلك تغيير للأخلاق والقول الكاشف للغطاء عن ذلك أن نقول
الموجودات منقسمة إلى ما لا مدخل للآدمي واختياره في أصله وتفصيله كالسماء
والكواكب بل أعضاء البدن داخلا وخارجا وسائر أجزاء الحيوانات وبالجملة كل
ما هو حاصل كامل وقع الفراغ من وجوده وكماله وإلى ما وجد وجودا ناقصا وجعل
فيه قوة لقبول الكمال بعد أن وجد شرطه وشرطه قد يرتبط باختيار العبد فإن
النواة ليست بتفاح ولا نخل إلا أنها خلقت خلقة يمكن أن تصير نخلة إذا انضاف
التربية إليها ولا تصير تفاحا أصلا ولا بالتربية فإذا صارت النواة متأثرة
بالاختيار حتى تقبل بعض الأحوال دون بعض فكذلك الغضب والشهوة لو أردنا
قمعهما وقهرهما بالكلية حتى لا يبقى لهما أثر لم نقدر عليه أصلا ولو أردنا
سلاستهما وقودهما بالرياضة والمجاهدة قدرنا عليه وقد أمرنا بذلك وصار ذلك
سبب نجاتنا ووصولنا إلى الله تعالى نعم الجبلات مختلفة بعضها سريعة القبول
وبعضها بطيئة القبول ولاختلافها سببان
أحدهما قوة الغريزة في أصل الجبلة وامتداد مدة الوجود فإن قوة الشهوة
والغضب والتكبر موجودة في الإنسان ولكن أصعبها أمرا وأعصاها على التغيير
قوة الشهوة فإنها أقدم  وجودا إذ الصبي في مبدإ الفطرة تخلق له الشهوة ثم
بعد سبع سنين ربما يخلق له الغضب وبعد ذلك يخلق له قوة التمييز
والسبب الثاني أن الخلق قد يتأكد بكثرة العمل بمقتضاه والطاعة له
وباعتقاد كونه حسنا ومرضيا والناس فيه على أربع مراتب
الأولى وهو الإنسان الغفل الذي لا يميز بين الحق والباطل والجميل والقبيح
بل بقي كما فطر عليه خاليا عن جميع الاعتقادات ولم تستتم شهوته أيضا باتباع
اللذات فهذا سريع القبول للعلاج جدا فلا يحتاج إلا إلى معلم ومرشد وإلى
باعث من نفسه يحمله على المجاهدة فيحسن خلقه في أقرب زمان
والثانية أن يكون قد عرف قبح القبيح ولكنه لم يتعود العمل الصالح بل زين
له سوء عمله فتعاطاه انقيادا لشهواته وإعراضا عن صواب رأيه لاستيلاء الشهوة
عليه ولكن علم تقصيره في عمله فأمره أصعب من الأول إذ قد تضاعفت الوظيفة
عليه إذ عليه قلع ما رسخ في نفسه أولا من كثرة الاعتياد للفساد والآخر أن
يغرس في نفسه صفة الاعتياد للصلاح ولكنه بالجملة محل قابل للرياضة إن انتهض
لها بجد وتشمير وحزم
والثالثة أن يعتقد في الأخلاق القبيحة أنها الواجبة المستحسنة وأنها حق
وجميل وتربى عليها فهذا يكاد تمتنع معالجته ولا يرجى صلاحه إلا على الندور
وذلك لتضاعف أسباب الضلال
والرابعة أن يكون مع نشئه على الرأي الفاسد وتربيته على العمل به يرى
الفضيلة في كثرة الشر واستهلاك النفوس ويباهي به ويظن أن ذلك يرفع قدره
وهذا هو أصعب المراتب وفي مثله قيل ومن العناء رياضة الهرم ومن التعذيب
تهذيب الذيب
والأول من هؤلاء جاهل فقط
والثاني جاهل وضال
والثالث جاهل وضال وفاسق
والرابع جاهل وضال وفاسق وشرير
وأما الخيال الآخر الذي استدلوا به وهو قولهم إن الآدمي ما دام حيا فلا
تنقطع عنه الشهوة والغضب وحب الدنيا وسائر هذه الأخلاق فهذا غلط وقع لطائفة
ظنوا أن المقصود من المجاهدة قمع هذه الصفات بالكلية ومحوها وهيهات فإن
الشهوة خلقت لفائدة وهي ضرورية في الجبلة فلو انقطعت شهوة  الطعام لهلك
الإنسان ولو انقطعت PageV03P056
شهوة الوقاع لانقطع النسل ولو انعدم الغضب بالكلية لم يدفع الإنسان عن
نفسه ما يهلكه ولهلك
ومهما بقي أصل الشهوة فيبقى لا محالة حب المال الذي يوصله إلى الشهوة حتى
يحمله ذلك على إمساك المال وليس المطلوب إماطة ذلك بالكلية بل المطلوب ردها
إلى الاعتدال الذي هو وسط بين الإفراط والتفريط والمطلوب في صفة الغضب حسن
الحمية وذلك بأن يخلو عن التهور وعن الجبن جميعا وبالجملة أن يكون في نفسه
قويا ومع قوته منقادا للعقل ولذلك قال الله تعالى أشداء على الكفار رحماء
بينهم وصفهم بالشدة وإنما تصدر الشدة عن الغضب ولو بطل الغضب لبطل الجهاد
وكيف يقصد قلع الشهوة والغضب بالكلية والأنبياء عليهم السلام لم ينفكوا عن
ذلك إذ قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما أنا بشر أغضب كما يغضب البشر (1) حديث
أنه كان يتكلم بين يديه بما يكرهه فيغضب حتى تحمر وجنتاه ولكن لا يقول إلا
حقا فكان الغضب لا يخرجه عن الحق أخرجه الشيخان من حديث عبد الله بن الزبير
في قصة شراج الحرة فقال لأن كان ابن عمتك فتلون وجه رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم ولهما من حديث أبي سعيد الخدري وكان إذا كره شيئا عرفناه في وجهه
ولهما من حديث عائشة وما انتقم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لنفسه إلا أن
تنتهك حرمة الله ولمسلم ما ينال منه شيء قط فينتقم من صاحبه الحديث (2)
حديث خير الأمور أوساطها أخرجه البيهقي في شعب الإيمان من رواية مطرف بن
عبد الله معضلا وهذا له سر وتحقيق وهو أن السعادة منوطة بسلامة القلب عن
عوارض هذا العالم قال الله تعالى إلا من أتى الله بقلب سليم والبخل من
عوارض الدنيا والتبذير أيضا من عوارض الدنيا وشرط القلب أن يكون سليما
منهما أي لا يكون ملتفتا إلى المال ولا يكون حريصا على إنفاقه ولا على
إمساكه فإن الحريص على الإنفاق مصروف القلب إلى الإنفاق كما أن الحريص على
الإمساك مصروف القلب إلى  الإمساك فكان كمال القلب أن يصفو عن الوصفين جميعا
وإذا لم يكن ذلك في الدنيا طلبنا ما هو الأشبه لعدم الوصفين وأبعد عن
الطرفين وهو الوسط فإن الفاتر لا حار ولا بارد بل هو وسط بينهما فكأنه خال
عن الوصفين فكذلك السخاء بين التبذير والتقتير والشجاعة بين الجبن التهور
والعفة بين الشره والجمود وكذلك سائر الأخلاق فكلا طرفي الأمور ذميم هذا هو
المطلوب وهو ممكن نعم يجب على الشيخ المرشد للمريد أن يقبح عنده الغضب رأسا
ويذم إمساك المال رأسا ولا يرخص له في شيء منه لأنه لو رخص له في أدنى شيء
اتخذ ذلك عذرا في استبقاء بخله وغضبه وظن أنه القدر المرخص فيه فإذا قصد
الأصل وبالغ فيه ولم يتيسر له إلا كسر PageV03P057
سورته بحيث يعود إلى الاعتدال فالصواب له أن يقصد قلع الأصل حتى يتيسر له
القدر المقصود فلا يكشف هذا السر للمريد فإنه موضع غرور الحمقى إذ يظن
بنفسه أن غضبه بحق وأن إمساكه بحق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Creation, measurement, estimation; the inherent pattern or constitution of a thing—both its outward form (khalq) and inward disposition (khuluq)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely-originated constitution of the soul; moral character as the stable form of the inner self, parallel to the physical form of the outer self
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for physical creation (khalq); metaphorical extension (majāz) for the acquired or modifiable inward disposition (khuluq), since the latter is not fixed by nature alone
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (law, idhā) and exceptive phrases (illā) to delineate the limits of human capacity versus divine ordainment, requiring careful parsing of the protasis-apodosis relationships.
chapters.translation:
Know that some of those whom idleness has overcome found the spiritual struggle (mujāhadah), discipline (riyāḍah), and occupation with the purification of the soul and the refinement of moral character too burdensome. Their souls would not permit them to acknowledge that this failure stemmed from their own deficiency, imperfection, and the corruption of their inner motives. So they claimed that moral character cannot be conceived as changeable, for natural temperaments do not undergo alteration.

They adduced two arguments for this:

**The First:** Moral character (al-khuluq) is the form of the inner self, just as physical constitution (al-khalq) is the form of the outer self. The outward physical form cannot be changed—the short man cannot make himself tall, nor the tall man make himself short, nor the ugly man improve his appearance. Likewise, they said, inner ugliness runs the same course.

**The Second:** They said that good moral character requires the suppression of appetite (shahwah) and anger (ghaḍab). But we have tested this through prolonged spiritual struggle and come to know that these are exigencies of temperament and natural constitution—they never cease from the human being entirely. Thus, occupying oneself with their suppression is a waste of time without benefit, for what is sought is the complete severance of the heart's attention from immediate gratifications, and that is impossible to achieve.

We respond: If moral character did not admit of change, then all exhortations, counsels, and disciplinary instructions would be nullified, and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) would not have said: {«حَسِّنُوا أَخْلَاقَكُمْ»} ("Improve your moral characters"). How can this be denied regarding the human being, when the transformation of the beast's character is possible? The falcon is transferred from wildness to tameness, the dog from voracious eating to discipline and restraint, the horse from recalcitrance to gentleness and submission—and all of this is a change of character.

The statement that unveils the covering from this matter is to say: Existing things are divided into two categories. First, that which admits no entry for human agency or choice in its origin or its details—such as the heavens, the stars, indeed the bodily members both internal and external, and all the parts of animals—in short, everything that has come into existence complete, with its existence and perfection already finished. Second, that which came into existence in an incomplete state, having been endowed with a capacity for receiving perfection once its condition is fulfilled—and its condition may be linked to the servant's choice. The date-pit is neither an apple nor a palm-tree, yet it was created with a constitution that can become a palm-tree if cultivation is added to it; but it can never become an apple, even with cultivation. Now, if the date-pit is thus affected by choice so as to receive some states and not others, then likewise anger and appetite—if we wished to suppress and subjugate them entirely so that no trace of them remained, we would have no power over that at all. But if we wish to render them gentle and submissive through discipline and spiritual struggle, we are able to do so. And we have been commanded to do precisely this, and it has become the cause of our salvation and our arrival at Allah, the Exalted.

Indeed, natural constitutions (jibillāt) differ—some are quick to accept, others slow. There are two causes for this difference:

**The First:** The strength of the instinct in the original constitution and the extension of the duration of existence. For the power of appetite, anger, and pride exists in the human being, but the most difficult of them in matter and the most resistant to change is the power of appetite—for it is the most ancient in existence, since the child at the beginning of his natural disposition has appetite created in him, then after seven years anger is perhaps created in him, and after that the power of discernment is created.

**The Second:** A moral trait may become firmly established through frequent action in accordance with it, obedience to it, and the belief that it is good and pleasing.

People in this regard fall into four ranks:

**The First Rank:** The heedless person who does not distinguish between truth and falsehood, or between the beautiful and the ugly. Rather, he remains as he was created, devoid of all beliefs, and his appetite has not yet been completed by the pursuit of pleasures. This one is very quick to accept treatment—he needs only a teacher and a guide, and a motivator from within himself that impels him to spiritual struggle, and his character will improve in the shortest time.

**The Second Rank:** One who has come to know the ugliness of the ugly, but has not accustomed himself to righteous action. Rather, his evil deed has been adorned for him, so he engages in it, yielding to his appetites and turning away from his sound judgment because appetite has gained mastery over him. Yet he knows his shortcoming in his deed. His matter is more difficult than the first, for the task has been doubled upon him: he must first uproot what has become entrenched in his soul through much habituation to corruption, and secondly, he must plant in himself the trait of habituation to righteousness. But in sum, he is a receptacle capable of discipline if he rises to it with earnestness, rolled-up sleeves, and resolve.

**The Third Rank:** One who believes that the ugly moral traits are the obligatory and commendable ones, that they are right and beautiful, and he has been raised upon them. This one's treatment is almost impossible, and his reform is not hoped for except rarely—this due to the multiplication of the causes of error.

**The Fourth Rank:** One who, along with his upbringing upon corrupt opinion and his cultivation upon acting by it, sees virtue in the abundance of evil and the destruction of souls, boasts of it, and imagines that this elevates his standing. This is the most difficult of the ranks. Regarding the like of him it was said: "And from affliction is the training of the decrepit, and from torment is the refinement of the wolf."

The first of these is merely ignorant.
The second is ignorant and erring.
The third is ignorant, erring, and corrupt.
The fourth is ignorant, erring, corrupt, and wicked.

As for the other illusion they adduced—their statement that as long as the human being is alive, appetite, anger, love of the world, and all these moral traits never cease from him—this is an error that befell a group who imagined that the purpose of spiritual struggle is to suppress these traits entirely and erase them. Far from it! For appetite was created for a benefit, and it is necessary in the natural constitution. If the appetite for food were cut off, the human being would perish. If the appetite for intercourse were cut off, progeny would cease. If anger were entirely annihilated, the human being would not defend himself against what would destroy him, and he would perish.

And as long as the root of appetite remains, the love of wealth that leads to appetite must necessarily remain, so that this impels him to retain wealth. What is sought is not the complete removal of these things, but rather their return to moderation (iʿtidāl)—which is the middle between excess and deficiency. What is sought in the trait of anger is good zeal (ḥusn al-ḥamiyyah)—namely, that one be free of both recklessness and cowardice. In sum, one should be strong in himself, yet with his strength submissive to reason. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: {«أَشِدَّاءُ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ»} ("Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves")—He described them with severity, and severity issues only from anger. If anger were nullified, jihad would be nullified.

How could one intend to uproot appetite and anger entirely, when the Prophets (peace be upon them) were not free of them? For he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ أَغْضَبُ كَمَا يَغْضَبُ الْبَشَرُ»} ("I am but a human being; I become angry as human beings become angry"). It is reported that something displeasing was spoken in his presence, and he became angry until his cheeks reddened—but he said nothing but the truth. Thus his anger did not remove him from the truth. This was narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) from the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr in the story of the Ḥarrah incident: "Even if he were the son of your maternal aunt"—and the face of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) changed color. And from them both, from the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: "When he disliked something, we recognized it in his face." And from them both, from the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) never took revenge for himself, except when the sanctity of Allah was violated." And Muslim has: "Nothing was ever done to him from which he took revenge upon its doer."

The ḥadīth {«خَيْرُ الْأُمُورِ أَوْسَاطُهَا»} ("The best of affairs is their middle course") was narrated by al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān from the narration of Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh as a disconnected (muʿḍal) report.

This matter has a secret and a realization: happiness is tied to the soundness of the heart from the accidents of this world. Allah, the Exalted, said: {«إِلَّا مَنْ أَتَى اللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ»} ("Except him who comes to Allah with a sound heart"). Stinginess (bukhl) is among the accidents of this world, and extravagance (tabdhīr) is also among the accidents of this world. The condition of the heart is that it be sound from both—that is, neither turned toward wealth nor eager to spend it nor eager to retain it. For the one eager to spend has his heart diverted toward spending, just as the one eager to retain has his heart diverted toward retention. Thus the perfection of the heart is that it be pure of both descriptions entirely.

And since this is not attainable in this world, we seek what is most similar to being devoid of both descriptions and farthest from both extremes—namely, the middle. For lukewarm water is neither hot nor cold, but is the middle between them, as if devoid of both descriptions. Likewise, generosity (sakhāʾ) lies between extravagance and miserliness; courage (shajāʿah) between cowardice and recklessness; chastity (ʿiffah) between voracity and frigidity; and so on for all the moral traits. For both extremes of affairs are blameworthy. This is what is sought, and it is possible.

Indeed, it is incumbent upon the guiding Shaykh to make anger appear utterly reprehensible to the disciple, and to condemn the retention of wealth absolutely, granting him no concession in any of it. For if he granted him the slightest concession, the disciple would take that as an excuse to preserve his miserliness and anger, imagining that this was the permitted measure. So when one aims at the root and strives mightily in it, and only the breaking of its force is achieved—such that he returns to moderation—then the correct course for him is to aim at uprooting the root entirely, so that the intended measure becomes attainable for him. But this secret must not be disclosed to the disciple, for it is a place of self-deception for fools—since each one imagines of himself that his anger is righteous and his retention is righteous.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Means by Which Good Character is Attained in General
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان السبب الذي به ينال حسن الخلق على الجملة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ي-ن (b-y-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clarity, separation, and making distinct; the act of rendering something evident after concealment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, bayān denotes the divine or prophetic clarification of what is ambiguous in matters of faith and practice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical separation or disclosure; metaphorical (majāz) — intellectual or moral elucidation, as here.
- Root: س-ب-ب (s-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A cord, rope, or tie; then extended to any means, cause, or connection by which something is reached.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, sabab denotes an instrumental cause (not an independent agent), subordinate to divine will.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — a physical binding; metaphorical — a causal pathway or occasion.
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beauty, goodness, and excellence in form or conduct; the opposite of ugliness (qubḥ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥusn al-khuluq (good character) is the soul’s disposition toward praiseworthy acts, aligning with the sharīʿah and reason.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — visible comeliness; metaphorical — moral and spiritual excellence.
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Inherent nature, disposition, or character; also creation and measure (taqdīr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khuluq is the inner form of the soul (al-ṣūrah al-bāṭinah), parallel to khalq as the outer form.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical creation; metaphorical — settled moral temperament.
- Root: ج-م-ل (j-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Totality, wholeness, and comprehensive gathering of parts.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAlā al-jumlah indicates a universal, non-particularized treatment — here, the general principle rather than detailed cases.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — gathering all parts; metaphorical — speaking in summary or general terms.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "على الجملة" functions as a qualifier restricting the scope of the preceding noun (السبب), indicating that the cause is being explained in its universal aspect, not in its particular applications.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the exposition of the means by which good character (ḥusn al-khuluq) is attained, in a general and comprehensive manner.

chapters.title_en: The Acquisition of Noble Character Traits through Spiritual Discipline and Habituation
chapters.arabic_text:
قد عرفت أن حسن الخلق يرجع إلى اعتدال قوة العقل وكمال الحكمة وإلى
اعتدال قوة الغضب والشهوة وكونها للعقل مطيعة وللشرع أيضا وهذا الاعتدال
يحصل على وجهين
أحدهما بجود إلهي وكمال فطري بحيث يخلق الإنسان ويولد كامل العقل حسن
الخلق قد كفي سلطان الشهوة والغضب بل خلقتا معتدلتين منقادتين للعقل والشرع
فيصير عالما بغير تعليم ومؤدبا بغير تأديب كعيسى بن مريم ويحيى بن زكريا
عليهما السلام وكذا سائر الأنبياء صلوات الله عليهم أجمعين ولا يبعد أن
يكون في الطبع والفطرة ما قد ينال بالاكتساب فرب صبي خلق صادق اللهجة سخيا
جريا وربما يخلق بخلافه فيحصل ذلك فيه بالاعتياد ومخالطة المتخلقين بهذه
الأخلاق وربما يحصل بالتعلم
والوجه الثاني اكتساب هذه الأخلاق بالمجاهدة والرياضة وأعني به حمل النفس
على الأعمال التي يقتضيها الخلق المطلوب فمن أراد مثلا أن يحصل لنفسه خلق
الجود فطريقه أن يتكلف تعاطي فعل الجواد وهو بذل المال فلا يزال يطالب  نفسه
ويواظب عليه تكلفا مجاهدا نفسه فيه حتى يصير ذلك طبعا له ويتيسر عليه فيصير
به جوادا وكذا من أراد أن يحصل لنفسه خلق التواضع وقد غلب عليه الكبر
فطريقه أن يواظب على أفعال المتواضعين مدة مديدة وهو فيها مجاهد نفسه
ومتكلف إلى أن يصير ذلك خلقا له وطبعا فيتيسر عليه
وجميع الأخلاق المحمودة شرعا تحصل بهذا الطريق وغايته أن يصير الفعل
الصادر منه لذيذا فالسخي هو الذي يستلذ بذل المال الذي يبذله دون الذي
يبذله عن كراهة والمتواضع هو الذي يستلذ التواضع ولن ترسخ الأخلاق الدينية
في النفس ما لم تتعود النفس جميع العادات الحسنة وما لم تترك جميع الأفعال
السيئة وما لم تواظب عليه مواظبة من يشتاق إلى الأفعال الجميلة ويتنعم بها
ويكره الأفعال القبيحة ويتألم بها كما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم وجعلت قرة
عيني في الصلاة (1) ومهما كانت العبادات وترك المحظورات مع كراهة واستثقال
فهو النقصان ولا ينال كمال السعادة به نعم المواظبة عليها بالمجاهدة خير
ولكن بالإضافة إلى تركها لا بالإضافة إلى فعلها عن طوع ولذلك قال الله
تعالى وإنها لكبيرة إلا على الخاشعين وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم اعبد الله في
الرضا فإن لم تستطع ففي الصبر على ما تكره خير كثير (2) ثم لا يكن في نيل
السعادة الموعودة على حسن الخلق استلذاذ الطاعة واستكراه المعصية في زمان
دون زمان بل ينبغي أن يكون ذلك على الدوام وفي جملة العمر وكلما كان العمر
أطول كانت الفضيلة ارسخ وأكمل ولذلك لما سئل صلى الله عليه وسلم عن السعادة
فقال طول العمر في طاعة الله تعالى (3) ولذلك كره الأنبياء والأولياء الموت
فإن الدنيا مزرعة الآخرة وكلما كانت العبادات أكثر بطول العمر كان الثواب
أجزل والنفس أزكى وأطهر والأخلاق أقوى وأرسخ وإنما مقصود العبادات تأثيرها
في القلب وإنما يتأكد تأثيرها بكثرة المواظبة على العبادات وغاية هذه
الأخلاق أن ينقطع عن النفس حب الدنيا ويرسخ فيها حب الله تعالى فلا يكون
PageV03P058
شيء أحب إليه من لقاء الله تعالى  عز وجل فلا يستعمل جميع ماله إلا على
الوجه الذي يوصله إليه وغضبه وشهوته من المسخرات له فلا يستعملهما إلا على
الوجه الذي يوصله إلى الله تعالى وذلك بأن يكون موزونا بميزان الشرع والعقل
ثم يكون بعد ذلك فرحا به مستلذا له ولا ينبغي أن يستبعد مصير الصلاة إلى حد
تصير هي قرة العين ومصير العبادات لذيذة فإن العادة تقتضي في النفس عجائب
أغرب من ذلك فإنا قد نرى الملوك والمنعمين في أحزان دائمة ونرى المقامر قد
يغلب عليه من الفرح واللذة بقماره وما هو فيه ما يستثقل معه فرح الناس بغير
قمار مع أن القمار ربما سلبه ماله وخرب بيته وتركه مفلسا ومع ذلك فهو يحبه
ويلتذ به وذلك لطول إلفه له وصرف نفسه إليه مدة وكذلك اللاعب بالحمام قد
يقف طول النهار في حر الشمس قائما على رجليه وهو لا يحس بألمها لفرحه
بالطيور وحركاتها وطيرانها وتحليقها في جو السماء بل نرى الفاجر العيار
يفتخر بما يلقاه من الضرب والقطع والصبر على السياط وعلى أن يتقدم به للصلب
وهو مع ذلك متبجح بنفسه وبقوته بالصبر على ذلك حتى يرى ذلك فخرا لنفسه
ويقطع الواحد منهم إربا إربا على أن يقر بما تعاطاه أو تعاطاه غيره فيصر
على الإنكار ولا يبالي بالعقوبات فرحا بما يعتقده كمالا وشجاعة ورجولية فقد
صارت أحواله مع ما فيها من النكال قرة عينه وسبب افتخاره بل لا حالة أخس
وأقبح من حال المخنث في تشبهه بالإناث في نتف الشعر ووشم الوجه ومخالطة
النساء فترى المخنث في فرح بحاله وافتخار بكماله في تخنثه يتباهى به مع
المخنثين حتى يجري بين الحجامين والكناسين التفاخر والمباهاة كما يجري بين
الملوك والعلماء فكل ذلك نتيجة العادة والمواظبة على نمط واحد على الدوام
مدة مديدة ومشاهدة ذلك في المخالطين والمعارف فإذا كانت النفس بالعادة
تستلذ الباطل وتميل إليه وإلى المقابح فكيف لا تستلذ الحق لو ردت إليه مدة
والتزمت المواظبة عليه بل ميل النفس إلى هذه الأمور الشنيعة خارج  عن الطبع
يضاهي الميل إلى أكل الطين فقد يغلب على بعض الناس ذلك بالعادة فأما ميله
إلى الحكمة وحب الله تعالى ومعرفته وعبادته فهو كالميل إلى الطعام والشراب
فإنه مقتضى طبع القلب فإنه أمر رباني وميله إلى مقتضيات الشهوة غريب من
ذاته وعارض على طبعه وإنما غذاء القلب الحكمة والمعرفة وحب الله عز وجل
ولكن انصرف عن مقتضى طبعه لمرض قد حل به كما قد يحل المرض بالمعدة فلا
تشتهي الطعام والشراب وهما سببان لحياتها فكل قلب مال إلى حب شيء سوى الله
تعالى فلا ينفك عن مرض بقدر ميله إلا إذا كان أحب ذلك الشيء لكونه معينا له
على حب الله تعالى وعلى دينه فعند ذلك لا يدل ذلك على المرض
فإذن قد عرفت بهذا قطعا أن هذه الأخلاق الجميلة يمكن اكتسابها بالرياضة
وهي تكلف الأفعال الصادرة عنها ابتداء لتصير طبعا انتهاء وهذا من عجيب
العلاقة بين القلب والجوارح أعني النفس والبدن فإن كل صفة تظهر في القلب
يفيض أثرها على الجوارح حتى لا تتحرك إلا على وفقها لا محالة وكل فعل يجري
على الجوارح فإنه قد يرتفع منه أثر إلى القلب والأمر فيه دور ويعرف ذلك
بمثال وهو أن من أراد أن يصير الحذق في الكتابة له صفة نفسية حتى يصير
كاتبا بالطبع فلا طريق له إلا أن يتعاطى بجارحة اليد ما يتعاطاه الكاتب
الحاذق ويواظب عليه مدة طويلة يحاكي الخط الحسن فإن فعل الكاتب هو الخط
الحسن فيتشبه بالكاتب تكلفا ثم لا يزال يواظب عليه حتى يصير صفة راسخة في
نفسه فيصدر منه في الآخر الخط الحسن طبعا كما كان يصدر منه في الابتداء
تكلفا فكان الخط الحسن هو الذي جعل خطه حسنا ولكن الأول بتكلف إلا أنه
ارتفع منه أثر إلى القلب ثم انخفض من القلب إلى الجارحة فصار يكتب الخط
الحسن بالطبع
PageV03P059
وكذلك من أراد أن يصير فقيه النفس فلا طريق له إلا أن يتعاطى أفعال
الفقهاء وهو التكرار للفقه حتى تنعطف منه على قلبه  صفة الفقه فيصير فقيه
النفس وكذلك من أراد أن يصير سخيا عفيف النفس حليما متواضعا فيلزمه أن
يتعاطى أفعال هؤلاء تكلفا حتى يصير ذلك طبعا له فلا علاج له إلا ذلك وكما
أن طالب فقه النفس لا ييأس من نيل هذه الرتبة بتعطيل ليلة ولا ينالها
بتكرار ليلة فكذلك طالب تزكية النفس وتكميلها وتحليتها بالأعمال الحسنة لا
ينالها بعبادة يوم ولا يحرم عنها بعصيان يوم وهو معنى قولنا أن الكبيرة
الواحدة لا توجب الشقاء المؤبد ولكن العطلة في يوم واحد تدعو إلى مثلها ثم
تتداعى قليلا قليلا حتى تأنس النفس بالكسل وتهجر التحصيل رأسا فيفوتها
فضيلة الفقه وكذلك صغائر المعاصي يجر بعضها إلى بعض حتى يفوت أصل السعادة
بهدم أصل الإيمان عند الخاتمة وكما أن تكرار ليلة لا يحس تأثيره في فقه
النفس بل يظهر فقه النفس شيئا فشيئا على التدريج مثل نمو البدن وارتفاع
القامة فكذلك الطاعة الواحدة لا يحس تأثيرها في تزكية النفس وتطهيرها في
الحال ولكن لا ينبغي أن يستهان بقليل الطاعة فإن الجملة الكثيرة منها مؤثرة
وإنما اجتمعت الجملة من الآحاد فلكل واحد منها تأثير فما من طاعة إلا ولها
أثر وإن خفي فله ثواب لا محالة فإن الثواب بإزاء الأثر وكذلك المعصية وكم
من فقيه يستهين بتعطيل يوم وليلة وهكذا على التوالي يسوف نفسه يوما فيوما
إلى أن يخرج طبعه عن قبول الفقه فكذا من يستهين صغائر المعاصي ويسوف نفسه
بالتوبة على التوالي إلى أن يختطفه الموت بغتة أو تتراكم ظلمة الذنوب على
قلبه وتتعذر عليه التوبة إذ القليل يدعو إلى الكثير فيصير القلب مقيدا
بسلاسل شهوات لا يمكن تخليصه من مخالبها وهو المعنى بانسداد باب التوبة وهو
المراد بقوله تعالى وجعلنا من بين أيديهم سدا ومن خلفهم سدا الآية ولذلك
قال رضي الله تعالى عنه إن الإيمان ليبدو في القلب نكتة بيضاء كلما ازداد
الإيمان ازداد ذلك البياض فإذا استكمل العبد الإيمان أبيض القلب كله وإن
النفاق ليبدو في القلب نكتة سوداء كلما ازداد  النفاق ازداد ذلك السواد فإذا
استكمل النفاق أسود القلب كله فإذا عرفت أن الأخلاق الحسنة تارة تكون
بالطبع والفطرة وتارة تكون باعتياد الأفعال الجميلة وتارة بمشاهدة أرباب
الفعال الجميلة ومصاحبتهم وهم قرناء الخير وإخوان الصلاح إذ الطبع يسرق من
الطبع الشر والخير جميعا فمن تظاهرت في حقه الجهات الثلاثة حتى صار ذا
فضيلة طبعا واعتيادا وتعلما فهو في غاية الفضيلة ومن كان رذلا بالطبع واتفق
له قرناء السوء فتعلم منهم وتيسرت له أسباب الشر حتى اعتادها فهو في غاية
البعد من الله عز وجل وبين الرتبتين من اختلفت فيه من هذه الجهات ولكل درجة
في القرب والبعد بحسب ما تقتضيه صورته وحالته فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره
ومن يعمل مثقال ذرة شرا يره وما ظلمهم الله ولكن كانوا أنفسهم يظلمون
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Creation, measurement, and the inherent constitution or disposition of a thing
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The inner form (ṣūrah bāṭinah) of the soul from which actions proceed naturally
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used both literally (innate disposition) and metaphorically (acquired second nature)
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional sentence structure (sharṭ/jazā') governing the "if...then" logical progression of habituation

- Root: ر-و-ض (r-w-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taming, training, and breaking in (as of a horse)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The disciplined exercise of the soul against its base inclinations
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of animal training extended metaphorically to soul-training
- Sībawayh Rule: Maṣdar construction (riyāḍah) indicating the processual nature of the action

- Root: ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Returning, repetition, and becoming accustomed
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The mechanism by which repeated acts become second nature (malakah)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal repetition transformed into metaphorical "habit" as settled disposition
- Sībawayh Rule: Verbal noun (ʿādah) with implied repetition marking the iterative aspect
chapters.translation:
You have come to know that excellence of character (ḥusn al-khuluq) reduces to the moderation of the power of intellect, the perfection of wisdom, the moderation of the powers of anger and appetite, and their being obedient to the intellect and likewise to the Sacred Law. This moderation is attained in two ways.

The first is through divine generosity and innate perfection (kamāl fiṭrī), such that a person is created and born with complete intellect and excellent character, having been spared the dominion of appetite and anger—rather, these two are created moderate and submissive to intellect and Law. Such a one becomes learned without instruction and disciplined without discipline, like Jesus son of Mary and John son of Zechariah, peace be upon them both, and likewise the rest of the prophets, may God's blessings be upon them all. Nor is it far-fetched that what is attainable through acquisition may also be present in one's natural temperament. For there may be a boy created truthful of speech, generous, and courageous; and another may be created the opposite, yet attain these traits through habituation, through mixing with those who possess such characters, and perhaps through learning.

The second way is the acquisition of these traits through striving (mujāhadah) and discipline (riyāḍah). By this I mean compelling the soul to perform the actions that the desired trait requires. For example, whoever wishes to acquire for himself the trait of generosity (jūd), his path is to undertake deliberately the act of the generous person—namely, expending wealth. He continues to demand this of himself and persists in it, straining and striving against his soul, until it becomes natural to him and easy, and thereby he becomes generous. Likewise, whoever wishes to acquire humility while pride has overcome him, his path is to persist in the acts of the humble for a long period, all the while striving against his soul and forcing himself, until that becomes his character and nature and thus easy for him.

All praiseworthy traits sanctioned by the Law are attained through this path. Its ultimate goal is that the action issuing from one becomes pleasurable. For the generous person is one who takes delight in expending wealth, not one who gives it reluctantly. The humble person is one who delights in humility. Religious traits will never take root in the soul unless the soul becomes accustomed to all good habits, abandons all evil actions, and persists in them with the persistence of one who yearns for beautiful acts and delights in them, and abhors ugly acts and suffers from them—as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And the coolness of my eye was placed in prayer" {«وجعلت قرة عيني في الصلاة»}. Whenever acts of worship and the avoidance of prohibitions are performed with aversion and burden, that is deficiency, and the perfection of felicity is not attained thereby. Indeed, persistence in them through striving is good, but only relative to abandoning them—not relative to performing them willingly. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: {«وإنها لكبيرة إلا على الخاشعين»} "And indeed it is grievous except for the humble." And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Worship God in contentment; if you cannot, then patience in what you dislike contains much good."

Then, attaining the promised felicity through excellent character should not consist in delighting in obedience and finding sin burdensome at one time but not another. Rather, this should be perpetual and throughout the whole of one's life. The longer the life, the more firmly rooted and complete the virtue. For this reason, when he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about felicity, he said: "Long life in obedience to God, exalted is He." And for this reason the prophets and saints disliked death, for this world is the tillage of the Hereafter. The more abundant the acts of worship through long life, the more ample the reward, the purer and cleaner the soul, and the stronger and firmer the traits. The very purpose of acts of worship is their effect upon the heart, and this effect is only strengthened through the frequency of persistence in worship. The ultimate end of these traits is that love of this world is severed from the soul and love of God, exalted is He, becomes firmly rooted in it, so that nothing is more beloved to one than meeting God, mighty and majestic. One then uses all one's wealth only in the way that leads to Him; one's anger and appetite are subjugated to one, used only in the way that leads to God—namely, weighed by the balance of the Sacred Law and the intellect. Thereafter one is joyful in this and delights in it.

One should not deem it far-fetched that prayer should reach the point of becoming the coolness of one's eye, and that acts of worship become pleasurable. For habit produces in the soul wonders stranger than that. We see kings and the affluent in perpetual sorrows; we see the gambler overcome by joy and delight in his gambling to such a degree that he finds the joy of others in non-gambling burdensome—even though gambling may strip him of his wealth, ruin his home, and leave him bankrupt.
