The butcher went to his place, and the cloud inclined with him. The messenger — peace be upon him — said: "You claimed you had no righteous deed. I supplicated, and you said 'Amen,' and a cloud shaded us — then it followed you. Tell me your story." So he told him. The messenger said: "Indeed, the repentant holds a station with God — may He be exalted — that no one else among people holds."

And from Aḥmad ibn Saʿīd al-ʿĀbid, from his father, he said: There was with us in Kūfah a young man devoted to worship, constant in the congregational mosque, hardly leaving it. He was handsome of face, fine of stature, and excellent in demeanor. A woman of beauty and intelligence looked upon him and became enamored with him, and this continued for a long time. One day she stood in his path as he was heading to the mosque and said to him: "O young man, hear from me some words I will speak to you, then do as you wish." He passed by without speaking to her. Then she stood in his path again as he was heading to his home and said: "O young man, hear from me some words I will speak to you." He lowered his head for a long while, then said to her: "This is a place of suspicion, and I dislike being a locus of suspicion." She said to him: "By God, I did not stand in this place out of ignorance of your affair. But God forbid that people should aspire to such from me. What drove me to meet you in such a matter myself is my knowledge that a little of this is much in people's eyes — and you, O company of worshippers, are like glass vessels: the slightest thing flaws them. The sum of what I say to you is that all my limbs are occupied with you. So God, God — be mindful of my affair and yours."

He said: The young man went to his home and wanted to pray, but he could not comprehend how to pray. So he took a sheet of paper and wrote a letter, then went out of his home — and behold, the woman was standing in her place. He threw the letter to her and returned to his home. In it was: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Know, O woman, that God — might and majesty be His — when His servant disobeys Him, He forbears; and if he returns to disobedience a second time, He conceals him; but when he dons the garments of disobedience, God — may He be exalted — becomes wrathful for His own sake with a wrath from which the heavens, the earth, the mountains, the trees, and the beasts shrink. So who can endure His wrath? If what you mentioned is false, then I remind you of a Day when the sky will be like molten lead, the mountains will become like carded wool, and the nations will kneel before the onslaught of the Mighty, the Magnificent. And I — by God — have weakened in reforming my own soul, so how [can I reform] another? And if what you mentioned is true, then I will direct you to a Physician of guidance who heals festering wounds and burning pains — that is God, Lord of the worlds. Seek Him with sincere supplication, for I am occupied from you by His saying — may He be exalted: {وأنذرهم يوم الآزفة إذ القلوب لدى الحناجر كاظمين ما للظالمين من حميم ولا شفيع يطاع يعلم خائنة الأعين وما تخفي الصدور} ("And warn them of the Day of Imminence, when hearts are at throats, choked — the wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor intercessor to be obeyed. He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal") (Q. 40:18-19). So where is the escape from this verse?"

Then she came after that by some days and stood in his path. When he saw her from afar, he wanted to return to his home so as not to see her. She said: "O young man, do not turn back. There will be no meeting after this day ever, except tomorrow before God — may He be exalted." Then she wept intensely and said: "I ask God — He who holds the keys of your heart — to ease what has become difficult of your affair." Then she followed him and said: "Bestow upon me a counsel I may carry from you, and enjoin upon me an injunction I may act upon." He said to her: "I enjoin you to guard your soul from your soul, and I remind you of His saying — may He be exalted: {وهو الذي يتوفاكم بالليل ويعلم ما جرحتم بالنهار} ("And He it is who takes you by night and knows what you have committed by day") (Q. 6:60)."

He said: She lowered her head and wept intensely — more intensely than her first weeping. Then she recovered, confined herself to her house, and took up worship. She continued thus until she died of grief (kamaḍan). The young man would remember her after her death and then weep. It was said to him: "Why do you weep, when you have despaired her of yourself?" He would say: "I slaughtered her hope at the beginning of her affair, and I made her severance a stored treasure (dhukhrah) for myself with God — may He be exalted. So I am ashamed before Him to reclaim a treasure I have stored with Him — may He be exalted."

The Book of Breaking the Two Desires is completed, by the praise of God — may He be exalted — and His generosity. It will be followed, God willing, by the Book of the Afflictions of the Tongue. And all praise belongs to God, first and last, outwardly and inwardly; and His blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the best of His creation, and upon every chosen servant among the people of the earth and the heavens; and abundant peace.

chapters.title_en: The Book of the Blights of the Tongue — Being the Fourth Book of the Quarter of the Destroyers from The Revival of the Religious Sciences
chapters.arabic_text:
### || كتاب آفات اللسان وهو الكتاب الرابع من ربع المهلكات من كتاب إحياء علوم الدين

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذي أحسن خلق الإنسان وعدله وألهمه نور الإيمان فزينه به
وجمله وعلمه البيان فقدمه به وفضله وأفاض على قلبه خزائن العلوم فأكمله ثم
أرسل عليه سترا من رحمته وأسبله ثم أمده بلسان يترجم به عما حواه القلب
وعقله ويكشف عنه ستره الذي أرسله وأطلق بالحق مقوله وأفصح بالشكر عما أولاه
وخوله
PageV03P107
من علم حصله ونطق سهله وأشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له وأن
محمدا عبده ورسوله الذي أكرمه وبجله ونبيه الذي أرسله بكتاب أنزله وأسمى
فضله وبين سبله صلى الله عليه وسلم ومن قبله ما كبر الله عبد وهلله
أما بعد فإن اللسان من نعم الله العظيمة ولطائف صنعه الغريبه فإنه صغير
جرمه عظيم طاعته وجرمه إذا لا يستبين الكفر والإيمان إلا بشهادة اللسان
وهما غاية الطاعة والعصيان ثم إنه ما من موجود أو معدوم خالق أو مخلوق
متخيل أو معلوم مظنون أو موهوم إلا واللسان يتناوله ويتعرض له بإثبات أو
نفي فإن كل ما يتناوله العلم يعرب عنه اللسان إما بحق أو باطل ولا شيء إلا
والعلم متناول له وهذه خاصية لا توجد في سائر الأعضاء فإن العين لا تصل إلى
غير الألوان والصور والآذان لا تصل إلى غير الأصوات واليد لا تصل إلى غير
الأجسام وكذا سائر الأعضاء واللسان رحب الميدان ليس له مرد ولا لمجاله
منتهى وحد له في الخير مجال رحب وله في الشر ذيل سحب فمن أطلق عذبة اللسان
وأهمله مرخى العنان سلك به الشيطان في كل ميدان  وساقه إلى شفا جرف هار إلى
أن يضطره إلى البوار ولا يكب الناس في النار على مناخرهم إلا حصائد ألسنتهم
ولا ينجو من شر اللسان إلا من قيده بلجام الشرع فلا يطلقه إلا فيما ينفعه
في الدنيا والآخرة ويكفه عن كل ما يخشى غائلته في عاجله وآجله وعلم ما يحمد
فيه إطلاق اللسان أو يذم غامض عزيز والعمل بمقتضاه على من عرفه ثقل عسير
وأعصى الأعضاء على الإنسان اللسان فإنه لا تعب في إطلاقه ولا مؤنة في
تحريكه وقد تساهل الخلق في الاحتراز عن آفاته وغوائله والحذر من مصائده
وحبائله وإنه أعظم آلة الشيطان في استغواء الإنسان ونحن بتوفيق الله وحسن
تدبيره نفصل مجامع آفات اللسان ونذكرها واحدة واحدة بحدودها وأسبابها
وغوائلها ونعرف طريق الاحتراز عنها ونورد ما ورد من الأخبار والآثار في
ذمها فنذكر أولا فضل الصمت ونردفه بذكر آفة الكلام فيما لا يعني ثم آفة
فضول الكلام ثم آفة الخوض في الباطل ثم آفة المراء والجدال ثم آفة الخصومة
ثم آفة التقعر في الكلام بالتشدق وتكلف السجع والفصاحة والتصنع فيه وغير
ذلك مما جرت به عادة المتفاصحين المدعين للخطابة ثم آفة الفحش والسب وبذاءة
اللسان ثم آفة اللعن إما لحيوان أو جماد أو إنسان ثم آفة الغناء بالشعر وقد
ذكرنا في كتاب السماع ما يحرم من الغناء وما يحل فلا نعيده ثم آفة المزاح
ثم آفة السخرية والاستهزاء ثم آفة إفشاء السر ثم آفة الوعد الكاذب ثم آفة
الكذب في القول واليمين ثم بيان التعاريض في الكذب ثم آفة الغيبة ثم آفة
النميمة ثم آفة ذي اللسانين الذي يتردد بين المتعاديين فيكلم كل واحد بكلام
يوافقه ثم آفة المدح ثم آفة الغفلة عن دقائق الخطأ في فحوى الكلام لا سيما
فيما يتعلق بالله وصفاته ويرتبط بأصول الدين ثم آفة سؤال العوام عن صفات
الله عز وجل وعن الحروف أهي قديمة أو محدثة وهي آخر الآفات وما يتعلق بذلك
وجملتها عشرون آفة ونسأل الله حسن التوفيق بمنه وكرمه

### ||| بيان  عظيم خطر اللسان وفضيلة الصمت
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-س-ن (l-s-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The physical organ of speech; the tongue; also used for language and dialect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The instrument by which the heart's knowledge is expressed; a trust (amānah) that translates inward realities into outward testimony.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the bodily member; metaphorical for eloquent speech or a messenger's tongue (lisān al-ḥāl).
- Root: ص-م-ت (ṣ-m-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Silence; refraining from speech; also the stillness of a camel's bell (i.e., cessation of sound).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A praiseworthy state of restraint, distinct from ʿiyy (inability to speak) — it is voluntary and virtuous.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for silence; metaphorical for the heart's stillness from vain thoughts.
- Root: غ-و-ل (gh-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cause destruction; a calamity that befalls unexpectedly; the ghūl of the desert that misleads travelers.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ruinous consequence of an action, especially of the tongue's misuse.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for sudden destruction; metaphorical for the hidden traps of speech.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Sabab (Coordination on the Cause) — When the author coordinates "small in its body, great in its obedience and its crime," the predicate applies to both, indicating that the tongue's physical smallness contrasts with its immense moral weight.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, who perfected the creation of man and made him just, and inspired him with the light of faith, adorning him thereby and beautifying him; and taught him eloquence, thus advancing him and preferring him; and poured forth upon his heart the treasuries of the sciences, completing him thereby; then cast over him a veil of His mercy and let it down; then supplied him with a tongue by which he translates what his heart and intellect contain, and uncovers the veil He had cast over it; and He loosed his utterance with truth, and made him fluent in gratitude for what He bestowed and granted him — from knowledge he acquired and speech he made easy. And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, whom He honored and magnified, and His Prophet whom He sent with a Book He revealed, exalting its merit and clarifying its paths — may God's blessings and peace be upon him and upon those before him, as long as any servant magnifies God and declares His oneness.

To proceed: The tongue is among the great blessings of God and the wondrous subtleties of His craftsmanship. For it is small in its body, yet immense in its obedience and its crime — since unbelief and faith are not made manifest except through the tongue's testimony, and these two are the utmost of obedience and disobedience. Moreover, there is no existent or non-existent, no creator or created, no imagined or known, no presumed or fancied thing, except that the tongue reaches it and engages with it by affirmation or denial. For everything that knowledge encompasses, the tongue expresses — either truthfully or falsely — and there is nothing but that knowledge encompasses it. This is a property found in no other limb: the eye reaches only colors and forms; the ear reaches only sounds; the hand reaches only bodies; and likewise the rest of the limbs. But the tongue has a spacious field with no barrier, and its domain has no limit. In good it has a wide expanse, and in evil it has a trailing train. Whoever unleashes the rein of his tongue and lets it loose with slackened bridle — Satan will lead him through every field and drive him to the brink of a crumbling precipice, until he forces him to ruin. For nothing casts people into the Fire upon their nostrils more than the harvests of their tongues. And none is saved from the evil of the tongue except one who bridles it with the rein of the Sacred Law, releasing it only in what benefits him in this world and the next, and restraining it from everything whose consequence he fears in his immediate and future state. And knowing where the tongue's release is praiseworthy or blameworthy is a subtle and precious matter, and acting upon it, for one who knows it, is a heavy and difficult burden. The most rebellious of limbs against man is the tongue: for there is no toil in releasing it, no cost in moving it. And mankind has been negligent in guarding against its blights and calamities, and in fearing its snares and traps. Yet it is the greatest instrument of Satan in leading man astray.

Now, with God's success and good direction, we shall detail the comprehensive categories of the tongue's blights, mentioning them one by one with their definitions, causes, and ruinous consequences; and we shall make known the way of guarding against them; and we shall cite what has come down of reports and traditions condemning them. So we shall first mention the virtue of silence, then follow it with the blight of speaking about what does not concern one; then the blight of excessive speech; then the blight of plunging into falsehood; then the blight of disputation and argumentation; then the blight of quarrelsomeness; then the blight of affectation in speech through over-elaboration, artificial rhyming prose, and pretentious eloquence and mannerism — and other such habits of those who parade their rhetoric and claim oratory; then the blight of obscenity, insult, and foulness of tongue; then the blight of cursing — whether of an animal, an inanimate object, or a person; then the blight of singing poetry — and we have already mentioned in the Book of Listening what is forbidden of singing and what is permissible, so we shall not repeat it; then the blight of jesting; then the blight of mockery and ridicule; then the blight of divulging secrets; then the blight of false promises; then the blight of lying in speech and in oaths; then the exposition of equivocation (taʿrīḍ) in lying; then the blight of backbiting (ghībah); then the blight of slander (namīmah); then the blight of the double-tongued one who oscillates between two enemies, speaking to each with words that please him; then the blight of praise; then the blight of heedlessness regarding subtle errors in the purport of speech — especially concerning God and His attributes, and what relates to the principles of religion; then the blight of the common folk asking about God's attributes, and about the letters — whether they are eternal or originated — and this is the last of the blights and what pertains to it. Their total is twenty blights. And we ask God for good success, by His grace and generosity.

chapters.title_en: The Peril of the Tongue and the Virtue of Silence
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن خطر اللسان عظيم ولا نجاة من خطره إلا بالصمت فلذلك مدح الشرع
الصمت وحث عليه فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من صمت نجا (1) وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم الصمت حكم وقليل فاعله (2) بلفظ حكم بدل حكمة وقال غلط فيه عثمان بن
سعد والصحيح رواية ثابت قال والصحيح عن أنس أن لقمان قال ورواه كذلك هو
وابن حبان في كتاب روضة العقلاء بسند صحيح إلى أنس أي حكمة وحزم وروي
PageV03P108
عبد الله بن سفيان عن أبيه قال قلت يا رسول الله أخبرني عن الإسلام بأمر
لا أسأل عنه أحدا بعدك قال قل آمنت بالله ثم استقم قال قلت فما أتقي فأوما
بيده إلى لسانه (1) وقال عقبة بن عامر قلت يا رسول الله ما النجاة قال أمسك
عليك لسانك وليسعك بيتك وابك على خطيئتك (2) وقال سهل بن سعد الساعدي
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من يتكفل لي بما بين لحييه ورجليه
أتكفل له بالجنة (3) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من وقي شر قبقبه وذبذبه
ولقلقه فقد وقي الشر كله (4) القبقب هو البطن والذبذب الفرج واللقلق اللسان
فهذه الشهوات الثلاث بها يهلك أكثر الخلق ولذلك اشتغلنا بذكر آفات اللسان
لما فرغنا من ذكر آفة الشهوتين البطن والفرج وقد سئل رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم عن أكثر ما يدخل الناسالجنة فقال تقوى الله وحسن الخلق وسئل عن
أكثر ما يدخل النار فقال الأجوفان الفم والفرج (5) فيحتمل أن يكون المراد
بالفم آفات اللسان لأنه محله ويحتمل أن يكون المراد به البطن لأنه منفذه
فقد قال معاذ بن جبل قلت يا رسول الله أنؤاخذ بما نقول فقال ثكلتك أمك يا
ابن جبل وهل يكب الناس في النار على مناخرهم إلا حصائد ألسنتهم (6) حديث
عبد الله الثقفي قلت يا رسول الله حدثني بأمر أعتصم به الحديث رواه النسائي
قال ابن عساكر وهو خطأ والصواب سفيان بن عبد الله الثقفي كما رواه الترمذي
وصححه ابن ماجه وقد تقدم  قبل هذا بخمسة أحاديث (7) حديث أن معاذا قال يا
رسول الله أي الأعمال أفضل فأخرج لسانه ثم وضع يده عليه أخرجه الطبراني
وابن أبي الدنيا في الصمت قال أصبعه مكان يده (8) حديث أنس لا يستقيم إيمان
عبد حتى يستقيم قلبه ولا يستقيم قلبه حتى يستقيم لسانه الحديث أخرجه ابن
أبي الدنيا في الصمت والخرائطي في مكارم الأخلاق بسند فيه ضعف (9) حديث من
سره أن يسلم فليلزم الصمت أخرجه ابن أبي الدنيا في الصمت وأبو الشيخ في
فضائل الأعمال والبيهقي في الشعب من حديث أنس بإسناد ضعيف (10) حديث إذا
أصبح ابن آدم أصبحت الأعضاء كلها تذكر اللسان الحديث أخرجه الترمذي من حديث
أبي سعيد الخدري رفعه ووقع في الإحياء عن سعيد بن جبير مرفوعا وإنما هو عن
سعيد بن جبير عن أبي سعيد رفعه ورواه الترمذي موقوفا على عمار بن زيد وقال
هذا أصح (11) حديث إن عمر اطلع على أبي بكر وهو يمد لسانه فقال ما تصنع يا
خليفة رسول الله قال إن هذا أوردني الموارد أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم قال ليس شيء من الجسد إلا يشكو إلى الله عز وجل اللسان على حدته أخرجه
ابن أبي الدنيا في الصمت وأبو يعلى في مسنده والدارقطني في العلل والبيهقي
في الشعب من رواية أسلم مولى عمر وقال الدارقطني إن المرفوع وهم على
الدراوردي قال وروي هذا الحديث عن قيس بن أبي حازم عن أبي بكر ولا علة له
// وعن ابن مسعود PageV03P109
أنه كان على الصفا يلبي ويقول يا لسان قل خيرا تغنم واسكت عن شر تسلم من
قبل أن تندم فقيل له يا أبا عبد الرحمن أهذا شيء تقوله أو شيء سمعته فقال
لا بل سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول إن أكثر خطايا ابن آدم في
لسانه (1) وقال ابن عمر قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من كف لسانه ستر
الله عورته ومن ملك غضبه وقاه الله عذابه ومن اعتذر إلى الله قبل الله عذره
(2) وروي أن معاذ بن جبل قال يا رسول الله أوصني قال اعبد الله كأنك تراه
وعد نفسك في الموتى وإن شئت أنبأتك بما هو أملك لك من هذا كله وأشار بيده
إلى لسانه (3) وعن صفوان بن سليم قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلا
أخبركم بأيسر العبادة وأهونها على البدن الصمت وحسن الخلق (4) حديث أبي
هريرة من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليقل خيرا أو ليسكت متفق عليه (5)
حديث الحسن ذكر لنا أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال رحم الله عبدا
تكلم فغنم أو سكت فسلم أخرجه ابن أبي الدنيا في الصمت والبيهقي في الشعب من
حديث أنس بسند فيه ضعف فإنه من رواية إسماعيل بن عياش عن الحجازيين وقيل
لعيسى عليه السلام دلنا على عمل ندخل به الجنة قال لا تنطقوا أبدا قالوا لا
نستطيع ذلك فقال فلا تنطقوا إلا بخير وقال سليمان بن داود عليهما السلام إن
كان الكلام من فضة فالسكوت من ذهب وعن البراء بن عازب قال جاء أعرابي إلى
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال دلني على عمل يدخلني الجنة قال أطعم
الجائع واسق الظمآن وأمر بالمعروف وانه عن المنكر فإن لم تطق فكف لسانك إلا
من خير (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم اخزن لسانك إلا من خير فإنك بذلك تغلب الشيطان
(7) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله عند لسان كل قائل فليتق الله امرؤ علم
ما يقول وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا رأيتم المؤمن صموتا وقورا فادنوا منه
فإنه يلقن الحكمة (8)
وقال ابن مسعود قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الناس ثلاثة غانم وسالم
وشاحب فالغانم الذي يذكر الله تعالى والسالم الساكت والشاحب الذي يخوض في
الباطل (9) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن لسان المؤمن وراء قلبه فإذا أراد أن
يتكلم بشيء تدبره بقلبه ثم أمضاه بلسانه وإن لسان المنافق أمام قلبه فإذا
هم بشيء أمضاه بلسانه ولم يتدبره بقلبه (10) وقال عيسى عليه السلام العبادة
عشرة  أجزاء تسعة منها في الصمت PageV03P110
وجزء في الفرار من الناس وقال نبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم من كثر كلامه كثر
سقطه ومن كثر سقطه كثرت ذنوبه ومن كثرت ذنوبه كانت النار أولى به (1)
الآثار كان أبو بكر الصديق رضي الله عنه يضع حصاة في فيه يمنع بها نفسه
عن الكلام وكان يشير إلى لسانه ويقول هذا الذي أوردني الموارد وقال عبد
الله بن مسعود والله الذي لا إله إلا هو ما شيء أحوج إلى طول سجن من لسان
وقال طاوس لساني سبع إن أرسلته أكلني وقال وهب بن منبه في حكمة آل داود حق
على العاقل أن يكون عارفا بزمانه حافظا للسانه مقبلا على شأنه وقال الحسن
ما عقل دينه من لم يحفظ لسانه وقال الأوزاعي كتب إلينا عمر بن عبد العزيز
رحمه الله أما بعد فإن من أكثر ذكر الموت رضي من الدنيا باليسير ومن عد
كلامه من عمله قل كلامه إلا فيما يعنيه وقال بعضهم الصمت يجمع للرجل
فضيلتين السلامة في دينه والفهم عن صاحبه وقال محمد بن واسع لمالك بن دينار
يا أبا يحيى حفظ اللسان أشد على الناس من حفظ الدينار والدرهم وقال يونس بن
عبيد ما من الناس أحد يكون منه لسانه على بال إلا رأيت صلاح ذلك في سائر
عمله وقال الحسن تكلم قوم عند معاوية رحمه الله والأحنف بن قيس ساكت فقال
له مالك يا أبا بحر لا تتكلم فقال له أخشى الله إن كذبت وأخشاك إن صدقت
وقال أبو بكر بن عياش اجتمع أربعة ملوك ملك الهند وملك الصين وكسرى وقيصر
فقال أحدهم أنا أندم على ما قلت ولا أندم على ما لم أقل وقال الآخر إني إذا
تكلمت بكلمة ملكتني ولم أملكها وإذا لم أتكلم بها ملكتها ولم تملكني وقال
الثالث عجبت للمتكلم إن رجعت عليه كلمته ضرته وإن لم ترجع لم تنفعه وقال
الرابع أنا على رد ما لم أقل أقدر مني على رد ما قلت وقيل أقام المنصور بن
المعتز لم يتكلم بكلمة بعد العشاء الآخرة أربعين سنة وقيل ما تكلم الربيع
بن خيثم بكلام الدنيا عشرين سنة وكان إذا أصبح وضع دواة وقرطاسا وقلما فكل
ما تكلم به كتبه ثم يحاسب نفسه عند المساء
فإن قلت فهذا الفضل الكبير للصمت ما سببه فاعلم أن سببه كثرة آفات اللسان
من الخطأ والكذب والغيبة والنميمة والرياء والنفاق والفحش والمراء وتزكية
النفس والخوض في الباطل والخصومة والفضول والتحريف والزيادة والنقصان
وإيذاء الخلق وهتك العورات
فهذه آفات كثيرة وهي سيانة إلى اللسان لا تثقل عليه ولها حلاوة في القلب
وعليها بواعث من الطبع ومن الشيطان والخائض فيها قلما يقدر أن يمسك اللسان
فيطلقه بما يحب ويكفه عما لا يحب فإن ذلك من غوامض العلم كما سيأتي تفصيله
ففي الخوض خطر وفي الصمت سلامة فلذلك عظمت فضيلته هذا مع ما فيه من جمع
الهم ودوام الوقار والفراغ للفكر والذكر والعبادة والسلامة من تبعات القول
في الدنيا ومن حسابه في الآخرة فقد قال الله تعالى {ما يلفظ من قول إلا
لديه رقيب عتيد}
ويدلك على فضل لزوم الصمت أمر وهو أن الكلام أربعة أقسام قسم هو ضرر محض
وقسم هو نفع محض وقسم فيه ضرر ومنفعة وقسم ليس فيه ضرر ولا منفعة
أما الذي هو ضرر محض فلا بد من السكوت عنه وكذلك ما فيه ضرر ومنفعة لا
تفي بالضرر
وأما ما لا منفعة فيه ولا ضرر فهو فضول والاشتغال به تضييع زمان وهو عين
الخسران فلا يبقى إلا القسم الرابع فقد سقط ثلاثة أرباع الكلام وبقي ربع
وهذا الربع فيه خطر إذ يمتزج بما فيه إثم من دقائق الرياء والتصنع والغيبة
وتزكية النفس وفضول الكلام امتزاجا يخفى دركه فيكون الإنسان به مخاطرا ومن
عرف دقائق PageV03P111
آفات اللسان على ما سنذكره علم قطعا أن ما ذكره صلى الله عليه وسلم هو
فصل الخطاب حيث قال من صمت نجا (1)
فلقد أوتى والله جواهر الحكم قطعا وجوامع الكلم (2) ولا يعرف ما تحت آحاد
كلماته من بحار  المعاني إلا خواص العلماء وفيما سنذكره من الآفات وعسر
الاحتراز عنها ما يعرفك حقيقة ذلك إن شاء الله تعالى
ونحن الآن نعد آفات اللسان ونبتديء بأخفها ونترقى إلى الأغلظ قليلا ونؤخر
الكلام في الغيبة والنميمة والكذب فإن النظر فيها أطول وهي عشرون آفة فاعلم
ذلك ترشد بعون الله تعالى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ ط ر (kha-ṭa-ra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be in peril, to hover between safety and destruction; a dangerous precipice
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The state of exposure to harm where one's fate hangs in balance—applied here to the tongue as a locus of moral hazard
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical danger; metaphorically extended to spiritual peril (khaṭar al-lisān) as a recognized rhetorical transference
- Root: ص م ت (ṣa-ma-ta)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Silence, refraining from speech; the cessation of utterance
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The disciplined withholding of speech as an act of worship and self-restraint (imsāk)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal silence versus the metaphorical "silence of the heart" from vain thoughts—here used literally
- Root: ن ج و (n-j-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deliverance, escape from harm
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Salvation from divine punishment through protective action
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal rescue; in religious discourse, eschatological deliverance
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Propositions (al-sharṭ wa-l-jazāʾ) — The prophetic formula "man ṣamata najā" (whoever is silent is saved) employs a conditional construction where the protasis (silence) is the sufficient condition for the apodosis (salvation), a structure used throughout this section to establish causal religious principles.
chapters.translation:
Know that the peril of the tongue is immense, and there is no deliverance from its peril except through silence. For this reason, the Sacred Law praised silence and urged it. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «من صمت نجا» ("Whoever remains silent is saved"). And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «الصمت حكم وقليل فاعله» ("Silence is wisdom, and few are its practitioners")—with the word "ḥukm" (judgment) instead of "ḥikmah" (wisdom). It was said that ʿUthmān ibn Saʿd erred in this, and the correct version is the narration of Thābit. It is also said that the correct view, according to Anas, is that Luqmān said this—and it was likewise narrated by him and by Ibn Ḥibbān in the book Rawḍat al-ʿUqalāʾ with a sound chain to Anas—meaning "wisdom and resoluteness."

It was narrated that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sufyān reported from his father, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Islam with a matter after which I will not ask anyone else.' He said: 'Say: I believe in Allah, then remain steadfast.' I said: 'Then what should I guard against?' He pointed with his hand to his tongue."

And ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, what is deliverance?' He said: 'Restrain your tongue, let your house suffice you, and weep over your sins.'"

And Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Whoever guarantees for me what is between his jaws and his legs, I guarantee Paradise for him.'"

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «من وقي شر قبقبه وذبذبه ولقلقه فقد وقي الشر كله» ("Whoever is protected from the evil of his qabqab, his dhabdhab, and his laqlaq has been protected from all evil"). The qabqab is the belly, the dhabdhab is the private parts, and the laqlaq is the tongue. These are the three appetites through which most of creation perish. For this reason, we have occupied ourselves with mentioning the afflictions of the tongue after finishing the mention of the affliction of the two appetites—the belly and the private parts.

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked about what most causes people to enter Paradise, and he said: "Fear of Allah and good character." And he was asked about what most causes people to enter the Fire, and he said: "The two hollows: the mouth and the private parts." It is possible that by "the mouth" is meant the afflictions of the tongue, because it is its locus; and it is possible that by it is meant the belly, because it is its passage.

Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we say?' He said: 'May your mother lose you, O son of Jabal! Is anything that topples people into the Fire on their faces—or on their nostrils—other than the harvests of their tongues?'"

Regarding the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me a matter by which I may hold fast'"—al-Nasāʾī narrated it. Ibn ʿAsākir said it is an error, and the correct version is Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī, as al-Tirmidhī narrated it and Ibn Mājah authenticated it. It has preceded this by five ḥadīths.

Regarding the ḥadīth that Muʿādh said: "O Messenger of Allah, which deeds are best?"—he brought out his tongue, then placed his hand upon it. Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt narrated it; he said: "His finger, instead of his hand."

Regarding the ḥadīth of Anas: «لا يستقيم إيمان عبد حتى يستقيم قلبه ولا يستقيم قلبه حتى يستقيم لسانه» ("A servant's faith is not upright until his heart is upright, and his heart is not upright until his tongue is upright")—Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt and al-Kharāʾiṭī in Makārim al-Akhlāq narrated it with a chain containing weakness.

Regarding the ḥadīth: «من سره أن يسلم فليلزم الصمت» ("Whoever is pleased to be safe, let him adhere to silence")—Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt, Abū al-Shaykh in Faḍāʾil al-Aʿmāl, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab narrated it from the ḥadīth of Anas with a weak chain.

Regarding the ḥadīth: «إذا أصبح ابن آدم أصبحت الأعضاء كلها تذكر اللسان» ("When the son of Adam wakes in the morning, all his limbs admonish the tongue")—al-Tirmidhī narrated it from the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, raised to the Prophet. In the Iḥyāʾ it appears from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, raised to the Prophet, but it is only from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Abū Saʿīd, raised. Al-Tirmidhī narrated it as stopped (mawqūf) on ʿAmmār ibn Zayd and said: "This is more correct."

Regarding the ḥadīth that ʿUmar looked upon Abū Bakr while he was stretching out his tongue and said: "What are you doing, O Successor of the Messenger of Allah?" He said: "This has led me into perilous places. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'There is nothing of the body except that it complains to Allah Almighty of the tongue, on its own account.'" Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt, Abū Yaʿlā in his Musnad, al-Dāraquṭnī in al-ʿIlal, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab narrated it from the narration of Aslam, the freed slave of ʿUmar. Al-Dāraquṭnī said that the raising of it to the Prophet is an error on the part of al-Darāwardī. He said: "This ḥadīth was also narrated from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim from Abū Bakr, and there is no defect in it."

And from Ibn Masʿūd, that he was on al-Ṣafā saying the talbiyah and saying: "O tongue, speak good and you will profit, or be silent about evil and you will be safe, before you regret." It was said to him: "O Abā ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, is this something you say yourself, or something you heard?" He said: "No, rather I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) say: 'Most of the sins of the son of Adam are in his tongue.'"

And Ibn ʿUmar said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Whoever restrains his tongue, Allah conceals his shame; whoever masters his anger, Allah protects him from His punishment; and whoever apologizes to Allah, Allah accepts his excuse.'"

It is narrated that Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: "O Messenger of Allah, advise me." He said: "Worship Allah as though you see Him, and count yourself among the dead. And if you wish, I will inform you of what is more controlling of you than all of this"—and he pointed with his hand to his tongue.

From Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'Shall I not inform you of the easiest of worship and the lightest upon the body? Silence and good character.'"

Regarding the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah: «من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليقل خيرا أو ليسكت» ("Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent")—agreed upon.

Regarding the ḥadīth of al-Ḥasan: "It was related to us that the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'May Allah have mercy on a servant who spoke and profited, or was silent and was safe.'" Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab narrated it from the ḥadīth of Anas with a chain containing weakness, for it is from the narration of Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh from the Ḥijāzīs.

It was said to Jesus (peace be upon him): "Guide us to a deed by which we may enter Paradise." He said: "Do not speak at all." They said: "We cannot do that." He said: "Then do not speak except good."

And Solomon son of David (peace be upon them both) said: "If speech is of silver, then silence is of gold."

From al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) and said: 'Guide me to a deed that will admit me to Paradise.' He said: 'Feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, enjoin good and forbid evil; and if you cannot, then restrain your tongue except from good.'"

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «اخزن لسانك إلا من خير فإنك بذلك تغلب الشيطان» ("Store up your tongue except from good, for by that you will overcome Satan").

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «إن الله عند لسان كل قائل فليتق الله امرؤ علم ما يقول» ("Indeed, Allah is at the tongue of every speaker; so let a man who knows what he says fear Allah").

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «إذا رأيتم المؤمن صموتا وقورا فادنوا منه فإنه يلقن الحكمة» ("When you see a believer silent and dignified, draw near to him, for he is taught wisdom").

And Ibn Masʿūd said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'People are three: a gainer, a safe one, and a ruined one. The gainer is he who remembers Allah Almighty; the safe one is he who is silent; and the ruined one is he who plunges into falsehood.'"

And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «إن لسان المؤمن وراء قلبه فإذا أراد أن يتكلم بشيء تدبره بقلبه ثم أمضاه بلسانه وإن لسان المنافق أمام قلبه فإذا هم بشيء أمضاه بلسانه ولم يتدبره بقلبه» ("The tongue of the believer is behind his heart: when he wishes to speak of something, he deliberates it with his heart, then passes it with his tongue. The tongue of the hypocrite is before his heart: when he intends something, he passes it with his tongue without deliberating it with his heart").

And Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "Worship is ten parts; nine of them are in silence, and one part is in fleeing from people."

And our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «من كثر كلامه كثر سقطه ومن كثر سقطه كثرت ذنوبه ومن كثرت ذنوبه كانت النار أولى به» ("Whoever's speech multiplies, his errors multiply; whoever's errors multiply, his sins multiply; and whoever's sins multiply, the Fire is more deserving of him").

THE TRADITIONS (ĀTHĀR): Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) used to place a pebble in his mouth to restrain himself from speech, and he would point to his tongue and say: "This is what has led me into perilous places."

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "By Allah, there is no god but Him—nothing is more in need of prolonged imprisonment than the tongue."

Ṭāwūs said: "My tongue is a beast of prey; if I release it, it devours me."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said, in the wisdom of the family of David: "It is incumbent upon the intelligent person to be cognizant of his time, to guard his tongue, and to attend to his own affairs."

Al-Ḥasan said: "He has not understood his religion who does not guard his tongue."

Al-Awzāʿī said: "ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote to us: 'To proceed: whoever frequently remembers death is content with little of this world, and whoever counts his speech as part of his deeds speaks little except in what concerns him.'"

Some of them said: "Silence gathers for a man two virtues: safety in his religion and understanding from his companion."

Muhammad ibn Wāsiʿ said to Mālik ibn Dīnār: "O Abā Yaḥyā, guarding the tongue is harder upon people than guarding the dīnār and the dirham."

Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd said: "There is no one among people whose tongue is on his mind except that I see rectitude in the rest of his deeds."

Al-Ḥasan said: "People spoke before Muʿāwiyah (may Allah have mercy on him) while al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays was silent. He said to him: 'What is the matter with you, O Abā Baḥr, that you do not speak?' He said to him: 'I fear Allah if I lie, and I fear you if I tell the truth.'"

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said: "Four kings gathered: the king of India, the king of China, Kisrā, and Qayṣar. One of them said: 'I regret what I have said, and I do not regret what I have not said.' Another said: 'When I speak a word, it masters me and I do not master it; and when I do not speak it, I master it and it does not master me.' The third said: 'I marvel at the speaker: if his word returns upon him, it harms him; and if it does not return, it does not benefit him.' The fourth said: 'I am more able to retract what I have not said than to retract what I have said.'"

It was said that al-Mansūr ibn al-Muʿtazz refrained from speaking a single word after the night prayer for forty years. And it was said that al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym did not speak a word of worldly matters for twenty years. When morning came, he would place an inkwell, a sheet, and a pen; whatever he spoke, he would write it down, then hold himself to account in the evening.

If you say: "This great virtue of silence—what is its cause?" Know that its cause is the multitude of the afflictions of the tongue: error, lying, backbiting, slander, hypocrisy, dissimulation, obscenity, disputation, self-justification, plunging into falsehood, quarrelsomeness, excess, distortion, addition, and omission, harming creation, and tearing open shameful secrets.

These are many afflictions, and they are attached to the tongue, weighing not heavily upon it; they have sweetness in the heart, and upon them there are prompters from nature and from Satan. The one who plunges into them can rarely restrain his tongue—to release it upon what he loves and to hold it back from what he dislikes. For that is among the subtleties of knowledge, as will be detailed hereafter. In plunging there is peril, and in silence there is safety. Therefore its virtue is magnified. This is in addition to what it contains of gathering one's concern, constancy of dignity, leisure for reflection, remembrance, and worship, and safety from the consequences of speech in this world and from its reckoning in the Hereafter. For Allah Almighty has said: {ما يلفظ من قول إلا لديه رقيب عتيد} ("He utters not a word but that there is with him a watcher, ready").

And what indicates to you the virtue of adhering to silence is a matter: speech is four divisions. A division that is pure harm; a division that is pure benefit; a division in which there is harm and benefit; and a division in which there is neither harm nor benefit.

As for that which is pure harm, silence about it is obligatory. Likewise, that in which there is harm and benefit that does not outweigh the harm.

As for that in which there is no benefit and no harm, it is excess, and occupying oneself with it is wasting time, which is sheer loss. Nothing remains except the fourth division. Thus three-quarters of speech have fallen away, and one quarter remains. And this quarter contains peril, for it becomes mixed with what involves sin—from the subtleties of hypocrisy, affectation, backbiting, self-justification, and excess of speech—a mixing whose perception is hidden. So a person is thereby placed in peril. And whoever knows the subtleties of the afflictions of the tongue, as we shall mention, knows with certainty that what the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) mentioned is the decisive word, where he said: «من صمت نجا» ("Whoever remains silent is saved").

By Allah, he was surely given the jewels of wisdom and the comprehensive words. And none knows what lies beneath the individual words of his speech of the seas of meanings except the elite of the scholars. And in what we shall mention of the afflictions and the difficulty of guarding against them, there is that which will make you know the reality of this, if Allah Almighty wills.

We now enumerate the afflictions of the tongue. We begin with the lightest of them and ascend gradually to the gravest. We defer the discussion of backbiting, slander, and lying, for the examination of them is longer. They are twenty afflictions. Know this, and you will be guided by the help of Allah Almighty.

chapters.title_en: The First Affliction: Speaking About What Does Not Concern You
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| الآفة الأولى الكلام فيما لا يعنيك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ل-م (k-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes wounding, cutting, or affecting through speech; kalām is that which leaves an impression on the hearer, whether beneficial or harmful.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Kalām in theological usage refers to discourse that conveys meaning (maʿnā) through articulated sound; here it is the act of speech as a moral and spiritual liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — articulated utterance; metaphorical (majāz) — engaging in matters that are extraneous to one’s religious and worldly welfare.
- Root: ع-ن-ي (ʿ-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ʿInāyah means care, concern, or that which occupies one’s attention; mā yaʿnīka is that which pertains to you, your duty, or your benefit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ethical-religious context, it denotes what is incumbent upon the servant (ʿabd) by virtue of divine command and personal accountability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — that which concerns you directly; metaphorical — that which yields spiritual profit or safeguards against harm in the Hereafter.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal sentence with definite subject (al-āfah al-ūlā) followed by a verbal clause (al-kalām fī...), where the genitive construction (mā lā yaʿnīka) functions as a restrictive qualifier — the negation (lā) is absolute, not temporal, indicating a permanent prohibition of engaging in irrelevant speech.
chapters.translation:
### The First Affliction: Speaking About What Does Not Concern You

I say — may Allah guide you and us to the path of truth and grant us success in attaining the felicity of the Hereafter — know that the tongue is among the greatest of Allah’s blessings upon His servants, yet it is also among the most perilous of their limbs. For speech is the instrument by which a servant either ascends to the highest ranks of righteousness or plunges into the deepest pits of ruin. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: {«مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ»} — "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent." And he, peace be upon him, also said: {«طُوبَى لِمَنْ أَمْسَكَ الْفَضْلَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ»} — "Blessed is he who restrains the excess of his tongue."

Know that the root of all afflictions of the tongue is the habit of speaking about that which does not concern one — that is, every utterance that is neither beneficial for one’s religion nor necessary for one’s worldly affairs. For when a servant habituates himself to such speech, his tongue becomes unbridled, and he slips from irrelevant talk into forbidden talk, from forbidden talk into slander and backbiting, and from slander into falsehood and calumny. Thus, the first gate of the tongue’s destruction is this very affliction: speaking about what does not concern you.

And the evidence for the prohibition of this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: {«مِنْ حُسْنِ إِسْلَامِ الْمَرْءِ تَرْكُهُ مَا لَا يَعْنِيهِ»} — "From the perfection of a man’s Islam is his leaving alone that which does not concern him." This hadith is among the most comprehensive statements regarding the discipline of the tongue, for it commands the servant to abandon all speech that is not his concern, and it makes such abandonment a sign of the excellence of his submission.

Know that "that which does not concern you" (mā lā yaʿnīka) is of two kinds: first, that which does not concern you at all — neither in your religion nor in your worldly life — such as the hidden affairs of others, the details of their states, and the secrets of their conditions; second, that which concerns you in some respect but not in the manner you pursue it, such as asking about matters whose knowledge is not obligatory upon you, or delving into questions whose answers are not required of you, or speaking about things whose benefit is outweighed by their harm.

And the wise servant is he who weighs his words before uttering them, as he weighs his deeds before performing them. For just as he would not spend his wealth except on that which brings him benefit, so too should he not expend his breath except on that which yields him profit in his religion. The breath is a treasure that is spent, and the tongue is a pen that writes — either for you or against you. Whoever speaks, let him speak for his own benefit, and whoever remains silent, let him remain silent for his own safety. For the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: {«الصَّمْتُ حِكْمَةٌ وَقَلِيلٌ فَاعِلُهُ»} — "Silence is wisdom, but few practice it."

Therefore, O servant of Allah, guard your tongue from speaking about what does not concern you, for in that is the preservation of your heart, the soundness of your religion, and the safety of your Hereafter. And know that the tongue is the interpreter of the heart — when the heart is sound, the tongue is sound, and when the heart is corrupt, the tongue is corrupt. So purify your heart, and your tongue will be purified; discipline your inner self, and your outer speech will be disciplined. This is the first affliction, and it is the gate through which all other afflictions of the tongue enter.

chapters.title_en: On Restraining the Tongue from What Does Not Concern One — The Definition, Cause, and Remedy of Superfluous Speech
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن أحسن أحوالك أن تحفظ ألفاظك من جميع الآفات التي ذكرناها من
الغيبة والنميمة والكذب والمراء والجدال وغيرها وتتكلم فيما هو مباح لا ضرر
عليك فيه ولا على مسلم أصلا إلا أنك تتكلم بما أنت مستغن عنه ولا حاجة بك
إليه فإنك مضيع به زمانك ومحاسب على عمل لسانك وتستبدل الذي هو أدنى بالذي
هو خير لأنك لو صرفت زمان الكلامإلى الفكر ربما كان ينفتح لك من نفحات رحمة
الله عند الفكر ما يعظم جدواه ولو هللت الله سبحانه وذكرته وسبحته لكان
خيرا لك فكم من كلمة يبنى بها قصرا في الجنة ومن قدر على أن يأخذ كنزا من
الكنوز فأخذ مكانه مدرة لا ينتفع بها كان خاسرا خسرانا مبينا وهذا مثال من
ترك ذكر الله تعالى واشتغل بمباح لا يعنيه فإنه وإن لم يأثم فقد خسر حيث
فاته الربح العظيم بذكر الله تعالى فإن المؤمن لا يكون صمته إلا فكرا ونظره
إلا عبرة ونطقه إلا ذكرا (3) هكذا قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
بل رأس مال العبد أوقاته ومهما صرفها إلى مالا يعنيه ولم يدخر بها ثوابا
في الآخرة فقد ضيع رأس ماله ولهذا قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من حسن
إسلام المرء تركه مالا يعنيه (4)
بل ورد ما هو أشد من هذا قال أنس استشهد غلام منا يوم أحد فوجدنا على
بطنه حجرا مربوطا من الجوع فمسحت أمه عن وجهه التراب وقالت هنيئا لك الجنة
يا بني فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم وما يدريك لعله كان يتكلم فيما لا يعنيه
ويمنع ما لا يضره (5)
وفي حديث آخر إن النبي صلى الله  عليه وسلم فقد كعبا فسأل عنه فقالوا مريض
فخرج يمشي حتى أتاه فلما دخل عليه قال أبشر يا كعب فقالت أمه هنيئا لك
الجنة يا كعب فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من هذه المتألية على الله قال هي أمي
يا رسول الله قال وما يدريك يا أم كعب لعل كعبا قال ما لا يعنيه أو منع ما
لا يغنيه (6)
ومعناه أنه إنما تتهيأ الجنة لمن لا يحاسب ومن تكلم فيما لا يعنيه حوسب
عليه وإن كان كلامه غير مباح فلا تتهيأ الجنة مع المناقشة في الحساب فإنه
نوع من العذاب PageV03P112
وعن محمد بن كعب قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن أول من يدخل من
هذا الباب رجل من أهل الجنة فدخل عبد الله بن سلام فقام إليه ناس من أصحاب
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فأخبروه بذلك وقالوا أخبرنا بأوثق عمل في
نفسك ترجو به فقال إني لضعيف وإن أوثق ما أرجو به الله سلامة الصدر وترك ما
لا يعنيني (1)
وقال أبو ذر قال لي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلا أعلمك بعمل خفيف
على البدن ثقيل في الميزان قلت بلى يا رسول الله قال هو الصمت وحسن الخلق
وترك ما لا يعنيك (2) وقال مجاهد سمعت ابن عباس يقول خمس لهن أحب إلى من
الدهم الموقوفة لا تتكلم فيما لا يعنيك فإنه فضل ولا آمن عليك الوزر ولا
تتكلم فيما يعنيك حتى تجد له موضعا فإنه رب متكلم في أمر يعنيه قد وضعه في
غير موضعه فعنت ولا تمار حليما ولا سفيها فإن الحليم يقليك والسفيه يؤذيك
واذكر أخاك إذا غاب عنك بما تحب أن يذكرك به وأعفه مما تحب أن يعفيك منه
وعامل أخاك بما تحب أن يعاملك به واعمل عمل رجل يعلم أنه مجازى بالإحسان
مأخوذ بالاحترام وقيل للقمان الحكيم ما حكمتك قال لا أسأل عما كفيت ولا
أتكلف ما لا يعنيني وقال مورق العجلي أمر أنا في طلبه منذ عشرين سنة لم
أقدر عليه ولست بتارك طلبه قالوا وما هو قال السكوت عما لا يعنيني وقال عمر
رضي الله عنه لا تتعرض لما لا يعنيك واعتزل عدوك وأحذر صديقك من القوم إلا
الأمين ولا أمين إلا من خشى الله تعالى ولا تصحب الفاجر فتتعلم من فجوره
ولا تطلعه على سرك واستشر في أمرك الذين يخشون الله تعالى
وحد الكلام فيما لا يعنيك أن تتكلم بكلام ولو سكت عنه لم تأثم ولم تستضر
به في حال ولا مال مثاله أن تجلس مع قوم فتذكر لهم أسفارك وما رأيت فيها من
جبال وأنهار وما وقع لك من الوقائع وما استحسنته من الأطعمة والثياب وما
تعجبت منه من مشايخ البلاد ووقائعهم فهذه أمور لو سكت عنها لم تأثم ولم
تستضر وإذا بالغت في الجهاد حتى لم يمتزج بحكايتك زيادة ولا نقصان ولا
تزكية نفس من حيث التفاخر بمشاهدة الأحوال العظيمة ولا اغتياب لشخص ولا
مذمة لشيء مما خلقه الله تعالى فأنت مع ذلك كله مضيع زمانك وأنى تسلم من
الآفات التي ذكرناها ومن جملتها أن تسأل غيرك عما لا يعنيك فأنت بالسؤال
مضيع وقتك وقد الجأت صاحبك أيضا بالجواب إلى التضييع هذا إذا كان الشيء مما
يتطرق إلى السؤال عنه آفة وأكثر الأسئلة فيها آفات فإنك تسأل غيرك عن
عبادته مثلا فتقول له هل أنت صائم فإن قال نعم كان مظهرا لعبادته فيدخل
عليه الرياء وإن لم يدخل سقطت عبادته من ديوان السر وعبادة السر تفضل عبادة
الجهر بدرجات وإن قال لا كان كاذبا وإن سكت كان مستحقرا لك وتأذيت به وإن
احتال لمدافعة الجواب افتقر إلى جهد وتعب فيه فقد عرضته بالسؤال إما للرياء
أو للكذب أو للاستحقار أو للتعب في حيلة الدفع وكذلك سؤالك عن سائر عباداته
وكذلك سؤالك عن المعاصي وعن كل ما يخفيه ويستحي منه وسؤالك عما حدث به غيرك
فتقول له ماذا تقول وفيم أنت وكذلك ترى إنسانا في الطريق فتقول من أين
فربما يمنعه مانع من ذكره فإن ذكره  تأذى به واستحيا وإن لم يصدق وقع في
الكذب وكنت السبب فيه
وكذلك تسأل عن مسألة لا حاجة بك إليها والمسئول ربما لم تسمح نفسه بأن
يقول لا أدري فيجيب عن غير بصيرة PageV03P113
ولست أعني بالتكلم فيما لا يعني هذه الأجناس فإن هذا يتطرق إليه إثم أو
ضرر
وإنما مثال ما لا يعني ما روي أن لقمان الحكيم دخل على داود عليه السلام
وهو يسرد درعا ولم يكن رآها قبل ذلك اليوم فجعل يتعجب مما رأى فأراد أن
يسأله عن ذلك فمنعته حكمته فأمسك نفسه ولم يسأله فلما فرغ قام داود ولبسه
ثم قال نعم الدرع للحرب فقال لقمان الصمت حكم وقليل فاعله أي حصل العلم به
من غير سؤال فاستغنى عن السؤال وقيل انه كان يتردد إليه سنة وهو يريد أن
يعلم ذلك من غير سؤال فهذا وأمثاله من الأسئلة إذا لم يكن فيه ضرر وهتك ستر
وتوريط في رياء وكذب هو مما لا يعني وتركه من حسن الإسلام فهذا حده
وأما سببه الباعث عليه فالحرص على معرفة ما لا حاجة به إليه أو المباسطة
بالكلام على سبيل التودد أو تزجية الأوقات بحكايات أحوال لا فائدة فيها
وعلاج ذلك كله أن يعلم أن الموت بين يديه وأنه مسؤول عن كل كلمة وأن
أنفاسه رأس ماله وأن لسانه شبكة يقدر أن يقتنص بها الحور العين فإهماله ذلك
وتضييعه خسران مبين هذا علاجه من حيث العلم وأما من حيث العمل فالعزلة أو
أن يضع حصاة في فيه وأن يلزم نفسه السكوت بها عن بعض ما يعنيه حتى يعتاد
اللسان ترك ما لا يعنيه وضبط اللسان في هذا على غير المعتزل شديد جدا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ض-ض (ghaḍḍa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To lower, restrain, withhold; the physical act of casting down the gaze or holding back
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The disciplined restraint of a faculty from its natural inclination toward excess — a moral virtue of self-governance
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the eye (ghaḍḍ al-baṣar); here extended metaphorically to the tongue as a parallel organ of perception and expression
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional apodosis with law (لو) — expressing counterfactual or hypothetical benefit, as in "if you had diverted the time of speech to reflection, perhaps there would open for you..."
chapters.translation:
Know that the most excellent of your states is that you guard your utterances from all the afflictions we have mentioned — backbiting, slander, lying, disputation, argumentation, and the rest — and that you speak only concerning what is permissible (mubāḥ), wherein there is no harm upon you nor upon any Muslim whatsoever. However, if you speak of that which you are independent of and have no need for, then you are squandering your time thereby and will be called to account for the deed of your tongue; you are exchanging that which is lower for that which is better. For if you had diverted the time of speech toward reflection (fikr), perhaps there would open upon you, from the breezes of Allah's mercy at the moment of reflection, that whose benefit is immense. And if you had uttered the tahlīl — glorifying and praising Allah — it would have been better for you. How many a word builds a palace in Paradise! And whoever is able to take a treasure from among the treasures, yet takes in its place a lump of clay that profits him nothing — he is a loser with a manifest loss. This is the parable of one who abandons the remembrance of Allah (dhikr) and occupies himself with the permissible that does not concern him. For even though he commits no sin, he has lost, since the great profit of Allah's remembrance has escaped him. Indeed, the believer's silence is nothing but reflection, his gaze nothing but a lesson (ʿibrah), and his speech nothing but remembrance (dhikr). Thus said the Prophet ﷺ.

Nay, the capital of the servant is his hours (awqāt). Whenever he spends them upon what does not concern him, and stores up no reward thereby for the Hereafter, he has squandered his capital. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: «من حسن إسلام المرء تركه ما لا يعنيه» — "From the excellence of a man's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him."

Nay, there has come what is more severe than this. Anas said: A young man of ours was martyred on the Day of Uḥud. We found upon his belly a stone bound [against hunger]. His mother wiped the dust from his face and said, "Congratulations to you, O my son, for Paradise!" The Prophet ﷺ said: «وما يدريك لعله كان يتكلم فيما لا يعنيه ويمنع ما لا يضره» — "And what makes you know? Perhaps he used to speak concerning what did not concern him, and withhold what did not harm him."

And in another ḥadīth: The Prophet ﷺ missed Kaʿb and asked about him. They said, "He is ill." So he went out walking until he reached him. When he entered upon him, he said, "Rejoice, O Kaʿb!" His mother said, "Congratulations to you, O Kaʿb, for Paradise!" The Prophet ﷺ said: «من هذه المتألية على الله» — "Who is this one who presumes to swear an oath concerning Allah?" She said, "She is my mother, O Messenger of Allah." He said: «وما يدريك يا أم كعب لعل كعبا قال ما لا يعنيه أو منع ما لا يغنيه» — "And what makes you know, O mother of Kaʿb? Perhaps Kaʿb said what did not concern him, or withheld what did not avail him."

Its meaning is that Paradise is only prepared for one who will not be subjected to strict reckoning. And whoever speaks concerning what does not concern him will be reckoned for it. And if his speech is not even permissible, then Paradise is not prepared for him along with the strictness of the reckoning — for that is a kind of torment.

And it is related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first one to enter through this door is a man from the people of Paradise." Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām entered. A group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to him, informed him of that, and said: "Inform us of the most trustworthy deed in yourself by which you hope [for Paradise]." He said: "Indeed I am weak. The most trustworthy thing by which I hope for Allah is soundness of heart (salāmat al-ṣadr) and leaving what does not concern me."

And Abū Dharr said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: «ألا أعلمك بعمل خفيف على البدن ثقيل في الميزان» — "Shall I not teach you a deed light upon the body, heavy in the Balance?" I said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It is silence (al-ṣamt), good character, and leaving what does not concern you."

And Mujāhid said: I heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: "Five things are dearer to me than the finest camels: Do not speak concerning what does not concern you, for it is superfluous, and I am not safe for you from sin. Do not speak concerning what does concern you until you find a proper place for it, for many a speaker concerning a matter that concerns him has placed it in an improper place and suffered distress. Do not dispute (tumāri) with a forbearing man nor with a fool — for the forbearing one will despise you and the fool will harm you. Mention your brother in his absence as you would love him to mention you, and excuse him from what you would love him to excuse you from. Deal with your brother as you would love him to deal with you. And do the deed of a man who knows he will be recompensed for good and seized for transgression."

And it was said to Luqmān the Wise: "What is your wisdom?" He said: "I do not ask about what I have been spared, and I do not burden myself with what does not concern me."

And Muwarriq al-ʿIjlī said: "A matter I have been seeking for twenty years — I have not attained it, and I will not abandon seeking it." They said: "What is it?" He said: "Silence concerning what does not concern me."

And ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not expose yourself to what does not concern you. Keep away from your enemy. And beware of your friend — except the trustworthy one, and there is no trustworthy one except he who fears Allah. Do not accompany the wicked, lest you learn from his wickedness. Do not reveal your secret to him. And consult in your affairs those who fear Allah."

The definition (ḥadd) of speaking concerning what does not concern you is: that you speak words which, were you to remain silent about them, you would commit no sin and suffer no harm thereby — neither in circumstance nor in wealth. Its example: that you sit with a people and relate to them your travels, and what you saw therein of mountains and rivers, and what befell you of events, and what you admired of foods and garments, and what astonished you of the elders of the lands and their affairs. These are matters which, were you silent about them, you would commit no sin and suffer no harm. Even if you exert yourself in [truthfulness] until your narration is not mixed with increase or decrease, nor self-praise by way of boasting at witnessing great spectacles, nor backbiting of any person, nor disparagement of anything Allah created — you are nonetheless, with all of that, squandering your time. And how can you be safe from the afflictions we have mentioned?

Among these afflictions is that you ask another concerning what does not concern you. By your question you squander your own time, and you have also compelled your companion, through the answer, into squandering his. This is [the case] when the thing asked about is susceptible to affliction. And most questions contain afflictions. For example, you ask another about his worship, saying to him: "Are you fasting?" If he says "Yes," he has made his worship manifest, and ostentation (riyāʾ) enters upon him. And even if it does not enter, his worship has fallen from the register of the secret — and the worship of the secret excels the worship of the open by degrees. If he says "No," he has lied. If he remains silent, he has deemed you contemptible and is harmed by you. If he resorts to evasion in repelling the answer, he is reduced to effort and toil therein. So you have exposed him by your question — either to ostentation, or to lying, or to contempt, or to toil in the stratagem of repulsion. Likewise is your question concerning his other acts of worship. And likewise your question concerning sins, and concerning everything he conceals and is ashamed of. And your question concerning what another has related to him — you say to him: "What do you say? What are you about?" And likewise you see a man on the road and say: "From where?" Perhaps some impediment prevents him from mentioning it — if he mentions it, he is harmed and ashamed; and if he does not tell the truth, he falls into lying, and you were the cause of it.

Likewise, you ask about a question for which you have no need, and the one asked perhaps does not permit his soul to say "I do not know," so he answers without insight.

I do not mean by "speaking concerning what does not concern you" these kinds [of speech] — for sin or harm attaches to them.

Rather, the example of what does not concern [one] is what is related: that Luqmān the Wise entered upon Dāwūd, peace be upon him, while he was weaving a coat of mail — and he had not seen such a thing before that day. He began marveling at what he saw and wished to ask him about it, but his wisdom prevented him. He restrained himself and did not ask. When he finished, Dāwūd stood and put it on, then said: "Excellent is the coat of mail for battle!" Luqmān said: "Silence is wisdom, and few are its doers" — meaning, he obtained knowledge of it without asking, and so was spared the need to ask. It is said that he kept returning to him for a year, desiring to know that without asking. This, and its like among questions — when there is in it no harm, no tearing of a veil, no entangling in ostentation or lying — is what does not concern one, and leaving it is from the excellence of Islam. This is its definition.

As for its cause that impels it: it is eagerness to know what one has no need for, or the free expansion of speech by way of seeking affection, or the passing of time with narrations of matters in which there is no benefit.

The remedy for all of that is: to know that death is before him, that he is accountable for every word, that his breaths are his capital, and that his tongue is a net by which he is able to hunt the ḥūr al-ʿayn. His neglect of that and his squandering of it is a manifest loss. This is its remedy from the aspect of knowledge. As for the aspect of practice: it is seclusion (al-ʿuzlah), or that he place a pebble in his mouth, and that he oblige himself to silence thereby from some of what does concern him, until the tongue becomes accustomed to leaving what does not concern him. And the restraint of the tongue in this matter is, for one who does not practice seclusion, very severe indeed.
