His brain becomes like a cave in which a fire has blazed: its atmosphere blackens, its recesses burn, its sides fill with smoke, and within it was a weak lamp whose light is effaced or extinguished—so no foot stands firm in it, no speech is heard in it, no form is seen in it, and it cannot be extinguished from within or without. Rather, one must wait until all that is combustible burns up. Thus does anger do to the heart and the brain.

The fire of anger may intensify until it consumes the moisture by which the heart lives, and its possessor dies of rage—just as fire intensifies in the cave until it splits and its upper parts collapse upon its lower, that being the annihilation by the fire of what is in its sides of the cohesive force that holds its parts together. Such is the state of the heart at anger. In truth, a ship amid clashing waves, when winds disturb it in the deep of the sea, is in a better state and more hopeful of safety than the soul disturbed by rage—for in the ship there is one who devises means to calm it, manages it, looks to it, and steers it. But the heart is the owner of the ship, and its device has fallen when anger has blinded and deafened it.

Among the effects of this anger outwardly: the change of color, intense trembling in the limbs, the departure of actions from order and system, and the disturbance of movement and speech—until foam appears on the jaws, the eye-whites redden, the nostrils flare, and the form is transformed. Were the angry man to see the ugliness of his form in his state of anger, his anger would settle out of shame at the ugliness of his form and the transformation of his constitution. The ugliness of his interior is greater than the ugliness of his exterior, for the exterior is the title-page of the interior. The ugliness of the inner form is first, then its ugliness spreads to the exterior secondarily; so the exterior change is the fruit of the interior change. Measure the fruit by the tree.

This is its effect on the body. As for its effect on the tongue: its release into abuse and obscene speech, which the intelligent man is ashamed of and which its speaker is ashamed of when anger cools—and that, along with confused order and disturbed utterance.

As for its effect on the limbs: striking, assaulting, tearing, killing, and wounding when one has the power, without heed. If the object of anger flees from him or escapes him by some cause, and he is unable to gain vindictive satisfaction, the anger turns back upon its owner: he tears his own garment, slaps his own face, may strike his hand upon the ground, and runs the run of a distracted, intoxicated, bewildered, perplexed man. He may fall quickly, unable to run or rise, due to the intensity of anger, and a swoon-like state befalls him. He may strike inanimate objects and animals—striking a bowl, for example, upon the ground, and may break a table if angry at it. He engages in the acts of madmen: he reviles beasts and inanimate objects, addresses them, and says: "How long this from you, O so-and-so?"—as though addressing a rational being. Perhaps a beast kicks him, and he kicks the beast and repays it in kind.

As for its effect in the heart toward the object of anger: rancor, envy, harboring evil, rejoicing at misfortunes, grieving at joys, resolve to divulge secrets, tearing of veils, mockery, and other such abominations. These are the fruits of excessive anger.

As for the fruit of weak protective zeal: the lack of indignation at what should provoke indignation—such as the violation of one's sanctity, wife, and slave-girl; the endurance of humiliation from the base; pettiness of soul and abasement. This too is blameworthy, for among its fruits is the absence of jealousy (ghayrah) over the forbidden—which is effeminacy. He—peace be upon him—said: "Saʿd is indeed jealous, and I am more jealous than Saʿd, and Allah is more jealous than I." Jealousy was created only for the preservation of lineages; were people to be lax in that, lineages would become mixed. Therefore it was said: "Every nation that places jealousy in its men places modesty in its women." From the weakness of anger comes cowardice and silence at the sight of abominations. He—peace be upon him—said: "The best of my community are its sharp-tempered ones"—meaning in religion. And Allah—Exalted is He—said: {«ولا تأخذكم بهما رأفة في دين الله»} ("Let not pity for the two seize you in the religion of Allah"). Rather, whoever loses anger is incapable of disciplining his own soul, for discipline is not accomplished except by the subjugation of anger over appetite—so that one becomes angry at his own soul when it inclines toward base appetites. Thus the loss of anger is blameworthy. The praiseworthy anger is only that which awaits the signal of intellect and religion: it surges where protective zeal is obligatory, and is extinguished where forbearance is fitting. Preserving it upon the limit of moderation is the uprightness (istiqāmah) with which Allah charged His servants, and it is the middle which the Messenger of Allah—peace be upon him—described when he said: "The best of affairs are their middles."

So whoever's anger inclines toward languor, until he senses in himself weakness of jealousy and baseness of soul in enduring humiliation and oppression in their improper place—he should treat his soul until his anger is strengthened. And whoever's anger inclines toward excess, until it drags him into recklessness and the plunging into indecencies—he should treat his soul to diminish the fury of anger and stand upon the true middle between the two extremes. That is the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm), which is finer than a hair and sharper than a sword. If one is incapable of it, let him seek closeness to it. Allah—Exalted is He—said: {«ولن تستطيعوا أن تعدلوا بين النساء ولو حرصتم فلا تميلوا كل الميل فتذروها كالمعلقة»} ("You will never be able to be just between women, even if you strive; so do not incline with all inclination, leaving her like one suspended"). Not everyone who is incapable of doing all good should do all evil; rather, some evil is lighter than other evil, and some good is higher than other good.

This is the reality of anger and its degrees. We ask Allah for good success toward what pleases Him—verily, He over what He wills is All-Powerful.

chapters.title_en: Exposition on Anger — Whether Its Root Can Be Eradicated Through Spiritual Discipline (Riyāḍah) or Not
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان الغضب  هل يمكن إزالة أصله بالرياضة أم لا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ض-ب (gh-ḍ-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning — boiling agitation of the blood of the heart, seeking retaliation; intensity of heat and swelling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, anger (ghaḍab) is a natural human faculty (quwwah) that, when unrestrained, leads to blameworthy acts; its root is not inherently evil but becomes so through excess or deficiency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical boiling; metaphorical (majāz) — the soul's fervent impulse toward vengeance. Here, the question concerns the literal root (aṣl) as a created disposition.
- Root: ر-و-ض (r-w-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taming, training, breaking in (as a beast); gradual habituation to obedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Riyāḍah in the spiritual path is the disciplined exercise of the soul to subdue its passions, not annihilation of the faculty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical training of animals; metaphorical — disciplining the soul's faculties.
- Sībawayh Rule: Istifhām Taqrīrī (Interrogative of Affirmation/Confirmation) — The question "هل" here is not for genuine inquiry but for establishing a settled truth, requiring a nuanced answer distinguishing eradication (izālah) from management (taʿdīl).
chapters.translation: I say: Know that the root of anger (ghaḍab) is a natural disposition (gharīzah) created by God in man, and it is not possible to eradicate it entirely from its very foundation, for it is an inseparable part of human nature. Rather, what is possible through spiritual discipline (riyāḍah) is to bring it into moderation (iʿtidāl) — to tame it so that it moves only when appropriate and rests when it should. For if anger were wholly removed, man would lose the very drive that impels him to defend truth, repel injustice, and strive against his own lower self. Thus, the aim of discipline is not annihilation (izālah) but equilibrium (taʿdīl), just as one trains a spirited horse not to kill its vigor but to direct it.

chapters.title_en: On the Extirpation of Anger: Its Possibility, Degrees, and the Path of Discipline (Riyāḍah)
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أنه ظن ظانون أنه يتصور محو الغضب بالكلية وزعموا أن الرياضة إليه
تتوجه وإياه تقصد وظن آخرون أنه أصل لا يقبل العلاج وهذا رأي من يظن أن
الخلق كالخلق وكلاهما لا يقبل التغيير وكلا الرأيين ضعيف بل الحق فيه ما
نذكره وهو أنه ما بقي الإنسان يحب شيئا ويكره شيئا فلا يخلو من الغيظ
والغضب وما دام يوافقه شيء ويخالفه آخر فلا بد من أن يحب ما يوافقه ويكره
ما يخالفه
والغضب يتبع ذلك فإنه مهما أخذ منه محبوبه غضب لا محالة وإذا قصد بمكروه
غضب لا محالة
إلا أن ما يحبه الإنسان ينقسم إلى ثلاثة أقسام
الأول ما هو ضرورة في حق الكافة كالقوت والمسكن والملبس وصحة البدن فمن
قصد بدنه بالضرب والجرح فلا بد وأن يغضب وكذلك إذا أخذ منه ثوبه الذي يستر
عورته وكذلك إذا أخرج من داره التي هي مسكنه أو أريق ماؤه الذي لعطشه فهذه
ضرورات لا يخلو الإنسان من كراهة زوالها ومن غيظ على من يتعرض لها
القسم الثاني ما ليس ضروريا لأحد من الخلق كالجاه والمال الكثير والغلمان
والدواب فإن هذه الأمور صارت محبوبة بالعادة والجهل بمقاصد الأمور حتى صار
الذهب والفضة محبوبين في أنفسهما فيكنزان ويغضب على من يسرقهما وإن كان
مستغنيا عنهما في القوت فهذا الجنس مما يتصور أن ينفك الإنسان عن أصل الغيظ
عليه فإذا كانت له دار زائدة على مسكنه فهدمه ظالم فيجوز أن لا يغضب إذ
يجوز أن يكون بصيرا بأمر الدنيا فيزهد في الزيادة على الحاجة فلا يغضب
بأخذها فإنه لا يحب وجودها ولو أحب وجودها لغضب على الضرورة بأخذها وأكثر
غضب الناس على ما هو غير ضروري كالجاه والصيت والتصدر في المجالس والمباهاة
في العلم فمن غلب هذا الحب عليه فلا محالة يغضب إذا زاحمه مزاحم على التصدر
في المحافل ومن لا يحب ذلك فلا يبالي ولو جلس في صف النعال فلا يغضب إذا
جلس غيره فوقه وهذه  العادات الرديئة هي التي أكثرت محاب الإنسان ومكارهه
فأكثرت غضبه وكلما كانت الإرادات والشهوات أكثر كان صاحبها أحط رتبة وأنقص
لأن الحاجة صفة نقص فمهما كثرة كثر النقص والجاهل أبدا جهده في أن يزيد في
حاجاته وفي شهواته وهو لا يدري أنه مستكثر من أسباب الغم والحزم حتى ينتى
بعض الجهال بالعادات الرديئة ومخالطة قرناء السوء إلى أن يغضب لو قيل له
إنك لا تحسن اللعب بالطيور واللعب بالشطرنج ولا تقدر على شرب الخمر الكثير
وتناول الطعام الكثير وما يجري مجراه من الرذائل فالغضب على هذا الجنس ليس
بضروري لأن حبه ليس بضروري PageV03P169
القسم الثالث ما يكون ضروريا في حق بعض الناس دون البعض كالكتاب مثلا في
حق العالم لأنه مضطر إليه فيحبه فيغضب على من يحرقه ويغرقه وكذلك أدوات
الصناعات في حق المكتسب الذي لا يمكنه التوصل إلى القوت إلا بها فإنما هو
وسيلة إلى الضروري والمحبوب يصير ضروريا ومحبوبا وهذا يختلف بالأشخاص وإنما
الحب الضروري ما أشار إليه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بقوله من أصبح
آمنا في سربه معافى في بدنه وله قوت يومه فكأنما حيزت له الدنيا بحذافيرها
(1)
ومن كان بصيرا بحقائق الأمور وسلم له هذه الثلاثة يتصور أن لا يغضب في
غيرها فهذه ثلاثة أقسام فلنذكر غاية الرياضة في كل واحد منها
أما القسم الأول فليست الرياضة فيها لينعدم غيظ القلب ولكن لكي يقدر على
أن لا يطيع الغضب ولا يستعمله في الظاهر إلا على حد يستحبه الشرع ويستحسنه
العقل وذلك ممكن بالمجاهدة وتكلف الحلم والاحتمال مدة حتى يصير الحلم
والاحتمال خلقا راسخا فأما قمع أصل الغيظ من القلب فذلك ليس مقتضى الطبع
وهو غير ممكن نعم يمكن كسر سورته وتضعيفه حتى لا يشتد هيجان الغيظ في
الباطن وينتهي ضعفه إلى أن لا يظهر أثره في الوجه ولكن ذلك شديد جدا وهذا
حكم القسم الثالث أيضا لأن ما صار ضروريا في حق شخص فلا يمنعه من الغيظ
استغناء غيره عنه فالرياضة فيه تمنع العمل  به وتضعف هيجانه في الباطن حتى
لا يشتد التألم بالصبر عليه
وأما القسم الثاني فيمكن التوصل بالرياضة إلى الانفكاك عن الغضب عليه إذ
يمكن إخراج حبه من القلب وذلك بأن يعلم الإنسان أن وطنه القبر مستقره
الآخرة وأن الدنيا معبر يعبر عليها ويتزود منها قدر الضرورة وما وراء ذلك
عليه وبال في وطنه ومستقره فيزهد في الدنيا ويمحو حبها عن قلبه ولو كان
للإنسان كلب لا يحبه لا يغضب إذا ضربه غيره فالغضب تبع للحب فالرياضة في
هذا تنتهي إلى قمع أصل الغضب وهو نادر جدا وقد تنتهي إلى المنع من استعمال
الغضب والعمل بموجبه وهو أهون
فإن قلت الضروري من القسم الأول التألم بفوات المحتاج إليه دون الغضب فمن
له شاة مثلا وهي قوته فماتت لا يغضب على أحد وإن كان يحصل فيه كراهة وليس
من ضرورة كل كراهة غضب فإن الإنسان يتألم بالفصد والحجامة ولا يغضب على
الفصاد والحجام فمن غلب عليه التوحيد حتى يرى الأشياء كلها بيد الله ومنه
فلا يغضب على أحد من خلقه إذ يراهم مسخرين في قبضة قدرته كالقلم في يد
الكاتب ومن وقع ملك بضرب رقبته لم يغضب على القلم فلا يغضب على من يذبح
شاته التي هي قوته كما لا يغضب على موتها إذ يرى الذبح والموت من الله عز
وجل فيندفع الغضب بغلبة التوحيد ويندفع أيضا بحسن الظن بالله وهو أن يرى أن
الكل من الله تعالى وإن الله لا يقدر له إلا ما فيه الخيرة وربما تكون
الخيرة في مرضه وجوعه وجرحه وقتله فلا يغضب كما لا يغضب على الفصاد والحجام
لأنه يرى أن الخيرة فيه فيقول هذا على هذا الوجه غير محال ولكن غلبة
التوحيد إلى هذا الحد إنما تكون كالبرق الخاطف تغلب في أحوال مختلفة ولا
تدوم ويرجع القلب إلى الالتفات إلى الوسائط رجوعا طبيعيا لا يندفع عنه ولو
تصور ذلك على الدوام لبشر لتصور لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فإنه كان
يغضب حتى تحمر وجنتاه // حديث  كان صلى الله عليه وسلم يغضب حتى تحمر وجنتاه
أخرجه مسلم من حديث جابر كان إذا خطب احمرت عيناه وعلا صوته واشتد غضبه
وللحاكم كان إذا ذكر الساعة احمرت وجنتاه واشتد غضبه وقد تقدم في أخلاق
النبوة
حتى قال اللهم أنا بشر أغضب كما يغضب البشر فأيما مسلم سببته PageV03P170
أو لعنته أو ضربته فاجعلها مني صلاة عليه وزكاة وقربة تقربه بها إليك يوم
القيامة (1)
وقال عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص يا رسول الله أكتب عنك كل ما قلت في
الغضب والرضا فقال اكتب فوالذي بعثني بالحق نبيا ما يخرج منه إلا حق وأشار
إلى لسانه (2)
فلم يقل إني لا أغضب ولكن قال إن الغضب لا يخرجني عن الحق أي لا أعمل
بموجب الغضب وغضبت عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها مرة فقال لها رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم مالك جاءك شيطانك فقالت ومالك شيطان قال بلى ولكني دعوت
الله فأعانني عليه فأسلم فلا يأمرني إلا بالخير (3)
ولم يقل لا شيطان لي وأراد شيطان الغضب لكن قال لا يحملني على الشر وقال
علي رضي الله تعالى عنه كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يغضب للدنيا
فإذا أغضبه الحق لم يعرفه أحد ولم يقم لغضبه شيء حتى ينتصر له (4)
فكان يغضب على الحق وإن كان غضبه لله فهو التفات إلى الوسائط على الجملة
بل كل من يغضب على من يأخذ ضرورة قوته وحاجته التي لا بد له في دينه منها
فإنما غضب لله فلا يمكن الانفكاك عنه نعم قد يفقد أصل الغضب فيما هو ضروري
إذا كان القلب مشغولا بضروري أهم منه فلا يكون في القلب متسع للغضب
لاشتغاله بغيره فإن استغراق القلب ببعض المهمات يمنع الإحساس بما عداه
وهذا كما أن سلمان لما شتم قال إن خفت موازيني فأنا شر مما تقول وإن ثقلت
موازيني لم يضرني ما تقول فقد كان همه مصروفا إلى الآخرة فلم يتأثر قلبه
بالشتم وكذلك شتم الربيع بن خثيم فقال يا هذا قد  سمع الله كلامك وإن دون
الجنة عقبة إن قطعتها لم يضرني ما تقول وإن لم أقطعها فأنا شر مما تقول وسب
رجل أبا بكر رضي الله عنه فقال ما ستر الله عنك أكثر فكأنه كان مشغولا
بالنظر في تقصير نفسه عن أن يتقي الله حق تقاته ويعرفه حق معرفته فلم يغضبه
نسبة غيره إياه إلى نقصان إذ كان ينظر إلى نفسه بعين النقصان وذلك لجلالة
قدره
وقالت امرأة لمالك بن دينار يا مرائي فقال ما عرفني غيرك فكأنه كان
مشغولا بأن ينفي عن نفسه آفة الرياء ومنكرا على نفسه ما يلقيه الشيطان إليه
فلم يغضب لما نسب إليه وسب رجل الشعبي فقال إن كنت صادقا فغفر الله لي وإن
كنت كاذبا فغفر الله لك
فهذه الأقاويل دالة في الظاهر على أنهم لم يغضبوا لاشتغال قلوبهم بمهمات
دينهم ويحتمل أن يكون ذلك قد أثر في قلوبهم ولكنهم لم يشتغلوا به واشتغلوا
بما كان هو الأغلب على قلوبهم فإذا اشتغال القلب ببعض المهمات لا يبعد أن
يمنع هيجان الغضب عند فوات بعض المحاب فإذا يتصور فقد الغيظ إما باشتغال
القلب بمهم أو بغلبة نظر التوحيد أو بسبب ثالث وهو أن يعلم أن الله يحب منه
أن لا يغتاظ فيطفئ شدة حبه لله غيظه وذلك غير محال في أحوال نادرة وقد عرفت
بهذا أن الطريق للخلاص من نار الغضب محو حب الدنيا عن القلب وذلك بمعرفة
آفات الدنيا وغوائلها كما سيأتي في كتاب ذم الدنيا ومن أخرج حب المزايا عن
القلب تخلص من أكثر PageV03P171
أسباب الغضب وما لا يمكن محوه يمكن كسره وتضعيفه فيضعف الغضب بسببه ويهون
دفعه نسأل الله حسن التوفيق بلطفه وكرمه أنه على كل شيء قدير والحمد لله
وحده
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ض-ب (ghaḍiba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Boiling of the blood of the heart, seeking to repel harm; intense displeasure and irritation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A natural, God-given faculty (quwwah) in man; blameworthy when it exceeds the mean, praiseworthy when harnessed for religious defense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the internal emotion; metaphorical (majāz) when attributed to God or to inanimate causes.
- Root: ر-و-ض (rāḍa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tame, break in (an animal); to train and discipline gradually.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's habituation to virtuous acts until they become ingrained character (khuluq).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for animal taming; metaphorical for the soul's training against its passions.
- Root: ح-ب-ب (ḥabba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Affection, inclination of the heart toward what pleases it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The root of all action; love of the world is the source of all sin, love of God the source of all virtue.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for emotional attachment; metaphorical for the soul's orientation toward its ultimate end.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍarra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Necessity, need, harm; that without which one cannot subsist.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which is indispensable for religion or worldly survival; its absence causes distress.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical need; metaphorical for spiritual necessity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly uses "law" and "illā" to delineate the precise scope of possibility and impossibility, requiring careful parsing to distinguish absolute from conditional claims.
chapters.translation:
Know that some people have conjectured that the complete eradication of anger is conceivable, and they claimed that spiritual discipline (riyāḍah) is directed toward this end and aims at it. Others opined that it is a root [trait] that admits no treatment — this being the view of those who think that character (khuluq) is like physical constitution (khalq), and that neither admits of change. Both views are weak. Rather, the truth in this matter is what we shall now mention: namely, that as long as a man loves something and hates something, he cannot be free from rage and anger. And as long as one thing agrees with him and another opposes him, he must necessarily love what agrees with him and hate what opposes him.

Anger follows from this. For whenever his beloved is taken from him, he becomes angry without fail; and when he is afflicted with something hateful, he becomes angry without fail.

However, what a man loves divides into three categories:

**The First Category:** That which is a necessity for all people universally — such as food, shelter, clothing, and bodily health. If someone strikes his body or wounds it, he must necessarily become angry. Likewise, if his garment that covers his nakedness is taken from him, or if he is expelled from his house which is his dwelling, or if the water he needs for thirst is spilled — these are necessities, and a man cannot be free from hatred of their loss, nor from rage against whoever assaults them.

**The Second Category:** That which is not a necessity for anyone among creation — such as status, abundant wealth, servants, and riding beasts. These things have become beloved through habit and through ignorance of the true purposes of things, until gold and silver have come to be loved in themselves, hoarded, and anger is felt toward whoever steals them — even if one is independent of them for sustenance. This kind is that from which a man can conceivably be freed from the root of rage. For if a man has a house exceeding his dwelling-place and a tyrant demolishes it, it is permissible that he not become angry — for it is permissible that he be insightful about the affairs of this world, and thus renounce (zuhd) what exceeds his need, and so not become angry at its being taken. For he does not love its existence; and had he loved its existence, he would necessarily have become angry at its being taken. Most of people's anger is over what is non-necessary — such as status, reputation, sitting at the head of assemblies, and boasting in knowledge. Whoever is overcome by this love must necessarily become angry when someone vies with him for the head of gatherings. But whoever does not love that does not care — even if he sits in the row of sandals, he does not become angry when another sits above him. These base habits are what have multiplied people's loves and hates, and thus multiplied their anger. And the more one's desires and appetites multiply, the lower one's rank and the greater one's deficiency — for need is a mark of deficiency, and whenever it multiplies, deficiency multiplies. The ignorant man always strives to increase his needs and appetites, not knowing that he is accumulating causes of grief and ruin — until some of the ignorant, through base habits and the company of evil companions, reach the point of becoming angry if it is said to him: "You do not know how to play with birds, nor play chess, nor can you drink much wine or consume much food" — and similar vices. Anger over this kind is not necessary, because the love of it is not necessary.

**The Third Category:** That which is necessary for some people but not others — such as the book, for example, in the case of the scholar. For he is compelled to it, so he loves it, and thus becomes angry at whoever burns it or drowns it. Likewise, the tools of crafts in the case of the wage-earner who cannot attain sustenance except through them — for they are a means to the necessary, and the beloved becomes necessary and beloved. This varies according to persons. The necessary love is only that which the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) indicated in his saying: {«Whoever wakes up secure in his person, healthy in his body, having the provision of his day — it is as if the whole world had been gathered for him»}.

Whoever is insightful about the realities of things, and these three are secured for him, it is conceivable that he not become angry over anything else. These, then, are the three categories. Let us now mention the utmost limit of discipline (riyāḍah) in each of them.

**As for the first category:** The discipline therein is not that the heart's rage become extinct, but rather that one be able to not obey anger, and not employ it outwardly except to the limit that the Law (sharʿ) approves and reason deems good. This is possible through striving (mujāhadah) and through burdening oneself with forbearance (ḥilm) and endurance over a period, until forbearance and endurance become a firmly rooted character. As for suppressing the very root of rage from the heart — that is not required by nature, and it is not possible. Yes, it is possible to break its violence and weaken it, so that the stirring of rage in the inward does not become intense, and its weakness reaches the point that its trace does not appear on the face. But that is extremely difficult. This is also the ruling for the third category — for what has become necessary in the case of a person, the fact that another is independent of it does not prevent him from rage. The discipline therein prevents acting upon it and weakens its stirring inwardly, so that the pain of enduring it does not become intense.

**As for the second category:** It is possible through discipline to attain complete detachment from anger over it, since it is possible to expel its love from the heart. This is done by a man knowing that his homeland is the grave, his final abode is the Hereafter, and that this world is a passageway upon which one crosses, taking from it provision to the measure of necessity — and whatever is beyond that is a burden upon him in his homeland and final abode. Thus he renounces this world and erases its love from his heart. If a man had a dog that he did not love, he would not become angry if another struck it — for anger follows love. So discipline in this matter reaches the point of suppressing the root of anger — and that is extremely rare — and it may reach the point of preventing the employment of anger and acting upon its dictate — and that is easier.

If you say: "The necessary thing in the first category is the pain of losing what is needed — not anger. For a man who has a sheep, for example, which is his sustenance, and it dies — he does not become angry at anyone, though distress occurs in him. And it is not necessary that every distress entail anger. For a man feels pain at phlebotomy (faṣd) and cupping (ḥijāmah), yet does not become angry at the phlebotomist or the cupper."

Then know that whoever is overcome by tawḥīd (divine unity) to the point that he sees all things as being in God's hand and from Him, he does not become angry at any of His creatures — for he sees them as subjugated in the grasp of His power, like the pen in the hand of the writer. If a king strikes a man's neck, he does not become angry at the pen. So he does not become angry at whoever slaughters his sheep which is his sustenance — just as he does not become angry at its death — for he sees the slaughter and the death as both from God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus anger is repelled by the dominance of tawḥīd. It is also repelled by good opinion of God (ḥusn al-ẓann billāh) — namely, that he sees that everything is from God Most High, and that God does not decree for him except what contains the better choice (al-khiyarah). Perhaps the better choice lies in his illness, his hunger, his wound, or his being killed — so he does not become angry, just as he does not become angry at the phlebotomist and the cupper, because he sees that the better choice lies therein.

One might say: "This is not impossible in this manner." But the dominance of tawḥīd to this extent only occurs like a flashing lightning-bolt — it prevails in various moments but does not endure. The heart returns to attending to secondary causes (wasāʾiṭ) with a natural return that cannot be repelled. Had this been conceivable perpetually, it would have been fitting for the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) — for he used to become angry until his cheeks reddened. He said: {«O God, I am a human being; I become angry as human beings become angry. So any Muslim whom I have reviled, cursed, or struck — make it for him a prayer, a purification, and a means of nearness to You on the Day of Resurrection»}.

And ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said: "O Messenger of God, shall I write from you everything you say in anger and in pleasure?" He said: {«Write — for by Him who sent me with the truth as a Prophet, nothing comes out of it except truth»} — and he pointed to his tongue.

He did not say "I do not become angry," but rather said that anger does not take him out of the truth — i.e., he does not act upon anger's dictate. ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her) once became angry, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said to her: {«What is the matter with you? Your devil has come to you.»} She said: "And do you have a devil?" He said: {«Yes, but I called upon God and He aided me against him, so he submitted — he does not command me except to good.»} He did not say "I have no devil" — meaning the devil of anger — but rather said that he does not carry him to evil. And ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) did not become angry for the sake of this world. But when the truth angered him, no one recognized him, and nothing could withstand his anger until he prevailed for it." So he used to become angry for the truth — and even if his anger was for God, it is still an attending to secondary causes in general.

Rather, whoever becomes angry at one who takes his necessary sustenance and need which he cannot do without in his religion — his anger is for God, and detachment from it is not possible. Yes, the very root of anger may be absent in what is necessary, if the heart is occupied with a necessity more important than it — for then there is no room in the heart for anger, due to its occupation with something else. For the heart's total absorption in some important matter prevents sensation of what is other than it.

This is like Salmān — when he was reviled, he said: "If my scales are light, then I am worse than what you say; and if my scales are heavy, then what you say does not harm me." His concern was diverted to the Hereafter, so his heart was not affected by the reviling. Likewise, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym was reviled and said: "O this man — God has heard your words. Between me and Paradise there is a steep incline; if I cross it, what you say does not harm me; and if I do not cross it, then I am worse than what you say." A man reviled Abū Bakr (may God be pleased with him), and he said: "What God has concealed of you is more than [what you reveal]." It was as if he was occupied with examining his own shortcoming — that he had not feared God with the fear due to Him, nor known Him with the knowledge due to Him — so another's attribution of deficiency to him did not anger him, since he looked at himself with the eye of deficiency. And that was due to the greatness of his rank.

A woman said to Mālik ibn Dīnār: "O show-off (murāʾī)!" He said: "No one has known me except you." It was as if he was occupied with repelling from himself the affliction of ostentation, and censuring himself for what Satan cast into him — so he did not become angry at what was attributed to him. A man reviled al-Shaʿbī, and he said: "If you are truthful, may God forgive me; and if you are lying, may God forgive you."

These sayings outwardly indicate that they did not become angry because their hearts were occupied with the important matters of their religion. It is also possible that [the reviling] did affect their hearts, but they did not occupy themselves with it, and instead occupied themselves with what was dominant in their hearts. So the heart's occupation with some important matter is not far from preventing the stirring of anger at the loss of some beloved things. Thus the absence of rage is conceivable — either through the heart's occupation with something important, or through the dominance of the vision of tawḥīd, or through a third cause: namely, that one knows that God loves from him that he not become enraged — so the intensity of his love for God extinguishes his rage. And that is not impossible in rare moments.

You have thus come to know that the path of deliverance from the fire of anger is the erasure of love of this world from the heart — and that is through knowledge of the afflictions of this world and its perils, as will come in the Book of the Blame of this World (Kitāb Dhamm al-Dunyā). Whoever expels the love of privileges (mazāyā) from his heart is delivered from most of the causes of anger. And what cannot be erased can be broken and weakened — so anger is weakened by reason of it, and its repulsion becomes easy.

We ask God for good success (tawfīq) through His gentleness and generosity — verily He is powerful over all things. And praise be to God alone.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Causes that Provoke Anger
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان الأسباب المهيجة للغضب

قد عرفت أن علاج كل علة حسم مادتها وإزالة أسبابها فلا بد من معرفة أسباب
الغضب وقد قال يحيى لعيسى عليهما السلام أي شيء أشد قال غضب الله قال فما
يقرب من غضب الله قال أن تغضب  قال فما بيدي الغضب وما ينبته قال عيسى الكبر
والفخر والتعزز والحمية
والأسباب المهيجة للغضب هي الزهو والعجب والمزاح والهزل والهزء والتعيير
والمماراة والمضادة والغدر وشدة الحرص على فضول المال والجاه وهي بأجمعها
أخلاق رديئة مذمومة شرعا ولا خلاص من الغضب مع بقاء هذه الأسباب فلا بد من
إزالة هذه الأسباب بأضدادها
فينبغي أن تميت الزهو بالتواضع وتميت العجب بمعرفتك بنفسك كما سيأتي
بيانه في كتاب الكبر والعجب وتزيل الفخر بأنك من جنس عبدك إذ الناس يجمعهم
في الانتساب أب واحد وإنما اختلفوا في الفضل أشتاتا فبنو آدم جنس واحد
وإنما الفخر بالفضائل والفخر والعجب والكبر أكبر الرذائل وهي أصلها ورأسها
فإذا لم تخل عنها فلا فضل لك على غيرك فلم تفتخر وأنت من جنس عبدك من حيث
البنية والنسب والأعضاء الظاهرة والباطنة وأما المزاح فتزيله بالتشاغل
بالمهمات الدينية التي تستوعب العمر وتفضل عنه إذا عرفت ذلك وأما الهزل
فتزيله بالجد في طلب الفضائل والأخلاق الحسنة والعلوم الدينية التي تبلغك
إلى سعادة الآخرة وأما الهزء فتزيله بالتكرم عن إيذاء الناس وبصيانة النفس
عن أن يستهزأ بك وأما التعيير فالحذر عن القول القبيح وصيانة النفس عن مر
الجواب وأما شدة الحرص على مزايا العيش فتزال بالقناعة بقدر الضرورة طلبا
لعز الاستغناء وترفعا عن ذل الحاجة
وكل خلق من هذه الأخلاق وصفة من هذه الصفات يفتقر في علاجه إلى رياضة
وتحمل مشقة وحاصل رياضتها يرجع إلى معرفة غوائلها لترغب النفس عنها وتنفر
عن قبحها ثم المواظبة على مباشرة أضدادها مدة مديدة حتى تصير بالعادة
مألوفة هينة على النفس فإذا انمحت عن النفس فقد زكت وتطهرت عن هذه الرذائل
وتخلصت أيضا عن الغضب الذي يتولد منها
ومن أشد البواعث على الغضب عند أكثر الجهال تسميتهم الغضب شجاعة ورجولية
وعزة نفس وكبر همة وتلقيبه بالألقاب المحمودة غباوة وجهلا حتى تميل النفس
إليه وتستحسنه وقد يتأكد ذلك بحكاية شدة الغضب عن الأكابر في معرض المدح
بالشجاعة والنفوس مائلة إلى التشبه بالأكابر فيهيج الغضب إلى القلب  بسببه
وتسمية هذا عزة نفس وشجاعة جهل بل هو مرض قلب ونقصان عقل وهو لضعف النفس
ونقصانها وآية أنه لضعف النفس أن المريض أسرع غضبا من الصحيح والمرأة أسرع
غضبا من الرجل والصبي أسرع غضبا من الرجل الكبير والشيخ الضعيف أسرع غضبا
من الكهل وذو الخلق السيء والرذائل القبيحة أسرع غضبا من صاحب الفضائل
فالرذل يغضب لشهوته إذا فاتته اللقمة ولبخله إذا فاتته الحبة حتى أنه
يغضب على أهله وولده وأصحابه
بل القوي من يملك نفسه عند الغضب كما قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
ليس الشديد بالصرعة إنما الشديد الذي يملك نفسه عند الغضب (1) بل ينبغي أن
يعالج هذا الجاهل بأن تتلي عليه PageV03P172
حكايات أهل الحلم والعفو وما استحسن منهم من كظم الغيظ فإن ذلك منقول عن
الأنبياء والأولياء والحكماء والعلماء وأكابر الملوك الفضلاء وضد ذلك منقول
عن الأكراد والأتراك والجهلة والأغبياء الذين لا عقول لهم ولا فضل فيهم

### ||| بيان علاج الغضب بعد هيجانه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-ه-و (z-h-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Self-conceit, pride, and the swelling of the heart with self-regard
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral vice rooted in ignorance of one's own defects, opposed to the Quranic condemnation of self-praise {«فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ»}
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the blooming of a plant; metaphorically applied to the heart's inflation with vanity
- Root: غ-ض-ب (gh-d-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Boiling of the blood in the veins, the fiercest of which is divine wrath
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A passion of the soul seeking retaliation; in God, it is purely an attribute of justice, not a passion
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the boiling of a pot; metaphorical for the soul's agitation
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The listing of causes (الزهو والعجب والمزاح...) follows a coordinated sequence where each term is syntactically parallel, requiring the translator to preserve the cumulative force of the enumeration.
chapters.translation:
I say: You have already known that the treatment of every malady lies in cutting off its material cause and removing its sources. Therefore, one must necessarily know the causes of anger. It has been related that Yaḥyā (John) said to ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace be upon them both: "What thing is most severe?" He replied: "The wrath of God." He asked: "What brings one near to the wrath of God?" He answered: "That you become angry." He asked: "What is within my power regarding anger, and what causes it to grow?" ʿĪsā replied: "Pride, vainglory, self-exaltation, and protective zeal."

The causes that provoke anger are: self-conceit (al-zahw), vanity (al-ʿujb), jesting (al-mizāḥ), frivolity (al-hazl), mockery (al-huzʾ), reproach (al-taʿyīr), disputation (al-mirāʾ), opposition (al-muḍāddah), treachery (al-ghadr), and intense greed for superfluous wealth and status. All of these together are base traits, reprehensible by Sacred Law, and there is no deliverance from anger while these causes remain. Thus, one must necessarily remove these causes by their opposites.

So you should kill self-conceit (al-zahw) through humility (al-tawāḍuʿ), and kill vanity (al-ʿujb) through your knowledge of your own soul, as will be explained in the Book of Pride and Vanity. You should remove vainglory (al-fakhr) by recognizing that you are of the same kind as your servant, for all people are united in lineage through a single father, and they differ only in degrees of merit. The children of Adam are one species, and glory belongs only to virtues. Yet pride, vanity, and arrogance are the greatest of vices — they are their root and their head. If you are not free of these, then you have no merit over anyone else. So why do you boast, when you are of the same kind as your servant in terms of bodily constitution, lineage, and both outward and inward organs? As for jesting (al-mizāḥ), you remove it by occupying yourself with religious obligations that consume one's entire lifespan, and which leave no surplus for it once you know this. As for frivolity (al-hazl), you remove it through earnestness in seeking virtues, good character traits, and religious sciences that will convey you to the felicity of the Hereafter. As for mockery (al-huzʾ), you remove it through magnanimity that refrains from harming people, and through guarding your own soul against being mocked. As for reproach (al-taʿyīr), it is removed by caution against ugly speech and guarding the soul against bitter retorts. As for intense greed for the luxuries of life, it is removed through contentment (al-qanāʿah) with what necessity requires, seeking the honor of self-sufficiency and rising above the humiliation of need.

Every one of these traits and every one of these qualities requires, for its treatment, discipline (riyāḍah) and the endurance of hardship. The sum of their discipline reduces to knowledge of their harmful consequences, so that the soul becomes averse to them and repelled by their ugliness; then, perseverance in practicing their opposites for a long period, until they become familiar and easy to the soul through habit. When they are effaced from the soul, then it has been purified and cleansed of these vices, and it is also delivered from the anger that is generated from them.

Among the strongest incitements to anger among most of the ignorant is their naming anger "courage" (shajāʿah), "manliness" (rujūliyyah), "self-respect" (ʿizzat nafs), and "loftiness of aspiration" (kibar himmah), and their labeling it with praiseworthy epithets — out of stupidity and ignorance — until the soul inclines toward it and deems it good. This is further reinforced by narrating tales of intense anger from great men in the context of praising their courage, for souls incline toward imitating great men, and thus anger is stirred up in the heart because of this. Calling this "self-respect" and "courage" is sheer ignorance; rather, it is a sickness of the soul and a deficiency of intellect. It is due to the weakness of the soul and its deficiency. The proof that it stems from weakness of soul is that the sick person becomes angry more quickly than the healthy one, the woman more quickly than the man, the boy more quickly than the grown man, the weak old man more quickly than the middle-aged man, and the person of bad character and ugly vices more quickly than the possessor of virtues. Indeed, the base man becomes angry over his appetite when a morsel escapes him, and over his miserliness when a grain is lost, to the point that he becomes angry at his family, his children, and his companions.

Rather, the strong one is he who masters his soul at the moment of anger, as the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The strong man is not the one who wrestles well; rather, the strong man is he who masters his soul at the moment of anger" {«لَيْسَ الشَّدِيدُ بِالصُّرَعَةِ إِنَّمَا الشَّدِيدُ الَّذِي يَمْلِكُ نَفْسَهُ عِنْدَ الْغَضَبِ»}. Rather, this ignorant person should be treated by reciting to him the stories of the forbearing and the forgiving, and what was deemed excellent among them of suppressing rage (kaẓm al-ghayẓ) — for this is transmitted from the prophets, the saints, the sages, the scholars, and the virtuous great kings. The opposite of this is transmitted from the Kurds, the Turks, the ignorant, and the stupid who have no intellect and no merit in them.

### ||| Exposition of the Treatment of Anger After Its Provocation

chapters.title_en: The Cure for Anger: The Compound of Knowledge and Action
chapters.arabic_text:
ما ذكرناه هو حسم لمواد الغضب وقطع لأسبابه حتى لا يهيج فإذا جرى سبب
هيجه فعنده يجب التثبت حتى لا يضطر صاحبه إلى العمل به على الوجه المذموم
وإنما يعالج الغضب عند هيجانه بمعجون العلم والعمل
أما العلم فهو ستة أمور
الأول أن يتفكر في الأخبار التي سنوردها في فضل كظم الغيظ والعفو والحلم
والاحتمال فيرغب في ثوابه فتمنعه شدة الحرص على ثواب الكظم عن التشفي
والانتقام وينطفيء عنه غيظه قال مالك بن أوس ابن الحدثان غضب عمر على رجل
وأمر بضربه فقلت يا أمير المؤمنين {خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن
الجاهلين} فكان عمر يقول {خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين} فكان
يتأمل في الآية وكان وقافا عند كتاب الله مهما تلي عليه كثير التدبر فيه
فتدبر فيه وخلى الرجل
وأمر عمر بن عبد العزيز بضرب رجل ثم قرأ قوله تعالى {والكاظمين الغيظ}
فقال لغلامه خل عنه
الثاني أن يخوف نفسه بعقاب الله وهو أن يقول قدرة الله على أعظم من قدرتي
على هذا الإنسان فلو أمضيت غضبي عليه لم آمن أن يمضي الله غضبه علي يوم
القيامة أحوج ما أكون إلى العفو فقد قال تعالى في بعض الكتب القديمة يا ابن
آدم اذكرني حين تغضب أذكرك حين أغضب فلا أمحقك فيمن أمحق وبعث رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم وصيفا إلى حاجة فأبطأ عليه فلما جاء قال لولا القصاص
لأوجعتك (1)
أي القصاص في القيامة وقيل ما كان في بني إسرائيل ملك إلا ومعه حكيم إذا
غضب أعطاه صحيفة فيها ارحم المسكين واخش الموت واذكر الآخرة فكان يقرؤها
حتى يسكن غضبه
الثالث أن يحذر نفسه عاقبة العداوة والانتقام وتشمر العدو لمقابلته
والسعي في هدم أغراضه والشماتة بمصائبه وهو لا يخلو عن المصائب فيخوف نفسه
بعواقب الغضب في الدنيا إن كان لا يخاف من الآخرة وهذا يرجع إلى تسليط شهوة
على غضب وليس هذا من أعمال الآخرة ولا ثواب عليه لأنه متردد على حظوظه
العاجلة يقدم بعضها على بعض إلا أن يكون محذوره أن تتشوش عليه في الدنيا
فراغته للعلم والعمل وما يعينه على الآخرة فيكون مثابا عليه
الرابع أن يتفكر في قبح صورته عند الغضب بأن يتذكر صورة غيره في حالة
الغضب ويتفكر في قبح الغضب في نفسه ومشابهة صاحبه للكلب الضاري والسبع
العادي ومشابهة الحليم الهادي التارك للغضب للأنبياء والأولياء والعلماء
والحكماء ويخير نفسه بين أن يتشبه بالكلاب والسباع وأراذل الناس وبين أن
يتشبه بالعلماء والأنبياء في عادتهم لتميل نفسه إلى حب الاقتداء بهؤلاء إن
كان قد بقي معه مسكة من عقل
الخامس أن يتفكر في السبب الذي يدعوه إلى الانتقام ويمنعه من كظم الغيظ
ولا بد وأن يكون له سبب مثل قول الشيطان له إن هذا يحمل منك على العجز وصغر
النفس والذلة والمهانة وتصير حقيرا في أعين الناس فيقول لنفسه ما أعجبك
تأنفين من الاحتمال الآن ولا تأنفين من خزي يوم القيامة والافتضاح إذا أخذ
هذا بيدك وانتقم PageV03P173
منك وتحذرين من أن تصغري في أعين الناس ولا تحذرين من  أن تصغري عند الله
والملائكة والنبيين فمهما كظم الغيظ فينبغي أن يكظمه لله وذلك يعظمه عند
الله فما له وللناس وذل من ظلمه يوم القيامة أشد من ذله لو انتقم الآن أفلا
يحب أن يكون هو القائم إذا نودي يوم القيامة ليقم من أجره على الله فلا
يقوم إلا من عفا فهذا وأمثاله من معارف الإيمان ينبغي أن يكرره على قلبه
السادس أن يعلم أن غضبه من تعجبه من جريان الشيء على وفق مراد الله لا
على وفق مراده فكيف يقول مرادي أولى من مراد الله ويوشك أن يكون غضب الله
عليه أعظم من غضبه
وأما العمل فأن تقول بلسانك أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم هكذا أمر رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن يقال عند الغيظ (1) حديث كان إذا غضبت عائشة
أخذ بأنفها وقال يا عويش قولي اللهم رب النبي محمد اغفر لي ذنبي وأذهب غيظ
قلبي الحديث أخرجه ابن السني في اليوم والليلة من حديثها وتقدم في الأذكار
والدعوات
فيستحب أن تقول ذلك فإن لم يزل بذلك فاجلس إن كنت قائما واضجع إن كنت
جالسا واقرب من الأرض التي منها خلقت لتعرف بذلك ذل نفسك واطلب بالجلوس
والاضجاع السكون فإن سبب الغضب الحرارة وسبب الحرارة الحركة
فقد قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الغضب جمرة توقد في القلب (2)
ألم تروا إلى انتفاخ أوداجه وحمره عينيه فإذا وجد أحدكم من ذلك شيئا فإن
كان قائما فليجلس وإن كان جالسا فلينم فإن لم يزل ذلك فليتوضا بالماء
البارد أو يغتسل فإن النار لا يطفئها إلا الماء فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم
إذا غضب أحدكم فليتوضأ بالماء فإنما الغضب من النار (3)
وفي رواية إن الغضب من الشيطان وإن الشيطان خلق من النار وإنما تطفأ
النار بالماء فإذا غضب أحدكم فليتوضأ وقال ابن عباس قال رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم وإذا غضبت فاسكت (4)
وقال أبو هريرة كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا غضب وهو قائم جلس
وإذا غضب وهو جالس اضطجع فيذهب غضبه (5)
وقال أبو سعيد الخدري قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ألا إن الغضب جمرة في
قلب ابن آدم (6)
ألا ترون إلى حمرة عينيه وانتفاخ أوداجه فمن وجد من ذلك شيئا فليلصق خده
بالأرض وكأن هذا إشارة إلى السجود وتمكين أعز الأعضاء من أذل المواضع وهو
التراب لتستشعر به النفس الذل وتزايل به العزة والزهو الذي هو سبب الغضب
وروي أن عمر غضب يوما فدعا بماء فاستنشق وقال إن الغضب من الشيطان وهذا
يذهب الغضب وقال عروة PageV03P174
ابن محمد لما استعملت على اليمن قال لي أبي أوليت قلت نعم قال فإذا غضبت
فانظر إلى السماء فوقك وإلى الأرض تحتك ثم عظم خالقهما
وروي أن أبا ذر قال لرجل يا ابن الحمراء في خصومة بينهما فبلغ ذلك رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا أبا ذر بلغني أنك اليوم عيرت أخاك بأمه
فقال نعم فانطلق أبو ذر ليرضي صاحبه فسبقه الرجل فسلم عليه فذكر ذلك لرسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا أبا ذر ارفع رأسك فانظر ثم اعلم أنك لست
بأفضل من أحمر فيها ولا أسود إلا أن تفضله بعمل ثم قال إذا غضبت فإن كنت
قائما فاقعد وإن كنت قاعدا فاتكيء وإن كنت متكئا فاضطجع (1)
وقال المعتمر بن سليمان كان رجل ممن كان قبلكم يغضب فيشتد غضبه فكتب
صحائف وأعطى كل صحيفة رجلا وقال للأول إذا غضبت فأعطني هذه وقال للثاني إذا
سكن بعض غضبي فأعطني هذه وقال للثالث إذا ذهب غضبي فأعطني هذه فاشتد غضبه
يوما فأعطى الصحيفة الأولى فإذا فيها ما أنت وهذا الغضب إنك لست بإله إنما
أنت بشر يوشك أن يأكل بعضك بعضا فسكن بعض غضبه فأعطي الثانية فإذا فيها
ارحم من في الأرض يرحمك من في السماء فأعطي الثالثة فإذا فيها خذ الناس بحق
الله فإنه لا يصلهم إلا ذلك أي لا تعطل الحدود وغضب المهدي على رجل فقال
شبيب لا تغضب لله بأشد من غضبه  لنفسه فقال خلوا سبيله
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ض-ب (ghaḍaba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intense heat and swelling of the veins; the boiling of the blood in response to provocation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A divinely-instilled natural faculty (gharīzah) that, when unrestrained, veils the intellect (ʿaql) and drives toward vengeance (intiqām).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the physiological inflammation; metaphorical (majāz) for the soul's agitation — the Prophet's description of it as a "burning ember" (jamrah) is treated as quasi-literal in this therapeutic context.
- Root: ك-ظ-م (kaẓama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tie the mouth of a water-skin; to suppress and contain what would otherwise burst forth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The praiseworthy restraint of anger for divine reward — a central Quranic virtue (al-kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical containment; metaphorical for the soul's self-mastery against the eruption of rage.
- Root: ح-ل-م (ḥalima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Forbearance, clemency, and the deliberate postponement of retaliation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The mature virtue of the prophets and awliyā', opposed to the impulsiveness of jahl (ignorance-driven rashness).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the settled temperament; metaphorical for the deliberate choice of pardon over punishment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Prohibition (al-nahy fī ṣīghat al-sharṭ) — The imperative "if you are standing, sit" (fa-in kunta qāʾiman fa-qʿud) employs the conditional particle (in) followed by a command, indicating a causal therapeutic sequence: the physical posture change is syntactically bound to the emotional state, mirroring the natural causality of heat and motion.
chapters.translation:
I say: What we have mentioned is a severing of the materials of anger and a cutting off of its causes, so that it does not flare up. But when a cause of its agitation does occur, then at that point one must exercise self-restraint (al-tathabbut), so that its possessor is not compelled to act upon it in the blameworthy manner. Anger, when it is agitated, is only treated with the compound of knowledge (ʿilm) and action (ʿamal).

As for knowledge, it consists of six matters:

**The First:** That he reflect upon the reports (akhbār) which we shall cite concerning the merit of suppressing rage (kaẓm al-ghayẓ), pardon (al-ʿafw), forbearance (al-ḥilm), and endurance (al-iḥtimāl). Thus he will be drawn to desire its reward, and the intensity of his craving for the reward of suppression will prevent him from venting his spite (al-tashaffī) and taking revenge, and his rage will be extinguished. Mālik ibn Aws ibn al-Ḥadathān said: ʿUmar became angry with a man and ordered that he be beaten. I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, {«Take forgiveness, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant»} (7:199)." And ʿUmar would (thereafter) recite {«Take forgiveness, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant»} — he would ponder the verse, and he was one who halted at the Book of God whenever it was recited to him, given to much reflection upon it. So he reflected upon it and released the man.

And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ordered a man to be beaten, then he recited the words of God Most High: {«And those who suppress their rage»} (3:134). He said to his servant: "Let him go."

**The Second:** That he frighten himself with God's punishment, by saying: God's power over me is greater than my power over this man. If I execute my anger upon him, I am not safe from God executing His anger upon me on the Day of Resurrection, at the very time I am most in need of pardon. For God Most High has said in some of the ancient books: "O son of Adam, remember Me when you are angry, and I will remember you when I am angry, and I will not annihilate you among those whom I annihilate." And the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) sent a servant-boy on an errand, and he was slow in returning. When he came, he (the Prophet) said: "Were it not for retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ), I would have hurt you" — meaning retaliation on the Day of Resurrection. And it is said: There was no king among the Children of Israel except that he had a sage with him; when he became angry, the sage would hand him a scroll containing: "Have mercy on the poor, fear death, and remember the Hereafter." He would read it until his anger subsided.

**The Third:** That he warn himself against the consequence of enmity and vengeance — that the enemy will gird himself to retaliate, strive to demolish his aims, and gloat over his misfortunes — and he is not free from misfortunes. So he frightens himself with the worldly consequences of anger, if he does not fear the Hereafter. This reverts to subjugating one appetite (shahwah) to another appetite (ghaḍab), and it is not among the works of the Hereafter, nor is there reward upon it, because he is deliberating over his immediate shares (ḥuẓūẓ), preferring some over others — unless his fear is that his worldly leisure for knowledge and action, and what aids him toward the Hereafter, would be disturbed; in that case he is rewarded for it.

**The Fourth:** That he reflect upon the ugliness of his own form when angry, by recalling the form of another person in a state of anger, and reflect upon the ugliness of anger in itself — that its possessor resembles a predatory dog (al-kalb al-ḍārī) and a ferocious beast (al-sabuʿ al-ʿādī) — while the forbearing, rightly-guided one who abandons anger resembles the prophets, the awliyā', the scholars, and the sages. He should give himself the choice between resembling dogs, beasts, and the dregs of mankind, or resembling the scholars and prophets in their habit, so that his soul may incline toward loving emulation of these — if any shred of intellect (muskah min ʿaql) remains with him.

**The Fifth:** That he reflect upon the cause that summons him to vengeance and prevents him from suppressing his rage. There must be some cause, such as the devil's whisper to him: "This (forbearance) will be taken from you as weakness, smallness of soul, abasement, and humiliation, and you will become contemptible in people's eyes." So he should say to himself: "How strange of you! You are too proud to endure now, yet you are not too proud to face disgrace on the Day of Resurrection and exposure when this man seizes you and takes vengeance upon you. You fear becoming small in people's eyes, yet you do not fear becoming small before God, the angels, and the prophets." So whenever one suppresses his rage, he should suppress it for God — and that magnifies him before God. What has he to do with people? The humiliation of the one wronged on the Day of Resurrection is more severe than his humiliation were he to take revenge now. Would he not love to be among those who stand when the call is made on the Day of Resurrection: "Let stand those whose reward is due from God" — and none stand except those who pardoned? This and its like are among the cognitions of faith (maʿārif al-īmān) which he should repeat to his heart.

**The Sixth:** That he know that his anger arises from his astonishment that a thing proceeds according to God's will rather than his own will. How can he say: "My will is more worthy than God's will"? It is likely that God's anger upon him is greater than his anger (upon another).

As for **action**, it is that you say with your tongue: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan" (aʿūdhu billāhi min al-shayṭān al-rajīm). Thus did the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) command that it be said at the moment of rage. (A ḥadīth: When ʿĀʾishah became angry, he would take her by the nose and say: "O ʿUwaysh, say: O God, Lord of the Prophet Muhammad, forgive me my sin and remove the rage of my heart." This ḥadīth was narrated by Ibn al-Sunnī in al-Yawm wa al-Laylah from her report, and it has preceded in the section on remembrances and supplications.)

So it is recommended (yustaḥabb) that you say this. If it does not cease by that, then sit if you are standing, and lie down if you are sitting. Draw near to the earth from which you were created, so that by this you recognize the abasement of your soul. Seek tranquility through sitting and lying down, for the cause of anger is heat, and the cause of heat is motion.

The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Anger is an ember (jamrah) kindled in the heart — do you not see the swelling of his jugular veins and the redness of his eyes? So when any of you finds something of that, if he is standing, let him sit; and if he is sitting, let him lie down." If it does not cease by that, then let him perform ablution with cold water, or bathe — for fire is only extinguished by water. He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "When one of you becomes angry, let him perform ablution with water, for anger is from fire." In another narration: "Anger is from Satan, and Satan was created from fire, and fire is only extinguished by water. So when one of you becomes angry, let him perform ablution."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "And when you become angry, be silent."

Abū Hurayrah said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), when he became angry while standing, would sit; and when he became angry while sitting, he would lie down — and his anger would depart.

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Verily, anger is an ember in the heart of the son of Adam — do you not see the redness of his eyes and the swelling of his jugular veins? So whoever finds something of that, let him press his cheek to the ground." This appears to be an allusion to prostration (sujūd) — placing the most honored of limbs upon the most abased of places, which is dust — so that the soul may sense abasement thereby, and the pride and haughtiness that are the cause of anger may depart from it.

It is narrated that ʿUmar became angry one day, so he called for water and sniffed it (into his nose), saying: "Anger is from Satan, and this removes anger."

ʿUrwah ibn Muḥammad said: When I was appointed governor over Yemen, my father said to me: "Have you been appointed?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then when you become angry, look to the sky above you and the earth below you, then magnify their Creator."

It is narrated that Abū Dharr said to a man, "O son of a red woman" (yā ibn al-ḥamrāʾ), during a dispute between them. That reached the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and he said: "O Abū Dharr, it has reached me that today you insulted your brother by (mentioning) his mother." He said: "Yes." So Abū Dharr went off to appease his companion, but the man preceded him and greeted him (first). That was mentioned to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and he said: "O Abū Dharr, raise your head and look, then know that you are not better than a red man or a black man therein, except that you surpass him by (righteous) deed." Then he said: "When you become angry — if you are standing, sit; if you are sitting, recline; if you are reclining, lie down."

Al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān said: There was a man among those before you who would become angry, and his anger would intensify. He wrote scrolls and gave each scroll to a man. He said to the first: "When I become angry, give me this." He said to the second: "When my anger has partially subsided, give me this." He said to the third: "When my anger has gone, give me this." One day his anger intensified, so the first scroll was given to him, and in it was: "What are you and this anger? You are not a god; you are only a mortal — soon one part of you will consume another." So part of his anger subsided, and the second was given to him, and in it was: "Have mercy on those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy on you." Then the third was given to him, and in it was: "Take people by the right of God, for nothing else will benefit them" — meaning: do not suspend the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd).

And al-Mahdī became angry with a man, and Shabīb said: "Do not become angry for God more intensely than His own anger for Himself." So he said: "Let him go free."

chapters.title_en: The Virtue of Suppressing Anger (Faḍīlat Kaẓm al-Ghayẓ)
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| فضيلة كظم الغيظ

قال الله تعالى {والكاظمين الغيظ} وذكر ذلك في معرض المدح وقال رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم من كف غضبه كف الله عنه عذابه ومن اعتذر إلى ربه قبل
الله عذره ومن خزن لسانه ستر الله عورته (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أشدكم من غلب نفسه عند الغضب وأحلمكم من عفا عند
القدرة (3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من كظم غيظا ولو شاء أن يمضيه لأمضاه ملأ الله
قلبه يوم القيامة رضا وفي رواية ملأ الله قلبه أمنا وإيمانا (4)
وقال ابن عمر قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما جرع عبد جرعة أعظم
أجرا من جرعة غيظ كظمها ابتغاء وجه الله تعالى (5)
وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن لجهنم بابا
PageV03P175
لا يدخله إلا من شفى غيظه بمعصية الله تعالى (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما من جرعة أحب إلى الله تعالى من جرعة غيظ
كظمها عبد وما كظمها عبد إلا ملأ الله قلبه إيمانا (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من كظم غيظا وهو قادر على أن ينفذه دعاه الله
على رءوس الخلائق ويخيره من أي الحور شاء (3)
الآثار قال عمر رضي الله عنه من اتقى الله لم يشف غيظه ومن خاف الله لم
يفعل ما يشاء ولولا يوم القيامة لكان غير ما ترون وقال لقمان لابنه يا بني
لا تذهب ماء وجهك بالمسألة ولا تشف غيظك بفضيحتك واعرف قدرك تنفعك معيشتك
وقال أيوب حلم ساعة يدفع شرا كثيرا
واجتمع سفيان الثوري وأبو خزيمة اليربوعي والفضيل بن عياض فتذاكروا الزهد
فأجمعوا على أن أفضل الأعمال الحلم عند الغضب والصبر عند الجزع
وقال رجل لعمر رضي الله عنه والله ما تقضي بالعدل ولا تعطي الجزل فغضب
عمر حتى عرف ذلك في وجهه فقال له رجل يا أمير المؤمنين ألا تسمع إلى الله
تعالى يقول {خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين} فهذا من الجاهلين
فقال عمر صدقت فكأنما  كانت نارا فأطفئت وقال محمد بن كعب ثلاث من كن فيه
استكمل الإيمان بالله إذا رضي لم يدخله رضاه في الباطل وإذا غضب لم يخرجه
غضبه عن الحق وإذا قدر لم يتناول ما ليس له وجاء رجل إلى سلمان فقال يا عبد
الله أوصني قال لا تغضب قال لا أقدر قال فإن غضبت فأمسك لسانك ويدك

### ||| بيان فضيلة الحلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ظ-م (Ka-Ẓa-Ma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is to tie the mouth of a waterskin, to hold back, to restrain, to suppress what is within — specifically the retention of that which seeks to escape.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, kaẓm denotes the deliberate retention of the soul's agitation (ghayẓ) — a volitional act of self-mastery that prevents the internal fire of wrath from manifesting in outward speech or action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physically tying a vessel's opening; metaphorical (majāz) — restraining the self from venting its fury. The metaphor is sustained throughout the prophetic traditions cited here.
- Root: غ-ي-ظ (Ghayn-Yā-Ẓā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intense, boiling anger that fills the chest — a deeper, more concealed rage than mere ḥadab (irritation).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ghayẓ is the internal state of wrath; kaẓm is the virtuous act of swallowing it back. The pairing of the two roots in the Quranic verse {والكاظمين الغيظ} establishes the moral paradigm: the internal passion is natural, the suppression is meritorious.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The Quranic phrase is literal in its moral application — the "swallowing" is a real, though non-physical, act of the soul.
- Root: ح-ل-م (Ḥā-Lām-Mīm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Forbearance, clemency, the quality of one who possesses sound judgment and does not react impulsively; also dream (as a distinct homonym).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥilm is the settled disposition of the intellect that restrains the self from retaliatory passion when one has the power to do so — the mature virtue that kaẓm cultivates.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥilm is used literally for the moral trait; the rhetorical force lies in its contrast with jahl (ignorance/folly) in the Quranic command {وأعرض عن الجاهلين}.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The prophetic traditions employ repeated conditional clauses (من كظم... ملأ الله) where the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) are linked by the particle man (whoever), establishing a causal nexus between human action and divine recompense. The apodosis frequently employs the perfect tense (ملأ) for future certainty, a classical usage indicating the assured nature of the divine promise.
chapters.translation:
### ||| The Virtue of Suppressing Anger

Allah Most High has said: {«والكاظمين الغيظ»} (and those who suppress their anger) — and He mentioned this in the context of praise. And the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever restrains his anger, Allah restrains His punishment from him; whoever makes an excuse to his Lord, Allah accepts his excuse; whoever guards his tongue, Allah conceals his shame."

And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "The strongest among you is he who overcomes his own self at the moment of anger, and the most forbearing among you is he who pardons when he has the power [to retaliate]."

And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever suppresses his anger — and had he wished to vent it, he could have done so — Allah will fill his heart with contentment on the Day of Resurrection." In another narration: "Allah will fill his heart with security and faith."

And Ibn ʿUmar said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "No servant has swallowed a draught greater in reward than a draught of anger which he suppressed, seeking thereby the Face of Allah Most High."

And Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Verily, Hell has a gate which none shall enter except the one who has vented his anger through disobedience to Allah Most High."

And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "There is no draught more beloved to Allah Most High than a draught of anger which a servant suppresses; and no servant suppresses it except that Allah fills his heart with faith."

And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever suppresses his anger while being able to give it full vent, Allah will call him on the Day of Resurrection before the heads of all creation, and will give him the choice of whichever of the ḥūr (maidens of Paradise) he wishes."

**The Reports (Āthār):**

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever fears Allah does not vent his anger; whoever dreads Allah does not do whatever he wishes. Were it not for the Day of Resurrection, things would be other than what you see."

And Luqmān said to his son: "O my son, do not squander the water of your face by begging, and do not vent your anger by disgracing yourself. Know your own worth, and your livelihood will benefit you."

And Ayyūb said: "An hour of forbearance repels much evil."

Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Khuzaymah al-Yarbūʿī, and al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ gathered together and discussed asceticism (zuhd), and they agreed that the most excellent of deeds are forbearance at the moment of anger and patience at the moment of distress.

A man said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "By Allah, you do not judge with justice, nor do you give generously!" ʿUmar became angry until it was recognized in his face. Then a man said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, will you not listen to what Allah Most High says: {«خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين»} (Take the forgiveness, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant) — and this man is among the ignorant?" ʿUmar said: "You have spoken the truth." And it was as though a fire had been lit within him and was then extinguished.

And Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb said: "Whoever possesses three qualities has perfected his faith in Allah: when he is pleased, his pleasure does not lead him into falsehood; when he is angry, his anger does not drive him from the truth; and when he has power, he does not seize what is not rightfully his."

A man came to Salmān and said: "O servant of Allah, counsel me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man said: "I cannot [help it]." He said: "Then if you become angry, restrain your tongue and your hand."

### ||| Exposition of the Virtue of Forbearance (Ḥilm)

chapters.title_en: On Forbearance (Ḥilm) Being Superior to Restraining Anger (Kaẓm al-Ghayẓ), and the Path to Acquiring It
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الحلم أفضل من كظم الغيظ لأن كظم الغيظ عبارة عن التحلم أي تكلف
الحلم ولا يحتاج إلى كظم الغيظ إلا من هاج غيظه ويحتاج فيه إلى مجاهدة
شديدة ولكن إذا تعود ذلك مدة صار ذلك اعتيادا فلا يهيج الغيظ وإن هاج فلا
يكون في كظمه تعب وهو الحلم الطبيعي وهو دلالة كمال العقل واستيلائه
وانكسار قوة الغضب وخضوعها للعقل ولكن ابتداؤه التحلم وكظم الغيظ تكلفا
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما العلم بالتعلم والحلم بالتحلم ومن يتخير
الخير يعطه ومن يتوق الشر يوقه (4) وأشار بهذا إلى أن اكتساب الحلم طريقه
التحلم أولا وتكلفه كما أن اكتساب العلم طريقه التعلم
وقال أبو هريرة
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اطلبوا العلم واطلبوا مع العلم السكينة
والحلم لينوا لمن تعلمون ولمن تتعلمون منه ولا تكونوا من جبابرة العلماء
فيغلب جهلكم حلمكم (5)
وأشار بهذا إلى أن التكبر والتجبر هو الذي يهيج الغضب ويمنع من الحلم
واللين
وكان من دعائه صلى الله عليه وسلم اللهم أغنني بالعلم وزيني بالحلم
وأكرمني بالتقوى وجملني بالعافية (6)
وقال أبو هريرة قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم {ابتغوا} PageV03P176
الرفعة عند الله قالوا وما هي يا رسول الله قال تصل من قطعك وتعطي من
حرمك وتحلم عمن جهل عليك (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم خمس من سنن المرسلين الحياء والحلم والحجامة
والسواك والتعطر (2) حديث علي إن الرجل المسلم ليدرك بالحلم درجة الصائم
القائم الحديث أخرجه الطبراني في الأوسط بسند ضعيف (3) حديث أبي هريرة أن
رجلا قال يا رسول الله إن لي قرابة أصلهم ويقطعوني وأحسن إليهم ويسيئون إلي
ويجهلون علي وأحلم عنهم الحديث رواه مسلم (4) حديث قال رجل من المسلمين
اللهم ليس عندي صدقة أتصدق بها فأيما رجل أصاب من عرضي شيئا فهو صدقة عليه
الحديث أخرجه أبو نعيم في الصحابة والبيهقي في الشعب من رواية عبد المجيد
بن أبي عبس بن جبر عن أبيه عن جده بإسناد لين زاد البيهقي عن علية بن زيد
وعلية هو الذي قال ذلك كما في أثناء الحديث وذكر ابن عبد البر في الاستيعاب
أنه رواه ابن عيينة عن عمرو بن دينار عن أبي صالح عن أبي هريرة أن رجلا من
المسلمين ولم يسمه وقال أظنه أبا ضمضم قلت وليس بأبي ضمضم إنما هو علية بن
زيد وأبو ضمضم ليس له صحبة وإنما هو متقدم (5) حديث أيعجز أحدكم أن يكون
كأبي ضمضم الحديث تقدم في آفات اللسان (6) حديث أن ابن مسعود مر بلغو معرضا
فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أصبح ابن مسعود وأمسى كريما أخرجه ابن
المبارك في البر والصلة (7) حديث اللهم لا يدركني ولا أدركه زمان لا يتعبون
فيه العليم ولا يستحيون فيه من الحليم الحديث أخرجه أحمد من حديث سهل بن
سعد بسند ضعيف (8) حديث ليليني منكم أولو الأحلام والنهى الحديث أخرجه مسلم
من حديث ابن مسعود دون قوله ولا تختلفوا فتختلف قلوبكم فهي عند أبي داود
والترمذي وحسنه وهي عند مسلم في حديث آخر لابن مسعود //
وروي أنه وفد على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الأشج فأناخ راحلته ثم عقلها
وطرح عنه ثوبين كانا عليه وأخرج من العيبة ثوبين حسنين فلبسهما وذلك بعين
رسول الله PageV03P177
صلى الله عليه وسلم يرى ما يصنع ثم أقبل يمشي إلى رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم فقال عليه السلام إن فيك يا أشج خلقين يحبهما الله ورسوله قال ما
هما بأبي أنت وأمي يا رسول الله قال الحلم والأناة فقال خلتان تخلقتهما أو
خلقان جبلت عليهما فقال بل خلقان جبلك الله عليهما فقال الحمد الله الذي
جبلني على خلقين يحبهما الله ورسوله  (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله يحب الحليم الحي الغني المتعفف أبا
العيال التقي ويبغض الفاحش البذي السائل الملحف الغبي (2)
وقال ابن عباس قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاث من لم تكن فيه واحدة
منهن فلا تعتدوا بشيء من عمله تقوى تحجزه عن معاصي الله عز وجل وحلم يكف به
السفيه وخلق يعيش به في الناس (3)
وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا جمع الله الخلائق يوم القيامة
نادى مناد أين أهل الفضل فيقوم ناس وهم يسير فينطلقون سراعا إلى الجنة
فتتلقاهم الملائكة فتقولون لهم إنا نراكم سراعا إلى الجنة فيقولون نحن أهل
الفضل فيقولون لهم ما كان فضلكم فيقولون كنا إذا ظلمنا صبرنا وإذا أسيء
إلينا عفونا وإذ جهل علينا حلمنا فيقال لهم ادخلوا الجنة فنعم أجر العاملين
// حديث إذا جمع الخلائق نادى مناد أين أهل الفضل فيقوم ناس الحديث وفيه
إذا جهل علينا حلمنا أخرجه البيهقي في شعب الإيمان من رواية عمرو بن شعيب
عن أبيه عن جده قال البيهقي في إسناده ضعف
الآثار قال عمر رضي الله عنه تعلموا العلم وتعلموا للعلم السكينة والحلم
وقال علي رضي الله عنه ليس الخير أن يكثر مالك وولدك ولكن الخير أن يكثر
علمك ويعظم حلمك وأن لا تباهي الناس بعبادة الله وإذا أحسنت حمدت الله
تعالى وإذا أسأت استغفرت الله تعالى وقال الحسن اطلبوا العلم وزينوه
بالوقار والحلم وقال أكثم بن صيفي دعامة العقل الحلم وجماع الأمر الصبر
وقال أبو الدرداء أدركت الناس ورقا لا شوك فيه فأصبحوا شوكا لا ورق فيه إن
عرفتهم نقدوك وإن تركتهم لم يتركوك قالوا كيف نصنع قال تقرضهم عن عرضك ليوم
فقرك وقال علي رضي الله عنه أن أول ما عوض الحليم من حلمه أن الناس كلهم
أعوانه على الجاهل وقال معاوية رحمه الله تعالى لا يبلغ العبد مبلغ الرأي
حتى يغلب حلمه جهله وصبره شهوته ولا يبلغ ذلك إلا بقوة العلم وقال معاوية
لعمرو بن الأهتم أي الرجال أشجع قال  من رد جهله بحلمه قال أي الرجال أسخى
قال من بذل دنياه لصلاح دينه وقال أنس بن مالك في قوله تعالى {فإذا الذي
بينك وبينه عداوة كأنه ولي حميم} إلى قوله {عظيم} هو الرجل يشتمه أخوه
فيقول إن كنت كاذبا فغفر الله لك وإن كنت صادقا فغفر الله لي وقال بعضهم
شتمت فلانا من أهل البصرة فحلم علي فاستعبدني بها زمانا وقال معاوية لعرابة
بن أوس بم سدت قومك يا عرابة قال يا أمير المؤمنين كنت أحلم عن جاهلهم
وأعطي سائلهم وأسعى في حوائجهم فمن فعل فعلي فهو مثلي ومن جاوزني فهو أفضل
مني ومن قصر عني فأنا خير منه وسب رجل ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما فلما فرغ
قال يا عكرمة هل للرجل حاجة فنقضيها فنكس الرجل رأسه واستحى وقال رجل لعمر
بن عبد العزيز أشهد أنك من الفاسقين فقال ليس تقبل شهادتك وعن علي بن
الحسين بن علي رضي الله عنهم أنه سبه رجل فرمى إليه بخميصة كانت عليه وأمر
له بألف درهم فقال بعضهم جمع له خمس خصال محمودة الحلم وإسقاط الأذى وتخليص
الرجل مما يبعد من الله عز وجل وحمله على الندم والتوبة ورجوعه إلى مدح بعد
الذم اشترى جميع ذلك بشيء من الدنيا يسير وقال رجل لجعفر بن محمد
PageV03P178
إنه قد وقع بيني وبين قوم منازعة في أمر وإني أريد أن أتركه فأخشى أن
يقال لي إن تركك له ذل فقال جعفر إنما الذليل الظالم وقال الخليل بن أحمد
كان يقال من أساء فأحسن إليه فقد جعل له حاجز من قلبه يردعه عن مثل إساءته
وقال الأحنف بن قيس لست بحليم ولكنني أتحلم وقال وهب بن منبه من يرحم يرحم
ومن يصمت يسلم ومن يجهل يغلب ومن يعجل يخطيء ومن يحرص على الشر لا يسلم ومن
لا يدع المراء يشتم ومن لا يكره الشر يأثم ومن يكره الشر يعصم ومن يتبع
وصية الله يحفظ ومن يحذر الله يأمن ومن يتول الله يمنع ومن لا يسأل  الله
يفتقر ومن يأمن مكر الله يخذل ومن يستعن بالله يظفر وقال رجل لمالك بن
دينار بلغني أنك ذكرتني بسوء قال أنت إذن أكرم علي من نفسي إني إذا فعلت
ذلك أهديت لك حسناتي وقال بعض العلماء الحلم أرفع من العقل لأن الله تعالى
تسمى به وقال رجل لبعض الحكماء والله لأسبنك سبا يدخل معك في قبرك فقال معك
يدخل لا معي ومر المسيح ابن مريم عليه الصلاة والسلام بقوم من اليهود
فقالوا له شرا فقال لهم خيرا فقيل له إنهم يقولون شرا وأنت تقول خيرا فقال
كل ينفق مما عنده وقال لقمان ثلاثة لا يعرفون إلا عند ثلاث لا يعرف الحليم
إلا عند الغضب ولا الشجاع إلا عند الحرب ولا الأخ إلى عند الحاجة إليه ودخل
على بعض الحكماء صديق له فقدم إليه طعاما فخرجت امرأة الحكيم وكانت سيئة
الخلق فرفعت المائدة وأقبلت على شتم الحكيم فخرج الصديق مغضبا فتبعه الحكيم
وقال له تذكر يوم كنا في منزلك نطعم فسقطت دجاجة على المائدة فأفسدت ما
عليها فلم يغضب أحد منا قال نعم قال فاحسب أن هذه مثل تلك الدجاجة فسرى عن
الرجل غضبه وانصرف وقال صدق الحكيم الحلم شفاء من كل ألم وضرب رجل قدم حكيم
فأوجعه فلم يغضب فقيل له في ذلك فقال أقمته مقام حجر تعثرت به فذبحت الغضب
وقال محمود الوراق
سألزم نفسي الصفح عن كل مذنب ... وإن كثرت منه علي الجرائم
وما الناس إلا واحد من ثلاثة ... شريف ومشروف ومثلي مقاوم
فأما الذي فوقي فأعرف قدره ... وأتبع فيه الحق والحق لازم
وأما الذي دوني فإن قال صنت عن ... إجابته عرضي وإن لام لائم
وأما الذي مثل فإن زل أو هفا ... تفضلت إن الفضل بالحلم حاكم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح ل م (Ḥ-L-M)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is forbearance, clemency, and the quality of deliberate restraint; also used for the dream-state (ru'yā) as a suspension of hasty action. Al-Farāhīdī notes it as a virtue of the mature intellect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, ḥilm is the rational faculty's governance over the irascible appetite (quwwat al-ghaḍab), a trait of the prophets and the godly; it is the mean between recklessness (ṭaysh) and cowardly passivity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally (ḥaqīqah), ḥilm is an innate settled disposition; metaphorically (majāz), it is applied to acquired forbearance (taḥallum) as if it were natural, since the acquired state becomes second nature.
- Root: غ ي ظ (Gh-Y-Ẓ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intense internal rage or choler that boils within the breast, distinct from external wrath (ghaḍab) in that it is the concealed inflammation of the spirit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Kaẓm al-ghayẓ is the act of swallowing or suppressing this internal fire—a commanded virtue in the Qur'an {«وَالْكَاظِمِينَ الْغَيْظَ»}—signifying the soul's victory over its lower impulse.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Kaẓm is literal (ḥaqīqah) for sealing a waterskin; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for containing the boiling of rage, implying effort and strain.
- Root: ع ق ل (ʿ-Q-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The intellect as a fetter (ʿiqāl) that binds the soul from reckless action; its perfection is manifest in ḥilm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): ʿAql is the instrument of discernment (tamyīz) and the substrate of moral responsibility (taklīf); its dominance over the passions is the goal of spiritual striving (mujāhadah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the rational faculty; metaphorically for the practical wisdom that restrains, as in "he is possessed of ʿaql" meaning he is fettered from folly.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Causal Clauses (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The sentence "إذا تعود ذلك مدة صار ذلك اعتيادا" employs a temporal-conditional structure where the protasis (condition) establishes a habitual action, and the apodosis (result) follows as a necessary consequence, mirroring the naturalization of acquired virtue.
chapters.translation:
Know that forbearance (ḥilm) is superior to restraining anger (kaẓm al-ghayẓ), because restraining anger is but an expression for feigning forbearance (taḥallum)—that is, undertaking the burden of forbearance with effort. None needs to restrain his anger save one whose rage has been provoked, and therein he requires severe striving (mujāhadah). Yet when one becomes accustomed to this over a period, it becomes a habit, so that rage is no longer provoked; and if it is provoked, there is no fatigue in restraining it. This is natural forbearance (al-ḥilm al-ṭabīʿī), and it is the indication of the perfection of the intellect, its dominance, the breaking of the power of anger, and its submission to reason. But its beginning is feigned forbearance (taḥallum) and restraining anger as a deliberate effort.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Knowledge is only attained by learning, and forbearance is only attained by feigning forbearance. Whoever seeks after good is given it, and whoever guards against evil is protected from it." (4) By this he indicated that the path to acquiring forbearance is first to feign it and undertake it as a burden, just as the path to acquiring knowledge is learning.

Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Seek knowledge, and seek with knowledge tranquility (sakīnah) and forbearance. Be gentle with those you teach and those from whom you learn, and do not be among the tyrants of the scholars, lest your ignorance overcome your forbearance." (5) By this he indicated that arrogance and domineering pride are what provoke anger and prevent forbearance and gentleness.

Among his supplications ﷺ was: "O Allah, enrich me with knowledge, adorn me with forbearance, honor me with piety, and beautify me with well-being." (6)

Abū Hurayrah said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Seek elevation before Allah." They said: "What is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "That you join the one who cuts you off, give to the one who deprives you, and forbear with the one who acts ignorantly toward you." (1)

He ﷺ also said: "Five are from the traditions (sunan) of the messengers: modesty, forbearance, cupping, the toothstick, and perfuming oneself." (2)

[Regarding the ḥadīth of ʿAlī: "A Muslim man attains by forbearance the rank of the one who fasts and stands in prayer" — al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Awsaṭ with a weak chain.] (3)

[Regarding the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have relatives whom I join but they cut me off, I treat them well but they treat me ill, and they act ignorantly toward me, yet I forbear with them" — Muslim narrated it.] (4)

[Regarding the ḥadīth: A man from the Muslims said: "O Allah, I have no charity to give, so whatever man takes from my honor, let it be charity for him" — Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab from the narration of ʿAbd al-Majīd ibn Abī ʿAbs ibn Jabr from his father from his grandfather with a lenient chain. Al-Bayhaqī added from ʿAlīyah ibn Zayd, and ʿAlīyah is the one who said that, as appears in the body of the ḥadīth. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned in al-Istīʿāb that Ibn ʿUyaynah narrated it from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Abū Hurayrah that a man from the Muslims—without naming him—said: "I think he was Abū Ḍamḍam." I say: He was not Abū Ḍamḍam; rather, he was ʿAlīyah ibn Zayd. Abū Ḍamḍam had no companionship (ṣuḥbah); he was merely an earlier figure.] (5)

[Regarding the ḥadīth: "Is any of you unable to be like Abū Ḍamḍam?" — it has preceded in the section on the afflictions of the tongue.] (6)

[Regarding the ḥadīth that Ibn Masʿūd passed by idle talk, turning away from it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Ibn Masʿūd has become noble morning and evening" — Ibn al-Mubārak narrated it in al-Birr wa al-Ṣilah.] (7)
