  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic and Kalām discourse, mathal (parable) is a didactic device that renders abstract metaphysical truths perceptible through sensory analogies, as in {«وَتِلْكَ الْأَمْثَالُ نَضْرِبُهَا لِلنَّاسِ»} (And these parables We strike for mankind).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "likeness"; metaphorical sense here is "exemplary illustration" (tamthīl) — a rhetorical method of clarifying the unseen (ghayb) via the seen (shahādah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʾiḍāfah (genitive construction) — "bayān ṣifati al-dunyā" (exposition of the attribute of the world) is an annexation where the first term (bayān) governs the second (ṣifah), which in turn governs the third (al-dunyā), creating a nested chain of specification; the preposition "bi" (with/by) introduces the instrumental means (al-amthilah), indicating that the exposition is effected through parables.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us proceed to the exposition of the attribute of the world (ṣifat al-dunyā) by way of parables (amthilah) — for the comprehension of its true nature is not attained by bare definition, but by the striking of similitudes that unveil its reality to the discerning eye. Know that the world, in its essence, is a passing shadow and a fleeting dream; its delights are but mirages, and its terrors are but phantoms. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«الدُّنْيَا مَلْعُونَةٌ مَلْعُونٌ مَا فِيهَا إِلَّا ذِكْرُ اللَّهِ وَمَا وَالَاهُ»} (The world is cursed, and cursed is all that is in it, except the remembrance of God and what draws near to Him). So I shall strike for you parables from the visible realm (shahādah) that you may grasp the hidden reality (ghayb) of this abode — for the similitude of the world is like that of a traveler who stops beneath a tree for shade, then departs and leaves it behind; or like a sleeper who dreams of vast treasures, then awakens to find his hands empty. Thus the wise man does not incline to it, nor does he build his hopes upon it, but rather he takes from it only as a provision (zād) for the journey to the abode of permanence.

chapters.title_en: On the World (al-Dunyā) and Its Similitudes: Its Swift Passing, Deceptive Allure, and Perilous Consequences
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الدنيا سريعة الفناء قريبة الانقضاء تعد بالبقاء ثم تخلف في
الوفاء تنظر إليها فتراها ساكنة مستقرة وهي سائرة سيرا عنيفا ومرتحلة
ارتحالا سريعا ولكن الناظر إليها قد لا يحس بحركتها فيطمئن إليها وإنما يحس
عند انقضائها ومثالها الظل فإنه متحرك ساكن متحرك في الحقيقة ساكن الظاهر
لا تدرك حركته بالبصر الظاهر بل بالبصيرة الباطنة ولما ذكرت الدنيا عند
الحسن البصري رحمه الله أنشد وقال
أحلام نوم أو كظل زائل ... إن اللبيب بمثلها لا يخدع
وكان الحسن بن علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله وجهه يتمثل كثيرا ويقول
يا أهل لذات دنيا لا بقاء لها ... إن اغترارا بظل زائل حمق
وقيل إن هذا من قوله ويقال إن أعرابيا نزل بقوم فقدموا إليه طعاما فأكل
ثم قام إلى ظل خيمة لهم فنام هناك فاقتلعوا الخيمة فأصابته الشمس فانتبه
فقام وهو يقول
ألا إنما الدنيا كظل ثنية ... ولا بد يوما أن ظلك زائل
وكذلك قيل
وإن امرأ دنياه أكبر همه ... لمستمسك منها بحبل غرور
مثال آخر للدنيا من حيث التغرير بخيالاتها ثم الإفلاس منها بعد إفلاتها
تشبه خيالات المنام وأضغاث الأحلام قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
الدنيا حلم وأهلها عليها مجازون ومعاقبون (1) وقال يونس بن عبيد ما شبهت
نفسي في الدنيا إلا كرجل نام فرأى في منامه ما يكره وما يحب فبينما هو كذلك
إذ انتبه فكذلك الناس نيام فإذا ماتوا انتبهوا فإذا ليس بأيديهم شيء مما
ركنوا إليه وفرحوا به وقيل لبعض الحكماء أي شيء أشبه بالدنيا قال أحلام
النائم
مثال آخر للدنيا في عداوتها لأهلها وإهلاكها لبنيها اعلم أن طبع الدنيا
التلطف في الاستدراج أولا والتوصل إلى الإهلاك آخرا وهي كامرأة تتزين
للخطاب حتى إذا نكحتهم ذبحتهم وقد روي أن عيسى عليه السلام كوشف بالدنيا
فرآها في صورة عجوز هتماء عليها من كل زينة فقال لها كم تزوجت قالت لا
أحصيهم قال PageV03P214
فكلهم مات عنك أم كلهم طلقك قالت بل كلهم قتلت فقال عيسى عليه السلام
بؤسا لأزواجك الباقين كيف لا يعتبرون بأزواجك الماضين كيف تهلكينهم واحدا
بعد واحد ولا يكونون منك على حذر
مثال آخر للدنيا في مخالفة ظاهرها لباطنها اعلم أن الدنيا مزينة الظواهر
قبيحة السرائر وهي شبه عجوز متزينة تخدع الناس بظاهرها فإذا وقفوا على
باطنها وكشفوا القناع عن وجهها تمثل لهم قبائحها فندموا على اتباعها وخجلوا
من ضعف عقولهم في الاغترار بظاهرها
وقال العلاء بن زياد رأيت في المنام عجوزا كبيرة متعصبة الجلد عليها من
كل زينة الدنيا والناس عكوف عليها معجبون ينظرون إليها فجئت ونظرت وتعجبت
من نظرهم إليها وإقبالهم عليها فقلت لها ويلك من أنت قالت أو ما تعرفني قلت
لا أدري من أنت قالت أنا الدنيا قلت أعوذ بالله من شرك قالت إن أحببت أن
تعاذ من شري فابغض الدرهم قال أبو بكر بن عياش رأيت الدنيا في النوم عجوزا
مشوهة شمطاء تصفق بيديها وخلفها خلق يتبعونها ويصفقون ويرقصون فلما كانت
بحذائي أقبلت علي فقالت لو ظفرت بك لصنعت بك مثل ما صنعت بهؤلاء ثم بكى أبو
بكر وقال رأيت هذا قبل أن أقدم إلى بغداد وقال الفضيل بن عياض قال ابن عباس
يؤتى بالدنيا يوم القيامة في صورة عجوز شمطاء زرقاء أنيابها بادية ومشوه
خلقها فتشرف على الخلائق  فيقال لهم أتعرفون هذه فيقولون نعوذ بالله من
معرفة هذه فيقال هذه الدنيا التي تناحرتم عليها بها تقاطعتم الأرحام وبها
تحاسدتم وتباغضتم واغتررتم ثم يقذف بها في جهنم فتنادي أي رب أين أتباعي
وأشياعي فيقول الله عز وجل ألحقوا بها أتباعها وأشياعها وقال الفضيل بلغني
أن رجلا عرج بروحه فإذا امرأة على قارعة الطريق عليها من كل زينة من الحلي
والثياب وإذا لا يمر بها أحد إلا جرحته فإذا هي أدبرت كانت أحسن شيء رآه
الناس وإذا هي أقبلت كانت أقبح شيء رآه الناس عجوز شمطاء زرقاء عمشاء قال
فقلت أعوذ بالله منك قالت لا والله لا يعيذك الله مني حتى تبغض الدرهم قال
فقلت من أنت قالت أنا الدنيا
مثال آخر للدنيا وعبور الإنسان بها اعلم أن الأحوال ثلاثة حالة لم تكن
فيها شيئا وهي ما قبل وجودك إلى الأزل وحالة لا تكون فيها مشاهدا للدنيا
وهي ما بعد موتك إلى الأبد وحالة متوسطة بين الأبد والأزل وهي أيام حياتك
في الدنيا فانظر إلى مقدار طولها وانسبه إلى طرفي الأزل والأبد حتى تعلم
أنه أقل من منزل قصير في سفر بعيد ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم مالي
وللدنيا وإنما مثلي ومثل الدنيا كمثل راكب سار في يوم صائف فرفعت شجرة فقال
تحت ظلها ساعة ثم راح وتركها (1)
ومن رأى الدنيا بهذه العين لم يركن إليها ولم يبال كيف انقضت أيامه في ضر
وضيق أو في سعة ورفاهية بل لا يبني لبنة على لبنة
توفي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وما وضع لبنة على لبنة ولا قصبة على
قصبة (2)
ورأى بعض الصحابة يبني بيتا من جص فقال أرى الأمر أعجل من هذا وأنكر ذلك
(3) وإلى هذا أشار عيسى عليه السلام حيث قال الدنيا قنطرة فاعبروها ولا
تعمروها وهو مثال واضح فإن الحياة الدنيا معبر إلى الآخرة والمهد هو الميل
الأول على رأس القنطرة واللحد هو الميل الآخر PageV03P215
وبينهما مسافة محدودة فمن الناس من قطع نصف القنطرة ومنهم من  قطع ثلثها
ومنهم من قطع ثلثيها ومنهم من لم يبق له إلا خطوة واحدة وهو غافل عنها
وكيفما كان فلا بد له من العبور والبناء على القنطرة وتزيينها بأصناف
الزينة وأنت عابر عليها غاية الجهل والخذلان
مثال آخر للدنيا في لين موردها وخشونة مصدرها اعلم أن أوائل الدنيا تبدو
هينة لينة يظن الخائض فيها أن حلاوة خفضها كحلاوة الخوض فيها وهيهات فإن
الخوض في الدنيا سهل والخروج منها مع السلامة شديد وقد كتب علي رضي الله
عنه إلى سلمان الفارسي بمثالها فقال مثل الدنيا مثل الحية لين مسها ويقتل
سمها فأعرض عما يعجبك منها لقلة ما يصحبك منها وضع عنك همومها بما أيقنت من
فراقها وكن أسر ما تكون فيها أحذر ما تكون لها فإن صاحبها كلما اطمأن منها
إلى سرور أشخصه عنه مكروه والسلام
مثال آخر للدنيا في تعذر الخلاص من تبعتها بعد الخوض فيها قال رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما مثل صاحب الدنيا كالماشي في الماء هل يستطيع الذي
يمشي في الماء أن لا تبتل قدماه (1)
وهذا يعرفك جهالة قوم ظنوا أنهم يخوضون في نعيم الدنيا بأبدانهم وقلوبهم
منها مطهرة وعلائقها عن بواطنهم منقطعة وذلك مكيدة من الشيطان بل لو أخرجوا
مما هم فيه لكانوا من أعظم المتفجعين بفراقها فكما أن المشي على الماء
يقتضي بللا لا محالة يلتصق بالقدم فكذلك ملابسة الدنيا تقتضي علاقة وظلمة
في القلب بل علاقة الدنيا مع القلب تمنع حلاوة العبادة
قال عيسى عليه السلام بحق أقول لكم كما ينظر المريض إلى الطعام فلا يلتذ
به من شدة الوجع كذلك صاحب الدنيا لا يلتذ بالعبادة ولا يجد حلاوتها مع ما
يجد من حب الدنيا وبحق أقول لكم إن الدابة إذا لم تركب وتمتهن تصعب ويتغير
خلقها كذلك القلوب إذا لم ترقق بذكر الموت ونصب العبادة تقسو وتغلظ وبحق
أقول لكم إن الزق ما لم ينخرق أو يقحل يوشك أن يكون وعاء للعسل كذلك القلوب
ما لم تخرقها الشهوات أو يدنسها الطمع  أو يقسيها النعيم فسوف تكون أوعية
للحكمة وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما بقي من الدنيا بلاء وفتنة وإنما
مثل عمل أحدكم كمثل الوعاء إذا طاب أعلاه طاب أسفله وإذا خبث أعلاه خبث
أسفله (2)
مثال آخر لما بقي من الدنيا وقلته بالإضافة لما سبق قال رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم مثل هذه الدنيا مثل ثوب شق من أوله إلى آخره فبقي متعلقا
بخيط في آخره فيوشك ذلك الخيط أن ينقطع (3)
مثال آخر لتأدية علائق الدنيا بعضها إلى بعض حتى الهلاك قال عيسى عليه
السلام مثل طالب الدنيا مثل شارب ماء البحر كلما ازداد شربا ازداد عطشا حتى
يقتله
مثال آخر لمخالفة آخر الدنيا أولها ولنضارة أوائلها وخبث عواقبها اعلم أن
شهوات الدنيا في القلب لذيذة كشهوات الأطعمة في المعدة وسيجد العبد عند
الموت لشهوات الدنيا في قلبه من الكراهة والنتن والقبح ما يجده للأطعمة
اللذيذة إذا بلغت في المعدة غايتها وكما أن الطعام كلما كان ألذ طعما وأكثر
دسما وأظهر حلاوة كان رجيعه أقذر وأشد نتنا فكذلك كل شهوة في القلب هي أشهى
وألذ وأقوى فنتنها وكراهتها والتأذي بها عند الموت أشد PageV03P216
بل هي في الدنيا مشاهدة فإن من نهبت داره وأخذ أهله وماله وولده فتكون
مصيبته وألمه وتفجعه في كل ما فقد بقدر لذته به وحبه له وحرصه عليه فكل ما
كان عند الوجود أشهى عنده وألذ فهو عند الفقد أدهى وأمر ولا معنى للموت إلا
فقد ما في الدنيا وقد روي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال للضحاك بن سفيان
الكلابي الست تؤتى بطعامك وقد ملح وقزح ثم تشرب عليه اللبن والماء قال بلى
قال فإلام يصير قال إلى ما قد علمت يا رسول لله قال فإن الله عز وجل ضرب
مثل الدنيا بما يصير إليه طعام ابن آدم (1)
وقال أبي بن كعب قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الدنيا ضربت مثلا
لابن آدم فانظر إلى ما يخرج من ابن آدم وإن قزحه  وملحه إلام يصير (2) وقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم إن الله ضرب الدنيا لمطعم ابن آدم مثلا وضرب مطعم ابن
آدم للدنيا مثلا وإن قزحه وملحه (3)
وقال الحسن قد رأيتهم يطيبونه بالأفاويه والطيب ثم يرمون به حيث رأيتم
وقد قال الله عز وجل فلينظر الإنسان إلى طعامه قال ابن عباس إلى رجيعه وقال
رجل لابن عمر إني أريد أن أسألك وأستحي قال فلا تستحي واسأل قال إذا قضى
أحدنا حاجته فقام ينظر إلى ذلك منه قال نعم إن الملك يقول له انظر إلى ما
بخلت به انظر إلى ماذا صار وكان بشر بن كعب يقول انطلقوا حتى أريكم الدنيا
فيذهب بهم إلى مزبلة فيقول انظروا إلى ثمارهم ودجاجهم وعسلهم وسمنهم
مثال آخر في نسبة الدنيا إلى الآخرة قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما
الدنيا في الآخرة إلا كمثل ما يجعل أحدكم إصبعه في اليم فلينظر أحدكم بم
يرجع إليه (4)
مثال آخر للدنيا وأهلها في اشتغالهم بنعيم الدنيا وغفلتهم عن الآخرة
وخسرانهم العظيم بسببها اعلم أن أهل الدنيا مثلهم في غفلتهم مثل قوم ركبوا
سفينة فانتهت بهم إلى جزيرة فأمرهم الملاح بالخروج إلى قضاء الحاجة وحذرهم
المقام وخوفهم مرور السفينة واستعجالها فتفرقوا في نواحي الجزيرة فقضى
بعضهم حاجته وبادر إلى السفينة فصادف المكان خاليا فأخذ أوسع الأماكن
وألينها وأوفقها لمراده وبعضهم توقف في الجزيرة ينظر إلى أنوارها وأزهارها
العجيبة وغياضها الملتفة ونغمات طيورها الطيبة وألحانها الموزونة الغريبة
وصار يلحظ من بريتها أحجارها وجواهرها ومعادنها المختلفة الألوان والأشكال
الحسنة المنظر العجيبة النقوش السالبة أعين الناظرين بحسن زبرجدها وعجائب
صورها ثم تنبه لخطر فوات السفينة فرجع إليها فلم يصادف إلا مكانا ضيقا حرجا
فاستقر فيه وبعضهم أكب على تلك الأصداف والأحجار وأعجبه حسنها ولم تسمح
نفسه بإهمالها فاستصحب منها جملة فلم يجد في السفينة إلا مكانا ضيقا وزاده
ما حمله من الحجارة ضيقا وصار ثقيلا عليه ووبالا فندم على أخذه ولم يقدر
على رميه ولم يجد مكانا لوضعه فحمله في السفينة على  عنقه وهو متأسف على
أخذه وليس ينفعه التأسف
وبعضهم تولج الغياض ونسي المركب وبعد في متفرجه ومتنزهه منه حتى لم يبلغه
نداء الملاح لاشتغاله بأكل تلك الثمار واستشمام تلك الأنوار والتفرج بين
تلك الأشجار وهو مع ذلك خائف على نفسه من السباع وغير خال من السقطات
PageV03P217
والنكبات ولا منفك عن شوك ينشب بثيابه وغضن يجرح بدنه وشوكة تدخل في رجله
وصوت هائل يفزع منه وعوسج يخرق ثيابه ويهتك عورته ويمنعه عن الانصراف لو
أراده فلما بلغه نداء أهل السفينة انصرف مثقلا بما معه ولم يجد في المركب
موضعا فبقي في الشط حتى مات جوعا وبعضهم لم يبلغه النداء وسارت السفينة
فمنهم من افترسته السباع ومنهم من تاه فهام على وجهه حتى هلك ومنهم من مات
في الأوحال ومنهم من نهشته الحيات فتفرقوا كالجيف المنتنة
وأما من وصل إلى المركب بثقل ما أخذه من الأزهار والأحجار فقد استرقته
وشغله الحزن بحفظها والخوف من فوتها وقد ضيقت عليه مكانه فلم يلبث أن ذبلت
تلك الأزهار وكمدت تلك الألوان والأحجار فظهر نتن رائحتها فصارت مع كونها
مضيقة عليه مؤذية له بنتنها ووحشتها فلم يجد حيلة إلا أن ألقاها في البحر
هربا منها وقد أثر فيه ما أكل منها فلم ينته إلى الوطن إلا بعد أن ظهرت
عليه الأسقام بتلك الروائح فبلغ سقيما مدبرا ومن رجع قريبا ما فاته إلا سعة
المحل فتأدى بضيق المكان مدة ولكن لما وصل إلى الوطن استراح ومن رجع أولا
وجد المكان الأوسع ووصل إلى الوطن سالما فهذا مثال أهل الدنيا في اشتغالهم
بحظوظهم العاجلة ونسيانهم موردهم ومصدرهم وغفلتهم عن عاقبة أمورهم وما أقبح
من يزعم أنه بصير عاقل أن تغره أحجار الأرض وهي الذهب والفضة وهشيم النبت
وهي زينة الدنيا وشيء من ذلك لا يصحبه عند الموت بل يصير كلا ووبالا عليه
وهو في الحال شاغل له بالحزن والخوف عليه وهذه حال الخلق كلهم إلا من عصمه
الله عز وجل
مثال آخر لاغتزار الخلق بالدنيا وضعف إيمانهم قال  الحسن رحمه الله بلغني
أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال لأصحابه إنما مثلي ومثلكم ومثل الدنيا
كمثل قوم سلكوا مفازة غبراء حتى إذا لم يدروا ما سلكوا منها أكثر أو ما بقي
أنفدوا الزاد وخسروا الظهر وبقوا بين ظهراني المفازة ولا زاد ولا حمولة
فأيقنوا بالهلكة فبينما هم كذلك إذ خرج عليهم رجل في حلة تقطر رأسه فقالوا
هذا قريب عهد بريف وما جاءكم هذا إلا من قريب فلما انتهى إليهم قال يا
هؤلاء فقالوا يا هذا فقال علام أنتم فقالوا على ما ترى فقال أرأيتم إن
هديتكم إلى ماء رواء ورياض خضر ما تعملون قالوا لا نعصيك شيئا قال عهودكم
ومواثيقكم بالله فأعطوه عهودهم ومواثيقهم بالله لا يعصونه شيئا قال فأوردهم
ماء رواء ورياضا خضرا فمكث فيهم ما شاء الله ثم قال يا هؤلاء قالوا يا هذا
قال الرحيل قالوا إلى أين قال إلى ماء ليس كمائكم وإلى رياض ليست كرياضكم
فقال أكثرهم والله ما وجدنا هذا حتى ظننا أنا لن نجده وما نصنع بعيش خير من
هذا وقالت طائفة وهم أقلهم ألم تعطوا هذا الرجل عهودكم ومواثيقكم بالله أن
لا تعصوه شيئا وقد صدقكم في أول حديثه فوالله ليصدقنكم في آخره فراح فيمن
اتبعه وتخلف بقيتهم فبدرهم عدو فأصبحوا بين أسير وقتيل (1)
ومثال آخر لتنعم الناس بالدنيا ثم تفجعهم على فراقها اعلم أن مثل الناس
فيما أعطوا من الدنيا مثل رجل هيأ دارا وزينها وهو يدعو إلى داره على
الترتيب قوما واحدا بعد واحد فدخل واحد داره فقدم إليه طبق ذهب عليه بخور
ورياحين ليشمه ويتركه لمن يلحقه لا ليتملكه ويأخذه فجهل رسمه وظن أنه قد
وهب ذلك فتعلق به قلبه لما ظن أنه له فلما استرجع منه ضجر وتفجع ومن كان
عالما برسمه انتفع به وشكره ورده بطيب قلب PageV03P218
وانشراح صدر وكذلك من عرف سنة الله في الدنيا علم أنها دار ضيافة سبلت
على المجتازين لا على المقيمين ليتزودوا منها وينتفعوا بما فيها كما ينتفع
المسافرون بالعواري ولا يصرفون إليها كل قلوبهم حتى تعظم مصيبتهم عند
فراقها
فهذه أمثلة الدنيا وآفاتها وغوائلها نسأل الله تعالى اللطيف الخبير حسن
العون بكرمه وحلمه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف ن ي (f-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cessation, passing away, extinction; the state of being transient and evanescent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ontological finitude of contingent beings; the world's essential characteristic of non-endurance (fanāʾ) as opposed to divine permanence (baqāʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the world's actual passing; metaphorically for the swiftness of its departure, as in "sariʿat al-fanāʾ" (quick to perish).
- Root: غ ر ر (gh-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deception, delusion, heedlessness; to be beguiled by appearances.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The state of being deceived by the lower world's ephemeral pleasures, leading to neglect of the Hereafter; a moral-spiritual blindness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of deceiving; metaphorical for the world's seductive presentation of itself as enduring while it is inherently transient.
- Root: م ث ل (m-th-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Likeness, similitude, example; to stand in representation of something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Quranic and prophetic method of conveying metaphysical truths through sensory parables (amthāl) to awaken the intellect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical likeness; metaphorical for the analogical correspondence between the world's nature and familiar objects (shadow, dream, bridge).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Ḥāl (Circumstantial Clause) — The frequent use of circumstantial accusatives (e.g., "wa-hiya sāʾiratun") to depict simultaneous states, emphasizing the world's hidden motion and deceptive stillness.
chapters.translation:
Know that the world (al-dunyā) is swift in its passing (fanāʾ), near in its termination. It promises permanence, then fails in its pledge. You look upon it and see it still and settled, yet it is traveling with violent motion and departing with swift journeying. But the beholder may not perceive its movement, and so feels secure toward it; he only perceives it at its end. Its likeness is the shadow: it is moving yet still—moving in reality, still in appearance. Its motion is not grasped by the outer eye, but by the inner insight (al-baṣīrah al-bāṭinah). When the world was mentioned before al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may God have mercy on him), he recited and said:

"Dreams of sleep, or a passing shadow—truly, the intelligent one is not deceived by the like of this."

And al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God honor his face) would frequently recite and say:

"O people of pleasures, of a world with no endurance—truly, being deluded by a fleeting shadow is folly."

It is said this is from his own words, and it is also said that a Bedouin alighted upon a people, and they set food before him. He ate, then rose to the shade of their tent and slept there. They pulled up the tent, and the sun struck him. He awoke and stood, saying:

"Indeed, the world is but like the shade of a mountain pass—and inevitably, one day, your shade will depart."

Likewise, it was said:

"Whosoever's world is his greatest concern—he clings to a rope of delusion."

Another similitude of the world, regarding its deception through its phantasms and then its bankruptcy after their release: It resembles the visions of sleep and the confused dreams of slumber. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: «The world is a dream, and its people are requited and punished upon it.» (1) And Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd said: "I have likened myself in the world only to a man who slept and saw in his dream what he disliked and what he loved. While he was in that state, he awoke. Thus are people asleep; when they die, they awaken—and behold, they hold in their hands nothing of what they had leaned upon and rejoiced in." It was said to one of the sages: "What thing most resembles the world?" He said: "The dreams of a sleeper."

Another similitude of the world, regarding its enmity toward its people and its destruction of its children: Know that the nature of the world is to be gentle in enticement at first, and to reach destruction at last. It is like a woman who adorns herself for suitors, until when she has married them, she slaughters them. It has been narrated that Jesus (peace be upon him) was shown the world, and he saw it in the form of a toothless old woman (hutmāʾ) adorned with every kind of ornament. He said to her: "How many husbands have you had?" She said: "I cannot count them." He said: "Did they all die of you, or did they all divorce you?" She said: "Rather, I killed them all." Then Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "Woe to your remaining husbands! How do they not take heed from your past husbands? How do you destroy them one after another, and they remain not on guard against you?"

Another similitude of the world, regarding the contradiction between its outward and its inward: Know that the world is adorned in its outward aspects (ẓawāhir), ugly in its hidden secrets (sarāʾir). It is like an adorned old woman who deceives people by her exterior; when they come upon her interior and lift the veil from her face, her ugliness appears to them, and they regret following her and are ashamed of the weakness of their intellects in being deluded by her exterior.

And al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Ziyād said: "I saw in a dream an old woman, large, with wrinkled skin, upon her every ornament of the world, and people were crowding around her, admiring and gazing at her. I came and looked, and I marveled at their gazing at her and their turning toward her. I said to her: 'Woe to you! Who are you?' She said: 'Do you not recognize me?' I said: 'I do not know who you are.' She said: 'I am the world.' I said: 'I seek refuge in God from your evil.' She said: 'If you wish to be protected from my evil, then despise the dirham.'"

Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said: "I saw the world in sleep as an old woman, deformed, with gray hair (shamṭāʾ), clapping her hands, and behind her a creation following her, clapping and dancing. When she was opposite me, she turned to me and said: 'Had I gotten hold of you, I would have done to you as I did to these.'" Then Abū Bakr wept and said: "I saw this before I came to Baghdad."

And al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The world will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a gray-haired old woman, blue-eyed, with protruding fangs, deformed in her creation. She will overlook the creatures, and it will be said to them: 'Do you recognize this?' They will say: 'We seek refuge in God from knowing this.' It will be said: 'This is the world over which you contended, through which you cut ties of kinship, through which you envied and hated one another, and by which you were deluded.' Then she will be cast into Hellfire, and she will cry out: 'O Lord, where are my followers and my partisans?' God (mighty and majestic) will say: 'Join to her her followers and her partisans.'"

And al-Fuḍayl said: "It reached me that a man's spirit was ascended, and behold, there was a woman at the crossroads, upon her every ornament of jewelry and garments, and no one passed by her but she wounded him. When she turned away, she was the most beautiful thing people had seen; when she turned toward, she was the ugliest thing people had seen—a gray-haired, blue-eyed, bleary-eyed old woman." He said: "I said: 'I seek refuge in God from you.' She said: 'No, by God, God will not protect you from me until you despise the dirham.'" He said: "I said: 'Who are you?' She said: 'I am the world.'"

Another similitude of the world and man's crossing through it: Know that the states are three: a state in which you were nothing—that is, before your existence, back to eternity past (al-azal); a state in which you will not be a beholder of the world—that is, after your death, to eternity future (al-abad); and an intermediate state between the two eternities—that is, the days of your life in the world. So look at the measure of its length, and compare it to the two extremes of eternity past and eternity future, until you know that it is less than a brief station in a long journey. For this reason, he (peace be upon him) said: «What have I to do with the world? My likeness and the likeness of the world is like a rider who traveled on a scorching day, and a tree was raised up, so he said: 'Under its shade for an hour,' then he departed and left it.» (1)

Whoever sees the world with this eye does not lean toward it, nor does he care how his days pass—whether in harm and constriction or in expanse and comfort. Rather, he does not place one brick upon another. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) died, and he had not placed a brick upon a brick, nor a reed upon a reed. (2)

And one of the Companions saw a man building a house of plaster, and he said: "I see the matter is more urgent than this," and he disapproved of that. (3) To this Jesus (peace be upon him) alluded when he said: "The world is a bridge (qanṭarah)—so cross it, and do not build upon it." This is a clear similitude: the life of this world is a crossing to the Hereafter. The cradle is the first incline at the head of the bridge, and the grave is the last incline. Between them is a limited distance. Among people, some have crossed half the bridge, some a third, some two-thirds, and some have only one step remaining while heedless of it. However it may be, crossing is inevitable—and to build upon the bridge and adorn it with various ornaments while you are a passer-by upon it is the utmost ignorance and abandonment.

Another similitude of the world, regarding the softness of its entry and the roughness of its exit: Know that the beginnings of the world appear easy and soft. The one who wades into it thinks that the sweetness of its descent is like the sweetness of wading into it. Far from it! For wading into the world is easy, but coming out of it safely is severe. ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) wrote to Salmān al-Fārsī with its similitude, saying: "The likeness of the world is like the serpent: soft to the touch, deadly in its venom. Turn away from what pleases you of it, for the little that accompanies you from it. Cast off its cares by your certainty of parting from it. Be, when you are most at ease in it, most wary of it. For its companion, whenever he is tranquil in a joy from it, a disliked thing removes him from it. And peace."

Another similitude of the world, regarding the difficulty of escaping its attachments after wading into it: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: «The likeness of the companion of the world is like one walking in water—can the one who walks in water keep his feet from getting wet?» (1)

This informs you of the ignorance of a people who thought they could wade into the world's delights with their bodies while their hearts were purified from it and its attachments severed from their inner selves. That is a stratagem from Satan. Rather, were they to be removed from what they are in, they would be among the greatest of those grieving over parting from it. For just as walking on water necessitates wetness that inevitably clings to the foot, so too does contact with the world necessitate an attachment and darkness in the heart. Indeed, the world's attachment to the heart prevents the sweetness of worship.

Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "Truly, I say to you: as the sick man looks at food and takes no pleasure in it due to the severity of his pain, so too the companion of the world takes no pleasure in worship and finds not its sweetness, along with what he finds of love for the world. And truly, I say to you: if the beast is not ridden and broken, it becomes wild and its nature changes. Likewise, if hearts are not softened by the remembrance of death and the exertion of worship, they harden and become coarse. And truly, I say to you: the waterskin, as long as it is not pierced or dried up, is likely to be a vessel for honey. Likewise, hearts, as long as they are not pierced by desires, or defiled by greed, or hardened by comfort, will be vessels for wisdom."

And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: «Nothing remains of the world but tribulation and trial. The likeness of the deed of any one of you is like a vessel: if its top is good, its bottom is good; if its top is corrupt, its bottom is corrupt.» (2)

Another similitude of what remains of the world and its scantiness relative to what has passed: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: «The likeness of this world is like a garment torn from its beginning to its end, leaving it hanging by a thread at its end—and soon that thread will snap.» (3)

Another similitude of the world's attachments leading one to another until destruction: Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "The likeness of the seeker of the world is like one drinking seawater: the more he drinks, the thirstier he becomes, until it kills him."

Another similitude of the contradiction between the world's end and its beginning, and of the freshness of its beginnings and the foulness of its consequences: Know that the desires of the world in the heart are delicious, like the desires of foods in the stomach. The servant will find at death, for the world's desires in his heart, a degree of repulsion, stench, and ugliness like what he finds for delicious foods when they reach their limit in the stomach. And just as food, the more delicious in taste, the more fatty and manifestly sweet, the filthier and more stench-ridden is its excrement—so too, every desire in the heart that is more appetizing, more delicious, and stronger, its stench, repulsion, and harm at death are more severe.

Rather, this is observable in the world itself: whoever's house is plundered, and his family, wealth, and children are taken, his calamity, pain, and grief over all he has lost are proportionate to his pleasure in it, his love for it, and his craving for it. So whatever is more appetizing and delicious at the time of possession is more dire and bitter at the time of loss. And death is nothing but the loss of what is in the world. It has been narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān al-Kilābī: "Do you not bring your food, salted and spiced, then drink milk and water over it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then to what does it become?" He said: "To what you know, O Messenger of God." He said: "Indeed, God (mighty and majestic) has struck the world as a similitude of what the food of the son of Adam becomes." (1)

And Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: «Indeed, the world has been struck as a similitude for the son of Adam—so look at what comes out of the son of Adam, even if it is spiced and salted: to what does it become?» (2) And he (peace be upon him) said: «Indeed, God has struck the world as a similitude for the food of the son of Adam, and the food of the son of Adam as a similitude for the world—even if it is spiced and salted.» (3)

And al-Ḥasan said: "I have seen them flavoring it with aromatic spices and perfume, then throwing it where you have seen." And God (mighty and majestic) has said: {So let man look at his food} (Q. 80:24). Ibn ʿAbbās said: "At his excrement." A man said to Ibn ʿUmar: "I wish to ask you, but I am ashamed." He said: "Do not be ashamed; ask." He said: "When one of us relieves himself and stands to look at that from him—?" He said: "Yes. Indeed, the angel says to him: 'Look at what you were stingy with. Look at what it has become.'" And Bishr ibn Kaʿb used to say: "Come, let me show you the world." He would take them to a dunghill and say: "Look at their fruits, their chickens, their honey, and their butter."

Another similitude of the world's proportion to the Hereafter: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: «The world in the Hereafter is but like what one of you places his finger in the sea—so let him look at what he brings back.» (4)

Another similitude of the world and its people, regarding their occupation with the world's delights, their heedlessness of the Hereafter, and their great loss because of it: Know that the people of the world, in their heedlessness, are like a people who boarded a ship, and it brought them to an island. The captain ordered them to go out to relieve themselves, warned them against staying, and frightened them of the ship's passing and its haste. They scattered across the island's corners. Some of them relieved themselves and hurried back to the ship, finding the place empty, and took the widest, softest, and most suitable spot for his purpose. Some of them lingered on the island, gazing at its lights, its wondrous flowers, its dense thickets, the sweet songs of its birds, and their strange, measured melodies. He began to observe its stones, jewels, and mines of various colors and forms, beautiful in appearance, wondrous in engravings, robbing the eyes of beholders with the beauty of their emeralds and the wonders of their shapes. Then he became alert to the danger of missing the ship, returned to it, and found only a narrow, constricted place, and settled there. Some of them bent over those shells and stones, admired their beauty, and his soul did not permit him to neglect them, so he took a quantity of them with him. He found in the ship only a narrow place, and his load of stones made it narrower, becoming heavy upon him and a burden. He regretted taking them, could not throw them away, and found no place to put them, so he carried them in the ship on his neck, grieving over having taken them—and grief did not avail him.

And some of them entered the thickets, forgot the vessel, and went far in his stroll and recreation from it, until the captain's call did not reach him, occupied as he was with eating those fruits, smelling those flowers, and strolling among those trees. Yet he was fearful for himself of wild beasts, not free from falls and calamities, nor free from thorns catching in his clothes, a branch tearing his body, a thorn entering his foot, a terrifying sound frightening him, and a bramble tearing his clothes and exposing his nakedness, preventing his return even if he wished it. When the call of the ship's people reached him, he turned back laden with what he had, found no place in the vessel, and remained on the shore until he died of hunger. And some of them—the call did not reach them, and the ship sailed. Among them, some were preyed upon by wild beasts; some wandered astray, roaming aimlessly until they perished; some died in the mud; some were bitten by snakes—so they scattered like putrid carcasses.

As for the one who reached the vessel with the weight of what he had taken of flowers and stones, grief over preserving them and fear of losing them enslaved him and occupied him, and they narrowed his place. It was not long before those flowers withered, those colors faded, and the stones—their stench appeared, and they became, besides being constricting, harmful to him with their stench and desolation. He found no stratagem but to cast them into the sea, fleeing from them—yet what he had eaten of them had already affected him, and he did not reach his homeland until sicknesses appeared upon him from those odors, arriving sick and ruined. And the one who returned early—he missed only the spaciousness of the place, and endured the narrowness for a time, but when he reached his homeland, he rested. And the one who returned first found the widest place and reached his homeland safely. This is the similitude of the people of the world in their occupation with their immediate shares, their forgetfulness of their origin and destination, and their heedlessness of the end of their affairs. How ugly is the one who claims to be insightful and intelligent, that he is deceived by the stones of the earth—which are gold and silver—and the dried plants—which are the world's adornments—while nothing of that accompanies him at death, but rather becomes a burden and a calamity upon him, and in the present it occupies him with grief and fear over it. This is the state of all creatures, except those whom God (mighty and majestic) protects.

Another similitude of creatures' delusion by the world and the weakness of their faith: Al-Ḥasan (may God have mercy on him) said: "It reached me that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said to his Companions: «My likeness, your likeness, and the likeness of the world is like a people who traversed a barren desert (mafāzah ghabrāʾ), until they did not know whether they had traversed more of it or what remained. They exhausted their provisions, lost their mounts, and remained in the midst of the desert with no provision and no mount, certain of destruction. While they were in that state, a man came out upon them in a garment with his head dripping. They said: 'This one is recently from the green land—and he has only come to us from nearby.' When he reached them, he said: 'O people!' They said: 'Yes, O this one.' He said: 'What are you upon?' They said: 'Upon what you see.' He said: 'What do you think—if I guide you to abundant water and green meadows, what will you do?' They said: 'We will not disobey you in anything.' He said: 'Your covenants and pledges by God.' So they gave him their covenants and pledges by God that they would not disobey him in anything. He said: 'Then he brought them to abundant water and green meadows, and he stayed among them as long as God willed. Then he said: 'O people!' They said: 'Yes, O this one.' He said: 'The departure.' They said: 'To where?' He said: 'To water not like your water, and meadows not like your meadows.' The majority of them said: 'By God, we did not find this until we thought we would never find it—and what shall we do with a life better than this?' And a group—the lesser of them—said: 'Did you not give this man your covenants and pledges by God not to disobey him in anything? And he was truthful to you in his first speech—by God, he will be truthful to you in his last.' So he departed with those who followed him, and the rest of them lagged behind. An enemy rushed upon them, and they awoke among captive and slain.» (1)

And another similitude of people's enjoyment of the world and then their grief over parting from it: Know that the likeness of people in what they are given of the world is like a man who prepared a house and adorned it, and he invites people to his house in order, one after another. One man entered his house, and a golden tray was set before him with incense and fragrant herbs, for him to smell and leave for the one after him—not to possess and take. But he was ignorant of the custom, thought it had been given to him, and his heart clung to it, thinking it was his. When it was taken back from him, he was vexed and grieved. But the one who knew the custom benefited from it, gave thanks, and returned it with a good heart and an expanded breast. Likewise, whoever knows God's way (sunnah) in the world knows that it is a house of hospitality (dār ḍiyāfah), laid out for passers-by, not for residents—so that they may take provision from it and benefit from what is in it, as travelers benefit from borrowed things, and not turn all their hearts to it such that their calamity becomes great at parting from it.

These are the similitudes of the world, its afflictions, and its perils. We ask God the Most High, the Subtle, the Aware, for good assistance, by His generosity and His forbearance.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Reality of the World and Its Quiddity in Relation to the Servant
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان حقيقة الدنيا وماهيتها في حق العبد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ن-ي (d-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, lowness, that which is near or inferior; the world as the "nearer" (al-dunyā) in contrast to the hereafter (al-ākhirah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The world as the lower abode of trial and temporal attachment, opposed to the eternal abode; its "quiddity" (māhiyyah) is relational, not absolute.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense — the nearer life; metaphorical sense — the sum of worldly pursuits that veil one from God.
- Root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Reality, truth, due right, that which is firmly established.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The true nature of a thing as it exists in itself, distinct from mere appearance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — established fact; metaphorical — the inner reality of the world as a testing ground.
- Root: ع-ب-د (ʿ-b-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Servant, worshipper; one who is subjugated and devoted.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The human as ʿabd — bound by covenant to God, whose relation to the world defines his station.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — slave; metaphorical — the believer who uses the world as a means, not an end.
- Sībawayh Rule: Idāfah (Construct State) — "ḥaqīqat al-dunyā" and "māhiyyatuhā fī ḥaqq al-ʿabd" establish a genitive relation that specifies the scope: the world's reality is not absolute but relative to the servant's condition.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the exposition of the reality of the world and its quiddity in relation to the servant — that is, what the world truly is in itself, and how it stands with respect to the one who is tried by it. For the world is not a single thing with a fixed essence, but rather a station of passage, whose reality is known only by him who perceives its end and its beginning. And its quiddity, in relation to the servant, is that it is a place of sowing for the hereafter, a bridge to the abode of permanence, and a veil for the heedless, even as it is a mirror for the discerning. So know that the world, in its true nature, is nothing but the days and hours that pass, and the breaths that expire; and the servant's portion of it is but his deeds, which are stored for him, whether for good or for evil. Thus, whoever looks upon the world with the eye of reality sees it as a fleeting shadow and a borrowed garment, and he takes from it only what carries him to his Lord; but whoever looks upon it with the eye of delusion is deceived by its adornment and perishes in its pursuit. And this is the meaning of its quiddity in relation to the servant: that it is a trial and a test, not a home and a resting place.

chapters.title_en: The True Nature of the Blameworthy World and Its Divisions
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن معرفة ذم الدنيا لا تكفيك ما لم تعرف الدنيا المذمومة ما هي وما
الذي ينبغي أن يجتنب منها وما الذي لا يجتنب فلا بد وأن نبين الدنيا
المذمومة المأمور باجتنابها لكونها عدوة قاطعة لطريق الله ما هي فنقول
دنياك وآخرتك عبارة عن حالتين من أحوال قلبك فالقريب الداني منها يسمى دنيا
وهو كل ما قبل الموت والمتراخي المتأخر يسمى آخرة وهو ما بعد الموت فكل ما
لك فيه حظ ونصيب وغرض وشهوة ولذة عاجل الحال قبل الوفاة فهي الدنيا في حقك
إلا أن جميع مالك إليه ميل وفيه نصيب وحظ فليس بمذموم بل هو ثلاثة أقسام
القسم الأول ما يصحبك في الآخرة وتبقى معك ثمرته بعد الموت وهو شيئان
العلم والعمل فقط وأعني بالعلم العلم بالله وصفاته وأفعاله وملائكته وكتبه
ورسله وملكوت أرضه وسمائه والعلم بشريعة نبيه وأعني بالعمل العبادة الخالصة
لوجه الله تعالى وقد يأنس العالم بالعلم حتى يصير ذلك ألذ الأشياء عنده
فيهجر النوم والمطعم والمنكح في لذته لأنه أشهى عنده من جميع ذلك فقد صار
حظا عاجلا في الدنيا
ولكنا إذا ذكرنا الدنيا المذمومة لم نعد هذا من الدنيا أصلا بل قلنا إنه
من الآخرة وكذلك العابد قد يأنس بعبادته فيستلذها بحيث لو منع عنها لكان
ذلك أعظم العقوبات عليه حتى قال بعضهم ما أخاف من الموت إلا من حيث يحول
بيني وبين قيام الليل وكان آخر يقول اللهم ارزقني قوة الصلاة والركوع
والسجود في القبر فهذا قد صارت الصلاة عنده من حظوظه العاجلة وكل حظ عاجل
فاسم الدنيا ينطلق عليه من حيث الاشتقاق من الدنو ولكنا لسنا نعني بالدنيا
المذمومة ذلك وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم حبب إلي من دنياكم ثلاث النساء
والطيب وقرة عيني في الصلاة (1)
فجعل الصلاة من  جملة ملاذ الدنيا وكذلك كل ما يدخل في الحس والمشاهدة فهو
من عالم الشهادة وهو من الدنيا والتلذذ بتحريك الجوارح بالركوع والسجود
إنما يكون في الدنيا فلذلك أضافها إلى الدنيا إلا أنا لسنا في هذا الكتاب
نتعرض إلا للدنيا المذمومة فنقول هذه ليست من الدنيا
القسم الثاني وهو المقابل له على الطرف الأقصى كل ما فيه حظ عاجل ولا
ثمرة له في الآخرة أصلا كالتلذذ بالمعاصي كلها والتنعم بالمباحاة الزائدة
على قدر الحاجات والضرورات الداخلة في جملة الرفاهية والرعونات كالتنعم
بالقناطير المقنطرة من الذهب والفضة والخيل المسومة والأنعام والحرث
والغلمان والجواري والخيول والمواشي والقصور والدور ورفيع الثياب ولذائذ
الأطعمة فحظ العبد من هذا كله هي الدنيا المذمومة وفيما يعد فضولا أوفى محل
الحاجة نظر طويل إذ روي عن عمر رضي الله عنه أنه استعمل أبا الدرداء على
حمص فاتخذ كنيفا أنفق عليه درهمين فكتب إليه عمر من عمر بن الخطاب أمير
المؤمنين إلى عويمر قد كان لك في بناء فارس والروم ما تكتفي به عن عمران
الدنيا حين أراد الله خرابها فإذا أتاك كتابي هذا فقد سيرتك إلى دمشق أنت
وأهلك فلم يزل بها حتى مات فهذا رآه فضولا من الدنيا فتأمل فيه PageV03P219
القسم الثالث وهو متوسط بين الطرفين كل حظ في العاجل معين على أعمال
الآخرة كقدر القوت من الطعام والقميص الواحد الخشن وكل ما لا بد منه لبتأتي
للإنسان البقاء والصحة التي بها يتوصل إلى العلم والعمل وهذا ليس من الدنيا
كالقسم الأول لأنه معين على القسم الأول ووسيلة إليه فمهما تناوله العبد
على قصد الاستعانة به على العلم والعمل لم يكن به متناولا للدنيا ولم يصر
به من أبناء الدنيا وإن كان باعثه الحظ العاجل دون الاستعانة على التقوى
التحق بالقسم الثاني وصار من جملة الدنيا ولا يبقى مع العبد عند الموت إلا
ثلاث صفات صفاء القلب أعني طهارته من الأدناس وأنسه بذكر الله تعالى وحبه
لله عز وجل
وصفاء القلب وطهارته لا يحصلان إلا بالكف عن  شهوات الدنيا والأنس لا يحصل
إلا بكثرة ذكر الله تعالى والمواظبة عليه والحب لا يحصل إلا بالمعرفة ولا
تحصل معرفة الله إلا بدوام الفكر وهذه الصفات الثلاث هي المنجيات المسعدات
بعد الموت
أما طهارة القلب عن شهوات الدنيا فهي من المنجيات إذ تكون جنة بن العبد
وبين عذاب الله كما ورد في الأخبار إن أعمال العبد تناضل عنه فإذا جاء
العذاب من قبل رجليه جاء قيام الليل يدفع عنه وإذا جاء من جهة يديه جاءت
الصدقة تدفع عنه (1) الحديث
وأما الأنس والحب فهما من المسعدات وهما موصلان العبد إلى لذة اللقاء
والمشاهدة وهذه السعادة تتعجل عقيب الموت إلى أن يدخل أوان الرؤية في الجنة
فيصير القبر روضة من رياض الجنة وكيف لا يكون القبر عليه روضة من رياض
الجنة ولم يكن له إلا محبوب واحد وكانت العوائق تعوقه عن دوام الأنس بدوام
ذكره ومطالعة جماله فارتفعت العوائق وأفلت من السجن وخلي بينه وبين محبوبه
فقدم عليه مسرورا سليما من الموانع آمنا من العوائق وكيف لا يكون محب
الدنيا عند الموت معذبا ولم يكن له محبوب إلا الدنيا وقد غصب منه وحيل بينه
وبينه وسدت عليه طرق الحيلة في الرجوع إليه ولذلك قيل
ما حال من كان له واحد ... غيب عنه ذلك الواحد
وليس الموت عدما إنما هو فراق لمحاب الدنيا وقدوم على الله تعالى فإذا
سالك طريق الآخرة هو المواظب على أسباب هذه الصفات الثلاث وهي الذكر والفكر
والعمل الذي يفطمه عن شهوات الدنيا ويبغض إليه ملاذها ويقطعه عنها وكل ذلك
لا يمكن إلا بصحة البدن وصحة البدن لا تنال إلا بقوت وملبس ومسكن ويحتاج كل
واحد إلى أسباب فالقدر الذي لا بد منه من هذه الثلاثة إذا أخذه العبد من
الدنيا للآخرة لم يكن من أبناء الدنيا وكانت الدنيا في حقه مزرعة للآخرة
وإن أخذ ذلك لحظ النفس وعلى قصد التنعم صار من أبناء الدنيا والراغبين في
حظوظها إلا أن الرغبة في حظوظ الدنيا تنقسم إلى ما يعرض صاحبه  لعذاب الآخرة
ويسمى ذلك حراما وإلى ما يحول بينه وبين الدرجات العلا ويعرضه لطول الحساب
ويسمى ذلك حلالا والبصير يعلم أن طول الموقف في عرصات القيامة لأجل
المحاسبة أيضا عذاب فمن نوقش الحساب عذب (2)
إذ قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حلالها حساب وحرامها عذاب (3)
وقد قال أيضا حلالها عذاب إلا أنه عذاب أخف من عذاب الحرام PageV03P220
بل لو لم يكن الحساب لكان ما يفوت من الدرجات العلا في الجنة وما يرد على
القلب من التحسر على تفوتها لحظوظ حقيرة خسيسة لا بقاء لها هو أيضا عذاب
وقس به حالك في الدنيا إذا نظرت إلى أقرانك وقد سبقوك بسعادات دنيوية كيف
يتقطع قلبك عليها حسرات مع علمك بأنها سعادات منصرمة لا بقاء لها منغصة
بكدورات لا صفاء لها فما حالك في فوات سعادة لا يحيط الوصف بعظمتها وتنقطع
الدهور دون غايتها فكل من تنعم في الدنيا ولو بسماع صوت من طائر أو بالنظر
إلى خضرة أو شربة ماء بارد فإنه ينقص من حظه في الآخرة أضعافه وهو المعنى
بقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم لعمر رضي الله عنه هذا من النعيم الذي تسئل عنه
(1)
أشار به إلى الماء البارد والتعرض لجواب السؤال فيه ذل وخوف وخطر ومشقة
وانتظار وكل ذلك من نقصان الحظ ولذلك قال عمر رضي الله عنه اعزلوا عني
حسابها حين كان به عطش فعرض عليه ماء بارد بعسل فأداره في كفه ثم امتنع عن
شربه فالدنيا قليلها وكثيرها حرامها وحلالها ملعونة إلا ما أعان على تقوى
الله فإن ذلك القدر ليس من الدنيا وكل من كانت معرفته أقوى وأتقن كان حذره
من نعيم الدنيا أشد حتى أن عيسى عليه السلام وضع رأسه على حجر لما نام ثم
رماه إذ تمثل له إبليس وقال رغبت في الدنيا وحتى أن سليمان عليه السلام في
ملكه كان يطعم الناس لذائذ الأطعمة وهو يأكل خبز الشعير فجعل الملك على
نفسه بهذا الطريق امتهانا وشدة فإن الصبر على لذائذ الأطعمة مع القدرة
عليها ووجودها أشد ولهذا روي أن الله تعالى زوى الدنيا عن نبينا صلى الله
عليه وسلم فكان يطوي أياما (2)
وكان يشد الحجر على بطنه من الجوع (3)
ولهذا سلط الله البلاء والمحن على الأنبياء والأولياء ثم الأمثل فالأمثل
كل ذلك نظرا لهم وامتنانا عليهم ليتوفر من الآخرة حظهم كما يمنع الوالد
الشفيق ولده لذة الفواكه ويلزم ألم الفصد والحجامة شفقة عليه وحبا له لا
بخلا عليه وقد عرفت بهذا أن كل ما ليس لله فهو من الدنيا وما هو لله فذلك
ليس من الدنيا
فإن قلت فما الذي هو لله فأقول الأشياء ثلاثة أقسام منها مالا يتصور أن
يكون لله وهو الذي يعبر عنه بالمعاصي والمحظورات وأنواع التنعمات في
المباحات وهي الدنيا المحضة المذمومة فهي الدنيا صورة ومعنى ومنها ما صورته
لله ويمكن أن يجعل لغير الله وهو ثلاثة الفكر والذكر والكف عن الشهوات فإن
هذه الثلاثة إذا جرت سرا ولم يكن عليها باعث سوى أمر الله واليوم الآخر فهي
لله وليست من الدنيا وإن كان الغرض من الفكر طلب العلم للتشرف به وطلب
القبول بين الخلق بإظهار المعرفة أو كان الغرض من ترك الشهوة حفظ المال أو
الحمية لصحة البدن والاشتهار بالزهد فقد صار هذا من الدنيا بالمعنى وإن كان
يظن بصورته أنه لله تعالى ومنها ما صورته لحظ النفس ويمكن أن يكون معناه
لله وذلك كالأكل والنكاح وكل ما يرتبط به بقاؤه وبقاء ولده فإن كان القصد
حظ النفس فهو من الدنيا وإن كان القصد الاستعانة به على التقوى فهو لله
بمعناه وإن كانت صورته صورة الدنيا قال صلى الله عليه وسلم من طلب الدنيا
حلالا مكاثرا مفاخرا لقي الله وهو عليه غضبان ومن طلبها استعفافا عن
المسألة وصيانة لنفسه جاء يوم القيامة ووجهه كالقمر ليلة البدر (4)
فانظر كيف اختلف ذلك بالقصد فإذا الدنيا حظ نفسك العاجل الذي لا حاجة
إليه لأمر الآخرة ويعبر عنه بالهوى وإليه الإشارة بقوله تعالى ونهى النفس
عن PageV03P221
الهوى فإن الجنة هي المأوى ومجامع  الهوى خمسة أمور وهي ما جمعه الله
تعالى في قوله أنما الحياة الدنيا لعب ولهو وزينة وتفاخر بينكم وتكاثر في
الأموال والأولاد والأعيان التي تحصل منها هذه الخمسة سبعة يجمعها قوله
تعالى زين للناس حب الشهوات من النساء والبنين والقناطير المقنطرة من الذهب
والفضة والخيل المسومة والأنعام والحرث ذلك متاع الحياة الدنيا فقد عرفت أن
كل ما هو لله فليس من الدنيا وقدر ضرورة القوت وما لا بد منه من مسكن وملبس
هو لله إن قصد به وجه الله والاستكثار منه تنعم وهو لغير الله وبين التنعم
والضرورة درجة يعبر عنها بالحاجة ولها طرفان وواسطة طرف يقرب من حد الضرورة
فلا يضر فإن الاقتصار على حد الضرورة غير ممكن وطرف يزاحم جانب التنعم
ويقرب منه وينبغي أن يحذر منه وبينهما وسائط متشابهة ومن حام حول الحمى
يوشك أن يقع فيه
والحزم في الحذر والتقوى والتقرب من حد الضرورة ما أمكن اقتداء بالأنبياء
والأولياء عليهم السلام إذا كانوا يردون أنفسهم إلى حد الضرورة حتى إن
أويسا القرنى كان يظن أهله أنه مجنون لشدة تضييقه على نفسه فبنوا له بيتا
على باب دارهم فكان يأتي عليهم السنة والسنتان والثلاث لا يرون له وجها
وكان يخرج أول الآذان ويأتي إلى منزله بعد العشاء الآخرة وكان طعامه أن
يلتقط النوى وكلما أصاب حشفة خبأها لإفطاره وإن لم يصب ما يقوته من الحشف
باع النوى واشترى بثمنه ما يقوته وكان لباسه مما يلتقط من المزابل من قطع
الأكسية فيغسلها في الفرات ويلفق بعضها إلى بعض ثم يلبسها فكان ذلك لباسه
وكان ربما مر الصبيان فيرمونه ويظنون أنه مجنون فيقول لهم يا أخوتاه إن
كنتم ولا بد أن ترموني فارموني بأحجار صغار فإني أخاف أن تدموا عقبي فيحضر
وقت الصلاة ولا أصيب الماء فهكذا كانت سيرته ولقد عظم رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم أمره فقال إني لأجد نفس الرحمن من جانب اليمن إشارة إليه رحمه
الله (1) ولما ولي الخلافة عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى  عنه قال أيها
الناس من كان منكم من العراق فليقم قالوا فقاموا فقال اجلسوا إلا من كان من
أهل الكوفة فجلسوا فقال اجلسوا إلا من كان من مراد فجلسوا فقال اجلسوا إلا
من كان من قرن فجلسوا كلهم إلا رجلا واحدا فقال له عمر أقرني أنت فقال نعم
فقال أتعرف أويس بن عامر القرني فوصفه له فقال نعم وما ذاك تسأل عنه يا
أمير المؤمنين والله ما فينا أحمق منه ولا أجن منه ولا أوحش منه ولا أدنى
منه فبكى عمر رضي الله تعالى عنه ثم قال ما قلت ما قلت إلا لأني سمعت رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول يدخل في شفاعته مثل ربيعة ومضر (2)
فقال هرم بن حيان لما سمعت هذا القول من عمر بن الخطاب قدمت الكوفة فلم
يكن لي هم إلا أن أطلب أويسا القرني وأسأل عنه حتى سقطت عليه جالسا على
شاطيء الفرات نصف النهار يتوضأ ويغسل ثوبه فعرفته بالنعت الذي نعت لي فإذا
رجل لحيم شديد الأدمة محلوق الرأس كث اللحية متغير جدا كريه الوجه متهيب
المنظر قال فسلمت عليه فرد علي السلام ونظر إلي فقلت حياك الله من رجل
ومددت يدي لأصافحه فأبى أن يصافحني فقلت رحمك الله يا أويس وغفر لك كيف أنت
رحمك الله ثم خنقتني العبرة من حبي إياه ورقتي عليه إذ رأيت من حاله ما
رأيت حتى بكيت وبكى فقال وأنت فحياك الله يا هرم بن حيان كيف أنت يا أخي
ومن دلك علي قال قلت الله فقال PageV03P222
لا إله إلا الله سبحان الله إن كان وعد ربنا لمفعولا قال فعجبت حين عرفني
ولا والله ما رأيته قبل ذلك ولا رآني فقلت من أين عرفت اسمي واسم أبي وما
رأيتك قبل اليوم قال نبأني العليم الخبير وعرفت روحي روحك حين كلمت نفسي
نفسك إن الأرواح لها أنفس كأنفس الأجساد وإن المؤمنين ليعرف بعضهم بعضا
ويتحابون بروح الله وإن لم يلتقوا يتعارفون ويتكلمون وإن نأت بهم الدار
وتفرقت بهم  المنازل قال قلت حدثني رحمك الله عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم بحديث أسمعه منك قال إني لم أدرك رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ولم
تكن لي معه صحبة بأبي وأمي رسول الله ولكن رأيت رجالا قد صحبوه وبلغني من
حديثه كما بلغك ولست أحب أن أفتح على نفسي هذا الباب أن أكون محدثا أو
مفتيا أو قاضيا في نفسي شغل عن الناس يا هرم بن حيان فقلت يا أخي اقرأ علي
آية من القرآن أسمعها منك وادع لي بدعوات وأوصني بوصية أحفظها عنك فإني
أحبك في الله حبا شديدا قال فقام وأخذ بيدي على شاطيء الفرات ثم قال أعوذ
بالله السميع العليم من الشيطان الرجيم ثم بكى ثم قال قال ربي والحق قول
ربي وأصدق الحديث حديثه وأصدق الكلام كلامه ثم قرأ وما خلقنا السموات
والأرض وما بينهما لاعبين ما خلقناهما إلا بالحق ولكن أكثرهم لا يعلمون حتى
انتهى إلى قوله إنه هو العزيز الرحيم فشهق شهقة ظننت أنه قد غشي عليه ثم
قال يا ابن حيان مات أبوك حيان وتوشك أن تموت فإما إلى جنة وإما إلى نار
ومات أبوك آدم وماتت أمك حواء ومات نوح ومات إبراهيم خليل الرحمن ومات موسى
نجى الرحمن ومات داود خليفة الرحمن ومات محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو رسول
رب العالمين ومات أبو بكر خليفة المسلمين ومات عمر بن الخطاب أخي وصفي ثم
قال يا عمراه يا عمراه قال فقلت رحمك الله إن عمر لم يمت قال فقد نعاه إلي
ربي ونعى إلى نفسي ثم قال أنا وأنت في الموت كأنه قد كان ثم صلى على النبي
صلى الله عليه وسلم ثم دعا بدعوات خفيات ثم قال هذه وصيتي إياك يا هرم بن
حيان كتاب الله ونهج الصالحين المؤمنين فقد نعيت إلى نفسي ونفسك عليك بذكر
الموت لا يفارق قلبك طرفة عين ما بقيت وأنذر قومك إذا رجعت إليهم وانصح
للأمة جميعا وإياك أن تفارق الجماعة قيد شبر فتفارق  دينك وأنت لا تعلم
فتدخل النار يوم القيامة ادع لي ولنفسك ثم قال اللهم إن هذا يزعم أنه يحبني
فيك وزارني من أجلك فعرفني وجهه في الجنة وأدخله علي في دارك دار السلام
واحفظه ما دام في الدنيا حيثما كان وضم عليه ضيعته وأرضه من الدنيا باليسير
وما أعطيته من الدنيا فيسره له تيسيرا واجعله لما أعطيته من نعمائك من
الشاكرين وأجزه عني خير الجزاء ثم قال أستودعك الله يا هرم بن حيان والسلام
عليك ورحمة الله وبركاته لا أراك بعد اليوم رحمك الله تطلبني فإني أكره
الشهرة والوحدة أحب إلي أن كثير الهم شديد الغم مع هؤلاء الناس ما دمت حيا
فلا تسأل عني ولا تطلبني واعلم أنك مني على بال وإن لم أرك ولم ترني
فاذكرني وادع لي فإني سأذكرك وأدعو لك إن شاء الله انطلق أنت ههنا حتى
أنطلق أنا ههنا
فحرصت أن أمشي معه ساعة فأبى علي وفارقته فبكى وأبكاني وجعلت أنظر في
قفاه حتى دخل بعض السكك ثم سألت عنه بعد ذلك فما وجدت أحدا يخبرني عنه بشيء
رحمه الله وغفر له
فهكذا كانت سيرة أبناء الآخرة المعرضين عن الدنيا
وقد عرفت مما سبق في بيان الدنيا ومن سيرة الأنبياء والأولياء أن حد
الدنيا كل ما أظلته الخضراء وأقلته الغبراء إلا ما كان لله عز وجل من ذلك
وضد الدنيا الآخرة وهو كل ما أريد به الله تعالى مما يؤخذ بقدر الضرورة من
الدنيا لأجل قوة طاعة الله وذلك ليس من الدنيا
ويتبين هذا بمثال وهو أن الحاج إذا حلف أنه في طريق الحج
PageV03P223
لا يشتغل بغير الحج بل يتجرد له ثم اشتغل بحفظ الزاد وعلف الجمل وخرز
الرواية وكل ما لا بد للحج منه لم يحنث في يمينه ولم يكن مشغولا بغير الحج
فكذلك البدن مركب النفس تقطع به مسافة العمر فتعهد البدن بما تبقى به قوته
على سلوك الطريق بالعلم والعمل هو من الآخرة لا من الدنيا نعم إذا قصد تلذذ
البدن وتنعمه  بشيء من هذه الأسباب كان منحرفا عن الآخرة ويخشى على قلبه
القسوة قال الطنافسي كنت على باب بني شيبة في المسجد الحرام سبعة أيام
طاويا فسمعت في الليلة الثامنة مناديا وأنا بين اليقظة والنوم ألا من أخذ
من الدنيا أكثر مما يحتاج إليه أعمى الله عين قلبه
فهذا بيان حقيقة الدنيا في حقك فاعلم ذلك ترشد إن شاء الله تعالى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ن-و (d-n-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, nearness, closeness in spatial or temporal terms; the nearer of two things.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The worldly life (al-dunyā) as that which is immediate and proximate, contrasted with the hereafter (al-ākhirah) as that which is remote and deferred; a technical Kalām term for the present abode of trial.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "nearness" (qurb) versus metaphorical extension to designate all that precedes death; the blameworthy world is not a physical entity but a relational category of the heart's attachments.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (in kāna... fa-) and exceptive particles (illā) to delineate precise boundaries between categories, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the logical structure of the divisions.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that knowledge of the blameworthiness of the world does not suffice you unless you know what the blameworthy world is, what it is that ought to be shunned from it, and what is not to be shunned. It is therefore necessary that we clarify the blameworthy world, which one is commanded to avoid because it is an enemy that cuts off the path of God — what it is. So we say:

Your world and your hereafter are two expressions for two states of your heart. That which is near and proximate to you is called "world" (dunyā) — namely, everything before death. That which is remote and deferred is called "hereafter" (ākhirah) — namely, everything after death. Thus, everything in which you have a share, a portion, an aim, an appetite, and an immediate pleasure prior to death — that is the world in your regard. However, not everything toward which you incline and in which you have a portion and share is blameworthy. Rather, it is of three divisions:

**The First Division:** That which accompanies you into the hereafter and whose fruit remains with you after death. This is two things only: knowledge (ʿilm) and action (ʿamal). By knowledge I mean knowledge of God, His attributes, His acts, His angels, His books, His messengers, the dominion (malakūt) of His earth and heavens, and knowledge of the sacred law of His Prophet. By action I mean worship (ʿibādah) purified solely for the face of God, the Exalted. The scholar may become so intimate with knowledge that it becomes the most delightful of things to him, and he abandons sleep, food, and marriage for its pleasure, because it is more desirable to him than all of that. Thus it has become an immediate share in the world.

Yet when we mention the blameworthy world, we do not count this as part of the world at all. Rather, we say it belongs to the hereafter. Likewise, the worshipper may become intimate with his worship and find pleasure in it to such a degree that were he prevented from it, that would be the greatest of punishments upon him. Some of them said: "I do not fear death except because it intervenes between me and the night prayer." Another used to say: "O God, grant me strength for prayer, bowing, and prostration in the grave." For such a one, prayer has become among his immediate shares. And every immediate share falls under the name "world" (dunyā) by way of etymological derivation from proximity (dunūw). But we do not mean by the blameworthy world that [kind of share]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three things of your world have been made beloved to me: women, perfume, and the coolness of my eye in prayer." (1) He thus made prayer part of the pleasures of the world. Likewise, everything that enters into sense perception and witnessing belongs to the world of testimony (ʿālam al-shahādah), which is part of the world. The delight in moving one's limbs in bowing and prostration occurs only in the world; therefore he attributed it to the world. However, in this book we are concerned only with the blameworthy world, and we say: this is not of the world.

**The Second Division:** That which is its opposite at the farthest extreme — everything in which there is an immediate share with no fruit whatsoever in the hereafter, such as delighting in all acts of disobedience, and enjoying what is permissible beyond the measure of needs and necessities that fall within the scope of luxury and ostentation — like enjoying heaped-up treasures of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, tillage, male servants, female servants, steeds, livestock, palaces, dwellings, fine garments, and delicious foods. The servant's share in all of this is the blameworthy world. Regarding what is counted as superfluous (fuḍūl) beyond the place of need, there is a lengthy consideration. For it is narrated that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, appointed Abū al-Dardāʾ over Ḥimṣ, and he built a privy upon which he spent two dirhams. ʿUmar wrote to him: "From ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Commander of the Faithful, to ʿUwaymir. You had in the building of Persia and Rome enough to suffice you from the construction of the world when God willed its ruin. When this letter of mine reaches you, I have dispatched you to Damascus, you and your family." He remained there until he died. This [ʿUmar] considered it superfluous of the world. Reflect upon this. [Page V03P219]

**The Third Division:** That which is intermediate between the two extremes — every immediate share that assists in the works of the hereafter, such as the measure of sustenance from food, a single coarse shirt, and everything indispensable for the preservation of one's existence and health by which one attains to knowledge and action. This is not of the world, like the first division, because it assists the first division and is a means to it. Whenever the servant partakes of it with the intention of seeking aid thereby for knowledge and action, he has not partaken of the world thereby, nor has he become among the children of the world. But if his motive is the immediate share without seeking aid for piety, it is annexed to the second division and becomes part of the world.

Nothing remains with the servant at death except three qualities: purity of heart — I mean its cleanliness from filth — intimacy (uns) with the remembrance of God, the Exalted, and love (ḥubb) for God, the Mighty and Majestic.

Purity of heart and its cleanliness are attained only by refraining from the appetites of the world. Intimacy is attained only by abundant remembrance of God, the Exalted, and persistence therein. Love is attained only through knowledge (maʿrifah), and knowledge of God is attained only through continuous reflection (fikr). These three qualities are the saving and felicitating ones after death.

As for the purity of the heart from the appetites of the world, it is among the saving things, for it becomes a shield between the servant and God's punishment. As has come in the reports: "The deeds of the servant fight on his behalf. When punishment comes from the direction of his feet, the night prayer comes to repel it; when it comes from the direction of his hands, charity comes to repel it." (1) — the hadith.

As for intimacy and love, they are among the felicitating things, and they are the two that convey the servant to the pleasure of the encounter (liqāʾ) and the vision (mushāhadah). This felicity is hastened immediately after death until the time of vision (ruʾyah) arrives in Paradise, and the grave becomes a garden from the gardens of Paradise. How could the grave not be for him a garden from the gardens of Paradise, when he had but one Beloved, and the obstacles hindered him from continuous intimacy through continuous remembrance of Him and contemplation of His beauty? The obstacles have been removed, he has escaped from the prison, and he has been left alone with his Beloved. He arrives before Him joyful, safe from impediments, secure from obstacles. And how could the lover of the world not be tormented at death, when he had no beloved but the world, which has been seized from him, a barrier placed between him and it, and all paths of stratagem for returning to it have been closed? Therefore it was said:

"What is the state of one who had a single one... when that single one is veiled from him?"

Death is not annihilation; it is only separation from the beloved things of the world and arrival before God, the Exalted. Thus, the wayfarer of the hereafter is the one who persists in the causes of these three qualities — namely, remembrance (dhikr), reflection (fikr), and the action that weans him from the appetites of the world, makes its pleasures hateful to him, and cuts him off from them. All of that is possible only through a sound body, and a sound body is attained only through food, clothing, and shelter. Each one requires means. The measure that is indispensable from these three — when the servant takes it from the world for the sake of the hereafter — he is not among the children of the world, and the world is in his regard a tillage for the hereafter. But if he takes it for the share of the soul and with the intention of enjoyment, he becomes among the children of the world and those desirous of its shares.

However, desire for the shares of the world divides into what exposes its possessor to the punishment of the hereafter — this is called forbidden (ḥarām) — and what intervenes between him and the highest stations and exposes him to the length of the reckoning — this is called permissible (ḥalāl). The insightful one knows that the length of standing in the plains of the Resurrection for the sake of accounting is itself a punishment. For whoever is scrutinized in the reckoning is tormented. (2) The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Its permissible is a reckoning, and its forbidden is a punishment." (3) He also said: "Its permissible is a punishment, except that it is a lighter punishment than the punishment of the forbidden." [Page V03P220]

Nay, even were there no reckoning, what is lost of the highest stations in Paradise and what descends upon the heart of regret over their loss — for the sake of base, contemptible shares that have no permanence — that too is a punishment. Measure by this your own state in the world: when you look at your peers who have preceded you in worldly felicities, how your heart is torn apart with regrets over them, even while you know they are fleeting felicities with no permanence, embittered by turbidities with no purity. Then what is your state in the loss of a felicity whose greatness description cannot encompass and whose limit the ages cannot reach? Thus, whoever delights in the world — even by hearing the voice of a bird, or looking at greenery, or a drink of cold water — is diminished from his share in the hereafter by multiples thereof. This is the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, to ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him: "This is of the bliss about which you will be questioned." (1) He pointed thereby to the cold water. And exposure to answering the question entails humiliation, fear, peril, hardship, and waiting — all of which is from the diminishment of the share. Therefore ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "Set aside from me its reckoning," when he was afflicted with thirst and cold water mixed with honey was presented to him. He turned it in his palm, then refrained from drinking it.

So the world — its little and its much, its forbidden and its permissible — is accursed, except what aids in the piety of God. For that measure is not of the world. And whoever's knowledge (maʿrifah) is stronger and more precise, his caution against the bliss of the world is more severe. So much so that Jesus, peace be upon him, placed his head on a stone when he slept, then cast it away when Satan appeared to him and said: "You have desired the world." And so much so that Solomon, peace be upon him, in his kingdom fed the people the most delicious foods while he himself ate barley bread. He made kingship upon himself, by this path, a humiliation and severity. For patience over delicious foods while having the power over them and their availability is more severe. For this reason it is narrated that God, the Exalted, folded up the world from our Prophet, peace be upon him, and he would go hungry for days (2) and would bind a stone upon his belly from hunger. (3)

For this reason God, the Exalted, imposed trials and afflictions upon the prophets and the saints, then upon the most excellent, then the most excellent. All of that is solicitude for them and grace upon them, so that their share of the hereafter might be complete — just as the compassionate father prevents his child the pleasure of fruits and imposes upon him the pain of bloodletting and cupping, out of tenderness and love for him, not out of miserliness toward him.

You have come to know by this that everything that is not for God is of the world, and what is for God — that is not of the world.

If you say: "Then what is that which is for God?" I say: Things are of three divisions:

Among them is what cannot be conceived to be for God — that which is expressed as acts of disobedience and prohibitions, and the various enjoyments in permissible things. This is the pure blameworthy world; it is the world in form and meaning.

Among them is what is for God in form but can be made for other than God — and this is three: reflection (fikr), remembrance (dhikr), and refraining from appetites (kaf ʿan al-shahawāt). For these three, when they proceed secretly and have no motive upon them save the command of God and the Last Day, they are for God and not of the world. But if the purpose of reflection is seeking knowledge for self-aggrandizement, or seeking acceptance among creatures by displaying knowledge; or if the purpose of abandoning appetite is preserving wealth, or guarding the health of the body, or gaining fame for asceticism — then this has become of the world in meaning, even if in form it is thought to be for God, the Exalted.

Among them is what is for the share of the soul in form but can be for God in meaning — such as eating, marriage, and everything connected to one's survival and the survival of one's offspring. If the intention is the share of the soul, it is of the world. If the intention is seeking aid thereby for piety, it is for God in its meaning, even if its form is the form of the world. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever seeks the world lawfully, multiplying and boasting, will meet God while He is angry with him. And whoever seeks it to preserve himself from begging and to protect his dignity will come on the Day of Resurrection with a face like the full moon on the night of the full moon." (4)

See how this differs by intention. Thus, the world is your soul's immediate share that has no need for the matter of the hereafter — and this is expressed as caprice (hawā). To this points the saying of God, the Exalted: {«وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ»} "And forbade the soul its caprice" — {«فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ»} "for indeed Paradise is the refuge." [Page V03P221]

The gathering points of caprice are five things — what God, the Exalted, has collected in His saying: {«إِنَّمَا الْحَيَاةُ الدُّنْيَا لَعِبٌ وَلَهْوٌ وَزِينَةٌ وَتَفَاخُرٌ بَيْنَكُمْ وَتَكَاثُرٌ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْأَوْلَادِ»} "The life of this world is but play, diversion, adornment, boasting among yourselves, and rivalry in wealth and children." The concrete things (aʿyān) from which these five are obtained are seven, gathered by His saying, the Exalted: {«زُيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ حُبُّ الشَّهَوَاتِ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ وَالْبَنِينَ وَالْقَنَاطِيرِ الْمُقَنْطَرَةِ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَالْخَيْلِ الْمُسَوَّمَةِ وَالْأَنْعَامِ وَالْحَرْثِ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ مَتَاعُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا»} "Made attractive to people is the love of appetites: women, sons, heaped-up treasures of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tillage. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life."

You have thus known that everything that is for God is not of the world. The measure of necessity of sustenance and what is indispensable of shelter and clothing is for God if one intends thereby the face of God. Seeking abundance thereof is enjoyment, and it is for other than God. Between enjoyment and necessity there is a degree expressed as need (ḥājah), which has two extremes and a middle. One extreme approaches the limit of necessity and does not harm — for restricting oneself to the very limit of necessity is not possible. The other extreme encroaches upon the side of enjoyment and approaches it, and one ought to be wary of it. Between them are ambiguous intermediates. "Whoever grazes around the sanctuary is likely to fall into it."

Prudence lies in caution, piety, and drawing near to the limit of necessity as much as possible, following the example of the prophets and saints, peace be upon them — for they would drive themselves back to the limit of necessity. So much so that Uways al-Qaranī's family thought him mad due to the severity of his restriction upon himself. They built for him a house at the door of their courtyard, and a year, two years, three years would pass without them seeing his face. He would go out at the first call to prayer and return to his dwelling after the night prayer. His food was to pick up date pits, and whenever he found a shriveled date he would store it for his breaking of the fast. If he found nothing to sustain him from shriveled dates, he would sell the pits and buy with their price what would sustain him. His clothing was what he picked from rubbish heaps — pieces of cloaks — which he would wash in the Euphrates, patch together, and then wear. That was his garment. Sometimes the boys would pass by and throw stones at him, thinking him mad. He would say to them: "O my brothers, if you must throw at me, throw at me with small stones, for I fear you will wound my heels, and the time of prayer will come and I will not find water." Such was his way.

The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, magnified his matter and said: "I find the breath of the Merciful from the direction of Yemen" — pointing to him, may God have mercy on him. (1) When ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God the Exalted be pleased with him, assumed the caliphate, he said: "O people, whoever among you is from Iraq, let him stand." They stood. He said: "Sit down, except whoever is from the people of Kufa." They sat. He said: "Sit down, except whoever is from Murād." They sat. He said: "Sit down, except whoever is from Qaran." They all sat except one man. ʿUmar said to him: "Are you from Qaran?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you know Uways ibn ʿĀmir al-Qaranī?" He described him to him. He said: "Yes. And what is this you ask about, O Commander of the Faithful? By God, there is none among us more foolish than him, nor more mad, nor more wild, nor more base." ʿUmar, may God the Exalted be pleased with him, wept, then said: "I said what I said only because I heard the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, say: 'There will enter through his intercession the like of Rabīʿah and Muḍar.'" (2)

Hirm ibn Ḥayyān said: "When I heard this saying from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, I came to Kufa, and I had no concern but to seek Uways al-Qaranī and ask about him, until I came upon him sitting on the bank of the Euphrates at midday, performing ablution and washing his garment. I recognized him by the description given to me. There was a fleshy man, intensely dark, shaven-headed, thick-bearded, greatly altered, repulsive of face, awe-inspiring of appearance." He said: "I greeted him, and he returned the greeting and looked at me. I said: 'May God give you life, O man.' I extended my hand to shake his, but he refused to shake my hand. I said: 'May God have mercy on you, O Uways, and forgive you. How are you? May God have mercy on you.' Then tears choked me from my love for him and my tenderness toward him, when I saw of his state what I saw, until I wept and he wept. He said: 'And you — may God give you life, O Hirm ibn Ḥayyān. How are you, O my brother? And who pointed you to me?' I said: 'God.' He said: [Page V03P222] 'There is no god but God. Glory be to God. Indeed, the promise of our Lord is to be fulfilled.'"

He said: "I marveled when he knew me — by God, I had not seen him before that, nor had he seen me. I said: 'From where did you know my name and my father's name, when I have not seen you before today?' He said: 'The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me. And I knew your soul by my soul when I spoke to myself and you spoke to yourself. For souls have breaths like the breaths of bodies, and the believers know one another and love one another by the spirit of God, even if they have not met — they recognize one another and speak, even if the abode is distant and the dwellings are separated.'"

He said: "I said: 'Narrate to me, may God have mercy on you, a hadith from the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, that I may hear it from you.' He said: 'I did not reach the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, nor did I have companionship with him — by my father and mother, the Messenger of God — but I saw men who accompanied him, and his hadith reached me as it reached you. And I do not love to open this door upon myself, to be a narrator, or a mufti, or a judge. In myself I have occupation from the people, O Hirm ibn Ḥayyān.'"

He said: "I said: 'O my brother, recite to me a verse of the Quran that I may hear it from you, and supplicate for me with supplications, and counsel me with a counsel I will preserve from you, for I love you intensely for the sake of God.'"

He said: "He stood and took my hand on the bank of the Euphrates, then said: 'I seek refuge in God, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed.' Then he wept. Then he said: 'My Lord said — and the truth is the word of my Lord, and the truest speech is His speech, and the truest words are His words.' Then he recited: {«وَمَا خَلَقْنَا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا لَاعِبِينَ * مَا خَلَقْنَاهُمَا إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكْثَرَهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ»} "And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know" — until he reached His saying: {«إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ»} "Indeed, He is the Mighty, the Merciful." Then he sobbed a sob that I thought he had fainted. Then he said: "O Ibn Ḥayyān, your father Ḥayyān has died, and soon you will die — either to Paradise or to the Fire. Your father Adam died, your mother Eve died, Noah died, Abraham the friend of the Merciful died, Moses the deliverance of the Merciful died, David the vicegerent of the Merciful died, and Muhammad, peace be upon him — the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds — died. Abū Bakr, the vicegerent of the Muslims, died, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, my brother and my chosen one, died." Then he said: "O ʿUmar! O ʿUmar!" He said: "I said: 'May God have mercy on you — ʿUmar has not died.' He said: 'My Lord has announced his death to me, and announced to myself my own death.' Then he said: 'I and you are in death as if it had already been.' Then he prayed upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, then supplicated with hidden supplications. Then he said: 'This is my counsel to you, O Hirm ibn Ḥayyān: the Book of God and the path of the righteous believers. I have announced death to myself and to yourself. Upon you is the remembrance of death — let it not depart from your heart for the blink of an eye as long as you remain. Warn your people when you return to them, and counsel the entire community. Beware of separating from the congregation by a handspan, lest you separate from your religion without knowing, and enter the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. Supplicate for me and for yourself.'"

"Then he said: 'O God, this one claims that he loves me for Your sake and has visited me for Your sake. Show me his face in Paradise, and admit him upon me in Your abode, the Abode of Peace. Preserve him as long as he is in the world, wherever he is. Cover his negligence, and content him from the world with little. Whatever You give him of the world, make it easy for him with ease. Make him among the thankful for what You have given him of Your blessings. And recompense him on my behalf with the best recompense.' Then he said: 'I entrust you to God, O Hirm ibn Ḥayyān. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings. I will not see you after today, may God have mercy on you — do not seek me, for I dislike fame, and solitude is more beloved to me. I am much worried, intensely grieved, among these people as long as I live. So do not ask about me, and do not seek me. Know that you are on my mind even if I do not see you and you do not see me. Remember me and supplicate for me, for I will remember you and supplicate for you, God willing. Go you this way, and I will go this way.'"

"I was eager to walk with him for an hour, but he refused me, and I parted from him. He wept and made me weep. I kept looking at his back until he entered one of the alleys.
