قال الله تعالى يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تلهكم أموالكم ولا أولادكم عن ذكر
الله ومن يفعل ذلك فأولئك هم الخاسرون وقال تعالى إنما أموالكم وأولادكم
فتنة والله عنده أجر عظيم فمن اختار ماله وولده على ما عند الله فقد خسر
وغبن خسرانا عظيما وقال عز وجل من كان يريد الحياة الدنيا وزينتها الآية
وقال تعالى إن الإنسان ليطغى أن رآه استغنى فلا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله
العلي العظيم وقال تعالى ألهاكم التكاثر وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
حب المال والشرف ينبتان النفاق في القلب كما ينبت الماء البقل (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما ذئبان ضاريان أرسلا في زريبة غنم بأكثر
إفسادا فيها من حب الشرف والمال والجاه في دين الرجل المسلم (2)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم هلك المكثرون إلا من قال به في عباد الله هكذا
وهكذا وقليل ما هم (3)
وقيل يا رسول الله أي أمتك شر قال الأغنياء (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم سيأتي بعدكم قوم يأكلون أطايب الدنيا وألوانها
ويركبون فره الخيل وألوانها وينكحون أجمل النساء وألوانها ويلبسون أجمل
الثياب وألوانها لهم بطون من القليل لا تشبع وأنفس بالكثير لا تقنع عاكفون
على الدنيا يغدون ويروحون إليها اتخذوها آلهة من دون إلههم وربا دون ربهم
إلى أمرها ينتهون ولهواهم يتبعون فعزيمة من محمد بن عبد الله لمن أدركه ذلك
الزمان من عقب عقبكم وخلف خلفكم أن لا يسلم عليهم ولا يعود مرضاهم ولا يتبع
جنائزهم ولا يوقر كبيرهم فمن فعل ذلك فقد أعان على هدم الإسلام (5)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم دعوا الدنيا لأهلها من أخذ من الدنيا فوق ما
يكفيه أخذ حتفه وهو لا يشعر (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول ابن آدم مالي مالي وهل لك من مالك إلا ما
أكلت فأفنيت أو لبست فأبليت أو تصدقت فأمضيت (7)
وقال رجل يا رسول الله مالي لا أحب الموت فقال هل معك من مال قال نعم يا
رسول الله قال قدم مالك فإن قلب المؤمن مع ماله إن قدمه PageV03P232
أحب أن يلحقه وإن خلفه أحب أن يتخلف معه (1)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أخلاء ابن آدم ثلاثة واحد يتبعه إلى قبض روحه
والثاني إلى قبره والثالث إلى محشرة فالذي يتبعه إلى قبض روحه فهو ماله
والذي يتبعه إلى قبره فهو أهله والذي يتعبه إلى محشره فهو عمله (2)
وقال الحواريون لعيسى عليه السلام مالك تمشي على الماء ولا نقدر على ذلك
فقال  لهم ما منزلة الدينار والدرهم عندكم قالوا حسنة قال لكنهما والمدر
عندي سواء وكتب سلمان الفارسي إلى أبي الدرداء رضي الله عنهما يا أخي إياك
أن تجمع من الدنيا مالا تؤدي شكره فإني سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
يقول يجاء بصاحب الدنيا الذي أطاع الله فيها وماله بين يديه كلما تكفأ به
الصراط قال له ماله امض فقد أديت حق الله في ثم يجاء بصاحب الدنيا الذي لم
يطع الله فيها وماله بين كتفيه كلما تكفأ به الصراط قال له ماله ويلك ألا
أديت حق الله في فما يزال كذلك حتى يدعو بالويل والثبور (3)
وكل ما أوردناه في كتاب الزهد والفقر في ذم الغنى ومدح الفقر يرجع جميعه
إلى ذم المال فلا نطول بتكريره وكذا كل ما ذكرناه في ذم الدنيا فيتناول ذم
المال بحكم العموم لأن المال أعظم أركان الدنيا وإنما نذكر الآن ما ورد في
المال خاصة
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا مات العبد قالت الملائكة ما قدم وقال الناس
ما خلف (4) حديث لا تتخذوا الضيعة فتحبوا الدنيا أخرجه الترمذي والحاكم
وصحح إسناده من حديث ابن مسعود بلفظ فترغبوا //
الآثار روي أن رجلا نال من أبي الدرداء وأراه سوءا فقال اللهم من فعل بي
سوءا فأصح جسمه وأطل عمره وأكثر ماله فانظر كيف رأى كثرة المال غاية البلاء
مع صحة الجسم وطول العمر لأنه لا بد وأن يفضي إلى الطغيان ووضع علي كرم
الله وجهه درهما على كفه ثم قال أما إنك ما لم تخرج عني لا تنفعني وروي أن
عمر رضي الله عنه أرسل إلى زينب بنت جحش بعطائها فقالت ما هذا قالوا أرسل
إليك عمر بن الخطاب قالت غفر الله له ثم سلت سترا كان لها فقطعته وجعلته
صررا وقسمته في أهل بيتها ورحمها وأيتامها ثم رفعت يديها وقالت اللهم لا
يدركني عطاء عمر بعد عامي هذا فكانت أول نساء رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
لحوقا به وقال الحسن والله ما أعز  الدرهم أحد إلا أذله الله وقيل إن أول ما
ضرب الدينار والدرهم رفعهما إبليس ثم وضعهما على جبهته ثم قبلهما وقال من
أحبكما فهو عبدي حقا وقال سميط بن عجلان إن الدراهم والدنانير أزمة
المنافقين يقادون بها إلى النار وقال يحيى بن معاذ الدرهم عقرب فإن لم تحسن
رقيته فلا تأخذه فإنه إن لدغك قتلك سمه قيل وما رقيته قال أخذه من حله
ووضعه في حقه وقال العلاء بن زياد تمثلت لي الدنيا وعليها من كل زينة فقلت
أعوذ PageV03P233
بالله من شرك فقالت إن سرك أن يعيذك الله مني فابغض الدرهم والدينار وذلك
لأن الدرهم والدينار هما الدنيا كلها إذ يتوصل بهما إلى جميع أصنافها فمن
صبر عنهما صبر عن الدنيا وفي ذلك قيل
إني وجدت فلا تظنوا غيره ... أن التورع عند هذا الدرهم
فإذا قدرت عليه ثم تركته ... فاعلم بأن تقاك تقوى المسلم
وفي ذلك قيل أيضا
لا يغرنك من المر قميص رقعه ... أو إزار فوق عظم الساق منه رفعه
أو جبين لاح فيه أثر قد خلعه ... أره الدرهم تعرف حبه أو ورعه
ويروى عن مسلمة بن عبد الملك أنه دخل على عمر بن عبد العزيز رحمه الله
عند موته فقال يا أمير المؤمنين صنعت صنيعا لم يصنعه أحد قبلك تركت ولدك
ليس لهم درهم ولا دينار وكان له ثلاثة عشر من الولد فقال عمر أقعدوني
فأقعدوه فقال أما قولك لم أدع لهم دينار ولا درهما فإني لم أمنعهم حقا لهم
ولم أعطهم حقا لغيرهم وإنما ولدي أحد رجلين إما مطيع لله فالله كافيه والله
يتولى الصالحين وإما عاص لله فلا أبالي على ما وقع وروي أن محمد بن كعب
القرظي أصاب مالا كثيرا فقيل له لو ادخرته لولدك من بعدك قال لا ولكني
أدخره لنفسي عند ربي وأدخر ربي لولدي ويروى أن رجلا قال لأبي عبد ربه يا
أخي لا تذهب بشر وتترك أولادك بخير فأخرج أبو عبد ربه من ماله مائة ألف
درهم
وقال يحيى بن معاذ  مصيبتان لم يسمع الأولون والآخرون بمثلهما للعبد في
ماله عند موته قبل وما هما قال يؤخذ منه كله ويسئل عنه كله
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-ه-ي (lahiya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To divert, distract, or turn away from something; heedless engrossment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The soul's occupation with worldly matters that veils it from divine remembrance (dhikr), a state of spiritual negligence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of turning aside; here metaphorically extended to the heart's captivity by possessions.
- Root: ف-ت-ن (fatana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Trial, affliction, seduction; to burn or smelt gold to test purity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A divinely ordained test that distinguishes the sincere from the corrupt, often through worldly allurements.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphorical usage — wealth as a crucible that exposes the soul's true mettle.
- Root: ط-غ-ي (ṭaghā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To exceed bounds, transgress, overflow violently (as a flood).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The arrogant rebellion of the soul against God when satiated with worldly sufficiency (istighnāʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal overflowing water; metaphorically, the soul's insolence when it perceives itself self-sufficient.
- Root: ك-ث-ر (kathura)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Abundance, multiplicity, exceeding in number or quantity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The competitive accumulation of worldly goods that diverts from the Hereafter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for numerical abundance, but rhetorically as a censure of acquisitive rivalry.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-ʿAṭf wa al-Tafṣīl (Coordination and Detailing) — The repeated use of "وقال" (and He said) to sequentially coordinate independent Quranic citations and prophetic reports, each functioning as an independent proof (shāhid) within the cumulative argumentative structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: God Most High has said: {«O you who believe, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of God. And whoever does that — then those are the losers»} (Q 63:9). And He Most High said: {«Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and God — with Him is a mighty reward»} (Q 64:15). So whoever chooses his wealth and his children over what is with God has indeed lost and been defrauded with a tremendous loss. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment...»} (Q 11:15) — the verse. And He Most High said: {«Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient»} (Q 96:6-7). There is no might and no power except through God, the Exalted, the Magnificent. And He Most High said: {«Competition in abundance diverts you»} (Q 102:1).

And the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The love of wealth and status sprouts hypocrisy in the heart just as water sprouts vegetation." (1)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Two hungry wolves sent into a pen of sheep do not cause more corruption therein than the love of status, wealth, and prestige does to the religion of a Muslim man." (2)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The accumulators of much have perished — except those who spent it in the path of God's servants, thus and thus — and few they are." (3)

And it was said: "O Messenger of God, which of your community is the worst?" He said: "The wealthy." (4)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "There will come after you a people who eat the delicacies of this world and its varieties, ride the finest horses and their varieties, marry the most beautiful women and their varieties, and wear the most beautiful garments and their varieties. They have bellies that are not satisfied by little, and souls that are not content with much. They are devoted to this world, going out morning and evening to it. They have taken it as a god besides their God, and as a lord besides their Lord. To its command they submit, and their whims they follow. So it is a firm resolve from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh — for whoever reaches that time from among your descendants and your successors — that they should not greet them with peace, nor visit their sick, nor follow their funerals, nor honor their elders. For whoever does that has aided in the demolition of Islam." (5)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Leave this world to its people. Whoever takes from this world more than what suffices him has taken his death-blow without perceiving it." (6)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The son of Adam says: 'My wealth! My wealth!' But is there anything of your wealth for you except what you ate and consumed, or wore and wore out, or gave in charity and forwarded?" (7)

And a man said: "O Messenger of God, why is it that I do not love death?" He said: "Do you have wealth with you?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Send your wealth ahead of you. For the heart of the believer is with his wealth — if he sends it ahead, he loves to join it; and if he leaves it behind, he loves to remain behind with it." (1)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The companions of the son of Adam are three: one accompanies him until the seizure of his soul, the second until his grave, and the third until his place of resurrection. The one who accompanies him until the seizure of his soul is his wealth; the one who accompanies him to his grave is his family; and the one who accompanies him to his resurrection is his deeds." (2)

And the disciples said to Jesus, peace be upon him: "Why is it that you walk upon the water and we are not able to do so?" He said to them: "What is the station of the dinar and the dirham with you?" They said: "Good." He said: "But they and the dust are equal in my sight."

And Salmān al-Fārsī wrote to Abū al-Dardāʾ, may God be pleased with them both: "O my brother, beware of accumulating from this world wealth whose gratitude you cannot discharge. For I heard the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, say: 'The master of worldly wealth who obeyed God therein will be brought forth with his wealth before him. Whenever he stumbles upon the Path (al-ṣirāṭ), his wealth says to him: "Proceed, for you have discharged God's right concerning me." Then the master of worldly wealth who did not obey God therein will be brought forth with his wealth upon his shoulders. Whenever he stumbles upon the Path, his wealth says to him: "Woe to you! Did you not discharge God's right concerning me?" And it continues thus until he calls for woe and destruction.'" (3)

And everything we have cited in the Book of Asceticism and Poverty concerning the censure of wealth and the praise of poverty all reverts to the censure of wealth itself, so we shall not prolong by repeating it. Likewise, everything we have mentioned in the censure of this world encompasses the censure of wealth by virtue of generality, for wealth is the greatest pillar of this world. We now mention only what has come specifically concerning wealth.

He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When the servant dies, the angels say: 'What has he sent ahead?' And the people say: 'What has he left behind?'" (4)

A hadith: "Do not take up landed estates, lest you love this world" — narrated by al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated its chain from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd with the wording "lest you become desirous of it."

THE TRADITIONS (ĀTHĀR):

It is related that a man spoke ill of Abū al-Dardāʾ and showed him evil. He said: "O God, whoever does evil to me — make his body sound, prolong his life, and increase his wealth." Observe how he regarded abundance of wealth as the ultimate affliction, along with soundness of body and length of life — because it inevitably leads to transgression.

And ʿAlī, may God honor his face, placed a dirham upon his palm and said: "Indeed, as long as you do not depart from me, you will not benefit me."

And it is related that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, sent to Zaynab bint Jaḥsh her stipend. She said: "What is this?" They said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb has sent this to you." She said: "May God forgive him." Then she took out a curtain she had, cut it into pieces, made them into bundles, and distributed them among her household, her relatives, and her orphans. Then she raised her hands and said: "O God, let not ʿUmar's gift reach me after this year of mine." And she was the first of the wives of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, to join him (in death).

And al-Ḥasan said: "By God, no one has honored the dirham except that God has humiliated him."

And it was said: When the dinar and the dirham were first struck, Iblīs raised them up, then placed them upon his forehead, then kissed them, and said: "Whoever loves you both is truly my slave."

And Samīṭ ibn ʿAjlān said: "The dirhams and dinars are the reins of the hypocrites, by which they are led to the Fire."

And Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "The dirham is a scorpion — if you do not master its incantation, do not take it, for if it stings you, its venom kills you." It was said: "And what is its incantation?" He said: "Taking it from its lawful source and placing it in its rightful place."

And al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Ziyād said: "This world appeared to me in a vision adorned with every ornament. I said: 'I seek refuge with God from your evil.' She said: 'If you wish God to protect you from me, then despise the dirham and the dinar.'" That is because the dirham and the dinar are this world entirely, for through them one reaches all its varieties. Whoever is patient regarding them is patient regarding this world. Concerning this it was said:

"I have found — and think not otherwise — that scrupulous piety (al-tawarruʿ) is at this dirham. When you have power over it and then leave it, know that your god-fearing is the god-fearing of a Muslim."

And concerning this it was also said:

"Let not a patched shirt deceive you about a man, nor a waist-wrapper raised above the shinbone, nor a forehead showing the trace of prostration. Show him a dirham, and you will know his love or his piety."

And it is related from Maslamah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik that he entered upon ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, may God have mercy on him, at the time of his death and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, you have done something that no one before you has done — you have left your children with not a single dirham or dinar." And he had thirteen children. ʿUmar said: "Seat me up." So they seated him. He said: "As for your saying that I have left them no dinar or dirham — I have not withheld from them any right that was theirs, nor have I given them any right that belonged to others. My children are but one of two men: either obedient to God — then God suffices him, and God takes charge of the righteous; or disobedient to God — then I care not upon what he falls."

And it is related that Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī acquired much wealth, and it was said to him: "Would you not store it up for your children after you?" He said: "No, but I store it up for myself with my Lord, and I leave my children to my Lord."

And it is related that a man said to Abū ʿAbd Rabbih: "O my brother, do not go with evil and leave your children with good." So Abū ʿAbd Rabbih brought out from his wealth one hundred thousand dirhams.

And Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "Two calamities — the earlier and later peoples have heard of nothing like them — befall the servant regarding his wealth at his death." It was said: "What are they?" He said: "All of it is taken from him, and he is questioned about all of it."

### ||| بيان مدح المال والجمع بينه وبين الذم

اعلم أن الله تعالى قد سمى المال خيرا في مواضع من كتابه العزيز فقال جل
وعز {إن ترك خيرا} الآية وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم نعم المال
الصالح للرجل الصالح (1)
وكل ما جاء في ثواب الصدقة والحج فهو ثناء على المال إذ لا يمكن الوصول
إليهما إلا به وقال تعالى {ويستخرجا كنزهما رحمة من ربك} وقال تعالى ممتنا
على عباده {ويمددكم بأموال وبنين ويجعل لكم جنات ويجعل لكم أنهارا} وقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم كاد الفقر أن يكون كفرا (2) حديث من أكرم الناس وأكيسهم
قال أكثرهم للموت ذكرا الحديث أخرجه ابن ماجه من حديث ابن عمر بلفظ أي
المؤمنين أكيس ورواه ابن أبي الدنيا في الموت بلفظ المصنف وإسناده جيد //
PageV03P234
وهذه السعادة لا تنال إلا بثلاث وسائل في الدنيا وهي الفضائل النفسية
كالعلم وحسن الخلق والفضائل البدنية كالصحة والسلامة والفضائل الخارجة عن
البدن كالمال وسائر الأسباب وأعلاها النفسية ثم البدنية ثم الخارجة
فالخارجة أخسها والمال من جملة الخارجات وأدناها الدراهم والدنانير
فإنهما خادمان ولا خادم لهما ومرادان لغيرهما
ولا يرادان لذاتهما إذ النفس هي الجوهر النفيس المطلوب سعادتها وأنها
تخدم العلم والمعرفة ومكارم الأخلاق لتحصلها صفة في ذاتها والبدن يخدم
النفس بواسطة الحواس والأعضاء والمطاعم والملابس تخدم البدن وقد سبق أن
المقصود من المطاعم إبقاء البدن ومن المناكح إبقاء النسل ومن البدن تمكيل
النفس وتزكيتها وتزيينها بالعلم والخلق
ومن عرف هذا الترتيب فقد عرف قدر المال ووجه شرفه وأنه من حيث هو ضرورة
المطاعم والملابس التي هي ضرورة بقاء البدن الذي هو ضرورة كمال النفس الذي
هو خير ومن عرف فائدة الشيء وغايته ومقصده واستعمله لتلك الغاية ملتفتا
إليها غير ناس لها فقد أحسن وانتفع وكان ما حصل له الغرض محمودا في حقه
فإذا المال آلة ووسيلة إلى مقصود صحيح  ويصلح أن يتخذ آلة ووسيلة إلى مقاصد
فاسدة وهي المقاصد الصادة عن سعادة الآخرة وتسد سبيل العلم والعمل فهو إذن
محمود مذموم محمود بالإضافة إلى المقصد المحمود ومذموم بالإضافة إلى المقصد
المذموم فمن أخذ من الدنيا أكثر مما يكفيه فقد أخذ حتفه وهو لا يشعر (1)
حديث اللهم اجعل قوت آل محمد كفافا متفق عليه من حديث أبي هريرة (2) حديث
اللهم أحيني مسكينا وأمتني مسكينا أخرجه الترمذي من حديث أنس وابن ماجه
والحاكم وصحح إسناده من حديث أبي سعيد وقد تقدم (3) حديث تعس عبد الدينار
تعس عبد الدرهم الحديث أخرجه البخاري من حديث أبي هريرة ولم يقل وانتفش
وإنما علق آخره بلفظ تعس وانتكس ووصل ذلك ابن ماجه والحاكم //
فبين أن محبهما عابد لهما ومن عبد حجرا فهو عابد صنم بل كان من كان عبدا
لغير الله فهو عابد صنم أي قطعه ذلك عن الله تعالى وعن أداء حقه فهو كعابد
صنم وهو شرك إلا أن الشرك شركان شرك خفي لا يوجب الخلود في النار وقلما
ينفك عنه المؤمنون فإنه أخفى من دبيب النمل وشرك جلي يوجب الخلود في النار
نعوذ بالله من الجميع

### ||| بيان تفصيل آفات المال وفوائده
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-ن-ن (m-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Bestowal of a favor (niʿmah) with graciousness; the act of conferring a benefit upon another without expectation of return.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine munificence (imtinān) as an attribute of God's gratuitous generosity in creation and provision, distinct from human obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of "granting a favor"; here used metaphorically (majāz) to denote God's reminding His servants of His blessings as an act of grace.
- Root: خ-د-م (kh-d-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To serve, to attend upon; a servant (khādim) who acts for the benefit of another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Instrumentality in the cosmic hierarchy—lower beings serve higher ones in the order of existence (tartīb al-wujūd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal servitude of persons; metaphorical extension to inanimate things (wealth, food, clothing) as "servants" of the soul's perfection.
- Root: ع-ب-د (ʿ-b-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Worship, servitude, utter submission; the state of being a slave (ʿabd).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): True worship is exclusive devotion to God; devotion to anything else constitutes shirk (associationism), whether manifest (jaliyy) or hidden (khafiyy).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal worship of idols; metaphorical application to the love of wealth that enslaves the heart, equated with idolatry in spiritual effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Coordination) — The phrase "وهي الفضائل النفسية" (which are the soul's virtues) functions as explicative apposition clarifying the three means, while the subsequent "ثم" (then) sequences a graded hierarchy (tafdīl) requiring the accusative of specification (tamyīz) in the implied ranking.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that God—Exalted and Glorified—has named wealth "good" (khayr) in places within His Mighty Book. He—Glorious and Majestic—said: {«إن ترك خيرا»} ("if he leaves behind good") — the verse. And the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—said: "Excellent is righteous wealth for a righteous man." (1)

And everything that has come regarding the reward for almsgiving (ṣadaqah) and pilgrimage (ḥajj) is itself praise of wealth, for neither can be attained except through it. And He—Exalted—said: {«ويستخرجا كنزهما رحمة من ربك»} ("And they would extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord"). And He—Exalted—said, bestowing favor upon His servants: {«ويمددكم بأموال وبنين ويجعل لكم جنات ويجعل لكم أنهارا»} ("And He will extend you with wealth and sons, and make for you gardens, and make for you rivers"). And he—peace be upon him—said: "Poverty nearly becomes unbelief." (2) The hadith: "Who is the most honorable and most astute of people?" He said: "The one who remembers death most." — recorded by Ibn Mājah from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar with the wording "Which of the believers is most astute?" And Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated it in his book on death with the author's wording, and its chain is sound. // PageV03P234

And this felicity (saʿādah) is not attained except through three means in this world: the soul's virtues (al-faḍāʾil al-nafsiyyah) such as knowledge and excellence of character; the body's virtues (al-faḍāʾil al-badaniyyah) such as health and soundness; and the virtues external to the body (al-faḍāʾil al-khārijah) such as wealth and all other instruments. The highest of these are the soul's virtues, then the body's, then the external. Thus the external are the basest of them, and wealth is among the external things—and the lowest of them are dirhams and dīnārs.

For the two of them are servants, and they have no servant; they are desired for the sake of other things, and are not desired for their own essences. For the soul is the precious substance (al-jawhar al-nafīs) whose felicity is sought, and it serves knowledge, gnosis, and noble character traits so that these may become attributes within its essence. The body serves the soul by means of the senses and limbs. And foods and garments serve the body. It has already been established that the purpose of foods is the preservation of the body, the purpose of marriage is the preservation of progeny, and the purpose of the body is the perfection of the soul, its purification, and its adornment with knowledge and character.

Whoever knows this hierarchy has known the measure of wealth and the aspect of its honor—namely, that inasmuch as it is a necessity for foods and garments, which are a necessity for the body's survival, which is a necessity for the soul's perfection, which is the good itself. And whoever knows the benefit of a thing, its end, and its purpose, and employs it for that end—attentive to it, not forgetful of it—has done well and profited, and what he has attained becomes praiseworthy in his regard.

Thus wealth is an instrument and a means to a sound purpose. And it may also be taken as an instrument and means to corrupt purposes—namely, those purposes that bar one from the felicity of the Hereafter and obstruct the path of knowledge and action. It is therefore both praiseworthy and blameworthy: praiseworthy in relation to the praiseworthy purpose, and blameworthy in relation to the blameworthy purpose. So whoever takes from this world more than suffices him has taken his own destruction while he does not perceive it. (1) The hadith: "O God, make the sustenance of the family of Muhammad sufficient (kafāf)" — agreed upon, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah. (2) The hadith: "O God, cause me to live as a poor man, and cause me to die as a poor man" — recorded by al-Tirmidhī from the hadith of Anas, and by Ibn Mājah and al-Ḥākim, who declared its chain sound, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, and it has preceded. (3) The hadith: "Perished is the slave of the dīnār; perished is the slave of the dirham" — recorded by al-Bukhārī from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, though he did not add "and may he be puffed up"; rather, he appended its ending with the wording "perished and overturned," and Ibn Mājah and al-Ḥākim connected that addition. //

Thus it is made clear that the lover of the two (dirham and dīnār) is a worshiper of them. And whoever worships a stone is a worshiper of an idol. Rather, whoever is a servant of anything other than God is a worshiper of an idol—that is, it has cut him off from God—Exalted—and from fulfilling His right, so he is like a worshiper of an idol. And this is shirk, except that shirk is of two kinds: a hidden shirk (shirk khafiyy) that does not necessitate eternal abiding in the Fire—and the believers are rarely free from it, for it is more concealed than the creeping of ants—and a manifest shirk (shirk jaliyy) that necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire. We seek refuge with God from all of it.

chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن المال مثل حية فيها سم وترياق ففوائده ترياقه وغوائله سمومه فمن
عرف غوائله وفوائده أمكنه أن يحترز من شره ويستدر من خيره PageV03P235
أما الفوائد فهي تنقسم إلى دنيوية ودينية أما الدنيوية فلا حاجة إلى
ذكرها فإن معرفتها مشهورة مشتركة بين أصناف الخلق ولولا ذلك لم يتهالكوا
على طلبها
وأما الدينية فتنحصر جميعها في ثلاثة أنواع
النوع الأول أن ينفقه على نفسه إما في عبادة أو في الاستعانة على عبادة
أما في العبادة فهو كالاستعانة به على الحج والجهاد فإنه لا يتوصل إليهما
إلا بالمال وهما من أمهات القربات والفقير محروم من فضلهما وأما فيما يقويه
على العبادة فذلك هو المطعم والملبس والمسكن والمنكح وضرورات المعيشة فإن
هذه الحاجات إذا لم تتيسر كان القلب مصروفا إلى تدبيرها فلا يتفرغ للدين
وما  لا يتوصل إلى العبادة إلا به فهو عبادة فأخذ الكفاية من الدنيا لأجل
الاستعانة على الدين من الفوائد الدينية ولا يدخل في هذا التنعم والزيادة
على الحاجة فإن ذلك من حظوظ الدنيا فقط
النوع الثاني ما يصرفه إلى الناس وهو أربعة أقسام الصدقة والمروءة ووقاية
العرض وأجرة الاستخدام
أما الصدقة فلا يخفى ثوابها وإنها لتطفيء غضب الرب تعالى وقد ذكرنا فضلها
فيما تقدم
وأما المروءة فنعني بها صرف المال إلى الأغنياء والأشراف في ضيافة وهدية
وإعانة وما يجري مجراها فإن هذه لا تسمى صدقة بل الصدقة ما يسلم إلى
المحتاج إلا أن هذا من الفوائد الدينية إذ به يكتسب العبد الإخوان
والأصدقاء وبه يكتسب صفة السخاء ويلتحق بزمرة الأسخياء فلا يوصف بالجود إلا
من يصطنع المعروف ويسلك سبيل المروءة والفتوة وهذا أيضا مما يعظم الثواب
فيه فقد وردت أخبار كثيرة في الهدايا والضيافات وإطعام الطعام من غير
اشتراط الفقر والفاقة في مصارفها
وأما وقاية العرض فنعني به بذل المال لدفع هجو الشعراء وثلب السفهاء وقطع
ألسنتهم ودفع شرهم وهو أيضا مع تنجز فائدته بالعاجلة من الحظوظ الدينية قال
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما وقى به المرء عرضه كتب له به صدقة (1)
وكيف لا وفيه منع المغتاب عن معصية الغيبة واحتراز عما يثور من كلامه من
العداوة التي تحمل في المكافئة والانتقام على مجاوزة حدود الشريعة
وأما الاستخدام فهو أن الأعمال التي يحتاج إليها الإنسان لتهيئة أسبابه
كثيرة ولو تولاها بنفسه ضاعت أوقاته وتعذر عليه سلوك سبيل الآخرة بالفكر
والذكر الذي هو أعلى مقامات السالكين ومن لا مال له فيفتقر إلى أن يتولى
بنفسه خدمة نفسه من شراء الطعام وطحنه وكنس البيت حتى نسخ الكتاب الذي
يحتاج إليه وكل ما يتصور أن يقوم به غيرك ويحصل به غرضك فأنت متعوب إذا
اشتغلت به إذ عليك من العلم والعمل والذكر والفكر ما لا يتصور أن يقوم به
غيرك فتضييع الوقت في غيره خسران
النوع الثالث ما لا يصرفه إلى إنسان  معين ولكن يحصل به خير عام كبناء
المساجد والقناطر والرباطات ودور المرضى ونصب الجباب في الطريق وغير ذلك من
الأوقاف المرصدة للخيرات وهي من الخيرات المؤبدة الدارة بعد الموت
المستجلبة بركة أدعية الصالحين إلى أوقات متمادية وناهيك بها خيرا فهذه
جملة فوائد المال في الدين سوى ما يتعلق بالحظوظ العاجلة من الخلاص من ذل
السؤال وحقارة الفقر والوصول إلى العز والمجد بين الخلق وكثرة الإخوان
والأعوان والأصدقاء والوقار والكرامة في القلوب فكل ذلك مما يقتضيه المال
من الحظوظ الدنيوية PageV03P236
وأما الآفات فدينية ودنيوية وأما الدينية فثلاث
الأولى أن تجر إلى المعاصي فإن الشهوات متفاضلة والعجز قد يحول بين المرء
والمعصية ومن العصمة أن لا يجد ومهما كان الإنسان آيسا عن نوع من المعصية
لم تتحرك داعيته فإذا استشعر القدرة عليها انبعثت داعيته والمال نوع من
القدرة يحرك داعية المعاصي وارتكاب الفجور فإن اقتحم ما اشتهاه هلك وإن صبر
وقع في شدة إذ الصبر مع القدرة أشد وفتنة السراء أعظم من فتنة الضراء
الثانية أنه يجر إلى التنعم في المباحات وهذا أول الدرجات فمتى يقدر صاحب
المال على أن يتناول خبز الشعير ويلبس الثوب الخشن ويترك لذائذ الأطعمة كما
كان يقدر عليه سليمان بن داود عليهما الصلاة والسلام في ملكه فأحسن أحواله
أن لا يتنعم بالدنيا ويمرن عليها نفسه فيصير التنعم مألوفا عنده ومحبوبا لا
يصبر عنه ويجره البعض منه إلى البعض فإذا اشتد أنسه به ربما لا يقدر على
التوصل إليه بالكسب الحلال فيقتحم الشبهات ويخوض في المراءاة والمداهنة
والكذب والنفاق وسائر الأخلاق الرديئة لينتظم له أمر دنياه ويتيسر له تنعمه
فإن من كثر ماله كثرت حاجته إلى الناس ومن احتاج إلى الناس فلا بد وأن
ينافقهم ويعصي الله في طلب رضاهم فإن سلم الإنسان من الآفة الأولى وهي
مباشرة الحظوظ فلا يسلم عن هذه أصلا ومن الحاجة إلى الخلق تثور العداوة
والصداقة وينشأ عنه الحسد والحقد والرياء والكبر والكذب والنميمة والغيبة
وسائر المعاصي التي تخص القلب واللسان ولا يخلو  عن التعدي أيضا إلى سائر
الجوارح وكل ذلك يلزم من شؤم المال والحاجة إلى حفظه وإصلاحه
الثالثة وهي التي لا ينفك عنها أحد وهو أنه يلهيه إصلاح ماله عن ذكر الله
تعالى وكل ما شغل العبد عن الله فهو خسران ولذلك قال عيسى عليه الصلاة
والسلام في المال ثلاث آفات أن يأخذه من غير حله فقيل إن أخذه من حله فقال
يضعه في غير حقه فقيل إن وضعه في حقه فقال يشغله إصلاحه عن الله تعالى وهذا
هو الداء العضال فإن أصل العبادات ومخها وسرها ذكر الله والتفكر في جلاله
وذلك يستدعي قلبا فارغا وصاحب الضيعة يمسي ويصبح متفكرا في خصومة الفلاح
ومحاسبته وفي خصومة الشركاء ومنازعتهم في المال والحدود وخصومة أعوان
السلطان في الخراج وخصومة الأجراء على التقصير في العمارة وخصومة الفلاحين
في خيانتهم وسرقتهم وصاحب التجارة يكون متفكرا في خيانة شريكه وانفراده
بالربح وتقصيره في العمل وتضييعه للمال وكذلك صاحب المواشي وهكذا سائر
أصناف الأموال
وأبعدها عن كثرة الشغل النقد المكنوز تحت الأرض ولا يزال الفكر مترددا
فيما يصرف إليه وفي كيفية حفظه وفي الخوف مما يعثر عليه وفي دفع أطماع
الناس عنه وأودية أفكار الدنيا لا نهاية لها والذي معه قوت يومه في سلامة
من جميع ذلك فهذه جملة الآفات الدنيوية سوى ما يقاسيه أرباب الأموال في
الدنيا من الخوف والحزن والغم والهم والتعب في دفع الحساد وتجشم المصاعب في
حفظ المال وكسبه فإذن ترياق المال أخذ القوت منه وصرف الباقي إلى الخيرات
وما عدا ذلك سموم وآفات نسأل الله تعالى السلامة وحسن العون بلطفه وكرمه
إنه على ذلك قدير
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-و-ل (gh-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That which destroys or corrupts; the ruinous consequence of a thing; also used for the sudden calamity that seizes one unawares.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The harmful, destructive aspect of a created thing that leads one away from felicity (saʿādah) — contrasted with its beneficial aspect (manfaʿah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for the venomous bite of a serpent; metaphorical extension to any hidden peril that undermines one's ultimate good.
- Root: ت-ر-ي-ا-ق (t-r-y-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The antidote (tiryāq) — a compound remedy against poison; by extension, that which neutralizes harm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the moral sphere, the corrective measure that transforms a potential source of ruin into a means of salvation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphorical usage — wealth is likened to a serpent whose poison is its harms and whose antidote is its benefits, requiring discernment to extract the latter.
- Root: م-ر-و-ء-ة (m-r-w-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Manliness, chivalrous virtue; the quality of one who is complete in manhood (murūʾah) — generosity and noble conduct toward others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A praiseworthy moral disposition (khuluq) that perfects the soul through beneficence toward fellow creatures, distinct from obligatory charity (ṣadaqah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of manly virtue; here used in its technical ethical sense of voluntary generosity toward the affluent, not the needy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The opening sentence employs a simile (tashbīh) with an implied conditional: "whoever knows the harms and benefits [of wealth] is able to guard against its evil and extract its good," where the protasis governs the apodosis, requiring the reader to supply the logical connection between knowledge and action.
chapters.translation:
Know that wealth is like a serpent containing both venom and antidote — its benefits are its antidote, and its harms are its poisons. Whoever recognizes its harms and its benefits is able to guard against its evil and to extract its good.

As for the benefits, they divide into worldly and religious. As for the worldly, there is no need to mention them, for knowledge of them is well-known and shared among all classes of creatures — were it not so, they would not vie so desperately in seeking them.

As for the religious benefits, they are entirely encompassed in three kinds:

The first kind: that one spends it upon oneself — either in worship, or in seeking aid for worship. As for [spending] in worship, it is like using it to aid in the Pilgrimage (Ḥajj) and the Holy War (Jihād), for neither can be attained except through wealth, and both are among the greatest acts of devotion (qurubāt); the poor man is deprived of their excellence. As for [spending] on what strengthens one for worship, that is food, clothing, shelter, marriage, and the necessities of livelihood — for when these needs are not readily available, the heart is diverted to managing them and cannot devote itself freely to religion. And whatever cannot be attained except through [some means] is itself an act of worship — so taking sufficiency from this world for the sake of aiding one's religion is among the religious benefits. But this does not include indulgence (tanʿum) or excess beyond need, for that pertains only to worldly pleasures.

The second kind: what one spends upon other people — and this is of four divisions: charity (ṣadaqah), chivalrous generosity (murūʾah), protection of one's honor (ʿirḍ), and the wages of service (ujrat al-istikhdām).

As for charity, its reward is not hidden, and indeed it extinguishes the wrath of the Lord, Exalted is He — and we have already mentioned its excellence in what preceded.

As for chivalrous generosity, we mean by it the expenditure of wealth upon the wealthy and the noble — in hospitality, gifts, assistance, and what runs in that course. For these are not called charity; rather, charity is what is given to the needy. Yet this too is among the religious benefits, for through it the servant acquires brothers and friends, and through it he acquires the attribute of generosity (sakhāʾ) and joins the company of the generous. For none is described as munificent (jawd) except one who performs acts of kindness and treads the path of chivalrous virtue and manly excellence (futūwah). This too is a matter of great reward — for many reports (akhbār) have come concerning gifts, hospitality, and feeding others without stipulating poverty or need as conditions for their expenditure.

As for protection of one's honor, we mean by it the expenditure of wealth to repel the lampoons of poets, the slander of the foolish, to cut off their tongues, and to repel their harm. This too — along with the immediate benefit it secures in this world — is among the religious benefits. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: {«ما وقى به المرء عرضه كتب له به صدقة»} — "Whatever a man protects his honor with is recorded for him as charity." And how could it not be so, for in it there is the prevention of the backbiter from the sin of backbiting, and the avoidance of what arises from his speech — namely, the enmity that drives one to retaliation and vengeance beyond the bounds of the Sacred Law.

As for the wages of service: the tasks that a man needs for the preparation of his affairs are many, and were he to undertake them himself, his time would be wasted and the path of the Hereafter would become difficult for him — [the path] of reflection (fikr) and remembrance (dhikr), which are the highest stations of the wayfarers (sālikīn). And whoever has no wealth is compelled to undertake himself the service of his own person — from buying food, grinding it, sweeping the house, even to copying the book he needs. And everything that another can perform for you while your purpose is thereby achieved — you are being burdened if you occupy yourself with it, for upon you rests [the duty of] knowledge, action, remembrance, and reflection, which no other can perform in your stead. So wasting time on other than that is sheer loss.

The third kind: what one does not spend upon any particular person, but through which general good is achieved — such as building mosques, bridges, caravanserais (ribāṭāt), houses for the sick, installing water-troughs on the road, and other endowments (awqāf) dedicated to good works. These are among the perpetual goods that continue after death, drawing the blessings of the prayers of the righteous for extended periods — and sufficient is this as good. This then is the sum of the benefits of wealth in religion — apart from what pertains to immediate worldly advantages: deliverance from the humiliation of begging, the contemptibility of poverty, the attainment of honor and glory among creatures, the abundance of brothers, helpers, and friends, and the dignity and reverence in hearts. All of that is among the worldly advantages that wealth procures.

As for the harms (āfāt), they are religious and worldly. As for the religious, they are three:

The first: that wealth drags one into sins. For the appetites (shahawāt) are of varying degrees, and incapacity may stand between a man and sin — and part of divine protection (ʿiṣmah) is that one finds no means [to sin]. Whenever a man is despairing of a particular kind of sin, his inclination toward it does not stir; but when he becomes conscious of his ability to commit it, his inclination is aroused. And wealth is a kind of ability that stirs the inclination toward sins and the commission of lewdness. If he plunges into what he desires, he perishes; and if he shows patience, he falls into hardship — for patience with ability is more severe, and the trial of prosperity (fitnat al-sarāʾ) is greater than the trial of adversity (fitnat al-ḍarrāʾ).

The second: that it drags one into indulgence in permissible things — and this is the first step [downward]. For when is the owner of wealth able to content himself with barley bread, to wear coarse garments, and to abandon the delicacies of food — as Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both, was able to do despite his kingdom? So the best of his states is that he does not indulge in this world and trains his soul against it — for indulgence becomes familiar to him and beloved, and he cannot bear to part with it, and it drags him from one [pleasure] to another. And when his intimacy with it intensifies, perhaps he cannot attain it through lawful earning, so he plunges into ambiguities (shubuhāt) and wades into flattery, sycophancy, lying, hypocrisy, and all other base traits of character — in order to set in order his worldly affairs and make his indulgence easy. For whoever's wealth increases, his need for people increases; and whoever needs people must inevitably dissimulate with them and disobey Allah in seeking their pleasure. For even if a man is safe from the first harm — namely, the direct pursuit of pleasures — he is not safe from this one at all. And from need of creatures arises enmity and friendship, and from it are born envy, rancor, hypocrisy, pride, lying, slander, backbiting, and the rest of the sins that pertain specifically to the heart and tongue — nor is one free from transgression extending also to the other limbs. And all of this follows from the ill-omen of wealth and the need to preserve and manage it.

The third — and this is the one from which no one is free — is that managing his wealth distracts him from the remembrance of Allah, Exalted is He. And everything that occupies the servant away from Allah is loss. For this reason, Jesus, peace be upon him, said concerning wealth: "It has three harms: that one takes it from an unlawful source." It was said: "What if he takes it from a lawful source?" He said: "That he places it in an improper purpose." It was said: "What if he places it in a proper purpose?" He said: "That its management distracts him from Allah, Exalted is He." And this is the chronic disease (al-dāʾ al-ʿuḍāl). For the root of acts of worship, their marrow, and their secret is the remembrance of Allah and reflection upon His Majesty — and that requires an empty heart. The owner of an estate passes his evening and morning reflecting upon disputes with the farmer and settling accounts with him, upon quarrels with partners and their contentions over the property and its boundaries, upon disputes with the agents of the Sultan over the land-tax (kharāj), upon disputes with the laborers over their negligence in cultivation, and upon disputes with the farmers over their treachery and theft. The merchant is absorbed in reflection upon the treachery of his partner, his taking sole profit, his negligence in work, and his squandering of wealth. Likewise the owner of livestock, and so too all other kinds of wealth.

And the farthest of these from much occupation is coined money buried beneath the earth — yet even then, thought continues to oscillate over how to spend it, how to preserve it, fear of someone discovering it, and repelling people's covetousness from it. And the valleys of worldly thoughts have no end. But the one who has with him only his day's provision is safe from all of that. This then is the sum of the worldly harms — apart from what the owners of wealth endure in this world of fear, sorrow, grief, anxiety, and toil in repelling the envious and surmounting difficulties in preserving and earning wealth.

So then: the antidote of wealth is to take from it one's provision (qūt) and to expend the remainder upon good works. And whatever is beyond that is poisons and harms. We ask Allah, Exalted is He, for safety and good assistance, through His grace and generosity — verily, He is powerful over that.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Blameworthiness of Greed and Covetousness, and the Praiseworthiness of Contentment and Despair of What Is in People’s Hands
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان ذم الحرص والطمع ومدح القناعة واليأس مما في أيدي الناس
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ر-ص (ḥ-r-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is intense, unrelenting pursuit of something, often with restless eagerness; also used for the predator’s clinging to prey.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ḥirṣ denotes an inordinate attachment to worldly goods that opposes trust in God (tawakkul) and veils the heart from the Hereafter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = physical clinging or eager striving; metaphorical (majāz) = the soul’s insatiable craving that enslaves the rational faculty.
- Root: ط-م-ع (ṭ-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Aspiration or longing for something hoped for, often with an element of expectation; can be praiseworthy (for divine mercy) or blameworthy (for worldly gain).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ṭamaʿ is the soul’s inclination toward what it desires; when directed to creatures, it breeds humiliation and dependence, whereas despair (yaʾs) of creatures is a station of the veracious (ṣiddīqīn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = stretching the neck toward a desired object; metaphorical = the heart’s fixation on what others possess, which is censured here.
- Root: ق-ن-ع (q-n-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Satisfaction with one’s allotted share; also the act of being content with little, without restless seeking.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Qanāʿah is a praiseworthy virtue that frees the soul from servitude to others and aligns with the prophetic counsel of richness of the soul (ghinā al-nafs).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = being filled or satisfied (as with water); metaphorical = the heart’s sufficiency with God’s decree, a state of inner wealth.
- Root: ي-أ-س (y-ʾ-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Despair or cessation of hope; in this context, it is not negative but a deliberate severing of expectation from creatures.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Yaʾs from what is in people’s hands is the foundation of true reliance on God; it is the opposite of ṭamaʿ and is praised when directed away from creation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = cutting off hope; metaphorical = the heart’s detachment from created causes, a spiritual discipline (riyāḍah) for the seeker.
- Sībawayh Rule: The construction “بيان ذمّ الحرص والطمع ومدح القناعة واليأس” employs a genitive chain (iḍāfah) where the verbal nouns (maṣādir) “ذمّ” and “مدح” govern their objects. The conjunction “و” links two coordinated pairs, each with a blameworthy and a praiseworthy trait, creating a balanced antithesis (muqābalah) that is rhetorically deliberate.
chapters.translation: I say: This section is an exposition of the blameworthiness of greed (ḥirṣ) and covetousness (ṭamaʿ), and the praiseworthiness of contentment (qanāʿah) and despair (yaʾs) of what is in the hands of people. Know that the root of every servitude to creatures is the soul’s eager clinging to their possessions, and its aspiration toward what they hold. For when the heart stretches toward what others possess, it is humiliated by them, and when it despairs of them, it is freed from them. Thus, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: «الْيَأْسُ مِمَّا فِي أَيْدِي النَّاسِ عِزٌّ لِلْمُؤْمِنِ» — “Despair of what is in people’s hands is honor for the believer.” And contentment is the wealth that never diminishes, for the rich is not the one whose wealth abounds, but the one whose soul is satisfied with what God has apportioned. So sever your hope from creatures, and you will be independent of them; and be content with your share, and you will be the richest of people. For greed is a chain upon the neck, and covetousness is a humiliation that never lifts, while contentment is a crown that never falls.

chapters.title_en: On Contentment (Qanāʿah) and the Censure of Greed and Ambition
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الفقر محمود كما أوردناه في كتاب الفقر ولكن ينبغي أن يكون
الفقير قانعا منقطع الطمع عن الخلق غير ملتفت إلى ما في أيديهم ولا حريصا
على اكتساب المال كيف كان ولا يمكنه ذلك إلا بأن يقنع بقدر الضرورة
PageV03P237
من المطعم والملبس والمسكن ويقتصر على  أقله قدرا وأخسه نوعا ويرد أمله
إلى يومه أو إلى شهره ولا يشغل قلبه بما بعد شهر فإن تشوق إلى الكثير أو
طول أمله فاته عز القناعة وتدنس لا محالة بالطمع وذل الحرص وجره الحرص
والطمع إلى مساوئ الأخلاق وارتكاب المنكرات الخارقة للمروءات وقد جبل
الآدمي على الحرص والطمع وقلة القناعة قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لو
كان لابن آدم واديان من ذهب لابتغى لهما ثالثا ولا يملأ جوف ابن آدم إلا
التراب ويتوب الله على من تاب (1) وعن أبي واقد الليثي قال كان رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا أوحى أليه أتيناه يعلمنا مما أوحى إليه فجئته ذات
يوم فقال إن الله عز وجل يقول إنا أنزلنا المال لإقام الصلاة وإيتاء الزكاة
ولو كان لابن آدم واد من ذهب لأحب أن يكون له ثان ولو كان له الثاني لأحب
أن يكون لهما ثالث ولا يملأ جوف ابن آدم إلا التراب ويتوب الله على من تاب
(2) وقال أبو موسى الأشعري نزلت سورة نحو براءة ثم رفعت وحفظ منها إن الله
يؤيد هذا الدين بأقوام لا خلاق لهم ولو أن لابن آدم واديين من مال لتمنى
واديا ثالثا ولا يملأ جوف ابن آدم إلا التراب ويتوب الله على من تاب (3)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم منهومان لا يشبعان منهوم العلم ومنهوم المال (4)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم يهرم ابن آدم ويشب معه اثنتان الأمل وحب المال
أو كما قال (5)
ولما كانت هذه جبلة للآدمي مضلة وغريزة مهلكه أثنى الله تعالى ورسوله على
القناعة فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم طوبى لمن هدي للإسلام وكان عيشه كفافا
وقنع به (6)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ما من أحد فقير ولا غني إلا ود يوم القيامة أنه
كان أوتي قوتا في الدنيا (7)
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ليس الغنى عن كثرة العرض إنما الغنى غنى النفس
(8)
ونهى عن شدة الحرص والمبالغة في الطلب فقال أيها الناس أجملوا في الطلب
فإنه ليس لعبد  إلا ما كتب له ولن يذهب عبد من الدنيا حتى يأتيه ما كتب له
من الدنيا وهي راغمة (9)
وروي أن موسى عليه السلام سأل ربه تعالى فقال أي عبادك أغنى قال أقنعهم
مما أعطيته قال فأيهم أعدل قال من أنصف من نفسه (10) حديث ابن مسعود إن روح
القدس نفث في روعى إن نفسا لن تموت حتى تستكمل رزقها الحديث أخرجه ابن أبي
الدنيا في القناعة والحاكم مع اختلاف وقد تقدم فيه (11) حديث أبي هريرة كن
ورعا تكن أعبد الناس الحديث أخرجه ابن ماجه وقد تقدم // PageV03P238
ونهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الطمع فيما رواه أبو أيوب الأنصاري
أن أعرابيا أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا رسول الله عظني وأوجز
فقال إذا صليت فصل صلاة مودع ولا تحدثن بحديث تعتذر منه غدا وأجمع اليأس
مما في أيدي الناس (1)
وقال عوف بن مالك الأشجعي كنا عند رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم تسع أو
ثمانية أو سبعة فقال ألا تبايعون رسول الله قلنا أو ليس قد بايعناك يا رسول
الله ثم قال ألا تبايعون رسول الله فبسطنا أيدينا فبايعناه فقال قائل منا
قد بايعناك فعلى ماذا نبايعك قال أن تعبدوا الله ولا تشركوا به شيئا وتصلوا
الخمس وأن تسمعوا وتطيعوا وأسر كلمة خفية ولا تسألوا الناس شيئا (2) قال
