chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-خ-و (s-kh-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be generous, to give freely, to be ample or abundant" — the root denotes an innate disposition of open-handedness, as opposed to constriction (ḍīq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, sakhaʾ is the praiseworthy moral trait (khuluq) by which one expends what is not needed for the sake of another, mirroring divine bounty (jūd) — it is a perfection of the soul's faculty of giving.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally (ḥaqīqah), sakhaʾ is the physical act of bestowal; metaphorically (majāz), it denotes the soul's liberality even when the hand is empty — the rhetorical shift from act to character.
- Root: أ-ث-ر (ʾ-th-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root means "to prefer, to choose, to single out" — from ʾathara, "he preferred," and ʾithār, "preference of another over oneself."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic lexicon, īthār is the supreme degree of generosity — giving to another while in dire need (khaṣāṣah), as in {«وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ»} (They prefer others over themselves, even if they are in need). It is the virtue of the Companions and the summit of moral excellence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, īthār is the act of preference; metaphorically, it is the annihilation of self-interest — the rhetorical figure of hyperbole (mubālaghah) where the giver is described as "preferring" even when it entails self-harm.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs "لو" (law) for counterfactual conditions (e.g., "لو وجدها مجانا لأكلها"), and "إنما" (innamā) for restriction (ḥaṣr), which Sībawayh parses as a nominal sentence with an implied predicate, restricting the definition of sakhaʾ to its essential act.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that generosity (sakhāʾ) and miserliness (bukhl) — each of them is divided into degrees.

The highest degree of generosity is self-sacrifice (īthār), which is to be bountiful with wealth while in need. For generosity is but an expression of expending what one does not need, whether for one in need or for one not in need; but expending while in need is more severe.

Just as generosity may reach the point where a man is generous toward another while in need, so miserliness may reach the point where a man is miserly toward himself while in need. How many a miser hoards wealth, then falls ill and does not treat himself, and desires a craving and nothing prevents him from it save the miserliness of the price — had he found it free, he would have eaten it. This one is miserly toward himself while in need; that one prefers another over himself while he is in need of it. So behold the difference between the two men! For moral traits are gifts (ʿaṭāyā) that God places wherever He wills, and there is no degree after self-sacrifice in generosity.

God — exalted — praised the Companions, may God be pleased with them, for it, saying: {«وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ»} (And they prefer others over themselves, even if they are in need) [Q. 59:9]. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Any man who craves a craving, then suppresses his craving and prefers another over himself — it is forgiven him." (1) The hadith of ʿĀʾishah: "The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, never filled his stomach for three consecutive days; had we wished, we would have been full, but we used to prefer others over ourselves." Al-Bayhaqī transmitted it in al-Shuʿab with the wording: "But he used to prefer himself over others" — and the beginning of the hadith is in Muslim with the wording: "The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, never filled his stomach for three consecutive days with barley bread until he passed away." And for the Two Shaykhs: "The family of Muhammad never filled their stomachs for three consecutive nights since they arrived in Medina until he was taken." Muslim added: "from food."

A guest descended upon the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he found nothing with his family. Then a man from the Anṣār entered upon him and took the guest to his family. Then he placed food before him and ordered his wife to extinguish the lamp, and he kept extending his hand to the food as if he were eating, but he was not eating, until the guest had eaten. When morning came, the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said to him: "God indeed marveled at your deed last night toward your guest," and the verse was revealed: {«وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ»} — the hadith of the guest descending and finding nothing with his family, and a man of the Anṣār entering upon him and taking him to his family — the hadith concerning the revelation of His saying, exalted: {«وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ»}, is agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh) from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.

So generosity is a trait of the traits of God — exalted — and self-sacrifice is the highest degree of generosity. This was of the character (adab) of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, until God — exalted — called it "great," saying: {«وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ»} (And indeed, you are upon a great character) [Q. 68:4].

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said: Moses, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, show me some of the degrees of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his community." He said: "O Moses, you will not be able to bear that, but I will show you one of his stations, noble and great, by which I favored him over you and over all My creation." He said: So He unveiled for him the dominion of the heavens (malakūt al-samāwāt), and he looked upon a station whose lights and proximity to God — exalted — nearly destroyed his soul. He said: "O Lord, by what did he attain this honor?" He said: "By a trait I singled him out with among them — and it is self-sacrifice (īthār). O Moses, no one among them comes to Me having acted upon it for a time of his life, except that I am ashamed to call him to account, and I lodge him in My Garden wherever he wills."

It is said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar went out to an estate of his, and he alighted at some palm trees of a people, in which there was a black slave working. When the slave's provision came to him, a dog entered the garden and drew near the slave. The slave threw a loaf to it, and it ate it; then he threw the second and the third, and it ate them — while ʿAbd Allāh was watching him. He said: "O slave, how much is your provision each day?" He said: "What you have seen." He said: "Then why did you prefer this dog over yourself?" He said: "This is not a land of dogs; it came from a distant distance, hungry, and I disliked that I should be full while it is hungry." He said: "Then what will you do today?" He said: "I will fast this day of mine." So ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar said: "Am I to be blamed for generosity? This slave is more generous than I." So he bought the garden, the slave, and all the implements in it, freed the slave, and gifted it to him.

And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: A sheep's head was gifted to a man among the Companions of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he said: "My brother is more in need of it than I." So he sent it to him, and one kept sending it to another until seven households passed it around, and it returned to the first.

And ʿAlī, may God honor his face, spent the night on the bed of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him. God — exalted — revealed to Gabriel and Michael, peace be upon them: "I have made you brothers and made the life of one of you longer than the life of the other; so which of you will prefer his companion with life?" Both chose life and loved it. So God — mighty and majestic — revealed to them: "Will you not be like ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib? I made brotherhood between him and My Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and he spent the night on his bed, ransoming him with his own soul and preferring him with life. Descend to the earth and protect him from his enemy." So Gabriel was at his head and Michael at his feet, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, was saying: "Bravo, bravo! Who is like you, O son of Abī Ṭālib? God — exalted — boasts of you to the angels." So God — exalted — revealed: {«وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَن يَشْرِي نَفْسَهُ ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ وَاللَّهُ رَءُوفٌ بِالْعِبَادِ»} (And among the people is one who sells his soul seeking the pleasure of God, and God is kind to the servants) [Q. 2:207]. — The hadith of ʿAlī spending the night on the bed of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and God revealing to Gabriel and Michael, "I have made you brothers and made the life of one of you longer than the other" — the hadith concerning the revelation of His saying, exalted: {«وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَن يَشْرِي نَفْسَهُ ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ»}. Aḥmad transmitted it in abbreviated form from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "He sold himself, wore the garment of the Prophet, peace be upon him, then slept in his place" — the hadith, but it does not mention Gabriel and Michael. I have not found a source for this addition, and in it is Abū Balj, who is disputed, and the hadith is rejected (munkar).

And from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Anṭākī: About thirty-three souls gathered with him in a village near al-Rayy, and they had a few counted loaves that would not satisfy all of them. So they broke the loaves, extinguished the lamp, and sat down to eat. When it was lifted, the food was as it was — no one had eaten anything from it, each preferring his companion over himself.

And it is related that Shuʿbah was approached by a beggar while he had nothing, so he pulled a beam from the ceiling of his house and gave it to him, then apologized to him.

And Ḥudhayfah al-ʿAdawī said: On the day of al-Yarmūk, I went out seeking a cousin of mine, and with me was some water. I was saying: "If he has any breath left, I will give him to drink and wipe his face with it." Then I came upon him, and I said: "Shall I give you to drink?" He gestured to me: "Yes." Then a man said: "Ah!" So my cousin gestured to me to go to him. I came to him, and he was Hishām ibn al-ʿĀṣ. I said: "Shall I give you to drink?" Another heard him and said: "Ah!" So Hishām gestured: "Go to him." I came to him, and he had died. So I returned to Hishām, and he had died. Then I returned to my cousin, and he had died. May God's mercy be upon them all.

And ʿAbbās ibn Dahqān said: No one left this world as he entered it except Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith — for a man came to him in his illness and complained to him of need, so he pulled off his shirt and gave it to him, and borrowed a garment and died in it.

And from some of the Sufis, he said: We were in Ṭarsūs, and a group of us gathered and went out to the gate of jihad. A dog from the city followed us. When we reached the outer part of the gate, there was a dead animal, so we climbed to a high place and sat. When the dog looked at the carcass, it returned to the city, then came back after an hour with about twenty dogs. It came to that carcass and sat aside, and the dogs fell upon the carcass and kept eating it, while that dog sat watching them, until they had eaten the carcass and only the bone remained. The dogs returned to the city, and that dog arose, came to those bones, ate a little of what remained on them, then departed.

We have already mentioned a number of reports on self-sacrifice and the states of the saints (awliyāʾ) in the Book of Poverty and Asceticism (Kitāb al-Faqr wa al-Zuhd), so there is no need to repeat them here. And with God is success, and upon Him is reliance in what pleases Him — mighty and majestic.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Definition of Generosity and Stinginess and Their True Reality
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان حد السخاء والبخل وحقيقتهما
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-خ-و (s-kh-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "ease, softness, and liberality" — the opposite of hardness and constriction; also denotes a soft, yielding palm (nakhla sakhwāʾ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, sakhāʾ is the virtue of the soul that disposes one to expend what is due without reluctance — a mean between squandering (tabdhīr) and stinginess (bukhl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to the natural ease of giving; metaphorical (majāz) extends to the soul's liberality in knowledge, praise, or life itself.
- Root: ب-خ-ل (b-kh-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "niggardliness, withholding, and avarice" — the opposite of sakhāʾ; also used for a tight, constricted state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Bukhl is the soul's vice of withholding what is obligatory or commendable — a deficiency in the irāda (will) to expend for the sake of God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is withholding wealth; metaphorical is withholding one's self, effort, or truth — a spiritual constriction.
- Root: ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "boundary, limit, definition" — the precise demarcation separating one thing from another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, ḥadd is the logical definition that captures the essence (māhiyya) of a thing, distinguishing it from all else.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is a physical boundary; metaphorical is the conceptual limit that defines a moral or metaphysical reality.
- Root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "truth, reality, due right" — that which is firmly established and undeniable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥaqīqa is the inner reality of a thing as it truly is, as opposed to its outward appearance or metaphorical sense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is the fixed truth; metaphorical is the essential nature of an act or virtue.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taḍādd (Mutual Opposition) — When two terms are defined as opposites (sakhāʾ vs. bukhl), their definitions must be mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive, each clarified by negation of the other's defining property.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us expound the definition (ḥadd) of generosity (sakhāʾ) and stinginess (bukhl), and their true realities (ḥaqīqatuhumā). Know that every moral quality (khuluq) is known by its definition and its opposite, for things are made clear by their contraries. Generosity is a disposition of the soul (malakat al-nafs) whereby one parts with what is due (al-wājib) and what is commendable (al-mandūb) with ease and willingness, without hesitation or regret. Stinginess, on the other hand, is a disposition of the soul whereby one withholds what is due and what is commendable, clinging to it with tightness and reluctance, even when the expenditure is obligatory. The true reality of generosity is not the mere act of giving, nor is the true reality of stinginess the mere act of withholding; rather, each is a settled state (hayʾa rāsikha) in the soul from which the acts flow naturally. For the generous man gives when giving is fitting, and refrains when refraining is fitting; the stingy man withholds even when giving is incumbent upon him, and his withholding is a sickness of the heart, not a virtue of prudence. Thus, the definition of each is bound to the state of the soul, not to the outward act alone — for acts are but the fruits of the inner dispositions, and the root is the soul's inclination toward ease or constriction.

chapters.title_en: The True Reality of Stinginess (Bukhl) and Generosity (Jūd/Sakhāʾ) — Section 489
chapters.arabic_text:
لعلك تقول قد عرف بشواهد الشرع أن البخل من المهلكات ولكن ما حد البخل
وبماذا يصير الإنسان بخيلا وما من إنسان إلا وهو يرى نفسه سخيا وربما يراه
غيره بخيلا وقد يصدر فعل من إنسان فيختلف فيه الناس فيقول قوم هذا بخل
ويقول آخرون ليس هذا من البخل
وما من إنسان إلا ويجد من نفسه حبا للمال ولأجله يحفظ المال ويمسكه فإن
كان يصير بإمساك المال بخيلا فإذا لا ينفك أحد عن البخل
وإذا كان الإمساك مطلقا لا يوجب البخل ولا معنى للبخل إلا الإمساك فما
البخل الذي يوجب الهلاك وما حد السخاء الذي يستحق به البعد صفة السخاوة
وثوابها فنقول قد قال قائلون حد البخل منع الواجب فكل من أدى ما يجب عليه
فليس ببخيل 4 وهذا غير كاف فإن من يرد اللحم مثلا إلى القصاب والخبز للخباز
بنقصان حبة أو نصف حبة فإنه يعد بخيلا بالاتفاق
وكذلك من يسلم إلى عياله القدر الذي يفرضه القاضي ثم يضايقهم في لقمة
ازدادوها عليه أو تمرة أكلوها من ماله يعد بخيلا
ومن كان بين يديه رغيف فحضر من يظن أنه يأكل معه فأخفاه عنه عد بخيلا
وقال قائلون البخيل هو الذي يستصعب العطية وهو أيضا قاصر فإنه إن أريد به
أنه يستصعب كل عطية فكم من بخيل لا يستصعب العطية القليلة كالحبة وما يقرب
منها ويستصعب ما فوق ذلك وإن أريد به أنه يستصعب بعض العطايا فمن من جواد
إلا  وقد يستصعب بعض العطايا وهو ما يستغرق جميع ماله أو المال العظيم
فهذا لا يوجب الحكم بالبخل
وكذلك تكلموا في الجود فقيل الجود عطاء بلا من وإسعاف من غير روية
وقيل الجود عطاء من غير مسألة على رؤية التقليل
وقيل الجود السرور بالسائل والفرح بالعطاء لما أمكن
وقيل الجود عطاء على رؤية أن المال لله تعالى والعبد لله عز وجل فيعطى
عبد الله مال الله على غير رؤية الفقر
وقيل من أعطى البعض وأبقى البعض فهو صاحب سخاء ومن بذل الأكثر وأبقى
لنفسه شيئا فهو صاحب جود ومن قاسى الضر وآثر غيره بالبلغة فهو صاحب إيثار
ومن لم يبذل شيئا فهو صاحب بخل
وجملة هذه الكلمات غير محيطة بحقيقة الجود والبخل بل نقول المال خلق
لحكمة ومقصود وهو صلاحه لحاجات الخلق ويمكن إمساكه عن الصرف إلى ما خلق
للصرف إليه ويمكن بذله بالصرف إلى ما لا يحسن الصرف إليه ويمكن التصرف فيه
بالعدل وهو أن يحفظ حيث يجب الحفظ ويبذل حيث يجب البذل
فالإمساك حيث يجب البذل بخل والبذل حيث يجب الإمساك تبذير
وبينهما وسط وهو المحمود وينبغي أن يكون السخاء والجود عبارة عنه إذ لم
يؤمر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلا بالسخاء وقد قيل له ولا تجعل يدك
مغلولة إلى عنقك ولا تبسطها كل البسط وقال تعالى والذين إذا أنفقوا لم
يسرفوا ولم يقتروا وكان بين ذلك قواما فالجود وسط بين الإسراف والإقتار
وبين البسط والقبض وهو أن يقدر بذله وإمساكه بقدر الواجب ولا يكفي أن يفعل
ذلك بجوارحه ما لم يكن قلبه طيبا به غير منازع له فيه
فإن بذل في محل وجوب البذل ونفسه تنازعه وهو يصابرها فهو متسخ وليس بسخي
بل ينبغي أن لا يكون لقلبه علاقة مع المال إلا من حيث يراد المال له وهو
صرفه إلى ما يجب صرفه إليه
PageV03P259
فإن قلت فقد صار هذا موقوفا على معرفة الواجب فما الذي يجب بذله
فأقول إن الواجب قسمان واجب بالشرع وواجب بالمروءة والعادة
والسخي هو الذي لا يمنع واجب الشرع ولا واجب المروءة فإن منع واحدا منهما
فهو بخيل ولكن الذي يمنع واجب الشرع أبخل كالذي يمنع أداء الزكاة ويمنع
عياله وأهله النفقة أو يؤديها ولكنه يشق عليه فإنه بخيل بالطبع وإنما يتسخى
بالتكلف أو الذي يتيمم الخبيث من ماله ولا يطيب قلبه أن يعطي من أطيب ماله
أو من وسطه فهذا كله بخل
وأما واجب المروءة فهو ترك المضايقة والاستقصاء في المحقرات فإن ذلك
مستقبح واستقباح ذلك يختلف بالأحوال والأشخاص
فمن كثر ماله استقبح منه ما لا يستقبح من الفقير من المضايقة ويستقبح من
الرجل المضايقة مع أهله وأقاربه ومماليكه ما لا يستقبح مع الأجانب ويستقبح
من الجار ما لا يستقبح مع البعيد ويستقبح في الضيافة من المضايقة ما لا
يستقبح في المعاملة فيختلف ذلك بما فيه من المضايقة في ضيافة أو معاملة
وبما به المضايقة من طعام أو ثوب إذ يستقبح في الأطعمة ما لا يستقبح في
غيرها ويستقبح في شراء الكفن مثلا أو شراء الأضحية أو شراء خبز الصدقة ما
لا يستقبح في غيره من المضايقة
وكذلك بمن معه المضايقة من صديق أو أخ أو قريب أو زوجة أو ولد أو أجنبي
وبمن منه المضايقة من صبي أو امرأة أو شيخ أو شاب أو عالم أو جاهل أو
موسر أو فقير
فالبخيل هو الذي يمنع حيث ينبغي أن لا يمنع إما بحكم الشرع وإما بحكم
المروءة وذلك لا يمكن التنصيص على مقداره
ولعل حد البخل هو إمساك المال عن غرض ذلك الغرض هو أهم من حفظ المال فإن
صيانة الدين أهم من حفظ المال فمانع الزكاة والنفقة بخيل
وصيانة المروءة أهم من حفظ المال والمضايق في الدقائق مع من لا تحسن
المضايقة معه هاتك ستر المروءة لحب المال فهو بخيل
ثم تبقى درجة أخرى وهو أن يكون الرجل ممن يؤدي الواجب ويحفظ المروءة ولكن
معه مال كثير قد جمعه ليس يصرفه إلى الصدقات وإلى المحتاجين فقد تقابل غرض
حفظ المال  ليكون له عدة على نوائب الزمان وغرض الثواب ليكون رافعا لدرجاته
في الآخرة وإمساك المال عن هذا الغرض بخل عند الأكياس وليس ببخل عند عوام
الخلق وذلك لأن نظر العوام مقصور على حظوظ الدنيا فيرون إمساكه لدفع نوائب
الزمان مهما وربما يظهر عند العوام أيضا سمة البخل عليه إن كان في جواره
محتاج فمنعه وقال قد أديت الزكاة الواجبة وليس على غيرها
ويختلف استقباح ذلك باختلاف مقدار ماله وباختلاف شدة حاجة المحتاج وصلاح
دينه واستحقاقه
فمن أدى واجب الشرع وواجب المروءة اللائقة به فقد تبرأ من البخل
نعم لا يتصف بصفة الجود والسخاء ما لم يبذل زيادة على ذلك لطلب الفضيلة
ونيل الدرجات فإذا اتسعت نفسه لبذل المال حيث لا يوجبه الشرع ولا تتوجه
إليه الملامة في العادة فهو جواد بقدر ما تتسع له نفسه من قليل أو كثير
ودرجات ذلك لا تحصر وبعض الناس أجود من بعض فاصطناع المعروف وراء ما
توجبه العادة والمروءة هو الجود ولكن بشرط أن يكون عن طيب نفس ولا يكون طمع
ورجاء خدمة أو مكافأة أو شكر أو ثناء فإن من طمع في الشكر والثناء فهو بياع
وليس بجواد فإنه يشتري المدح بماله والمدح لذيذ وهو مقصود في نفسه والجود
هو بذل الشيء من غير عوض
هذا هو الحقيقة ولا يتصور ذلك إلا من الله تعالى أما الآدمي فاسم الجود
عليه مجاز إذ لا يبذل الشيء إلا لغرض ولكنه إذا لم يكن غرضه إلا
PageV03P260
الثواب في الآخرة أو اكتساب فضيلة الجود وتطهير النفس عن رذالة البخل
فيسمى جوادا فإن كان الباعث عليه الخوف من الهجاء مثلا أو من ملامة الخلق
أو ما يتوقعه من نفع يناله من المنعم عليه فكل ذلك ليس من الجود لأنه مضطر
إليه بهذه البواعث وهي أعواض معجلة له عليه فهو معتاض لا جواد كما روي عن
بعض المتعبدات أنها وقفت على حبان بن هلال وهو جالس مع أصحابه فقالت هل
فيكم من أسأله عن مسألة فقالوا لها سلي عما  شئت وأشاروا إلى حبان بن هلال
فقالت ما السخاء عندكم قالوا العطاء والبذل والإيثار قالت هذا السخاء في
الدنيا فما السخاء في الدين قالوا أن نعبد الله سبحانه سخية بها أنفسنا غير
مكرهة قالت فتريدون على ذلك أجرا قالوا نعم قالت ولم قالوا لأن الله تعالى
وعدنا بالحسنة عشر أمثالها قالت سبحان الله فإذا أعطيتم واحدة وأخذتم عشرة
فبأي شيء تسخيتم عليه قالوا لها فما السخاء عندك يرحمك الله قالت السخاء
عندي أن تعبدوا الله متنعمين متلذذين بطاعته غير كارهين لا تريدون على ذلك
أجرا حتى يكون مولاكم يفعل بكم ما يشاء ألا تستحيون من الله أن يطلع على
قلوبكم فيعلم منها أنكم تريدون شيئا بشيء إن هذا في الدنيا لقبيح وقالت بعض
المتعبدات أتحسبون أن السخاء في الدرهم والدينار فقط قيل ففيم قالت السخاء
عندي في المهج
وقال المحاسبي السخاء في الدين أن تسخوا بنفسك تتلفها لله عز وجل ويسخو
قلبك ببذل مهجتك وإهراق دمك لله تعالى بسماحة من غير إكراه ولا تريد بذلك
ثوابا عاجلا ولا آجلا وإن كنت غير مستغن عن الثواب ولكن يغلب على ظنك حسن
كمال السخاء بترك الاختيار على الله حتى يكون مولاك هو الذي يفعل لك ما لا
تحسن أن تختار لنفسك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-خ-ل (B-Kh-L)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is withholding, niggardliness, and constriction of the hand from what should be given; the opposite of generosity (jūd).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, bukhl is a vice of the soul (radhīlah nafsāniyyah) that prevents the discharge of obligatory rights (ḥuqūq), whether divine or human; it is blameworthy because it opposes the divine attribute of generosity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, bukhl is the withholding of property; metaphorically (majāz), it extends to withholding of the self, effort, or knowledge — as in "stingy with one's life" (bukhl bi-l-muhjah).
- Root: ج-و-د (J-W-D)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is excellence, munificence, and giving freely; al-jawād is the one who gives abundantly without constraint.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Jūd is the mean (wasat) between extravagance (isrāf) and miserliness (iqtār); it is the soul's natural inclination to expend wealth in its proper place (ṣarf al-māl fī mawḍiʿihi).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, jūd is giving without recompense; metaphorically, it is the purity of the heart in giving, such that the giver seeks no worldly or even otherworldly return.
- Root: س-خ-و (S-Kh-W)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is ease, liberality, and softness of disposition; sakhāʾ is the quality of one whose soul is expansive (inshirāḥ) in giving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sakhāʾ is the virtue of the heart that makes giving effortless and pleasant; its perfection is giving without expectation of reward, even in the afterlife.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, sakhāʾ is open-handedness; metaphorically, it is the soul's willingness to sacrifice itself for God — "sakhāʾ bi-l-nafs" (generosity with the self).
- Root: ق-ت-ر (Q-T-R)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is narrowness, scantiness, and withholding; iqtār is the extreme of stinginess.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iqtār is the blameworthy constriction of expenditure, contrasted with isrāf (extravagance); the Quranic mean is qiwām (moderation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, iqtār is poverty-induced withholding; metaphorically, it is the soul's constriction even when wealth is abundant.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa-l-Istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly uses "in kāna... fa-" (if it were... then) and "lā... illā" (nothing but) to delimit definitions, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions.
chapters.translation:
I say: You might say, "It has been established by the evidences of the Sacred Law that stinginess (al-bukhl) is among the destructive vices. But what is the definition (ḥadd) of stinginess? And by what does a person become stingy? For there is no person who does not see himself as generous, while perhaps others see him as stingy. And an act may issue from a person concerning which people differ — some say, 'This is stinginess,' while others say, 'This is not stinginess.'

Moreover, there is no person who does not find in himself a love of wealth, and for its sake he preserves wealth and withholds it. If withholding wealth (imsāk al-māl) made one stingy, then no one would be free of stinginess. And if withholding in an absolute sense does not necessitate stinginess — yet there is no meaning of stinginess except withholding — then what is the stinginess that necessitates destruction? And what is the definition of generosity (al-sakhāʾ) by which one merits the attribute of generosity and its reward?"

We say: Some have said, "The definition of stinginess is the refusal of what is obligatory (manʿ al-wājib). Whoever discharges what is obligatory upon him is not stingy." But this is insufficient. For one who returns meat to the butcher, or bread to the baker, deficient by a grain or half a grain, is deemed stingy by unanimous agreement. Likewise, one who hands over to his family the amount that a judge would decree, but then tightens upon them regarding a morsel they add beyond it, or a date they eat from his wealth, is deemed stingy. And one before whom a loaf of bread is placed, and a person arrives whom he suspects will eat with him, and he hides it from him — he is deemed stingy.

Others have said, "The stingy person is one for whom giving is difficult (yastaṣʿibu al-ʿaṭiyyah)." This too is deficient. For if what is meant is that every gift is difficult for him — how many a stingy person finds no difficulty in a small gift like a grain or the like, but finds difficulty in what is above that? And if what is meant is that some gifts are difficult for him — then who among the generous does not find some gifts difficult, namely what would consume all his wealth, or a great sum? This does not necessitate the judgment of stinginess.

Likewise, they spoke concerning liberality (al-jūd). It was said: "Jūd is giving without reproach (minn), and aiding without deliberation." It was said: "Jūd is giving without being asked, upon the view of deeming it little." It was said: "Jūd is rejoicing in the petitioner and delighting in the gift, whenever possible." It was said: "Jūd is giving upon the view that wealth belongs to God, and the servant belongs to God — so the servant of God gives the wealth of God without the view of poverty." It was said: "Whoever gives some and keeps some is a man of sakhāʾ; whoever expends most and keeps something for himself is a man of jūd; whoever endures hardship and prefers others over himself in sustenance is a man of īthār (self-sacrifice); and whoever expends nothing is a man of bukhl."

The sum of these sayings does not encompass the reality of jūd and bukhl. Rather, we say: Wealth was created for a wisdom and purpose — namely, its suitability for the needs of creation. It is possible to withhold it from being spent toward that for which it was created to be spent; it is possible to expend it by spending toward what is not fitting to spend toward; and it is possible to dispose of it with justice — namely, to preserve it where preservation is obligatory, and to expend it where expenditure is obligatory.

Thus, withholding where expenditure is obligatory is stinginess (bukhl); expenditure where withholding is obligatory is extravagance (tabdhīr). Between the two is a mean (wasat), and that is the praiseworthy one. It is fitting that sakhāʾ and jūd be expressions of this mean — for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was commanded only with sakhāʾ. It was said to him: {«وَلَا تَجْعَلْ يَدَكَ مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ وَلَا تَبْسُطْهَا كُلَّ الْبَسْطِ»} ("And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely" — Qurʾān 17:29). And God Most High said: {«وَالَّذِينَ إِذَا أَنفَقُوا لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا وَكَانَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ قَوَامًا»} ("And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but hold a just balance between the two" — Qurʾān 25:67). So jūd is the mean between isrāf and iqtār, and between open-handedness and constriction — namely, that one measures his expenditure and withholding according to what is obligatory.

And it is not sufficient that one do this with his limbs unless his heart is content with it, not disputing against it. For if one expends in a place where expenditure is obligatory while his soul disputes against him and he struggles against it, he is one who forces himself to be generous (mutasakhkhī), not a generous one (sakhī). Rather, it is necessary that his heart have no attachment to wealth except insofar as wealth is desired for him — namely, its expenditure toward what must be expended toward.

Page V03P259

If you say: "This has become dependent upon knowledge of the obligatory. So what is it that must be expended?"

I say: The obligatory is of two kinds: obligatory by the Sacred Law (wājib bi-l-sharʿ), and obligatory by manly virtue and custom (wājib bi-l-murūʾah wa-l-ʿādah). The generous one is he who withholds neither the obligation of the Sacred Law nor the obligation of murūʾah. Whoever withholds either of them is stingy. But the one who withholds the obligation of the Sacred Law is more stingy — like the one who withholds the payment of zakāh, or withholds from his family and dependents their maintenance (nafaqah), or pays it but finds it burdensome — for he is stingy by nature, only forcing generosity upon himself by effort. Or the one who earmarks the inferior portion of his wealth [for giving], his heart not being content to give from his best wealth or from its middle — all of this is stinginess.

As for the obligation of murūʾah, it is the abandonment of tightness (al-muḍāyaqah) and exactingness (al-istiqṣāʾ) in trivial matters (al-muḥaqqirāt). For that is deemed ugly (mustaqbaḥ), and the deeming of it ugly varies according to circumstances and persons. Thus, from one of abundant wealth, tightness is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly from a poor man. From a man, tightness with his family, relatives, and slaves is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly with strangers. From a neighbor, tightness is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly with one who is distant. In hospitality, tightness is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly in commercial transactions. This varies according to what the tightness occurs in — hospitality or transaction — and by what the tightness occurs with — food or clothing — for tightness in foods is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly in other things. And tightness in purchasing a shroud, for example, or purchasing a sacrificial animal, or purchasing bread for charity, is deemed ugly that would not be deemed ugly in other matters.

Likewise, it varies by the person with whom one is tight — a friend, brother, relative, wife, child, or stranger — and by the person from whom the tightness proceeds — a boy, woman, elder, youth, scholar, ignoramus, wealthy man, or poor man.

So the stingy one is he who withholds where he ought not to withhold — either by the rule of the Sacred Law or by the rule of murūʾah. And it is not possible to specify its exact measure.

Perhaps the definition of stinginess is: the withholding of wealth from a purpose, where that purpose is more important than the preservation of wealth. For the safeguarding of religion (ṣiyānat al-dīn) is more important than the preservation of wealth — so the one who withholds zakāh and maintenance is stingy. And the safeguarding of murūʾah is more important than the preservation of wealth — so the one who is tight in trivialities with those with whom tightness is not fitting is a tearer of the veil of murūʾah for love of wealth — he is stingy.

Then there remains another degree: that a man discharges the obligatory and preserves murūʾah, but he has much wealth that he has amassed, not expending it in charities and to the needy. For the purpose of preserving wealth — to have provision against the vicissitudes of time — may conflict with the purpose of reward — to raise his ranks in the afterlife. Withholding wealth from this purpose is stinginess in the view of the discerning (al-akyās), but it is not stinginess in the view of the common folk (ʿawāmm al-khalq). For the view of the common folk is confined to the shares of this world, so they see his withholding as provision against the vicissitudes of time. But perhaps the mark of stinginess may also appear upon him in the view of the common folk if there is a needy person in his vicinity whom he refuses, saying, "I have paid the obligatory zakāh, and there is nothing beyond it."

And the deeming of this as ugly varies according to the measure of his wealth, the severity of the needy person's need, the soundness of his religion, and his worthiness.

So whoever discharges the obligation of the Sacred Law and the obligation of murūʾah befitting him has absolved himself of stinginess.

Yes, he does not become characterized by the attribute of jūd and sakhāʾ unless he expends beyond that, seeking virtue (al-faḍīlah) and attaining ranks. So when his soul expands to expend wealth where the Sacred Law does not require it and where no blame attaches to him by custom — then he is generous (jawād) to the extent that his soul expands, whether little or much. And the degrees of this cannot be enumerated; some people are more generous than others. So the doing of good (iṣṭināʿ al-maʿrūf) beyond what custom and murūʾah require — that is jūd. But on the condition that it be from a contented soul, and that there be no covetousness or hope of service, recompense, gratitude, or praise. For whoever covets gratitude and praise is a seller (bayyāʿ), not a generous one — for he purchases praise with his wealth, and praise is delightful and sought for its own sake. Jūd is the expenditure of a thing without recompense (ʿiwaḍ).

This is the reality. And it is not conceivable except from God Most High. As for the human being, the name jūd is applied to him metaphorically (majāz), for he does not expend a thing except for some purpose. But when his purpose is nothing other than

Page V03P260

reward in the afterlife, or the acquisition of the virtue of jūd and the purification of the soul from the vice of stinginess — then he is called generous (jawād). For if the motive is fear of satire (hijāʾ), for example, or fear of people's blame, or what he anticipates of benefit to be obtained from the one upon whom he bestows — all of that is not from jūd, because he is compelled to it by these motives, and they are immediate compensations (aʿwāḍ muʿajjalah) for him. So he is one who takes compensation (muʿtāḍ), not a generous one.

This is as related from one of the female ascetics (al-mutaʿabbidāt): she stopped by Ḥibbān ibn Hilāl while he was sitting with his companions and said, "Is there among you one whom I might ask about a question?" They said, "Ask whatever you wish," and they gestured to Ḥibbān ibn Hilāl. She said, "What is sakhāʾ in your view?" They said, "Giving, expending, and self-sacrifice (al-īthār)." She said, "This is sakhāʾ in this world. So what is sakhāʾ in religion?" They said, "That we worship God, glorified be He, with our souls generously (sakhiyyatan bihā anfusunā), not coerced." She said, "And do you seek a reward for that?" They said, "Yes." She said, "Why?" They said, "Because God Most High has promised us ten times the like of every good deed." She said, "Glory be to God! If you give one and take ten, then by what have you been generous?" They said to her, "So what is sakhāʾ in your view, may God have mercy on you?" She said, "Sakhāʾ in my view is that you worship God delighting and taking pleasure in His obedience, not disliking it, not seeking a reward for it — so that your Master (mawlākum) may do with you as He wills. Are you not ashamed before God that He should look upon your hearts and know from them that you desire something for something? This is indeed ugly in this world."

And another of the female ascetics said, "Do you reckon that sakhāʾ is only in the dirham and the dīnār?" It was said, "Then in what?" She said, "Sakhāʾ in my view is in the souls (al-muhaj)."

And al-Muḥāsibī said: "Sakhāʾ in religion is that you be generous with your soul, expending it for God, and that your heart be generous in expending your life's blood (muhjatika) and shedding your blood for God Most High, with open-handedness (samāḥah) without coercion, not seeking thereby a reward, whether immediate or deferred — even though you are not independent of reward. But your dominant conviction is the perfection of sakhāʾ by abandoning choice (al-ikhtiyār) before God, so that your Master is the one who does for you what you do not know how to choose for yourself."

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Remedy for Stinginess (Bayān ʿIlāj al-Bukhl)
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| بيان علاج البخل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع ل ج (ʿ-l-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to set right, to rectify, to treat a wound or ailment" — implying a direct, practical intervention upon a diseased state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ʿilāj denotes the remedial discipline applied to the soul’s moral maladies (adwiyat al-qulūb), contrasting with mere theoretical knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — medical treatment of the body; metaphorical (majāz) — spiritual therapy for the heart’s vices.
- Root: ب خ ل (b-kh-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "niggardliness, avarice, withholding what is due" — a contraction of the hand and heart from rightful expenditure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Bukhl is the vice opposed to generosity (jūd); it is a sickness of the soul (marad al-nafs) rooted in excessive love of worldly accumulation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical withholding of wealth; metaphorical — spiritual constriction of the heart’s capacity for divine giving.
- Sībawayh Rule: Idāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "علاج البخل" (ʿilāj al-bukhl) is an annexation where the first term (ʿilāj) is indefinite and the second (al-bukhl) is definite, yielding a specific, targeted remedy for a known ailment.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that stinginess (al-bukhl) is a malady of the heart, and its remedy (ʿilāj) lies not in mere exhortation, but in the uprooting of its cause. For the heart is like a limb afflicted with a chronic disease; it cannot be healed by a single dose, but requires a sustained regimen. The root of stinginess is the excessive love of wealth (ḥubb al-māl), and the love of wealth is itself a branch of the love of self (ḥubb al-nafs). Therefore, the cure must proceed in stages: first, to weaken the love of wealth by reflecting upon its fleeting nature and the certainty of parting from it; second, to habituate the soul to giving, even in small measures, until generosity becomes a second nature; and third, to contemplate the rewards promised by God for the generous and the punishments threatened for the miserly. For the soul, when it tastes the sweetness of giving and the peace that follows it, will find that the pleasure of generosity outweighs the pleasure of hoarding. Thus, the remedy is achieved by combining knowledge (ʿilm) with practice (ʿamal), until the vice is uprooted and replaced by its opposite virtue.

chapters.title_en: The Roots of Miserliness and Its Comprehensive Cure
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن البخل سببه حب المال
ولحب 2 المال سببان أحدهما حب الشهوات التي لا وصول إليها إلا بالمال مع
طول الأمل فإن الإنسان لو علم أنه يموت بعد يوم ربما أنه كان لا يبخل بماله
إذ القدر الذي يحتاج إليه في يوم أو في شهر أو في سنة قريب وإن كان قصير
الأمل ولكن كان له أولاد أقام الولد مقام طول الأمل فإنه يقدر بقاءهم كبقاء
نفسه فيمسك لأجلهم
ولذلك قال صلى الله عليه وسلم عليه السلام الولد مبخلة مجبنة مجهلة //
حديث الولد مبخلة زاد في رواية محزنة ابن ماجه من حديث يعلى بن مره دون
قوله محزنة رواه بهذه الزيادة أبو يعلى والبزار من حديث أبي  سعيد والحاكم
من حديث الأسود بن خلف وإسناده صحيح
فإذا انضاف إلى ذلك خوف الفقر وقلة الثقة بمجيء الرزق قوي البخل لا محالة
السبب الثاني أن يحب عين المال فمن الناس من معه ما يكفيه لبقية عمره إذا
اقتصر على ما جرت به عادته بنفقته وتفضل آلاف وهو شيخ بلا ولد ومعه أموال
كثيرة ولا تسمح نفسه بإخراج الزكاة ولا بمداواة نفسه عند المرض بل صار محبا
للدنانير عاشقا لها يلتذ بوجودها في يده وبقدرته عليها فيكنزها تحت الأرض
وهو يعلم أنه يموت فتضيع أو يأخذها أعداؤه هذا فلا تسمح نفسه بأن يأكل أو
يتصدق منها بحبة واحدة وهذا مرض للقلب عظيم عسير العلاج لا سيما في كبر
السن وهو مرض مزمن لا يرجى علاجه
ومثال صاحبه مثال رجل عشق شخصا فأحب رسوله لنفسه ثم نسي محبوبه واشتغل
برسوله فإن الدنانير رسول يبلغ إلى الحاجات فصارت محبوبة لذلك لأن الموصل
إلى اللذيذ لذيذ ثم قد تنسى الحاجات ويصير الذهب عنده كأنه محبوب في نفسه
وهو غاية الضلال بل من رأى بينه وبين الحجر فرقا فهو جاهل إلا من حيث قضاء
حاجته به فالفاضل عن قدر حاجته والحجر بمثابة واحدة
فهذه أسباب حب المال
وإنما علاج كل علة بمضادة سببها فتعالج حب الشهوات بالقناعة
PageV03P261
باليسير وبالصبر وتعالج طول الأمل بكثرة ذكر الموت والنظر في موت الأقران
وطول تعبهم في جمع المال وضياعه بعدهم وتعالج التفات القلب إلى الولد بأن
خالقه خلق معه رزقه وكم من ولد ولم يرث من أبيه مالا وحاله أحسن ممن ورث
وبأن يعلم أنه يجمع المال لولده يريد أن يترك ولده بخير وينقلب هو إلى شر
وأن ولده إن كان تقيا صالحا فالله كافيه وإن كان فاسقا فيستعين بماله على
المعصية وترجع مظلمته إليه
ويعالج أيضا قلبه بكثرة التأمل في الأخبار الواردة في ذم البخل ومدح
السخاء وما توعد الله به على البخل من العقاب العظيم
ومن الأدوية النافعة كثرة التأمل في أحوال البخلاء ونفرة الطبع عنهم
واستقباحهم له فإنه ما من بخيل إلا ويستقبح البخل من غيره ويستثقل كل بخيل
من أصحابه فيعلم أنه مستثقل ومستقذر في قلوب الناس مثل سائر البخلاء في
قلبه
ويعالج أيضا قلبه بأن يتفكر في مقاصد المال وأنه لماذا خلق ولا يحفظ من
المال إلا بقدر حاجته إليه والباقي يدخره لنفسه في الآخرة بأن يحصل له ثواب
بذله
فهذه الأدوية من جهة المعرفة والعلم فإذا عرف بنور البصيرة أن البذل خير
له من الإمساك في الدنيا والآخرة هاجت رغبته في البذل إن كان عاقلا فإن
تحركت الشهوة فينبغي أن يجيب الخاطر الأول ولا يتوقف فإن الشيطان يعده
الفقر ويخوفه ويصده عنه
حكي أن أبا الحسن البوشنجي كان ذات يوم في الخلاء فدعا تلميذا له وقال
انزع عني القميص وادفعه إلى فلان فقال هلا صبرت حتى تخرج قال لم آمن على
نفسي أن تتغير وكان قد خطر لي بذله ولا تزول صفة البخل إلا بالبذل تكلفا
كما لا يزول العشق إلا بمفارقة المعشوق بالسفر عن مستقره حتى إذا سافر
وفارق تكلفا وصبر عنه مدة تسلى عنه قلبه فكذلك الذي يريد علاج البخل ينبغي
أن يفارق المال تكلفا بأن يبذله بل لو رماه في الماء كان أولى به من إمساكه
إياه مع الحب له
ومن لطائف الحيل فيه أن يخدع نفسه بحسن الاسم والاشتهار بالسخاء فيبذل
على قصد الرياء حتى تسمح نفسه بالبذل طمعا في حشمة الجود فيكون قد أزال عن
نفسه خبث البخل واكتسب بها خبث الرياء ولكن ينعطف بعد ذلك على الرياء
ويزيله بعلاجه ويكون طلب الاسم كالتسلية للنفس عند فطامها عن المال كما
يسلي الصبي عند الفطام عن الثدي باللعب بالعصافير وغيرها لا ليخلى واللعب
ولكن لينفك عن الثدي إليه ثم ينقل عنه إلى غيره فكذلك هذه الصفات الخبيثة
ينبغي أن يسلط بعضها على بعض كما تسلط الشهوة على الغضب وتكسر سورته بها
ويسلط الغضب على الشهوة وتكسر رعونتها به إلا أن هذا مفيد في حق من كان
البخل أغلب  عليه من حب الجاه والرياء فيبذل الأقوى بالأضعف فإن كان الجاه
محبوبا عنده كالمال فلا فائدة فيه فإنه يقلع من علة ويزيد في أخرى مثلها
إلا أن علامة ذلك أن لا يثقل عليه البذل لأجل الرياء فلذلك يتبين أن الرياء
أغلب عليه فإن كان البذل يشق عليه مع الرياء فينبغي أن يبذل فإن ذلك يدل
على أن مرض البخل أغلب على قلبه
ومثال دفع هذه الصفات بعضها ببعض ما يقال إن الميت تستحيل جمع أجزائه
دودا ثم يأكل بعض الديدان البعض حتى يقل عددها ثم يأكل بعضها بعضا حتى ترجع
إلى اثنتين قويتين عظيمتين ثم لا تزالان تتقاتلان إلى أن تغلب إحداهما
الأخرى فتأكلها وتسمن بها ثم لا تزال تبقى جائعة وحدها إلى أن تموت فكذلك
هذه الصفات الخبيثة يمكن أن يسلط بعضها على بعض حتى يقمعها ويجعل الأضعف
قوتا للأقوى إلى أن لا يبقى إلا واحدة ثم تقع العناية بمحوها وإذابتها
بالمجاهدة وهو منع القوت عنها
ومنع القوت عن الصفات أن لا يعمل بمقتضاها فإنها تقتضي لا محالة أعمالا
وإذا خولفت خمدت الصفات وماتت
مثل البخل فإنه يقتضي إمساك
PageV03P262
المال فإذا منع مقتضاه وبذل المال مع الجهد مرة بعد أخرى ماتت صفة البخل
وصار البذل طبعا وسقط التعب فيه فإن علاج البخل بعلم وعمل فالعلم يرجع إلى
معرفة آفة البخل وفائدة الجود والعمل يرجع إلى الجود والبذل على سبيل
التكلف ولكن قد يقوى البخل بحيث يعمي ويصم فيمنع تحقق المعرفة فيه وإذا لم
تتحقق المعرفة لم تتحرك الرغبة فلم يتيسر العمل فتبقى العلة مزمنة كالمرض
الذي يمنع معرفة الدواء وإمكان استعماله فإنه لا حيلة فيه إلا الصبر إلى
الموت
وكان من عادة بعض شيوخ الصوفية في معالجة / علة البخل في المريدين أن
يمنعهم من الاختصاص بزواياهم
وكان إذا توهم في مريد فرحه بزاويته وما فيها نقله إلى زاوية غيرها ونقل
زاوية غيره إليه وأخرجه عن جميع ما ملكه وإذا رآه يلتفت إلى ثوب جديد يلبسه
أو سجادة يفرح بها  يأمره بتسليمها إلى غيره ويلبسه ثوبا خلقا لا يميل إليه
قلبه
فبهذا يتجافى القلب عن متاع الدنيا
فمن لم يسلك هذا السبيل أنس بالدنيا وأحبها فإن كان له ألف متاع كان له
ألف محبوب ولذلك إذا سرق كل واحد منه ألمت به مصيبة بقدر حبه له فإذا مات
نزل به ألف مصيبة دفعة واحدة لأنه كان يحب الكل وقد سلب عنه بل هو في حياته
على خطر المصيبة بالفقد والهلاك
حمل إلى بعض الملوك قدح من فيروزج مرصع بالجواهر لم ير له نظير ففرح
الملك بذلك فرحا شديدا فقال لبعض الحكماء عنده كيف ترى هذا قال أراه مصيبة
أو فقرا قال كيف قال إن كسر كان مصيبة لا جبر لها وإن سرق صرت فقيرا إليه
ولم تجد مثله وقد كنت قبل أن يحمل إليك في أمن من المصيبة والفقر ثم اتفق
يوما أن كسر أو سرق وعظمت مصيبة الملك عليه فقال صدق الحكيم ليته لم يحمل
إلينا وهذا شأن جميع أسباب الدنيا فإن الدنيا عدوة لأعداء الله تسوقهم إلى
النار وعدوة أولياء الله إذ تغمهم بالصبر عنها وعدوة الله إذ تقطع طريقه
على عباده وعدوة نفسها فإنها تأكل نفسها فإن المال لا يحفظ إلا بالخزائن
والحراس
والخزائن والحراس لا يمكن تحصيلها إلا بالمال وهو بذل الدراهم والدنانير
فالمال يأكل نفسه ويضاد ذاته حتى يفنى ومن عرف آفة المال لم يأنس به ولم
يفرح ولم يأخذ منه إلا بقدر حاجته ومن قنع بقدر الحاجة فلا يبخل لأن ما
أمسكه لحاجته فليس ببخل ولا يحتاج إليه فلا يتعب نفسه بحفظه فيبذله بل هو
كالماء على شط الدجلة إذ لا يبخل به أحد لقناعة الناس منه بمقدار الحاجة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-خ-ل (b-kh-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "narrowness/tightness" — withholding what should be given; the opposite of generosity (jūd/sakhāʾ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral disease of the soul (marad al-qalb) wherein one clings to wealth (māl) against the claims of religious duty and human need; it is blameworthy (madhmūm) in contrast to divine liberality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = physical tightness of the hand; metaphorical (majāz) = spiritual constriction preventing expenditure (badhl) even when abundance exists.
- Root: ش-ه-و-ة (sh-h-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Inclination of the soul toward what pleases it; appetite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lower appetitive faculty (al-quwwah al-shahwāniyyah) which, when ungoverned, becomes the root of attachment to means (like wealth).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for bodily desires; metaphorically extended to the soul's craving for possessions as instruments of pleasure.
- Root: أ-م-ل (a-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Hope/expectation of future good; prolonged expectation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ṭūl al-amal (length of hope) is a cardinal vice — it blinds one to death's proximity and breeds accumulation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = expectation; in ethical discourse, it is the psychological extension of one's concerns beyond the present moment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and causal coordination (al-ʿaṭf wa al-sharṭ) — the text uses layered causal chains (sabab…sababān) with embedded conditions (law…la-) to build a periodic argument; the translator must preserve the logical subordination.
chapters.translation:
Know that the cause of miserliness (al-bukhl) is love of wealth (ḥubb al-māl). And love of wealth has two causes. The first is love of the appetites (al-shahawāt) which cannot be attained except through wealth, combined with length of hope (ṭūl al-amal). For if a man knew that he would die after a single day, perhaps he would not be miserly with his wealth — since the amount he needs for a day, a month, or a year is small, even if his hope were short. But if he has children, the child takes the place of length of hope, for he estimates their survival as his own survival, and so he withholds for their sake.

For this reason, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The child is a cause of miserliness, a cause of cowardice, a cause of ignorance." {«الولد مبخلة مجبنة مجهلة»} — In one narration, the addition "a cause of grief" (muḥzinah) appears. Ibn Mājah recorded it from the ḥadīth of Yaʿlā ibn Murrah without the word "muḥzinah"; Abū Yaʿlā and al-Bazzār narrated it with this addition from the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd, and al-Ḥākim from the ḥadīth of al-Aswad ibn Khalaf, and its chain is sound (ṣaḥīḥ).

When, in addition to this, there is fear of poverty (khawf al-faqr) and little trust in the arrival of provision (rizq), miserliness is inevitably strengthened.

The second cause is that one loves the very substance of wealth (ʿayn al-māl). Among people there is one who possesses what suffices him for the remainder of his life, if he restricts himself to his customary expenditure — and he has thousands to spare — yet he is an old man without a child, possessing abundant wealth, and his soul does not permit him to pay the alms-tax (zakāh), nor to treat himself in illness. Rather, he has become a lover of dinars, a passionate devotee of them, delighting in their presence in his hand and in his power over them. He hoards them beneath the earth, knowing full well that he will die and they will be lost, or his enemies will take them. Yet his soul does not permit him to eat from them or to give a single grain in charity. This is a grave disease of the heart, difficult of cure — especially in old age — and it is a chronic illness from which no cure is hoped.

The likeness of its possessor is the likeness of a man who fell in love with a person, and so loved that person's messenger for his own sake; then he forgot the beloved and occupied himself with the messenger. For the dinar is a messenger that conveys one to one's needs; it became beloved for that reason, because that which leads to the pleasurable is itself pleasurable. Then the needs may be forgotten, and gold becomes, in his view, as though beloved in itself — and this is the extreme of error. Nay, whoever sees a difference between himself and a stone is ignorant, except from the aspect of fulfilling his need through it. So what exceeds the measure of his need, and a stone, are of one rank.

These, then, are the causes of love of wealth.

The cure of every ailment is only through opposing its cause. So the love of appetites is treated by contentment (al-qanāʿah) with little, and by patience (al-ṣabr). Length of hope is treated by frequent remembrance of death, and by reflecting on the death of one's peers — their long toil in amassing wealth and its loss after them. The heart's attachment to children is treated by knowing that their Creator created their provision along with them; how many a child has inherited no wealth from his father, yet his state is better than one who inherited! And by knowing that he amasses wealth for his child, intending to leave his child in good while he himself turns to evil — and that if his child is pious and righteous, God suffices him; but if he is wicked, he will use that wealth to aid him in disobedience, and its injustice reverts upon the father.

He also treats his heart by much reflection on the reports (akhbār) concerning the blame of miserliness and the praise of generosity, and what God has threatened against miserliness of tremendous punishment.

Among the beneficial remedies is much reflection on the states of misers and the natural aversion of the temperament from them, and one's deeming them repugnant. For there is no miser who does not deem miserliness repugnant in others, and who does not find every miser among his companions burdensome. So he knows that he himself is burdensome and loathsome in people's hearts, just as other misers are in his own heart.

He also treats his heart by reflecting on the purposes of wealth — why it was created — and that he should not retain of wealth except the measure of his need; the remainder he should store up for himself in the Hereafter by acquiring the reward of expending it.

These, then, are the remedies from the direction of knowledge and understanding (al-maʿrifah wa al-ʿilm). When, by the light of insight (nūr al-baṣīrah), he knows that expending (al-badhl) is better for him than withholding (al-imsāk) in this world and the next, his desire for expending is stirred — if he is rational. And if the appetite is stirred, he should answer the first thought (al-khāṭir al-awwal) and not hesitate, for Satan promises him poverty and frightens him and turns him away from it.

It is related that Abū al-Ḥasan al-Būshanjī was one day in seclusion (khalāʾ). He called a disciple of his and said: "Remove the shirt from me and give it to so-and-so." The disciple said: "Would you not wait until you go out?" He replied: "I do not feel safe that my state might change" — for the thought of expending it had occurred to him.

The trait of miserliness is not removed except by expending with self-imposition (takalluf), just as passionate love (al-ʿishq) is not removed except by separation from the beloved — by traveling away from one's abode. When one travels and separates with self-imposition, and endures patiently for a while, the heart is consoled of it. Likewise, whoever wishes to cure miserliness must separate from wealth with self-imposition, by expending it. Nay, even if he threw it into water, that would be better for him than withholding it while loving it.

Among the subtle stratagems (al-ḥiyal) in this matter is that he deceive his soul by the good name and fame of generosity — so he expends with the intention of ostentation (riyāʾ), until his soul permits expenditure out of desire for the prestige of liberality. Thus he removes from himself the impurity of miserliness, though he acquires thereby the impurity of ostentation. But afterward he turns upon the ostentation and removes it by its own cure. Seeking the name is like a consolation for the soul at its weaning from wealth — just as a child at weaning from the breast is consoled by playing with birds and other things, not for the sake of the play itself, but so that he may detach from the breast to it; then he is transferred from it to something else. Likewise, these evil traits should be set one against another — as appetite is set against anger to break its violence, and anger is set against appetite to break its rashness. However, this is beneficial only for one in whom miserliness predominates over love of status and ostentation, so that he expends the stronger by the weaker. But if status is as beloved to him as wealth, there is no benefit in it, for he uproots one ailment and increases another like it. The sign of this is that expending for the sake of ostentation is not burdensome to him — for then it becomes clear that ostentation predominates over him. But if expending is burdensome to him even with ostentation, then he should expend, for that indicates that the disease of miserliness predominates over his heart.

An example of repelling these traits by means of one another is what is said: that a corpse's parts turn into worms; then some worms eat others until their number decreases; then they continue eating one another until they return to two, strong and mighty; then the two keep fighting until one overcomes the other, eats it, and fattens on it; then it remains alone, hungry, until it dies. Likewise, these evil traits can be set one against another until one suppresses them, making the weaker a nourishment for the stronger, until only one remains. Then one's care is directed to erasing and dissolving it by spiritual striving (al-mujāhadah) — which is the withholding of nourishment from it.

And the withholding of nourishment from the traits is that one does not act according to their dictates. For they inevitably dictate actions; and when they are opposed, the traits subside and die.

For example, miserliness dictates withholding wealth. So when its dictate is prevented, and wealth is expended with effort, time after time, the trait of miserliness dies, expenditure becomes natural, and the effort in it falls away. For the cure of miserliness is by knowledge and by action: the knowledge reverts to recognizing the harm of miserliness and the benefit of generosity; the action reverts to generosity and expenditure by way of self-imposition. But miserliness may become so strong that it blinds and deafens, preventing the realization of knowledge within one. And when knowledge is not realized, desire is not stirred, action does not become feasible, and the ailment remains chronic — like a disease that prevents knowledge of the remedy and the possibility of using it. In that case there is no stratagem except patience until death.

It was the practice of some Sufi masters (mashāyikh al-ṣūfiyyah) in treating the ailment of miserliness in disciples (murīdīn) that they would prevent them from being attached to their private cells (zawāyā). When a master suspected in a disciple delight in his cell and what it contained, he would move him to another cell, and move another's cell to him, and strip him of all that he owned. And when he saw him turning toward a new garment he wore, or a prayer rug he delighted in, he would command him to surrender it to another, and clothe him in a worn garment toward which his heart had no inclination.

By this means the heart becomes detached (tajāfā) from the goods of this world.

Whoever does not tread this path becomes familiar with the world and loves it. If he has a thousand possessions, he has a thousand beloveds. Therefore, when each one is stolen, a calamity befalls him proportionate to his love for it. And when he dies, a thousand calamities descend upon him at once — because he loved them all and was stripped of them. Nay, even in his life he is in danger of calamity through loss and destruction.

A goblet of turquoise (fīrūzaj) studded with jewels, with no equal seen, was carried to one of the kings. The king rejoiced at it with intense joy, and said to one of the sages in his presence: "How do you see this?" He said: "I see it as a calamity — or as poverty." The king said: "How so?" He said: "If it is broken, it is a calamity with no recompense; and if it is stolen, you become poor for want of it, finding no equal to it. Yet before it was brought to you, you were secure from calamity and poverty." Then one day it happened that it was broken — or stolen — and the king's calamity over it was immense. He said: "The sage spoke truly. Would that it had never been brought to us!"

And such is the affair of all the causes of this world. For the world is an enemy to the enemies of God, driving them to the Fire; and an enemy to the friends of God (awliyāʾ), for it grieves them by the patience required in abstaining from it; and an enemy to God, for it cuts off His path from His servants; and an enemy to itself, for it consumes itself. For wealth is not preserved except by treasuries and guards; and treasuries and guards cannot be obtained except by wealth — that is, by expending dirhams and dinars. So wealth eats itself and opposes its own essence until it perishes. Whoever knows the harm of wealth does not grow familiar with it, does not rejoice in it, and takes from it only the measure of his need. And whoever is content with the measure of need is not miserly — for what he withholds for his need is not miserliness — and he has no need of it, so he does not weary himself in preserving it; rather, he expends it. It is like water on the bank of the Tigris: no one is miserly with it, because people are content with the measure of need from it.

### ||| بيان مجموع الوظائف التي على العبد في ماله

اعلم أن المال كما وصفناه خير من وجه وشر من وجه
ومثاله مثال حية يأخذها الراقي ويستخرج منها الترياق ويأخذها الغافل
فيقتله سمها من حيث لا يدري ولا يخلو أحد عن سم المال إلا بالمحافظة على
خمس  وظائف
الأولى أن يعرف مقصود المال وأنه لماذا خلق وأنه لم يحتج إليه حتى يكتسب
ولا يحفظ إلا قدر الحاجة ولا يعطيه من همته فوق ما يستحقه
الثانية أن يراعي جهة دخل المال فيجتنب الحرام المحض وما الغالب عليه
الحرام كمال السلطان ويجتنب الجهات المكروهة القادحة في المروءة كالهدايا
التي فيها شوائب الرشوة وكالسؤال الذي فيه الذلة وهتك المروءة وما يجري
مجراه
الثالثة في المقدار الذي يكتسبه فلا يستكثر منه ولا يستقل بل القدر
الواجب ومعياره الحاجة والحاجة
PageV03P263
ملبس ومسكن ومطعم
ولكل واحد ثلاث درجات أدنى وأوسط وأعلى
وما دام مائلا إلى جانب القلة ومتقربا من حد الضرورة كان محقا ويجيء من
جملة المحقين وإن جاوز ذلك وقع في هاوية لا آخر لعمقها
وقد ذكرنا تفصيل هذه الدرجات في كتاب الزهد
الرابعة أن يراعي جهة المخرج ويقتصد في الإنفاق غير مبذر ولا مقتر كما
ذكرناه فيضع ما اكتسبه من حله في حقه ولا يضعه في غير حقه فإن الإثم في
الأخذ من غير حقه والوضع في غير حقه سواء
الخامسة أن يصلح نيته في الأخذ والترك والإنفاق والإمساك فيأخذ ما يأخذ
ليستعين به على العبادة ويترك ما يترك زهدا فيه واستحقارا له إذا فعل ذلك
لم يضره وجود المال ولذلك قال علي رضي الله عنه لو أن رجلا أخذ جميع ما في
الأرض وأراد به وجه الله تعالى فهو زاهد ولو أنه ترك الجميع ولم يرد به وجه
الله تعالى فليس بزاهد
فلتكن جميع حركاتك وسكناتك لله مقصورة على عبادة أو ما يعين على العبادة
فإن أبعد الحركات عن العبادة الأكل وقضاء الحاجة وهما معينان على العبادة
فإذا كان ذلك قصدك بهما صار ذلك عبادة في حقك
وكذلك ينبغي أن تكون نيتك في كل ما يحفظك من قميص وإزار وفراش وآنية لأن
كل ذلك مما يحتاج إليه في الدين وما فضل من الحاجة ينبغي أن يقصد به أن
ينتفع به عبد من عباد الله ولا يمنعه منه عند حاجته فمن  فعل ذلك فهو الذي
أخذ من حية المال جوهرها وترياقها واتقى سمها فلا تضره كثرة المال ولكن لا
يتأتى ذلك إلا لمن رسخ في الدين قدمه وعظم فيه علمه
والعامي إذا تشبه بالعالم في الاستكثار من المال وزعم أنه يشبه أغنياء
الصحابة شابه الصبي الذي يرى المعزم الحاذق يأخذ الحية ويتصرف فيها فيخرج
ترياقها فيقتدي به ويظن أنه أخذها مستحسنا صورتها وشكلها ومستلينا جلدها
فيأخذها اقتداء به فتقتله في الحال إلا أن قتيل الحية يدري أنه قتيل وقتيل
المال قد لا يعرف
وقد شبهت الدنيا بالحية فقيل
هي دنيا كحية تنفث السم ... وإن كانت المجسة لانت
وكما يستحيل أن يتشبه الأعمى بالبصير في تخطي قلل الجبال وأطراف البحر
والطرق المشوكة فمحال أن يتشبه العامي بالعالم الكامل في تناول المال

- Root: و-ظ-ف (wa-ẓa-fa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Assignment of a recurring, fixed task; a stipulated obligation binding one's conduct.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely ordained functional role of wealth as a test (ibtilāʾ) and instrument, not an end.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "appointed duty" (waẓīfah); here metaphorically extended to moral-religious imperatives.
- Root: ح-ي-ة (ḥayyah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Serpent; creature whose venom is lethal yet whose body yields theriac (tiryāq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Symbol of worldly wealth (māl) — inherently ambivalent, both perilous and medicinal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz (metaphor) — wealth likened to a snake; the wise extract its antidote, the heedless perish by its poison.
- Root: ق-ص-د (qa-ṣa-da)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intent, aim, moderation; the middle path.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sincere intention (niyyah) directing action toward divine worship (ʿibādah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "straight path" vs. metaphorical "upright intention" in acquisition and expenditure.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — "If he does that, then..." (fa-idhā faʿala dhālika...) governing the apodosis of moral consequence.
chapters.translation:
### ||| Exposition of the Aggregate Duties Incumbent upon the Servant Regarding His Wealth

Know that wealth, as we have described it, is good in one respect and evil in another. Its likeness is the likeness of a serpent which the snake-charmer seizes and extracts from it the theriac, whereas the heedless man seizes it and its venom kills him, though he knows not whence. And no one is safe from the venom of wealth except by guarding five duties:

**The First:** That he know the purpose of wealth — why it was created, and that he has no need of it save to acquire and preserve only the measure of necessity, and that he not grant it from his aspiration more than it deserves.

**The Second:** That he observe the source of wealth's income, shunning the purely unlawful (ḥarām maḥḍ) and that which is predominantly unlawful, such as the wealth of rulers; and shunning the detestable channels that impugn manly virtue (murūʾah), such as gifts containing traces of bribery, and such as begging which entails humiliation and the tearing of murūʾah, and whatever runs in that course.

**The Third:** Concerning the quantity he acquires — he should neither seek much of it nor deem it little, but rather the obligatory measure, whose standard is need. And need is of three kinds: clothing, dwelling, and food. For each of these there are three degrees: the lowest, the middle, and the highest. So long as he inclines toward the side of scarcity and draws near the limit of necessity, he is among the truthful (muḥiqqūn) and comes within their company. But if he exceeds that, he falls into an abyss whose depth has no end. We have already mentioned the detailing of these degrees in the Book of Asceticism (Kitāb al-Zuhd).

**The Fourth:** That he observe the channel of expenditure and be moderate in spending — neither wasteful nor miserly, as we have mentioned — placing what he has earned lawfully in its rightful place, and not placing it in other than its rightful place. For the sin in taking from other than its rightful source and placing in other than its rightful destination is equal.

**The Fifth:** That he rectify his intention (niyyah) in taking, leaving, spending, and withholding. He takes what he takes to aid himself in worship, and he leaves what he leaves out of ascetic detachment (zuhd) and contempt for it. When he does this, the possession of wealth harms him not. For this reason ʿAlī — may God be pleased with him — said: "If a man took all that is upon the earth, intending thereby the Face of God Most High, he would be an ascetic (zāhid); and if he left all of it without intending the Face of God Most High, he would not be an ascetic."

Let all your movements and stillnesses be for God, confined to worship or to that which aids worship. For the farthest of movements from worship are eating and the relieving of nature, yet both are aids to worship. When that is your intention in them, they become worship in your regard. Likewise should your intention be in everything that preserves you — shirt, waist-wrapper, bedding, and vessels — for all of that is needed for the religion. And whatever exceeds need, you should intend thereby that a servant of God's servants benefit from it, and not withhold it from him at his time of need. Whoever does this is the one who has taken from the serpent of wealth its jewel and its theriac, and has guarded against its venom. So the abundance of wealth harms him not. But this is attainable only for one whose foot is firmly rooted in the religion and whose knowledge therein is great.

As for the common man (ʿāmmī) who imitates the scholar in amassing wealth, claiming that he resembles the wealthy Companions — he is like a boy who sees a skilled exorcist seize a serpent and handle it, extracting its theriac, and so imitates him, thinking he has seized it while admiring its form and shape and stroking its skin. He takes it in emulation, and it kills him on the spot — except that the one slain by the serpent knows he is slain, whereas the one slain by wealth may not recognize it.

And the world has been likened to a serpent, for it was said:

*It is a world like a serpent that breathes venom —*  
*Even though, when stroked, it feels soft.*

And just as it is impossible for the blind man to imitate the sighted in crossing mountain peaks, sea shores, and thorny paths, so it is impossible for the common man to imitate the perfect scholar in the handling of wealth.
