chapters.translation:
Know that pride (kibr) is among the destroyers, and no one among creation is entirely free from some measure of it. Its removal is an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn). It does not vanish by mere wishing, but rather by treatment and the application of repressive remedies.

In its treatment there are two stations:
The first is the eradication of its root from its very source and the uprooting of its tree from its planting place in the heart.
The second is the repulsion of what arises from it through the specific causes by which a person becomes proud over others.

**THE FIRST STATION: ERADICATING ITS ROOT**

Its treatment is both theoretical (ʿilmī) and practical (ʿamalī), and healing is not complete except through both combined.

As for the theoretical: it is that a person knows himself and knows his Lord, may He be exalted—and that suffices him in removing pride. For whenever he truly knows himself, he knows that he is more abased than every abased thing and less than every little thing, and that nothing befits him except humility, lowliness, and degradation. And when he knows his Lord, he knows that grandeur and majesty befit none but God.

As for his knowledge of his Lord, His greatness and His glory—the discourse on that is lengthy, and it is the ultimate end of the science of unveiling (ʿilm al-mukāshafah). As for his knowledge of himself, that too is lengthy; but we shall mention from it what is beneficial in arousing humility and lowliness.

It suffices him to understand the meaning of a single verse in the Book of God, for in the Qur'an is the knowledge of the first and the last for one whose inner sight has been opened. God, may He be exalted, has said: {قُتِلَ الْإِنسَانُ مَا أَكْفَرَهُ ۝ مِنْ أَيِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ ۝ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ ۝ ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ ۝ ثُمَّ أَمَاتَهُ فَأَقْبَرَهُ ۝ ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنشَرَهُ} ("Destroyed is man; how ungrateful he is! From what thing did He create him? From a drop of fluid He created him and proportioned him. Then He made the path easy for him. Then He caused him to die and buried him. Then when He wills, He will resurrect him.") [Q. 80:17-22]

The verse points to the beginning of man's creation, to his final end, and to his middle state. Let man then contemplate this to understand the meaning of this verse.

**As for man's beginning:** he was nothing worth mentioning, and he was in the realm of non-existence for ages upon ages—rather, his non-existence had no beginning. And what is more base and less than obliteration and non-existence? Such he was in eternity past. Then God created him from the most despicable of things, then from the filthiest of them—for He created him from dust, then from a drop of fluid, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, then made him bones, then clothed the bones with flesh. This was the beginning of his existence, when he became something worth mentioning. And he did not become something worth mentioning except while being upon the most base of descriptions and attributes—for he was not created complete at his inception, but rather was created as an inanimate dead thing, not hearing, not seeing, not sensing, not moving, not speaking, not grasping, not perceiving, not knowing. He began with his death before his life, his weakness before his strength, his ignorance before his knowledge, his blindness before his sight, his deafness before his hearing, his muteness before his speech, his error before his guidance, his poverty before his wealth, and his incapacity before his power.

This is the meaning of His saying: {مِنْ أَيِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ ۝ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ} ("From what thing did He create him? From a drop of fluid He created him and proportioned him.") And the meaning of His saying: {هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى الْإِنسَانِ حِينٌ مِّنَ الدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُن شَيْئًا مَّذْكُورًا ۝ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَا الْإِنسَانَ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ أَمْشَاجٍ نَّبْتَلِيهِ} ("Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning? Indeed, We created man from a mixed drop, testing him.") [Q. 76:1-2] Thus He created him at first, then He bestowed favor upon him, saying: {ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ} ("Then He made the path easy for him")—an indication of what was facilitated for him during the duration of his life until death. Likewise He said: {مِن نُّطْفَةٍ أَمْشَاجٍ نَّبْتَلِيهِ فَجَعَلْنَاهُ سَمِيعًا بَصِيرًا ۝ إِنَّا هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ إِمَّا شَاكِرًا وَإِمَّا كَفُورًا} ("From a mixed drop, testing him, and We made him hearing and seeing. Indeed, We guided him to the path, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.") [Q. 76:2-3] Its meaning: that He gave him life after he had been an inanimate dead thing—dust at first, then a drop secondly. He gave him hearing after he had been deaf, sight after he had lacked sight, strength after weakness, knowledge after ignorance. He created for him the limbs with all the wonders and signs within them, after he had lacked them. He enriched him after poverty, satiated him after hunger, clothed him after nakedness, and guided him after error.

So see how He managed him and formed him—and to the path, how He made it easy—and to man's transgression, how ungrateful he is!—and to man's ignorance, how He exposed it! For He said: {أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الْإِنسَانُ أَنَّا خَلَقْنَاهُ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ فَإِذَا هُوَ خَصِيمٌ مُّبِينٌ} ("Does man not see that We created him from a drop, yet behold, he is an open adversary?") [Q. 36:77] And He said: {وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ خَلَقَكُم مِّن تُرَابٍ ثُمَّ إِذَا أَنتُم بَشَرٌ تَنتَشِرُونَ} ("And of His signs is that He created you from dust; then behold, you are humans spreading abroad.") [Q. 30:20]

So look at God's blessing—how He transferred him from that abasement, paucity, vileness, and filth to this elevation and honor. He became existent after non-existence, alive after death, speaking after muteness, seeing after blindness, strong after weakness, knowing after ignorance, guided after error, capable after incapacity, and rich after poverty. He was in himself nothing—and what is more base than nothing? And what paucity is less than pure non-existence? Then he became something through God.

He only created him from the abased dust that is trodden under feet, and the filthy drop after pure non-existence as well—to make him know the vileness of his essence, so that he might thereby know himself. And He only completed the blessing upon him so that he might thereby know his Lord, and know thereby His greatness and majesty, and that pride befits none but Him, may He be glorified and exalted.

For this reason He bestowed favor upon him, saying: {أَلَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُ عَيْنَيْنِ ۝ وَلِسَانًا وَشَفَتَيْنِ ۝ وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ} ("Did We not make for him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips, and guide him to the two clear paths?") [Q. 90:8-10] And He made known his vileness at first, saying: {أَلَمْ يَكُ نُطْفَةً مِّن مَّنِيٍّ يُمْنَىٰ ۝ ثُمَّ كَانَ عَلَقَةً} ("Was he not a drop of emitted fluid? Then he was a clinging clot?") [Q. 75:37-38] Then He mentioned His favor upon him, saying: {فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ ۝ فَجَعَلَ مِنْهُ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنثَىٰ} ("Then He created and proportioned, and made from him the two mates, male and female.") [Q. 75:38-39]—so that his existence might continue through procreation, just as his existence was first obtained through origination (ikhtirāʿ).

So whoever has this beginning and these states—from where does he get insolence, pride, vainglory, and haughtiness, when he is in truth the most base of the base and the weakest of the weak? But this is the habit of the base: when he is raised from his baseness, he turns up his nose and magnifies himself—and that itself is evidence of the baseness of his beginning. There is no might and no power except through God.

Yes—had He perfected him, entrusted his affair to him, and perpetuated his existence by his own choice, then it would be permissible for him to transgress and forget the beginning and the end. But He has imposed upon him, in the continuation of his existence, terrifying diseases, great sicknesses, various afflictions, and opposing temperaments—of bile, phlegm, wind, and blood—demolishing some of his parts with others, whether he wills or not, whether he is pleased or displeased. He hungers against his will, thirsts against his will, falls ill against his will, and dies against his will. He owns for himself neither benefit nor harm, neither good nor evil. He wants to know a thing and is ignorant of it; he wants to remember a thing and forgets it; he wants to forget a thing and be heedless of it, yet he is not heedless of it; he wants to turn his heart to what concerns him, yet it wanders in the valleys of whisperings and thoughts by compulsion. He does not own his heart—his heart—nor his self—his self. He desires a thing, and perhaps his destruction is in it; he dislikes a thing, and perhaps his life is in it. He finds delight in foods that destroy and ruin him, and finds repulsive the medicines that benefit and revive him. He is not safe for a single moment of his night or day from having his hearing and sight stripped away, his limbs paralyzed, his intellect snatched, his spirit seized, and all that he desires in his world taken from him.

So he is compelled and abased: if left, he remains; if seized, he perishes. A slave, owned, having no power over anything of himself nor anything of others. So what is more abased than him, if he knew himself? And how does pride befit him, were it not for his ignorance? This is his middle state—let him contemplate it.

**As for his end and final destination:** it is death, referred to in His saying, may He be exalted: {ثُمَّ أَمَاتَهُ فَأَقْبَرَهُ ۝ ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنشَرَهُ} ("Then He caused him to die and buried him. Then when He wills, He will resurrect him.") [Q. 80:21-22] Its meaning: that his spirit, hearing, sight, knowledge, power, sensation, perception, and movement are stripped from him, and he returns to being an inanimate thing as he was the first time. Nothing remains but the shape of his limbs and his form—no sensation in it, no movement. Then he is placed in the dust and becomes a putrid, filthy corpse, just as he was at first a despised drop. Then his limbs decay, his parts crumble, his bones rot, and he becomes decayed bones and scattered dust. Worms eat his parts—beginning with his eye-sockets, plucking them out; then his cheeks, cutting them off; then the rest of his parts—until he becomes dung in the bellies of worms. He becomes a corpse from which animals flee and every person deems filthy, fleeing from it due to the intensity of the stench. And the best of his states is that he returns to what he was, becoming dust from which jugs are made and from which buildings are constructed. He becomes non-existent after having been existent, and becomes as though he had not dwelt [in the world] but yesterday—cut down—just as he was in his first affair for a long span. And would that he had remained so—how good it would be if he were left as dust!

Nay—rather, He revives him after the long decay to endure severe tribulation. He comes out of his grave after the gathering of his scattered parts, and goes out to the terrors of the Resurrection. He beholds a standing resurrection, a sky split and rent asunder, an earth changed, mountains set in motion, stars extinguished, sun darkened, dark conditions, angels harsh and severe, Hell-fire exhaling, and Paradise at which the criminal looks and grieves. He sees scrolls spread open, and it is said to him: {اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ} ("Read your book!") [Q. 17:14] He says, "What is this?" It is said: "There were appointed over you, in your life which you rejoiced in and were proud of its comforts and boasted of its means, two recording angels writing down upon you whatever you uttered or did—little and much, the speck and the husk—eating and drinking, standing and sitting. You forgot all that, but God has enumerated it against you. So come to the reckoning and prepare for the answer"—or he is dragged to the abode of punishment. His heart is cut asunder in terror from the horror of this address before the scroll is even spread out and he beholds what is in it of his disgraceful deeds. When he beholds it, he says: {يَا وَيْلَتَنَا مَالِ هَٰذَا الْكِتَابِ لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةً وَلَا كَبِيرَةً إِلَّا أَحْصَاهَا} ("O woe to us! What is this book that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it!") [Q. 18:49]

This is his final affair, and it is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: {ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنشَرَهُ} ("Then when He wills, He will resurrect him.") So what does one whose state is this have to do with pride and self-magnification? Rather, what does he have to do with rejoicing for a single moment, let alone insolence and exultation? His first state and his middle state have become manifest to him—and were his final state to become manifest (God forbid!), perhaps he would choose to be a dog or a pig, so that he might become dust along with the beasts, and not be a human who hears an address or meets a punishment. For if he is deserving of the Fire in God's sight, then the pig is nobler than him, and more pleasant and more elevated—for its beginning is dust and its end is dust, and it is far removed from the reckoning and the punishment. And the dog and the pig—creation does not flee from them.

Were the people of this world to see the sinful servant in the Fire, they would be thunderstruck by the horror of his form and the ugliness of his image. Were they to find his odor, they would die from his stench. Were a single drop of the drink he is given to fall into the seas of this world, it would become more putrid than a corpse. So how does one whose final state is this—unless God pardons him, and he is in doubt of pardon—how does he rejoice and exult? How does he become proud and tyrannical? How does he see himself as something, so as to believe he has merit? For what servant has not committed a sin by which he deserves punishment—unless God the Generous pardons him by His bounty and mends the break by His grace? And hope in Him for that is due to His generosity and good opinion of Him. There is no might and no power except through God.

Have you seen one who committed an offense against some king and thereby deserved a thousand lashes, and was imprisoned awaiting his being brought out for the display and the punishment carried out upon him before a gathering of creation—not knowing whether he will be pardoned or not? How is his abasement in prison? Do you think he would be proud over those in prison? And there is no sinful servant except that this world is his prison, and he has deserved punishment from God, may He be exalted, and does not know how his final affair will be. That suffices him as grief, fear, dread, degradation, and abasement.

This is the theoretical treatment that represses the root of pride.

**As for the practical treatment:** it is humility toward God in action, and toward the rest of creation by persisting in the character traits of the humble—as we have described and narrated from the states of the righteous and from the states of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him—to the point that he used to eat on the ground and say: "I am only a servant; I eat as the servant eats." [Hadith of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, that I would not prostrate except standing"—narrated by Aḥmad, abbreviated, with a hidden discontinuity.]

Since prostration was, in their view, the ultimate limit of abasement and lowliness, they were commanded to do it so that their haughtiness might be broken by it, their pride removed, and humility settled in their hearts. And by it the rest of creation was commanded—for bowing, prostrating, and standing in attendance are the actions that humility requires. Likewise, whoever knows himself should look at every action that pride demands and persist in its opposite, until humility becomes a character trait for him. For hearts do not acquire praiseworthy character traits except through knowledge and action combined—due to the hidden connection between hearts and limbs, and the secret of the link between the world of dominion (ʿālam al-mulk) and the world of sovereignty (ʿālam al-malakūt). And the heart belongs to the world of sovereignty.

**THE SECOND STATION: WHAT ARISES FROM PRIDE THROUGH THE SEVEN MENTIONED CAUSES**

We have mentioned in the Book of the Blame of Ignorance that true perfection is knowledge and action. As for what is other than that, which perishes with death, it is illusory perfection. From this, it is difficult for the scholar not to be proud—but we shall mention the path of treatment, both theoretical and practical, for all seven causes.

**The First Cause: Lineage (al-nasab)**

Whoever is afflicted with pride on account of lineage should treat his heart by knowing two matters:

The first: that this is ignorance, because he is magnifying himself by the perfection of another. Therefore it was said:

"If you boast of noble fathers, you have spoken truly—but what an evil thing they have begotten!"

The one who is proud of his lineage—if he is base in the attributes of his own self, then from where does he compensate his baseness with the perfection of another? Rather, were the one to whom he attributes himself alive, he would have the right to say: "The merit is mine—and who are you? You are but a worm created from my urine!" Do you think the worm created from a man's urine is nobler than the worm created from a horse's urine? Far from it—they are equal. And honor belongs to the man, not to the worm.

The second: that he know his true lineage—his father and his grandfather. For his near father is a filthy drop, and his distant grandfather is abased dust. God, may He be exalted, has made known his lineage to him, saying: {الَّذِي أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ ۖ وَبَدَأَ خَلْقَ الْإِنسَانِ مِن طِينٍ ۝ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ نَسْلَهُ مِن سُلَالَةٍ مِّن مَّاءٍ مَّهِينٍ} ("He who perfected everything He created and began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his progeny from an extract of despised fluid.") [Q. 32:7-8] So his origin is the despised dust that is trodden under feet; then his clay was fermented until it became fetid black mud. How can he be proud, when the most base of things is that to which he traces his lineage? For it is said: "O more abased than dust! O more putrid than fetid mud! O filthier than a clinging clot!"

If it is said that his being from his father is nearer than his being from dust, we say: boast of the near rather than the distant! The drop and the clot are nearer to him than the father—so let him hold himself in contempt by that. Then if that nearness entails elevation, the highest father is dust—so from where does its elevation come? And if it has no elevation, from where does elevation come to its offspring? Thus his origin is from dust and his branch is from a drop—so he has neither origin nor branch.

This is the ultimate vileness of lineage: the origin is trodden under feet, and the branch is washed from bodies. This is the true lineage of man. Whoever knows it will not be proud of lineage. After this knowledge and the uncovering of the veil from the reality of his origin, he is like a man who always considered himself among the Banū Hāshim, having been told so by his parents, and continued in the haughtiness of honor—when suddenly trustworthy witnesses, whose word he cannot doubt, informed him that he is the son of an Indian cupper who deals in filth, and they exposed to him the deception practiced upon him. No doubt remains in his mind of their truthfulness. Do you think that would leave anything of his pride? No—rather, he becomes in his own eyes the most contemptible and abased of people, occupied with the sense of disgrace at his baseness, too busy to be proud over others.

Such is the state of the insightful person when he reflects on his origin and knows that he is from the drop, the clot, and the dust. For were his father one who deals in carrying dust or in bloodletting or the like, he would know the baseness of his self by the touching of his father's limbs to dust and blood—so how about when he knows that he himself is from dust, blood, and filthy things from which he himself recoils?

**The Second Cause: Pride in Beauty (al-jamāl)**

Its remedy is that he look at his interior with the look of the intelligent, and not look at his exterior with the look of beasts. Whenever he looks at his interior, he sees such ugliness as would cloud his self-magnification by beauty. For he is entrusted with filth in all his parts: excrement in his intestines, urine in his bladder, mucus in his nose, saliva in his mouth, wax in his ears, blood in his veins, pus beneath his skin, and stench beneath his armpits. He washes away his feces with his hand once or twice every day, and goes to the privy once or twice daily to expel from his interior what, were he to see it with his eye, he would deem filthy—let alone touch it or smell it. All of this is so that he might know his filth and abasement. This is his middle state.

And in his first state, he was created from loathsome filths—from the drop and menstrual blood—and emerged from the passage of filth. For he came out from the loins, then from the penis—the passage of urine—then from the womb—the outlet of menstrual blood—then he emerged from the passage of excrement. Anas, may God have mercy on him, said: "Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, used to address us and make us despise ourselves, saying: 'Each of you came out from the passage of urine twice.'" Likewise Ṭāwūs said to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—when he saw him strutting—"What is this gait of one whose belly contains excrement?" And that was before his caliphate. This is his first and middle state.

Were he to leave himself for a single day of his life without attending to cleansing and washing, stenches and filths would erupt from him, and he would become more putrid and filthier than neglected beasts that never attend to themselves at all.

So when he sees that he was created from filths, dwells among filths, and will die and become a corpse filthier than all other filths—he will not boast of his beauty, which is like green vegetation upon a dunghill, like the color of flowers in the wilderness: while he is thus, it becomes dry chaff scattered by the winds. How so, even if his beauty were lasting? And even if it were free of these uglinesses, he still should not be proud of it over the ugly one—for the ugliness of the ugly is not directed at him that he should negate it, nor is the beauty of the beautiful from him that he should be praised for it. How, when it has no permanence—rather, at every moment it is conceivable that it will vanish through illness, smallpox, an ulcer, or some other cause? How many beautiful faces have been disfigured by such causes! Knowledge of these matters removes from the heart the disease of pride in beauty, for one who reflects upon them much.

**The Third Cause: Pride in Strength and Physical Power (al-quwwah wa al-aydī)**

What prevents him from this is that he know what has been imposed upon him of ailments and diseases—that were a single vein in his hand to ache, he would become more incapable than every incapable one and more abased than every abased one; that were a fly to snatch something from him, he could not retrieve it; that were a bedbug to enter his nose or an ant his ear, it would kill him; that were a thorn to enter his foot, it would incapacitate him; that a single day of fever dissolves from his strength what cannot be restored in a long period.

So whoever cannot bear a thorn, cannot resist a bedbug, and cannot repel a fly from himself—he should not boast of his strength. Then, even if a man is strong, he is not stronger than a donkey, a cow, an elephant, or a camel. And what pride is there in an attribute in which beasts surpass you?

**The Fourth and Fifth Causes: Wealth and Abundance of Property (al-ghinā wa kathrat al-māl)**

And in their meaning: abundance of followers and supporters, and pride in the authority of rulers and being established through them. All of that is pride in something external to the human self—like beauty, strength, and knowledge.

This is the ugliest type of pride. For the one proud of his wealth is as though proud of his horse and his house—were his horse to die and his house to collapse, he would return to abasement. And the one proud of a ruler's establishment and authority—not of any attribute in himself—has built his affair upon a heart that boils more intensely than a cooking pot: if it turns against him, he becomes the most abased of creation.

Every one who is proud of something external to his self is manifestly ignorant. How so? The one proud of wealth, were he to reflect, would see among the Jews those who surpass him in wealth, riches, and elegance. Fie on an honor in which the Jew surpasses you! Fie on an honor that a thief takes in a single moment, leaving its owner abased and bankrupt! These are causes not in his self; and what is in his self has no permanence of existence; and in the Hereafter it is a burden and a punishment. So boasting of it is the ultimate ignorance. And everything that is not in your power is not yours—and none of these things is in your power; rather, it belongs to its Bestower: if He preserves it for you, it remains; if He takes it back, it departs from you. And you are but an owned slave, having power over nothing.

Whoever knows this, his pride must inevitably depart.

Its example: a heedless man boasts of his strength, beauty, wealth, freedom, independence, spacious dwellings, many horses, and servants—when two just witnesses testify against him before a fair judge that he is a slave of so-and-so, and that his parents were his slaves. He learns of this, and the judge rules accordingly. His master comes and takes him and takes everything in his hand—while he fears that his master will punish and chastise him for his negligence with his master's wealth and his failure to seek his master. Then the slave looks and sees himself imprisoned in a dwelling surrounded by snakes, scorpions, and vermin, in constant dread of each one of them, having no power over himself or his wealth, and knowing no path of escape whatsoever.

Do you think one whose state is this would boast of his power, wealth, strength, and perfection—or would he abase himself and submit? Such is the state of every intelligent, insightful person: he sees himself thus—not owning his neck, his body, his limbs, or his wealth—and is, moreover, amidst afflictions, desires, diseases, and sicknesses that are like scorpions and snakes, fearing destruction from them. So one whose state is this does not become proud of his strength and power, for he knows he has no power and no strength.

This is the path of treating pride in external causes—and it is easier than treating pride in knowledge and action, for those two are perfections in the soul, worthy of rejoicing in. But pride in them too is a type of hidden ignorance, as we shall mention.

**The Sixth Cause: Pride in Knowledge (al-ʿilm)**

This is the greatest of afflictions, the most dominant of diseases, and the farthest from accepting treatment except with severe hardship and great effort. That is because the worth of knowledge is great with God and great with people—and it is greater than the worth of wealth, beauty, and other things. Rather, those have no worth at all except when accompanied by knowledge and action.

Therefore Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: "Knowledge has a tyranny like the tyranny of wealth." Likewise ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "When the scholar slips, the whole world slips with his slipping." The scholar is unable not to magnify himself in relation to the ignorant one, due to the abundance of what the Sacred Law has stated regarding the virtues of knowledge.

The scholar will not be able to repel pride except by knowing two matters:

**The first:** that he know that God's proof against the people of knowledge is more binding, and that what is tolerated from the ignorant one is not tolerated even to a tenth of it from the scholar. For whoever disobeys God with knowledge and understanding, his offense is more heinous—since he has not fulfilled the due of God's blessing upon him in knowledge. Therefore he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The scholar will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and cast into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out, and he will circle around them as the donkey circles the millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'What is the matter with you?' He will say: 'I used to command good and not do it, and forbid evil and do it.'" [Hadith: "The scholar will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and cast into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out"—agreed upon, from the hadith of Usāmah ibn Zayd, with the wording "a man will be brought," and it has preceded in the Book of Knowledge.]

God, glorified and exalted, has likened the one who knows but does not act to the donkey and the dog. He said, might and majesty be His: {مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ حُمِّلُوا التَّوْرَاةَ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَحْمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ الْحِمَارِ يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا} ("The example of those who were charged with the Torah then did not carry it is like the donkey carrying books.") [Q. 62:5]—meaning the scholars of the Jews. And He said concerning Balaam son of Beor: {وَاتْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبَأَ الَّذِي آتَيْنَاهُ آيَاتِنَا فَانسَلَخَ مِنْهَا} ("And recite to them the news of him to whom We gave Our signs, and he slipped away from them") until His saying: {فَمَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ الْكَلْبِ إِن تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْهِ يَلْهَثْ أَوْ تَتْرُكْهُ يَلْهَثْ} ("So his example is like the dog: if you drive him away he pants, or leave him, he pants.") [Q. 7:175-176] Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Balaam was given a book, and he inclined to the desires of the earth—that is, his love of it settled in him—so he was likened to the

chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان غاية الرياضة في خلق التواضع

اعلم أن هذا الخلق كسائر الأخلاق له طرفان وواسطة فطرفه الذي يميل إلى
الزيادة يسمى تكبرا وطرفه الذي يميل إلى النقصان يسمى تخاسسا ومذلة والوسط
يسمى تواضعا
والمحمود أن يتواضع في غير مذلة ومن غير تخاسس فإن كلا طرفي الأمور ذميم
وأحب الأمور إلى الله تعالى أوساطها
فمن يتقدم على أمثاله فهو متكبر ومن يتأخر عنهم فهو متواضع أي وضع شيئا
من قدره الذي يستحقه
والعالم إذا دخل عليه إسكاف فتنحى له عن مجلسه وأجلسه فيه ثم تقدم وسوى
له نعله وعدا إلى باب الدار خلفه فقد تخاسس وتذلل وهذا أيضا غير محمود بل
المحمود عند الله العدل وهو أن يعطي كل ذي حق حقه فينبغي أن يتواضع بمثل
هذا لأقرانه ومن يقرب من درجته فأما تواضعه للسوقي فبالقيام والبشر في
الكلام والرفق في السؤال وإجابة دعوته والسعي في حاجته وأمثال ذلك وأن لا
يرى نفسه خيرا منه بل يكون على نفسه أخوف منه على غيره فلا يحتقره ولا
يستصغره وهو لا يعرف خاتمة PageV03P368
أمره
فإذن سبيله في اكتساب التواضع أن يتواضع للأقران ولمن دونهم حتى يخف عليه
التواضع المحمود في محاسن العادات ليزول به الكبر عنه فإن خف عليه ذلك فقد
حصل له خلق التواضع وإن كان يثقل عليه وهو يفعل ذلك فهو متكلف لا متواضع بل
الخلق ما يصدر عنه الفعل بسهولة من غير ثقل ومن غير روية فإن خف ذلك وصار
بحيث يثقل عليه رعاية قدره حتى أحب التملق والتخاسس فقد خرج إلى طرف
النقصان فليرفع نفسه إذ  ليس للمؤمن أن تذل نفسه إلى أن يعود إلى الوسط الذي
هو الصراط المستقيم وذلك غامض في هذا الخلق وفي سائر الأخلاق
والميل عن الوسط إلى طرف النقصان وهو التملق أهون من الميل إلى طرف
الزيادة بالتكبر كما أن الميل إلى طرف التبذير في المال أحمد عند الناس من
الميل إلى طرف البخل فنهاية التبذير ونهاية البخل مذمومان وأحدهما أفحش
وكذلك نهاية التكبر ونهاية التنقص والتذلل مذمومان وأحدهما أقبح من الآخر
والمحمود المطلق هو العدل ووضع الأمور مواضعها كما يجب وعلى ما يجب كما
يعرف ذلك بالشرع والعادة ولنقتصر على هذا القدر من بيان أخلاق الكبر
والتواضع
الشطر الثاني من الكتاب في العجب وفيه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The middle point, the center, that which is equidistant between two extremes; moderation as a spatial metaphor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The praiseworthy mean (wasat) in moral character, aligning with the Quranic notion of the "middle nation" (ummatan wasaṭan) — the balanced path of justice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical centrality; here employed metaphorically (majāz) for the ethical mean between excess and deficiency.
- Root: ذ-ل-ل (dh-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lowness, abasement, submissiveness; the state of being humbled or degraded.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Distinguishes between praiseworthy humility (tawāḍuʿ) and blameworthy abasement (madhalla) — the latter being a voluntary self-degradation contrary to human dignity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of physical lowness; metaphorical sense of moral self-deprecation that exceeds the bounds of justice.
- Root: ك-ب-ر (k-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Greatness, magnitude; in moral context, arrogance and self-magnification.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The blameworthy trait of considering oneself greater than others, a vice opposed to humility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal greatness of stature; metaphorical usage for pride and haughtiness (istikbār).
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Balanced Predication (al-ʿadl fī al-ḥaml) — When attributing moral qualities, the predicate must reflect the precise degree of the subject's worth, neither exceeding nor diminishing it, as in the phrase "he placed something of his due rank" (waḍaʿa shayʾan min qadrihi).
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that this trait, like all other moral traits, has two extremes and a middle. Its extreme that inclines toward excess is called arrogance (takabbur), and its extreme that inclines toward deficiency is called abasement (takhāsus) and degradation (madhalla). The middle is called humility (tawāḍuʿ).

What is praiseworthy is that one be humble without degradation and without abasement, for both extremes of matters are blameworthy. And the most beloved of matters to God Almighty are their middles.

Thus, whoever advances himself above his peers is arrogant, and whoever holds himself back from them is humble — that is, he has lowered something of the rank that he rightfully deserves.

Now, if a scholar has a cobbler enter upon him, and he moves aside from his seat for him, seats him in it, then steps forward and straightens his sandal for him, and walks to the door of the house behind him — then he has abased and degraded himself. This too is not praiseworthy. Rather, what is praiseworthy before God is justice (al-ʿadl), which is to give every possessor of a right his due right. So one ought to be humble in this manner toward his peers and those close to his rank. As for his humility toward the common market-man, it is through standing up for him, cheerfulness in speech, gentleness in asking, responding to his invitation, striving in his need, and the like — and that he not see himself as better than him, but rather be more fearful for himself than for him, so that he neither despises him nor regards him as insignificant, for he does not know the final outcome of his affair. [Page V03P368]

Therefore, his way in acquiring humility is to be humble toward his peers and those below him, until praiseworthy humility becomes easy for him among the beautiful habits, so that arrogance departs from him thereby. For if it becomes easy for him, then the trait of humility has been attained. But if it is burdensome for him and he still does it, then he is forcing himself (mutakallif), not humble. Rather, the trait is that from which the action issues forth with ease, without burden and without deliberation. If it becomes easy and reaches the point where observing his own rank becomes burdensome to him, so that he comes to love flattery and abasement, then he has gone out to the extreme of deficiency. So let him raise himself up — for it is not for a believer to degrade himself — until he returns to the middle, which is the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm). And this is subtle in this trait and in all other traits.

The inclination from the middle toward the extreme of deficiency — namely flattery — is easier than the inclination toward the extreme of excess through arrogance. Just as the inclination toward the extreme of extravagance in wealth is more agreeable to people than the inclination toward the extreme of miserliness. For the ultimate of extravagance and the ultimate of miserliness are both blameworthy, yet one of them is more heinous. Likewise, the ultimate of arrogance and the ultimate of self-deprecation and degradation are both blameworthy, yet one of them is uglier than the other. What is absolutely praiseworthy is justice — placing things in their proper places as is obligatory and in the manner that is obligatory, as is known through the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ) and custom (al-ʿādah). And let us suffice with this measure in the exposition of the traits of arrogance and humility.

THE SECOND PART OF THE BOOK: ON SELF-ADMIRATION (al-ʿujb), AND IN IT:

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Blameworthiness of Self-Admiration (ʿUjb) and Its Afflictions
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| بيان ذم العجب وآفاته

وبيان حقيقة العجب والإدلال وحدهما وبيان علاج العجب على الجملة وبيان
أقسام ما به العجب وتفصيل علاجه بيان ذم العجب وآفاته
اعلم أن العجب مذموم في كتاب الله تعالى وسنة رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم
قال الله تعالى {ويوم حنين إذ أعجبتكم كثرتكم فلم تغن عنكم شيئا} ذكر ذلك
في معرض الإنكار وقال عز وجل {وظنوا أنهم مانعتهم حصونهم من الله فأتاهم
الله من حيث لم يحتسبوا} فرد على الكفار في إعجابهم بحصونهم وشوكتهم وقال
تعالى {وهم يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا} وهذا أيضا يرجع إلى العجب بالعمل
وقد يعجب الإنسان بالعمل هو مخطئ فيه كما يعجب بعمل هو مصيب فيه
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاث مهلكات شح مطاع وهوى متبع وإعجاب المرء
بنفسه (1) حديث أبي ثعلبة إذا رأيت شحا مطاعا وهوى متبعا وإعجاب كل ذي رأي
برأيه فعليك نفسك أخرجه أبو داود والترمذي وحسنه وابن ماجه وقد تقدم
وقال ابن مسعود الهالك في اثنتين القنوط والعجب
وإنما جمع بينهما لأن السعادة لا تنال إلا بالسعي والطلب والجد والتشمر
والقانط لا يسعى ولا يطلب والمعجب يعتقد أنه قد سعد وقد ظفر بمراده فلا
يسعى
فالموجود لا يطلب والمحال لا يطلب والسعادة موجودة في اعتقاد المعجب
حاصلة له ومستحيلة في اعتقاد القانط فمن  ههنا جمع بينهما
وقد قال تعالى {فلا تزكوا أنفسكم} قال ابن جريج معناه إذا عملت خيرا فلا
تقل عملت
وقال زيد بن أسلم
لا تبروها أي لا تعتقدوا أنها بارة وهو معنى العجب
ووقى طلحة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوم أحد بنفسه فأكب عليه حتى
أصيبت كفه فكأنه أعجبه فعله العظيم إذ فداه بروحه حتى جرح فتفرس ذلك عمر
فيه فقال
مازال يعرف في طلحة فأو منذ أصيبت إصبعه مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
// حديث وقى طلحة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بنفسه وأكب عليه حتى أصيبت
كفه أخرجه البخاري من وراية قيس بن أبي حازم قال رأيت يد طلحة شلاء وقى بها
النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
والنأو هو العجب في اللغة إلا أنه لم ينقل فيه أنه أظهره واحتقر مسلما
ولما كان وقت الشورى قال له ابن عباس أين أنت من طلحة قال ذلك رجل فيه تحوة
فإذا كان لا يتخلص من العجب أمثالهم فكيف يتخلص من الضعفاء إن
PageV03P369
لم يأخذوا حذرهم وقال مطرف لأن أبيت نائما وأصبح نادما أحب إلي من أبيت
قائما وأصبح معجبا
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم لو لم تذنبوا لخشيت عليكم ما هو أكبر من ذلك
العجب العجب // حديث لو لم تذنبوا لخشيت عليكم ما هو أكبر من ذلك العجب
العجب أخرجه البزار وابن حبان في الضعفاء والبيهقي في الشعب من حديث أنس
وفيه سلام بن أبي الصهباء قال البخاري منكر الحديث
وقال أحمد حسن الحديث ورواه أبو منصور الديلمي في مسند الفردوس من حديث
أبي سعيد بسند ضعيف جدا
فجعل العجب أكبر الذنوب
وكان بشر بن منصور من الذين إذا رءوا ذكر الله تعالى والدار الآخرة
لمواظبته على العبادة فأطال الصلاة يوما ورجل خلفه ينظر ففطن له بشر فلما
انصرف عن الصلاة قال له لا يعجبنك ما رأيت مني فإن إبليس لعنه الله قد عبد
الله تعالى مع الملائكة مدة طويلة ثم صار إلى ما صار إليه
وقيل لعائشة رضي الله عنها متى يكون الرجل مسيئا قالت إذا ظن أنه محسن
وقد قال تعالى {لا تبطلوا صدقاتكم بالمن والأذى} والمن نتيجة استعظام
الصدقة واستعظام العمل هو العجب
فظهر بهذا أن العجب مذموم جدا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ج-ب (ʿ-j-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Astonishment, wonderment; the state of being struck with amazement at something extraordinary, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Self-admiration (ʿujb) as a spiritual disease wherein one magnifies one's own deeds or attributes, leading to neglect of divine grace and accountability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is wonder; metaphorical (majāz) usage denotes the heart's complacency with one's own state, often veiling one's faults.
- Root: إ-د-ل-ا-ل (idlāl) — from د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Reliance, presumption; leaning upon something as a support.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Presumptuous reliance upon one's own deeds or status as sufficient for salvation, neglecting divine mercy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: leaning on a staff; metaphorical: trusting in one's own merit as a guarantee.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal sentence with predicate emphasis (al-mubtadaʾ wa al-khabar) — used to establish the categorical blameworthiness of ʿujb as a fixed attribute, not a contingent state.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that self-admiration (ʿujb) is blameworthy in the Book of God Most High and in the Sunnah of His Messenger, peace be upon him. God Most High said: {«And on the Day of Ḥunayn, when your great number pleased you (aʿjabatkum kathratukum), but it availed you nothing»} — He mentioned this in the context of rebuke. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said: {«And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from God, but God came upon them from where they did not expect»} — thus He reproached the disbelievers for their admiration of their fortresses and their might. And He Most High said: {«While they think that they are doing good work»} — this too reverts to self-admiration in one's deed. A man may admire himself for a deed in which he is mistaken, just as he may admire himself for a deed in which he is correct.

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Three destructive things: avarice obeyed, passion followed, and a man's admiration of himself" — the ḥadīth of Abū Thaʿlabah: "When you see avarice obeyed, passion followed, and every man of opinion admiring his own opinion, then look to yourself" — narrated by Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī (who deemed it good), and Ibn Mājah, and it has preceded.

And Ibn Masʿūd said: "The one who perishes does so through two things: despair (qunūṭ) and self-admiration (ʿujb)." He joined them together only because happiness (saʿādah) is attained only through striving, seeking, earnestness, and girding oneself; the despairing one neither strives nor seeks, and the self-admiring one believes that he has already attained happiness and secured his goal, so he does not strive. For what is already present is not sought, and what is impossible is not sought. Happiness, in the belief of the self-admiring one, is present and attained; while in the belief of the despairing one, it is impossible. From this angle, he joined the two together.

And God Most High said: {«So do not declare yourselves pure (lā tuzakkū anfusakum)»}. Ibn Jurayj said: Its meaning is — when you do good, do not say "I have done good." And Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Do not declare them pure (lā tabarrūhā)" — i.e., do not believe that they are righteous; and this is the meaning of self-admiration.

Ṭalḥah shielded the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, on the Day of Uḥud with his own body, bending over him until his hand was struck — and it seems he admired his great deed, since he ransomed him with his soul until he was wounded. ʿUmar perceived this in him and said: "He has not ceased to be known in Ṭalḥah — or rather, since his finger was struck alongside the Messenger of God, peace be upon him." [The ḥadīth of Ṭalḥah shielding the Prophet with his body and bending over him until his hand was struck is narrated by al-Bukhārī from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, who said: "I saw Ṭalḥah's hand paralyzed, with which he shielded the Prophet, peace be upon him."] And "al-naʾw" is self-admiration in the language, except that it is not reported that he displayed it or held any Muslim in contempt. And when the time of the Shūrā (council) came, Ibn ʿAbbās said to him: "Where are you with Ṭalḥah?" He said: "That is a man in whom there is some self-admiration (taḥwah)." If such as they cannot escape self-admiration, how can the weak escape it — unless they take their precaution? [Page V03P369]

And Muṭarrif said: "That I spend the night sleeping and wake up regretful is dearer to me than spending the night standing (in prayer) and waking up self-admiring."

And he, peace be upon him, said: "Were you not to sin, I would fear for you what is greater than that: self-admiration, self-admiration." [The ḥadīth "Were you not to sin, I would fear for you what is greater than that: self-admiration, self-admiration" is narrated by al-Bazzār and Ibn Ḥibbān in al-Ḍuʿafāʾ, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab, from Anas; in it is Sallām ibn Abī al-Ṣahbāʾ, whom al-Bukhārī declared a denier of ḥadīth, while Aḥmad said he is good in ḥadīth. Abū Manṣūr al-Daylamī also narrated it in Musnad al-Firdaws from Abū Saʿīd with a very weak chain.] Thus he made self-admiration the greatest of sins.

And Bishr ibn Manṣūr was among those who, when they saw the remembrance of God Most High and the Hereafter, [persisted] due to their constancy in worship. One day he lengthened his prayer, and a man behind him was watching him. Bishr perceived him, and when he finished his prayer, he said to him: "Do not let what you saw of me impress you, for Iblīs, may God curse him, worshipped God Most High alongside the angels for a long period, then he came to what he came to."

And it was said to ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her: "When is a man considered sinful?" She said: "When he thinks he is virtuous."

And God Most High said: {«Do not nullify your charities by reproach and injury»} — and reproach (al-mann) is the result of deeming one's charity great; and deeming one's deed great is self-admiration.

Thus it has become clear from all this that self-admiration is exceedingly blameworthy.
