chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح س س (ḥ-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sensory perception; the faculty by which the living being apprehends external objects.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The lowest tier of cognition; perception of particulars without rational judgment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical sensation; metaphorically for intellectual apprehension.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Propositions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The repeated use of "law" (if) and "fa" (then) structures the argument as a chain of hypothetical necessities, each contingent on the prior.
chapters.translation:
Know that sensory perception (al-ḥiss) yields nothing but apprehension, and volition (al-irādah) has no meaning other than the inclination toward seeking and fleeing. Yet this is insufficient unless there exists within you an instrument for seeking and fleeing. For how many a sick person longs for something distant, perceives it, yet cannot walk to it for lack of a leg, or cannot grasp it for lack of a hand, or due to paralysis and numbness therein. Thus, instruments of movement are indispensable, along with a power (qudrah) in those instruments for movement, so that their motion occurs in accordance with appetite as pursuit, and in accordance with aversion as flight. For this reason, God—exalted is He—created for you the limbs whose outward forms you behold but whose inner secrets you do not know. Among them are those for pursuit and flight, such as the leg for man, the wing for the bird, and the legs for beasts; and among them are those for defense, such as weapons for man and horns for animals. In this, animals differ greatly: some have many enemies and distant sustenance, thus requiring swift motion—so He created for them the wing to fly swiftly; some He created with four legs; some with two; some that crawl. The enumeration of this would be lengthy, so let us mention only the limbs by which eating is accomplished, that others may be measured against them.

We say: your seeing food from afar and your moving toward it suffice not unless you are able to take it. Thus you stood in need of a grasping instrument, and God—exalted is He—bestowed upon you the creation of two hands: long, extending toward things, comprising many joints so that they move in all directions, stretching and bending toward you—not like a fixed wooden post. Then He made the extremity of the hand broad by creating the palm, then divided the extremity of the palm into five divisions, which are the fingers, and arranged them in two rows such that the thumb stands on one side and rotates around the remaining four. Had they been clustered together or piled upon one another, your purpose would not have been fully achieved. So He positioned them such that if you spread them, they are a shovel for you; if you cup them, they are a ladle; if you clench them, they are an instrument for striking; and if you extend them then grasp, they are an instrument for seizing. Then He created for them nails, attaching them to the tips of the fingers so that they do not crumble, and so that you may pick up with them the fine objects that the fingers cannot encompass—you take them with the tips of your nails.

Then suppose you have taken the food with your hands—how would this suffice you unless it reaches the stomach, which lies within? There must be a vestibule from the exterior leading to it, through which food enters. So He made the mouth a passage to the stomach, along with the many wisdoms it contains besides being a passage for food. Then, if you place the food in the mouth as a single morsel, swallowing it is not facilitated; you need a mill to grind it. So He created for you the two jaws from two bones, set in them the teeth, and fitted the upper molars upon the lower ones to grind food therewith. Now food sometimes requires breaking, sometimes cutting, and then grinding thereafter. So He divided the teeth into broad grinders like the molars, sharp incisors like the foreteeth, and those suited for tearing like the canines. Then He made the joint of the jaws loose, such that the lower jaw advances and retreats, rotating upon the upper jaw as the rotation of a hand-mill. Were it not for this, only a striking of one upon the other would occur—like the clapping of hands, for instance—and by that grinding would not be accomplished. So He made the lower jaw move with a rotary motion, while the upper jaw remains fixed, unmoving.

Consider then the wondrous workmanship of God—exalted is He! For every mill made by creatures has its lower stone fixed and its upper stone rotating—except this mill made by God, for its lower part rotates upon the upper. Glory be to Him! How immense is His majesty, how mighty His dominion, how complete His proof, how vast His beneficence!

Then suppose you have placed the food in the cavity of the mouth—how does the food move to beneath the teeth, or how do the teeth draw it to themselves, or how is the hand to maneuver inside the mouth? Consider how God—exalted is He—has favored you by creating the tongue: it roams about the sides of the mouth, returning the food from the center to the teeth according to need, like the shovel that returns grain to the mill. This is besides the benefit of taste it contains, and the wonders of the power of speech, and the wisdoms which we shall not elaborate upon.

Then suppose you have cut and ground the food, and it is dry—you cannot swallow it unless it slides down the throat by means of some moisture. Consider how God—exalted is He—created beneath the tongue a spring from which saliva flows and pours forth in measure according to need, so that the food is kneaded with it. Consider how He subjugated it to this task: you see food from afar, and the two palates stir to service, and saliva pours until your jaws water—while the food is still distant from you.

Then this ground, kneaded food—who conveys it to the stomach while it is in the mouth? You cannot push it with your hand, and there is no hand in the stomach to extend and draw the food. Consider how God—exalted is He—prepared the esophagus and the larynx, placing upon its head layers that open to receive the food, then contract so that the food is turned over by their pressure and descends into the stomach through the vestibule of the esophagus.

When the food arrives at the stomach as bread and cut fruit, it is not fit to become flesh, bone, and blood in that form. Rather, it must be cooked thoroughly until its parts become homogeneous. So God—exalted is He—created the stomach in the form of a cooking pot: the food falls into it, it encloses it, and the doors close upon it. It remains therein until digestion and maturation are completed by the heat that surrounds the stomach from the internal organs—for on its right side is the liver, on its left the spleen, in front the breastbone, and behind the flesh of the spine. Heat thus reaches it from the warming of these organs on all sides, until the food is cooked and becomes a homogeneous fluid, fit to penetrate the channels of the veins. At that point it resembles barley-water in the homogeneity of its parts and its consistency. Yet it is still not fit for nourishment.

So God—exalted is He—created between it and the liver channels of veins, giving them many openings, so that the food pours into them and reaches the liver. The liver is kneaded from the clay of blood—as if it were blood itself—and within it are many hair-like veins spread through its parts. The thin food penetrates them and spreads through its parts until the liver's power overcomes it, dyeing it with the color of blood. It settles therein until a second maturation occurs, and it acquires the form of pure blood fit for the nourishment of the organs—except that the liver's heat is what matures this blood.

From this blood two residues are generated, just as residues are generated in all cooked things: one resembling dregs and sediment—this is the black bile (al-khilt al-sawdāwī); the other resembling foam—this is the yellow bile (al-ṣafrā'). Were these two residues not separated, the temperament of the organs would be corrupted. So God—exalted is He—created the gall bladder and the spleen, giving each a neck extended to the liver, entering into its cavity. The gall bladder draws the bilious residue, and the spleen draws the black sediment, leaving the blood pure, containing nothing but an excess of thinness and moisture due to its watery content. Were it not for this, it would not spread through those hair-like veins, nor would it ascend from them to the organs.

So God—glory be to Him—created the two kidneys, extending from each a long neck toward the liver. Among the wonders of God's wisdom is that their necks do not enter the liver's cavity but rather connect to the veins rising from the hump of the liver, so that they draw what is near them after its ascent from the fine veins within the liver. Had they drawn it before that, it would have been too thick and would not have emerged from the veins. When the watery content is separated from it, the blood becomes pure of the three residues, clean of everything that would corrupt nourishment.

Then God—exalted is He—caused veins to issue from the liver, then divided them after their emergence into branches, and branched each branch into further branches, spreading throughout the entire body from head to foot, outwardly and inwardly. The pure blood flows through them, reaching all the organs, until the divided veins become hair-like—like the veins of leaves and trees—imperceptible to sight. Through them nourishment reaches all the organs by seepage.

Were the gall bladder afflicted with a malady such that it failed to draw the bilious residue, the blood would be corrupted and bilious diseases would arise—such as jaundice, pustules, and erysipelas. Were the spleen afflicted such that it failed to draw the black humor, black-bilious diseases would occur—such as vitiligo, leprosy, melancholia, and others. Were the watery content not driven toward the kidneys, dropsy and other ailments would result.

Then consider the wisdom of the Wise Originator (al-Fāṭir al-Ḥakīm)—how He arranged benefits upon these three base residues. As for the gall bladder, it draws with one of its necks and discharges with the other neck into the intestines, so that a lubricating moisture is obtained in the food's dregs, and a pungency arises in the intestines that stirs them to expulsion—they contract until the dregs are pushed out and slide away. Its yellowness serves that purpose. As for the spleen, it transforms that residue into a transformation by which acidity and astringency are produced therein, then sends from it each day something to the mouth of the stomach, stirring the appetite by its acidity, awakening and arousing it; the remainder exits with the dregs. As for the kidney, it feeds upon the blood contained in that watery content and sends the remainder to the bladder.

Let us be content with this measure in explaining the blessings of God—exalted is He—in the causes prepared for eating. Were we to mention how the liver stands in need of the heart and the brain, how each of these principal organs stands in need of its companion, how the pulsating arteries branch from the heart to the rest of the body and through them sensation reaches, how the non-pulsating veins branch from the liver to the rest of the body and through them nourishment reaches, then the composition of the organs, the number of their bones, muscles, veins, tendons, ligaments, cartilages, and moistures—the discourse would become long. All of that is needed for eating and for other purposes besides. Indeed, in the human being there are thousands of muscles, veins, and nerves, varying in smallness and greatness, fineness and coarseness, abundance and paucity of division—and there is none among them but contains one, two, three, four, up to ten or more wisdoms. All of these are blessings from God—exalted is He—upon you. Were but a single moving vein to become still, or a still vein to move, you would perish, O wretched one!

Consider then God's blessing upon you—will you not, so that you may thereby be strengthened for gratitude? For you know of God's blessing—glory be to Him—nothing but eating, which is the basest of them. And even of that, you know only that you hunger and eat. The donkey also knows that it hungers and eats, tires and sleeps, desires and copulates, is roused and rises, and kicks. If you know of yourself nothing but what the donkey knows, how can you fulfill gratitude for God's blessing upon you?

This which we have indicated briefly is but a drop from a single sea among the seas of God's blessings. Measure by this summary what we have omitted from what we know, out of fear of prolixity. And all that we know—and all that creation knows—compared to what they do not know of God's blessings, is less than a drop from a sea. Yet whoever knows something of this apprehends a fragrance of the meaning of His saying—exalted is He: {«And if you should count the blessings of God, you could not enumerate them»} (Ibrāhīm 14:34).

Then consider how God—exalted is He—has tied the subsistence of these organs, the subsistence of their benefits, their perceptions, and their powers to a subtle vapor that ascends from the four humors, whose seat is the heart, and which courses through the entire body by means of the pulsating arteries. It reaches no part of the body except that, upon its arrival, there arises in that part what is needed of the power of sensation, perception, movement, and other things—like a lamp carried through the corners of a house: it reaches no part except that, by its arrival, light is produced upon the parts of the house, from God's creation and invention—yet He made the lamp a cause thereof by His wisdom.

This subtle vapor is what the physicians call the spirit (al-rūḥ). Its locus is the heart. Its likeness is the body of the lamp's flame; the heart is to it as the lamp-holder; the black blood within the heart is to it as the wick; nourishment is to it as the oil; and the apparent life in all the body's organs is by its means, as the light of the lamp in the whole house. And just as the lamp, when its oil is cut off, is extinguished, so too the lamp of the spirit is extinguished whenever its nourishment is cut off. And just as the wick may burn and become ash such that it no longer accepts oil, and the lamp is extinguished despite an abundance of oil, so too the blood to which this vapor clings in the heart may burn by the excessive heat of the heart, and the spirit is extinguished despite the presence of nourishment—for it does not accept the nourishment by which the spirit would subsist, just as ash does not accept oil in a manner by which fire would cling to it.

And just as the lamp is sometimes extinguished by an internal cause, as we have mentioned, and sometimes by an external cause—like a violent wind—so too the spirit is sometimes extinguished by an internal cause and sometimes by an external one, which is killing. And just as the extinguishing of the lamp—by the exhaustion of oil, or the corruption of the wick, or a violent wind, or a man's extinguishing it—occurs only by causes decreed in God's knowledge, arranged in order, all by measure (qadar), so too is the extinguishing of the spirit. And just as the extinguishing of the lamp is the terminus of its time of existence, being its appointed term (ajal) decreed for it in the Mother of the Book, so too is the extinguishing of the spirit. And just as, when the lamp is extinguished, the whole house darkens, so too, when the spirit is extinguished, the whole body darkens, and the lights it used to derive from the spirit depart from it—namely, the lights of sensations, powers, volitions, and all that the meaning of the word "life" encompasses.

This too is a brief symbol pointing to another world among the worlds of God's blessings and the wonders of His workmanship and wisdom—so that one may know that {«If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted»} (al-Kahf 18:109)—mighty and majestic is He. Perdition to him who disbelieves in God—perdition! And ruin to him who denies His blessing—ruin!

If you say: "You have described the spirit and likened it, yet the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—was asked about the spirit and added nothing beyond saying: {«Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord»} (al-Isrā' 17:85). He did not describe it to them in this manner."

Know that this is a negligence regarding the homonymy (ishtirāk) occurring in the word "spirit" (al-rūḥ). For "spirit" is applied to many meanings, which we shall not elaborate upon. We have described only one of them: a subtle body which the physicians call spirit. They have known its description, its existence, the manner of its coursing through the organs, and how sensation and powers arise in the organs by means of it—such that when a limb becomes numb, they know that this is due to an obstruction (suddat) occurring in the channel of this spirit. They do not treat the site of numbness but rather the origins of the nerves and the locations of the obstruction therein, treating them with what opens the obstruction. For this body, by its subtlety, penetrates the mesh of the nerve, and by its mediation, [the spirit] is conveyed from the heart to all the organs. Whatever the physicians' knowledge attains to is an easy, lowly matter.

As for the spirit that is the principle—the one whose corruption corrupts the entire body—that is a secret of God's secrets. We have not described it, nor is there license to describe it except by saying it is a divine command (amr rabbānī), as He—exalted is He—said: {«Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord»}. The divine commands do not admit of description by intellects; rather, the intellects of most creatures are bewildered by them. As for fancies and delusions, they fall short of them by necessity—as sight falls short of apprehending sounds. And in mentioning the principles of its description, the anchoring points of intellects—confined as they are to substance and accident, imprisoned in their narrow strait—are shaken. Nothing of its description is apprehended by the intellect, but rather by another light higher and nobler than the intellect. That light shines in the world of prophethood and sainthood (al-wilāyah). Its relation to the intellect is like the relation of the intellect to fancy and imagination.

God—exalted is He—created creation in stages (aṭwār). Just as the child apprehends sensibles but does not apprehend intelligibles—because that is a stage he has not yet reached—so too the adult apprehends intelligibles but does not apprehend what lies beyond them, because that is a stage he has not yet reached. It is a noble station, a sweet drinking-place, and a lofty rank in which one beholds the gardens of Truth by the light of faith and certainty. That drinking-place is too precious to be a thoroughfare for every comer; rather, none attains to it save one after one. The court of the Truth has a breast, and at the forefront of the breast is a field and a spacious arena. At the beginning of the arena is a threshold, which is the resting-place of that divine command. Whoever has no passage upon that threshold, and no vision of the threshold's keeper, it is impossible for him to reach the arena—how then to arrive at what lies beyond it of lofty visions?

For this reason it was said: "He who does not know himself does not know his Lord." How could the physicians' treasury encounter this? Whence would a physician behold it? Rather, the meaning called "spirit" by the physician, in relation to this divine command, is like the ball that the king's polo-stick moves in relation to the king. Whoever knows the medical spirit and supposes he has apprehended the divine command is like one who sees the ball moved by the king's polo-stick and supposes he has seen the king. There is no doubt that his error is gross—and this error is grosser than it by far.

And since the intellects by which obligation (taklīf) is effected and by which the interests of this world are apprehended are intellects that fall short of beholding the reality of this matter, God—exalted is He—did not permit His Messenger—peace be upon him—to speak about it. Rather, He commanded him to speak to people according to the measure of their intellects. God—exalted is He—mentioned nothing in His Book of the reality of this matter, but mentioned its relation and its act, and did not mention its essence. As for its relation, it is in His saying—exalted is He: {«Of the command of my Lord»}. As for its act, He mentioned it in His saying—exalted is He: {«O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing, and enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise»} (al-Fajr 89:27–30).

Let us now return to the purpose, for the aim is the mention of God's blessings in eating. We have mentioned some of God's blessings in the instruments of eating.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Aspect: On the Divine Blessings in the Primary Elements from Which Foods Arise and Become Fit for Human Craftsmanship
chapters.arabic_text: ### |||||| الطرف الرابع في نعم الله تعالى في الأصول التي يحصل منها الأطعمة وتصير صالحة لأن يصلحها الآدمي بعد ذلك بصنعته
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط ر ف (ṭ-r-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The side, edge, or extremity of a thing; also a novel or fresh matter (ṭaraf = a part, a section, a category).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A division or branch of a subject, often used to denote a distinct mode of inquiry within a broader discourse.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical extremity; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for a "section" or "aspect" of a systematic exposition.
- Root: ن ع م (n-ʿ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Softness, ease, abundance; blessings (niʿam) as the gracious gifts of God.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine beneficence (niʿmah) as that which brings about well-being (naʿīm) in this world and the next, contingent upon God's gratuitous favor.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: pleasantness of life; metaphorical: all forms of divine provision (rizq) and favor.
- Root: أ ص ل (a-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root, foundation, origin; the base from which branches derive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The primordial elements (uṣūl) — earth, water, air, fire — as the ontological bases of all generated things (mawālīd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: root of a tree; metaphorical: the elemental causes underlying material sustenance.
- Root: ص ن ع (ṣ-n-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Craftsmanship, skilled making, artifice.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Human industry (ṣināʿah) as a secondary agency, subordinate to divine creation (khalq).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical fabrication; metaphorical: the human role in transforming raw provision into consumable goods.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "التي يحصل منها الأطعمة" is a relative clause (ṣilah) modifying "الأصول", with the verb "يحصل" in the imperfect tense indicating habitual occurrence, and "وتصير صالحة" coordinated by wa (ʿaṭf) to express a sequential state change.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us turn to the fourth aspect — namely, the blessings of God Most High in the primary elements (uṣūl) from which foods are produced, and which then become suitable for the human being to refine afterward through his own craftsmanship (ṣināʿah). For God, exalted be He, has not merely created these elements in a state of raw potential, but has so ordered them that, through His wisdom, they yield the various grains, fruits, and provisions which sustain the body. And He has further endowed the human being with the capacity, the tools, and the discernment to transform these raw materials — by grinding, baking, cooking, and combining — into wholesome nourishment. Thus, every stage of this process, from the primordial element to the finished dish, is a chain of divine favors, each link of which calls for gratitude and reflection.

chapters.title_en: On the Marvels of Divine Providence in the Sustenance of Plants
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الأطعمة كثيرة ولله تعالى في خلقها عجائب كثيرة لا تحصى وأسباب
متوالية لا تتناهى وذكر ذلك في كل طعام مما يطول فإن الأطعمة إما أدوية
وإما فواكه وإما أغذية فلنأخذ الأغذية فإنها الأصل ولنأخذ من جملتها حبة من
البر ولندع سائر الأغذية فنقول إذا وجدت حبة أو حبات فلو أكلتها فنيت وبقيت
جائعا فما أحوجك إلى أن تنمو الحبة في نفسها وتزيد وتتضاعف حتى تفي بتمام
حاجتك فخلق الله تعالى في حبة الحنطة من القوى ما يغتذى به كما خلق فيك فإن
النبات إنما يفارقك في الحس والحركة ولا يخالفك في الاغتذاء لأنه يغتذي
بالماء ويجتذب إلى باطنه بواسطة العروق كما تغتذى أنت وتجتذب ولسنا نطنب في
ذكر آلات النبات في اجتذاب الغذاء إلى نفسه ولكن نشير إلى غذائه فنقول كما
أن الخشب والتراب لا يغذيك بل تحتاج إلى طعام مخصوص فكذلك الحبة لا تغتذي
بكل شيء بل تحتاج إلى شيء مخصوص بدليل أنك لو تركتها في البيت لم تزد لأنه
ليس يحيط بها إلا هواء  ومجرد الهواء لا يصلح لغذائها ولو تركنها في الماء
لم تزد ولو تركنها في أرض لا ماء فيها لم تزد بل لا بد من أرض فيها ماء
يمتزج ماؤها بالأرض فيصير طينا وإليه الإشارة بقوله تعالى {فلينظر الإنسان
إلى طعامه أنا صببنا الماء صبا ثم شققنا الأرض شقا فأنبتنا فيها حبا وعنبا
وقضبا وزيتونا ونخلا} الآية ثم لا يكفي الماء والتراب إذ لو تركت في أرض
ندية صلبة متراكمة لم تنبت لفقد الهواء فيحتاج إلى تركها في أرض رجوة
متخلخلة يتغلغل الهواء إليها ثم الهواء لا يتحرك إليها بنفسه فيحتاج إلى
ريح تحرك الهواء وتضربه بقهر وعنف على الأرض حتى ينفذ فيها وإليه الإشارة
بقوله تعالى {وأرسلنا الرياح لواقح} وإنما إلقاحها في إيقاع الازدواج بين
الهواء والماء والأرض ثم كل ذلك لا يغنيك لو كان في برد مفرط وشتاء شات
فتحتاج إلى حرارة الربيع والصيف فقد بان احتياج غذائه إلى هذه الأربعة
فانظر إلى ماذا يحتاج كل واحد إذ يحتاج الماء لينساق إلى أرض الزراعة من
البحار والعيون والأنهار والسواقي فانظر كيف خلق الله البحار وفجر العيون
وأجرى منها الأنهار ثم الأرض ربما تكون مرتفعة والمياه لا ترتفع إليها
فانظر كيف خلق الله تعالى الغيوم وكيف سلط الرياح عليها لتسوقها بإذنه إلى
أقطار الأرض وهي سحب ثقال حوامل بالماء ثم انظر كيف يرسله مدرارا على
الأراضي في وقت الربيع والخريف على حسب الحاجة وانظر كيف خلق الجبال حافظة
للمياه تتفجر منها العيون تدريجا فلو خرجت دفعة لغرقت البلاد وهلك الزرع
والمواشي ونعم الله في الجبال والسحاب والبحار والأمطار لا يمكن إحصاؤها
وأما الحرارة فإنها لا تحصل بين الماء والأرض وكلاهما باردان فانظر كيف سخر
الشمس وكيف خلقها مع بعدها عن الأرض مسخنة للأرض في وقت دون وقت ليحصل
البرد عند الحاجة إلى البرد والحر عند الحاجة إلى الحر فهذه إحدى حكم الشمس
والحكم فيها أكثر من أن تحصى ثم النبات إذا ارتفع عن الأرض كان في الفواكه
انعقاد وصلابة فتفتقر  إلى رطوبة تنضجها فانظر كيف خلق القمر وجعل من خاصيته
الترطيب كما جعل من خاصية الشمس التسخين فهو ينضج الفواكه ويصبغها بتقدير
الفاطر الحكيم ولذلك لو كانت الأشجار في ظل يمنع شروق الشمس والقمر وسائر
PageV04P116
الكواكب عليها لكانت فاسدة ناقصة حتى إن الشجرة الصغيرة تفسد إذا ظللتها
شجرة كبيرة وتعرف ترطيب القمر بأن تكشف رأسك له بالليل فتغلب على رأسك
الرطوبة التي يعبر عنها بالزكام فكما يرطب رأسك يرطب الفاكهة أيضا ولا نطول
فيما لا مطمع في استقصائه بل نقول كل كوكب في السماء فقد سخر لنوع فائدة
كما سخرت الشمس للتسخين والقمر للترطيب فلا يخلو واحد منها عن حكم كثيرة لا
تفي قوة البشر بإحصائها ولو لم يكن كذلك لكان خلقها عبثا وباطلا ولم يصح
قوله تعالى {ربنا ما خلقت هذا باطلا} وقوله عز وجل وما خلقنا السموات
والأرض وما بينهما لاعبين وكما أنه ليس في أعضاء بدنك عضو إلا لفائدة فليس
في أعضاء بدن العالم عضو إلا لفائدة والعالم كله كشخص واحد وآحاد أجسامه
كالأعضاء له وهي متعاونة تعاون أعضاء بدنك في جملة بدنك وشرح ذلك يطول ولا
ينبغي أن تظن أن الإيمان بأن النجوم والشمس والقمر مسخرات بأمر الله سبحانه
في أمور جعلت أسبابا لها بحكم الحكمة مخالف للشرع لما ورد فيه من النهي عن
تصديق المنجمين وعن علم النجوم // حديث النهي عن تصديق المنجمين وعن علم
النجوم أخرجه أبو داود وابن ماجه بسند صحيح من حديث ابن عباس من اقتبس علما
من النجوم اقتبس شعبة من السحر زاد ما زاد وللطبرانى من حديث ابن مسعود
وثوبان إذا ذكرت النجوم فأمسكوا وإسنادهما ضعيف وقد تقدم فى العلم ولمسلم
من حديث معاوية بن الحكم السلمى قال قلت يا رسول لله أمورا كنا نصنعها فى
الجاهلية كنا نأتى الكهان قال فلا تأتوا الكهان الحديث
بل المنهي عنه في النجوم أمران أحدهما أن تصدق بأنها فاعلة لآثارها
مستقلة بها وأنها ليست مسخرة تحت تدبير مدبر خلقها وقهرها وهذا كفر والثاني
تصديق المنجمين في تفصيل ما يخبرون عنه من الآثار التي لا يشترك كافة الخلق
في دركها لأنهم يقولون ذلك عن جهل فإن علم أحكام النجوم كان معجزة لبعض
الأنبياء عليهم السلام ثم اندرس ذلك العلم فلم يبق إلا ما هو مختلط لا
يتميز فيه الصواب عن الخطأ فاعتقاد كون الكواكب أسبابا لآثار تحصل بخلق
الله تعالى في الأرض وفي النبات وفي الحيوان ليس قادحا في الدين بل هو حق
ولكن دعوى العلم بتلك الآثار على التفصيل مع الجهل قادح في الدين ولذلك إذا
كان معك ثوب غسلته وتريد تجفيفه فقال لك غيرك أخرج الثوب وابسطه فإن الشمس
قد طلعت وحمي النهار والهواء لا يلزمك تكذيبه ولا يلزمك الإنكار عليه
بحوالته حمي الهواء على طلوع الشمس وإذا سألت عن تغيير وجه الإنسان فقال
قرعتني الشمس في الطريق فاسود وجهي لم يلزمك تكذيبه بذلك وقس بهذا سائر
الآثار إلا أن الآثار بعضها معلوم وبعضها مجهول فالمجهول لا يجوز دعوى
العلم فيه والمعلوم بعضه معلوم للناس كافة كحصول الضياء والحرارة بطلوع
الشمس وبعضه لبعض الناس كحصول الزكام بشروق القمر فإذن الكواكب ما خلقت
عبثا بل فيها حكم كثيرة لا تحصى ولهذا نظر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
إلى السماء وقرأ قوله تعالى ربنا ما خلقت هذا باطلا سبحانك فقنا عذاب النار
ثم قال صلى الله عليه وسلم ويل لمن قرأ هذه الآية ثم مسح بها سبلته
حديث قرأ قوله تعالى ربنا ما خلقت هذا باطلا سبحانك فقنا عذاب النار ثم
قال ويل لمن قرأ هذه الآية ثم مسح بها سبلته أى ترك تأملها أخرجه الثعلبى
من حديث ابن عباس بلفظ ولم يتفكر فيها وفيه أبو جناب يحيى بن أبى حبة ضعيف
ومعناه أن يقرأ ويترك التأمل ويقتصر من فهم ملكوت السموات على أن يعرف
لون السماء وضوء الكواكب وذلك مما تعرفه البهائم أيضا فمن قنع منه بمعرفة
ذلك فهو الذي مسح بها سبلته فلله تعالى في ملكوت السموات والآفاق والأنفس
والحيوانات عجائب  يطلب معرفتها المحبون لله تعالى فإن من أحب عالما فلا
يزال مشغولا بطلب تصانيفه ليزداد بمزيد الوقوف على عجائب علمه حبا له فكذلك
الأمر في عجائب صنع الله تعالى فإن العالم
PageV04P117
كله من تصنيفه بل تصنيف المصنفين من تصنيفه الذي صنفه بواسطة قلوب عباده
فإن تعجبت من تصنيف فلا تتعجب من المصنف بل من الذي سخر المصنف لتصنيفه بما
أنعم عليه من هدايته وتسديده وتعريفه كما إذا رأيت لعب المشعوذ ترقص وتتحرك
حركات موزونة متناسبة فلا تعجب من اللعب فإنها خرق محركة لا متحركة ولكن
تعجب من حذق المشعوذ المحرك لها بروابط دقيقة خفية عن الأبصار فإذن المقصود
أن غذاء النبات لا يتم إلا بالماء والهواء والشمس والقمر والكواكب ولا يتم
ذلك إلا بالأفلاك التي هي مركوزة فيها ولا تتم الأفلاك إلا بحركانها ولا
تتم حركاتها إلا بملائكة سماوية يحركونها وكذلك يتمادى ذلك إلى أسباب بعيدة
تركنا ذكرها تنبيها بما ذكرناه على ما أهملناه ولنقتصر على هذا من ذكر
أسباب غذاء النبات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ذ-و (gh-dh-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to nourish, to feed," denoting the intake by which a living being attains growth and preservation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, it signifies the divinely ordained means (sabab) by which created bodies are sustained, distinct from the Creator's direct act of origination (ījād).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for physical nutriment; metaphorically (majāz) for spiritual sustenance, though here it remains literal.
- Root: س-خ-ر (s-kh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To subjugate, to compel, to employ for a purpose," implying a superior power directing an inferior.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, it denotes the divine imposition of order upon celestial and terrestrial bodies, making them causes (asbāb) under God's command, not independent agents.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the subjugation of inanimate objects; the rhetorical force lies in the implied contrast with God's absolute sovereignty.
- Root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Judgment, wisdom, purpose," rooted in preventing corruption and attaining benefit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The teleological principle that every created thing has a divinely appointed end (ghāyah), negating futility (ʿabath).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the wise ordering of causes; metaphorically extended to the hidden benefits (maṣāliḥ) imperceptible to most.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Causal Coordination (al-ʿaṭf bi-sababiyyah) — The text employs lengthy periodic sentences where subordinate clauses (e.g., "if you found a grain...") are coordinated to establish a chain of necessary conditions, each linked by fa- (consequence) to demonstrate the cumulative dependence of effects on multiple causes.
chapters.translation:
Know that foods are many, and for God Most High—in their creation—there are marvels beyond enumeration and successive causes that do not come to an end. To mention this for every food would be lengthy, for foods are either medicines, or fruits, or nourishments. Let us take the nourishments, for they are the foundation; and from among them let us take a single grain of wheat, leaving aside all other nourishments. We say: If you found a grain or grains, and you ate them, they would perish and you would remain hungry—so how much more do you need the grain to grow within itself, to increase and multiply, until it suffices for your complete need? Thus God Most High created in the grain of wheat powers by which it is nourished, just as He created in you. For the plant differs from you only in sensation and movement; it does not differ from you in nourishment, because it is nourished by water and draws it into its interior by means of roots, just as you are nourished and draw in. We shall not elaborate at length on the instruments of the plant in drawing nourishment to itself, but we shall point to its nourishment and say: Just as wood and earth do not nourish you—rather, you need specific food—so likewise the grain is not nourished by everything; rather, it needs something specific. The proof is that if you left it in a house, it would not increase, because nothing surrounds it but air, and mere air is not suitable for its nourishment. If you left it in water, it would not increase. If you left it in earth without water, it would not increase. Rather, there must be earth containing water, whose water mixes with the earth and becomes clay. To this points His saying, Most High: {«Then let man look at his food—that We pour down water in abundance, then We cleave the earth in clefts, and We cause to grow therein grain, and grapes, and fresh vegetation, and olives, and palms»}—the verse. Then water and earth alone do not suffice, for if you left it in moist, hard, compacted earth, it would not sprout due to the lack of air. Thus it needs to be left in loose, crumbled earth into which air penetrates. Then the air does not move to it by itself, so it needs a wind that moves the air and strikes it with force and violence upon the earth until it penetrates therein. To this points His saying, Most High: {«And We sent the winds as fertilizing agents»}. Its fertilization lies in effecting the union between air, water, and earth. Then all that would not avail you if it were in extreme cold and a wintry season—so you need the heat of spring and summer. Thus it has become clear that its nourishment requires these four things. So consider what each one requires: for water needs to flow to the cultivated land from seas, springs, rivers, and channels. Consider how God created the seas, caused the springs to gush forth, and made the rivers flow from them. Then the earth may be elevated, and waters do not rise to it—so consider how God Most High created the clouds, and how He subjected the winds to them, to drive them by His leave to the regions of the earth, they being heavy clouds bearing water. Then consider how He sends it down in abundance upon the lands in the time of spring and autumn, according to need. And consider how He created the mountains as preservers of water, from which springs burst forth gradually—for if it gushed forth all at once, the lands would be flooded, and the crops and livestock would perish. The blessings of God in the mountains, clouds, seas, and rains cannot be enumerated. As for heat, it cannot be obtained between water and earth, for both are cold—so consider how He subjected the sun, and how He created it, despite its distance from the earth, as a heater of the earth at one time and not another, so that cold is obtained when cold is needed, and heat when heat is needed. This is one of the wisdoms of the sun; its wisdoms are more than can be counted. Then when the plant rises above the earth, the fruits undergo formation and hardness, so they need moisture to ripen them. Consider how He created the moon and made its property that of moistening, just as He made the sun's property that of heating. Thus it ripens the fruits and colors them by the ordainment of the Wise Originator. For this reason, if the trees were in a shade that blocked the rising of the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars upon them, they would be corrupt and deficient—even a small tree is corrupted if a large tree shades it. You can recognize the moistening of the moon by exposing your head to it at night, for moisture—which is called catarrh—overcomes your head. Just as it moistens your head, so it moistens the fruit as well. We shall not prolong in what there is no hope of exhausting; rather, we say: Every star in the sky has been subjected for a type of benefit, just as the sun is subjected for heating and the moon for moistening. Not one of them is devoid of many wisdoms that human power cannot enumerate. Were it not so, their creation would be futility and falsehood, and the saying of God Most High would not hold: {«Our Lord, You have not created this in vain»}—and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {«And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play»}. And just as there is no organ in your body except for a benefit, so there is no organ in the body of the world except for a benefit. The entire world is like a single person, and the individual bodies within it are like his organs, cooperating as the organs of your body cooperate within the whole of your body. The explanation of this would be lengthy.

You should not think that believing the stars, the sun, and the moon are subjected by the command of God, Glorified be He, in matters for which they were made causes by the dictate of wisdom, is contrary to the Sacred Law—despite what has come therein of the prohibition against believing astrologers and against the science of the stars. [Hadith: The prohibition against believing astrologers and the science of the stars is reported by Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah with a sound chain from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Whoever acquires a branch of the science of the stars has acquired a branch of sorcery; the more he increases, the more he increases." And al-Ṭabarānī reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Thawbān: "When the stars are mentioned, desist"—but their chains are weak, and it has preceded in the Book of Knowledge. And Muslim reports from Muʿāwiyah ibn al-Ḥakam al-Sulamī, who said: "I said, O Messenger of God, we used to do things in the Jāhiliyyah—we used to come to soothsayers." He said: "Then do not come to soothsayers."]

Rather, what is prohibited regarding the stars are two matters: First, that you believe they are agents of their effects independently, and that they are not subjected under the direction of a Director who created them and subdued them—this is unbelief. Second, believing astrologers in the detail of what they report of effects that not all creatures share in perceiving, because they say this from ignorance. For the science of astral judgments was a miracle for some of the prophets, peace be upon them; then that science became extinct, and nothing remained but what is mixed, in which right cannot be distinguished from error. Thus, believing that the planets are causes for effects that occur by the creation of God Most High in the earth, in the plant, and in the animal is not a defect in religion—rather, it is true. But claiming knowledge of those effects in detail, while ignorant, is a defect in religion. For this reason, if you had a garment that you washed and wished to dry, and someone said to you: "Take out the garment and spread it, for the sun has risen and the day has become hot, and the air is warm"—you are not obliged to declare him a liar, nor are you obliged to deny his attribution of the warming of the air to the rising of the sun. And if you ask about the change of a person's face, and he says: "The sun struck me on the road, and my face blackened"—you are not obliged to declare him a liar in that. Measure by this all other effects, except that some effects are known and some are unknown. The unknown may not be claimed as knowledge; and of the known, some is known to all people—like the obtaining of light and heat by the rising of the sun—and some is known to some people—like the obtaining of catarrh by the rising of the moon. Thus, the planets were not created in vain; rather, in them are many wisdoms beyond count. For this reason, the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, looked to the sky and recited the saying of God Most High: {«Our Lord, You have not created this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire»}. Then he said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Woe to the one who recites this verse and then wipes his mustache with it." [Hadith: He recited the saying of God Most High: {«Our Lord, You have not created this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire»}, then said: "Woe to the one who recites this verse and then wipes his mustache with it"—i.e., he leaves off contemplating it. Al-Thaʿlabī reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās with the wording "and does not reflect upon it," and in it is Abū Janāb Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ḥabbah, who is weak. Its meaning is that he recites and leaves off reflection, and confines his understanding of the kingdom of the heavens to knowing the color of the sky and the light of the stars—which even beasts know. Whoever is content with knowing that is the one who wiped his mustache with it.]

For God Most High—in the kingdom of the heavens, the horizons, the souls, and the animals—there are marvels that the lovers of God Most High seek to know. For whoever loves a scholar does not cease to be occupied with seeking his writings, to increase in love for him by increasing in acquaintance with the marvels of his knowledge. Likewise is the matter in the marvels of God's handiwork—for the entire world is of His composition. Rather, the composition of composers is of His composition, which He composed by means of the hearts of His servants. If you marvel at a composition, do not marvel at the composer, but at the One who subjected the composer to his composition, by what He bestowed upon him of His guidance, His direction, and His instruction. It is as when you see the tricks of a juggler—the puppets dance and move with measured, proportionate motions. Do not marvel at the puppets, for they are rags moved, not movers; rather, marvel at the skill of the juggler who moves them by subtle cords hidden from sight. Thus, the intent is that the nourishment of the plant is not completed except by water, air, sun, moon, and stars; and that is not completed except by the spheres in which they are fixed; and the spheres are not completed except by their motions; and their motions are not completed except by celestial angels who move them. And so it continues to distant causes, which we have omitted to mention, alerting by what we have mentioned to what we have neglected. Let us confine ourselves to this much of the mention of the causes of the nourishment of the plant.

chapters.title_en: On the Divine Favors in the Means Conveying Sustenance to You, and on the Preparation of Foods
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||||| الطرف الخامس في نعم الله تعالى في الأسباب الموصلة للأطعمة إليك

اعلم أن هذه الأطعمة كلها لا توجد في كل مكان بل لها شروط مخصوصة لأجلها
توجد في بعض الأماكن دون بعض والناس منتشرون على وجه الأرض وقد تبعد عنهم
الأطعمة ويحول بينهم وبينها البحار والبراري فانظر كيف سخر الله تعالى
التجار وسلط عليهم حرص حب المال وشهوة الربح مع أنهم لا يغنيهم في غالب
الأمر شيء بل يجمعون فإما أن تغرق بها السفن أو تنهبها قطاع الطريق أو
يموتوا في بعض البلاد فيأخذها السلاطين وأحسن أحوالهم أن يأخذها ورثتهم وهم
أشد أعدائهم لو عرفوا فانظر كيف سلط الله الجهل والغفلة عليهم حتى يقاسوا
الشدائد في طلب الربح ويركبوا الأخطار ويغرروا بالأرواح في ركوب البحر
فيحملون الأطعمة وأنواع الحوائج من أقصى الشرق والغرب إليك وانظر كيف علمهم
الله تعالى صناعة السفن وكيفية الركوب فيها وانظر كيف خلق الحيوانات وسخرها
للركوب والحمل في البراري وانظر إلى الإبل كيف خلقت  وإلى الفرس كيف أمدت
بسرعة الحركة وإلى الحمار كيف جعل صبورا على التعب وإلى الجمال كيف تقطع
البراري وتطوي المراحل تحت الأعباء الثقيلة على الجوع والعطش وانظر كيف
سيرهم الله تعالى بواسطة السفن والحيوانات في البر والبحر ليحملوا إليك
الأطعمة وسائر الحوائج وتأمل ما يحتاج إليه الحيوانات من أسبابها وأدواتها
وعلفها وما تحتاج إليه السفن فقد خلق الله تعالى جميع ذلك إلى حد الحاجة
وفوق الحاجة وإحصاء ذلك غير ممكن ويتمادى ذلك إلى أمور خارجة عن الحصر نرى
تركها طلبا للإيجاز

### |||||| الطرف السادس في إصلاح الأطعمة

اعلم أن الذي ينبت في الأرض من النبات وما يخلق من الحيوانات لا يمكن أن
يقضم ويؤكل وهو كذلك بل لا بد في كل واحد من إصلاح وطبخ وتركيب وتنظيف
بإلقاء البعض وإبقاء البعض إلى أمور أخر لا تحصى واستقصاء ذلك في كل طعام
يطول فلنعين رغيفا واحدا ولننظر إلى ما يحتاج إليه الرغيف الواحد حتى
يستدير ويصلح للأكل من بعد إلقاء البذر في الأرض فأول ما يحتاج إليه الحارث
ليزرع ويصلح الأرض ثم الثور الذي يثير الأرض والفدان وجميع أسبابه ثم بعد
ذلك التعهد بسقي الماء مدة ثم تنقية الأرض من الحشيش ثم الحصاد ثم الفرك
والتنقية ثم الطحن ثم العجين ثم الخير فتأمل عدد هذه الأفعال التي ذكرناها
وما لم نذكره وعدد الأشخاص القائمين بها وعدد الآلات التي يحتاج إليها من
الحديد والخشب والحجر وغيره وانظر إلى أعمال الصناع في إصلاح آلات الحراثة
والطحن والخبز من نجار وحداد وغيرهما وانظر إلى حاجة الحداد إلى الحديد
والرصاص والنحاس وانظر كيف خلق الله تعالى
PageV04P118
الجبال والأحجار والمعادن وكيف جعل الأرض قطعا متجاورات مختلفة فإن فتشت
علمت أن رغيفا واحدا لا يستدير بحيث يصلح لأكلك يا مسكين مالم يعمل عليه
أكثر من ألف صانع فابتدىء من الملك الذي يزجي السحاب لينزل الماء إلى آخر
الأعمال من جهة الملائكة حتى تنتهى النوبة إلى عمل الإنسان فإذا استدار
طلبه قريب من سبعة آلاف صانع كل صانع أصل  من أصول الصنائع التي بها تتم
مصلحة الخلق ثم تأمل كثرة أعمال الإنسان في تلك الآلات حتى إن الإبرة التي
هي آلة صغيرة فائدتها خياطة اللباس الذي يمنع البرد عنك لا تكمل صورتها من
حديدة تصلح للإبرة إلا بعد أن تمر على يد الإبري خمسا وعشرين مرة ويتعاطى
في كل مرة منها عملا فلو لم يجمع الله تعالى البلاد ولم يسخر العباد
وافتقرت إلى عمل المنجل الذي تحصد به البر مثلا بعد نباته لنفذ عمرك وعجزت
عنه أفلا ترى كيف هدى الله عبده الذي خلقه من نطفة قذرة لأن يعمل هذه
الأعمال العجيبة والصنائع الغريبة فانظر إلى المقراض مثلا وهما جلمان
متطابقان ينطبق أحدهما على الآخر فيتناولان الشيء معا ويقطعانه بسرعة ولو
لم يكشف الله تعالى طريق اتخاذه بفضله وكرمه لمن قبلنا وافتقرنا إلى
استنباط الطريق فيه بفكرنا ثم إلى استخراج الحديد من الحجر وإلى تحصيل
الآلات التي بها يعمل المقراض وعمر الواحد منا عمر نوح وأوتي أكمل العقول
لقصر عمره عن استنباط الطريق في إصلاح هذه الآلة وحدها فضلا عن غيرها
فسبحان من الحق ذوي الأبصار بالعميان وسبحان من منع النبيين مع هذا البيان
فانظر الآن لو خلا بلدك عن الطحان مثلا أو عن الحداد أو عن الحجام الذي هو
أخس العمال أو عن الحائك أو عن واحد من جملة الصناع ماذا يصيبك من الأذى
وكيف تضطرب عليك أمورك كلها فسبحان من سخر بعض العباد لبعض حتى نفذت به
مشيئته وتمت به حكمته ولنوجز القول في هذه الطبقة أيضا فإن الغرض التنبيه
على النعم دون الاستقصاء
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-خ-ر (s-kh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To subjugate, compel, or employ something against its natural inclination for a purpose.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine subjugation (taskhīr) of creation as a sign of God's sole agency (tawḥīd) — creatures act as instruments of divine providence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to God's power; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to creatures, who are merely compelled vehicles.
- Root: ح-ر-ث (ḥ-r-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Tilling the soil; the act of preparing earth for cultivation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Earthly labor as a microcosm of divine causation — the farmer's work is a shadow of God's creative act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for agriculture; extended metaphorically for "acquiring merit" (ḥarth al-ākhirah).
- Root: ص-ن-ع (ṣ-n-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Skilled making, craftsmanship, precise fabrication.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Human artifice (ṣunʿ) contrasted with divine creation (khalq) — the former is derivative, the latter ex nihilo.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for human craft; when applied to God, it is metaphorical (majāz) indicating perfect ordering.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The repeated "law" (if) clauses with implied apodoses (e.g., "if you investigated, you would know") create a cumulative argumentative structure, each condition escalating the preceding one.
chapters.translation:
**The Fifth Section: On the Favors of God Most High in the Means That Convey Foods to You**

Know that all these foods are not found in every place; rather, they have specific conditions on account of which they exist in some locations and not others. People are scattered across the face of the earth, and foods may be distant from them, with seas and wildernesses intervening between them and those foods. So behold how God Most High subjugated (sakhkhara) the merchants and imposed upon them the greed for wealth and the appetite for profit — even though, in most cases, nothing avails them; rather, they amass goods, and then either the ships sink with their cargo, or highway robbers plunder them, or they die in some land and the rulers seize their wealth. And the best of their circumstances is that their heirs take it — heirs who would be their fiercest enemies, if only they knew. So behold how God imposed ignorance and heedlessness upon them, until they endure hardships in pursuit of profit, mount dangers, and gamble with their very souls in embarking upon the sea — all so that they may carry foods and all manner of necessities to you from the farthest East and West. And behold how God taught them the craft of shipbuilding and the manner of sailing therein. And behold how He created the animals and subjugated them for riding and for burden-bearing across the wildernesses. And behold the camel — how it was created; and the horse — how it was endowed with swiftness of motion; and the donkey — how it was made patient under toil; and the caravan beasts — how they traverse the wastelands and fold up the stages of the journey beneath heavy loads, upon hunger and thirst. And behold how God conveyed them, by means of ships and animals, over land and sea, so that they might carry to you foods and all other necessities. And reflect upon what the animals require of their means, their implements, and their fodder, and what the ships require — for God Most High has created all of that to the limit of need and beyond need. The enumeration of all this is not possible, and it extends to matters beyond all reckoning, which we omit in pursuit of brevity.

**The Sixth Section: On the Preparation of Foods**

Know that what grows from the earth of plants and what is created of animals cannot be gnawed and eaten as it is; rather, every single item requires preparation, cooking, combining, and cleansing — by discarding some parts and retaining others — along with countless other matters. Exhaustively detailing this for every food would be lengthy. So let us single out one single loaf of bread, and let us examine what that one loaf requires until it becomes round and fit for eating, from the moment the seed is cast into the earth. The first thing needed is the plowman (al-ḥārith) to sow and to prepare the soil; then the ox that turns the earth; then the plow (faddān) with all its appurtenances; then, after that, the ongoing care of watering it with irrigation for a period; then clearing the ground of weeds; then the harvest; then the threshing and winnowing; then the grinding; then the kneading; then the baking. So reflect upon the number of these acts that we have mentioned — and those we have not mentioned — and the number of persons engaged in them, and the number of implements required therein, of iron, wood, stone, and other materials. And behold the labors of the craftsmen in preparing the tools of plowing, grinding, and baking — the carpenter, the blacksmith, and others. And behold the blacksmith's need for iron, lead, and copper. And behold how God Most High created the mountains, the stones, and the minerals, and how He made the earth into adjacent, variegated plots. For if you investigated, you would know that a single loaf does not become round so as to be fit for your eating, O wretched one, unless more than a thousand craftsmen have worked upon it. Begin from the king who drives the clouds to send down water, to the final operations on the part of the angels, until the turn of office reaches the work of man. And when it becomes round, its requisition approaches seven thousand craftsmen — each craftsman being a root (aṣl) among the roots of the crafts by which the welfare of creation is perfected. Then reflect upon the multiplicity of man's labors in those implements — so much so that the needle, which is a tiny implement whose benefit is the sewing of the garment that wards off cold from you, does not complete its form from an iron suitable for a needle except after it passes through the hands of the needle-maker (ibriy) twenty-five times, and in each time a distinct operation is performed upon it. Had God not gathered together the lands and subjugated the servants, and had you been reduced to needing to make the sickle with which you harvest the wheat, for example, after its growth — your lifespan would have expired and you would have failed at it. Do you not see how God guided His servant — whom He created from a filthy drop of sperm — to perform these wondrous works and strange crafts? So behold the scissors, for example: they are two matching blades, one folding upon the other, and together they seize the object and cut it swiftly. Had God not unveiled, by His bounty and generosity, the way of making them to those before us, and had we been reduced to deriving the method by our own thought — then to extracting the iron from the stone, and to procuring the implements by which the scissors are made — the lifespan of any one of us, even were it the lifespan of Noah, and even were he given the most perfect intellects, would fall short of deriving the method for perfecting this single implement alone, let alone others. So glorified be He who afflicted the possessors of insight with blindness, and glorified be He who withheld this from the prophets, despite this elucidation! Now behold: if your town were emptied of the miller, for example, or of the blacksmith, or of the cupper (ḥajjām) — who is the meanest of laborers — or of the weaver, or of any one among the totality of craftsmen, what harm would befall you, and how would all your affairs be thrown into disarray? So glorified be He who subjugated some servants to others, until His will was executed thereby and His wisdom was completed thereby. And let us be brief in this stratum as well, for the purpose is to alert to the favors, not to exhaust them.

chapters.title_en: The Seventh Aspect: On the Rectification of the Rectifiers
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||||| الطرف السابع في إصلاح المصلحين

اعلم أن هؤلاء الصناع المصلحين للأطعمة وغيرها لو تفرقت آراؤهم وتنافرت
طباعهم تنافر طباع الوحش لتبددوا وتباعدوا ولم ينتفع بعضهم ببعض بل كانوا
كالوحوش لا يحويهم مكان واحد ولا يجمعهم غرض واحد فانظر كيف ألف الله تعالى
بين قلوبهم وسلط الأنس والمحبة عليهم {لو أنفقت ما في الأرض جميعا ما ألفت
بين قلوبهم ولكن الله ألف بينهم} فلأجل  الإلف وتعارف الأرواح اجتمعوا
وائتلفوا وبنوا المدن والبلاد ورتبوا المساكن والدور متقاربة متجاورة
ورتبوا الأسواق والخانات وسائر أصناف البقاع مما يطول إحصاؤه ثم هذه المحبة
تزول بأغراض يتزاحمون عليها ويتنافسون فيها ففي جبلة الإنسان الغيظ والحسد
والمنافسة وذلك مما يؤدي إلى التقاتل والتنافر فانظر كيف سلط الله تعالى
السلاطين وأمدهم بالقوة والعدة والأسباب وألقى رعبهم في قلوب الرعايا حتى
أذعنوا لهم طوعا وكرها وكيف هدى السلاطين إلى طريق إصلاح البلاد حتى رتبوا
أجزاء البلد كأنها أجزاء شخص واحد تتعاون على غرض واحد ينتفع البعض منها
بالبعض فرتبوا الرؤساء والقضاة والسجن وزعماء الأسواق واضطروا الخلق إلى
قانون العدل وألزموهم التساعد والتعاون حتى صار الحداد ينتفع بالقصاب
والخباز وسائر أهل البلد وكلهم ينتفعون بالحداد وصار الحجام ينتفع بالحراث
والحراث بالحجام وينتفع كل واحد بكل واحد بسبب ترتيبهم واجتماعهم وانضباطهم
تحت ترتيب السلطان وجمعه كما يتعاون جميع أعضاء البدن وينتفع بعضها ببعض
وانظر كيف بعث الأنبياء عليهم السلام حتى أصلحوا السلاطين المصلحين للرعايا
وعرفوهم قوانين الشرع في حفظ العدل بين الخلق وقوانين السياسة في ضبطهم
وكشفوا من أحكام الإمامة والسلطنة وأحكام الفقه
PageV04P119
ما اهتدوا به إلى إصلاح الدنيا فضلا عما أرشدوهم إليه من إصلاح الدين
وانظر كيف أصلح الله تعالى الأنبياء بالملائكة وكيف أصلح الملائكة بعضهم
ببعض إلى أن ينتهي إلى الملك المقرب الذى لاواسطه بينه وبين الله تعالى
فالخباز يخبز العجين والطحان يصلح الحب بالطحن والحراث يصلحه بالحصاد
والحداد يصلح آلات الحراثة والنجار يصلح آلات الحداد وكذا جميع أرباب
الصناعات المصلحين لآلات الأطعمة والسلطان يصلح الصناع والأنبياء يصلحون
العلماء الذين هم ورثتهم والعلماء يصلحون السلاطين والملائكة يصلحون
الأنبياء إلى أن ينتهي إلى حضرة الربوبية التي هي ينبوع كل نظام ومطلع كل
حسن وجمال ومنشأ كل ترتيب وتأليف وكل ذلك نعم من رب الأرباب ومسبب الأسباب
ولولا فضله وكرمه إذ قال تعالى {والذين جاهدوا فينا لنهدينهم سبلنا} لما
اهتدينا إلى هذه النبذة اليسيرة من نعم الله تعالى ولولا عزله إيانا عن أن
نطمح  بعين الطمع إلى الإحاطة بكنه نعمه لتشوفنا إلى طلب الإحاطة والاستقصاء
ولكنه تعالى عزلنا بحكم القهر والقدرة فقال تعالى {وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا
تحصوها} فإن تكلمنا فبإذنه انبسطنا وإن سكنا فبقهره انقبضنا إذ لا معطي لما
منع ولا مانع لما أعطى لأنا في كل لحظة من لحظات العمر قبل الموت نسمع بسمع
القلوب نداء الملك الجبار {لمن الملك اليوم لله الواحد القهار} فالحمد لله
الذي ميزنا عن الكفار وأسمعنا هذا النداء قبل انقضاء الأعمار

### |||||| الطرف الثامن في بيان نعمة الله تعالى في خلق الملائكة عليهم السلام
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ل-ف (alifa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intimate companionship, harmonious union, the drawing together of hearts in concord.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely-wrought bond of affection that transforms disparate souls into a cohesive social whole—a metaphysical grace (luṭf) rather than a natural accident.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in reference to the heart's inclination; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to the ordering of cities and markets, as the physical arrangement mirrors the spiritual reality.
- Root: ص-ل-ح (ṣaluḥa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To set right, to amend, to restore to a state of uprightness and proper function.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The rectification of that which is corrupt (fasād)—whether in souls, in social order, or in material instruments—by restoring it to its intended purpose (ghāyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the craftsman's repair of tools; metaphorically for the prophet's rectification of the ruler, and the ruler's rectification of the subjects—a graded chain of amendment.
- Root: ق-ه-ر (qahara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Overpowering dominion, subjugation by superior force.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divine attribute of al-Qahhār—the irresistible sovereignty that compels all creation into submission, whether willingly or unwillingly.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of physical compulsion; metaphorical when describing the awe (ruʿb) cast into hearts, which is a psychological subjugation.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Periodic Conditional Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The sentence «{وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها}» employs the conditional particle (in) with the apodosis in the jussive, establishing an irrefutable logical nexus between human incapacity and divine abundance.
chapters.translation:
Know that these craftsmen who rectify foods and other things—if their opinions were to diverge and their temperaments were to clash with the savagery of wild beasts, they would scatter and disperse, and none would benefit from another. Rather, they would be like beasts, not gathered in a single place nor united by a single purpose. So behold how Allah, the Exalted, brought harmony between their hearts and imposed familiarity and love upon them: {«Even if you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have brought their hearts together; but Allah brought them together»} (8:63). It is by virtue of this familiarity and the mutual recognition of spirits that they assembled and united, built cities and towns, arranged dwellings and houses in close proximity and adjacency, and organized markets, caravanserais, and all manner of places—the enumeration of which would be lengthy.

Then this love vanishes due to competing aims upon which they crowd and vie. For in the human constitution (jibillah) there is rage, envy, and rivalry—and these lead to fighting and estrangement. So behold how Allah, the Exalted, empowered the sultans, supplied them with force, weaponry, and means, and cast their awe (ruʿb) into the hearts of the subjects until they submitted to them willingly and unwillingly. And how He guided the sultans to the path of rectifying the lands, until they arranged the parts of the city as though they were the parts of a single person, cooperating toward a single purpose, each part benefiting from the other. Thus they appointed the chiefs, the judges, the prison, and the market wardens, and compelled the creation to the law of justice, obliging them to mutual aid and cooperation—until the blacksmith benefits from the butcher, the baker, and all the people of the town, and all of them benefit from the blacksmith. And the cupper benefits from the plowman, and the plowman from the cupper—each one benefits from every other, by virtue of their arrangement, their gathering, and their discipline under the order of the sultan and his uniting of them, just as all the limbs of the body cooperate and benefit one another.

And behold how Allah sent the prophets, peace be upon them, until they rectified the sultans who rectify the subjects, and taught them the laws of the Sacred Law (sharʿ) in preserving justice among the creation, and the laws of governance (siyāsah) in restraining them. And they disclosed from the rulings of the imamate and sovereignty, and the rulings of jurisprudence (fiqh)—[Page V04P119]—that by which they were guided to the rectification of this world, let alone what they directed them toward of the rectification of religion.

And behold how Allah, the Exalted, rectified the prophets by the angels, and how He rectified the angels by one another, until it terminates at the angel brought near (al-malāʾikah al-muqarrabūn) who has no intermediary between him and Allah, the Exalted. So the baker bakes the dough, and the miller rectifies the grain by grinding, and the plowman rectifies it by harvesting, and the blacksmith rectifies the plowman's tools, and the carpenter rectifies the blacksmith's tools. Likewise, all the masters of crafts who rectify the instruments of foods. And the sultan rectifies the craftsmen, and the prophets rectify the scholars who are their inheritors, and the scholars rectify the sultans, and the angels rectify the prophets—until it terminates at the Presence of Lordship (ḥaḍrat al-rubūbiyyah), which is the fountainhead of every order, the source of every beauty and comeliness, and the origin of every arrangement and composition. And all of this is a grace from the Lord of Lords (rabb al-arbāb) and the Causer of Causes (musabbib al-asbāb).

Were it not for His bounty and generosity—when He said, the Exalted: {«And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths»} (29:69)—we would not have been guided to this paltry portion of the graces of Allah, the Exalted. And were it not that He has debarred us from gazing with the eye of covetousness toward encompassing the inner reality (kunnh) of His graces, we would have yearned to seek encompassing and exhaustive knowledge. But He, the Exalted, has debarred us by the decree of overwhelming power (qahr) and might, saying: {«And if you count the graces of Allah, you could not enumerate them»} (14:34). If we speak, it is by His permission that we expand; and if we are silent, it is by His compulsion that we contract. For there is none who gives what He has withheld, and none who withholds what He has given—because in every moment of the moments of life before death, we hear with the ear of the hearts the call of the Mighty King: {«To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah, the One, the Irresistible»} (40:16). So praise be to Allah, who distinguished us from the disbelievers and made us hear this call before the expiration of our lifespans.

### |||||| The Eighth Aspect: On the Exposition of Allah's Grace in the Creation of the Angels, Peace Be Upon Them
