For God has elevated [His] good pleasure above the Gardens of Eden, just as He elevated His remembrance above the prayer, where He said: {«إن الصلاة تنهي عن الفحشاء والمنكر ولذكر الله أكبر»} [Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater] (Q. 29:45). So just as the vision of the Remembered One within the prayer is greater than the prayer itself, so too is the good pleasure of the Lord of the Garden higher than the Garden — nay, it is the ultimate object of pursuit for the inhabitants of the Gardens.

And in the ḥadīth: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, will manifest Himself to the believers and say: 'Ask of Me.' They will say: 'Your good pleasure.'" (1) Their asking for [His] good pleasure after [having been granted] the vision is the utmost degree of favor and distinction.

As for the servant's good pleasure [in God], we shall mention its reality [later]. As for God's good pleasure (riḍwān) with the servant, it carries another meaning, approximating what we have already mentioned concerning God's love (ḥubb) for the servant. It is not permissible to unveil its true reality, for the understandings of creatures fall short of grasping it, and none has the strength to comprehend it independently from himself.

In sum, there is no station above the vision of Him (al-naẓar ilayhi). For they asked only for [His] good pleasure because it is the cause of the perpetuity of the vision. It is as though they saw it as the ultimate of all ends and the farthest reach of all aspirations, having attained the bliss of the vision. When they were commanded to ask, they asked only for its perpetuity, knowing that good pleasure is the cause of the continued lifting of the veil.

And God, the Exalted, said: {«ولدينا مزيد»} [And with Us is more] (Q. 50:35). Some commentators said: The people of Paradise will be visited, at the time of the "increase" (mazīd), with three gifts from the Lord of the Worlds. The first is a gift from God, the Exalted, the like of which they do not possess in the Gardens — and that is His saying, the Exalted: {«فلا تعلم نفس ما أخفي لهم من قرة عين»} [No soul knows what comfort has been concealed for them] (Q. 32:17). The second is the salutation of peace upon them from their Lord, which surpasses the gift in excellence — and that is His saying, the Exalted: {«سلام قولا من رب رحيم»} [Peace — a word from a Merciful Lord] (Q. 36:58). The third is that God, the Exalted, says: "I am well pleased with you" — and that is more excellent than the gift and the salutation. And that is His saying, the Exalted: {«ورضوان من الله أكبر»} [And good pleasure from Allah is greater] — that is, greater than the bliss in which they are. This, then, is the excellence of God's good pleasure, and it is the fruit of the servant's good pleasure [in God].

As for the reports (akhbār): It is related that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked a group of his Companions: "What are you?" They said: "Believers." He said: "What is the sign of your faith?" They said: "We are patient in affliction, grateful in ease, and content with the places of the decree (riḍā bi-mawāqiʿ al-qaḍāʾ)." He said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah!" (2)

In another report, he said: "They are wise scholars who, by virtue of their understanding, nearly became prophets." (3) And in the report: "Blessed (ṭūbā) is he who is guided to Islam, whose provision is sufficient, and who is content with it." (4) And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever is content with God, the Exalted, for the little of provision, God, the Exalted, will be content with him for the little of deeds." (5)

And he also said: "When God, the Exalted, loves a servant, He tests him; if he is patient, He elects him (ijtabāhu); if he is content, He chooses him (iṣṭafāhu)."

And he also said: "On the Day of Resurrection, God, the Exalted, will cause wings to grow for a group of my community, and they will fly from their graves to the Gardens, roaming therein and delighting therein as they wish. The angels will say to them: 'Have you seen the Reckoning?' They will say: 'We have seen no reckoning.' The angels will say: 'Have you crossed the Ṣirāṭ?' They will say: 'We have seen no Ṣirāṭ.' The angels will say: 'Have you seen Hellfire?' They will say: 'We have seen nothing.' The angels will say: 'Of which community are you?' They will say: 'We are of the community of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him.' The angels will say: 'We adjure you by God — tell us what your deeds were in the world.' They will say: 'Two qualities were in us, and by the grace of God's mercy we have reached this station.' The angels will say: 'And what are they?' They will say: 'When we were alone, we were ashamed to disobey Him, and we were content with the little of what He apportioned to us.' The angels will say: 'This is rightfully yours.'" (1)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "O company of the poor! Give God the contentment of your hearts, and you will attain the reward of your poverty — otherwise, you will not." (2)

And in the reports concerning Moses, peace be upon him: The Children of Israel said to him: "Ask your Lord for us for a matter which, if we do it, He will be pleased with us." Moses, peace be upon him, said: "My God, I have heard what they said." He said: "O Moses, tell them: Let them be pleased with Me, and I will be pleased with them."

And this is corroborated by what is related from our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "Whoever loves to know his standing with God, the Mighty and Majestic, let him look at what standing God has in his own heart — for God, the Blessed and Exalted, places the servant with Himself according to where the servant places Him in himself." (3)

And the ḥadīth: "God said: 'I am Allah; there is no god but I. Whoever is not patient with My affliction...'" — al-Ṭabarānī related it in al-Kabīr, and Ibn Ḥibbān in al-Ḍuʿafāʾ, from the ḥadīth of Abī Hind al-Dārī, restricting it to his saying: "Whoever is not content with My decree and patient with My affliction, let him seek a lord other than Me" — and its chain is weak. (4)

And in the well-known report, God, the Exalted, says: "I created good and evil. Blessed is he whom I created for good and upon whose hands I caused good to flow. And woe to him whom I created for evil and upon whose hands I caused evil to flow. Woe, then woe, to him who says: 'Why?' and 'How?'" (5)

And in the earlier reports: A prophet among the prophets complained to God, the Mighty and Majestic, of hunger, poverty, and lice for ten years, and he was not answered with what he desired. Then God, the Exalted, revealed to him: "How long will you complain? Thus was your beginning with Me in the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb) before I created the heavens and the earth, and thus was it decreed for you from Me, and thus did I ordain upon you before I created the world. Do you wish Me to recreate the world for your sake? Or do you wish Me to change what I have decreed for you, so that what you love prevails over what I love, and what you will prevails over what I will? By My Might and My Majesty, if this [complaint] lingers in your breast once more, I will erase you from the register of prophethood."

And it is related that Adam, peace be upon him, had some of his young children climbing upon his body and descending — one of them would place his foot upon his ribs as upon a ladder, climbing to his head, while another descended upon his ribs likewise — and he remained bowed to the ground, not speaking nor raising his head. One of his sons said to him: "O father, do you not see what this one does to you? Would you not forbid him from this?" He said: "O my son, I have seen what you have not seen, and I have known what you have not known. I made a single movement, and I was cast down from the Abode of Honor to the Abode of Humiliation, and from the Abode of Bliss to the Abode of Misery. I fear that if I make another movement, something will befall me that I do not know."

And Anas ibn Mālik, may God be pleased with him, said: "I served the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, for ten years. He never said to me regarding anything I did: 'Why did you do it?' nor regarding anything I did not do: 'Why did you not do it?' Nor did he say of anything: 'Would that it had not been,' nor of anything absent: 'Would that it had been.' And when one of his family disputed with me, he would say: 'Leave him — if anything had been decreed, it would have been.'" (1)

And it is related that God, the Exalted, revealed to David, peace be upon him: "O David, you will [something] and I will [something], and only what I will comes to be. If you surrender to what I will, I will suffice you in what you will. But if you do not surrender to what I will, I will weary you in what you will — and still only what I will comes to be."

As for the sayings of the Salaf (āthār): Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "The first to be summoned to Paradise on the Day of Resurrection are those who praise God, the Exalted, in every state."

And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "No joy remains for me except in the places of the decree (mawāqiʿ al-qaḍāʾ)." And it was said to him: "What do you desire?" He said: "What God decrees."

And Maymūn ibn Mahrān said: "Whoever is not content with the decree — there is no cure for his foolishness."

And al-Fuḍayl said: "If you are not patient with God's ordainment (taqdīr), you will not be patient with your own ordainment."

And ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād said: "The matter is not in eating barley bread with vinegar, nor in wearing wool and hair-cloth — rather, the matter is in contentment with God, the Mighty and Majestic."

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: "That I should be a live ember that burns what it burns and leaves what it leaves is dearer to me than saying of something that happened: 'Would that it had not been,' or of something that did not happen: 'Would that it had been.'"

And a man looked at a sore on the leg of Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ and said: "I pity you for this sore." He said: "I have been thanking it ever since it appeared, for it did not appear in my eye."

And it is related in the Israʾīliyyāt that a worshipper worshipped God for a long time, and it was shown to him in a dream: "So-and-so, the shepherdess, is your companion in Paradise." He inquired about her until he found her, and he hosted himself with her for three days to observe her deeds. He would spend the night standing [in prayer] while she slept, and he would fast the day while she broke her fast. He said: "Do you have no deed other than what I have seen?" She said: "By God, it is nothing but what you have seen — I know nothing else." He kept saying: "Recall [more]," until she said: "One single quality — when I am in hardship, I do not wish to be in ease; when I am in illness, I do not wish to be in health; and when I am in the sun, I do not wish to be in the shade." The worshipper placed his hand upon his head and said: "Is this a [mere] quality? By God, this is a mighty quality, which the worshippers are incapable of [attaining]."

And it is related from some of the Salaf: "When God, the Exalted, decrees a decree in heaven, He loves that the people of the earth be content with His decree."

And Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "The summit of faith is patience under the judgment and contentment with the decree."

And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "I care not upon which state I rise and retire — whether of hardship or of ease."

And al-Thawrī said one day to Rābiʿah: "O God, be pleased with me." She said: "Are you not ashamed before God to ask Him for His good pleasure while you yourself are not pleased with Him?" He said: "I seek God's forgiveness." Then Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān al-Ḍubʿī said: "So when is the servant pleased with God, the Exalted?" She said: "When his joy at affliction is like his joy at blessing."

And al-Fuḍayl used to say: "When deprivation and giving become equal in his sight, then he has been pleased with God, the Exalted."

And Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said: Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "God, the Mighty and Majestic, out of His generosity, has been pleased from His servants with what servants are pleased with from their masters." I said: "How is that?" He said: "Is not the servant's aim from creatures that his master be pleased with him?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then God's love from His servants is that they be pleased with Him."

And Sahl said: "The share of servants from certainty (yaqīn) is according to their share of contentment (riḍā), and their share of contentment is according to their living with God, the Mighty and Majestic."

And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed God, the Mighty and Majestic, by His wisdom and majesty, has placed spirit and joy in contentment and certainty, and has placed grief and sorrow in doubt and displeasure." (1)

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Reality of Contentment (Riḍā) and Its Conceptualization in What Opposes Caprice (Hawa)
chapters.arabic_text: ### |||| بيان حقيقة الرضا وتصوره فيما يخالف الهوى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ض-ي (r-ḍ-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of being pleased, satisfied, or consenting; opposite of anger (ghaḍab) and displeasure (sakhaṭ). Denotes a state of the heart’s acquiescence to what befalls it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, riḍā is the soul’s tranquil acceptance of divine decree (qaḍāʾ) and its cessation of resistance—an inward submission that aligns with the will of God, not mere outward compliance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense: satisfaction with a given state. Metaphorical (majāz) sense: the heart’s “sweetening” of bitter trials, as when one is pleased with what is inherently painful—a figurative extension of consent to the unseen wisdom of God.
- Root: ه-و-ى (h-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of falling, plunging, or inclination downward; also denotes desire or caprice that drags the soul toward base appetites.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic and Kalām discourse, hawā is the unregulated inclination of the self (nafs) that opposes revealed truth and rational guidance—often condemned as a false deity (cf. {أَفَرَأَيْتَ مَنِ اتَّخَذَ إِلَٰهَهُ هَوَاهُ}).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical falling or descent. Metaphorical: the soul’s gravitational pull toward passion, used rhetorically to contrast with the upward ascent of reason and obedience.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase “fīmā yukhālifu al-hawā” (in what opposes caprice) is a prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr) attached to the verbal noun “taṣawwuruhu” (its conceptualization), governing the scope of the exposition. The definite article on “al-hawā” marks generic reference, indicating all forms of caprice, not a particular instance.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the reality of contentment (riḍā) and how it is to be conceived in matters that run contrary to caprice (hawā). Know that contentment is not the mere absence of aversion, nor is it a passive resignation of the tongue; rather, it is a settled state of the heart whereby it welcomes the decree of God—whether pleasing or painful—with an inward serenity, such that the soul finds no rancor against what has been ordained, and its agitation is stilled. For the essence of riḍā lies in the heart’s harmony with the divine will, even when the object of that will clashes with the appetites of the self. Thus, when the believer confronts that which opposes his inclination, he does not recoil in resentment, but perceives therein the hidden wisdom of his Lord, and his heart acquiesces as naturally as the thirsty soul rejoices in water. This is the true conceptualization of riḍā: not the extinction of desire, but its subordination to the command of God, so that what was bitter becomes sweet, and what was repugnant becomes beloved, through the light of certainty (yaqīn) that illuminates the heart.

chapters.title_en: On the Reality of Contentment (Riḍā) with What Contradicts Desire, and Its Two Aspects
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن من قال ليس فيما يخالف الهوى وأنواع البلاء إلا الصبر فأما الرضا
فلا يتصور فإنما أتى من ناحية إنكار المحبة فأما إذا ثبت تصور الحب لله
تعالى واستغراق الهم به فلا يخفى أن الحب يورث الرضا بأفعال الحبيب ويكون
ذلك من وجهين
{أحدهما} أن يبطل الإحساس بالألم حتى يجري عليه المؤلم ولا يحس وتصيبه
جراحة ولا يدرك ألمها
ومثاله الرجل المحارب فإنه في حال غضبه أو في حال خوفه قد تصيبه جراحة
وهو لا يحس بألم ذلك لشغل قلبه
بل الذي يحجم أو يحلق رأسه بحديدة كآلة يتألم به فإن كان مشغول القلب
بمهم من مهماته فرغ المزين والحجام وهو لا يشعر به
وكل ذلك لأن القلب إذا صار مستغرقا بأمر من الأمور مستوفى به لم يدرك ما
عداه فكذلك العاشق المستغرق الهم بمشاهدة معشوقه أو بحبه قد يصيبه ما كان
يتألم به أو يغتم له لولا عشقه ثم لا يدرك غمه وألمه لفرط استيلاء الحب على
قلبه
هذا إذا أصابه من غير حبيبه فكيف إذا أصابه من حبيبه وشغل القلب بالحب
والعشق من أعظم الشواغل وإذا تصور هذا في ألم يسير بسبب حب خفيف تصور في
الألم العظيم بالحب العظيم فإن الحب أيضا يتصور تضاعفه في القوة كما يتصور
تضاعف الألم وكما يقوى حب الصور الجميلة المدركة بحاسة البصر فكذا يقوى حب
الصور الجميلة الباطنة المدركة بنور البصيرة وجمال حضرة الربوبية وجلالها
لا يقاس به جمال ولا جلال فمن ينكشف له شيء  منه فقد يبهره بحث يدهش ويغشى
عليه فلا يحس مما يجري عليه
فقد روي أن امرأة فتح الموصلي عثرت فانقطع ظفرها فضحكت فقيل لها أما
تجدين الوجع فقالت إن لذة ثوابه أزالت عن قلبي مرارة وجعه
وكان سهل رحمه الله تعالى به علة يعالج غيره منها ولا يعالج نفسه فقيل له
في ذلك فقال يا دوست ضرب الحبيب لا يوجع
وأما الوجه الثاني فهو أن يحس به ويدرك ألمه ولكن يكون راضيا به بل راغبا
فيه مريدا له أعني بعقله وإن كان كارها بطبعه كالذي يلتمس من الفصاد الفصد
والحجامة فإنه يدرك ألم ذلك إلا انه راض به وراغب فيه ومتقلد من الفصاد به
منة بفعله فهذا حال الراضي بما يجري عليه من الألم
وكذلك كل من يسافر في طلب الربح يدرك مشقة السفر ولكن حبه لثمرة سفره طيب
عنده مشقة السفر وجعله راضيا بها
ومهما أصابه بلية من الله تعالى وكان له يقين بأن ثوابه الذي ادخر له فوق
ما فاته رضي به ورغب فيه وأحبه وشكر الله عليه هذا إن كان PageV04P347
يلاحظ الثواب والإحسان الذي يجازى به عليه ويجوز أن يغلب الحب بحيث يكون
حظ المحب في مراد محبوبه ورضاء لا لمعنى آخر وراءه فيكون مراد حبيبه ورضاه
محبوبا عنده ومطلوبا وكل ذلك موجود في المشاهدات في حب الخلق وقد تواصفها
المتواصفون في نظمهم ونثرهم ولا معنى له إلا ملاحظة جمال الصورة الظاهرة
بالبصر فإن نظر إلى الجمال فما هو إلا جلد ولحم ودم مشحون بالأقذار
والأخباث بدايته من نطفة مذرة ونهايته جيفة قذرة وهو فيما بين ذلك يحمل
العذرة
وإن نظر إلى المدرك للجمال فهي العين الخسيسة التي تغلط فيما ترى كبيرا
فترى الصغير كبيرا والكبير صغيرا والبعيد قريبا والقبيح جميلا فإذا تصور
استيلاء هذا الحب فمن أين يستحيل ذلك في حب الجمال الأزلي الأبدي الذي لا
منتهى لكماله المدرك بعين البصيرة التي لا يعتريها الغلط ولا يدور بها
الموت بل تبقى بعد الموت حية عند الله  فرحة برزق الله تعالى مستفيدة بالموت
مزيد تنبيه واستكشاف فهذا أمر واضح من حيث النظر بعين الاعتبار ويشهد لذلك
الوجود وحكايات أحوال المحبين وأقوالهم
فقد قال شقيق البلخي من يرى ثواب الشدة لا يشتهي المخرج منها وقال الجنيد
سألت سريا السقطي هل يجد المحب ألم البلاء قال لا قلت وإن ضرب بالسيف قال
نعم وإن ضرب بالسيف سبعين ضربة ضربة على ضربة
وقال بعضهم أحببت كل شيء يحبه حتى لو أحب النار أحببت دخول النار وقال
بشر بن الحارث مررت برجل وقد ضرب ألف سوط في شرقية بغداد ولم يتكلم ثم حمل
إلى الحبس فتبعته فقلت له لم ضربت فقال لأني عاشق فقلت له ولم سكت قال لأن
معشوقي كان بحذائي ينظر إلي فقلت فلو نظرت إلى المعشوق الأكبر قال فزعق
زعقة خر ميتا
وقال يحي بن معاذ الرازي رحمه الله تعالى إذا نظر أهل الجنة إلى الله
تعالى ذهبت عيونهم في قلوبهم من لذة النظر إلى الله تعالى ثمانمائة سنة لا
ترجع إليهم فما ظنك بقلوب وقعت بين جماله وجلاله إذا لاحظت جلاله هابت وإذا
لاحظت جماله تاهت وقال بشر قصدت عبادان في بدايتي فإذا برجل أعمى مجذوم
مجنون قد صرع والنمل يأكل لحمه فرفعت رأسه فوضعته في حجري وأنا أردد الكلام
فلما أفاق قال من هذا الفضولي الذي يدخل بيني وبين ربي لو قطعني إربا إربا
ما ازددت له إلا حبا قال بشر فما رأيت بعد ذلك نقمة بين عبد وبين ربه
فأنكرتها
وقال أبو عمرو محمد بن الأشعث إن أهل مصر مكثوا أربعة أشهر لم يكن لهم
غذاء إلا النظر إلى وجه يوسف الصديق عليه السلام كانوا إذا جاعوا نظروا إلى
وجهه فشغلهم جماله عن الإحساس بألم الجوع بل في القرآن ما هو أبلغ من ذلك
وهو قطع النسوة أيديهن لاستهتارهن بملاحظة جماله حتى ما أحسسن بذلك
وقال سعيد بن يحيى رأيت بالبصرة في خان عطاء بن مسلم شابا وفي يده مدية
وهو ينادي بأعلى صوته والناس  حوله وهو يقول
يوم الفراق من القيامة أطول ... والموت من ألم التفرق أجمل
قالوا الرحيل فقلت لست براحل ... لكن مهجتي التي تترحل
ثم بقر بالمدية بطنه وخر ميتا فسألت عنه وعن أمره فقيل لي إنه كان يهوى
فتى لبعض الملوك حجب عنه يوما واحدا
ويروى أن يونس عليه السلام قال لجبريل دلني على أعبد أهل الأرض فدله على
رجل قد قطع الجذام يديه ورجليه وذهب ببصره فسمعه وهو يقول إلهي متعتني بهما
ما شئت أنت وسلبتني ما شئت أنت وأبقيت لي فيك الأمل يا بر يا وصول
ويروى عن عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنه اشتكى له ابن فاشتد
PageV04P348
وجده عليه حتى قال بعض القوم لقد خشينا على هذا الشيخ إن حدث بهذا الغلام
حدث فمات الغلام فخرج ابن عمر في جنازته وما رجل أشد سرورا أبدا منه فقيل
له في ذلك فقال ابن عمر إنما كان حزني رحمة له فلما وقع أمر الله رضينا به
وقال مسروق كان رجل بالبادية له كلب وحمار وديك فالديك يوقظهم للصلاة
والحمار ينقلون عليه الماء ويحمل لهم خباءهم والكلب يحرسهم قال فجاء الثعلب
فأخذ الديك فحزنوا له وكان الرجل صالحا فقال عسى أن يكون خيرا ثم جاء ذئب
فخرق بطن الحمار فقتله فحزنوا عليه فقال الرجل عسى أن يكون خيرا ثم أصيب
الكلب بعد ذلك فقال عسى أن يكون خيرا ثم أصبحوا ذات يوم فنظروا فإذا قد سبي
من حولهم وبقوا هم قال وإنما أخذوا أولئك لما كان عندهم من أصوات الكلاب
والحمير والديكة فكانت الخيرة لهؤلاء في هلاك هذه الحيوانات كما قدره الله
تعالى
فإذن من عرف خفي لطف الله تعالى رضي بفعله على كل حال
ويروى أن عيسى عليه السلام مر برجل أعمى أبرص مقعد مضروب الجنبين بفالج
وقد تناثر لحمه من الجذام وهو يقول الحمد لله الذي عافاني مما ابتلي به
كثيرا من خلقه فقال له عيسى يا هذا أي شيء من البلاء أراه مصروفا عنك فقال
يا روح الله أنا خير ممن لم يجعل الله في قلبه ما جعل في قلبي من معرفته
فقال له صدقت هات يدك فناوله يده فإذا هو أحسن الناس وجها وأفضلهم هيئة وقد
أذهب الله عنه ما كان به فصحب عيسى عليه السلام وتعبد معه
وقطع عروة بن الزبير رجله من ركبته من أكلة خرجت بها ثم قال الحمد لله
الذي أخذ مني واحدة وليت لئن كنت أخذت لقد أبقيت ولئن كنت ابتليت لقد عافيت
ثم لم يدع ورده تلك الليلة
وكان ابن مسعود يقول الفقر والغنى مطيبتان ما أبالي أيتهما ركبت إن كان
الفقر فإن فيه الصبر وإن كان الغنى فإن فيه البذل
وقال أبو سليمان الداراني قلت قد نلت من كل مقام حالا إلا الرضا فمالى
منه إلا مشام الريح وعلى ذلك لو أدخل الخلائق كلهم الجنة وأدخلني النار كنت
بذلك راضيا
وقيل لعارف آخر هل نلت غاية الرضا عنه فقال أما الغاية فلا ولكن مقام
الرضا قد نلته لو جعلني جسرا على جهنم يعبر الخلائق علي إلى الجنة ثم ملأ
بي جهنم تحلة لقسمه وبدلا من خليقته لأحببت ذلك من حكمه ورضيت به من قسمه
وهذا كلام من علم أن الحب قد استغرق همه حتى منعه الإحساس بألم النار فإن
بقي إحساس فيغمره ما يحصل من لذته في استشعاره حصول رضا محبوبه بإلقائه
إياه في النار
واستيلاء هذه الحالة غير محال في نفسه وإن كان بعيدا من أحوالنا الضعيفة
ولكن لا ينبغي أن يستنكر الضعيف المحروم أحوال الأقوياء ويظن أن ما هو عاجز
عنه يعجز عنه الأولياء
وقال الروذباري قلت لأبي عبد الله بن الجلاء الدمشقي قول فلان وددت أن
جسدي قرض بالمقاريض وأن هذا الخلق أطاعوه ما معناه فقال يا هذا إن كان هذا
من طريق التعظيم والإجلال فلا أعرف وإن كان هذا من طريق الإشفاق والنصح
للخلق فأعرف قال ثم غشي عليه
وقد كان عمران بن الحصين قد استسقى بطنه فبقي ملقى على ظهره ثلاثين سنة
لا يقوم ولا يقعد قد نقب له في سرير من جريد كان عليه موضع لقضاء حاجته
فدخل عليه مطرف وأخوه العلاء فجعل يبكي لما يراه من حاله فقال لم تبكي قال
لأني أراك على هذه الحالة العظيمة قال لا تبك فإن أحبه إلى الله تعالى أحبه
إلي ثم قال أحدثك شيئا لعل الله أن ينفعك به واكتم علي حتى أموت إن
الملائكة تزورني فآنس بها وتسلم علي فأسمع تسليمها فأعلم بذلك أن هذا
البلاء ليس بعقوبة إذ هو سبب هذه النعمة الجسيمة فمن يشاهد هذا في بلائه
كيف لا يكون راضيا به قال ودخلنا على سوبد بن متعبه نعوده فرأيناه ثوبا
ملقى فما ظننا أن تحته شيئا حتى كشف فقالت له امرأته أهلي
PageV04P349
فداؤك ما نطعمك
ما نسقيك فقال طالت الضجعة ودبرت الحراقيف وأصبحت نضوا لا أطعم طعاما ولا
أسيغ شرابا منذ كذا فذكر أياما وما يسرني أني نقصت من هذا قلامة ظفر ولما
قدم سعد بن أبي وقاص إلى مكة وقد كان كف بصره جاءه الناس يهرعون إليه كل
واحد يسأله أن يدعو له فيدعو لهذا ولهذا وكان مجاب الدعوة قاله عبد الله بن
السائب فأتيته وأنا غلام فتعرفت إليه فعرفني وقال أنت قارئ أهل مكة قلت نعم
فذكر قصة قال في آخرها فقلت له يا عم أنت تدعو للناس فلو دعوت لنفسك فرد
الله عليك بصرك فتبسم وقال يا بني قضاء الله سبحانه عندي أحسن من بصري وضاع
لبعض الصوفية ولد صغير ثلاثة أيام لم يعرف له خبر فقيل له لو سألت الله
تعالى أن يرده عليك فقال اعتراضي عليه فيما قضي أشد علي من ذهاب ولدي
وعن بعض العباد أنه قال إني أذنبت ذنبا عظيما فأنا أبكي عليه منذ ستين
سنة وكان قد اجتهد في العبادة لأجل التوبة من الذنب فقيل له وما هو قال قلت
مرة لشيء كان ليته لم يكن
وقال بعض السلف لو قرض جسمي بالمقاريض لكان أحب إلي من أن أقول لشيءقضاه
الله  تعالى سبحانه ليته لم يقضه
وقيل لعبد الواحد بن زيد ههنا رجل قد تعبد خمسين سنة فقصده فقال له يا
حبيبي أخبرني عنك هل قنعت به قال لا قال أنست به قال لا قال فهل رضيت عنه
قال لا قال فإنما مزيدك منه الصوم والصلاة قال نعم قال لولا أني أستحيي منك
لأخبرتك بأن معاملتك خمسين سنة مدخولة ومعناه أنك لم يفتح لك باب القلب
فتترقى إلى درجات القرب بأعمال القلب وإنما أنت تعد في طبقات أصحاب اليمين
لأن مزيدك منه في أعمال الجوارح التى هى مزيد أهل العموم
ودخل جماعة من الناس على الشبلي رحمه الله تعالى في مارستان قد حبس فيه
وقد جمع بين يديه حجارة فقال من أنتم فقالوا محبوك فأقبل عليهم يرميهم
بالحجارة فتهاربوا فقال ما بالكم ادعيتم محبتي إن صدقتم فاصبروا على بلائي
وللشبلي رحمه الله تعالى
إن المحبة للرحمن أسكرني ... وهل رأيت محبا غير سكران
وقال بعض عباد أهل الشام كلكم يلقى الله عز وجل مصدقا ولعله قد كذبه وذلك
أن أحدكم لو كان له إصبع من ذهب ظل يشير بها ولو كان بها شلل ظل يواريها
يعني بذلك أن الذهب مذموم عند الله والناس يتفاخرون به والبلاء زينة أهل
الآخرة وهم يستنكفون منه
وقيل إنه وقع الحريق في السوق فقيل للسري احترق السوق وما احترق دكانك
فقال الحمد لله ثم قال كيف قلت الحمد لله على سلامتي دون المسلمين فتاب من
التجارة وترك الحانوت بقية عمره توبة واستغفارا من قوله الحمد لله
فإذا تأملت هذه الحكايات عرفت قطعا أن الرضا بما يخالف الهوى ليس مستحيلا
بل هو مقام عظيم من مقامات أهل الدين
ومهما كان ذلك ممكنا في حب الخلق وحظوظهم كان ممكنا في حق حب الله تعالى
وحظوظ الآخرة قطعا
وإمكانه من وجهين {أحدهما} الرضا بالألم لما يتوقع من الثواب الموجود
كالرضا بالفصد والحجامة وشرب الدواء انتظارا للشفاء
والثاني الرضا به لا لحظ وراءه بل لكونه مراد المحبوب ورضا له فقد يغلب
الحب بحيث ينغمر مراد المحب في مراد المحبوب فيكون ألذ الأشياء عنده سرور
قلب محبوبه ورضاه ونفوذ إرادته ولو في هلاك روحه كما قيل
فما لجرح إذا أرضاكم ألم ...
وهذا ممكن مع الإحساس بالألم وقد يستولي الحب بحيث يدهش عن إدراك الألم
فالقياس والتجربة والمشاهدة
PageV04P350
دالة على وجوده فلا ينبغي أن ينكره من فقده من نفسه لأنه إنما فقده لفقد
سببه وهو فرط حبه ومن لم يذق طعم الحب لم يعرف عجائبه فللمحبين عجائب أعظم
مما وصفناه
وقد روى عن عمرو بن الحارث الرافعي قال كنت في مجلس بالرقة عند صديق لي
وكان معنا فتى يتعشق جارية مغنية وكانت معنا في المجلس فضربت بالقضيب وغنت
علامة ذل الهوى ... على العاشقين البكا
ولا سيما عاشق ... إذا لم يجد مشتكى
فقال لها الفتى أحسنت والله يا سيدتي أفتأذنين لي أن أموت فقالت مت راشدا
قال فوضع رأسه على الوسادة وأطبق فمه وغمض عينيه فحركناه فإذا هو ميت
وقال الجنيد رأيت رجلا متعلقا بكم صبي وهو يتضرع إليه ويظهر له المحبة
فالتفت إليه الصبي وقال له إلى متى ذا النفاق الذي تظهر لي فقال قد علم
الله أني صادق فيما أورده حتى لو قلت لي مت لمت فقال إن كنت صادقا فمت قال
فتنحى الرجل وغمض عينيه فوجد ميتا وقال سمنون المحب كان في جيراننا رجل وله
جارية يحبها غاية الحب فاعتلت الجارية فجلس الرجل ليصلح لها حيسا فبينا هو
يحرك القدر إذ قالت الجارية آه قال فدهش الرجل وسقطت الملعقة من يده وجعل
يحرك ما في القدر بيده حتى سقطت أصابعه فقالت الجارية ما هذا قال هذا مكان
قولك آه
وحكى عن محمد ابن عبد الله البغدادي قال رأيت بالبصرة شابا على سطح مرتفع
وقد أشرف على الناس وهو يقول
من مات عشقا فليمت هكذا ... لا خير في عشق بلا موت
ثم رمى بنفسه إلى الأرض فحملوه ميتا
فهذا وأمثاله قد يصدق به في حب المخلوق والتصديق به في حب الخالق أولى
لأن البصيرة الباطنة أصدق من البصر الظاهر وجمال الحضرة الربانية أو في من
كل جمال بل كل جمال في العالم فهو حسنة من حسنات ذلك الجمال
نعم الذي فقد البصر ينكر جمال الصور والذي فقد السمع ينكر لذة الألحان
والنغمات الموزونة فالذي فقد القلب لا بد وأن ينكر أيضا هذه اللذات التي
لامظنة لها سوى القلب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ض-و (r-ḍ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be pleased, satisfied, contented" — the opposite of sakhaṭ (displeasure). It denotes a state of the heart's acquiescence to what befalls it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, riḍā is the soul's tranquil acceptance of divine decree (qaḍāʾ), rooted in the recognition that God's choice for the servant is superior to the servant's own choice for himself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage pertains to the heart's settled satisfaction; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to verbal expressions of praise (ḥamd) even when inner turmoil remains — a distinction the author implicitly refines here.
- Root: ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Love" — the inclination of the heart toward what it perceives as agreeable; its intensity is termed ʿishq (passionate love).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Love of God is the soul's yearning for proximity to Him, generated by knowledge (maʿrifah) of His perfections; it is the root from which riḍā necessarily branches.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal love involves sensory perception; metaphorical love of the unseen (al-ghayb) is higher, since its object is the eternal Beauty perceived by the inner eye (baṣīrah).
- Root: أ-ل-م (ʾ-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "Pain, suffering" — a sensory or psychic distress.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Pain is a divine trial (balāʾ) that tests the servant's love; its perception can be overridden by the heart's engrossment (istighrāq) in a beloved object.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal pain is bodily sensation; metaphorical usage extends to the "pain" of separation (furqah) which lovers describe as sweeter than death.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs "law" (if) and "fa-in" (for if) to structure hypothetical proofs, and "illā" (except) to delimit the scope of denial, requiring precise parsing to preserve the logical force of each argument.
chapters.translation:
Know that whoever says that in what contradicts desire and the varieties of affliction there is nothing but patience (ṣabr) — and that as for contentment (riḍā), it is inconceivable — has only erred from the quarter of denying love (maḥabbah). But once the conceivability of love for God — exalted is He — and the engrossment of one's whole concern in Him is established, it is not hidden that love necessarily engenders contentment with the acts of the Beloved. And this occurs from two aspects:

{The first} is that the perception of pain is annihilated, so that the painful thing passes over him and he does not feel it; a wound strikes him and he does not perceive its pain.

Its example is the warrior: in the state of his anger or in the state of his fear, a wound may strike him and he does not feel its pain, because of the occupation of his heart.

Rather, even the one who is cupped or who has his head shaved with an iron instrument as a tool — he feels pain from it; but if his heart is occupied with some important matter of his concerns, the barber and the cupper finish while he is unaware of it.

All of that is because when the heart becomes engrossed in one of the affairs, fully taken up by it, it does not perceive what is other than it. Likewise, the passionate lover whose concern is engrossed in beholding his beloved, or in his love of him — there may strike him what he would have felt pain from, or grieved over, were it not for his passion; then he does not perceive his grief and pain, due to the overwhelming dominance of love over his heart.

This is when it strikes him from other than his beloved. How then, when it strikes him from his beloved himself? And the occupation of the heart with love and passion is among the greatest of occupations. If this is conceivable in a slight pain due to a light love, it is conceivable in a great pain due to a great love. For love, too, is conceivable as multiplying in strength, just as pain multiplies. And just as the love of beautiful forms perceived by the sense of sight grows strong, so too does the love of beautiful inner forms perceived by the light of insight (nūr al-baṣīrah) grow strong. And the Beauty of the Presence of Lordship and its Majesty — no beauty or majesty can be compared to it. Whoever has something of it unveiled to him, it may overwhelm him with a bewilderment that stupefies him, and he swoons, and he does not feel what passes over him.

It has been related that a woman of the family of Fath al-Mawsilī stumbled, and her fingernail was torn off, and she laughed. It was said to her: "Do you not feel the pain?" She said: "The delight of its reward has removed from my heart the bitterness of its pain."

And Sahl — may God have mercy on him — had an ailment, and he would treat others for it but would not treat himself. It was said to him about that, and he said: "O friend, the blow of the Beloved does not hurt."

As for the second aspect: he feels it and perceives its pain, but he is content with it — rather, desirous of it, willing it — I mean, with his intellect, even though he is averse to it by his nature. Like the one who seeks phlebotomy and cupping from the phlebotomist: he perceives the pain of that, yet he is content with it, desirous of it, and regards the phlebotomist with gratitude for his act. Such is the state of the one content with what passes over him of pain.

Likewise, whoever travels seeking profit perceives the hardship of travel, but his love for the fruit of his journey makes the hardship of travel pleasant to him and renders him content with it.

And whenever an affliction befalls him from God — exalted is He — and he has certainty that the reward which has been stored up for him is greater than what has escaped him, he is content with it, desires it, loves it, and thanks God for it. This is if he observes the reward and the beneficence with which he will be recompensed for it. And it is possible that love should dominate to the point that the lover's portion is in the will of his Beloved and His contentment, not for any other meaning beyond that — so that the will of his Beloved and His contentment become beloved to him and sought after. All of this exists in observable reality in the love of creatures, and those who describe it have described it in their poetry and prose. And there is no meaning to it except the observation of the beauty of the outward form by the eye. For if one looks at the beauty, it is nothing but skin, flesh, and blood packed with filth and impurities — its beginning is a drop of despised fluid, its end a putrid corpse, and in between it carries excrement.

And if one looks at the perceiver of beauty, it is the base eye that errs in what it sees — seeing the small as large, the large as small, the distant as near, and the ugly as beautiful. So if the dominance of this love is conceivable, how could that be impossible in the love of the eternal, everlasting Beauty, which has no limit to its perfection, perceived by the eye of insight (ʿayn al-baṣīrah) which is not subject to error and around which death does not revolve — rather, it remains after death, alive with God, rejoicing in God's provision, gaining increase through death?

A further clarification and uncovering: This matter is clear from the standpoint of consideration with the eye of reflection, and existence bears witness to it, along with the stories of the states of lovers and their sayings.

Shuqayq al-Balkhī said: "Whoever sees the reward of severity does not crave an exit from it." And al-Junayd said: "I asked Sari al-Saqatī: 'Does the lover feel the pain of affliction?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'Even if he is struck with the sword?' He said: 'Yes, even if he is struck with the sword seventy blows, blow upon blow.'"

And one of them said: "I loved everything he loves, so much so that if he loved the Fire, I would love entering the Fire." And Bishr ibn al-Hārith said: "I passed by a man who had been struck a thousand lashes in eastern Baghdad, and he did not speak. Then he was carried to prison, and I followed him and said to him: 'Why were you struck?' He said: 'Because I am a lover.' I said to him: 'And why did you remain silent?' He said: 'Because my beloved was opposite me, looking at me.' I said: 'Then what if you looked at the Greater Beloved?' He cried out a cry and fell dead."

And Yahyā ibn Muʿādh al-Rāzī — may God have mercy on him — said: "When the people of Paradise look upon God — exalted is He — their eyes will be lost in their hearts from the delight of looking upon God for eight hundred years, not returning to them. So what do you think of hearts that have fallen between His Beauty and His Majesty? When they observe His Majesty they are awed, and when they observe His Beauty they are enraptured."

And Bishr said: "I set out for ʿAbbādān in my early days, and there was a blind man, leprous, mad, struck with epilepsy, and ants were eating his flesh. I lifted his head and placed it in my lap, repeating words. When he regained consciousness, he said: 'Who is this meddler who comes between me and my Lord? If He cut me to pieces, piece by piece, I would only increase in love for Him.'" Bishr said: "After that I never saw a punishment between a servant and his Lord that I denied."

And Abu ʿAmr Muhammad ibn al-Ashʿath said: "The people of Egypt remained for four months with no nourishment except looking upon the face of Yūsuf the Truthful — peace be upon him. When they were hungry, they would look upon his face, and his beauty occupied them from perceiving the pain of hunger." Rather, in the Qurʾān there is what is more eloquent than that — namely, the cutting of the women's hands due to their being utterly captivated by observing his beauty, until they did not feel it. {«فَلَمَّا سَمِعْنَ مَكْرَهُنَّ أَرْسَلْنَ إِلَيْهِنَّ وَأَعْتَدْنَ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَأً وَآتَتْ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُنَّ سِكِّينًا فَقَالَتِ اخْرُجْ عَلَيْهِنَّ فَلَمَّا رَأَيْنَهُ أَكْبَرْنَهُ وَقَطَّعْنَ أَيْدِيَهُنَّ»} (Yūsuf 12:31).

And Saʿīd ibn Yahyā said: "I saw in Basra, in the caravanserai of ʿAṭāʾ ibn Muslim, a young man with a dagger in his hand, crying out at the top of his voice while people surrounded him, saying:

'The day of parting is longer than the Resurrection, / And death is more beautiful than the pain of separation.'
'They said: Depart. I said: I am not departing, / But rather my soul is what departs.'

Then he ripped open his belly with the dagger and fell dead. I asked about him and his affair, and it was said to me: 'He was enamored of a youth belonging to one of the kings, who was veiled from him for a single day.'"

And it is related that Yūnus — peace be upon him — said to Gabriel: "Show me the most devout servant on earth." So he showed him a man whose leprosy had cut off his hands and feet and taken his sight. He heard him saying: "My God, You gave me enjoyment with them as long as You willed, and You took them away as You willed, and You left me hope in You. O Beneficent, O Responsive!"

And it is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with them both — that his son fell ill, and his grief over him intensified, until one of the people said: "We fear for this old man if something happens to this boy." Then the boy died, and Ibn ʿUmar went out in his funeral procession, and there was no man ever more joyful than he. It was said to him about that, and Ibn ʿUmar said: "My grief was only mercy for him. When God's command occurred, we were content with it."

And Masrūq said: "There was a man in the desert who had a dog, a donkey, and a rooster. The rooster woke them for prayer, the donkey carried water for them and bore their tent, and the dog guarded them." He said: "A fox came and took the rooster, and they grieved over it. The man was righteous and said: 'Perhaps it is good.' Then a wolf came and tore open the donkey's belly and killed it, and they grieved over it, and the man said: 'Perhaps it is good.' Then the dog was stricken after that, and he said: 'Perhaps it is good.' Then one morning they woke and looked, and behold, those around them had been taken captive, and they remained. He said: 'They were only taken because of what they had of the sounds of dogs, donkeys, and roosters. So the good was for these in the destruction of those animals, just as God — exalted is He — had decreed it.'"

So whoever knows the hidden subtlety of God's grace (luṭf) is content with His act in every state.

And it is related that Jesus — peace be upon him — passed by a blind, leprous, paralyzed man, struck on both sides with palsy, whose flesh had fallen away from leprosy, and he was saying: "Praise be to God who has spared me from what He has afflicted many of His creatures with." Jesus said to him: "O you, what affliction do I see turned away from you?" He said: "O Spirit of God, I am better than one in whose heart God has not placed what He has placed in my heart of knowledge of Him." He said: "You have spoken truly. Give me your hand." So he gave him his hand, and behold, he was the most handsome of people in face and the best of them in form, and God had removed from him what he had. He accompanied Jesus — peace be upon him — and worshipped with him.

And ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr cut off his leg from the knee due to an ulcer that had appeared on it, then said: "Praise be to God who has taken from me one, and I hope that if He has taken, He has spared; and if He has afflicted, He has healed." Then he did not abandon his nightly devotion that night.

And Ibn Masʿūd used to say: "Poverty and wealth are two mounts of ease; I do not care which of them I ride. If it is poverty, then in it is patience; and if it is wealth, then in it is generosity."

And Abu Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: "I have attained from every station a state, except contentment (riḍā); I have from it only the scent of the breeze." And despite that: "If all creatures were admitted to Paradise and I were admitted to the Fire, I would be content with that."

And it was said to another knower (ʿārif): "Have you attained the utmost of contentment with Him?" He said: "As for the utmost, no. But the station of contentment I have attained: if He made me a bridge over Hell over which creatures cross to Paradise, then filled me with Hell as a fulfillment of His oath and a substitute for His creation, I would love that from His judgment and be content with it from His decree."

This is the speech of one who knows that love has engrossed his concern until it prevented him from perceiving the pain of the Fire. And if any perception remains, it is overwhelmed by the delight he obtains in sensing the occurrence of his Beloved's contentment with his being cast into the Fire.

The dominance of this state is not impossible in itself, even if it is far from our weak states. But the weak and deprived one should not deny the states of the strong, nor suppose that what he is incapable of is beyond the capacities of the saints (awliyāʾ).

And al-Rūdhabārī said: "I said to Abu ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jallāʾ al-Dimashqī: 'The saying of so-and-so — "I wish my body were cut with shears and that these creatures obeyed him" — what is its meaning?' He said: 'O you, if this is from the way of magnification and veneration, then I do not recognize it; but if it is from the way of compassion and sincere counsel for creatures, then I recognize it.' He said: 'Then he swooned.'"

And ʿImrān ibn al-Husayn had dropsy in his belly, and he remained lying on his back for thirty years, unable to sit or stand; a hole had been cut in a bed of palm branches on which he lay, as a place for relieving himself. Mutarrif and his brother al-ʿAlāʾ entered upon him, and Mutarrif began to weep at what he saw of his state. He said: "Why do you weep?" He said: "Because I see you in this terrible state." He said: "Do not weep, for what is most beloved to God of it is most beloved to me." Then he said: "I will tell you something; perhaps God will benefit you with it. Keep it secret until I die: the angels visit me, and I find companionship with them, and they greet me, and I hear their greeting. So I know that this affliction is not a punishment, since it is the cause of this immense grace." So whoever observes this in his affliction, how could he not be content with it?

He said: "And we entered upon Suwayd ibn Muʿtabah to visit him, and we saw a garment thrown down, and we did not think there was anything beneath it until it was uncovered. His wife said to him: 'May my family be your ransom — we do not feed you, we do not give you to drink.' He said: 'Long has been the lying down, and the hipbones have wasted away, and I have become emaciated, not eating food nor swallowing drink for such-and-such.' He mentioned days, then said: 'And it would not please me that I had been diminished from this by the paring of a fingernail.'"

And when Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ came to Mecca — and his sight had been lost — people came rushing to him, each one asking him to pray for him, and he would pray for this one and that one, and his supplication was answered. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib said: "I came to him as a young boy, and I introduced myself to him, and he recognized me and said: 'You are the reciter of the people of Mecca.' I said: 'Yes.'" He mentioned a story, and at its end he said: "I said to him: 'O uncle, you pray for people; would you not pray for yourself, that God might return your sight to you?' He smiled and said: 'O my son, God's decree — glory be to Him — is more excellent to me than my sight.'"

And a small son of one of the Sufis was lost for three days, with no news of him. It was said to him: "Would you not ask God — exalted is He — to return him to you?" He said: "My objecting to Him over what He has decreed is more severe to me than the loss of my son."

And it is related from one of the worshippers that he said: "I committed a great sin, and I have been weeping over it for sixty years." He had striven in worship for the sake of repentance from that sin. It was said to him: "And what is it?" He said: "I said once, regarding something, 'Would that it had not been.'"

And one of the Salaf said: "If my body were cut with shears, it would be more beloved to me than that I should say of something God — exalted is He — has decreed: 'Would that He had not decreed it.'"

And it was said to ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Zayd: "Here is a man who has worshipped for fifty years." So he went to him and said: "O my beloved, tell me about yourself: have you been content with Him?" He said: "No." He said: "Have you found companionship with Him?" He said: "No." He said: "Are you content with Him?" He said: "No." He said: "Then your increase from Him is only fasting and prayer?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Were I not ashamed before you, I would tell you that your dealing with Him for fifty years is defective." Its meaning: you have not had the door of the heart opened for you, so as to ascend to the degrees of proximity through the works of the heart. Rather, you are counted among the ranks of the Companions of the Right, because your increase from Him is in the works of the limbs, which are the increase of the common folk.

And a group of people entered upon al-Shiblī — may God have mercy on him — in the madhouse in which he had been confined, and stones had been gathered before him. He said: "Who are you?" They said: "Your lovers." So he turned to them and pelted them with stones, and they fled. He said: "What is the matter with you? You claimed to love me. If you are truthful, then be patient with my affliction."

And al-Shiblī — may God have mercy on him — said:

"Love of the Merciful has intoxicated me — / Have you ever seen a lover who is not drunk?"

And one of the worshippers of the people of Syria said: "All of you will meet God — mighty and majestic is He — affirming Him, but perhaps one has denied Him. That is because if one of you had a finger of gold, he would keep pointing with it; but if it were paralyzed, he would keep hiding it." He meant by that: gold is blameworthy before God, and people boast of it; while affliction is the adornment of the people of the Hereafter, and they disdain it.

And it is related that a fire broke out in the market, and it was said to al-Sarī: "The market has burned, but your shop has not burned." He said: "Praise be to God." Then he said: "How did I say 'Praise be to God' for my safety, without the Muslims?" So he repented from trade and abandoned his shop for the rest of his life, as repentance and seeking forgiveness for his saying "Praise be to God."

So if you contemplate these stories, you will know with certainty that contentment with what contradicts desire is not impossible. Rather, it is a mighty station among the stations of the people of religion.

And whenever that is possible in the love of creatures and their shares, it is possible — with certainty — in the case of love for God — exalted is He — and the shares of the Hereafter.

Its possibility is from two aspects: {The first} is contentment with pain for the sake of the expected reward that exists — like contentment with phlebotomy, cupping, and drinking medicine in anticipation of recovery.

{The second} is contentment with it not for any share beyond it, but because it is the will of the Beloved and His contentment. For love may dominate to the point that the lover's will is submerged in the Beloved's will, so that the most delicious of things to him is the joy of his Beloved's heart, His contentment, and the execution of His will — even if it be in the destruction of his own soul, as it was said:

"No wound, if it pleases you, has pain..."

And this is possible with the perception of pain. And love may so dominate that it stupefies one from perceiving pain. So analogy (qiyās), experience (tajribah), and direct observation (mushāhadah) all indicate its existence. Therefore, one who lacks it in himself should not deny it, for he only lacks it due to the lack of its cause — namely, the excess of his love. And whoever has not tasted the flavor of love does not know its wonders. For lovers have wonders greater than what we have described.

And it is related from ʿAmr ibn al-Hārith al-Rāfiʿī that he said: "I was in a gathering in al-Raqqah with a friend of mine, and with us was a young man who was passionately in love with a singing slave-girl, and she was with us in the gathering. She struck the rod and sang:

'The mark of the humiliation of passion / Upon lovers is weeping — / And especially a lover / Who finds no one to complain to.'

The young man said to her: 'You have done well, by God, O my lady. Will you permit me to die?' She said: 'Die, rightly guided.' He said: 'So he placed his head on the cushion, closed his mouth, and shut his eyes. We moved him, and behold, he was dead.'"

And al-Junayd said: "I saw a man clinging to the garment of a boy, supplicating him and showing him love. The boy turned to him and said: 'How long is this hypocrisy you show me?' He said: 'God knows that I am truthful in what I profess — even if you said to me "Die," I would die.' He said: 'If you are truthful, then die.' He said: 'So the man withdrew, shut his eyes, and was found dead.'"

And Sumnūn the Lover said: "There was a man among our neighbors who had a slave-girl he loved with utmost love. The slave-girl fell ill, and the man sat to prepare ḥays for her. While he was stirring the pot, the slave-girl said: 'Ah!' He said: 'The man was stupefied, the spoon fell from his hand, and he began stirring what was in the pot with his hand until his fingers fell off.' The slave-girl said: 'What is this?' He said: 'This is the place of your saying "Ah!"'"

And it is narrated from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Baghdādī that he said: "I saw in Basra a young man on a high rooftop, leaning over the people, saying:

'Whoever dies of love, let him die thus — / There is no good in love without death.'

Then he threw himself to the ground, and they carried him off dead."

So this and its like may be believed in the love of a creature; and believing it in the love of the Creator is more fitting, because the inner insight (al-baṣīrah al-bāṭinah) is truer than the outward eye (al-baṣar al-ẓāhir), and the Beauty of the Lordly Presence is greater than every beauty — rather, every beauty in the world is a single excellence among the excellences of that Beauty.

Yes — the one who has lost sight denies the beauty of forms, and the one who has lost hearing denies the delight of melodies and measured tones. So the one who has lost the heart must inevitably deny these delights as well, which have no locus other than the heart.

chapters.title_en: Exposition That Supplication Does Not Contradict Divine Contentment (Riḍā)
chapters.arabic_text: ### |||| بيان أن الدعاء غير مناقض للرضا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ع-و (da-ʿa-wa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning — calling, invoking, summoning; also includes the sense of requesting aid or beseeching with humility.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, duʿāʾ is the servant’s act of turning to God (tawajjuh) in need, expressing utter dependence (iftiqār) upon Him; it is an act of worship (ʿibādah) in itself, not merely a petition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — vocal or inward call; metaphorical (majāz) — the soul’s state of neediness that transcends words. Here, the term is used in its full literal sense as an intentional act, yet its deeper reality is the heart’s submission.
- Root: ن-ق-ض (na-qa-ḍa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning — to undo, break, or contradict; also to unravel a woven fabric, implying a reversal of established order.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, naqḍ denotes logical or practical opposition — a state where one thing invalidates another’s requirement. Here, it is negated: supplication does not invalidate or oppose riḍā.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical breaking; metaphorical — conceptual contradiction. The negation (ghayr munāqiḍ) is a definitive denial of any inherent conflict between the two acts.
- Root: ر-ض-و (ra-ḍa-wa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning — contentment, approval, satisfaction; also the absence of aversion or displeasure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Riḍā is the soul’s tranquil acceptance of divine decree (qaḍāʾ) and choice (qadar), rooted in love (maḥabbah) and trust (tawakkul). It is a station (maqām) of the heart, not a passive resignation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — emotional satisfaction; metaphorical — the will’s alignment with God’s will. Here, riḍā is the believer’s inner state, which coexists with the outward act of duʿāʾ.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Negation with "ghayr" (غَيْر) — When "ghayr" precedes an active participle (ism fāʿil) like "munāqiḍ," it forms a compound predicate denying the attribute entirely, without implying its opposite. Syntactically, the sentence "al-duʿāʾ ghayr munāqiḍ" is a nominal clause (jumlah ismiyyah) with a definite subject and indefinite predicate, establishing a permanent, non-temporal negation — thus, the contradiction is categorically impossible, not merely absent at a given moment.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that supplication (duʿāʾ) is not in opposition to contentment with divine decree (riḍā), nor does it contradict it. For the one who is content with God’s decree does not thereby abandon the command to supplicate, nor does he cease to seek from God what He has ordained. Rather, supplication itself is part of the decree — it is a divinely appointed means (sabab) through which the decree unfolds. The heart’s contentment is with the whole of God’s governance, including His command to call upon Him. Thus, the servant who is truly content prays, not because he opposes the decree, but because he submits to the One who decreed both the prayer and its answer. So do not imagine that the act of asking contradicts the state of acceptance; for the Prophet {ﷺ} said: «الدعاء هو العبادة» — "Supplication is worship" — and worship is the very essence of contentment. Therefore, the one who abandons supplication, imagining that it opposes riḍā, has erred in his understanding; for riḍā is to embrace God’s command, and His command includes the call upon Him. And God knows best.

chapters.title_en: The Station of Contentment (Ridā) and Its Reconciliation with the Abhorrence of Sin

أسبابها والسعي في إزالتها بالأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر لا يناقضه
أيضا
وقد غلط في ذلك بعض البطالين المغترين وزعم أن المعاصي والفجور والكفر من
قضاء الله وقدره عز وجل فيجب الرضا به وهذا جهل بالتأويل وغفلة عن أسرار
الشرع فأما الدعاء فقد تعبدنا به وكثرة دعوات رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
وسائر الأنبياء عليهم السلام على ما نقلناه في كتاب الدعوات تدل عليه ولقد
كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في أعلى المقامات من الرضا
وقد أثنى الله تعالى على بعض عباده بقوله {ويدعوننا رغبا ورهبا} وأما
إنكار المعاصي وكراهتها وعدم الرضا بها فقد تعبد الله به عباده وذمهم على
الرضا به فقال {ورضوا بالحياة الدنيا واطمأنوا بها} وقال تعالى {رضوا بأن
يكونوا مع الخوالف وطبع على قلوبهم} وفي الخبر المشهور من شهد منكرا فرضي
به فكأنه قد فعله وفي الحديث الدال على الشر كفاعله (1) وعن ابن مسعود إن
