ليهرب عن عدو له في منزله أو يتبرم بأهله وولده أو بشغل هو فيه فأراد أن
يستريح منه أياما أو ليغزو وليمارس الحرب ويتعلم أسبابه ويقدر به على تهيئة
العساكر وجرها أو يصلي بالليل وله غرض في دفع النعاس  عن نفسه به ليراقب
أهله أو رحله أو يتعلم العلم ليسهل عليه طلب ما يكفيه من المال أو ليكون
عزيزا بين العشيرة أو ليكون عقاره أو ماله محروسا بعز العلم عن الأطماع أو
اشتغل بالدرس والوعظ ليتخلص عن كرب الصمت ويتفرج بلذة الحديث
أو تكفل بخدمة العلماء الصوفية لتكون حرمته وافرة عندهم وعند الناس أو
لينال به رفقا في الدنيا أو كتب مصحفا ليجود بالمواظبة على الكتابة خطه أو
حج ماشيا ليخفف عن نفسه الكراء أو توضأ ليتنظف أو يتبرد
أو اغتسل لتطيب رائحته أو روى الحديث ليعرف بعلو الإسناد أو اعتكف في
المسجد ليخف كراء المسكن
أو صام ليخفف عن نفسه التردد في طبخ الطعام أو ليتفرغ لأشغاله فلا يشغله
الأكل عنها أو تصدق على السائل ليقطع إبرامه في السؤال عن نفسه أو يعود
مريضا ليعاد إذا مرض أو يشيع جنازة ليشيع جنائز أهله أو يفعل شيئا من ذلك
ليعرف بالخير ويذكر به وينظر إليه بعين الصلاح والوقار فمهما كان باعثه هو
التقرب إلى الله تعالى PageV04P379
ولكن انضاف إليه خطرة من هذه الخطرات حتى صار العمل أخف عليه بسبب هذه
الأمور فقد خرج عمله عن حد الإخلاص وخرج عن أن يكون خالصا لوجه الله تعالى
وتطرق إليه الشرك
وقد قال تعالى أنا أغني الشركاء عن الشركة وبالجملة كل حظ من حظوظ الدنيا
تستريح إليه النفس ويميل إليه القلب قل أم كثر إذا تطرق إلى العمل تكدر به
صفوه وزال به إخلاصه
والإنسان مرتبط في حظوظه منغمس في شهواته قلما ينفك فعل من أفعاله وعبادة
من عباداته عن حظوظ وأغراض عاجلة من هذه الأجناس
فلذلك قيل من سلم له من عمره لحظة واحده خالصة لوجه الله نجا وذلك لعزة
الإخلاص وعسر تنقية القلب عن هذه الشوائب بل الخالص هو الذي لا باعث عليه
إلا طلب القرب من الله تعالى
وهذه الحظوظ إن كانت هي الباعثة وحدها فلا يخفى شدة الأمر على صاحبه فيها
وإنما نظرنا فيما إذا كان القصد الأصلي  هو التقرب وانضافت إليه هذه الأمور
ثم هذه الشوائب إما أن تكون في رتبة الموافقة أو في رتبة المشاركة أو في
رتبة المعاونة كما سبق في النية وبالجملة فإما أن يكون الباعث النفسي مثل
الباعث الديني أو أقوى منه أو أضعف ولكل واحد حكم آخر كما سنذكره وإنما
الإخلاص تخليص العمل عن هذه الشوائب كلها قليلها وكثيرها حتى يتجرد فيه قصد
التقرب فلا يكون في باعث سواه
وهذا لا يتصور إلا من محب لله مستهتر بالله مستغرق الهم بالآخرة بحيث لم
يبق لحب الدنيا في قلبه قرار حتى لا يحب الأكل والشرب أيضا بل تكون رغبته
فيه كرغبته في قضاء الحاجة من حيث إنه ضرورة الجبلة فلا يشتهي الطعام لأنه
طعام بل لأنه يقويه على عبادة الله تعالى ويتمنى أن لو كفي شر الجوع حتى لا
يحتاج إلى الأكل فلا يبقى في قلبه حظ من الفضول الزائدة على الضرورة ويكون
قدر الضرورة مطلوبا عنده لأنه ضرورة دينه فلا يكون له هم إلا الله تعالى
فمثل هذا الشخص لو أكل أو شرب أو قضى حاجته كان خالص العمل صحيح النية في
جميع حركاته وسكناته فلو نام مثلا حتى يريح نفسه ليتقوى على العبادة بعده
كان نومه عبادة وكان له درجة المخلصين فيه ومن ليس كذلك فباب الإخلاص في
الأعمال مسدود عليه إلا على الندور وكما أن من غلب عليه حب الله وحب الآخرة
فاكتسبت حركاته الاعتيادية صفة همه وصارت إخلاصا فالذي يغلب على نفسه
الدنيا والعلو والرياسة وبالجملة غير الله فقد اكتسبت جميع حركاته تلك
الصفة فلا تسلم له عباداته من صوم وصلاة وغير ذلك إلا نادرا فإذن علاج
الإخلاص كسر حظوظ النفس وقطع الطمع عن الدنيا والتجرد للآخرة بحيث يغلب ذلك
على القلب فإذا ذاك يتيسر الإخلاص
وكم من أعمال يتعب الإنسان فيها ويظن أنها خالصة لوجه الله ويكون فيها
مغرور لأنه لا يرى وجه الآفة فيها كما حكي عن بعضهم أنه قال قضيت صلاة
ثلاثين سنة كنت صليتها في  المسجد في الصف الأول لأني تأخرت يوما لعذر فصليت
في الصف الثاني فاعترتني خجلة من الناس حيث رأوني في الصف الثاني فعرفت أن
نظر الناس إلي في الصف الأول كان مسرتي وسبب استراحة قلبي من حيث لا أشعر
وهذا دقيق غامض قلما تسلم الأعمال من أمثاله وقل من يتنبه له إلا من وفقه
الله تعالى والغافلون يرون حسناتهم كلها في الآخرة سيئات وهم المرادون
بقوله تعالى وبدا لهم من الله مالم يكونوا يحتسبون وبدا لهم سيئات ما كسبوا
وبقوله تعالى قل هل ننبئكم بالأخسرين أعمالا الذين ضل سعيهم في الحياة
الدنيا وهم يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا وأشد الخلق تعرضا لهذه الفتنة العلماء
فإن الباعث للأكثرين على نشر العلم لذة الاستيلاء والفرح بالاستتباع
والاستبشار بالحمد والثناء والشيطان يلبس عليهم ذلك ويقول غرضكم نشر دين
الله والنضال عن الشرع الذي شرعه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
وترى الواعظ يمن على الله تعالى بنصيحة الخلق ووعظه للسلاطين ويفرح بقبول
الناس قوله وإقبالهم عليه
PageV04P380
وهو يدعي أنه يفرح بما يسر له من نصرة الدين ولو ظهر من أقرانه من هو
أحسن منه وعظا وانصرف الناس عنه وأقبلوا عليه ساءه ذلك وغمه ولو كان باعثه
الدين لشكر الله تعالى إذ كفاه الله تعالى هذا المهم بغيره
ثم الشيطان مع ذلك لا يخليه ويقول إنما غمك لانقطاع الثواب عنك لا
لانصراف وجوه الناس عنك إلى غيرك إذ لو اتعظوا بقولك لكنت أنت المثاب
واغتمامك لفوات الثواب محمود ولا يدري المسكين أن انقياده للحق وتسليمه
الأمر أفضل وأجزل ثوابا وأعوذ عليه في الآخرة من انفراده
وليت شعري لو اغتم عمر رضي الله عنه بتصدي أبي بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه
للإمامة أكان غمه محمودا أو مذموما ولا يستريب ذو دين أن لو كان ذلك لكان
مذموما لأن انقياده للحق وتسليمه الأمر إلى من هو أصلح منه أعود عليه في
الدين من تكفله بمصالح الخلق مع ما فيه من الثواب الجزيل بل فرح عمر رضي
الله تعالى  عنه باستقلال من هو أولى منه بالأمر
فما بال العلماء لا يفرحون بمثل ذلك وقد ينخدع بعض أهل العلم بغرور
الشيطان فيحدث نفسه بأنه لو ظهر من هو أولى منه بالأمر لفرح به وإخباره
بذلك عن نفسه قبل التجربة والامتحان محض الجهل والغرور فإن النفس سهلة
القياد في الوعد بأمثال ذلك قبل نزول الأمر ثم إذا دهاه الأمر تغير ورجع
ولم يف بالوعد
وذلك لا يعرفه إلا من عرف مكايد الشيطان والنفس وطال اشتغاله بامتحانها
فمعرفة حقيقة الإخلاص والعمل به بحر عميق يغرق فيه الجميع إلا الشاذ النادر
والفرد الفذوهو المستثنى في قوله تعالى إلا عبادك منهم المخلصين فليكن
العبد شديد التفقد والمراقبة لهذه الدقائق وإلا التحق بأتباع الشياطين وهو
لا يشعر
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ص (kh-l-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity from admixture; the clear essence of a thing when separated from foreign elements — as milk (laban) is khāliṣ when free of blood and chyme.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ikhlāṣ denotes the purification of intention (qaṣd) so that only the pursuit of divine nearness (taqarrub) remains as motive — the opposite of shirk (associationism).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense: physical purity of a substance. Metaphorical extension (majāz): purity of the heart's aim from worldly admixtures — the term is conventionally (ʿurf) specialized to this spiritual sense.
- Root: ش-ر-ك (sh-r-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Partnership, sharing; to associate a thing with another in a common matter.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic register, shirk is the ascription of divinity to other than God — having degrees (darajāt) from open polytheism to hidden inclination of the heart.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: co-participation. Metaphorical: any motive that shares with the religious motive in driving an act — thus "hidden shirk" (shirk khafī).
- Root: ب-ع-ث (b-ʿ-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rouse, stir up, incite; the internal impulse that moves one to action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The bāʿith (motive) is that which impels the will; sincerity requires singularity of the bāʿith — that it be solely the quest of God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical arousal. Metaphorical: psychological motivation — the term is used for the inner springs of action.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause with Law (لو) and Its Apodosis — as in "لو ظهر من هو أولى منه بالأمر لفرح به" (if one more worthy had appeared, he would have rejoiced), where the protasis and apodosis are both governed by the conditional particle, indicating a counterfactual supposition whose truth is tested only by actual occurrence — a syntactic point al-Ghazali exploits to expose self-deception.
chapters.translation:
Know that everything which can conceivably be adulterated by something else — when it becomes pure of its adulterant and is cleared of it — is called "pure" (khāliṣ). And the act that is purified and cleared is called "sincerity" (ikhlāṣ). God Most High said: {«...from between dung and blood, milk pure (khāliṣan), palatable to drinkers»} (Q. 16:66). For the purity of milk consists only in there being in it no admixture of blood or dung, nor of anything that could possibly be mixed with it.

Sincerity is opposed by associationism (ishrāk). Whoever is not sincere is an associationist — except that associationism has degrees. Sincerity in tawḥīd (divine unity) is opposed by associating partners in divinity (ilāhiyyah). Of shirk there is the hidden and the manifest — and likewise of sincerity. Sincerity and its opposite both enter upon the heart, for their locus is the heart, and they occur only in intentions (qaṣd) and purposes (niyyāt).

We have already mentioned the reality of intention — that it reduces to the answering of motives (bawāʿith). Whenever the motive is single in its purity, the act issuing from it is called "sincere" (mukhliṣ) relative to what is intended. Thus one who gives charity with the sole aim of ostentation (riyāʾ) is "sincere" [in that sense]; and one whose aim is solely drawing near to God Most High is "sincere" [in the true sense]. But custom (ʿādah) has come to specialize the name "sincerity" to the purification of the intention of drawing near to God Most High from all adulterants — just as "heresy" (ilḥād) literally means "inclination," but custom has specialized it to mean deviation from the truth.

As for one whose motive is sheer ostentation, he is exposed to destruction — and we shall not speak of him here, for we have already mentioned what pertains to him in the Book of Ostentation (Kitāb al-Riyāʾ) from the Quarter of the Destroyers. The least of his matters is what has come in the report that the ostentatious one will be summoned on the Day of Resurrection by four names: "O ostentatious one! O deceiver! O associationist! O disbeliever!"

Rather, we now speak of one who is impelled by the intention of drawing near [to God], but another motive has become mixed with this motive — whether from ostentation or from other selfish appetites (ḥuẓūẓ al-nafs). An example: that he fasts to benefit from the dietary regimen (ḥimyah) obtained through fasting, along with the intention of drawing near; or that he frees a slave to be rid of his maintenance and bad character; or that he performs the pilgrimage to improve his constitution through the movement of travel, or to escape an evil that befalls him in his own land, or to flee an enemy in his abode, or because he is weary of his family and children, or of an occupation he is engaged in and wants to rest from it for some days; or that he goes on raiding expeditions to practice warfare and learn its means, and thereby is able to prepare armies and mobilize them; or that he prays at night with the aim of warding off sleepiness from himself so as to guard his family or his property; or that he studies knowledge to make easy the seeking of what suffices him of wealth, or to be honored among his clan, or so that his estate and property may be guarded by the prestige of knowledge against covetous designs; or that he occupies himself with lecturing and preaching to be relieved of the distress of silence and to divert himself with the pleasure of conversation; or that he undertakes to serve the scholars and Sufis so that his honor may be ample with them and with the people, or to obtain thereby some ease in this world; or that he copies a muṣḥaf to improve his handwriting through persistent practice; or that he performs the pilgrimage on foot to lighten for himself the hire; or that he performs ablution to clean himself or to cool off; or that he bathes to improve his odor; or that he transmits ḥadīth to be known for the elevation of his chain (ʿulūw al-isnād); or that he observes iʿtikāf in the mosque to reduce his rent for lodging; or that he fasts to lighten for himself the trouble of going back and forth in cooking food, or to free himself for his occupations so that eating does not distract him from them; or that he gives charity to a beggar to cut off his importunity in asking; or that he visits a sick person so that he himself will be visited when sick; or that he follows a funeral so that his own family's funerals will be followed; or that he does any of these things to be known for goodness, to be mentioned for it, and to be regarded with the eye of righteousness and dignity.

Now, whenever his motive is drawing near to God Most High, but there is joined to it one of these passing thoughts (khaṭarāt) — such that the act becomes lighter for him because of these matters — then his act has departed from the limit of sincerity, and has departed from being pure for the Face of God Most High, and associationism has found its way into it.

God Most High has said: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners from partnership" (ḥadīth qudsī). In sum: every worldly gratification (ḥaẓẓ) to which the soul inclines and toward which the heart leans — whether little or much — when it finds its way into the act, it clouds its purity and removes its sincerity.

Man is bound to his gratifications, immersed in his appetites. Scarcely does any of his acts or any of his devotions remain free of immediate gratifications and purposes of these kinds. Therefore it was said: "Whoever is granted a single moment of his life that is pure for the Face of God has attained salvation" — and that is because of the preciousness of sincerity and the difficulty of purifying the heart of these adulterants. Rather, the sincere one is he whom nothing impels except the quest of nearness to God Most High.

Now, if these gratifications are the sole impellers, then the severity of the matter for its possessor is not hidden. We have only considered the case where the primary intention is drawing near, and these matters are joined to it. Then these adulterants are either in the rank of concurrence (muwāfaqah), or in the rank of participation (mushārakah), or in the rank of assistance (muʿāwanah) — as has preceded in the discussion of intention. In sum: either the soul's motive is like the religious motive, or stronger than it, or weaker — and each has another ruling, as we shall mention.

Sincerity, rather, is the purification of the act from all these adulterants — their few and their many — until the intention of drawing near stands alone in it, with no motive besides it. And this is not conceivable except from one who loves God, who is infatuated with God, whose concern is wholly absorbed by the Hereafter — such that no place remains in his heart for the love of this world, to the point that he does not even love eating and drinking. Rather, his desire for them is like his desire to relieve a natural need — insofar as it is a necessity of his constitution (ḍarūrat al-jibillah). He does not crave food because it is food, but because it strengthens him for the worship of God Most High. And he wishes that he could be spared the evil of hunger so as not to need eating. Thus no gratification remains in his heart beyond what exceeds necessity; and the measure of necessity is sought by him only because it is a necessity for his religion. He has no concern but God Most High.

Such a person — if he eats, drinks, or relieves his need, his act is pure (khāliṣ al-ʿamal) and his intention sound (ṣaḥīḥ al-niyyah) in all his movements and stillnesses. If he sleeps, for example, to rest himself so as to gain strength for worship afterward, his sleep is worship, and he has the rank of the sincere (darajat al-mukhliṣīn) in it. As for one who is not like this, the door of sincerity in deeds is closed to him — except rarely.

And just as one whom the love of God and the love of the Hereafter has overcome — so that his habitual movements acquire the quality of his concern and become sincerity — likewise, one whom this world, elevation, and leadership — in sum, other than God — has overcome, all his movements acquire that [worldly] quality, and none of his devotions — fasting, prayer, and otherwise — remain safe for him, except rarely.

Therefore, the treatment (ʿilāj) of sincerity is the breaking of the soul's gratifications, the cutting off of hope from this world, and the total devotion to the Hereafter — such that this prevails over the heart. For then sincerity becomes attainable.

How many deeds does a man exhaust himself in, thinking they are pure for the Face of God, while he is deluded in them — because he does not see the face of the defect in them! As was related of one of them that he said: "I completed thirty years of prayer, which I had prayed in the mosque in the first row. Then one day I was delayed by an excuse and prayed in the second row, and I felt embarrassment before the people when they saw me in the second row. Then I knew that the people's looking at me in the first row had been my delight and the cause of my heart's ease — without my being aware of it."

This is subtle and obscure. Scarcely do deeds remain safe from its like, and few are those who become alert to it — except one whom God Most High has granted success. The heedless see all their good deeds as evil deeds in the Hereafter — and they are the ones meant by His saying: {«And there will appear to them from God that which they had not reckoned, and there will appear to them the evils of what they had earned»} (Q. 39:47-48), and by His saying: {«Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing good work»} (Q. 18:103-104).

And the most severely exposed of creatures to this trial are the scholars. For the motive of most of them in spreading knowledge is the pleasure of domination, the joy of attracting followers, and the delight in praise and commendation. Satan dresses this up for them and says: "Your aim is the spreading of God's religion and the defense of the Sacred Law which the Messenger of God ﷺ legislated."

You see the preacher bestowing favor upon God Most High for his advising of creation and his preaching to the sultans, rejoicing in the people's acceptance of his words and their turning toward him — while he claims that he rejoices in what has been facilitated for him of supporting the religion. Yet if one of his peers appeared who preached better than him, and the people turned away from him and toward that other, he would be pained and grieved by it. Had his motive been religion, he would have thanked God Most High — for God Most High had sufficed him this task through another.

Then Satan, despite all this, does not leave him alone, but says: "Your grief is only for the cutting off of reward from you — not for the turning of people's faces from you to another. For if they had been admonished by your words, you would have been the rewarded one. And your grief for the loss of reward is praiseworthy." The wretch does not know that his submission to the truth and his surrender of the matter [to one more worthy] is better and more abundant in reward — and more beneficial for him in the Hereafter than his sole undertaking of it.

Would that I knew: had ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) grieved over Abū Bakr's (may God be pleased with him) being confirmed in the caliphate — would his grief have been praiseworthy or blameworthy? No one possessed of religion would doubt that had that occurred, it would have been blameworthy — because his submission to the truth and his surrender of the matter to one more worthy than himself would have been more beneficial to him in religion than his own undertaking of the people's welfare, along with what is in that of abundant reward. Rather, ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) rejoiced in the self-sufficiency of one more worthy than himself of the matter.

Why then do the scholars not rejoice at the like of that?

And some people of knowledge may be deceived by Satan's delusion, telling himself that were one more worthy than himself of the matter to appear, he would rejoice at it. But his reporting this of himself before trial and testing is pure ignorance and delusion. For the soul is easily led in promising such things before the matter descends — but then when the matter befalls him, he changes and turns back, and does not fulfill the promise.

And that is known only to one who knows the wiles of Satan and the soul, and whose occupation with testing them has been long.

So the knowledge of the reality of sincerity and acting upon it is a deep sea in which all drown — except the rare and exceptional one, the singular individual. And he is the one excepted in His saying: {«Except Your sincere servants among them»} (Q. 15:40). Let the servant, then, be intensely vigilant and watchful over these subtleties — lest he join the followers of the devils without being aware.

chapters.arabic_text:
### |||| بيان أقاويل الشيوخ في الإخلاص

قال السوسي الإخلاص فقد رؤية الإخلاص فإن من شاهد في إخلاصه الإخلاص فقد
احتاج إخلاصه إلى إخلاص
وما ذكره إشارة إلى تصفية العمل عن العجب بالفعل فإن الالتفات إلى
الإخلاص والنظر إليه عجب وهو من جملة الآفات
والخالص ما صفا عن جميع الآفات فهذا تعرض لآفة واحد وقال سهل رحمه الله
تعالى الإخلاص أن يكون سكون العبد وحركاته لله تعالى خاصة وهذه كلمة جامعة
محيطة بالغرض وفي معناه قول إبراهيم بن أدهم الإخلاص صدق النية مع الله
تعالى
وقيل لسهل أي شيء أشد على النفس فقال الإخلاص إذ ليس لها فيه نصيب وقال
رويم الإخلاص في العمل هو أن لا يريد صاحبه عليه عوضا في الدارين
وهذا إشارة إلى أن حظوظ النفس آفة آجلا وعاجلا
والعابد لأجل التنعم بالشهوات في الجنة معلول بل الحقيقة أن لا يراد
بالعمل إلا وجه الله تعالى وهو إشارة إلى إخلاص الصديقين وهو الإخلاص
المطلق
فأما من يعمل لرجاء الجنة وخوف النار فهو مخلص بالإضافة إلى الحظوظ
العاجلة وإلا فهو في طلب حظ البطن والفرج وإنما المطلوب الحق لذوي الألباب
وجه الله تعالى فقط وهو القائل لا يتحرك الإنسان إلا لحظ والبراءة من
الحظوظ صفة الإلهية ومن ادعى  ذلك فهو كافر
وقد قضى القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني بتكفير من يدعي البراءة من الحظوظ وقال
هذا من صفات الإلهية وما ذكره حق ولكن القوم إنما أرادوا به البراءة عما
يسميه الناس حظوظا وهو الشهوات الموصوفة في الجنة فقط فأما التلذذ بمجرد
المعرفة والمناجاة والنظر إلى وجه الله تعالى فهذا حظ هؤلاء وهذا لا يعده
الناس حظا بل يتعجبون منه
وهؤلاء لو عوضوا عما هم فيه من لذة الطاعة والمناجاة وملازمة السجود
للحضرة الإلهية سرا وجهرا جميع نعيم الجنة لاستحقروه ولم يلتفتوا إليه
فحركتهم لحظ وطاعتهم لحظ ولكن حظهم معبودهم فقط دون غيره
وقال أبو عثمان الإخلاص نسيان روية
PageV04P381
الخلق بدوام النظر إلى الخالق فقط
وهذا إشارة إلى آفة الرياء فقط ولذلك قال بعضهم الإخلاص في العمل أن لا
يطلع عليه شيطان فيفسده ولا ملك فيكتبه فإنه إشارة إلى مجرد الإخفاء
وقد قيل الإخلاص ما استتر عن الخلق وصفا عن العلائق
وهذا أجمع للمقاصد
وقال المحاسبي الإخلاص هو إخراج الخلق عن معاملة الرب
وهذا إشارة إلى مجرد نفي الرياء
وكذلك قول الخواص من شرب من كأس الرياسة فقد خرج عن إخلاص العبودية
وقال الحواريون لعيسى عليه السلام ما الخالص من الأعمال فقال الذي يعمل
لله تعالى لا يحب أن يحمده عليه أحد
وهذا أيضا تعرض لترك الرياء وإنما خصه بالذكر لأنه أقوى الأسباب المشوشة
للإخلاص
وقال الجنيد الإخلاص تصفية العمل من الكدورات
وقال الفضيل ترك العمل من أجل الناس رياء والعمل من أجل الناس شرك
والإخلاص أن يعافيك الله منهما
وقيل الإخلاص دوام المراقبة ونسيان الحظوظ كلها
وهذا هو البيان الكامل والأقاويل في هذا كثيرة ولا فائدة في تكثير النقل
بعد انكشاف الحقيقة
وإنما البيان الشافي بيان سيد الأولين والآخرين صلى الله عليه وسلم إذ
سئل عن الإخلاص فقال أن تقول ربي الله ثم تستقيم كما أمرت (1) أي لا تعبد
هواك ونفسك ولا تعبد إلا ربك وتستقيم في عبادته كما أمرت وهذا إشارة إلى
قطع ما سوى الله عن مجرى  النظر وهو الإخلاص حقا

### |||| بيان درجات الشوائب والآفات المكدرة للإخلاص
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ص (khalasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity, clarity, and freedom from admixture; the pure core of a thing as opposed to its dross (al-khāliṣ is what is unmixed).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the theological register, ikhlāṣ is the purification of the act (ʿamal) from every motive other than the Divine Countenance (wajh Allāh); it is the opposite of shirk and riyāʾ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense: refining gold from alloy. Metaphorical (majāz) sense: purging the heart's intention from all creaturely regard.
- Root: ر-ء-ي (raʾā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Visual perception, sight, and also opinion or consideration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ruʾyat al-ikhlāṣ — the soul's reflexive glance at its own sincerity — introduces a secondary object of attention, thereby corrupting the purity of the act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical sight. Metaphorical: the inward gaze of the heart upon its own states, which is a subtle form of self-admiration (ʿujb).
- Root: ح-ظ-ظ (ḥaẓẓ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Portion, share, allotment of fortune or pleasure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qurʾānic idiom, al-ḥaẓẓ denotes the soul's share of worldly or otherworldly gratification; the sincere one seeks only God's face, not any ḥaẓẓ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a fixed portion. Metaphorical: every motive of the lower self (nafs) that competes with the Divine command.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When the author says "وهذا إشارة إلى..." (and this is an indication of...), the demonstrative (hādhā) functions as an anaphoric subject whose referent is the preceding quoted saying, and the predicate (ishārah ilā) specifies the precise defect (āfah) being addressed. This syntactic pattern allows the author to taxonomize each master's definition by its scope.
chapters.translation:
### |||| Exposition of the Sayings of the Masters Concerning Sincerity (al-Ikhlāṣ)

Al-Sūsī said: "Sincerity is the disappearance of the vision of sincerity. For whoever witnesses sincerity within his own sincerity, his sincerity stands in need of yet another sincerity."

What he mentioned is an allusion to purifying the deed from self-admiration (ʿujb) in the act itself. For turning one's attention to one's sincerity and gazing upon it is a form of self-admiration, and it is among the class of defects (āfāt). The pure (al-khāliṣ) is that which is clear of all defects. So this man addressed himself to a single defect.

Sahl (may God Most High have mercy on him) said: "Sincerity is that the servant's stillness and his movements be for God Most High alone." This is a comprehensive utterance that encompasses the entire purpose. In agreement with its meaning is the saying of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham: "Sincerity is the truthfulness of intention (ṣidq al-niyyah) with God Most High."

It was said to Sahl: "What thing is most severe upon the soul?" He replied: "Sincerity, for the soul has no share (naṣīb) in it."

Ruwaym said: "Sincerity in the deed is that its doer not desire any recompense (ʿiwaḍ) for it in either of the two abodes."

This is an allusion to the fact that the soul's shares (ḥuẓūẓ) are a defect, both deferred and immediate. For the worshipper who acts for the sake of delighting in the pleasures of Paradise is defective (maʿlūl). Rather, the truth is that nothing be intended by the deed except the Countenance of God Most High — and this is an allusion to the sincerity of the veracious ones (al-ṣiddīqīn), which is absolute sincerity (al-ikhlāṣ al-muṭlaq).

As for one who acts for hope of Paradise and fear of the Fire, he is sincere relative to immediate shares (bi-l-iḍāfah ilā al-ḥuẓūẓ al-ʿājilah) — but otherwise he is seeking the share of the belly and the private parts. Rather, what is sought by those possessed of intellects (ulū al-albāb) is only the Countenance of God Most High. And He is the One who said: "Man does not move except for a share (ḥaẓẓ)." And freedom from shares (al-barāʾah min al-ḥuẓūẓ) is an attribute of divinity (ṣifat al-ilāhiyyah). Whoever claims it [for himself] is an unbeliever (kāfir).

Indeed, the Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī pronounced the takfīr of anyone who claims freedom from shares, saying: "This is among the attributes of divinity." What he mentioned is true — but those people (the Sufi masters) only meant by it freedom from what people call "shares," namely, the appetites (al-shahawāt) described in Paradise alone. As for taking delight in sheer knowledge (al-maʿrifah), intimate communion (al-munājāh), and the vision of the Countenance of God Most High — this is the share of these people. And people do not count this as a share; rather, they marvel at it.

These people — if they were offered, in exchange for what they are in of the delight of obedience, intimate communion, and constant prostration before the Divine Presence (al-ḥaḍrah al-ilāhiyyah), secretly and openly, all the bliss of Paradise — they would deem it paltry and would not turn to it. So their movement is for a share, and their obedience is for a share — but their share is only their Worshipped One (maʿbūduhum), to the exclusion of all else.

Abū ʿUthmān said: "Sincerity is the forgetting of the vision of creatures (khalq) by dint of the perpetual gaze upon the Creator alone."

This is an allusion to the defect of ostentation (al-riyāʾ) only. For this reason, some of them said: "Sincerity in the deed is that neither a devil (shayṭān) should catch sight of it and corrupt it, nor an angel (malak) should see it and record it" — for this is an allusion to sheer concealment (al-ikhfāʾ).

And it has been said: "Sincerity is what is hidden from creatures and pure of attachments (al-ʿalāʾiq)." This is the most comprehensive of the purposes.

Al-Muḥāsibī said: "Sincerity is the exclusion of creatures from dealing with the Lord (muʿāmalat al-Rabb)." This is an allusion to the mere negation of ostentation.

Likewise is the saying of al-Khawwāṣ: "Whoever drinks from the cup of leadership (al-riyāsah) has departed from the sincerity of servanthood (ikhlāṣ al-ʿubūdiyyah)."

The disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn) said to Jesus (peace be upon him): "What is the purest of deeds?" He replied: "That which is done for God Most High, whose doer does not love that anyone praise him for it."

This too is an address to abandoning ostentation. He singled it out for mention because it is the strongest of the causes that disturb sincerity.

Al-Junayd said: "Sincerity is the purification of the deed from turbidities (al-kudūrāt)."

Al-Fuḍayl said: "Abandoning the deed for the sake of people is ostentation (riyāʾ); doing the deed for the sake of people is polytheism (shirk); and sincerity is that God Most High preserve you from both."

It has been said: "Sincerity is the constancy of watchfulness (dawām al-murāqabah) and the forgetting of all shares (nisyān al-ḥuẓūẓ kullihā)."

This is the complete exposition. The sayings on this matter are many, and there is no benefit in multiplying quotations after the truth has been disclosed.

Rather, the sufficient exposition (al-bayān al-shāfī) is the exposition of the Master of the first and the last (peace be upon him), when he was asked about sincerity and said: "That you say: 'My Lord is God,' then remain upright (tastaqīm) as you have been commanded" (1) — that is, that you not worship your caprice (hawāk) and your soul, and that you worship none but your Lord, and that you remain upright in His worship as you have been commanded. This is an allusion to severing everything other than God from the channel of the gaze (majrā al-naẓar) — and that is sincerity in truth.

### |||| Exposition of the Degrees of Admixtures and Defects that Turbid Sincerity

chapters.title_en: The Hidden Adulterants of Sincerity: Degrees of Ostentation (Riyāʾ) and Their Subtle Penetration
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن الآفات المشوشة للإخلاص بعضها جلي وبعضها خفي وبعضها ضعيف مع
الجلاء وبعضها قوي مع الخفاء ولا يفهم اختلاف درجاتها في الخفاء والجلاء
إلا بمثال
وأظهر مشوشات الإخلاص الرياء فلنذكر منه مثالا
فنقول الشيطان يدخل الآفة على المصلي مهما كان مخلصا في صلاته ثم نظر
إليه جماعة أو دخل عليه داخل فيقول له حسن صلاتك حتى ينظر إليك هذا الحاضر
بعين الوقار والصلاح ولا يزدريك ولا يغتابك فتخشع جوارحه وتسكن أطرافه
وتحسن صلاته وهذا هو الرياء الظاهر ولا يخفى ذلك على المبتدئين من المريدين
الدرجة الثانية يكون المريد قد فهم هذه الآفة وأخذ منها حذره فصار لا
يطيع الشيطان فيها ولا يلتفت إليه ويستمر في صلاته كما كان
فيأتيه في معرض الخير ويقول أنت متبوع ومقتدى بك ومنظور إليك وما تفعله
يؤثر عنك ويتأسى بك غيرك فيكون لك ثواب أعمالهم إن أحسنت وعليك الوزر إن
أسأت فأحسن عملك بين يديه فعساه يقتدي بك في الخشوع وتحسين العبادة وهذا
أغمض من الأول وقد ينخدع به من لا ينخدع بالأول وهو أيضا عين الرياء ومبطل
للإخلاص فإنه إن كان يرى الخشوع وحسن العبادة خيرا لا يرضى لغيره تركه فلم
لم يرتض لنفسه ذلك في الخلوة ولا يمكن أن تكون نفس غيره أعز عليه من نفسه
فهذا محض التلبيس بل المقتدي به هو الذى استقام في نفسه واستنار قلبه
فانتشر نوره إلى غيره فيكون له ثواب عليه PageV04P382
فأما هذا فمحض النفاق والتلبيس فمن اقتدى به أثيب عليه وأما هو فيطالب
بتلبيسه ويعاقب على إظهاره من نفسه ما ليس متصفا به
الدرجة الثالثة وهي أدق مما قبلها أن يجرب العبد نفسه في ذلك ويتنبه لكيد
الشيطان ويعلم أن مخالفته بين الخلوة والمشاهدة للغير محض الرياء ويعلم أن
الإخلاص في أن تكون صلاته في الخلوة مثل صلاته في الملأ ويستحيي من نفسه
ومن ربه أن يتخشع لمشاهدة خلقه تخشعا زائدا على عادته فيقبل على  نفسه في
الخلوة ويحسن صلاته على الوجه الذي يرتضيه في الملأ ويصلي في الملأ أيضا
كذلك
فهذا أيضا من الرياء الغامض لأنه حسن صلاته في الخلوة لتحسن في الملأ فلا
يكون قد فرق بينهما فالتفاته في الخلوة والملأ إلى الخلق
بل الإخلاص أن تكون مشاهدة البهائم لصلاته ومشاهدة الخلق على وتيرة واحدة
فكأن نفس هذا ليست تسمح بإساءة الصلاة بين أظهر الناس ثم يستحيي من نفسه أن
يكون في صورة المرائين ويظن أن ذلك يزول بأن تستوي صلاته في الخلا والملا
وهيهات بل زوال ذلك بأن لا يلتفت إلى الخلق كما لا يلتفت إلى الجمادات في
الخلا والملأ جميعا وهذا من شخص مشغول الهم بالخلق في الملأ والخلا جميعا
وهذا من المكايد الخفية للشيطان
الدرجة الرابعة وهي أدق وأخفى أن ينظر إليه الناس وهو في صلاته فيعجز
الشيطان عن أن يقول له اخشع لأجلهم فإنه قد عرف أنه قد تفطن لذلك فيقول له
الشيطان تفكر في عظمة الله تعالى وجلاله ومن أنت واقف بين يديه واستحي من
أن ينظر الله إلى قلبك وهو غافل عنه فيحضر بذلك قلبه وتخشع جوارحه ويظن أن
ذلك عين الإخلاص وهو عين المكر والخداع فإن خشوعه لو كان لنظره إلى جلاله
لكانت هذه الخطرة تلازمه في الخلوة ولكان لا يختص حضورها بحالة حضور غيره
وعلامة الأمن من هذه الآفة أن يكون هذا الخاطر مما يألفه في الخلوة كما
يألفه في الملأ ولا يكون حضور الغير هو السبب في حضور الخاطر كما لا يكون
حضور البهيمة سببا فما دام يفرق في أحواله بين مشاهدة إنسان ومشاهدة بهيمة
فهو بعد خارج عن صفو الإخلاص مدنس الباطن بالشرك الخفي من الرياء وهذا
الشرك أخفي في قلب ابن آدم من دبيب النملة السوداء في الليلة الظلماء على
الصخرة الصماء (1) كما ورد في الخبر ولا يسلم من الشيطان إلا من دق نظره
وسعد بعصمة الله تعالى وتوفيقه وهدايته وإلا فالشيطان ملازم للمتشعرين
لعبادة الله تعالى لا يغفل عنهم لحظة حتى  يحملهم على الرياء في كل حركة من
الحركات حتى في كحل العين وقص الشارب وطيب يوم الجمعة ولبس الثياب فإن هذه
سنن في أوقات مخصوصة وللنفس فيها حظ خفي لارتباط نظر الخلق بها ولاستئناس
الطبع بها فيدعوه الشيطان إلى فعل ذلك ويقول هذه سنة لا ينبغي أن تتركها
ويكون انبعاث القلب باطنا لها لأجل تلك الشهوة الخفية أو مشوبة بها شوبا
يخرج عن حد الإخلاص بسببه ومالا يسلم عن هذه الآفات كلها فليس بخالص بل من
يعتكف في مسجد معمور نظيف حسن العمارة يأنس إليه الطبع فالشيطان يرغبه فيه
ويكثر عليه من فضائل الاعتكاف وقد يكون المحرك الخفي في سره هو الأنس بحسن
صورة المسجد واستراحة الطبع إليه ويتبين ذلك في ميله إلى أحد المسجدين أو
أحد الموضعين إذا كان أحسن من الآخر وكل ذلك امتزاج بشوائب الطبع وكدورات
النفس ومبطل حقيقة الإخلاص لعمري الغش الذي يمزج بخالص الذهب له درجات
متفاوتة فمنها ما يغلب ومنها ما يقل لكن يسهل دركه
ومنها ما يدق بحيث لا يدركه إلا الناقد البصير
وغش القلب ودغل الشيطان وخبث النفس أغمض من ذلك وأدق كثيرا PageV04P383
ولهذا قيل ركعتان من عالم أفضل من عبادة سنة من جاهل وأريد به العالم
البصير بدقائق آفات الأعمال حتى يخلص عنها فإن الجاهل نظره إلى ظاهر
العبادة واغتراره بها كالنظر السوادي إلى حمرة الدينار المموه واستدارته
وهو مغشوش زائف في نفسه وقيراط من الخالص الذي يرتضيه الناقد البصير خير من
دينار يرتضيه الغر الغبي
فهكذا يتفاوت أمر العبادات بل أشد وأعظم ومداخل الآفات المتطرقة إلى فنون
الأعمال لا يمكن حصرها وإحصاؤها فلينتفع بما ذكرناه مثالا والفطن يغنيه
القليل عن الكثير والبليد لا يغنيه التطويل أيضا فلا فائدة في التفصيل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ي-ء (r-y-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To show, display, make visible; the act of presenting oneself for visual perception; riyāʾ is the act of performing deeds to be seen by others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological vice of directing an act of worship toward creatures rather than the Creator; it nullifies ikhlāṣ (pure sincerity) and constitutes a form of hidden shirk (associationism).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is visual perception (ruʾyah); metaphorically extended to the heart's orientation toward the gaze of others, making the creature's observation the operative motive.
- Root: خ-ل-ص (kh-l-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be pure, unmixed, unadulterated; the core sense of a substance free from alloy or contamination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ikhlāṣ is the purification of intention so that the act is directed solely to God, unmixed with any creaturely motive; it is the opposite of shirk.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal purity of gold or honey; metaphorically, the heart's freedom from the adulterating admixture of self-regard and social consideration.
- Root: غ-ش-ش (gh-sh-sh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To adulterate, debase, mix a base metal with precious metal; also to deceive, defraud.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The inward corruption of the heart's intention, analogous to the debasement of coinage; the soul's secret inclination that vitiates the apparent goodness of the act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal alloying of gold; metaphorically, the hidden admixture of base motive within an outwardly pious deed.
- Root: د-ق-ق (d-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be fine, thin, subtle; to be precise and penetrating in perception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The subtlety of spiritual discernment required to perceive the hidden defects of the soul; the fine-grained distinction between sincere and insincere acts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal fineness of texture; metaphorically, the acuity of the spiritual examiner (nāqid) who detects what the coarse eye misses.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional Clause with Repeated Protasis (al-sharṭ al-mukarrar) — The text employs repeated conditional constructions (fa-in kāna... fa-law... fa-law...) to articulate nested hypothetical scenarios, each refining the previous, demonstrating the graded progression of spiritual states through syntactic parallelism and escalation.
chapters.translation:
Know that the adulterating afflictions (āfāt) which disturb sincerity (ikhlāṣ) are of several kinds: some are manifest (jalī), some are hidden (khafī), some are weak despite their manifestness, and some are strong despite their hiddenness. The difference in their degrees of hiddenness and manifestness cannot be understood except through an example.

The most conspicuous of the adulterants of sincerity is ostentation (riyāʾ). Let us, therefore, mention an example of it.

We say: Satan introduces the affliction upon the one praying whenever he is sincere in his prayer, and then a group of people looks at him, or someone enters upon him. Satan says to him: "Perfect your prayer so that this present one may look upon you with the eye of dignity and righteousness, and neither despise you nor speak ill of you behind your back." So his limbs become submissive, his extremities become still, and his prayer becomes excellent. This is the manifest ostentation (al-riyāʾ al-ẓāhir), and it is not hidden from the beginners among the aspirants (murīdīn).

The second degree: The aspirant has understood this affliction and taken caution against it, so he no longer obeys Satan in it, nor pays attention to him, and he continues in his prayer as he was. Then Satan comes to him in the guise of goodness and says: "You are one who is followed, an exemplar, and one who is observed. What you do is transmitted from you, and others emulate you. You will have the reward of their deeds if you do well, and upon you will be the burden of sin if you do ill. So perfect your deed before him — perhaps he will emulate you in humility (khushūʿ) and the beautification of worship." This is more subtle than the first, and one who is not deceived by the first may be deceived by this. Yet this too is precisely ostentation and a nullifier of sincerity. For if he regards humility and the beautification of worship as good, and is not pleased that others should abandon it, then why does he not approve it for himself in solitude? It is impossible that another's self should be dearer to him than his own self. This is pure deception (talbīs). Rather, the one who is truly emulated is he who is upright in himself and whose heart is illumined, so that his light spreads to others — and he has reward for it. As for this one, it is pure hypocrisy (nifāq) and deception. Whoever emulates him is rewarded for his own act, but he himself is called to account for his deception and is punished for displaying from himself what he does not actually possess.

The third degree, which is more subtle than the preceding: That the servant tests himself in this matter and becomes alert to Satan's cunning, and knows that his differing between solitude and the presence of others is pure ostentation, and knows that sincerity consists in his prayer in solitude being like his prayer in public. He feels shame before himself and before his Lord that he should humble himself for the sight of creatures with a humility exceeding his custom. So he turns to himself in solitude and perfects his prayer in the manner he approves in public, and he prays in public likewise.

Yet this too is from the obscure ostentation (al-riyāʾ al-ghāmiḍ), because he perfected his prayer in solitude so that it might be excellent in public — thus he has not distinguished between them. His attention in both solitude and public remains directed toward creatures.

Rather, true sincerity is that the sight of beasts observing his prayer and the sight of creatures observing it should be on one and the same footing. It is as if this soul does not permit itself to pray badly in the midst of people, and then feels shame before itself at being in the form of the ostentatious, imagining that this is removed by making his prayer equal in solitude and in public. Far from it! Rather, its removal consists in not paying attention to creatures at all, just as he pays no attention to inanimate objects, in both solitude and public alike. This one is a person whose concern is occupied with creatures in both public and solitude — and this is among the hidden machinations of Satan.

The fourth degree, which is more subtle and more hidden: That people look at him while he is in prayer, and Satan is unable to say to him, "Be humble for their sake," for he knows that he has become alert to that. So Satan says to him: "Reflect upon the majesty of God Most High and His glory, and upon who you are standing before. Feel shame that God should look upon your heart while it is heedless of Him." So by this his heart becomes present and his limbs become humble, and he imagines that this is the very essence of sincerity — but it is the very essence of deceit and deception. For if his humility were due to his regard for the Divine Majesty, this thought would accompany him in solitude, and its presence would not be restricted to the presence of others. The sign of security from this affliction is that this thought should be familiar to him in solitude just as it is familiar in public, and that the presence of another should not be the cause of the thought's presence, just as the presence of a beast is not a cause. As long as he distinguishes in his states between the sight of a human being and the sight of a beast, he remains outside the purity of sincerity, his inward being defiled by the hidden associationism (al-shirk al-khafī) of ostentation. This associationism is more hidden in the heart of the son of Adam than the creeping of a black ant upon a smooth rock in the pitch-dark night, as has come in the report. None is saved from Satan except him whose perception is fine and who is blessed with God's protection, success, and guidance. Otherwise, Satan is ever-attendant upon those who devote themselves to the worship of God Most High; he does not neglect them for a single moment, until he drives them to ostentation in every one of their movements — even in the application of kohl to the eye, the trimming of the moustache, the perfuming on Friday, and the wearing of garments. For these are sunan (established practices) at particular times, yet the soul has in them a hidden share, because of the connection of creatures' gaze to them and the soul's familiarity with them. Satan calls him to do them and says: "This is a sunnah; it should not be abandoned." But the heart's inner impulse toward it is for the sake of that hidden desire, or mixed with it with a mixture that removes it from the limit of sincerity. Whatever is not saved from all these afflictions is not sincere. Rather, even one who secludes himself (iʿtikāf) in a well-maintained, clean, beautifully constructed mosque to which the soul is drawn — Satan makes it attractive to him and multiplies for him the virtues of seclusion, while the hidden mover in his secret heart is the comfort of the mosque's beautiful form and the soul's repose in it. This becomes evident in his inclination toward one of two mosques or one of two places when it is more beautiful than the other. All of this is a mingling with the impurities of nature and the turbidities of the soul, and a nullifier of the reality of sincerity.

By my life, the alloy (ghishsh) that is mixed with pure gold has varying degrees: some of it predominates, some of it is slight, but easy to perceive; and some of it is so fine that none perceives it except the discerning examiner (al-nāqid al-baṣīr). The adulteration of the heart, the deceit of Satan, and the malice of the soul are far more obscure and far more subtle than that.

For this reason it was said: "Two rakʿahs from a learned man are better than a year's worship from an ignorant man." By "learned" is meant one who is discerning of the subtle defects of deeds, so that he may be purified of them. For the ignorant one's gaze is upon the outward form of worship, and he is deceived by it — like the gaze of a common man upon the redness of a gilded dinar and its roundness, while it is in itself adulterated and counterfeit. A single carat of the pure gold which the discerning examiner approves is better than a dinar which the gullible fool approves.

Thus the matter of acts of worship varies — nay, more severely and more greatly. The entry-points of afflictions that penetrate the various kinds of deeds cannot be enumerated or counted. Let one benefit from what we have mentioned as an example. The intelligent one is sufficed by the little from the much, while the dull one is not sufficed even by prolixity — so there is no benefit in elaboration.

chapters.title_en: Exposition of the Ruling on Action Mixed with Defect and the Deservingness of Reward for It
chapters.arabic_text: ### |||| بيان حكم العمل المشوب واستحقاق الثواب به
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-و-ب (sh-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Mixing, blending, or adulterating one thing with another; the core sense is intermingling of two substances such that the original purity is compromised.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, refers to the admixture of worldly motives, heedlessness, or minor sins into an act of obedience, thereby diminishing its purity (ikhlāṣ) without necessarily nullifying its validity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical blending; metaphorical (majāz) for moral or intentional contamination of an act, where the act remains but its excellence is reduced.
- Root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be due, fitting, or necessary; the root conveys established rightness and entitlement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, istiḥqāq denotes the deservedness of recompense (thawāb) based on divine promise and justice, not on human merit alone.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for legal entitlement; metaphorical for the moral fittingness of reward as a divine grace (faḍl) rather than a necessary obligation.
- Root: ث-و-ب (th-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, recompense, or reward; the root implies a return for an action, whether good or evil.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Thawāb is the divinely ordained recompense for obedience, contingent upon sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and conformity to the Law (muwāfaqah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a contractual return; metaphorical for God’s gratuitous reward, which exceeds the act’s intrinsic worth.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal sentence with inchoative (mubtadaʾ) and predicate (khabar) — the phrase «بيان حكم العمل المشوب» functions as a genitive construct (iḍāfah) where «بيان» is the head noun, and the entire clause «واستحقاق الثواب به» is coordinated by the conjunction (ʿaṭf) with a second genitive noun, maintaining syntactic parallelism.
chapters.translation: I say: Now let us set forth the ruling concerning an act that is mixed with some defect, and the manner in which deservingness of reward attaches to it. Know that the acts of the servants, in their relation to the divine command, fall into degrees of purity and admixture. For an act may be wholly pure in its intention, directed solely toward God, exalted be He, with no admixture of worldly aim or self-regard; such an act is the most perfect in deservingness of reward, and its recompense is multiplied beyond measure. But an act may be mixed with some worldly motive, or with a trace of ostentation (riyāʾ), or with a lapse in the purity of intention — yet the act itself remains valid in its outward form, and the obedience is not nullified thereby. In this case, the deservingness of reward is not wholly negated, nor is it wholly affirmed; rather, it is diminished according to the measure of the admixture. For the reward is apportioned to the degree of sincerity (ikhlāṣ) present in the act, and the admixture reduces the purity, yet does not extinguish the root of obedience. And this is the justice of God, exalted be He, and His grace; for He does not cause the reward of the obedient to be lost, even if their acts are not free from every blemish. Rather, He takes account of the intention, and He weighs the act by its sincerity, and He forgives the admixture that does not reach the degree of nullifying the act’s validity. So let the servant not despair of the mercy of his Lord, nor let him be heedless of the subtlety of his own heart; for the matter is delicate, and the accounting is precise, and God, exalted be He, is the Knower of the unseen, the Seer of what is in the breasts.

chapters.title_en: On the Intermingling of Sincerity and Ostentation in Actions, and the Division of Reward and Punishment
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن العمل إذا لم يكن خالصا لوجه الله تعالى بل امتزج به شوب من
الرياء أو حظوظ النفس فقد اختلف الناس في أن ذلك هل يقتضي ثوابا أم يقتضي
عقابا أم لا  يقتضي شيئا أصلا فلا يكون له ولا عليه أما الذي لم يرد به إلا
الرياء فهو عليه قطعا وهو سبب المقت والعقاب
وأما الخالص لوجه الله تعالى فهو سبب الثواب وإنما النظر في المشوب وظاهر
الأخبار تدل على أنه لا ثواب له (1) وليس تخلو الأخبار عن تعارض فيه والذي
ينقدح لما فيه والعلم عند الله أن ينظر إلى قدر قوة الباعث فإن كان الباعث
الديني مساويا للباعث النفسي تقاوما وتساقطا وصار العمل لا له ولا عليه وإن
كان باعث الرياء أغلب وأقوى فهو ليس بنافع وهو مع ذلك مضر ومفض للعقاب
نعم العقاب الذي فيه أخف من عقاب العمل الذي تجرد للرياء ولم يمتزج به
شائبة التقرب
وإن كان قصد التقرب أغلب بالإضافة إلى الباعث الآخر فله ثواب بقدر ما فضل
من قوة الباعث الديني وهذا لقوله تعالى فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره ومن
يعمل مثقال ذرة شرا يره ولقوله تعالى إن الله لا يظلم مثقال ذرة وإن تك
حسنة يضاعفها فلا ينبغي أن يضيع قصد الخير بل إن كان غالبا على قصد الرياء
حبط منه القدر الذي يساويه وبقيت زيادة وإن كان مغلوبا سقط بسببه شيء من
عقوبة القصد الفاسد
وكشف الغطاء عن هذا أن الأعمال تأثيرها في القلوب بتأكيد صفاتها فداعية
الرياء من المهلكات وإنما غذاء هذا المهلك وقوته العمل على وفقه وداعية
الخير من المنجيات وإنما قوتها بالعمل على وفقها
فإذا اجتمعت الصفتان في القلب فهما متضادتان فإذا عمل على وفق مقتضى
الرياء فقد قوي تلك الصفة وإذا كان العمل على وفق مقتضى التقرب فقد قوي
أيضا تلك الصفة وأحدهما مهلك والآخر منج فإن كان تقوية هذا بقدر تقوية
الآخر فقد تقاوما فكان كالمستضر بالحرارة إذا تناول ما يضره ثم تناول من
المبردات ما يقاوم قدر قوته فيكون بعد تناولهما كأنه لم يتناولهما وإن كان
أحدهما غالبا لم يخل الغالب عن أثر فكما لا يضيع مثقال ذرة من الطعام
والشراب والأدوية ولا ينفك عن أثر في  الجسد بحكم سنة الله تعالى فكذلك لا
يضيع مثقال ذرة من الخير والشر ولا ينفك عن تأثيره في إنارة القلب أو
تسويده وفي تقريبه من الله أو إبعاده فإذا جاء بما يقربه شبرا مع ما يبعده
شبرا فقد عاد إلى ما كان PageV04P384
فلم يكن له ولا عليه وإن كان الفعل مما يقربه شبرين والآخر يبعده شبرا
واحدا فضل له لا محالة شبر وقد قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أتبع السيئة
الحسنة تمحها (1) فإذا كان الرياء المحض يمحوه الإخلاص المحض عقيبه فإذا
اجتمعا جميعا فلا بد وأن يتدافعا بالضرورة
ويشهد لهذا إجماع الأمة على أن من خرج حاجا ومعه تجارة صح حجه وأثيب عليه
وقد امتزج به حظ من حظوظ النفس
نعم يمكن أن يقال إنما يثاب على أعمال الحج عند انتهائه إلى مكة وتجارته
غير موقوفة عليه فهو خالص وإنما المشترك طول المسافة ولا ثواب فيه مهما قصد
التجارة
ولكن الصواب أن يقال مهما كان الحج هو المحرك الأصلي وكان غرض التجارة
كالمعين والتابع فلا ينفك نفس السفر عن ثواب ما
وعندي أن الغزاة لا يدركون في أنفسهم تفرقة بين غزو الكفار في جهة تكثر
فيها الغنائم وبين جهة لا غنيمة فيها ويبعد أن يقال إدراك هذه التفرقة يحبط
بالكلية ثواب جهادهم بل العدل أن يقال إذا كان الباعث الأصلي والمزعج القوي
هو إعلاء كلمة الله تعالى وإنما الرغبة في الغنيمة على سبيل التبعية فلا
يحبط به الثواب
نعم لا يساوي ثوابه ثواب من لا يلتفت قلبه إلى الغنيمة أصلا فإن هذا
الالتفات نقصان لا محالة
فإن قلت فالآيات والأخبار تدل على أن شوب الرياء محبط للثواب وفي معناه
شوب طلب الغنيمة والتجارة وسائر الحظوظ فقد روى طاوس وغيره من التابعين أن
رجلا سأل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عمن يصطنع المعروف أو قال يتصدق فيحب أن
يحمد ويؤجر فلم يدر ما يقول له حتى نزلت {فمن كان يرجو لقاء ربه فليعمل
عملا صالحا ولا يشرك بعبادة ربه أحدا}  (2) وقد قصد الأجر والحمد جميعا وروى
معاذ عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال أدنى الرياء شرك (3) وقال أبو
هريرة قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقال لمن أشرك في عمله خذ أجرك ممن
عملت له (4) وروي عن عبادة إن الله عز وجل يقول أنا أغنى الأغنياء عن
الشركة من عمل لي عملا فأشرك معي غيري ودعت نصيبي لشريكي وروى أبو موسى أن
أعرابيا أتى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا رسول الله الرجل يقاتل
حمية والرجل يقاتل شجاعة والرجل يقاتل ليرى مكانه فأيهم في سبيل الله فقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم من قاتل لتكون كلمة الله هي العليا فهو في سبيل الله
(5) وقال عمر رضي الله عنه تقولون فلان شهيد ولعله أن يكون قد ملأ دفتي
راحلته ورقا وقال ابن مسعود رضي الله تعالى عنه قال رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم من هاجر يبتغي شيئا من الدنيا فهو له (6) فنقول هذه الأحاديث لا
تناقض ما ذكرناه بل المراد بها من لم يرد بذلك إلا الدنيا كقوله من هاجر
يبتغي شيئا من الدنيا وكان ذلك هو الأغلب على همه وقد ذكرنا أن ذلك عصيان
وعدوان لا لأن طلب الدنيا حرام ولكن طلبها بأعمال الدين حرام لما فيه من
الرياء وتغيير العبادة عن موضعها وأما لفظ الشركة حيث ورد فمطلق للتساوي
وقد بينا أنه إذا تساوى القصدان تقاوما ولم يكن له PageV04P385
ولا عليه فلا ينبغي أن يرجى عليه ثواب ثم إن الإنسان عند الشركة أبدا في
خطر فإنه لا يدري أي الأمرين أغلب على قصده فربما يكون عليه وبالا ولذلك
قال تعالى {فمن كان يرجو لقاء ربه فليعمل عملا صالحا ولا يشرك بعبادة ربه
أحدا} أي لا يرجى اللقاء مع الشركة التي أحسن أحوالها التساقط ويجوز أن
يقال أيضا منصب الشهادة لا ينال إلا بالإخلاص في الغزو
وبعيد أن يقال من كانت له داعيته الدينية بحيث تزعجه إلى مجرد الغزو وإن
لم يكن غنيمة وقدر على غزو  طائفتين من الكفار إحداهما غنية والأخرى فقيرة
فمال إلى جهة الأغنياء لإعلاء كلمة الله وللغنيمة لاثواب له على غزوه البتة
ونعوذ بالله أن يكون الأمر كذلك فإن هذا حرج في الدين ومدخل لليأس على
المسلمين لأن أمثال هذه الشوائب التابعة قط لا ينفك الإنسان عنها إلا على
الندور فيكون تأثير هذا في نقصان الثواب فأما أن يكون في إحباطه فلا نعم
الإنسان فيه على خطر عظيم لأنه ربما يظن أن الباعث الأقوى هو قصد التقرب
إلى الله ويكون الأغلب على سره الحظ النفسي وذلك مما يخفى غاية الخفاء
فلا يحصل الأجر إلا بالإخلاص والإخلاص قلما يستيقنه العبد من نفسه وإن
بالغ في الاحتياط فلذلك ينبغي أن يكون أبدا بعد كمال الاجتهاد مترددا بين
الرد والقبول خائفا أن تكون في عبادته آفة يكون وبالها أكثر من ثوابها
وهكذا كان الخائفون من ذوي البصائر وهكذا ينبغي أن يكون كل ذي بصيرة
ولذلك قال سفيان رحمه الله لا أعتد بما ظهر من عملي
وقال عبد العزيز بن أبي رواد جاورت هذا البيت ستين سنة وحججت ستين حجة
فما دخلت في شيء من أعمال الله تعالى إلا وحاسبت نفسي فوجدت نصيب الشيطان
أوفى من نصيب الله ليته لا لي ولا علي
ومع هذا فلا ينبغي أن يترك العمل عند خوف الآفة والرياء فإن ذلك منتهى
بغية الشيطان منه إذ المقصود أن لا يفوت الإخلاص
ومهما ترك العمل فقد ضيع العمل والإخلاص جميعا
وقد حكي أن بعض الفقراء كان يخدم أبا سعيد الخراز وكيف في أعماله فتكلم
أبو سعيد في الإخلاص يوما يريد إخلاص الحركات فأخذ الفقير يتفقد قلبه عند
كل حركة ويطالبه بالإخلاص فتعذر عليه قضاء الحوائج واستضر الشيخ بذلك فسأله
عن أمره فأخبره بمطالبته نفسه بحقيقة الإخلاص وأنه يعجز عنها في أكثر
أعماله فيتركها فقال أبو سعيد لا تفعل إذ الإخلاص لا يقطع المعاملة فواظب
على العمل واجتهد في تحصيل الإخلاص فما قلت لك اترك العمل وإنما قلت لك
أخلص العمل وقد قال  الفضيل ترك العمل بسبب الخلق رياء وفعله لأجل الخلق شرك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ص (khalasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Purity, clarity, freedom from admixture; the core of a thing being unmixed with foreign elements.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ikhlāṣ denotes the purification of intention (niyyah) so that the act is directed solely to God, excluding all other motives.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical purity (e.g. pure water); metaphorically extended to the heart's purity from the taint of ostentation (riyāʾ).
- Root: ر-ي-ء (raʾā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To see, show; riyāʾ is the act of displaying one's deeds to be seen by others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Riyāʾ is a form of hidden shirk (associationism) — performing acts of worship for the sake of created beings rather than the Creator.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal seeing (ruʾyah) vs. metaphorical "making oneself seen" — the latter is the blameworthy showing-off.
- Root: ب-ع-ث (baʿatha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rouse, stir up, send forth; the motive force that impels action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The bāʿith (motive/incentive) is the psychological or spiritual drive that originates an act; in kalām, it relates to the causality of human action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical rousing; metaphorically, the inner impulse that "drives" (yuzʿij) a person to act.
- Root: ح-ب-ط (habita)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To become null, void, fruitless; a deed rendered worthless.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iḥbāṭ in Quranic theology — the cancellation of good deeds by disbelief or corrupt intention.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a camel's hump wasting away; metaphorical: the annihilation of an act's reward.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqābūl wa-tasāquṭ (Mutual opposition and cancellation) — When two opposing grammatical agents (fāʿil) act upon a single object with equal force, they negate each other's effect, analogous to two equal and opposite forces in a sentence where neither predicate dominates.
chapters.translation:
Know that when an act is not purely for the Face of God — may He be exalted — but is mixed with a taint of ostentation (riyāʾ) or selfish appetites, people have differed as to whether this entails a reward, a punishment, or neither at all, so that it is neither for nor against the doer. As for that which was intended solely for ostentation, it is against him definitively, and it is a cause of divine displeasure and punishment.

As for that which is purely for the Face of God, it is a cause of reward. The point of inquiry is only concerning the mixed act. The apparent import of the reports (akhbār) indicates that it has no reward, yet the reports are not free from apparent contradiction in this matter. What suggests itself to me — and knowledge is with God — is that one should consider the measure of the strength of the motive (bāʿith). If the religious motive equals the selfish motive, they mutually oppose and cancel each other out, and the act becomes neither for nor against him. If the motive of ostentation is more prevalent and stronger, then it is not beneficial; rather, it is harmful and leads to punishment. Indeed, the punishment in it is lighter than the punishment of an act that was purely for ostentation with no admixture of seeking nearness to God.

If the intention of seeking nearness is more prevalent relative to the other motive, then he has a reward proportionate to the surplus of the religious motive's strength. This is according to His saying — exalted is He: {«فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره ومن يعمل مثقال ذرة شرا يره»} ("So whoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil shall see it") [Q. 99:7-8], and His saying — exalted is He: {«إن الله لا يظلم مثقال ذرة وإن تك حسنة يضاعفها»} ("Indeed, God does not wrong anyone by an atom's weight, and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it") [Q. 4:40]. It is not fitting that an intention of good be wasted. Rather, if it is predominant over the intention of ostentation, then from it is cancelled only the amount equal to it, and the surplus remains. If it is outweighed, then some of the punishment for the corrupt intention is remitted by virtue of it.

The unveiling of this matter is that acts have their effect upon hearts by reinforcing their qualities. The impulse of ostentation is among the destructive things (muhlikāt), and the nourishment and strength of this destructive thing is only through acting in accordance with it. The impulse of good is among the saving things (munjiyāt), and its strength is only through acting in accordance with it.

When the two qualities are combined in the heart, they are mutually opposed. If one acts in accordance with the requirement of ostentation, that quality is strengthened; if one acts in accordance with the requirement of seeking nearness, that quality is likewise strengthened. One of them is destructive, the other saving. If the strengthening of one equals the strengthening of the other, they mutually cancel, and the person is like one harmed by heat who consumes something injurious to him, then consumes coolants that counterbalance its strength — after consuming both, it is as though he had consumed neither. If one of them is predominant, the predominant one is not devoid of effect. Just as an atom's weight of food, drink, or medicine is not lost and does not fail to have an effect upon the body by the decree of God's sunnah (established practice), so likewise an atom's weight of good or evil is not lost and does not fail to have its effect in illuminating the heart or blackening it, in drawing one nearer to God or farther from Him. If one brings that which draws him nearer by a span along with that which distances him by a span, he returns to where he was — thus it is neither for nor against him. If the act draws him nearer by two spans and the other distances him by one span, then a span necessarily remains in his favor.

The Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed; it will erase it." If pure ostentation is erased by pure sincerity that follows it, then when both are combined, they must necessarily repel each other.

Witnessing to this is the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the community that one who sets out for pilgrimage (ḥajj) with merchandise — his pilgrimage is valid and he is rewarded for it, even though a share of selfish appetites was mixed into it.

Indeed, it could be said: he is only rewarded for the rites of pilgrimage when he reaches Mecca, and his trade is not contingent upon it — so that part is pure. What is shared is merely the length of the journey, and there is no reward in it when trade is intended.

But the correct view is to say: whenever pilgrimage is the original motive (muḥarrik aṣlī) and the purpose of trade is like an auxiliary and follower, then the journey itself is not devoid of some reward.

In my view, warriors (ghuzāh) do not perceive in themselves a distinction between fighting the disbelievers in a direction where spoils are abundant versus a direction where there are no spoils. It is far-fetched to say that perceiving this distinction entirely nullifies the reward of their jihad. Rather, justice is to say: if the original and powerfully impelling motive is the elevation of God's word, and the desire for spoils is merely by way of subordination, then it does not nullify the reward.

Indeed, his reward does not equal the reward of one whose heart pays no attention to spoils at all, for this attention is a deficiency without doubt.

If you say: "The verses and reports indicate that the admixture of ostentation nullifies reward, and in its meaning is the admixture of seeking spoils, trade, and other selfish appetites. For Ṭāwūs and others among the Followers (tābiʿūn) narrated that a man asked the Prophet — peace be upon him — about one who does a good deed, or said: gives charity, and loves to be praised and rewarded — and he did not know what to say to him until this was revealed: {«فمن كان يرجو لقاء ربه فليعمل عملا صالحا ولا يشرك بعبادة ربه أحدا»} ("So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord") [Q. 18:110] — and he intended both reward and praise. Muʿādh narrated from the Prophet — peace be upon him — that he said: 'The least of ostentation is shirk.' Abū Hurayrah said: The Prophet — peace be upon him — said: 'It will be said to one who associated partners in his deed: Take your reward from the one for whom you worked.' It is narrated from ʿUbādah that God — mighty and majestic — says: 'I am the most independent of partners. Whoever does a deed for Me and associates another with Me in it, I abandon My share to My partner.' Abū Mūsā narrated that a Bedouin came to the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — and said: 'O Messenger of God, a man fights out of tribal zeal (ḥamiyyah), a man fights out of courage (shajāʿah), and a man fights to show his position — which of them is in the path of God?' He said — peace be upon him: 'Whoever fights so that the word of God is the highest — he is in the path of God.' ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — said: 'You say: So-and-so is a martyr, but perhaps he filled both saddlebags of his mount with paper (i.e. worldly gain).' Ibn Masʿūd — may God be pleased with him — said: The Messenger of God — peace be upon him — said: 'Whoever emigrates seeking something of this world, it is his.'"

We say: these hadiths do not contradict what we have mentioned. Rather, their intent is the one who intended nothing by his act except this world — like his saying: "Whoever emigrates seeking something of this world" — and that was the predominant concern of his heart. We have mentioned that this is disobedience and transgression — not because seeking this world is forbidden, but because seeking it through deeds of religion is forbidden, due to the ostentation involved and the displacement of worship from its proper station.

As for the word "partnership" (shirkah) wherever it occurs, it is unqualified and implies equality. We have explained that when the two intentions are equal, they mutually cancel and it is neither for nor against him — so no reward should be hoped for upon it. Moreover, a person in a state of partnership is always in danger, for he does not know which of the two matters is more predominant in his intention — perhaps it may be a burden upon him. For this reason God — exalted is He — said: {«فمن كان يرجو لقاء ربه فليعمل عملا صالحا ولا يشرك بعبادة ربه أحدا»} — that is, let him not hope for the meeting with partnership whose best state is mutual cancellation.

It may also be said: the station of martyrdom is not attained except through sincerity in fighting.

And it is far-fetched to say: a man whose religious motive impels him to mere fighting even without spoils, and who is able to fight either of two groups of disbelievers — one wealthy and one poor — and he inclines toward the wealthy direction for the elevation of God's word and for spoils — that he has no reward whatsoever for his fighting. We seek refuge in God from this being the case, for this would be a hardship (ḥaraj) in religion and an entry point for despair among Muslims, because such subordinate impurities are almost never absent from a person except rarely. Their effect is in diminishing the reward; as for nullifying it entirely — no.

Indeed, the person is in great danger in this matter, for perhaps he thinks the stronger motive is the intention of seeking nearness to God, while the predominant secret of his heart is the selfish appetite — and this is something hidden to the utmost degree of hiddenness. Thus reward is not attained except through sincerity (ikhlāṣ), and sincerity is rarely ascertained by the servant from himself, even if he is extremely cautious. Therefore, one should always — after complete striving (ijtihād) — remain oscillating between acceptance and rejection, fearful that there may be in his worship a defect whose burden is greater than its reward.

This is how the fearful ones among the people of insight (ahl al-baṣīrah) were, and this is how every person of insight should be. For this reason Sufyān — may God have mercy on him — said: "I do not count what is apparent of my deeds."

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Rawwād said: "I dwelt near this House (the Kaʿbah) for sixty years and performed sixty pilgrimages, and I never entered into any of God's deeds except that I called my soul to account and found the share of Satan more abundant than the share of God. Would that it were neither for me nor against me."

Yet despite this, one should not abandon action out of fear of defect and ostentation, for that is the ultimate goal of Satan from him — since the objective is that sincerity not be lost. Whenever one abandons action, he has wasted both the action and sincerity together.

It is narrated that one of the poor (fuqarāʾ) used to serve Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz and observe his deeds. One day Abū Saʿīd spoke about sincerity (ikhlāṣ), intending the sincerity of movements. The poor man began to scrutinize his heart at every movement and demand sincerity from it. This made it difficult for him to accomplish his needs, and the Shaykh was harmed by this. He asked him about his affair, and he informed him of his demanding from himself the reality of sincerity, and that he was incapable of it in most of his deeds, so he abandoned them. Abū Saʿīd said: "Do not do this, for sincerity does not cut off dealing (muʿāmalah). Persist in the action and strive to attain sincerity. I did not tell you to abandon action; I only told you to purify the action."

Al-Fuḍayl said: "Abandoning action due to people is ostentation (riyāʾ), and doing action for the sake of people is shirk."

chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| الباب الثالث في الصدق وفضيلته وحقيقته

### |||| فضيلة الصدق

قال الله تعالى {رجال صدقوا ما عاهدوا الله عليه} وقال النبي صلى الله
عليه وسلم إن الصدق يهدي إلى البر والبر يهدي إلى الجنة وإن الرجل ليصدق
حتى يكتب عند الله صديقا وإن الكذب يهدي إلى الفجور والفجور يهدي إلى النار
وإن الرجل ليكذب حتى يكتب عند الله كذابا (1) ويكفي في فضيلة الصدق أن
الصديق مشتق منه والله تعالى وصف الأنبياء به في معرض المدح والثناء فقال
{واذكر في الكتاب إبراهيم إنه كان صديقا نبيا} وقال PageV04P386
واذكر في الكتاب إسمعيل إنه كان صادق الوعد وكان رسولا نبيا وقال تعالى
{واذكر في الكتاب إدريس إنه كان صديقا نبيا} وقال ابن عباس أربع من كن فيه
فقد ربح الصدق والحياء وحسن الخلق والشكر
وقال بشر ابن الحارث من عامل الله بالصدق استوحش من الناس
وقال أبو عبد الله الرملي رأيت منصور الدينوري في المنام فقلت له ما فعل
الله بك قال غفر لي ورحمني وأعطاني ما لم أؤمل فقلت له أحسن ما توجه العبد
به إلى الله ماذا قال الصدق وأقبح ما توجه به الكذب
وقال أبو سليمان اجعل الصدق مطيتك والحق سيفك والله تعالى غاية طلبتك
وقال رجل لحكيم ما رأيت صادقا فقال له لو كنت صادقا لعرفت الصادقين
وعن محمد بن علي الكناني قال وجدنا دين الله تعالى مبنيا على ثلاثة أركان
على الحق والصدق والعدل فالحق على الجوارح والعدل على القلوب والصدق على
العقول
وقال الثوري في قوله تعالى {ويوم القيامة ترى الذين كذبوا على الله
وجوههم مسودة} قال هم الذين ادعوا محبة الله تعالى ولم يكونوا بها صادقين
وأوحى الله تعالى إلى داود عليه السلام يا داود من صدقني في سريرته صدقته
عند المخلوقين في علانيته
وصاح رجل في مجلس الشبلي ورمى نفسه في دجلة فقال الشبلي إن كان صادقا
فالله تعالى ينجيه كما نجى موسى عليه السلام وإن كان  كاذبا فالله تعالى
يغرقه كما أغرق فرعون
وقال بعضهم أجمع الفقهاء والعلماء على ثلاث خصال أنها إذا صحت ففيها
النجاة ولا يتم بعضها إلا ببعض الإسلام الخالص عن البدعة والهوى والصدق لله
تعالى في الأعمال وطيب المطعم
وقال وهب بن منبه وجدت على حاشية التوراة اثنين وعشرين حرفا كان صلحاء
بني إسرائيل يجتمعون فيقرءونها ويتدارسونها لا كنز أنفع من العلم ولا مال
أربح من الحلم ولا حسب أوضع من الغضب ولا قرين أزين من العمل ولا رفيق أشين
من الجهل ولا شرف أعز من التقوى ولا كرم أوفى من ترك الهوى ولا عمل أفضل من
الفكر ولا حسنة أعلى من الصبر ولا سيئة أخزى من الكبر ولا دواء ألين من
الرفق ولا داء أوجع من الخرق ولا رسول أعدل من الحق ولا دليل أنصح من الصدق
ولا فقر أذل من الطمع ولا غنى أشقى من الجمع ولا حياة أطيب من الصحة ولا
معيشة أهنأ من العفة ولا عبادة أحسن من الخشوع ولا زهد خير من القنوع ولا
حارس أحفظ من الصمت ولا غائب أقرب من الموت
وقال محمد بن سعيد المروزي إذا طلبت الله بالصدق آتاك الله تعالى مرآة
بيدك حتى تبصر كل شيء من عجائب الدنيا والآخرة
وقال أبو بكر الوراق احفظ الصدق فيما بينك وبين الله تعالى والرفق فيما
بينك وبين الخلق وقيل لذي النون هل للعبد إلى صلاح أموره سبيل فقال
قد بقينا من الذنوب حيارى ... نطلب الصدق ما إليه سبيل
فدعاوى الهوى تخف علينا ... وخلاف الهوى علينا ثقيل
وقيل لسهل ما أصل هذا الأمر الذي نحن عليه فقال الصدق والسخاء والشجاعة
فقيل زدنا فقال التقى والحياء وطيب الغذاء
وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل عن الكمال
فقال قول الحق والعمل بالصدق (1) وعن الجنيد في قوله تعالى {ليسأل الصادقين
عن صدقهم} قال يسأل الصادقين عند أنفسهم عن صدقهم عند ربهم وهذا أمر على
خطر
