Indeed, We created man from a mixed drop, that We might try him, and We made him hearing and seeing. Indeed, We guided him to the path—either grateful or ungrateful»} (Q. 76:1-3). So look at the gentleness and the generosity, then at the power and the wisdom—the wonders of the Divine Presence will dazzle you.

And the wonder of all wonders is the one who sees a beautiful script or a beautiful engraving on a wall, and admires it, and turns all his concern to reflecting upon the engraver and the calligrapher—how he engraved it and wrote it, and how he was able to do it—and he does not cease to deem it great in himself, saying, "How skillful he is! How complete his craft! How excellent his power!" Then he looks at these wonders in himself and in others, and then is heedless of their Maker and Fashioner—His greatness does not astound him, nor does His majesty and wisdom bewilder him.

This, then, is a sample of the wonders of your body, which cannot be exhaustively enumerated. It is the nearest field for your reflection and the clearest witness to the greatness of your Creator—and you are heedless of it, occupied with your belly and your private parts. You know nothing of yourself except that when you are hungry you eat, and when you are full you sleep, and when you desire you copulate, and when you are angry you fight. All the beasts share with you in that knowledge. The specific property of the human being, from which the beasts are veiled, is the knowledge of God—Exalted is He—through reflection upon the dominion (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth and the wonders of the horizons (āfāq) and the selves (anfus). For through it the servant enters the company of the angels brought near, and is gathered in the company of the prophets and the truthful ones, brought near to the Presence of the Lord of the worlds. This station is not for the beasts, nor for a human being who is content with the world and its bestial desires—for he is far worse than the beasts, since the beast has no capacity for that, whereas he has been given the capacity by God, then he has disabled it and disbelieved in God's blessing therein. Such are {«like cattle—nay, they are even more astray»} (Q. 7:179).

And when you have known the path of reflection in yourself, then reflect upon the earth which is your abode—then upon its rivers, its mountains, and its minerals—then rise from it to the dominion of the heavens. As for the earth: among His signs is that He created the earth as a bed and a resting-place, and threaded in it wide paths, and made it submissive, so that you might walk in its open ways. He made it firm, not moving, and anchored in it the mountains as pegs for it, preventing it from swaying. Then He widened its regions until the sons of Adam were incapable of reaching all its sides, even if their lifetimes were long and their wanderings many. He—Exalted is He—said: {«And the heaven—We built it with might, and indeed We are expanding it. And the earth—We spread it out, and how excellent a Spreader are We!»} (Q. 51:47-48). And He said: {«It is He who made the earth submissive to you, so walk in its open ways»} (Q. 67:15). And He said: {«He who made for you the earth a bed»} (Q. 2:22). And He has multiplied in His Mighty Book the mention of the earth, so that one might reflect upon its wonders. Its surface is an abode for the living, and its belly is a resting-place for the dead. He—Exalted is He—said: {«Have We not made the earth a receptacle for the living and the dead?»} (Q. 77:25-26).

So look at the earth—it is dead. When water is sent down upon it, it quivers, and swells, and grows green, and brings forth wondrous plants, and from it come out kinds of animals. Then look at how He made firm the sides of the earth with the towering, lofty, solid, hard mountains; and how He deposited waters beneath them, and caused springs to gush forth, and made rivers flow upon its surface; and brought forth from dry stones and turbid dust a fine, sweet, clear, pure water; and made everything alive through it. He brought forth thereby varieties of trees and plants—grain, grapes, green fodder, olives, date-palms, pomegranates, and fruits beyond counting, of different shapes, colors, tastes, attributes, and fragrances, some excelling others in eating—watered with a single water and brought forth from a single earth.

If you say, "Their difference is due to the difference of their seeds and their roots"—then when was there ever, in a date-stone, a date-palm laden with clusters of ripe dates? And when was there ever, in a single grain, ears of corn, in each ear a hundred grains? Then look at the land of the deserts, and search its surface and its interior—you will find it as similar dust. When water is sent down upon it, it quivers and swells, and brings forth from every delightful pair colors of different kinds, and plants similar and dissimilar—each one having a taste, a scent, a color, and a shape that differs from the other. So look at their multiplicity, the difference of their kinds, the abundance of their forms, then the difference of the natures of plants and the abundance of their benefits. And how God—Exalted is He—deposited in the medicinal herbs wondrous benefits: this plant nourishes, this strengthens, this revives, this kills, this cools, this heats, this—when it settles in the stomach—repels the yellow bile from the depths of the veins, this converts into the yellow bile, this repels the phlegm and the black bile, this converts into them both, this purifies the blood, this dissolves blood, this brings joy, this induces sleep, this strengthens, this weakens. Not a leaf nor a straw grows from the earth except that in it there are benefits that human beings are not able to grasp in their reality. And each one of these plants requires of the farmer, in its cultivation, a particular work: the date-palm prefers the vine-dresser to sweep; the crop is cleared of weeds and tares; some of that is cultivated by sowing seed in the earth, some by planting branches, some by grafting onto trees. Were we to wish to mention the difference of the genera of plants, their species, their benefits, their states, and their wonders, the days would not suffice for describing that. So let a small sample of each genus suffice you, to point you to the path of reflection. These, then, are the wonders of plants.

And among His signs are the jewels deposited beneath the mountains and the minerals produced from the earth. In the earth there are adjacent pieces of different kinds. So look at the mountains—how from them come forth precious jewels: gold, silver, turquoise, ruby, and others. Some are malleable under hammers, like gold, silver, copper, lead, and iron; and some are not malleable, like turquoise and ruby. And how God guided people to extract them, purify them, and make vessels, instruments, coins, and ornaments from them. Then look at the minerals of the earth—naphtha, sulfur, bitumen, and others. The least of them is salt, which is needed only to season food. Were a town to be devoid of it, destruction would hasten to it. So look at the mercy of God—Exalted is He—how He created some lands saline in their very substance, such that pure rainwater gathers in them and becomes salty, burning salt, of which one cannot take a single mithqāl—so that it might season your food when you eat it, and your life might be pleasant. There is no inanimate thing, no animal, and no plant except that in it there is wisdom and wisdoms of this kind. Nothing of them was created in vain, nor in play, nor in jest. Rather, He created all of it with truth (bil-ḥaqq), as is fitting, and in the manner that is fitting, and as befits His majesty, His generosity, and His gentleness. For this reason He—Exalted is He—said: {«And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth»} (Q. 44:38-39).

And among His signs are the kinds of animals and their division into what flies and what walks; and the division of what walks into what walks on two legs, what walks on four, on ten, and on a hundred—as is witnessed in some insects. Then their division in benefits, forms, shapes, temperaments, and natures. So look at the birds of the air, the wild beasts of the land, and the domestic animals—you will see in them wonders, with which you will not doubt the greatness of their Creator, the power of their Determiner, and the wisdom of their Fashioner. How could that be exhaustively enumerated? Indeed, were we to wish to mention the wonders of a gnat, or an ant, or a bee, or a spider—which are among the small animals—its building of its house, its gathering of its food, its familiarity with its mate, its storing for itself, its skill in the geometry of its house, and its guidance to its needs—we would not be able to do so.

You see the spider building its house at the edge of a river. It first seeks two adjacent places

### || كتاب ذكر الموت وما بعده وهو الكتاب العاشر من ربع المنجيات وبه اختتام كتاب إحياء علوم الدين

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذى قصم بالموت رقاب الجبابرة وكسر به ظهور الأكاسرة وقصر به
آمال القياصرة الذين لم تزل قلوبهم عن ذكر الموت نافرة حتى جاءهم الوعد
الحق فأرداهم فى الحافرة فنقلوا من القصور إلى القبور ومن ضياء المهود إلى
ظلمة اللحود ومن ملاعبة الجوارى والغلمان إلى مقاساة الهوام والديدان ومن
التنعم بالطعام والشراب إلى التمرغ فى التراب ومن أنس العشرة إلى وحشة
الوحدة ومن المضجع الوثير إلى المصرع الوبيل فانظر هل وجدوا من الموت حصنا
وعزا واتخذوا من دونه حجابا وحرزا وانظر هل تحس منهم من أحد أو تسمع لهم
ركزا فسبحان من انفرد بالقهر والاستيلاء واستأثر باستحقاق البقاء وأذل
أصناف الخلق بما كتب عليهم من الفناء ثم جعل الموت مخلصا للأتقياء وموعدا
فى حقهم للقاء وجعل القبر سجنا للأشقياء وحبسا ضيقا عليهم إلى يوم الفصل
والقضاء فله الإنعام بالنعم المتظاهرة وله الانتقام بالنقم القاهرة وله
الشكر فى السموات والأرض وله الحمد فى الأولى والآخرة والصلاة على محمد ذي
المعجزات الظاهرة والآيات الباهرة وعلى آله وأصحابه وسلم تسليما كثيرا
أما بعد فجدير بمن الموت مصرعه والتراب مضجعه والدود أنيسه ومنكر ونكير
جليسه والقبر مقره وبطن الأرض مستقره والقيامة موعده والجنة أو النار مورده
أن لا يكون له فكر إلا فى الموت ولا ذكر إلا له ولا استعداد إلا لأجله ولا
تدبير إلا فيه ولا تطلع إلا إليه ولا تعريج إلا عليه ولا اهتمام إلا به ولا
حول إلا حوله ولا انتظار وتربص إلا له وحقيق بأن يعد نفسه من الموتى ويراها
فى أصحاب القبور فإن كل ما هو آت قريب والبعيد ما ليس  بآت وقد قال رسول
الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الكيس من دان نفسه وعمل
PageV04P448
لما بعد الموت (1) ولن يتيسر الاستعداد للشيء إلا عند تجدد ذكره على
القلب ولا يتجدد ذكره إلا عند التذكر بالإصغاء إلى المذكرات له والنظر في
المنبهات عليه
ونحن نذكر من أمر الموت ومقدماته ولواحقه وأحوال الآخرة والقيامة والجنة
والنار ما لا بد للعبد من تذكاره على التكرار وملازمته بالافتكار
والاستبصار ليكون ذلك مستحثا على الاستعداد فقد قرب لما بعد الموت الرحيل
فما بقي من العمر إلا القليل والخلق عنه غافلون اقترب للناس حسابهم وهم في
غفلة معرضون ونحن نذكر ما يتعلق بالموت في شطرين

### ||| الشطر الأول في مقدماته وتوابعه إلى نفخة الصور وفيه ثمانية أبواب

الباب الأول في فضل ذكر الموت والترغيب فيه
الباب الثاني في ذكر طول الأمل وقصره
الباب الثالث في سكرات الموت وشدته وما يستحب من الأحوال عند الموت
الباب الرابع في وفاة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم والخلفاء الراشدين من
بعده
الباب الخامس في كلام المحتضرين من الخلفاء والأمراء والصالحين
الباب السادس في أقاويل العارفين على الجنائز والمقابر وحكم زيارة القبور
الباب السابع في حقيقة الموت وما يلقاه الميت في القبر إلى نفخة الصور
الباب الثامن فيما عرف من أحوال الموتى بالمكاشفة في المنام
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ص-م (qa-ṣa-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To break or snap something with force, severing it utterly — used of a bone or a neck, implying an irreversible fracture.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine punitive action that terminates the dominion of tyrants, marking the absolute limit of creaturely power before divine decree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in reference to physical breaking; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the abasement of kings, since their "necks" signify their pride and sovereignty.
- Root: ح-ف-ر (ḥa-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Digging; al-ḥāfirah is the pit or hollow dug in the earth — specifically the grave as a receptacle for the dead.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic usage, the "pit" (al-ḥāfirah) denotes the place of ruin and casting down, as in {«أَفَإِذَا مِتْنَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا ۖ ذَٰلِكَ رَجْعٌ بَعِيدٌ»} — the return to the dust of the grave.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the grave's excavation; metaphorical for the humiliation of being cast from elevated palaces into a lowly trench.
- Root: ل-ح-د (l-ḥ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The side-recess (lahd) in a grave where the corpse is placed; also deviation or slanting from the straight path.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The niche in the grave symbolizes the soul's transition from worldly light to the constricted darkness of the intermediate state (barzakh).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the burial niche; metaphorical for the "slanting" of the dead away from all worldly comforts.
- Root: ك-ي-س (k-y-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intelligence and acumen; al-kayyis is the shrewd one who perceives consequences before acting.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The "shrewd" believer is one who holds his soul to account (muḥāsabah) and works for what lies after death — a technical term in ascetic theology.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for mental sharpness; metaphorical for spiritual prudence in preparing for the afterlife.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Inceptive Clause with Emphasis (al-ibtidāʾ bi-l-tawkīd) — The opening "الحمد لله الذي..." employs a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) with an explicit subject and a relative clause (ṣilah) that carries a series of coordinated verbs (faʿala... kasara... qaṣara...), each governed by the relative pronoun, creating a periodic structure that piles divine acts upon one another to magnify the praise.
chapters.translation:
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, who broke with death the necks of tyrants, shattered thereby the backs of the Persian kings, and cut short the hopes of the Caesars — those whose hearts never ceased to recoil from the remembrance of death, until the true promise came upon them and cast them into the pit. So they were transferred from palaces to graves, from the brightness of cradles to the darkness of burial niches, from the play of slave-girls and pages to the endurance of vermin and worms, from delighting in food and drink to wallowing in dust, from the intimacy of companionship to the solitude of loneliness, and from the soft couch to the wretched place of falling. Consider: did they find in death any fortress or refuge? Did they take beyond it any veil or protection? Do you perceive any one of them, or hear from them even a whisper? Glory be to Him who is unique in subjugation and dominion, who alone deserves abiding existence, and who humbled all classes of creation by what He decreed upon them of extinction. Then He made death a deliverance for the pious and, in their case, an appointment for the encounter [with Him], and He made the grave a prison for the wretched and a narrow confinement upon them until the Day of Separation and Judgment. To Him belongs the bestowal of favors that follow one another, to Him belongs the infliction of overwhelming punishments, to Him is due gratitude in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is due praise in the First and the Last. And blessings upon Muhammad, possessor of manifest miracles and dazzling signs, and upon his family and companions, with abundant peace.

To proceed: Worthy is the one whose place of falling is death, whose bed is the dust, whose companion is the worm, whose boon-companions are Munkar and Nakīr, whose abode is the grave, whose resting place is the belly of the earth, whose appointment is the Resurrection, and whose destination is Paradise or the Fire — that he should have no thought except of death, no remembrance except of it, no preparation except for its sake, no deliberation except concerning it, no aspiration except toward it, no deviation except upon it, no concern except with it, no power except around it, and no waiting or tarrying except for it. And it is fitting that he count himself among the dead and see himself among the inhabitants of the graves, for everything that is coming is near, and that which is not coming is far. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The shrewd one is he who holds his soul to account and works for what comes after death."

And preparation for a thing will not be facilitated except when its remembrance is renewed upon the heart, and its remembrance is not renewed except through recollection by heeding the reminders of it and contemplating the awakeners to it.

We shall mention, concerning the matter of death, its preliminaries, its consequences, the states of the Hereafter, the Resurrection, Paradise, and the Fire, that which the servant must needs recall repeatedly and to which he must cling with reflection and insight, so that it may spur him to preparation — for the departure to what lies after death has drawn near, and nothing remains of life but a little, while creation is heedless of it. "The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they turn away in heedlessness" {«اقْتَرَبَ لِلنَّاسِ حِسَابُهُمْ وَهُمْ فِي غَفْلَةٍ مُعْرِضُونَ»}. And we shall mention what pertains to death in two parts.

### Part One: On Its Preliminaries and Consequences up to the Blast of the Trumpet, Containing Eight Chapters

Chapter One: On the Merit of Remembering Death and Encouraging It
Chapter Two: On the Length of Hope and Its Shortening
Chapter Three: On the Agonies of Death and Its Severity, and the States Recommended at the Time of Death
Chapter Four: On the Death of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs after him
Chapter Five: On the Utterances of the Dying among the Caliphs, Princes, and Righteous
Chapter Six: On the Sayings of the Knowers (al-ʿārifīn) at Funerals and Graves, and the Ruling on Visiting Graves
Chapter Seven: On the Reality of Death and What the Deceased Encounters in the Grave until the Blast of the Trumpet
Chapter Eight: On What Has Been Known of the States of the Dead through Unveiling (mukāshafah) in Dreams

### |||| الباب الأول في ذكر الموت والترغيب في الإكثار من ذكره

أعلم أن المنهمك في الدنيا المكب على غرورها المحب لشهواتها يغفل قلبه لا
محالة عن ذكر الموت فلا يذكره وإذا ذكر به كرهه ونفر منه أولئك هم الذين
قال الله فيهم قل إن الموت الذي تفرون منه فإنه ملاقيكم ثم تردون إلى عالم
الغيب والشهادة فينبئكم بما كنتم تعملون ثم الناس إما منهمك وإما تائب
مبتدئ أو عارف منته أما المنهمك فلا يذكر الموت وإن ذكره فيذكره للتأسف على
دنياه ويشتغل بمذمته وهذا يزيده ذكر الموت من الله بعدا
وأما التائب فإنه يكثر من ذكر الموت لينبعث به من قلبه الخوف والخشية
فيفي بتمام التوبة وربما يكره  الموت خيفة من أن يختطفه قبل تمام التوبة
وقبل إصلاح الزاد وهو معذور في كراهة الموت ولا يدخل هذا تحت قوله صلى الله
عليه وسلم من كره لقاء الله كره الله لقاءه (2) فإن هذا ليس يكره الموت
ولقاء الله وإنما يخاف فوت لقاء الله لقصوره وتقصيره وهو كالذي يتأخر عن
لقاء الحبيب مشتغلا بالاستعداد للقائه على وجه يرضاه فلا يعد كارها للقائه
وعلامة هذا أن يكون دائم الاستعداد له لا شغل له سواه وإلا التحق
بالمنهمك في الدنيا وأما العارف فإنه يذكر الموت دائما لأنه موعد لقائه
لحبيبه والمحب لا ينسى قط موعد لقاء الحبيب وهذا في غالب الأمر يستبطئ مجيء
الموت ويحب مجيئه ليتخلص من دار العاصين وينتقل إلى جوار رب العالمين
كما روي عن حذيفة أنه لما حضرته الوفاة قال حبيب جاء على فاقة لا أفلح من
ندم اللهم إن كنت تعلم PageV04P449
أن الفقر أحب إلي من الغنى والسقم أحب إلى من الصحة والموت احب إلى من
العيش فسهل على الموت حتى ألقاك فإذن التائب معذور في كراهة الموت وهذا
معذور في حب الموت وتمنيه وأعلى منهما رتبة من فوض أمره إلى الله تعالى
فصار لا يختار لنفسه موتا ولا حياة بل يكون أحب الأشياء إليه احبها إلى
مولاه
فهذا قد انتهى بفرط الحب والولاء إلى مقام التسليم والرضا وهو الغاية
والمنتهى
وعلى كل حال ففي ذكر الموت ثواب وفضل فإن المنهمك أيضا يستفيد بذكر الموت
التجافي عن الدنيا إذ ينغص عليه نعيمه ويكدر عليه صفو لذته
وكل ما يكدر على الإنسان اللذات والشهوات فهو من أسباب النجاة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ف-ل (gha-fa-la)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is heedlessness and absence of mind from a thing; the heart's neglect of what concerns it.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, denotes the heart's turning away from the remembrance of God and the Hereafter due to engrossment in worldly allurements—a moral failing, not mere cognitive lapse.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in reference to the heart's vacancy; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the soul's deliberate aversion from what it knows to be true.
- Root: ك-ر-ه (ka-ra-ha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Dislike and abhorrence; the soul's recoiling from something perceived as harmful or repugnant.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Distinguished between karāhah (aversion) and khawf (fear)—the former is a judgment of dislike, the latter an emotional response to anticipated harm; crucial for the author's distinction between the penitent's fear and the heedless man's hatred.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is aversion to an object; the metaphorical sense appears in the ḥadīth "whoever dislikes meeting God," where the object is not death itself but the state of being unprepared.
- Root: ع-ر-ف (ʿa-ra-fa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Knowledge and acquaintance; the root implies discernment and intimate cognition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿārif (gnostic) is one whose knowledge has transformed into direct experiential awareness (maʿrifah) of God, transcending mere discursive reasoning—the highest epistemic station in the author's hierarchy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes recognition of a person; metaphorical usage in the spiritual path denotes the soul's direct apprehension of divine realities, making death a longed-for encounter rather than a dreaded end.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (e.g., "if he mentions it, he mentions it with regret") and exceptive statements ("he is excused in disliking death; this does not fall under his saying...") requiring precise parsing to preserve the logical distinctions between the three classes of men.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the one engrossed in the world, bent over its delusions, and enamored of its lusts—his heart is inevitably heedless of the remembrance of death, so he does not mention it. And when it is mentioned to him, he detests it and recoils from it. These are the ones concerning whom God said: {«Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you, then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do»} (Q 62:8). Then mankind are of three kinds: either the engrossed one (munhamik), or the penitent beginner (tāʾib mubtadiʾ), or the gnostic who has reached the end (ʿārif muntahā).

As for the engrossed one, he does not remember death; and if he does remember it, he remembers it only to grieve over his world and occupies himself with blaming it. This remembrance of death only increases his distance from God.

As for the penitent, he multiplies the remembrance of death so that fear and dread may be stirred in his heart, thereby fulfilling the completion of his repentance. Yet perhaps he dislikes death out of apprehension that it might seize him before his repentance is complete and before he has set right his provisions. He is excused in this dislike of death, and this does not fall under his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever dislikes meeting God, God dislikes meeting him." For this one does not dislike death or the meeting of God; rather, he fears missing the meeting of God due to his shortcoming and negligence. He is like one who delays the meeting with the beloved, busying himself with preparation for the meeting in a manner that pleases him—such a one is not counted as disliking the meeting. The sign of this state is that he is perpetually in preparation for it, having no occupation other than it; otherwise, he joins the ranks of the engrossed in the world.

As for the gnostic, he remembers death constantly, for it is the appointed time of his meeting with his Beloved, and the lover never forgets the appointed time of meeting the beloved. This one, in most cases, deems the coming of death slow and loves its arrival, so that he may be delivered from the abode of the disobedient and pass on to the vicinity of the Lord of the Worlds. As is related of Ḥudhayfah—when death came upon him, he said: "A beloved has come upon destitution; he who regrets will not prosper. O God, if You know that poverty is dearer to me than wealth, and sickness dearer to me than health, and death dearer to me than life, then make death easy for me until I meet You."

Thus, the penitent is excused in disliking death, and this one is excused in loving death and longing for it. Higher in rank than both is the one who has delegated his affair entirely to God, exalted be He, so that he chooses for himself neither death nor life; rather, the most beloved of things to him is whatever is most beloved to his Master.

This one has arrived, through the excess of love and devotion, at the station of submission (taslīm) and contentment (riḍā)—and this is the ultimate goal and final end.

In any case, in the remembrance of death there is reward and merit. For even the engrossed one derives benefit from remembering death in turning away from the world, since it embitters his delights and clouds the clarity of his pleasures. And everything that clouds a man's pleasures and lusts is among the causes of salvation.

chapters.arabic_text:
### |||||| بيان فضل ذكر الموت كيفما كان

قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أكثروا من ذكر هاذم اللذات (1) ومعناه
نغصوا بذكره اللذات حتى ينقطع ركونهم إليها فتقبلوا على الله تعالى وقال
صلى الله عليه وسلم لو تعلم البهائم من الموت ما يعلم ابن آدم ما أكلتم
منها سمينا (2) وقالت عائشة رضي الله عنها يا رسول الله هل يحشر مع الشهداء
أحد قال نعم من يذكر الموت في اليوم والليلة عشرين مرة (3) وإنما سبب هذه
الفضيلة كلها أن ذكر الموت يوجب التجافي عن دار الغرور ويتقاضى الاستعداد
للآخرة والغفلة عن الموت تدعو إلى الانهماك في شهوات الدنيا
وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم تحفة المؤمن الموت (4) وإنما قال هذا لأن الدنيا
سجن المؤمن إذ لا يزال فيها في عناء من مقاساة نفسه ورياضة شهواته ومدافعه
شيطانه فالموت إطلاق له من هذا العذاب والإطلاق تحفة في حقه وقال صلى الله
عليه وسلم الموت كفارة لكل مسلم (5) واراد بهذا المسلم حقا المؤمن صدقا
الذي يسلم المسلمون من لسانه ويده ويتحقق فيه أخلاق المؤمنين ولم يتدنس من
المعاصي إلا باللمم والصغائر فالموت يطهره منها ويكفرها بعد اجتنابه
الكبائر وإقامته الفرائض قال عطاء الخراساني مر رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم بمجلس قد استعلى فيه الضحك فقال شوبوا مجلسكم بذكر مكدر اللذات قالوا
وما مكدر اللذات قال الموت (6) وقال أنس رضي الله تعالى عنه قال رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم أكثروا من ذكر الموت فإنه يمحص الذنوب ويزهد في الدنيا
(7) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم كفى بالموت مفرقا (8) وقال عليه السلام كفى
بالموت واعظا (9) وخرج رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى المسجد فإذا قوم
يتحدثون ويضحكون فقال اذكروا الموت أما والذي نفسي بيده لو تعلمون
PageV04P450
ما أعلم لضحكتم قليلا ولبكيتم كثيرا (1) وذكر عند رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم رجل فأحسنوا الثناء عليه فقال كيف ذكر صاحبكم للموت قالوا ما كنا
نكاد نسمعه يذكر الموت قال فإن صاحبكم ليس هنالك (2) وقال ابن عمر رضي الله
عنهما أتيت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عاشر عشرة فقال رجل من الأنصار من
أكيس الناس وأكرم الناس يا رسول الله فقال أكثرهم ذكرا للموت وأشدهم
استعدادا له أولئك هم الأكياس ذهبوا بشرف الدنيا وكرامة الآخرة (3)
أما الآثار فقد قال الحسن رحمه الله تعالى فضح الموت الدنيا فلم يترك لذى
لب فرحا
وقال الربيع بن خثيم
ما غائب ينتظره  المؤمن خيرا له من الموت وكان يقول لا تشعروا بي أحدا
وسلوني إلى ربي سلا
وكتب بعض الحكماء إلى رجل من إخوانه يا أخي أحذر الموت في هذه الدار قبل
أن تصير إلى دار تتمنى فيها الموت فلا تجده
وكان ابن سيرين إذا ذكر عنده الموت مات كل عضو منه
وكان عمر بن عبد العزيز يجمع كل ليلة الفقهاء فيتذا كرون الموت والقيامة
والآخرة ثم يبكون حتى كأن بين أيديهم جنازة
وقال إبراهيم التيمى شيئان قطعا عني لذة الدنيا ذكر الموت والوقوف بين
يدي الله عز وجل
وقال كعب من عرف الموت هانت عليه مصائب الدنيا وهمومها
وقال مطرف رأيت فيما يرى النائم كأن قائلا يقول في وسط مسجد البصرة قطع
ذكر الموت قلوب الخائفين فوالله ما تراهم إلا والهين
وقال أشعث كنا ندخل على الحسن فإنما هو النار وأمر الآخرة وذكر الموت
وقالت صفية رضي الله تعالى عنها أن امرأة اشتكت إلى عائشة رضي الله عنها
قساوة قلبها فقالت اكثري ذكر الموت يرق قلبك ففعلت فرق قلبها فجاءت تشكر
عائشة رضي الله عنها وكان عيسى عليه السلام إذا ذكر الموت عنده يقطر جلده
دما
وكان داود عليه السلام إذا ذكر الموت والقيامة يبكي حتى تنخلع أوصاله
فإذا ذكر الرحمة رجعت إليه نفسه
وقال الحسن ما رأيت عاقلا قط إلا أصبته من الموت حذرا وعليه حزينا
وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز لبعض العلماء عظني فقال لست أول خليفة تموت قال
زدني قال ليس من آبائك أحد إلى آدم إلا ذاق الموت وقد جاءت نويتك فبكى عمر
لذلك وكان الربيع بن خثيم قد حفر قبرا في داره فكان ينام فيه كل يوم مرات
يستديم بذلك ذكر الموت وكان يقول لو فارق ذكر الموت قلبي ساعة واحدة لفسد
وقال مطرف بن عبد الله بن الشخير إن هذا الموت قد نغص على أهل النعيم
نعيمهم فاطلبوا نعيما لا موت فيه وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز لعنبسة اكثر ذكر
الموت فإن كنت واسع العيش  ضيقه عليك وإن كنت ضيق العيش وسعه عليك وقال أبو
سليمان الداراني قلت لأم هرون أتحبين الموت قالت لا قلت لم قالت لو عصيت
آدميا ما اشتهيت لقاءه فكيف أحب لقاءه وقد عصيته
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ذ-ك-ر (dhakara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Remembrance, invocation, keeping something present in the mind; its opposite is forgetfulness (nisyān)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The heart's presence with an idea; in the Qur'an it denotes conscious mindfulness that transforms conduct, not mere lip-service
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) when the heart is truly engaged; metaphorical (majāz) when only the tongue moves without the heart
- Root: ه-د-م (hadama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To demolish, pull down, destroy a structure
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Death as the "demolisher of pleasures" (hādhimu al-ladhdhāt) — it dismantles the edifice of worldly delight
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphorical extension — death "demolishes" not physically but by severing attachment
- Root: غ-ر-ر (gharara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deception, delusion; a thing that appears beneficial but is harmful
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "Abode of delusion" (dār al-ghurūr) — the world deceives by promising permanence while delivering transience
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of deceiving; metaphorical for the world's inherent quality
- Root: ك-ف-ر (kafara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cover, conceal; to expiate, atone
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Expiation (kaffārah) — death covers minor sins like a veil, purifying the believer
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of covering; technical theological sense of atonement
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Apodosis (al-sharṭ bi-jawāb maḥdhūf) — in "لو تعلم البهائم" the result clause is omitted, requiring the listener to supply the terrifying consequence, heightening rhetorical impact
chapters.translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the path of truth:

### Exposition of the Merit of Remembering Death in Every Circumstance

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Multiply the remembrance of the demolisher of pleasures." Its meaning is: embitter the pleasures by remembering it, so that your reliance upon them is severed, and you turn toward Allah the Exalted. He also said, peace and blessings be upon him: "If the beasts knew of death what the son of Adam knows, you would never eat any of them fat." ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of Allah, will anyone be gathered with the martyrs?" He said: "Yes — whoever remembers death twenty times in a day and a night." The cause of all this merit is solely that the remembrance of death necessitates turning away from the abode of delusion, and it demands preparation for the Hereafter; while heedlessness of death invites immersion in the lusts of this world.

He said, peace and blessings be upon him: "The believer's gift is death." He only said this because this world is the believer's prison, for he never ceases therein to be in toil — struggling against his own soul, disciplining his appetites, and repelling his devil. Thus death is a release for him from this torment, and release is a gift in his regard. He said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Death is an expiation for every Muslim." By this he meant the true Muslim — the sincere believer from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe, who genuinely embodies the character of the believers, and who has not been defiled by sins except minor lapses and small faults. Death purifies him from these and expiates them, after his avoidance of grave sins and his performance of the obligatory duties.

ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, passed by a gathering in which laughter had prevailed, and said: "Mix your gathering with the remembrance of that which embitters pleasures." They asked: "And what embitters pleasures?" He said: "Death." Anas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Multiply the remembrance of death, for it purges sins and induces asceticism in this world." He said, peace and blessings be upon him: "Sufficient is death as a separator." And he said, peace be upon him: "Sufficient is death as an admonisher."

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, went out to the mosque and found a group conversing and laughing. He said: "Remember death. Verily, by Him in Whose hand is my soul, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much." A man was mentioned before the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and they praised him well. He said: "How does your companion remember death?" They said: "We could scarcely hear him mention death." He said: "Then your companion is not there" — meaning, not in that station of merit.

Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: I came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as the tenth of ten. A man of the Anṣār said: "Who is the most astute and most noble of people, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Those who remember death most and are most prepared for it — those are the astute ones. They have carried off the honor of this world and the dignity of the Hereafter."

As for the traditions of the pious predecessors (āthār):

Al-Ḥasan, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said: "Death has exposed this world's disgrace, leaving no possessor of intellect any joy in it."

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: "No absent thing that the believer awaits is better for him than death." He used to say: "Do not inform anyone of my condition, but commend me gently to my Lord."

One of the sages wrote to a brother of his: "O my brother, beware of death in this abode before you arrive at an abode where you will wish for death and not find it."

Ibn Sīrīn — when death was mentioned in his presence, every limb of him died (i.e., grew still and subdued).

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to gather the jurists every night, and they would discuss death, the Resurrection, and the Hereafter, then weep until it was as if a funeral bier lay before them.

Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: "Two things have cut off from me the pleasure of this world: the remembrance of death, and standing before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Kaʿb said: "Whoever knows death, the calamities and cares of this world become light upon him."

Muṭarrif said: "I saw in a dream as if a caller said in the middle of the mosque of Baṣrah: 'The remembrance of death has cut the hearts of the fearful.' By Allah, you see them only as distraught."

Ashʿath said: "We used to enter upon al-Ḥasan — and it was nothing but the Fire, the matter of the Hereafter, and the remembrance of death."

Ṣafiyyah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, said: A woman complained to ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, of the hardness of her heart. She said: "Multiply the remembrance of death, and your heart will soften." She did so, and her heart softened, and she came thanking ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

Jesus, peace be upon him — when death was mentioned in his presence, his skin would drip blood.

David, peace be upon him — when death and the Resurrection were mentioned, he would weep until his joints dislocated; then when mercy was mentioned, his soul would return to him.

Al-Ḥasan said: "I have never seen an intelligent man except that I found him wary of death and sorrowful over it."

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to one of the scholars: "Admonish me." He said: "You are not the first caliph to die." He said: "Add more." He said: "There is none among your forefathers down to Adam who has not tasted death — and your turn has come." ʿUmar wept at that.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym had dug a grave in his house, and he would sleep in it several times each day, thereby perpetuating the remembrance of death. He used to say: "If the remembrance of death were to leave my heart for a single hour, it would become corrupt."

Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr said: "This death has indeed embittered the bliss of those who enjoy ease — so seek a bliss in which there is no death."

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said to ʿAnbasah: "Multiply the remembrance of death. For if your livelihood is ample, it will narrow it for you; and if your livelihood is straitened, it will widen it for you."

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: I said to Umm Hārūn: "Do you love death?" She said: "No." I said: "Why?" She said: "If I had disobeyed a human being, I would not desire to meet him — so how can I love meeting Him when I have disobeyed Him?"

chapters.title_en: The Way to Realize the Remembrance of Death
chapters.arabic_text:
### |||||| بيان الطريق في تحقيق ذكر الموت

اعلم أن الموت هائل وخطره عظيم وغفلة الناس عنه لقلة فكرهم فيه وذكرهم له
ومن يذكره ليس يذكره بقلب فارغ بل بقلب مشغول بشهوة الدنيا فلا ينجع ذكر
الموت في قلبه
فالطريق فيه أن يفرغ العبد قلبه عن كل PageV04P451
شيء إلا عن ذكر الموت الذي هو بين يديه كالذي يريد أن يسافر إلى مفازة
مخطرة أو يركب البحر فإنه لا يتفكر إلا فيه فإذا باشر ذكر الموت قلبه فيوشك
أن يؤثر فيه وعند ذلك يقل فرحه وسروره بالدنيا وينكسر قلبه
وأنجع طريق فيه أن يكثر ذكر أشكاله وأقرانه الذين مضوا قبله فيتذكر موتهم
ومصارعهم تحت التراب ويتذكر صورهم في مناصبهم وأحوالهم ويتأمل كيف محا
التراب الآن حسن صورهم
وكيف تبددت أجزاؤهم في قبورهم وكيف أرملوا نساءهم وأيتموا أولادهم وضيعوا
أموالهم وخلت منهم مساجدهم ومجالسهم وانقطعت آثارهم فمهما تذكر رجل رجلا
وفصل في قلبه حاله وكيفية موته وتوهم صورته وتذكر نشاطه وتردده وتأمله
للعيش والبقاء ونسيانه للموت وانخداعه بمواتاة الأسباب وركونه إلى القوة
والشباب وميله إلى الضحك واللهو وغفلته عما بين يديه من الموت الذريع
والهلاك السريع
وأنه كيف كان يتردد والآن قد تهدمت رجلاه ومفاصله
وأنه كيف كان ينطق وقد أكل الدود لسانه
وكيف كان يضحك وقد أكل التراب أسنانه
وكيف كان يدبر لنفسه ما لا يحتاج إليه إلى عشر سنين في وقت لم يكن بينه
وبين الموت إلا شهر وهو غافل عما يراد به حتى جاءه الموت في وقت لم يحتسبه
فانكشف له صورة الملك وقرع سمعه النداء إما بالجنة أو بالنار فعند ذلك ينظر
في نفسه أنه مثلهم وغفلته كغفلتهم وستكون عاقبته كعاقبتهم
قال أبو الدرداء رضي الله عنه إذا ذكرت الموتى فعد نفسك كأحدهم
وقال ابن مسعود رضي  الله عنه السعيد من وعظ بغيره
وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز ألا ترون أنكم تجهزون كل يوم غاديا أو رائحا إلى
الله عز وجل تضعونه في صدع من الأرض قد توسد التراب وخلف الأحباب وقطع
الأسباب
فملازمة هذه الأفكار وأمثالها مع دخول المقابر ومشاهدة المرضى هو الذي
يجدد ذكر الموت في القلب حتى يغلب عليه بحيث يصير نصب عينيه فعند ذلك يوشك
أن يسند له ويتجافى عن دار الغرور وإلا فالذكر بظاهر القلب وعذبة اللسان
قليل الجدوى في التحذير والتنبيه ومهما طاب قلبه بشيء من الدنيا ينبغي أن
يتذكر في الحال أنه لا بد له من مفارقته نظر ابن مطيع ذات يوم إلى داره
فأعجبه حسنها ثم بكى فقال والله لولا الموت لكنت بك مسرورا ولولا ما نصير
إليه من ضيق القبور لقرت بالدنيا أعيننا ثم بكى بكاء شديدا حتى ارتفع صوته

### |||| الباب الثاني في طول الأمل وفضيلة قصر الأمل وسبب طوله وكيفية معالجته

### ||||| فضيلة قصر الأمل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ه-و-ل (h-w-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of terror, awe, and something that causes dread due to its magnitude.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological context, refers to the overwhelming awe of eschatological realities that shatter worldly complacency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the terrifying event of death itself, not metaphorically.
- Root: ف-ك-ر (f-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Reflection, deliberation, and the mind's movement over matters to grasp their reality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intellectual act that distinguishes humans; here, it is the means to awaken the heart from heedlessness (ghaflah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for contemplative thought, as opposed to mere verbal repetition.
- Root: م-ر-ض (m-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sickness, ailment, or weakness of the body.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In spiritual terms, the sickness of the heart (marad al-qalb) that requires the medicine of remembrance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical illness; here used literally for the sick, whose sight serves as a memento mori.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Apodosis (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The conditional structures (e.g., "if he remembers... then...") govern the logical sequence of spiritual cause and effect, requiring precise temporal alignment.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that death is terrifying (hā'il), its peril is immense, and people's heedlessness of it stems from their scant reflection upon it and their infrequent remembrance of it. And whoever does remember it does not remember it with an empty heart, but rather with a heart preoccupied by worldly desire (shahwah), so the remembrance of death does not penetrate his heart.

The way to achieve this is that the servant empties his heart of everything except the remembrance of death, which lies before him — like one who intends to travel across a perilous desert (mafāzah mukhṭirah) or to board a ship upon the sea, for he thinks of nothing else. When the remembrance of death takes hold of his heart, it is likely to affect him, and at that point his joy and delight in the world diminish, and his heart is broken.

The most effective way in this matter is to multiply the remembrance of those of his kind and peers who have passed away before him. He recalls their death and their resting places beneath the earth, and he recalls their forms in their former stations and conditions, and he contemplates how the earth has now effaced the beauty of their faces, how their limbs have disintegrated in their graves, how they have left their wives widowed, their children orphaned, their wealth wasted, their mosques and gatherings emptied of them, and their traces obliterated. Whenever a man recalls another man, and in his heart he details his condition and the manner of his death, and imagines his form, and remembers his vigor and his comings and goings, his striving for life and survival, his forgetfulness of death, his being deceived by the smooth flow of circumstances, his reliance upon strength and youth, his inclination to laughter and play, and his heedlessness of the swift death and rapid destruction before him — and that he used to walk about, yet now his legs and joints have crumbled; and that he used to speak, yet the worms have devoured his tongue; and that he used to laugh, yet the earth has consumed his teeth; and that he used to plan for himself what he would not need for ten years, at a time when there was between him and death but a month, while he was heedless of what was intended for him — until death came to him at a moment he had not anticipated. Then the form of the Angel was unveiled to him, and the call rang in his ears: either to Paradise or to the Fire. At that moment he looks upon himself and sees that he is like them, his heedlessness like their heedlessness, and his end will be like their end.

Abū al-Dardā' (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When you remember the dead, count yourself as one of them."

Ibn Mas'ūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The fortunate one is he who takes admonition from others."

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "Do you not see that every day you equip one who departs, whether going forth in the morning or the evening, unto Allah the Mighty and Majestic? You place him in a crevice of the earth, having taken the dust as his pillow, leaving behind his loved ones and severing all ties."

Thus, persisting in these reflections and their like, along with entering graveyards and witnessing the sick, is what renews the remembrance of death in the heart until it overwhelms it, such that it becomes set before one's very eyes. At that point, it is likely that he will be weaned from the world and turn away from the Abode of Delusion (dār al-ghurūr). Otherwise, remembrance by the outward heart and the sweetness of the tongue is of little avail in warning and admonition. And whenever his heart takes delight in anything of the world, he should immediately recall that he must inevitably part from it. Ibn Muṭīʿ once looked upon his house and admired its beauty, then wept and said: "By Allah, were it not for death, I would be joyful in you; and were it not for what awaits us of the constriction of graves, our eyes would find rest in the world." Then he wept intensely until his voice rose high.

### |||| The Second Chapter: On the Length of Hope (ṭūl al-amal), the Virtue of Shortening Hope, the Cause of Its Length, and the Method of Treating It

### ||||| The Virtue of Shortening Hope

chapters.title_en: The Censure of Long Hope (Dhamm Ṭūl al-Amal) — Section 736
chapters.arabic_text:
قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لعبد الله بن عمر إذا أصبحت فلا تحدث
نفسك بالمساء وإذا أمسيت فلا تحدث نفسك بالصباح وخذ من حياتك لموتك ومن
صحتك لسقمك فإنك يا عبد الله لا تدري ما اسمك غدا (1) وروى علي كرم الله
وجهه أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن أشد ما أخاف عليكم خصلتان اتباع الهوى
وطول الأمل فأما اتباع الهوى فإنه يصد عن الحق وأما طول الأمل فإنه الحب
للدنيا ثم قال إلا إن الله تعالى يعطي الدنيا من يحب ويبغض وإذا أحب عبدا
أعطاه الإيمان ألا إن للدين أبناء وللدنيا أبناء فكونوا من أبناء الدين ولا
تكونوا PageV04P452
من أبناء الدنيا ألا إن الدنيا قد ارتحلت مولية ألا إن الآخرة قد ارتحلت
مقبلة ألا وإنكم في يوم عمل ليس فيه حساب ألا وإنكم توشكون في يوم حساب ليس
فيه عمل (1) وقالت أم المنذر اطلع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ذات عشية
إلى الناس فقال أيها الناس إما تستحون من  الله قالوا وما ذاك يا رسول الله
قال تجمعون مالا تأكلون وتأملون ما لا تدركون وتبنون ما لا تسكنون (2) وقال
أبو سعيد الخدري اشترى أسامة بن زيد من زيد ابن ثابت وليدة بمائة دينار إلى
شهر فسمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول ألا تعجبون من أسامة المشترى
إلى شهر إن أسامة لطويل الأمل والذي نفسي بيده ما طرفت عيناي إلا ظننت أن
شفري لا يلتقيان حتى يقبض الله روحي ولا رفعت طرفي فظننت أنى واضعه حتى
أفيض ولا لقمت لقمة إلا ظننت أني لا أسيغها حتى أغص بها من الموت ثم قال يا
بني آدم إن كنتم تعقلون فعدوا أنفسكم من الموتى والذي نفسي بيده إن ما
توعدون لآت وما أنتم بمعجزين (3) وعن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إن رسول الله
صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يخرج يهريق الماء فيتمسح بالتراب فأقول له يا رسول
الله إن الماء منك قريب فيقول ما يدريني لعلي لا أبلغه (4) والبزاز بسند
ضعيف وروي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أخذ ثلاثة أعواد فغرز عودا بين يديه
والآخر إلى جنبه وأما الثالث فأبعده فقال هل تدرون ما هذا قالوا الله
ورسوله أعلم قال هذا الإنسان وهذا الأجل وذاك الأمل يتعاطاه ابن آدم
ويختلجه الأجل دون الأمل (5) وقال عليه السلام مثل ابن آدم وإلى جنبه تسع
وتسعون منية إن اخطأته المنايا وقع في الهرم (6) قال ابن مسعود هذا المرء
وهذه الحتوف حوله شوارع إليه والهرم وراء الحتوف والأمل وراء الهرم فهو
يؤمل وهذه الحتوف شوارع إليه فأيها أمر به أخذه فإن اخطأته الحتوف قتله
الهرم وهو ينتظر الأمل
قال عبد الله خط لنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم خطا مربعا وخط وسطه
خطا وخط خطوطا إلى جنب الخط وخط خطا خارجا وقال أتدرون ما هذا قلنا الله
ورسوله أعلم قال هذا الإنسان للخط الذي في الوسط وهذا الأجل محيط به وهذه
الأعراض للخطوط التي حوله تنهشه إن اخطأه هذا نهشه هذا وذاك الأمل  يعني
الخط الخط الخارج (7) وقال أنس قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يهرم ابن
آدم ويبقى معه اثنتان الحرص والأمل (8) وفي رواية وتشب معه اثنتان الحرص
على المال والحرص على العمر وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم PageV04P453
نجا أول هذه الأمة باليقين والزهد ويهلك آخر هذه الأمة بالبخل والأمل (1)
وقيل بينما عيسى عليه السلام جالس وشيخ يعمل بمسحاة يثير بها الأرض فقال
عيسى اللهم أنزع منه الأمل فوضع الشيخ المسحاة واضطجع فلبث ساعة فقال عيسى
اللهم اردد إليه الأمل فقام فجعل يعمل فسأله عيسى عن ذلك فقال بينما أنا
أعمل إذ قالت لي نفسي إلى متى تعمل وأنت شيخ كبير فألقيت المسحاة واضطجعت
ثم قالت لي نفسي والله لا بد لك من عيش ما بقيت فقمت إلى مسحاتي
وقال الحسن قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أكلكم يحب أن يدخل الجنة
قالوا نعم يا رسول الله قال قصروا من الأمل وثبتوا آجالكم بين أبصاركم
واستحيوا من الله حق الحياء (2) وكان صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول في دعائه
اللهم إني أعوذ بك من دنيا تمنع خير الآخرة وأعوذ بك من حياة تمنع خير
الممات وأعوذ بك من أمل يمنع خير العمل (3)
الآثار قال مطرف بن عبد الله لو علمت متى أجلي لخشيت على ذهاب عقلي ولكن
الله تعالى من على عباده بالغفلة عن الموت ولولا الغفلة ما تهنأوا بعيش ولا
قامت بينهم الأسواق
وقال الحسن السهو والأمل نعمتان عظيمتان على بني آدم ولولاهما ما مشى
المسلمون في الطرق وقال الثوري بلغني أن الإنسان خلق احمق ولولا ذلك لم
يهنأه العيش وقال أبو سعيد بن عبد الرحمن إنما عمرت الدنيا بقلة عقول أهلها
وقال سلمان الفارسي رضي الله عنه ثلاث أعجبتني حتى أضحكتني مؤمل الدنيا
والموت يطلبه وغافل وليس يغفل عنه وضاحك ملء فيه ولا يدري أساخط رب
العالمين عليه أم راض وثلاث أحزنتني حتى أبكتني فراق الأحبة محمد وحزبه
وهول المطلع والوقوف بين يدي الله ولا أدري إلى  الجنة يؤمر بي أو إلى النار
وقال بعضهم رأيت زرارة بن أبي أوفى بعد موته في المنام فقلت أي الأعمال
أبلغ عندكم قال التوكل وقصر الأمل
وقال الثوري الزهد في الدنيا قصر الأمل ليس بأكل الغليظ ولا لبس العباءة
وسأل المفضل بن فضالة ربه أن يرفع عنه الأمل فذهبت عن شهوة الطعام
والشراب ثم دعا ربه فرد عليه الأمل فرجع إلى الطعام والشراب وقيل للحسن يا
أبا سعيد ألا تغسل قميصك فقال الأمر أعجل من ذلك
وقال الحسن الموت معقود بنواصيكم والدنيا تطوى من ورائكم
وقال بعضهم أنا كرجل ماد عنقه والسيف عليه ينتظر متى تضرب عنقه
وقال داود الطائي لو أملت أن أعيش شهرا لرأيتني قد أتيت عظيما وكيف أؤمل
ذلك وأرى الفجائع تغشى الخلائق في ساعات الليل والنهار وحكى أنه جاء شقيق
البلخى إلى أستاذ له يقال له أبو هاشم الرمانى وفي طرف كسائه شيء مصرور
فقال له استاذه إيش هذا معك فقال لوزات دفعها إلى أخ لي وقال أحب أن تفطر
عليها فقال يا شقيق وأنت تحدث نفسك أنك تبقى إلى الليل لا كلمتك أبدا قال
فأغلق في وجهي الباب ودخل وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز في خطبته إن لكل سفر زادا
لا محالة فتزودوا لسفركم من الدنيا إلى الآخرة التقوى وكونوا كمن عاين ما
أعد الله من ثوابه وعقابه ترغبوا وترهبوا ولا يطولن عليكم الأمد فتقسو
قلوبكم وتنقادوا لعدوكم فإنه والله ما بسط أمل من لا يدرى لعله لا يصبح بعد
مسائه ولا يمسى بعد صباحه وربما كانت بين ذلك خطفات المنايا وكم رأيت
ورأيتم من كان بالدنيا مغترا وإنما تقر عين من PageV04P454
وثق بالنجاة من عذاب الله تعالى وإنما يفرح من أمن أهوال القيامة فأما من
لا يداوى كلما إلا أصابه جرح من ناحية أخرى فكيف يفرح أعوذ بالله من أن
آمركم بما لا أنهى عنه نفسي فتخسر صفقتي وتظهر عيبتي وتبدو مسكنتي في يوم
يبدو فيه الغنى والفقر والموازين فيه منصوبة لقد عنيتم بأمر  لو عنيت به
النجوم لانكدرت ولو عنيت به الجبال لذابت ولو عنيت به الأرض لتشققت أما
تعلمون أنه ليس بين الجنة والنار منزلة وإنكم صائرون إلى إحداهما
وكتب رجل إلى أخ له أما بعد فإن الدنيا حلم والآخرة يقظة والمتوسط بينهما
الموت ونحن في أضغات أحلام والسلام
وكتب آخر إلى أخ له إن الحزن على الدنيا طويل والموت من الإنسان قريب
وللنقص في كل يوم منه نصيب وللبلاء في جسمه دبيب فبادر قبل أن تنادى
بالرحيل والسلام
وقال الحسن كان آدم عليه السلام قبل أن يخطئ أمله خلف ظهره وأجله بين
عينيه فلما أصاب الخطيئة حول فجعل أمله بين عينيه وأجله خلف ظهره
وقال عبد الله بن سميط سمعت أبي يقول أيها المغتر بطول صحته أما رأيت
ميتا قط من غير سقم أيها المغتر بطول المهلة أما رأيت مأخوذا قط من غير عدة
إنك لو فكرت في طول عمرك لنسيت ما قد تقدم من لذاتك أبالصحة تغترون أم بطول
العافية تمرحون أم الموت تأمنون أم على ملك الموت تجترئون إن ملك الموت إذا
جاء لا يمنعه منك ثروة مالك ولا كثرة احتشادك أما علمت أن ساعة الموت ذات
كرب وغصص وندامة على التفريط ثم يقال رحم الله عبدا عمل لما بعد الموت رحم
الله عبدا نظر لنفسه قبل نزول الموت وقال أبو زكريا التيمي بينما سليمان بن
عبد الملك في المسجد الحرام إذ أتى بحجر منقور فطلب من يقرؤه فأتى بوهب بن
منبه فإذا فيه ابن آدم إنك لو رأيت قرب ما بقى من أجلك لزهدت في طول أملك
ولرغبت في الزيادة من عملك ولقصرت من حرصك وحيلك وإنما يلقاك غدا ندمك لو
قد زلت بك قدمك وأسلمك أهلك وحشمك وفارقك الوالد والقريب ورفضك الولد
والنسيب فلا أنت إلى دنياك عائد ولا في حسناتك زائد فاعمل ليوم القيامة قبل
الحسرة والندامة فبكى سليمان بكاء شديدا وقال بعضهم رأيت كتابا من محمد بن
يوسف إلى عبد الرحمن بن يوسف سلام عليك  فإني أحمد الله إليك الذي لا إله
إلا هو أما بعد فإني أحذرك متحولك من دار مهلتك إلى دار إقامتك وجزاء
أعمالك فتصير في قرار باطن الأرض بعد ظاهرها فيأتيك منكر ونكير فيقعدانك
وينتهرانك فإن يكن الله معك فلا يأس ولا وحشة ولا فاقة وإن يكن غير ذلك
فأعاذني الله وإياك من سوء مصرع وضيق مضجع ثم تبلغك صيحة الحشر ونفخ الصور
وقيام الجبار لفصل قضاء الخلائق وخلاء الأرض من أهلها والسماوات من سكانها
فباحت الأسرار وأسعرت النار ووضعت الموازين وجىء بالنبيين والشهداء وقضى
بينهم بالحق وقيل الحمد لله رب العالمين فكم من مفتضح ومستور وكم من هالك
وناج وكم من معذب ومرحوم فيا ليت شعري مالى وحالك يومئذ ففي هذا ما هدم
اللذات وأسلى عن الشهوات وقصر عن الأمل وأيقظ النائمين وحذر الغافلين
أعاننا الله وإياكم على هذا الخطر العظيم وأوقع الدنيا والآخرة من قلبي
وقلبك موقعهما من قلوب المتقين فإنما نحن به وله والسلام وخطب عمر بن عبد
العزيز فحمد الله وأثنى عليه وقال أيها الناس إنكم لم تخلقوا عبثا ولن
تتركوا سدى وإن لكم معادا يجمعكم الله فيه للحكم والفضل فيما بينكم فخاب
وشقى غدا عبد أخرجه الله من رحمته التي وسعت كل شيء وجنته التي عرضها
السموات والأرض وإنما يكون الأمان غدا لمن خاف واتقى وباع قليلا بكثير
وفانيا بباق وشقوة بسعادة ألا ترون أنكم في أسلاب الهالكين وسيخلف بعدكم
الباقون ألا ترون أنكم في كل يوم تشيعون غاديا ورائحا إلى الله عز وجل قد
قضى نحبه وانقطع أمله فتضعونه في بطن صدع من الأرض غير موسد ولا ممهد
PageV04P455
قد خلع الأسباب وفارق الأحباب وواجه الحساب وايم الله إني لأقول مقالتي
هذه ولا أعلم عند أحدكم من الذنوب أكثر مما أعلم من نفسي ولكنها سنن من
الله عادلة آمر فيها بطاعته وأنهى فيها عن معصيته واستغفر الله ووضع كمه
على وجهه وجعل يبكي حتى بلت دموعه لحيته وما عاد إلى مجلسه حتى مات
وقال القعقاع بن  حكيم قد استعددت للموت منذ ثلاثين سنة فلو أتاني ما
أحببت تأخير شيء عن شيء
وقال الثوري رأيت شيخا في مسجد الكوفة يقول أنا في هذا المسجد منذ ثلاثين
سنة لو أنتظر الموت أن ينزل بي ولو أتاني ما أمرته بشيء ولا نهيته عن شيء
ولا لى على أحد شيء ولا لأحد عندي شيء
وقال عبد الله بن ثعلبة تضحك ولعل أكفانك قد خرجت من عند القصار
وقال أبو محمد بن علي الزاهد خرجنا في جنازة بالكوفة وخرج فيها داود
الطائي فانتبذ فقعد ناحية وهي تدفن فجئت فقعدت قريبا منه فتكلم فقال من خاف
الوعيد قصر عليه البعيد ومن طال أمله ضعف عمله وكل ما هو آت قريب واعلم يا
أخي أن كل شيء يشغلك عن ربك فهو عليك مشؤم واعلم أن أهل الدنيا جميعا من
أهل القبور إنما يندمون على ما يخلفون ويفرحون بما يقدمون فما ندم عليه أهل
القبور أهل الدنيا عليه يقتتلون وفيه يتنافسون وعليه عند القضاة يختصمون
وروى أن معروفا الكرخي رحمه الله تعالى أقام الصلاة قال محمد بن أبي توبة
فقال لي تقدم فقلت إني إن صليت بكم هذه الصلاة لم أصل بكم غيرها فقال معروف
وأنت تحدث نفسك أن تصلي صلاة أخرى نعوذ بالله من طول الأمل فإنه يمنع من
خير العمل
وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز في خطبته إن الدنيا ليست بدار قراركم دار كتب
الله عليها الفناء وكتب على أهلها الظعن عنها فكم من عامر موثق عما قليل
يخرب وكم من مقيم مغتبط عما قليل يظعن فأحسنوا رحمكم الله منها الرحلة
بأحسن ما بحضرتكم من النقلة وتزودوا فإن خير الزاد التقوى إنما الدنيا كفىء
ظلال قلص فذهب بينا ابن آدم في الدنيا ينافس وهو قدير العين إذ دعاه الله
بقدره ورماه بيوم حتفه فسلبه آثاره ودنياه وصير لقوم آخرين مصانعه ومغناه
إن الدنيا لا تسر بقدر ما تضر إنها تسر قليلا وتحزن طويلا
وعن أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله تعالى عنه إنه  كان يقول في خطبته أين الوضاء
الحسنة وجوههم المعجبون بشبابهم أين الملوك الذين بنوا المدائن وحصنوها
بالحيطان أين الذين كانوا يعطون الغلبة في مواطن الحرب قد تضعضع بهم الدهر
فأصبحوا في ظلمات القبور الوحا الوحا ثم النجا النجا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-م-ل (ʾ-m-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to hope for something" or "to anticipate"; al-amal denotes expectation of a desired outcome, often extended to "hope for long life" or "deferred aspiration."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-amal is the soul's inclination toward future worldly prospects; when prolonged (ṭūl al-amal), it becomes a blameworthy trait that distracts from preparing for the Hereafter, contrasting with al-ajal (appointed term of death).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, amal is "hope" (ḥaqīqah); metaphorically (majāz), it signifies the deceptive extension of one's aspirations beyond the bounds of certainty, as in "long hope" being a veil over mortality.
- Root: أ-ج-ل (ʾ-j-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning is "a fixed term" or "appointed time"; al-ajal specifically denotes the decreed lifespan or the moment of death.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-ajal is the divinely ordained terminus of life, a certainty that renders all worldly planning provisional; it is the counterweight to al-amal in moral exhortation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to a set deadline; rhetorically, it is employed to emphasize the imminence of death against the illusion of extended hope.
- Root: ه-و-ى (h-w-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to fall" or "to descend"; hawā denotes the inclination of the soul toward base desires, often "passion" or "caprice."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Hawā is the soul's unchecked craving that veers from truth (ḥaqq); in Kalām, it is the antithesis of rational and revealed guidance, a primary cause of deviation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, it is physical falling; metaphorically, it signifies moral descent through following whims, as in the prophetic warning against it.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — For parsing sentences like "If you become morning, do not speak to yourself of evening" (idhā aṣbaḥta falā tuḥaddith nafsaka), where the protasis (sharṭ) sets a temporal condition and the apodosis (jawāb) delivers the imperative, requiring careful coordination of verb moods.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar: "When you enter the morning, do not speak to yourself of the evening; and when you enter the evening, do not speak to yourself of the morning. Take from your life for your death, and from your health for your sickness. For you, O ʿAbd Allāh, do not know what your name shall be tomorrow." (1) And ʿAlī, may God honor his face, narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Verily, the most severe thing I fear for you are two traits: following passion (hawā) and prolonged hope (ṭūl al-amal). As for following passion, it turns one away from the truth; and as for prolonged hope, it is the love of this world." Then he said: "Indeed, God Almighty gives the world to whom He loves and to whom He hates; and when He loves a servant, He grants him faith. Indeed, for religion there are sons, and for the world there are sons. So be among the sons of religion, and do not be among the sons of the world. Indeed, the world has departed turning away; indeed, the Hereafter has departed turning toward. Indeed, you are in a day of work in which there is no reckoning; and indeed, you will soon be in a day of reckoning in which there is no work." (1)

And Umm al-Mundhir said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, looked out to the people one evening and said: "O people, are you not ashamed before God?" They said: "And what is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: "You amass what you do not eat, and you hope for what you do not attain, and you build what you do not inhabit." (2)

And Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: Usāmah ibn Zayd purchased a slave-girl from Zayd ibn Thābit for one hundred dīnārs, payable within a month. So I heard the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, say: "Do you not marvel at Usāmah, who purchases on credit to a month? Verily, Usāmah has prolonged hope. By Him in Whose hand is my soul, my eyes did not blink but that I thought my eyelids would not meet until God takes my soul; nor did I raise my gaze but that I thought I would not lower it until I expire; nor did I take a morsel but that I thought I would not swallow it until I choke on it in death." Then he said: "O sons of Adam, if you possess reason, then count yourselves among the dead. By Him in Whose hand is my soul, what you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it." (3)

And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, would go out to relieve himself and then wipe himself with dust. I would say to him: "O Messenger of God, water is near you." He would say: "What makes me know that I shall reach it?" (4) — Al-Bazzār, with a weak chain. And it is narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, took three sticks and planted one before him, another beside him, and the third farther away. He said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is the human being, this is his appointed term (ajal), and that is his hope (amal). The son of Adam reaches for it, but the appointed term seizes him before the hope." (5)

And he, peace be upon him, said: "The likeness of the son of Adam is that beside him are ninety-nine deaths; if the deaths miss him, he falls into decrepitude." (6)

Ibn Masʿūd said: "This is the man, and these are the deaths surrounding him, rushing toward him; and decrepitude is behind the deaths, and hope is behind decrepitude. So he hopes, while these deaths rush toward him; whichever of them is commanded to take him, it takes him. If the deaths miss him, decrepitude kills him, while he awaits his hope."

ʿAbd Allāh said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, drew for us a square line, and drew a line in its middle, and drew lines beside the line, and drew a line outside. He said: "Do you know what this is?" We said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is the human being — the line in the middle; and this is his appointed term encompassing him; and these are the afflictions — the lines around him — gnawing at him: if this one misses him, that one bites him. And that is his hope — meaning the outside line." (7)

And Anas said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The son of Adam grows old, but two things remain with him: greed and hope." (8) And in another narration: "Two things remain with him: greed for wealth and greed for life."

And the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The first of this community was saved by certainty (yaqīn) and renunciation (zuhd), and the last of this community will be destroyed by miserliness and hope." (1)

And it is said: While Jesus, peace be upon him, was sitting, an old man was working with a spade, turning over the earth. Jesus said: "O God, remove hope from him." So the old man put down the spade and lay down, and remained for a while. Then Jesus said: "O God, return hope to him." So he stood up and began to work. Jesus asked him about that, and he said: "While I was working, my soul said to me: 'How long will you work, being an old man?' So I threw down the spade and lay down. Then my soul said to me: 'By God, you must have sustenance as long as you remain.' So I rose to my spade."

And al-Ḥasan said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Does every one of you love to enter Paradise?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Then shorten your hope, fix your appointed terms before your eyes, and be ashamed before God with true shame." (2)

And he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say in his supplication: "O God, I seek refuge in You from a world that prevents the good of the Hereafter; and I seek refuge in You from a life that prevents the good of death; and I seek refuge in You from a hope that prevents the good of work." (3)

THE SAYINGS OF THE PIOUS PREDECESSORS (Āthār):

Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: "If I knew when my appointed term was, I would fear for the loss of my reason. But God Almighty has bestowed upon His servants the grace of heedlessness of death. Were it not for heedlessness, they would not enjoy life, nor would markets stand among them."

And al-Ḥasan said: "Forgetfulness and hope are two great blessings upon the sons of Adam; were it not for them, Muslims would not walk in the streets."

And al-Thawrī said: "It has reached me that the human being was created foolish; were it not for that, life would not be enjoyable for him."

And Abū Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān said: "The world is only inhabited by the paucity of its people's intellects."

And Salmān al-Fārsī, may God be pleased with him, said: "Three things amazed me until they made me laugh: one who hopes for the world while death seeks him; one who is heedless while he is not forgotten; and one who laughs with his mouth full, not knowing whether the Lord of the Worlds is angry with him or pleased. And three things grieved me until they made me weep: the parting from the beloved — Muḥammad and his party; the terror of the place of inspection (muṭṭalaʿ); and standing before God, not knowing whether I shall be commanded to Paradise or to the Fire."

And some of them said: "I saw Zurārah ibn Abī Awfā after his death in a dream, and I said: 'Which deeds were most effective with you?' He said: 'Trust in God (tawakkul) and shortening of hope.'"

And al-Thawrī said: "Renunciation in this world is the shortening of hope; it is not eating coarse food nor wearing woolen garments."

And al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Fuḍālah asked his Lord to remove hope from him, so the desire for food and drink went away. Then he called upon his Lord to return hope to him, and he returned to food and drink.

And it was said to al-Ḥasan: "O Abū Saʿīd, will you not wash your shirt?" He said: "The matter is more urgent than that."

And al-Ḥasan said: "Death is tied to your forelocks, and the world is folded up behind you."

And some of them said: "I am like a man who stretches out his neck while the sword is upon him, waiting for when it will strike his neck."

And Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī said: "If I hoped to live a month, I would consider that I had committed a grave matter. How can I hope for that, when I see calamities overwhelming creatures in the hours of night and day?"

And it is narrated that Shaqīq al-Balkhī came to a teacher of his called Abū Hāshim al-Rummānī, and at the edge of his cloak there was something tied up. His teacher said to him: "What is this with you?" He said: "Pistachios that a brother of mine gave me, and he said: 'I would love for you to break your fast on them.'" He said: "O Shaqīq, and you speak to yourself that you will remain until evening? I will never speak to you again." He said: "So he closed the door in my face and went in."

And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said in his sermon: "Verily, for every journey there is a provision, inevitably. So provide for your journey from this world to the Hereafter with piety (taqwā). And be like one who has witnessed what God has prepared of His reward and His punishment, so that you may desire and fear. And let not the term be prolonged for you, lest your hearts harden and you yield to your enemy. For, by God, no one extends his hope but one who does not know — perhaps he will not see the morning after his evening, nor the evening after his morning. And between those, there may be the snatchings of death. How many have I seen, and you have seen, deluded by the world! Verily, the eye of one who trusts in deliverance from the punishment of God Almighty is only cooled; and only one who is secure from the terrors of the Day of Resurrection rejoices. As for one who is not cured — every time a wound heals on one side, another strikes him — how can he rejoice? I seek refuge in God from commanding you with what I do not forbid myself, lest my bargain be lost, my fault be exposed, and my destitution appear on a day when wealth and poverty appear, and the scales are set up. You have been burdened with a matter that, had the stars been burdened with it, they would have been dimmed; had the mountains been burdened with it, they would have melted; had the earth been burdened with it, it would have split apart. Do you not know that there is no station between Paradise and the Fire, and that you are destined for one of the two?"

And a man wrote to his brother: "To proceed: verily, this world is a dream, and the Hereafter is wakefulness, and the intermediary between them is death, and we are in the confused visions of dreams. Peace."

And another wrote to his brother: "Verily, grief over this world is long, and death from the human being is near. For diminishment, every day has its share of him, and affliction creeps through his body. So hasten before you are called to departure. Peace."

And al-Ḥasan said: "Adam, peace be upon him, before he erred, had his hope behind his back and his appointed term before his eyes. When he committed the sin, it was reversed, so his hope was placed before his eyes and his appointed term behind his back."

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sumayṭ said: "I heard my father say: 'O you who are deluded by long health — have you never seen a dead person without sickness? O you who are deluded by the long respite — have you never seen one seized without warning? If you reflected on the length of your life, you would forget the pleasures that have passed. Is it by health that you are deluded, or by long well-being that you exult, or of death that you feel secure, or against the Angel of Death that you dare? When the Angel of Death comes, neither the abundance of your wealth nor the multitude of your retinue will prevent him from you. Do you not know that the hour of death is full of distress, choking, and regret for negligence? Then it is said: 'May God have mercy on a servant who worked for what comes after death. May God have mercy on a servant who looked out for himself before the descent of death.'"

And Abū Zakariyyā al-Taymī said: While Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik was in the Sacred Mosque, a carved stone was brought to him, and he sought someone to read it. Wahb ibn Munabbih was brought, and on it was: "O son of Adam, if you saw how near is what remains of your appointed term, you would renounce the length of your hope, and you would desire increase in your work, and you would shorten your greed and your cunning. Verily, tomorrow your regret will meet you, when your foot slips, your family and retinue abandon you, your father and kin part from you, and your children and relatives forsake you. You will neither return to your world nor increase in your good deeds. So work for the Day of Resurrection before regret and remorse." Sulaymān wept intensely.

And some of them said: "I saw a letter from Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yūsuf: 'Peace be upon you. I praise God to you, besides Whom there is no god. To proceed: I warn you of your transfer from the abode of your respite to the abode of your permanence and the recompense of your deeds. You will come to rest in the hollow of the earth after its surface. Then Munkar and Nakīr will come to you, and they will sit you up and rebuke you. If God is with you, then there is no fear, no loneliness, and no want. But if it is otherwise — may God protect me and you from an evil end and a constricted resting place — then the blast of the Gathering will reach you, and the blowing of the Trumpet, and the rising of the Almighty for the separation of judgment among creatures, the earth emptied of its people, and the heavens of their inhabitants. Then secrets will be exposed, the Fire will be kindled, the scales will be set up, the prophets and martyrs will be brought, and judgment will be passed among them in truth, and it will be said: 'Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds.' How many are exposed and how many are veiled! How many are destroyed and how many are saved! How many are tormented and how many are shown mercy! Would that I knew what my state and your state will be on that day!' In this there is what demolishes pleasures, consoles against desires, shortens hope, awakens the sleeping, and warns the heedless. May God help us and you in this great peril, and place this world and the Hereafter in my heart and your heart in their proper place, as they are in the hearts of the God-fearing. For we are by Him and for Him. Peace."

And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz delivered a sermon, praised God, and extolled Him, then said: "O people, you were not created in vain, nor will you be left neglected. Verily, you have a return in which God will gather you for judgment and justice among you. Tomorrow, a servant will fail and be wretched whom God excludes from His mercy, which encompasses all things, and from His Garden, whose breadth is the heavens and the earth. Security tomorrow will only be for one who feared and was God-fearing, and sold a little for much, a perishable for an everlasting, and misery for happiness. Do you not see that you are in the spoils of the perished, and those who remain will succeed you? Do you not see that every day you escort one going forth and returning to God Almighty, whose term has been fulfilled and whose hope has been cut off, and you place him in the belly of a crack in the earth, neither cushioned nor spread — he has cast off the causes, parted from the beloved, and faced the reckoning? By God, I say this my saying, and I know not that any of you has more sins than what I know of myself. But these are just ways of God, in which I command obedience to Him and forbid disobedience to Him. And I seek God's forgiveness." And he placed his sleeve over his face and began to weep until his tears wet his beard, and he did not return to his seat until he died.

And al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Ḥakīm said: "I have prepared for death for thirty years. If it came to me, I would not love to delay anything for anything."

And al-Thawrī said: "I saw an old man in the mosque of Kūfah saying: 'I have been in this mosque for thirty years, as if I were waiting for death to descend upon me. If it came to me, I would not command it to do anything nor forbid it from anything, nor would I have authority over anyone, nor would anyone have a claim upon me.'"

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlabah said: "You laugh, while perhaps your shrouds have already come out from the washer's."

And Abū Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Zāhid said: "We went out to a funeral in Kūfah, and Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī went out with us. He withdrew and sat apart while it was being buried. I came and sat near him, and he spoke, saying: 'Whoever fears the threat, the distant becomes near to him. Whoever prolongs his hope, his work weakens. And everything that is coming is near. Know, O brother, that everything that occupies you from your Lord is ominous upon you. And know that the people of this world, all of them, are the people of the graves — they only regret what they leave behind, and rejoice in what they send ahead. So what the people of the graves regret, the people of this world fight over, compete for, and dispute about before the judges.'"

And it is narrated that Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, may God Almighty have mercy on him, stood for prayer. Muḥammad ibn Abī Tawbah said: "He said to me: 'Come forward.' I said: 'If I lead you in this prayer, I will not lead you in another.' Maʿrūf said: 'And you speak to yourself that you will pray another prayer? We seek refuge in God from prolonged hope, for it prevents the good of work.'"

And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said in his sermon: "Verily, this world is not an abode of permanence for you. It is an abode upon which God has written annihilation, and upon whose people He has written departure from it. How many a flourishing place will soon be ruined! How many a delighted resident will soon depart! So excel, may God have mercy on you, in departing from it with the best of what you have of provision for the journey. And provide for yourselves, for the best of provision is piety (taqwā). Verily, this world is like a shade that recedes; it goes away while the son of Adam is in it, competing, with his eye powerful — then God calls him by His decree and strikes him with the day of his destruction, stripping him of his traces and his world, and making his constructions and his wealth for others. Verily, this world does not delight as much as it harms; it delights a little and grieves for a long time."

And it is related from Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God Almighty be pleased with him, that he used to say in his sermon: "Where are those with radiant, beautiful faces, who marveled at their youth? Where are the kings who built cities and fortified them with walls? Where are those who were given victory in the arenas of war? Time has shaken them, and they have become in the darknesses of the graves. Hasten, hasten! Then escape, escape!"

chapters.title_en: The Explanation of the Cause of Length of Hope and Its Cure
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||||| بيان السبب في طول الأمل وعلاجه

اعلم أن طول الأمل له سببان أحدهما الجهل والآخر حب الدنيا
أما حب الدنيا فهو أنه إذا أنس بها وبشهواتها ولذاتها وعلائقها ثقل على
قلبه مفارقتها فامتنع قلبه من الفكر في الموت الذي هو سبب مفارقتها وكل من
كره شيئا دفعه عن نفسه والإنسان مشغوف بالأماني الباطلة فيمنى نفسه أبدا
بما يوافق مراده وإنما يوافق مراده البقاء في الدنيا فلا يزال يتوهمه
ويقدره في نفسه ويقدر توابع البقاء وما يحتاج إليه من مال وأهل ودار
وأصدقاء ودواب وسائر أسباب الدنيا فيصير قلبه عاكفا على هذا الفكر موقوفا
عليه فيلهو عن ذكر الموت فلا يقدر قربه فإن خطر له في بعض الأحوال أمر
الموت والحاجة إلى الإستعداد له سوف ووعد نفسه وقال الأيام بين يديك إلى أن
تكبر ثم تتوب وإذا كبر فيقول إلى أن تصير شيخا فإذا صار شيخا قال إلى أن
تفرغ من بناء هذه الدار وعمارة هذه الضيعة أو ترجع من هذه السفرة أو تفرغ
من تدبير هذا الولد وجهازه وتدبير مسكن له أو تفرغ من قهر هذا العدو الذي
يشمت بك
فلا يزال يسوف ويؤخر ولا يخوض في شغل إلا ويتعلق بإتمام ذلك الشغل عشرة
أشغال أخر وهكذا على التدريج
PageV04P456
يؤخر يوما بعد يوم ويفضي به شغل إلى شغل بل إلى أشغال إلى أن تختطفه
المنية في وقت لا يحتسبه فتطول عند ذلك حسرته وأكثر أهل النار وصياحهم من
سوف يقولون واحزناه من سوف
والمسوف المسكين لا يدري أن الذي يدعوه إلى التسويف اليوم هو معه غدا
وإنما يزداد بطول المدة قوة ورسوخا ويظن أنه يتصور أن يكون للخائض في
الدنيا والحافظ لها فراغ قط وهيهات فما يفرغ منها إلا من طرحها فما  قضى أحد
منها لبانته ... وما انتهى أرب إلا إلى أرب
وأصل هذه الأماني كلها حب الدنيا والأنس بها والغفلة عن معنى قوله صلى
الله عليه وسلم أحبب من أحببت فإنك مفارقه (1)
وأما الجهل فهو أن الإنسان قد يعول على شبابه فيستبعد قرب الموت مع
الشباب وليس يتفكر المسكين أن مشايخ بلده لو عدوا لكانوا أقل من عشر رجال
البلد وإنما قلوا لأن الموت في الشباب أكثر فإلى أن يموت شيخ يموت ألف صبي
وشاب
وقد يستبعد الموت لصحته ويستبعد الموت فجأة ولا يدري أن ذلك غير بعيد وإن
كان ذلك بعيدا فالمرض فجأة غير بعيد وكل مرض فإنما يقع فجأة وإذا مرض لم
يكن الموت بعيد ولو تفكر هذا الغافل وعلم أن الموت ليس له وقت مخصوص من
شباب وشيب وكهولة ومن صيف وشتاء وخريف وربيع من ليل ونهار لعظم استشعاره
واشتغل بالاستعداد له ولكن الجهل بهذه الأمور وحب الدنيا دعواه إلى طول
الأمل وإلى الغفلة عن تقدير الموت القريب فهو أبدا يظن أن الموت يكون بين
يديه ولا يقدر نزوله به ووقوعه فيه وهو أبدا يظن أنه يشيع الجنائز ولا يقدر
أن تشيع جنازته لأن هذا قد تكرر عليه وألفه وهو مشاهدة موت غيره فأما موت
نفسه فلم يألفه ولم يتصور أن يألفه فإنه لم يقع وإذا وقع في دفعه أخرى بعد
هذه فهو الأول وهو الآخر
وسبيله أن يقيس نفسه بغيره ويعلم أنه لا بد وأن تحمل جنازته ويدفن في
قبره ولعل اللبن الذي يغطي به لحده قد ضرب وفرغ منه وهو لا يدري فتسويفه
جهل محض
وإذا عرفت أن سببه الجهل وحب الدنيا فعلاجه دفع سببه
أما الجهل فيدفع بالفكر الصافي من القلب الحاضر وبسماع الحكمة البالغة من
القلوب الطاهرة
وأما حب الدنيا فالعلاج في إخراجه من القلب شديد وهو الداء العضال الذي
أعيا الأولين والآخرين علاجه ولا علاج له إلا الإيمان باليوم الآخر وبما
فيه من عظيم العقاب وجزيل الثواب ومهما حصل له اليقين بذلك ارتحل  عن قلبه
